stories.Headline: Kansas State proposes a master's degree in AI systems as the board of regents weighs it
stories.Summary:
The Kansas Board of Regents considered a new master's degree in artificial intelligence systems and their applications during the week of November 18, 2026. The University of Missouri Board of Curators unanimously approved a new bachelor's degree program in artificial intelligence on Thursday, November 19, 2026. This undergraduate program will be offered at Missouri University of Science and Technology, which is located in the city of Rolla, Missouri. The K-State degree will be part of the Department of Computer Science in the College of Engineering at Kansas State University. The Missouri S&T program is set to launch in fall 2027, pending approval from the Missouri Coordinating Board for Higher Education.

The Missouri S&T degree requires 120 credit hours and will be housed in the College of Engineering and Computing computer science department. Six new courses include Introduction to Modern AI Tools, Introduction to Artificial Intelligence, Introduction to Machine Learning, Intelligent Robots, Responsible AI and Computing, and AI Capstone. Students will study programming, algorithms, machine learning, data science, computer organization, databases, cybersecurity, calculus, linear algebra, statistics, and neuroscience. The program aligns with Missouri Executive Order 26-02, which directs higher education and workforce agencies to support the development of AI-focused degrees. This will be the first standalone undergraduate AI degree offered in Missouri, following a similar program at Southern Illinois University Carbondale.

Dr. David Borrok, the vice provost and dean of the College of Engineering and Computing at S&T, said demand for AI education grew. He stated that graduates will be prepared to understand and innovate within modern engineered systems that are increasingly using artificial intelligence technologies. Dr. Seung-Jong Jay Park, the Kummer Endowed Chair of Computer Science, said that experiential learning will be a key program component. He explained that students will complete project-based coursework and a senior capstone experience sponsored by government laboratories, university researchers, or industry. The K-State proposal stated that the new degree will help students compete in a changing job market as AI job demand grows.

Graduates will prepare for careers as AI application developers, machine learning engineers, data scientists, intelligent systems developers, AI solutions analysts, and AI-enabled cybersecurity analysts. The program will affect students by providing comprehensive preparation in both the theory and practice of artificial intelligence beyond traditional computer science. Educators noted that the curriculum will teach students about responsible AI practices and the societal effects of emerging technologies in the world. Missouri S&T projects that the new program will enroll approximately 110 students within five years of the official program launch date. The K-State degree targets students who need to compete in a market where AI engineer jobs have grown nearly 150 percent.

A market analysis by the AI company Veritone showed a 25.2 percent increase in AI jobs in early 2025 versus early 2024. AI technologies are becoming increasingly integrated into various industries, including financial services, healthcare, transportation, and manufacturing, according to the dean at Missouri S&T. The Missouri S&T proposal supports strategic goals related to academic innovation, workforce preparation, and enrollment growth for the university in Rolla. The K-State proposal was based on the fact that demand for AI-related jobs is growing rapidly across the current professional job market. These educational initiatives respond to a broader trend of increasing standalone undergraduate AI degrees appearing in recent years across the United States.

The next step for Missouri S&T is for the Missouri Coordinating Board for Higher Education to review the university's bachelor's degree proposal. Pending that specific approval, the university aims to admit its first group of students into the new major starting in fall 2027. The articles do not state if the Kansas Board of Regents has officially approved the master's degree for the Kansas State University students. There is no information regarding the specific start date or the total credit hours required for the proposed K-State master's degree program. The texts leave open whether other universities in Kansas or Missouri will launch similar standalone artificial intelligence degrees in the future.

stories.Headline: Bodhan AI partners with education groups to give one million teachers AI literacy across India
stories.Summary:
Bodhan AI, an IIT Madras incubated Centre of Excellence, will train one million teachers in AI literacy across India. This initiative was announced in November 2026 to help educators integrate artificial intelligence into their classroom teaching workflows. The program partners with the Learning Links Foundation and Vidya Shakti to implement these training efforts nationwide. Additionally, the Centre for Teacher Accreditation will support the rollout of this specific program within Andhra Pradesh. This project aims to create a scalable model for incorporating AI into existing teaching methods for educators.

The Wadhwani School of Data Science and Artificial Intelligence at IIT Madras proposed a responsible Frugal AI Framework. This framework, detailed in a white paper by the Centre for Responsible AI, seeks public value with minimum resources. It recommends that India develop smaller, domain-specific, and multilingual systems suited to its diverse population and local infrastructure. The proposal suggests using shared public AI infrastructure and vernacular-first development tested under varying Indian energy and bandwidth conditions. It also includes a seven-point checklist covering resource tracking, total cost of ownership, documentation, auditing, and human oversight.

IIT Madras director V Kamakoti stated that AI must be useful, affordable, and sustainable rather than knowing everything. He stressed that AI systems should know the right things deeply for the specific task they are performing. Balaraman Ravindran, head of CeRAI and WSAI, said India should not replicate capital-intensive models from China or USA. He argued that India can use its own strengths in engineering capabilities, frugal innovation, and digital public infrastructure. Gokul S Krishnan, research director at CeRAI, said the framework identifies the smallest sufficient AI model for outcomes.

The proposed framework affects the development of AI systems by suggesting alternatives to AI, such as rules-based systems. It recommends using retrieval-based approaches and conventional machine learning instead of complex AI when those methods are sufficient. The researchers believe India should not remain a downstream adopter of foreign AI technologies developed in other countries. This approach targets the diverse Indian population by focusing on systems that work with limited device capabilities. The framework aims to ensure that AI deployment is responsible and delivers actual value to the public.

The articles provide background on the creation of the Centre for Responsible AI and the Wadhwani School of Data Science. They describe the need for AI that operates with minimum computational resources, financial investment, and energy consumption in India. The text mentions that current AI development models in the US and China are too capital-intensive for India. It highlights the existing digital public infrastructure in India as a foundation for this new frugal innovation approach. The background emphasizes the importance of creating AI that is specifically tailored to the Indian domestic environment.

Next, the framework recommends publishing incidents and failures from AI deployments to help improve all future implementation efforts. The initiative will move forward with training one million teachers through the partnerships with various education organizations. The articles leave open how the seven-point checklist will be enforced across different AI deployment projects in India. They do not specify the exact timeline for when the one million teachers will complete their AI literacy. There is no mention of how the government will fund the shared public AI infrastructure being proposed.

stories.Headline: Frost & Sullivan forecasts cloud security to reach $26.8 billion by 2031
stories.Summary:
Frost & Sullivan issued three press releases on November 20, 2026, forecasting growth in cloud security, HVAC equipment and AI governance. The firm projected global cloud security revenues rising from $8.4 billion in 2025 to $26.8 billion by 2031. It projected the global HVAC equipment market reaching $383.6 billion by 2031 at a 7.0% CAGR from 2025. Frost & Sullivan also published analysis of AI governance platforms through 2030. The releases were issued from London through PR Newswire.

The cloud security analysis, Total Cloud Security Market, Global, 2025-2031, gives a 21.4% CAGR and covers extended cloud security platforms. The HVAC study, Frost Radar: HVAC Equipment, 2026, evaluated 25 qualified global participants and selected 10 for benchmarking. Those 10 are Bosch, Carrier, Daikin Industries, Johnson Controls, LG Electronics, Midea Group, Mitsubishi Electric Corporation, Panasonic Corporation, Samsung Electronics and Trane Technologies. The AI governance analysis, Applications and Growth Opportunities for AI Governance Platforms, covers the landscape through 2030 and cites the EU AI Act.

Anh Tien Vu, Industry Principal, Global Cybersecurity at Frost & Sullivan, said the market is moving beyond visibility, posture and fragmented control toward unified extended cloud security platforms. Vu said growth will be defined by platforms that validate and prioritize risk, assign ownership, accelerate remediation and support real-time detection and response. Jonathan Robinson, Practice Area Leader, Energy & Buildings, said the HVAC industry is moving toward an intelligent, connected and service-driven ecosystem. Robinson said companies combining energy-efficient technologies with digital intelligence and lifecycle services will be best positioned for the next wave of growth. Avinab Das, Industry Analyst in Frost & Sullivan's TechVision practice, said the real opportunity in AI governance lies in moving beyond compliance to enabling innovation at scale.

Frost & Sullivan said North America is expected to remain the largest regional cloud security market, with opportunities in Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Asia-Pacific and Latin America. Asia-Pacific remains the largest and fastest-growing HVAC equipment market, driven by urbanisation and infrastructure development. Europe and North America HVAC demand is fuelled by replacement and decarbonisation, the Middle East by energy-efficient and district cooling, and Latin America is an emerging market with more moderate growth. Frost & Sullivan said AI governance adoption faces high implementation costs, talent shortages, overlapping EU regulations and organisational resistance. Frost & Sullivan said managed security providers, systems integrators and cloud partners are positioned to help enterprises implement integrated security architectures.

Frost & Sullivan said enterprises are shifting from tools focused on visibility, configuration management and vulnerability detection toward extended cloud security platforms. It said generative AI applications, autonomous agents and AI-powered workloads are expanding the cloud attack surface. It said IoT-enabled sensors, AI-driven predictive analytics and cloud-based platforms enable real-time monitoring, predictive maintenance and energy optimisation. It said governments worldwide are introducing stricter energy-efficiency standards and environmental regulations. It said AI governance is evolving from a compliance-driven function into a strategic capability built on interoperability, data privacy and digital ethics.

Frost & Sullivan said competitive differentiation will depend less on the volume of threats identified and more on translating security intelligence into measurable risk reduction and operational resilience. It said AI infrastructure expansion is driving demand for advanced thermal management solutions. It said evolving regulations including the EU AI Act are driving demand for automated compliance monitoring, risk assessments and audit-ready governance solutions. Frost & Sullivan said it expects accelerating AI adoption and rising stakeholder expectations to sustain demand for governance solutions through 2030. The releases invite readers to explore the findings online and list Kristina Menzefricke of Frost & Sullivan for interview requests.

stories.Headline: U.N. talks extend debate on killer robots to 2028 without binding rules
stories.Summary:
Efforts to set firm rules on AI-powered killer robots and drones ran aground on Saturday, November 21, 2026, as U.N.-backed talks in Geneva produced a softened agreement to extend discussions for two more years. Scores of countries ended the weeklong U.N. conference on weapons by agreeing to “elaborate” a possible accord on lethal autonomous weapons systems by 2028. The outcome underscored the difficulty of achieving concrete results in diplomacy amid global conflicts as major military powers jockey for dominance. It also marked the latest failure to set guardrails for AI, at a time when some experts have warned about such systems breaking out of human control and going rogue. The talks this week centered on the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, ratified by 128 countries, where decisions are made by consensus.

The agreement extends discussions for two more years and sets 2028 as the target for elaborating a possible accord, but it does not commit to binding rules. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres had sought binding rules and set a 2026 deadline for launching negotiations toward an agreement on autonomous weapons systems. Before the meeting, seven countries, Austria, Belgium, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand, Panama and Brazil, proposed launching negotiations on a rulebook that could prevent or limit the ability of machines to kill without human control or accountability, and that effort fell short. Decisions under the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons are made by consensus, meaning any single country can thwart an agreement, and any deal is likely to be based on the lowest common denominator. Guterres leaves office at the end of the year.

Izumi Nakamitsu, the U.N. high representative for disarmament affairs, hailed a “significant achievement” but acknowledged a “glass half full or half empty” scenario, citing Guterres’ hopes for a legally binding deal this year. Nakamitsu called for countries to begin work as early as Monday and to “start thinking about how to get as strong as possible instrument to prohibit and regulate lethal autonomous weapon systems.” Ambassador Frederico Meyer of Brazil, which joined the seven-country proposal, said “Technology is moving faster than diplomacy” and “Diplomats are very slow.” The International Committee of the Red Cross said autonomous weapons can be “unpredictable,” unlike a bullet fired from a gun with a distinct and predictable trajectory. The ICRC said that for years it and many others have urged states to ensure that humans retain control over the use of force and that life-and-death decisions are never handed over to machines.

Activists accused military powers like Russia and the United States of blocking stronger language. Stop Killer Robots lamented a “watered-down mandate,” and Beatrice Fihn, founder of international law advocacy group Lex International, said the decision amounted to “pushing the can down the road for two more years.” Max Tegmark, a machine learning specialist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and founder of the Future of Life Institute, said states have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about the issue for the 14th year while these weapons enable atrocities. Advocacy groups bemoaned obstructionism at this week’s talks largely by Russia, which, like other leading developers of AI weapons including the United States, wants a freer hand to develop such high-tech weapons. Pope Leo XIV and humanitarian groups have framed the issue as an existential debate, urging quick action to rein in AI weapons before they become too commonplace to regulate easily.

Activists say armed drones that can independently strike targets have already been deployed in some select instances in conflict zones, but widespread rollout hasn’t happened. Opposition from big arms-producing nations like the United States and Russia had resulted in a watered-down agreement that left open the question of whether future measures would be legally binding. Delegates attended the United Nations Review Conference of the High Contracting Parties to the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, where discussions focused on Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems, often referred to as “killer robots,” in Geneva on November 16, 2026. A mock “killer robot” was pictured as part of the Campaign to Stop “Killer Robots,” which calls for the ban of lethal robot weapons that would be able to select and attack targets without any human intervention. The activists noted that most countries supported work toward a new treaty.

Nakamitsu called for countries to begin work as early as Monday, and Guterres leaves office at the end of the year. The agreement leaves open the question of whether future measures would be legally binding. The articles do not say what the countries will do at the 2028 target or how the two-year extension will be carried out. The articles do not say whether the seven countries that proposed negotiations will pursue alternative routes toward a deal. The articles do not say what the United States and Russia said in response to the accusations that they blocked stronger language.

stories.Headline: Trump and Xi agree humans must oversee military AI decisions
stories.Summary:
US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed that humans must stay involved in military decisions using artificial intelligence technologies. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced this agreement on November 20 after the leaders met in Shenzhen, China, on November 19. The meeting took place during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, which Bessent described as a major achievement of Trump's trip. This consensus ensures that no major military operation should be launched without a person involved in the decision making process. The two leaders agreed that super intelligence, or SI, should not be allowed to be autonomous for major military actions.

The agreement requires human oversight and other safeguards, but it will not change the competition between the two nations for AI supremacy. The Commerce Department took steps on November 16 to further restrict China's access to advanced AI chips and remote computing power. These restrictions include overseas data centres where Chinese entities can rent computing power, and the Treasury Department helped write the rule. China can only purchase the second tier H200 chip from Nvidia with licences, as Trump has taken a very firm line. Bessent noted a paucity of Chinese orders for H200s because China is trying to build its own chip stack.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, the lead American official on China relations, told CNBC that the agreement was a very important breakthrough. He stated that US AI labs must maintain their technological lead to defend against dangerous Chinese AI models used in cyberattacks. Bessent previously met with Vice Premier He Lifeng to create a dialogue where both countries can notify each other about AI threats. He also said that all Trump administration officials are committed to following the instructions of the president regarding these technology policies. Bessent downplayed previous differences he had voiced with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick regarding the restrictions on advanced AI chips.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has faced increasing scrutiny for his role in preventing the export of advanced AI chips to China. Former Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang was ousted after confirming a relationship with a suspected Chinese agent named Alice Huang. Alice Huang is an AI chips business executive under investigation by the US government for potentially smuggling chips into China. Bessent had previously criticized the Commerce Department for not adding Megaspeed International, a company tied to Alice Huang, to a blacklist. Both Trump and Bessent stated that the spying allegations involving Jensen Huang did not come up during the bilateral meeting.

The Trump administration recently moved to heighten scrutiny on processor exports to several countries and curtail remote access to AI servers. Trump told Fox News that he spoke with Xi about AI and that both leaders want regulations for the technology. The US government believes that China is probably many years behind the United States in developing its own chip stack. The National Security Council also helped direct the interim Commerce Department rule to restrict Chinese companies from obtaining remote chip access. These measures are intended to ensure that proper chip restrictions are in place to maintain a US technological advantage.

The US and China will continue to compete for AI supremacy while adhering to the agreement on human military oversight. The Treasury Department expects that remote access to advanced AI chips and servers will be further curtailed in the future. The articles do not state if the two countries will establish a formal treaty to enforce the human oversight agreement. It remains open whether the US will add Megaspeed International to the trade blacklist following the comments made by Bessent. The reports leave unclear how the two nations will monitor each other to ensure no autonomous military AI is used.

stories.Headline: China uses smuggling and front companies to bypass US export controls on AI chips
stories.Summary:
China used spies and smuggling to acquire super-powered computer chips from the United States. These illicit activities occurred recently to bypass strict American export controls on high-end technology. A woman ran a Singaporean front company to facilitate these illegal chip transfers. She established data centres in Southeast Asia to house the smuggled Taiwan-made hardware. Chinese companies then leased the use of these chips through this complex loophole.

The scheme requires Nvidia chips made by one specific manufacturing facility located in Taiwan. These chips rely on rare machines produced by a single company in the Netherlands. The U.S. government set export controls to limit which countries Nvidia can ship to. However, the Trump administration signed off on selling 900,000 chips to China over six months. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnik was reportedly lax with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang regarding these sales.

Kyle Chan from the Brookings Institution says the U.S. views AI as a winner-take-all race. He explains that some officials believe achieving Artificial General Intelligence provides an existential strategic advantage. Kenton Thibaut of the Atlantic Council says China views AI as a general purpose technology. He states that Chinese policies focus on making AI useful for society and the economy. Thibaut notes that the U.S. focuses on frontier systems while China supplies near frontier technology.

Chinese firms are affected by hardware constraints and focus on doing more with less computing power. They aim to automate factories and speed up drug discovery to benefit their overall economy. U.S. companies like Anthropic fear their models could run out of control and want more regulation. These American firms rely on the chip advantage to push the envelope of AI development. China seeks to integrate these advances holistically rather than focusing only on a singular goal.

The U.S. has more computing power than any other nation due to its chip access. China faces physical constraints that make discussions about runaway AI models largely moot for them. The Chinese government is predisposed to prevent any societal disruptions caused by new technology. They currently rely on a bridge of smuggled tech to maintain their competitive computing power. This strategy allows them to function while they work toward their own manufacturing capabilities.

China wants to eventually create its own version of the super-manufacturers found in Taiwan. They aim to separate themselves from the Western tech stack to achieve total independence. AI Czar David Sacks has explicitly advocated for selling more chips directly to China. The articles leave open whether the U.S. will tighten or loosen these export controls. It remains unclear if China will successfully build its own high-end chip manufacturing industry.

stories.Headline: Senator Mark Warner leads a bipartisan push for AI financial transparency to mitigate economic risks
stories.Summary:
Senator Mark Warner of Virginia and three other lawmakers introduced a bipartisan bill on Thursday, November 19, 2026, to increase financial transparency within the artificial intelligence sector. This legislative effort aims to scrutinize the complex web of funding fueling the current technology boom and identify potential risks to the broader economy. The senators are particularly concerned about the outsize influence of the industry and the possibility that a financial collapse could spread. They seek to uncover hidden financing arrangements that may not be immediately visible on corporate balance sheets.

The proposed legislation, titled the Advancing Uniform Disclosure of Investments and Transparency of Artificial Intelligence Act, requires publicly traded companies to disclose major AI-related financing. It also calls for the creation of formalized standards to ensure firms properly warn investors about risks associated with artificial intelligence. Senator Warner was joined in this effort by Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana, Senator Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, and Senator Mike Rounds of South Dakota. These requirements are intended to provide the public and investors with a clearer picture of the financial exposure behind the industry.

Senator Warner stated that while artificial intelligence has the potential to transform the economy, the trillions of dollars invested carry significant financial risks. He argued that policymakers and investors deserve to understand how these deals are financed to avoid a future financial crisis. Warner specifically expressed worry regarding circular investments, such as when Nvidia provides financial backing to businesses that then purchase its chips. He believes that bringing accountability to these investments is necessary to prevent massive financial exposure from building up behind the scenes.

This push for transparency follows the abrupt resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang amid a scandal involving a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The company is also facing national security investigations into export controls and questions regarding the long-term demand for AI infrastructure. These events, alongside the recent initial public offering of Anthropic, serve as critical tests for the future of the sector. Congress is now stepping up its oversight to ensure that the rapid expansion of the industry does not destabilize global financial markets.

stories.Headline: Bloomington mayor Kerry Thomson declines to sign superintelligence ordinance over enforcement concerns
stories.Summary:
Bloomington Mayor Kerry Thomson announced on Thursday, November 19, 2026, that she will not sign a city ordinance barring the distribution and deployment of artificial superintelligence, which the city council had passed unanimously by a 7-0 vote on November 4. The ordinance defined superintelligence as any artificial intelligence that can act autonomously, including operating without continuous human oversight on tasks affecting public safety, municipal infrastructure or financial markets, and that can outperform humans at nearly all mental tasks. The measure had drawn national attention and a mixed reception on social media, where some commenters criticized its definitions and questioned whether it could be enforced. Its author, Dave Rollo, conceded that the ordinance is currently unenforceable but said he hoped it would prompt action in other cities, and he described the risk as existential and expressed concern about public safety for the community.

The ordinance was written as an interim measure meant to regulate superintelligence in Bloomington until the Indiana General Assembly passes a framework, at which point the city ordinance would expire 91 days later. If violated, the city would be allowed to seek civil penalties, injunctive relief and referral to the county prosecutor. A memo accompanying the ordinance said developers of superintelligence have acknowledged the potential for a catastrophic outcome for humanity, potentially extinction, at an unacceptable level of risk. Under Indiana law, the mayor has 10 days from receipt to either sign or veto a piece of legislation passed by the city council, and if she takes no action it is considered vetoed.

Thomson acknowledged risks associated with artificial intelligence systems but said that passing a law carries responsibilities beyond stating a principle. She said the ordinance leaves significant questions about how the city would identify violations, what authority it has to regulate them and what enforcement would require, and she called the potential need to monitor private digital activity especially troubling given recent work to strengthen protections against government surveillance. She said she will not sign the ordinance as written, that she spoke with Rollo and appreciated his openness to revisions, and that she looks forward to continuing that work to support Bloomington's research and innovation economy while establishing clear, enforceable safeguards. She also said Bloomington is working hard to grow its innovation economy and that artificial intelligence plays an important role in that work.

stories.Headline: Together AI reports prompt leak after AI coding agent exposes private credential
stories.Summary:
Together AI disclosed on November 21, 2026, that an unauthorized party downloaded stored samples from a subset of customer prompts. This breach occurred because an AI coding agent exposed a private repository credential while the company developed its public xorl GitHub repository. The intruder used the credential to access a private Hugging Face repository containing requests for the MiniMax M3, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K2.6 models. These specific samples were primarily collected on June 24, July 4, July 8, and July 14, 2026.

The company is implementing scoped or short-lived credentials, keyless access, and credential checks on all pull requests to prevent future leaks. They have also updated development processes for AI coding agents and made zero data retention the default setting for new accounts. The intruder searched the downloaded prompts for other secrets and tested five canary credentials associated with a Dragos security experiment. Together AI now recommends that customers handling sensitive data manually enable zero data retention in their account settings.

Together AI worked with law enforcement and an external forensic firm to investigate the scope of the unauthorized activity. The company stated that its review found no evidence of additional prompt leakage and no reason to believe the data was shared further. They claimed to understand that the stolen data has been deleted, although they are still reviewing the content for sensitive personal information. The company said it will contact affected customers directly with any findings that are relevant to their specific data.

The incident highlights the security risks of using AI-assisted development tools alongside the retention of customer prompts for software testing. Together AI has documented new controls for both areas, but the ongoing content review remains the final step in the process. The company provides the email address security@together.ai for organizations with questions about the potential impact of this exposure. Future notifications to customers will depend on whether the review identifies the exposure of sensitive personal information.

stories.Headline: Nigeria data commissioner urges journalists to learn data protection and seek certification
stories.Summary:
Dr Vincent Olatunji, the National Commissioner of the National Data Protection Commission, addressed journalists on Friday in Abuja at a data protection enlightenment programme. He stressed the need for journalists to acquire adequate knowledge of data protection. He said the media has a crucial role in educating Nigerians on safeguarding personal information. He said journalists must properly understand data protection to communicate its importance to the public. He noted that reporting on issues they do not fully understand could affect public awareness and understanding.

Olatunji said the programme was designed to deepen journalists' knowledge of data privacy and equip them with qualifications to practise as data protection officers. He said the Federal Government has taken measures to introduce certification opportunities for journalists. He said the number of professionals in the ecosystem is very limited and more people are needed to understand private sector work in Nigeria. He said the Commission wants to take journalists to the level of certifications so they can practise as data privacy officers alongside their primary duties. He said there is no way journalists can create stories around what they do not really understand.

Olatunji said multinational companies were generally among the most compliant because they operate in jurisdictions with strict data protection requirements. He warned that organisations failing to comply with the law would face stricter enforcement measures. He said the Commission had spent considerable time creating awareness before moving towards stronger regulatory action. He said compliance levels have improved significantly, with more organisations approaching the Commission for guidance on meeting regulatory requirements. He said the Commission preferred collaboration and partnership but would not hesitate to enforce the law where there was persistent non-compliance or a data breach.

Dr Marlon-Ralph Nyakabau wrote in Techzim that POTRAZ was crowned Most Outstanding Data Protection Authority at the PICCASO Awards Africa 2026 in Lagos earlier this month. He wrote that POTRAZ beat a field reportedly including South Africa, Kenya, Egypt and Rwanda, on achievements including licensing over 2,500 data controllers and training and certifying more than 1,500 data protection officers. He wrote that South Africa's Information Regulator charges no licensing fee, registration is online and does not expire or require annual renewal. He wrote that Nigeria's NDPC classifies controllers of major importance into Ultra-High, Extra-High and Ordinary-High levels, and that Kenya's ODPC bases categorisation partly on employees and annual revenue or turnover. He wrote that Egypt's PDPC sets its registration threshold at a minimum of 100,000 personal data records, compared with just 50 in Zimbabwe.

Nyakabau wrote that Nigeria's registration fees for the corresponding category are as little as approximately US$7, Kenya's around US$30 and Zimbabwe's US$300. He wrote that a Nigerian DPO certification examination costs less than US$200, compared with approximately US$1,250 in Zimbabwe. He wrote that South Africa's Information Regulator must gazette proposed codes and consider submissions before approving them, while Zimbabwe's regulator may publish codes without seeking views. He wrote that Zimbabwe's Cyber and Data Protection Act did not establish a clearly articulated funding arrangement for the regulator. He wrote that POTRAZ is inviting submissions on amending the Cyber and Data Protection Regulations under Statutory Instrument 155 of 2024, with proposed revisions largely focused on strengthening enforcement powers including administrative penalties.

Olatunji said the Commission had spent considerable time creating awareness before moving towards stronger regulatory action. Nyakabau wrote that the founding legislation in South Africa, Kenya and Nigeria provides for public funding through government allocations and national treasury arrangements. He wrote that Zimbabwe's economy is a fraction of the size of the comparator countries, yet its regulatory charges are in some instances several times higher. He wrote that government has recently reviewed and reduced various licensing and registration fees, but data protection licensing costs appear to have escaped this exercise. He wrote that high compliance costs affect small enterprises, start-ups, NGOs and healthcare providers and add to the cost of doing business in Zimbabwe.

Nyakabau wrote that POTRAZ is currently inviting submissions as part of amending the Cyber and Data Protection Regulations under Statutory Instrument 155 of 2024. He wrote that the proposed direction of the revisions appears largely focused on strengthening the Authority's enforcement powers, including administrative penalties. He wrote that increasing punitive powers without first addressing disproportionate compliance costs risks making an already expensive regulatory environment more burdensome. He wrote that POTRAZ must be willing to examine the proportionality, affordability and effectiveness of its regulatory approach. He wrote that the best data protection regime is not the one that regulates the most, charges the most or punishes the most.

stories.Headline: J&K and Ladakh chief justice urges cautious AI use to strengthen justice delivery
stories.Summary:
Dr. Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati, Chief Justice of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, visited the District Court Complex in Budgam on Friday, November 20, 2026. He was accompanied by Justice Sindhu Sharma, the Administrative Judge for District Budgam. The Chief Justice received a ceremonial Guard of Honour at the complex. O.P. Bhagat, the Principal District and Sessions Judge of Budgam, warmly welcomed him. Deputy Commissioner Budgam Jatin Kishore and Senior Superintendent of Police Budgam Hariprasad KK were present along with other judicial and administrative officers.

The visit brought together judges from the Registry, including Registrar General M.K Sharma and Haq Nawaz Zargar, Principal Secretary to the Chief Justice. Members of the District Judiciary, court staff, officials of the District Legal Services Authority and Para Legal Volunteers also attended the programme. Advocates from all four Tehsils of District Budgam attended, represented by their respective Bar Association Presidents. The Chief Justice released a magazine published by the District Legal Services Authority, Budgam, under the supervision and guidance of the J&K Legal Services Authority. He is the Patron in Chief of the J&K Legal Services Authority.

The Chief Justice said the Bar, the Bench and the administration share a collective responsibility for strengthening the justice delivery system and upholding public trust. He stressed the importance of adopting emerging technologies, particularly Artificial Intelligence, with due caution to enhance transparency, efficiency and speedy delivery of justice. He called for strengthening the Bar and Bench and for promoting better facilities and opportunities for women lawyers. He urged the upholding of the highest standards of professionalism and judicial accountability. He assured that suggestions for institutional improvement would be considered.

The Chief Justice referred to the forthcoming centenary celebrations of the judicial institution on 28th March 2027 and called on the entire legal fraternity across Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh to participate actively. He described the occasion as a historic milestone and asked members to reaffirm their commitment to justice and public service. The articles state that the presence of Justice Sindhu Sharma was particularly significant in view of her administrative association with the district. The occasion acknowledged the role of the District Judiciary in ensuring effective judicial administration and the importance of coordinated efforts among all institutions associated with the justice delivery mechanism. The programme concluded with a formal Vote of Thanks presented by Additional District Judge Budgam, Yahya Firdous.

The District Bar Association Budgam, through its President, submitted a memorandum seeking urgent intervention to strengthen judicial infrastructure in the district. Its demands included construction of a new Court Complex at Budgam and establishment of a separate NIA Court and additional judicial courts. It also sought Court Complexes at Charar-i-Sharief and Beerwah and a Munsiff Court at Khansahib. Further demands were additional advocates' chambers, upgradation of the Ladies' Bar Room, development of parking facilities, and separate photocopy and canteen facilities for advocates. The Association said these measures are essential for improving judicial efficiency, addressing infrastructural deficiencies, facilitating the legal fraternity and ensuring better access and convenience for litigants and the general public.

The articles do not state what action followed the memorandum or how the demands will be addressed. They do not say whether the Chief Justice responded to the memorandum's specific demands. They do not give the name of the President of the District Bar Association Budgam who submitted it. They do not describe the contents of the magazine released by the Chief Justice. stories.Headline: Trump plans to tax US tech firms that build AI data centers abroad
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump announced on Friday, November 20, 2026, that he plans to penalize American technology companies for their overseas activities. He stated that these firms will face a tremendous tax if they build artificial intelligence data centers in other countries. The president spoke about this plan during a news conference held in Washington at the White House. He noted that he had not yet shared the details of this specific plan with his own officials. This announcement came as the president addressed the press in the James Brady Press Briefing Room.

The plan involves a tremendous tax for companies building AI data centers abroad, though Trump provided no further details on Friday. On Monday, the administration issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced U.S. computing chips and servers. These rules aim to limit the ability of China to use American chips to train its best AI models. Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were present during the president's Friday news conference. The president urged Americans to welcome data center construction in their communities and extract concessions from the developers.

President Trump told Americans they ought to take advantage of data centers and make them pay the local community. He urged citizens not to shut these facilities off, repeating a point he had made before the midterms. The president believes that AI is a positive force for the American economy despite the views of skeptics. He has been described as perhaps the biggest champion for the industry despite the current political toxicity. Trump wants developers to provide concessions to the communities that allow the construction of these server warehouses.

Officials from Google and Meta told The Associated Press they are trying to address mistrust by being more transparent. These companies are promising to take fewer taxpayer handouts and keep fewer secrets from the communities where they build. They are making pledges to reduce their environmental impact and offering assurances that data centers will boost property values. Host communities across the United States are turning against these gargantuan data centers, which have become a political issue. Many municipal permits are being blocked by community opposition, creating a bottleneck for the technology giants.

Anti-data center sentiment was a potent issue in the midterm elections, which resulted in Democrats taking control of Congress. A wave of Democrats was ushered in who pledged to clamp down on these energy-hungry behemoths. The technology industry says it has gotten the message and is ramping up financial incentives for host communities. The Republican-led Senate approved bipartisan legislation on Thursday to speed up permitting reviews for power plants and energy infrastructure. This legislative move comes as lawmakers seek to address the energy needs of the artificial intelligence boom.

A tougher regulatory environment for AI giants and data center developers is expected to follow the recent midterm elections. This regulatory shift may occur even if President Trump stalls any federal crackdown on the industry's current practices. The articles leave open the specific details of the tremendous tax Trump intends to levy on tech companies. It remains unclear how the administration will implement the penalties for building data centers in other foreign countries. The text does not specify when the proposed tax will be officially introduced or how it will be calculated.

stories.Headline: UAE AI Office, UNDP and Women in AI launch initiative to equip 100,000 Arab women with AI skills
stories.Summary:
The UAE Artificial Intelligence Office, in partnership with the United Nations Development Programme and the Women in AI organisation, launched the “100,000 Arab Women in AI” initiative. The regional effort aims to equip women with advanced artificial intelligence skills and accelerate women-led innovation and entrepreneurship. It also seeks to strengthen women’s leadership in shaping the AI economy across the Arab States. The initiative was announced during the Arab Women in AI Forum hosted by the Dubai Future Foundation. The forum took place as part of Dubai Future Week 2026, and the announcement was dated 20 November 2026 in Dubai.

The initiative establishes a collaborative framework to strengthen women’s participation and leadership in the AI economy across the Arab States. It combines capacity building, entrepreneurship support, innovation opportunities and policy engagement to give women skills, networks and opportunities. The initiative is structured around three interconnected tracks, the first covering AI skills and capacity development with specialised knowledge, technical expertise and practical competencies. The second track covers entrepreneurship and innovation, supporting women founders, entrepreneurs and innovators in developing and scaling AI-enabled solutions and businesses. The third track covers policy and the enabling ecosystem, promoting dialogue, evidence generation and frameworks that advance women’s participation and leadership in the AI and digital economies.

Omar Sultan Al Olama, Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence, said the UAE continues to strengthen its global leadership in investing in people and expanding access to knowledge. He said empowering women and advancing their participation across sectors are key priorities in building more competitive societies. He said investing in the AI capabilities of Arab women is an investment in the region’s future, in talent, ideas and ambitions. He said expanding women’s participation in AI will bring new experiences and perspectives into the ecosystem. He said the initiative aims to cultivate a new generation of Arab women leaders and AI professionals who will shape the future of the technology.

Zena Ali Ahmad, Deputy Regional Director for the Arab States, said artificial intelligence is transforming economies and societies across the Arab States, creating opportunities for innovation, growth and progress. She said women must be empowered not only to participate in the AI economy but also to lead and shape it. She said UNDP and its partners are working through the Women in AI initiative to expand opportunities for women through skills development, entrepreneurship, innovation and policy engagement. She said investing in women’s talent and leadership helps build a more inclusive AI future. She said it unlocks new pathways for sustainable development across the Arab States.

The Arab Women in AI Forum brought together government leaders, international experts, academics, technology companies, entrepreneurs and investors. The forum introduced the initiative’s vision and objectives and featured two panel discussions on opportunities for women in the region’s AI sector. The first discussion examined women’s participation in the AI economy across the Arab States. The second highlighted the experiences of entrepreneurs and innovators developing AI-enabled solutions and applications. The initiative seeks to equip women to contribute to and shape the development of artificial intelligence and the digital economy.

The articles do not state a schedule, funding figure or target date for reaching the 100,000 women named in the initiative. They do not name the specific countries covered beyond the Arab States, or list the participating technology companies, academics and investors beyond the organisations named. They do not give the number of women currently working in AI across the region or any measure for tracking the initiative’s progress. They do not say how women will be selected or where the tracks will be delivered. They do not describe any further events after the two panel discussions at the forum.
Orgs: women in artificial intelligence regional forum

stories.Headline: Lagarde calls AI-boosted cyber threat her top worry for finance
stories.Summary:
European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde said on Friday that the greatest immediate challenge facing the world of finance may be cyber threats supercharged by increasingly sophisticated AI agents. She made the remark at the European Banking Congress in Frankfurt, where she told the audience that this combination of AI and cyber threat is the one that keeps her awake. Lagarde added that many others in the room share that worry as well. She said policymakers have not paid enough attention to this threat.

Lagarde said attackers are often anonymous and difficult to track, and they rely on dubious funding that often comes from toxic states with a vested interest in disrupting the world. Her remarks were reported by CNA on Friday, November 20, 2026, in a story datelined Frankfurt. The report carried a file photo illustration taken on October 22, 2026, showing the words AI Hacking and PHP code on a screen. The article gave no further figures, dates or names beyond Lagarde, the congress and the ECB.

Lagarde is the president of the European Central Bank, and she used her speech at the congress to name AI applied together with cyber threat as her top worry. She said the threat deserves more attention from policymakers than it has received so far. The articles do not say what measures, if any, the ECB or other authorities plan to take in response. They also do not say what happens next.

stories.Headline: Dublin City Council trains 3,000 staff to use AI safely and responsibly
stories.Summary:
Dublin City Council staff will receive training on using artificial intelligence safely and responsibly starting in November 2026. This new multi-year AI Capacity Building Programme will train approximately 3,000 council staff members in their daily work. The initiative is delivered in partnership with BABLE Smart Cities to provide tools for responsible AI utilization. It begins with AI Fundamentals to help staff build the confidence and practical understanding needed for the technology. This training follows criticism regarding an unlabelled AI-generated image found in a recent council report in October.

The programme requires staff to learn AI Fundamentals to ensure they use the technology effectively and ethically. Lord Mayor Daryl Barron and Assistant Chief Executive Aidan Blighe attended the Smart City World Expo in Barcelona. BABLE CEO Alexander Schmidt worked with Digital Services and Innovation, Technology and Design teams to create the content. In New York, Council Speaker Julie Menin plans to vote on a suite of AI bills in January 2027. These bills include a twenty-five thousand dollar fine for businesses that deploy unvalidated AI models in New York City.

Lord Mayor Daryl Barron stated that AI opportunities must be matched by strong governance, transparency, and public trust. Assistant Chief Executive Aidan Blighe said the programme is a big step toward making staff effective and productive. BABLE CEO Alexander Schmidt noted the programme reflects the realities of public sector work rather than using generic examples. A council spokesperson said the structured approach combines governance, staff development, experimentation, and practical application for the organisation. These leaders believe investing in people first ensures that AI supports better public services for the local community.

Sinn Féin Councillor Ciaran Ó Meachair flagged concerns about transparency and accountability after seeing the unlabelled AI image. He argued that the arts community will lose out from the impact of AI and urged public bodies to pause. In New York, Mayor Zohran Mamdani believes AI regulation is a national issue that should be handled at the federal level. State Senator Andrew Gounardes questioned if a manual kill switch for AI systems would actually work from a technological perspective. OpenAI also expressed concerns to the New York City Council regarding how some of the proposed bills are written.

Dublin City Council has spent two years using a Generative AI Lab to test potential AI use cases safely. This lab allowed the council to work with business owners to evaluate AI in a controlled environment. In New York, Governor Kathy Hochul signed the RAISE Act to create a state oversight office for AI safety. She also launched a new AI center within the State University of New York to monitor large AI models. State lawmakers are now pursuing a RAISE Act 2.0 to limit computing powers and require annual compliance audits.

New York City Council members will continue soliciting input and tweaking the language of their ten proposed AI bills. The city aims to be the first jurisdiction in the country to pass meaningful regulation since this summer's incidents. President Donald Trump has rejected fears about AI development as a hoax and opposes robust regulation of super intelligence. It remains unclear if the New York City Council bills will conflict with or complement the state level proposals. The articles leave open whether the proposed manual kill switches for AI systems are technically feasible for implementation.

stories.Headline: Pennsylvania attorney general appoints privacy ombudsman to oversee Character.AI user data in bankruptcy sale
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania Attorney General Dave Sunday announced on November 20, 2026 that an independent consumer privacy ombudsman will advise the bankruptcy court on how user data held by Character Technologies, Inc., which operates the Character.AI chatbot platform, is handled in any sale. The appointment came as the company moves through bankruptcy proceedings while holding sensitive personal data from millions of minors. Pennsylvania and other states had opened an investigation after a 2024 wrongful death lawsuit alleging that the company's chatbots encouraged a child's suicidal thoughts and contributed to his death. Character.AI has more than 10 million current users averaging 120 minutes per day on the platform.

Before any assets of Character Technologies, Inc. can be sold, the ombudsman must file reports with the court evaluating data privacy issues and proposing protections, and the company plans to auction off user data on December 1, 2026. The appointment applies the consumer privacy ombudsman mechanism of the U.S. Bankruptcy Code, under 11 U.S.C. § 332, to an AI chatbot company holding minors' data, extending a tool previously used mainly for customer-list sales. The ombudsman's review of data-handling safeguards has not yet produced findings, and the scope of any proposed sale remains undisclosed. The ombudsman's findings will determine what privacy protections any buyer must honor.

Acting Alaska Attorney General Cori Mills announced that Alaska and a bipartisan coalition of states helped secure the appointment of the independent privacy watchdog, and the bankruptcy court ordered it at the coalition's urging. Mills said children and families should not have to worry that their private conversations can be sold to the highest bidder, and that companies have a responsibility to protect the information they collect, a responsibility that does not disappear when they file for bankruptcy. She said she was pleased the court had taken the important step to protect consumers. Alaska joined the bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general in October in raising concerns about Character.AI's privacy and safety practices, and the states' investigations identified potential consumer protection and privacy violations.

Character.AI allows users to interact with AI-generated characters, including fictional personalities and chatbots posing as therapists, psychologists, and other trusted professionals, and through these interactions the company has collected sensitive personal information including private conversations about mental health, relationships, and emotional struggles. Although Character.AI has voluntarily restricted minors' access to certain chatbot features, Mills has raised concerns that these measures are voluntary, incomplete, and could be circumvented or reversed by a future buyer. Sunday sent a letter to Congress in October 2026 calling for stronger children's online protections. Mills will remain actively engaged in the bankruptcy proceedings to protect consumers and address outstanding regulatory concerns, and users may see their data handled under a court-supervised review if the company's assets are sold.

stories.Headline: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung urges faster AI investment during data center visit
stories.Summary:
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung visited a data center under construction on Saturday to discuss the global artificial intelligence race. He urged the country to move fast because he believes that speed is decisive for competing in this technology sector. The president toured the construction site located in the southeastern city of Ulsan to highlight the need for faster investment. He stressed that governments and technology companies are racing to expand their capabilities to attract more computing capacity. This visit occurred while the world is competing right now to lead in the field of artificial intelligence.

The project is a joint development between Amazon Web Services and SK Group, which is the second largest conglomerate in South Korea. South Korea's science ministry estimated last year that the project will require 7 trillion won, or 5.2 billion dollars, until 2029. Initial operations at the Ulsan facility are scheduled to begin during the second half of 2027 to support the industry. SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won stated in September that initial capacity will be 103 megawatts by the year 2029. Future plans include expanding this capacity by nearly 900 megawatts to further increase the total computing power of the site.

President Lee Jae Myung said that speed is vital and that the Ulsan project shows regional growth is possible for Korea. He expressed hope that the success of this specific project would draw further investment from other global artificial intelligence companies. The president noted that AI investment had mainly been concentrated around Seoul before this development began in the southeastern region. He called on government ministries to consider how to train the workforce for building data centers and other AI infrastructure. Lee stated that advanced facilities were short of construction workers after learning that 900 people were working at the site.

The project could support demand for advanced semiconductors, which is an industry that is central to the technology exports of South Korea. Global technology companies are the target for further partnerships that SK Group is seeking as the construction project progresses. The president believes that strengthening the position of South Korea in the data center industry will help the national economy. Regional economic growth is affected by the location of major technology projects outside of the Seoul metropolitan area. Workers in the construction sector are affected by the current shortage of trained personnel for these advanced facility projects.

Data centers are a major source of chip demand, which links the project to the broader semiconductor industry in South Korea. The articles mention that President Lee and his wife, Kim Hea-kyung, attended an APEC meeting in Shenzhen on November 18, 2026. This meeting took place at the Shenzhen International Communication Center in Guangdong province before the president visited the Ulsan site. The science ministry provided the cost estimates for the project a year prior to the president's recent visit to Ulsan. These facts provide the context for the government's current push to accelerate the development of national artificial intelligence infrastructure.

SK Group plans to seek more partnerships with international technology companies as the construction of the Ulsan data center continues. Government ministries must now examine training programs to address the shortage of workers needed for these complex infrastructure projects. The project aims to reach its initial capacity of 103 megawatts by 2029 before moving into subsequent expansion phases. The articles leave open exactly how the government will implement the training for the workforce to build these facilities. They also do not specify which other global technology companies might partner with SK Group for future AI developments.

stories.Headline: Micron shares drop as investors reduce holdings in AI stocks
stories.Summary:
Micron Technology Inc. stock fell in Friday's premarket session as investors pulled back from AI-linked stocks, TradingView reported on 2026-11-20. The iShares PHLX SOX Semiconductor Sector Index Fund, which includes semiconductor players, was down over 3%. Memory rivals Western Digital Corp and Seagate Technology Holdings PLC were down 4-5%. NVIDIA Corp, Broadcom Inc, Marvell Technology Inc and Intel Corp were trading lower on Friday premarket. Micron shares were down 3.39% at $667 at last check during premarket trading on Friday, according to Benzinga Pro data.

Micron installed the first process tool at its high-bandwidth memory advanced-packaging facility in Singapore, keeping the project on track for initial output in early 2027, TechNode reported Friday. The company broke ground on the roughly $7 billion facility in January 2025 and expects it to create about 1,400 jobs. Micron is also developing an advanced wafer fabrication facility in Singapore, with wafer output expected in the second half of 2028. Micron is scheduled to report earnings on Dec. 17, 2026, with analysts expecting EPS of $38.22 versus $4.78 a year earlier and revenue of $61.93 billion versus $13.64 billion in the prior-year period. The stock trades at a P/E multiple of 9.3 times.

Micron Chief Executive Officer Sanjay Mehrotra said at the TomorrowX Summit in Austin, Texas, that the volume customers want to purchase over the next five years has exceeded what the company can currently commit to deliver. He expects that supply in 2027 and 2028 could be even tighter than in 2026. Micron has already pre-sold 75% of its projected 2027 supply and begun negotiating supply agreements for 2028 with customers. Micron has reportedly signed 26 multi-year supply and collaboration agreements involving a total of $32 billion in prepayments and other financial commitments. Some agreements require customers to purchase or pay as agreed, allowing Micron to determine how much future capacity already has buyers before investing capital to build wafer fabs.

TrendForce projects that wafers used by Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix and Micron to produce HBM will rise from about 23% of the three chipmakers' total DRAM wafer input in 2026 to nearly 30% in 2027. The research firm estimates that HBM4 prices will reach $3 to $5.50 per Gb in 2027, and commodity DRAM prices are expected to remain firm, though quarter-over-quarter price gains will narrow from 5% to 10% in the first quarter to 0% to 5% per quarter in the second half. Producing the same capacity of HBM consumes roughly three to four times as many wafers as commodity DRAM. CoreWeave shares fell from $53.13 to $39.51, while Micron declined from $778.31 to $594.51 between November 13 and November 20. CoreWeave reported $3.66 billion in revenue, representing 168% year-over-year growth, while its contracted revenue backlog reached approximately $132.5 billion.

Micron stock has gained more than 140% in 2026, alongside sharply higher demand and pricing for DRAM, NAND and HBM tied to the AI-driven memory market. At $658, Micron trades 17.8% below its 20-day SMA of $800.80, 28.5% below its 50-day SMA of $919.88 and 14.7% below its 200-day SMA of $771.48. Despite the pullback, the stock has gained 242.87% over the past 12 months. Micron carries a Buy consensus rating with an average price forecast of $1,622.38. RBC Capital maintained an Outperform rating and a $1,500 forecast on Nov. 18, Rosenblatt maintained Buy with a $1,900 forecast on Oct. 22, and Needham maintained Buy with a $1,650 forecast the same day.

Micron closed at $594.51 on the daily chart, breaking below its prior low of around $650 from early November and confirming a downward breakdown of its recent rebound structure. The stock lost the 1.272 Fibonacci extension reference level of $637.21, shifting price action from a consolidation above the prior low into an extended decline. In an optimistic rebound scenario, only if the daily chart first reclaims $637.21, then climbs back above the prior low of around $650 and holds it on a pullback, could this breakdown see initial repair. The next resistance on a rebound is the $669.00 to $676.01 zone, formed by the recent daily high and the 5-day exponential moving average. The primary risk is that the stock fails to recover after losing $585.25, which would cause the daily chart to form another lower low, with the 1.618 Fibonacci extension level of $509.15 viewed as the next support.

stories.Headline: California enacts first law governing lawyers use of generative AI
stories.Summary:
California became the first state to place a lawyer's obligations around generative artificial intelligence in statute when Governor Gavin Newsom signed Senate Bill 574 on September 30, 2026. Senator Thomas Umberg authored the bill, which passed the Legislature unanimously. The bill carries no urgency clause, so it takes effect on January 1, 2027. Lewellen Family Law Group P.C., a Northern California family law firm with offices in San Francisco and Sacramento, published an advisory on the statute on November 19, 2026. The firm practices exclusively in family law.

SB 574 adds section 6068.1 to the Business and Professions Code and section 1282.1 to the Code of Civil Procedure, and amends Code of Civil Procedure section 128.7 among other provisions. Section 6068.1 carries four duties: an attorney may not delegate the practice of law to generative artificial intelligence, must disclose generative AI use for documents submitted to a court, must take reasonable steps to verify the accuracy of generative AI output including all case and statutory citations and correct any erroneous or hallucinated output, and may not enter confidential, personal identifying or other nonpublic information into a generative AI system unless access is limited to the attorney and persons bound by the same duty of confidentiality. The amendment to section 128.7 provides that a brief, pleading, motion or other paper filed in any court may not contain a citation that the attorney responsible for submitting it has not personally read and verified. Parallel duties apply to arbitrators and alternative dispute resolution providers, who may not delegate decision making to generative AI and must disclose AI generated information used in a matter. Kimberly Lewellen is a Certified Family Law Specialist in California and the firm's shareholder, and has provided consultation to venture capitalists and technology founders over the past several years.

She says the practical risk in family law is distinctive. In a complex family law case, she says, an AI generated hallucinated legal citation, incorrect assumption or factual falsehood gets caught and the parties argue about sanctions. In a financial case the same failure can cost thousands if not hundreds of thousands of dollars before anyone fully untangles it, given the expediency of the proceedings and the complexity of the issues. She says the consequences are not symmetric, and the correction is not always retroactive if the mistake was preventable. Amrit Kullar, CIPP/US, CIPP/E, CIPP/C, CIPP/A and AIGP, is a data privacy subject matter expert who has presented on artificial intelligence and the ethics, discovery and family law practice issues that accompany it.

The statute does not state the form the disclosure must take, and it does not set the threshold of AI involvement that triggers it. Commentators have flagged an ambiguity in how the citation rule was inserted into section 128.7, and on one reading the protection that ordinarily shields a represented party from monetary sanctions attaches to the new citation provision rather than to the frivolous legal contention provision it was drafted against. A public tracker maintained by researcher Damien Charlotin documented 2,293 court decisions worldwide addressing AI generated hallucinated content as of November 14, 2026, of which 1,554 were in the United States. The tracker counts only matters where a court explicitly found or implied that a party relied on hallucinated content, rather than cases where the use of AI was merely alleged. California was already the first state to adopt a court rule governing generative artificial intelligence: Rule of Court 10.430, adopted in July 2025 and effective September 1, 2025, requires any court that does not prohibit generative AI use by court staff or judicial officers to adopt a use policy.

Those policies must keep confidential, personal identifying and other nonpublic information out of public generative AI systems, and must require anyone creating or using generative AI material to verify its accuracy and correct hallucinated output. A companion provision, Standard of Judicial Administration 10.80, covers judicial officers acting within their adjudicative role in advisory rather than mandatory language, and both followed a Generative AI Task Force established by Chief Justice Patricia Guerrero in May 2024. The rule's December 15, 2025 deadline reached every superior court in the state, including the family law courts in San Francisco and those in Sacramento County. The State Bar of California published its Practical Guidance for the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law in November 2023 and revised it in May 2026 to address agentic systems, and the American Bar Association issued Formal Opinion 512 in July 2024.

On September 12, 2025, in Noland v. Land of the Free, L.P., the Court of Appeal for the Second Appellate District, Division Three, issued what is understood to be the state's first published appellate opinion sanctioning a lawyer for AI fabricated citations, imposing a $10,000 sanction and directing that the opinion be forwarded to the State Bar. In the federal courts of California, a special master in the Central District imposed sanctions exceeding $31,000 in May 2025 against two firms whose ten page brief contained fabricated authority. In January 2026 the California Supreme Court directed the Third Appellate District to issue an order to show cause regarding sanctions over a prosecutor's filing that allegedly cited fabricated authority.

In March 2026 the Nebraska Supreme Court struck an appellant's brief, dismissed the appeal and referred counsel to its Counsel for Discipline in a marriage dissolution matter involving custody and property division, and in the disciplinary proceeding that followed, 57 of the brief's 63 citations were identified as defective. The court suspended the attorney from practice the following month pending a full disciplinary hearing. As of the advisory, no implementing guidance, advisory opinion or rules proposal interpreting the statute has issued from the Judicial Council or the State Bar, and firms have under three months to decide, without official direction, what their own practice will be. The disclosure question will be answered by local practice and by individual judges before it is answered by anyone else.

The ambiguity in section 128.7 may require either a legislative correction or a judicial answer, and until one arrives the prudent assumption is that the duty is personal to the attorney who signs. A practitioner appearing in more than one county is already working under more than one court policy. The articles leave open what form the disclosure must take and what threshold of AI involvement triggers it. More to follow.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave shares hit a one year low amid a broad sell off of AI infrastructure stocks
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave shares fell to a fresh one-year low of $39.51 on November 20, 2026, during a broad sell-off of AI infrastructure stocks. This drop took the stock 9.17% below the previous yearly extreme that was set on November 5, 2026. Other companies including IREN, Cipher Digital, and Applied Digital also saw their share prices fall sharply on the same day. The decline was part of a wider trend where AI-linked names were being repriced together across the market. This session saw the S&P 500 drop 3.00% to 6,954.60 and the Nasdaq 100 fall 4.63% to 25,237.50.

The sell-off affected the Dow Jones at 48,350.30 and the Russell 2000 at 2,594.94, while CoreWeave fell 6% to $42.17 in morning trading. Anthropic shares dropped 14% to $84.01 after opening at $111.50 on November 19 and closing that debut session at $97.17. Amazon, which owns 14.7% of Anthropic, slipped 2% to $251.39, while Alphabet owns 13.7% of the AI developer's capital stock. Applied Digital fell 17.81% and IREN dropped 18.0%, while Cipher Digital fell 17.4% and MARA saw a 19.38% drop. Other losses included SK hynix down 10.2%, Coherent down 10%, and DigitalOcean sliding 8.5% following an Alibaba earnings miss.

Market analysts noted that the selling was cohort-wide rather than tied to any specific company, reflecting a broad sector rotation. Bespoke stated on X that investors who wanted Anthropic at the IPO price of $83 could now do so. Eric Balchunas noted on X that Anthropic set a trading-volume record of $84 billion on its first day. The reports suggest that the floor investors had been watching for CoreWeave has finally given way during this session. Analysts believe the current swing in sentiment shows how quickly the initial debut-day enthusiasm for new AI stocks has cooled.

The sell-off affected GPU cloud providers, AI labs, hyperscalers, and enterprises that operate under multi-year contracts for data center capacity. Bitcoin miners like IREN and Cipher Digital were hit, with IREN leaving a market cap of $2.0 billion after its fall. Large-cap data-center REITs also suffered, with one seeing a 5.10% intraday slide to $164.18 during the heavy trading day. Money leaving the crypto and AI infrastructure sectors was absorbed by the healthcare and telecom industries, including HDFC Bank. Investors holding any AI-linked names felt the impact as the selling spread from Wall Street to Asia and Europe.

CoreWeave has worked steadily lower from a peak above $125, with each recovery attempt topping out below the previous one. The company rents purpose-built GPU data center capacity, which involves heavy capital spending and a large debt load for financing. Anthropic is a pure-play developer of frontier AI models, specifically the Claude family, and is listed in 82 ETFs. Amazon provides a different model by combining AWS with retail, marketplace, advertising, and subscription businesses that generate steady cash flow. Alphabet similarly pairs its Google Cloud unit with Google Search and YouTube advertising to spread its overall AI exposure.

Investors are now watching for signals about customer AI infrastructure spending, specifically from CoreWeave customer Meta and its science summit. The next major test is whether buyers will defend the $83 offer price for Anthropic as AI stocks remain under pressure. It remains open whether the largest IPO on record will slip below its offer price if the current sell-off deepens. The articles leave open if the current price levels for CoreWeave and its peers can eventually find a bottom. Amazon and Alphabet may also feel the outcome of the Anthropic price movement given their large stakes in the company.
