stories.Headline: Trump administration approves shipment of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China
stories.Summary:
The administration of President Donald Trump approved exports of nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips to Chinese companies. These sales occurred between December 2025 and May 2026, according to the House Foreign Affairs Committee. The approved chips were manufactured by Nvidia and AMD for use by various firms in China. This information was revealed by the committee on Thursday through an unusual release of licensing data. The approvals came despite previous restrictions on Chinese access to these prized artificial intelligence chips.

The Department of Commerce approved 879,000 chips, including 150,000 for Tencent, 75,000 for Alibaba, 43,000 for Baidu, and 4,000 for BYD. These four companies are on the Pentagon list of alleged Chinese military backed firms. The approved hardware included Nvidia H200 chips and the equivalent MI325X models made by AMD. Companies had actually sought permission to ship 3.4 million chips to China during this six month period. Trump gave the green light for H200 shipments in December, rolling back restrictions from the Biden era.

Committee Chair Brian Mast used the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 to publicly reveal this license application information. Mast stated that this release is the most detailed public disclosure in the history of that specific legislation. Nvidia said the approvals were subject to limited volumes and strict conditions, but they stopped shipping H200s. AMD stated that it maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance with all applicable United States export control laws. Commerce official Jeffrey Kessler testified in July that shipments had begun, although he noted there were very few.

Former US official Chris McGuire said it was astonishing that over 30 percent of chips went to military companies. McGuire questioned if the Commerce Department conducted any serious national security review before it approved these specific licenses. China hawks across the US political spectrum criticized the rollback of restrictions, fearing a supercharged Chinese military. The news affected markets, as Nvidia stock fell 3.3 percent and AMD shares slumped by 7.7 percent. The broader Nasdaq and S&P 500 also dropped by 2.2 percent and 1.8 percent, respectively.

Former President Joe Biden restricted these chips to protect the US lead in AI and prevent Chinese military growth. Scrutiny increased after news emerged that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. This scandal highlighted instances where Nvidia AI chips were smuggled into China without any punishment for the actors. Meanwhile, Tencent reported third quarter revenue of 207.34 billion yuan, while its capital spending hit 81.4 billion yuan. Tencent also leased 100,000 Nvidia class chips from Oracle for roughly 7 billion dollars over five years.

The Trump administration now faces pressure to crack down on technology threats as it coordinates AI rules with Xi Jinping. It remains unclear how many of the approved licenses actually resulted in physical shipments of chips to China. Some reports suggest only about ten companies were cleared to buy the H200, with few deliveries taking place. Investors are now waiting to see if heavy AI spending by Chinese firms turns into actual cloud revenue. The articles leave open whether the US will reinstate tougher restrictions following the recent House committee revelations.

stories.Headline: US government scrutinizes Nscale deal for providing ByteDance remote access to Nvidia GPUs
stories.Summary:
Bloomberg reported on November 19, 2026, that the US government is scrutinizing a deal between Nscale and ByteDance. The London based AI infrastructure company must now apply for a license to keep serving its client. This regulatory action follows a new rule regarding remote access to sensitive American technology. The rule aims to stop companies from using third country data centers to bypass export restrictions. Nscale provided Nvidia GPUs to ByteDance at data centers located in Iceland and Norway.

The interim final rule was released by the Bureau of Industry and Security on November 16, 2026. It takes effect on November 19 and gives operators already serving covered customers 90 days to obtain licenses. ByteDance subsidiary Spring used 2,304 Nvidia B200 chips at a data center in Glomfjord, Norway. This cluster exceeds the threshold of 12 million processing units, which is about 750 Nvidia H100s. Other high risk countries facing these licensing requirements include Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand.

The Commerce Department released the rule at the direction of the National Security Council and the Treasury Department. Officials stated the rule ensures that remote computing arrangements cannot be used to circumvent existing chip restrictions. They noted that cloud computing makes it easier to access advanced American capabilities from outside restricted countries. Nscale has not stated if it will apply for the license, nor has the government said if one will be granted. The rule focuses on the headquarters of the customer rather than the location of the data center.

ByteDance is affected because its Singapore unit Spring provided about 73 percent of Nscale's 2025 revenue. This single contract generated 24 million dollars out of a total 33 million dollars in annual revenue. Other firms are also affected, such as Moonshot AI, which dropped a 150 million dollar deal in Indonesia. Aolani Cloud saw banks pause a 480 million dollar loan for a ByteDance linked site in Malaysia. Tencent also faced similar issues with a five year Nvidia chip lease through Oracle in Southeast Asia.

Nscale planned a US listing on the New York Stock Exchange with a valuation of roughly 35 billion dollars. Macquarie Bank provided a 105 million dollar loan and required Nscale to report any suspicious compute configurations. Nvidia gave verbal guidance to cloud clients to sell at least 51 percent of services to non Chinese customers. The Nscale case is notable because it involves a NATO country and was disclosed in a public filing. Previous remote access debates focused mostly on Southeast Asia rather than European sites like Glomfjord.

Nscale must now decide whether to seek a license within the 90 day window or terminate the service. If the license is refused, Nscale will lose its main tenant and must resell the GPU capacity. The articles leave open whether the 90 day window is enough time for the government to reach a decision. It remains unclear how the rule treats existing contracts that were signed before November 16, 2026. No sources provided information on whether the laws of Iceland or Norway add further requirements to this deal.

stories.Headline: COP31 participants launch the Antalya AI Pledge to address technology and climate risks
stories.Summary:
Lord Mawuko-Yevugah and other authors wrote about the collision of artificial intelligence, climate change, and democratic governance in November 2026. They examined how these three structural forces reinforce and destabilize one another within the current international political landscape. The authors analyzed the intersection of computational systems, ecological crisis, and the legitimacy of liberal democratic institutions. They argued that technology is not a neutral instrument but is situated within a political economy of resource extraction. This analysis explores how these factors co-constitute a new world order through seven interconnected sections of critical examination.

The Antalya AI Pledge launched on November 16 at COP31 in Turkey recognizes AI's potential to track and cut emissions. This pledge acknowledges that AI increases demand for land, water, electricity, and critical materials like cobalt, lithium, and copper. The authors note that training large foundation models requires capital expenditures reaching tens of billions of dollars for specialized semiconductors. These systems rely on extreme ultraviolet lithography, hyperscale data centers, high-voltage transmission grids, and proprietary training corpora for their operation. This infrastructure creates natural monopolies dominated by a few American and Chinese technology conglomerates backed by state security apparatuses.

UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell described artificial intelligence as a double-edged sword during the COP31 meetings in Turkey. He noted that while AI can advance climate solutions, it also creates tangible demands for critical natural resources. Lord Mawuko-Yevugah stated that compute capacity has joined nuclear arsenals and oil reserves as a primary metric of national power. He argued that states now view algorithmic infrastructure as a core attribute of territorial sovereignty rather than a commercial sector. This securitization means international cooperation is often subordinated to zero-sum security dilemmas regarding autonomous warfare and cyber offense.

Civil society organizations and Indigenous groups expressed doubt that voluntary commitments can address the risks of expanding AI data centers. The Women and Gender Constituency voiced concerns regarding data privacy, energy consumption, and digital inequalities during the COP28 meetings. Affected communities in the Global South bear the costs of mineral extraction, including deforestation, toxic tailings, and aquifer depletion. These groups question who benefits from AI-driven solutions and who participates in the decisions regarding the supporting infrastructure. Many fear that without enforceable safeguards, AI will amplify the inequalities that climate action is intended to address.

The liberal international order previously rested on American military primacy and the assumption that global trade would socialize rising powers. This premise fractured by the mid-2020s, leading to a multipolar order defined by industrial nationalism and weaponized interdependence. AI was discussed at COP22 in 2016 for emissions and COP23 in 2017 for managing disaster risk. Subsequent discussions at COP25, COP26, and COP27 included adaptation and emissions monitoring before caution grew at COP28 in 2023. By COP29 in 2024, seventy-five countries and 1,170 non-state actors endorsed the voluntary Declaration on Green Digital Action.

Future steps include considering locally tailored AI tools and safeguards against social and environmental harm for the COP30 meetings. The Global Climate Action Agenda in Belém highlighted AI applications in food security, agriculture, and adaptation for further development. The articles leave open whether binding regulatory constraints can prevent the race for computational supremacy from cannibalizing ecological budgets. They question if democratic legislatures can satisfy competing constituencies while facing absolute biophysical limits and escalating disaster recovery costs. It remains unclear if institutional pathways can preserve human agency without succumbing to algorithmic authoritarianism or total ecological collapse.

stories.Headline: Anthropic stock crashes after IPO as AI shares lose over 50 percent in five months
stories.Summary:
Anthropic launched its initial public offering on the Nasdaq on November 19, 2026, but its stock crashed shortly after the debut. Gary Marcus reported on November 20, 2026, that AI stocks have lost over 50 percent of their value in five months. The company saw its share price drop steadily after opening, and it was set to fall nearly 10 percent more. This market decline is described as a crash that is happening faster than the original dot com debacle of the past. The overall technology sector on Wall Street fell across the board due to growing concerns over the weakening profitability of AI.

The IPO was priced at 83 dollars per share, which was above the earlier target range of 70 to 78 dollars. Anthropic raised 107.3 billion dollars, surpassing the 86.2 billion dollars raised by SpaceX in June, and was valued at 1.5 trillion dollars. Trading began at 111.50 dollars, reached a high of 114.99 dollars, and closed at 97.17 dollars on November 19 in New York. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1,101.11 points to 49,097.06, while the S&P 500 ended at 7,175.83 and the Nasdaq at 23,879.20. SpaceX is set to open below its IPO price of 135 dollars, and SoftBank fell 14.5 percent overnight.

Chief Executive Dario Amodei stated that the company would pace the training and deployment of AI systems to ensure the technology remains safe. He added that an obsession with the public interest and safety has been embedded in the DNA of Anthropic from the start. Gary Marcus claimed that the IPO is on pace to be one of the most embarrassing in history for retail investors. He noted that his inbox was filled with media think pieces glorifying the IPO that were filed too soon by various writers. Marcus warned that a death spiral for the market has begun, which he has long predicted in his newsletter.

Other affected companies include Apple, which fell 0.92 percent, Microsoft at 1.78 percent, Nvidia at 3.30 percent, and Amazon at 3.87 percent. Alphabet dropped 3.46 percent, Meta fell 3.27 percent, Tesla decreased 2.43 percent, and the semiconductor firm TSMC saw a decline of 2.90 percent. Broadcom fell 2.09 percent, Eli Lilly dropped 2.25 percent, Walmart fell 1.04 percent, SK hynix fell 2.67 percent, and Micron fell 2.10 percent. Asian markets collapsed, with the Nikkei plunging over 4 percent and Taiwan's stock index falling 16 percent during its worst week since COVID. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index also closed sharply lower, ending the session with a total decrease of 2.42 percent.

The background includes a period where AI stocks were highly valued, with some companies reaching valuations as high as one trillion dollars. The S&P 500 had already extended its losing streak to six sessions before the events of November 19 and November 20 occurred. In other news, President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping met in Shenzhen, China, to discuss oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. West Texas Intermediate crude settled at 83.21 dollars a barrel, while Brent crude traded at 91.98 dollars on the ICE Futures exchange. These events occurred amidst rising military tensions in the Middle East and expectations of a global oil supply glut.

In the coming months or days, Gary Marcus predicts that Nvidia and the Neoclouds will be hit hard by the market crash. He suggests that OpenAI cannot possibly IPO at a valuation of 1 trillion dollars in this environment and may run out of cash. The articles leave open whether the AI sector can recover from this selloff or if the death spiral will continue. It remains unclear how the safety pacing mentioned by Dario Amodei will affect the long term financial viability of the company. The reports do not state if other AI firms will delay their public offerings to avoid the current market volatility.

stories.Headline: AI chip demand creates structural high bandwidth memory shortage for top suppliers
stories.Summary:
A high bandwidth memory shortage occurred by November 21, 2026, as AI demand strained global silicon supplies. Samsung, SK hynix, and Micron caused this shift by dedicating more wafer capacity to HBM. This structural problem emerged because AI accelerators require far more memory bandwidth than ordinary DIMMs provide. The shortage is not a temporary inventory issue but a result of zero sum reallocation. Every wafer used for AI memory stacks is one that cannot become conventional DDR5.

TrendForce reports HBM took 23% of DRAM wafer input in 2026 and will reach nearly 30% by 2027. HBM requires three to four times the wafer capacity of general purpose DRAM to produce. HBM4 prices are at least 2.05 dollars per gigabit in 2026 and 3.00 to 5.50 dollars in 2027. Conventional DRAM contract prices are expected to rise 10% to 15% quarter over quarter in Q4 2026. Samsung is building an Onyang hub for HBM4E with operations moving up to June 2028.

SK hynix CEO Kwak Noh-jung stated that customer demand will exceed supply capacity even beyond 2030. Sales chief Kim Ki-tae noted that customers request more than twice the volume the company can supply. Samsung chairman Lee Jae-yong outlined plans for the Onyang complex, which costs 46 trillion to 56 trillion KRW. Micron announced high volume production of HBM4 for the Nvidia Vera Rubin platform to meet demand. These leaders agree that the supply chain cannot flex quickly to resolve the current structural imbalance.

Nvidia, AMD, and Google are primary buyers, with Nvidia's RTX Spark offering up to 128 GB of unified memory. Consumers of phones, PCs, and standard servers are affected by higher prices and longer lead times. Paul Triolo said securing advanced packaging and logic memory interfaces is the top priority for South Korea. Takashi Yunogami noted that TSMC holds a near 80% monopoly on the critical 2.5D packaging market. Douglas Fuller argued that industrial policy should prioritize dynamic efficiency and technological learning over short term costs.

HBM stacks several DRAM dies using through silicon vias and mounts them beside accelerators on a shared interposer. Counterpoint Research put SK hynix at 50% of HBM revenue in Q2 2026, down from 64% previously. Samsung rose to 33% and Micron held 18%, while Samsung's HBM4 revenue tripled in Q3 2026. SK hynix reported Q3 2026 revenue of 104.62 trillion KRW and an operating profit of 83.33 trillion KRW. China has raised its share of domestically supplied semiconductor equipment to between 20% and 30%.

SK hynix has sold out its HBM and related DRAM through 2029, while Micron covers only partial demand. Samsung continues pouring money into packaging capacity to catch up with its rivals in the HBM3E cycle. New capacity from China's CXMT and other major fabs may not add meaningful output before around 2028. The articles leave open whether Samsung's massive Onyang investment will create a memory glut after 2028. It remains uncertain if South Korean firms can break the TSMC monopoly on 2.5D packaging technology.

stories.Headline: Singapore launches three AI missions to combat financial crime and improve business lending
stories.Summary:
The Monetary Authority of Singapore and the Future of Finance Institute launched three national AI missions on Wednesday, November 18, 2026. These initiatives focus on preventing financial crime, improving business financing, and enabling the safe use of AI agents in financial transactions. Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong announced these plans during the Singapore FinTech Festival held at the Singapore Expo. The programs aim to bring together researchers, public agencies, technology companies, and financial institutions to develop shared capabilities. These missions are part of a wider national AI program that was first announced in the 2026 Budget.

The first initiative targets financial crime by improving the detection of suspicious transfers across banks to stop scams from moving quickly. The Monetary Authority of Singapore will begin a design study in early 2027 for an industry-wide Scam Detection Utility for domestic accounts. The second initiative uses synthetic data to help small and medium-sized enterprises and start-ups access credit without needing extensive collateral. The third initiative involves an Agentic Money Sandbox where AI agents can conduct transactions using digital money within defined limits. The Future of Finance Institute will also work with the Agency for Science, Technology and Research on speech-to-text AI applications.

Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong, who chairs the Monetary Authority of Singapore, said the missions build capabilities beyond individual institutions. He stated that scam proceeds move through several institutions in minutes, making it difficult for any single lender to intervene effectively. Gan explained that AI could help lenders assess a wider set of indicators to speed up decisions and lower borrowing costs. He stressed that greater autonomy for AI agents would not remove responsibility from the organisations that authorise those specific agents. He also noted that the government is engaging American officials regarding the implications of new United States export controls.

Five banks are already participating in a trial that securely combines transaction data to train and assess various AI models. Small and medium-sized enterprises and start-ups are affected because traditional credit assessments often overlook businesses with limited financial records. Technology companies are invited to develop lending tools using realistic synthetic data rather than relying on actual customer records initially. Participating businesses will be consulted to see if the proposed AI tools actually address their specific financing difficulties. Residents and visitors are affected by the second-phase report on PayNow, which includes an SGQR+ switching arrangement for payments.

The Future of Finance Institute began operations this month to coordinate work between financial institutions, technology developers, and various researchers. Its remit includes developing common standards and resources for managing AI risks that can be adopted beyond individual pilot projects. The AI Innovation Arena initiative provides developers with synthetic data to test AI solutions, focusing initially on preventing financial crime. The government wants to explore if AI can help lenders identify businesses approaching a financing need and offer options proactively. These initiatives follow the 2026 Budget, which established the broader national AI programme to strengthen the country's financial sector.

Authorities will assess promising applications against international practices before considering broader deployment rather than assuming demonstrations translate to commercial systems. The Monetary Authority of Singapore will examine the technical blueprint, governance arrangements, and operating model for the Scam Detection Utility. Officials want to establish how AI agents can use purpose-bound money without exceeding authority or compromising confidence in transactions. The articles leave open whether the Scam Detection Utility will eventually expand to include cross-border cooperation after the domestic phase. It remains unclear how the new United States export controls on advanced computing equipment will specifically impact Singapore's AI development.

stories.Headline: KPMG launches KCi AI audit platform in the US with agents in auditor workflows
stories.Summary:
KPMG LLP announced the U.S. rollout of KPMG Clara intelligence, or KCi, on November 17, 2026, from New York. The firm said KCi leads the profession to an AI-enabled, human-assured audit for audit committees, management teams, and KPMG auditors. KCi embeds specialized AI agents directly into auditor workflows rather than operating as a standalone tool. Auditors direct and review agent-orchestrated workflows, with agents automating routine tasks and first-pass documentation. The launch follows successful use in 2026, with KCi rolled out to more than 125 U.S. teams and 500 teams globally.

KPMG is aiming to deploy KCi in all private company audits in 2027 and plans a structured, phased rollout for public company audits. Automated data pipelines analyze 100% of transaction populations in selected audit areas, identifying outliers, trends, and anomalies for targeted auditor investigation. On some engagements, KPMG reports this shortened timelines by up to three and a half weeks and removed the need for clients to manually retrieve volumes of individual support documents. KCi operates within a governed environment grounded in KPMG audit methodology, professional standards, and the firm's Trusted AI framework. The technology foundation combines proprietary KPMG capabilities with enterprise technologies from relationships with Anthropic, Google Cloud, Microsoft, and OpenAI.

Christian Peo, Vice Chair of Audit and Assurance at KPMG U.S., said auditor judgment cannot be automated but technology helps remove barriers between data, analysis, and action. Peo said that when people spend less time assembling information and more time understanding it, they can focus on where the risk is and what needs to be challenged. He described the moment as defining for the profession, as fundamental as the transition from paper to digital workflows. KPMG said auditors retain responsibility for review and final judgment, and traceability lets teams inspect underlying data sources and corroborate findings. The firm said agents can generate and organize material, but responsibility does not transfer to the software.

KPMG is modernizing its audit operating model by strengthening role clarity, moving supervision and review earlier in the audit lifecycle, and creating greater consistency in how data is organized and used. The firm said nearly 1,000 Audit and Assurance interns attended training at its Lakehouse facility earlier this year on critical thinking, professional skepticism, and evaluation of AI-assisted work. KPMG said the approach simplifies the audit experience for client accounting teams by providing greater visibility into requests, milestones, and engagement activities. The announcement does not present the three-and-a-half-week result as an average across all engagements, describing it as a company-reported outcome from selected work. The announcement does not specify which provider powers each individual KCi function.

KPMG Clara is the firm's global smart audit platform, and KCi is built on it. KPMG said it was the first of the Big Four firms to organize itself along the same industry lines as clients. Over the past several years, the firm has built a secure data and technology foundation across KPMG Clara. KPMG said KCi is designed to evolve as technology advances and is the latest milestone in its long-term transformation of the audit experience. The articles state that KPMG has market-leading alliances with many of the world's leading software and services vendors.

KPMG's planned expansion in 2027 will test how consistently the model can operate across engagements while preserving human scrutiny. The articles leave open which provider powers each individual KCi function. The articles do not state how many public company audits the phased rollout will cover or on what timetable. The articles do not give the number of engagements behind the three-and-a-half-week result. The articles do not say what KCi costs or how the 2027 private company deployment will be sequenced.

stories.Headline: AI tools surface hidden software vulnerabilities as outages hit banks and airlines
stories.Summary:
Major U.S. businesses including Apple Pay, NASA's internal communication network, the Federal Aviation Administration and Microsoft's Outlook, Teams and Copilot experienced technical outages in recent weeks, TechGig reported on November 21, 2026. JPMorgan Chase confirmed on November 16 that a software bug in its systems caused disruptions affecting Chase and other banks making transactions with it. Microsoft's 365 suite, including Outlook, faced a global outage for millions of users for nearly 36 hours after a server update. The FAA cancelled over 10,000 flights following a router update, and a US Transport Secretary confirmed no AI link. A classified communications network at the National Security Agency went down due to routine maintenance.

Cybersecurity investor Dave DeWalt, a former McAfee CEO and CISA Advisory Council vice chairman, said AI tools like Mythos are surfacing existing vulnerabilities at unprecedented speed. Anusha Iyer, founder of Corsha, said industrial systems were not designed for the current level of secure connectivity and cited the FAA outage as modernization overwhelming legacy hardware. Senator Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intelligence Committee, called the disruptions a wake-up call and said AI is moving faster than the ability to manage its consequences. Iyer said the fault lies in rushed integration of legacy and modern systems without clear risk understanding. DeWalt recommended increased testing and prioritising what needs fixing, while Iyer advised tighter segmentation and access control.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on Wednesday that the outages were several unrelated issues and separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. Clayton said they were not a coordinated or state sponsored attack and that the rate of patching and upgrading of systems is increasing. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said he is 98% confident the outages have nothing to do with adversaries hacking and that DHS officials are convening a call with industry. Mullin said it would be helpful for the industry doing an upgrade to inform customers it is going to take place. Mullin added that patching and aging infrastructure are part of the challenge and that DHS is not pressuring industry.

Anjana Rajan, CEO of Atalanta and a former White House cyber official, said the private sector owns and operates most U.S. critical infrastructure and that understanding of systems is not keeping pace. Lauren Zabierek, CEO and co-founder of the Software Safety Institute and a former CISA official, said software does not have to be hacked to cause harm. Bob Lord, the institute's chief strategy officer, said the software sector lacks transparency and enough information. Mayank Morya, CTO at Mitigata, told India Today Tech the underlying vulnerability is a concentration of technology dependencies. Microsoft's 365 outage affected users in 74 countries including Indian airlines IndiGo and SpiceJet.

Saakar S Yadav, founder of Lexlegis.ai, said reliance on a few cloud, identity and payment providers increases disruption risk. Mandar Patil, executive VP at Cyble, warned AI may enable hackers to conduct autonomous attacks by interacting with APIs and enterprise applications. Google's Threat Intelligence Group reported hackers created an AI framework to scan security patches for flaws in older software versions and execute attacks. Sunil Peter, VP at Maveric Systems, recommended independent fallback mechanisms and crisis management communication through encrypted messaging tools. Professor Himanshu Joshi from IMI Delhi noted technical failures are not new but their impact is greater due to interconnected systems.

Zabierek said Mullin could reconstitute CISA's Cybersecurity Advisory Committee and the DHS Cyber Safety Review Board, which was disbanded last year. Lawmakers on the homeland security committee introduced a bipartisan bill Tuesday to reconstitute the board under a new name. Rajan pointed to a January 2025 report co-authored by CISA and other agencies on closing the software understanding gap. Lord suggested DHS strengthen the voluntary Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures program and said the question should be how to reduce recurring classes of coding error. DeWalt expects growth in AI-driven vulnerability management, autonomous remediation and safe patch deployment solutions.

stories.Headline: House lawmakers urge Trump administration to create US open-weight AI initiative to counter China
stories.Summary:
House lawmakers recommended on Friday that the Trump administration establish an initiative for American open-weight AI models. This proposal aims to entice organizations to turn away from Chinese open-weight models. The House Select Committee on China published a report detailing the widespread use of Chinese models. This report followed an investigation that began in April regarding specific American companies. The committee examined why firms like Airbnb, Anysphere, Cursor, and DoorDash used these models.

The committee highlighted the prevalence of Chinese open-weight models including DeepSeek, Kimi, Qwen, and GLM. They propose a national initiative pairing public compute, shared evaluation infrastructure, and lawful access to frontier models. Lawmakers want federal procurement to provide anchor demand and the White House to prohibit agencies from using Chinese models. The government should subject these models to consistent evaluation and sanction companies that illicitly distill U.S. models. Cursor, recently bought by SpaceX, plans to stop using Kimi K2.5 from Moonshot AI for Composer 2.

The House Select Committee on China stated that risks are increasing because Chinese models produce less secure code. They warned that these models can autonomously build cyber exploits, necessitating the creation of U.S. open-weight models. Lawmakers noted that Chinese models are widely used in the economy, though much of that use is hard to track. They also warned that many safety evaluations may not detect certain behaviors from these specific Chinese models. The committee believes the government must act to counter the growing influence of these foreign AI tools.

Organizations using Chinese models cite low cost, easy customization, and performance as the primary drivers for their adoption. Proponents of proprietary models believe that open-weight versions are less secure and not as capable as closed counterparts. Many experts told ISMG that open-weight models from Chinese labs are steadily closing in on frontier models. American companies like OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google primarily offer proprietary models that do not share weights or training data. These proprietary models are more restrictive than open-weight models, which allow users to customize parts of the system.

The articles explain that open-weight models provide weights to users, often costing a fraction of closed proprietary models. Some American open-weight options exist, such as Meta's Llama and Muse models, which operate under open-source licenses. Nvidia distributes the open-weight Nemotron, while OpenAI and Google offer open-weight models called oss and Gemma, respectively. Chinese labs may develop quickly through distillation, using responses from teacher models like Claude Fable as training data. The U.S. government says many Chinese labs perform this distillation illicitly and without permission from the original makers.

The Trump administration must now decide whether to implement the proposed national American open-weight AI initiative. Federal agencies may face new prohibitions against using Chinese models if the White House adopts the committee's recommendations. The government may begin sanctioning companies that are found to be illicitly distilling American-made AI models. The articles leave open whether the proposed public compute and shared infrastructure will be successfully established. It remains unclear if American open-weight models can effectively compete with the low cost of Chinese alternatives.

stories.Headline: Oracle says it secures full funding for OpenAI infrastructure contract
stories.Summary:
Oracle said on X on November 20, 2026, that it had secured all the funding needed to fulfill its infrastructure contract with OpenAI. Oracle posted the statement at 9:01 PM that day, and the post drew 655,000 views. Oracle said its final capital raise earlier that month made it the first hyperscaler fully funded for this investment cycle. Oracle said the financing it outlined at Oracle Investor Day, including vendor financing, is in place. Oracle said any further private discussions with vendors are just additional options.

Oracle said its ability to deliver on the OpenAI contract does not depend on those vendor discussions. Oracle said any media reports that will come out and say the contrary are incorrect and wrong. Oracle said it and OpenAI are making rapid progress on their infrastructure partnership. Oracle said its Abilene campus, where Astra-6 was trained, is nearly complete. Oracle said Shackelford, its next gigawatt-scale campus, is fully permitted.

Oracle said the handover of NVIDIA Vera Rubin racks in its data halls is on track for the coming weeks. Oracle said it continues to expect positive free cash flow in the second half of FY2028. Oracle said it is targeting more than $30 billion in free cash flow in FY2029. Oracle said it expects to self-fund future growth beginning that year. Oracle attached a forward-looking statements disclaimer saying statements about its future plans, expectations, beliefs and intentions are subject to material risks and uncertainties.

Ed Zitron replied to the post, thanking Oracle for what he called a very reassuring message delivered one minute after market close. Techmeme carried Oracle's statement on November 20, 2026, at 8:20 PM. stories.Headline: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns amid scandal involving a suspected Chinese spy
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as the head of Nvidia on Thursday, November 14, 2026. He stepped down after admitting to an affair with Alice Huang, a Singaporean executive. This woman is believed to be a spy for the government of China. A New York Times report also linked him to a second affair. This subordinate worked at the microchip company where Huang served as chief executive.

The scandal triggered federal investigations and a sell-off of Nvidia stock in Santa Clara, California. Huang lobbied Donald Trump to ease chip export controls established under President Joe Biden. The Commerce Department stopped investigating if Alice Huang smuggled chips after an Nvidia lawyer called. Nvidia is a major investor in a 1.4 trillion dollar IPO for Anthropic. This AI company warns that its technology poses catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.

Donald Trump said on Monday that he hoped there was no problem with Huang. He called the former executive an amazing, honorable, and very high quality guy. Trump believes that the microchip leader will eventually end up in good shape. He previously decided that AI companies should self police after meeting with tech executives. The president has facilitated the goals of a man potentially tied to China.

Stephen Witt told the New Yorker that sleeping with spies is generally regarded as bad. The New York Times reported that Trump was warned about the relationship last year. He received another warning in May before joining Huang on a trip to Beijing. The company board is populated by early investors and longtime associates of the cofounder. This board had no succession plan or clear replacement before the chief executive resigned.

Huang argued that the United States must sell more chips to maintain a chipmaking advantage. He served as the closest adviser to the president on artificial intelligence technology. The articles describe him as a leather swathed man who flattered the president for favors. The AI industry had previously issued warnings about the destructive potential of its own technology. These warnings failed to prevent the current mess involving the world's most valuable AI company.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will lead Nvidia while the search for a replacement begins. The new Congress includes members who promised to rein in data centers and AI. Some of these elected officials have a history of regulating various aspects of technology. The articles leave open whether the president will change his current laissez faire AI policy. It remains unclear if the new Congress will successfully implement these promised AI regulations.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang steps down as Nvidia becomes AI financing hub
stories.Summary:
NVIDIA’s longtime chief executive Jensen Huang has stepped down, and the company he led is now described by industry insiders as the “central bank” of the AI circular financing economy, a role that has drawn close attention from Wall Street and Silicon Valley. Under Huang, NVIDIA built the GPU chips that serve as the underlying foundation of the global AI wave and assembled what the article calls a huge capital ammunition depot. Regulatory filings show that as of September 30 the market value of NVIDIA’s shares in eight publicly listed companies exceeded 48 billion US dollars, with holdings concentrated in partners that buy its GPUs. Interim CEO Colette Kress said on Tuesday’s earnings call that NVIDIA is proud of the role it has played in supporting the industry and will keep evaluating future transactions with a rigorous attitude, adding that the company still has a lot of work to do to judge whether these are the right investments to make.

The article reports that NVIDIA’s total investment portfolio exceeds 1000 billion US dollars, covering equity stakes in cutting-edge labs and bets on power producers and cloud computing companies, and that its shareholding in cloud computing unicorn CoreWeave has reached 10 percent. Its capital has also extended to cloud platform Nebius Group, semiconductor firm Intel and xAI before it was merged into SpaceX, and during Huang’s tenure it placed large bets on Anthropic and OpenAI, which lack investment-grade ratings. As part of Anthropic’s initial public offering on Thursday, NVIDIA committed to buying 10 billion US dollars of Anthropic shares, and Anthropic has reportedly signed a 350 billion US dollar agreement with Lambda, another NVIDIA-backed company, to lease data center computing power run on NVIDIA chips. According to PitchBook, as of November 13 NVIDIA had taken part in 129 venture capital and startup accelerator transactions this year, with the total venture capital it joined other investors in reaching 2200 billion US dollars, or 27 percent of the global total of that kind, and at least 293 investment and acquisition deals since the AI boom heated up in 2023.

NVIDIA reported on Tuesday that its commitments in areas such as long-term supply agreements and data center leases total 5180 billion US dollars, up sharply from about 850 billion a year ago. One guarantee is that NVIDIA will provide up to 1050 billion US dollars in backing for SB Energy, a SoftBank subsidiary, for its planned Ohio data center to help it issue bonds for construction costs, along with a 1.5 billion US dollar equity investment, and OpenAI has agreed to lease the computing capacity once the center is complete, with NVIDIA holding exclusive chip supply rights for the first half of the project. In August, Huang led efforts to obtain commitments from Apollo, Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR to raise 5000 billion US dollars, with NVIDIA providing fallback arrangements and guarantees, to help startup customers finance chip purchases, but people familiar with the matter say no funds have actually been invested so far. The article notes real doubt about whether many of these commitments and guarantees can be fulfilled, and says that since NVIDIA’s stock hit an all-time peak on October 6, the combined market value of the eight listed companies it holds has fallen by 820 billion US dollars, with SpaceX and Intel accounting for most of the decline, while rising borrowing costs are straining many AI enterprises.

stories.Headline: Pandex launches an MCP and REST API for official European law with 2.8 million documents
stories.Summary:
Pandex launched on 21 November 2026 as an official European law service for AI agents, served over MCP and a REST API. The service aggregates legislation and highest-court decisions from the European Union, seven European countries and the European Court of Human Rights. It serves these documents through one API and one MCP server for every jurisdiction it holds. The product page counts about 2.8 million official documents, 37 million citation links and nightly updates as of November 2026. The launch was introduced on Hacker News by founder vasie, who framed the problem as models often getting European law wrong.

Pandex holds 2.8 million official documents, 33 of 41 institutions complete, 37 million citations linked to their text, and 8 more institutions next. The European Union holds 101,974 documents, with the Publications Office of the EU and the Court of Justice of the EU complete. France holds 907,232 documents, with Parlement, Gouvernement, Conseil d'État, Tribunal des conflits and Conseil constitutionnel complete, and Cour de cassation partial. Germany holds 177,101 documents, with Bundesamt für Justiz, Bundesgerichtshof, Bundesfinanzhof, Bundesarbeitsgericht, Bundessozialgericht and Gemeinsamer Senat complete, and Bundesverfassungsgericht and Bundesverwaltungsgericht partial. The Netherlands holds 335,852 documents, the United Kingdom 99,621, Austria 855,697, Switzerland 137,746, Luxembourg 41,891 and the Council of Europe 127,432.

Pandex says it is built for software that has to get the law right, offering keyword, semantic or hybrid search in any language. It offers point-in-time law, a full citation graph, exact lookup and official sources only, with responses in Markdown or JSON. The free tier gives 1,000 requests a day while in beta, the usage plan costs €1 per 1,000 requests, and the Feed costs from €1,000 a month. Founding customers get 10 places at €300 a month fixed for two years, with the API uncounted up to 1 million requests a month. The MCP endpoint is at https://api.pandex.io/mcp, and the site shows compatibility marks for Claude, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Windsurf, Zed and Gemini.

On Hacker News, founder vasie wrote that models often get European law wrong, quoting old versions or making up text, and that Pandex covers EU, Germany, France, Netherlands, UK, Austria, Switzerland, Luxembourg and ECHR case law with every past version of each law, refreshed nightly. The same comment advertises MCP install with no API key on the public HTTP endpoint. Explainx.ai advises builders to read Pandex terms before production use, noting that no key describes launch convenience, not a security audit. Explainx.ai also says Pandex does not interpret law but fixes stale or fabricated citations, and that teams should keep cite checking or human review. Explainx.ai lists vLex, Lexis and national portals as incumbents that already sell verified legal data.

The articles give coverage gaps institution by institution. Cour de cassation decisions published only through Judilibre since 2020 need a registered account there, and the dumps run about two months behind. Bundesverfassungsgericht chamber decisions of 1998 to 2009 are only on the court's site, which refuses clients that are not a browser. Bundesverwaltungsgericht is still loading, with 2,270 of about 20,321 documents held so far. About 27,700 older Dutch decisions have no text at Rechtspraak, and the council's own site shows them behind a Cloudflare challenge. About 900 UK House of Lords Appellate Committee judgments of 1996 to 2009 sit on archived parliament.uk pages the server cannot reach, and earlier ones are not online at an official site.

Switzerland's Bundesgericht is still loading, with 1,218 of about 20,904 and 131,167 of about 179,723 documents held so far. Luxembourg's Cour de cassation older judgments are only behind the search of justice.public.lu, which asks for a proof-of-work challenge. European Court of Human Rights texts of the amending Protocols are on the Treaty Office site, which answers the server with a Cloudflare block. The institution register is dated 17 November 2026, and the next countries listed are Spain, Italy, Ireland, Belgium, Poland, Czechia, Estonia and Finland. Explainx.ai notes the pitch emphasizes legislation and top courts, not every lower tribunal or administrative register.

Explainx.ai says the EU's AI Act enforcement timeline pushed deployers toward documented testing and monitoring, and that Claude's legal artifact templates assume connectors can fetch primary material. It describes the official MCP documentation as an open-source standard for connecting AI applications to external systems. It cites Stripe's Agent Wallet growth and Meta Muse transaction rails as signs that agents already spend and advise. It says national portals such as Légifrance and EUR-Lex already publish authoritative text, but each has different search semantics, HTML wrappers and session rules. It says Pandex's bet is that builders will pay integration time once for a normalized API with citation edges and version history.

Explainx.ai suggests builders run a version test on a directive with a known amendment, a cross-language test asking in English for a German Bundesgerichtshof holding, and a negative test asking for a fabricated article number. It advises scheduling long-running agent jobs outside any maintenance window, or retrying on 5xx responses during ingest if none is documented. It says the page does not list every crawler path, and that completeness claims should be treated as product statements until a jurisdiction is audited. It says connecting Pandex does not stop a model from mis-summarizing a correct passage, so retrieval should be paired with structured output checks. It leaves open whether Pandex documents a maintenance window and how its coverage claims hold up under audit.

stories.Headline: Harvard Berkman Klein Center seeks a director to lead its AI and youth safety research
stories.Summary:
Harvard University’s Berkman Klein Center for Internet & Society posted a hiring notice on Nov 20, 2026 for a Director of Research, also called Project Director, AI and Youth Safety. The center is an interfaculty research center at Harvard. The posting says the center seeks someone to lead its AI and Youth Safety initiative. The role involves defining unanswered questions about young people’s relationships with AI and developing a research agenda. The director will also convene leading thinkers across disciplines and translate research into evidence for public understanding and policy.

The basic qualifications are a bachelor’s degree and 8 years of progressive experience, or a related advanced degree with 5 years experience. The appointment is a term position currently expected to extend to June 30, 2027, with potential for renewal subject to departmental funding and need. Harvard says it is unable to provide visa sponsorship for the position. The position is salary grade level 059, and all offers are made by HLS Human Resources. The work format allows some duties at a non-Harvard location, and hybrid employees must work in a Harvard registered state when not at a Harvard or Harvard-designated location.

The posting says the director will lead day-to-day direction of the initiative, shape research design, conduct original research and writing, and ensure outputs meet standards for quality, rigor, ethics, and real-world relevance. The director will provide technical and methodological leadership, review research plans, instruments, analyses, and drafts, and select and justify quantitative, qualitative, or mixed methods. The role includes managing and mentoring research teams, hiring and supervising staff such as research coordinators, research associates, employee fellows, research assistants, and interns. The director will help shape the emerging field by identifying high-impact and underexplored questions and adapting the research agenda as new evidence and technologies emerge. The director will build an interdisciplinary community across Harvard and beyond, including researchers, youth-serving organizations, policymakers, technologists, educators, civil society organizations, and industry partners.

The posting says the director will design convenings, workshops, and ongoing collaborations, and support grant development and funder engagement, including proposal narratives, methods and measurement sections, project plans, and reporting deliverables. The director will oversee research program operations and communications with Center teams, manage timelines and outputs such as publications, tools, events, and reporting, and support public-facing outputs consistent with the Center’s Open Access Policy. The director will represent the Center’s AI and youth safety work at convenings and events such as working groups, symposia, and briefings. Qualifications include deep familiarity with AI and online safety issues such as generative AI and AI companions, youth online safety and development, platform governance, privacy and data protection, content moderation, age-appropriate design, human-computer interaction, evaluation and measurement, and the policy landscape shaping AI systems. The posting also lists a demonstrated record of AI or machine learning research, such as publications at peer-reviewed venues, open-source contributions, or equivalent technical work, and strong writing, presentation, and collaboration skills.

The posting says the center is committed to making sense of the digital environment and ensuring it promotes human agency, dignity, and genuine connection. It describes the opportunity as rare and unusual and the community as flourishing and intellectually robust, with faculty, staff, students, fellows, and affiliates from multiple disciplines and backgrounds. It says a successful candidate will be open to learning from experiments, taking good ideas from wherever they come, and changing course quickly. It says Harvard offers a comprehensive benefits package including paid time off, parental leave, medical, dental, and vision coverage starting on day one, retirement plans with university contributions, wellbeing and mental health resources, family and caregiver support, professional development including tuition assistance and reimbursement, and commuter benefits, discounts, and campus perks. It says Harvard is committed to equal opportunity and non-discrimination and seeks talent from all parts of society and the world.

The posting says the work schedule and location will be set by the department at its discretion based on operational needs, and certain visa types and funding sources may limit work location. It says individuals must meet work location sponsorship requirements prior to employment. It says additional details will be discussed during the interview process. It says the site and its contents are licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 Unported license unless otherwise noted. It says the page was last updated Nov 20, 2026.

stories.Headline: Mikhail Lukin leads a $12 million Harvard project to link quantum computing with AI
stories.Summary:
A $12 million federal grant will fund a Harvard-led collaboration aiming to link quantum computing with artificial intelligence. The project is called Application-Aware Error Correction Codesign for Scientific Quantum Computing, or ASQC. It is part of the Department of Energy's Genesis Mission. Mikhail Lukin, Harvard's Joshua and Beth Friedman University Professor and co-founder of QuEra Computing, will lead the effort. The collaboration unites researchers from MIT, Cornell University and three national labs alongside tech partners NVIDIA and Anthropic.

The project is one of 12 Phase II awards announced Oct. 9 under the Genesis Mission. The grant is administered by the Advanced Scientific Computing Research division of the Department of Energy. Lukin is the project's principal investigator and co-director of the Harvard Quantum Initiative. He will work with Harvard physicists Markus Greiner and Susanne Yelin and researchers at MIT, Cornell University, Los Alamos National Laboratory, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Sandia National Laboratories, QuEra Computing, NVIDIA and Anthropic. The team will train AI models to learn which errors matter for problems in quantum simulation, materials science, chemistry and nuclear science, use AI to design codes and decoders tailored to them, and test the results on hardware at Harvard, MIT and QuEra.

University President Alan M. Garber said Mikhail is a visionary leader who will do an excellent job driving progress and strengthening partnerships to ensure America's competitiveness in this area of vital importance. Lukin said this kind of collaborative approach is really needed in this case, and that the team wants to make something no one else has been able to make. He said the team will take all help. He said this is really an attempt to establish scientific foundations for useful fault-tolerant quantum computers and to really accelerate this progress using AI. He said that as we build larger and better quantum computers, we will really start making more and more scientific discoveries.

Garber said some of the most thrilling questions in science have long seemed out of reach, but the barriers to discovery are falling rapidly as quantum computing and artificial intelligence expand the realm of the possible. Lukin said you can really explore corners of the universe where you have never been, like a new kind of telescope. The team stated that we can really see these dreams the community has had for the last 40 years, for the first time, in the direct line of sight. Co-investigators on the program include Vladan Vuletić, Soonwon Choi and Hengyun "Harry" Zhou of MIT, Eun-Ah Kim of Cornell, Andrew Sornborger, Lukasz Cincio and Michael McKerns of Los Alamos, Wibe de Jong and Costin Iancu of Lawrence Berkeley, Andrew Landahl, Riley Chien and Kevin Thompson of Sandia, Nathan Gemelke and Michael Gullans of QuEra, Krysta Svore of NVIDIA and Alek Kemeny of Anthropic. The project will build on research Lukin and his collaborators published last year, which addressed a key challenge in quantum computing related to environmental noise and the inherently unstable quantum bits, or qubits, that make up quantum computers.

Through quantum error correction, the group suppressed errors to the point that adding qubits would reduce errors rather than add them, paving the way for larger, more complex calculations. Recent advances in quantum error correction have enabled the suppression of errors to the point where adding qubits now reduces, rather than increases, computational errors, a critical step toward building larger, more complex quantum computers. In an April preprint, Lukin, Yelin and colleagues described a neural-network decoder, software that identifies errors during computation, that cut error rates up to 17 times below existing versions and ran thousands of times faster. In another recent work, in collaboration with QuEra and Anthropic, the team used large language models to discover state-of-the-art quantum circuits for tasks spanning numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation and number theory. The Department of Energy grant specifically encourages partnerships between universities and national laboratories, an approach Lukin explained is unusual in quantum computing research, where institutions often operate more independently, and is essential to achieving goals previously considered unattainable.

The ASQC project will develop an AI-driven, fault-tolerant QEC system that can adapt to scientific problems relevant to the Energy Department. The Genesis Mission aims to integrate the world's best supercomputers, experimental facilities and AI systems to advance American research and innovation. Lukin and Greiner are co-founders of QuEra Computing, where Lukin is a chief scientist. Lukin views the resulting quantum computer not merely as a faster calculator, but as a novel scientific instrument capable of exploring previously inaccessible realms of knowledge. The articles do not say when the hardware tests will begin or how the $12 million will be divided among the partners.

The project is called Application-Aware Error Correction Codesign for Scientific Quantum Computing, or ASQC, and Cornell is one of several institutions taking part in the work. The award is one of 12 Phase II awards announced on October 9 under the Genesis Mission, according to the articles. stories.Headline: New Zealand cyber centre says hackers use AI tool Artex to automate attacks
stories.Summary:
New Zealand's National Cyber Security Centre warned on 21 November 2026 that hackers are using artificial intelligence to carry out cyber attacks, and it said organisations across the country must act. Its cyber defence operations director, Dr Emma Bickerstaffe, said there had been a rise over the past week in attackers using an open source AI tool called Artex to target organisations worldwide. Artex was developed by researchers to check for system vulnerabilities that hackers could exploit, and although it had been taken down from the internet, it had been replicated and was now being used to automate attacks on different organisations at the same time. Bickerstaffe said the key change was that phases of an attack could now be automated, which let threat actors act faster.

She said an attack that might previously have taken weeks could now go from initial reconnaissance and scanning of an organisation to exploitation in a matter of hours. Bickerstaffe said access to open source AI tools meant attackers could act opportunistically and were looking for any target they could gain access to. She said that if attackers got in using AI, they could move across a system, reach what she called an organisation's crown jewels, and access or change data. She said there had been instances in New Zealand where attackers used the tool to try to get into an organisation and failed, and other incidents where they successfully gained access and viewed data.

She advised organisations to limit the devices and systems they connect to the internet and to implement multi-factor authentication, which she said could stop an attack if a system was compromised. Her comments came after Forest & Bird and the New Zealand Defence Force both reported cyber security incidents on Friday, though the tools used by those hackers are not yet known. Forest & Bird confirmed supporters' details had been exposed, and chief executive Sam Rowland told RNZ it had taken immediate steps to secure its systems, including a forensic search of its website that uncovered malicious files. Rowland said the organisation was working with technology and cyber security experts to establish the full extent of the incident, was contacting people it knew were affected to explain what information had been accessed, and had notified NZ Police, the National Cyber Security Centre and the Office of the Privacy Commissioner.

Those affected were warned the stolen data could be used to create scam emails, phone calls or convincing text messages, and were told to be cautious about unexpected messages even if they contained personalised information. The New Zealand Defence Force took some of its websites down following a breach, after its website provider informed it of unauthorised access to its website systems. An NZDF spokesperson told RNZ that preliminary inquiries indicated a database associated with the Force4Families Defence Discounts scheme had been accessed, and that the database included names and email addresses of registered users. The NZDF said those who may have been affected had been contacted, and it advised individuals registered through the website to remain alert to phishing emails, scams and unsolicited requests for personal information.

stories.Headline: Schools and universities update curricula and policies to prepare students for an AI-driven workforce
stories.Summary:
Universities and schools are updating their curricula and policies to prepare students for a workforce reshaped by artificial intelligence. This shift follows reports that AI tools now perform many tasks previously handled by new hires in various companies. Professor Maurice Tse Kwok-sang wrote about these changes on November 20, 2026, for the HKU Business School. Meanwhile, community members gathered on November 15 at Woodstock Day School in Saugerties for an AI reality check. These educational adjustments aim to help students adapt as automation eliminates traditional entry level roles across the global economy.

Hong Kong's eight publicly funded universities will launch about 30 new programmes in AI, cybersecurity, and creative industries for 2025-28. The Education Bureau's 2026-27 undergraduate list includes intelligent information systems and AI business applications, while business curricula now integrate Python. In New York, Saugerties adopted a policy on January 14, 2025, and Onteora adopted one on August 18. Hunter-Tannersville aims to complete its policy by the end of the 2026-27 school year, and Kingston defines AI as plagiarism. Governor Kathy Hochul recently broke ground on Empire AI's permanent home at the University at Buffalo for shared use.

Bill Winters, chief executive of Standard Chartered Group, said the bank is replacing lower value human capital with investment capital. He announced plans to cut over 15 per cent of back office roles by 2030, affecting 7,800 global employees. Daniela Amodei, co-founder of Anthropic, believes companies will emphasize human communication, empathy, and collaboration more than before. She stated that these shifts will increase the importance of the humanities rather than diminish their value in education. Ashley Hughes, head of Woodstock Day School, said the school wants to hear from students about how they use AI.

Former Singaporean president Halimah Yacob described the phrasing used by Bill Winters as disturbing and cold regarding the bank's redundancies. Students like 17 year old Will Fox worry that degrees could become arbitrary or useless if AI replaces their future careers. Luca Kaufman, 16, noted that many students had ChatGPT open during a summer program at Columbia University. The World Economic Forum reports that 40 per cent of employers expect to reduce headcount in automatable areas by 2030. Regulators in Hong Kong and Singapore asked Standard Chartered to explain its redundancy arrangements after the bank's announcement.

The College Board reported that 84 per cent of surveyed high school students used generative AI for schoolwork in May 2025. An October 13 analysis by New York Focus found over half of New York's 678 school districts lacked formal policies. The New York State School Boards Association adopted a resolution on October 15 calling for safety and privacy legislation. Standard Chartered's strategy involves replacing human roles with capital, though some affected employees will receive chances to retrain. These developments occur as AI, robotics, and automation simultaneously create and eliminate jobs according to the World Economic Forum.

Schools will now emphasize oral presentations, staged assignments, and real world tasks to assess students without the use of AI. Woodstock Day School is looking to create a formal AI policy that incorporates direct input from its own students. The New York State School Boards Association is lobbying for notice when updates add AI features and school opt out options. Articles leave open how the meaning of work will be decided and which specific skills will be amplified. It remains uncertain if education can successfully reflect human capacities that are difficult for machines to replace in the future.

stories.Headline: IBM Philippines' Lope Doromal urges businesses to pair AI governance with orchestration for autonomous agents
stories.Summary:
Philippine businesses need to build real-time controls into their artificial intelligence systems as they move from individual AI applications to autonomous agents operating across enterprise workflows, an IBM Philippines executive said in an exclusive online interview with The Manila Times. Lope Doromal, technical community leader at IBM Philippines, said governance policies alone cannot ensure that AI systems operate within approved boundaries. Organizations must combine governance with orchestration to monitor AI agents, manage their access to data and applications, and intervene when their actions deviate from established rules. Doromal said that without orchestration, control remains separate from execution, leaving organizations to rely on teams to interpret and implement policies correctly. He said an enterprise can be fully compliant and still fully fragmented, adding that when AI systems cannot be coordinated under pressure, scale stops being an advantage and becomes a risk.

An IBM Institute for Business Value study cited by Doromal found that only 18 percent of surveyed organizations maintain a complete and current inventory of their AI assets. Just 27 percent know where AI is being used within their organizations. Doromal recommended establishing an agent registry, a continuously updated record identifying every AI agent deployed across an organization, including its purpose, owner, data access permissions, model version and operational status. He cited IBM Concert Observe, powered by IBM Instana Observability, as an example of technology that can discover AI components and map their interactions across applications. An IBV study on AI governance and business value found that 71 percent of organizations with high AI governance maturity had developed specific guidelines identifying acceptable and unacceptable uses of AI.

Doromal said every agent should also have a formal identity and access management framework defining its owner, authorized activities and access to enterprise systems. He said that access should be set to the minimum level needed to do the job, with the ability to revoke it instantly if behavior falls outside expected boundaries. He said a single misconfiguration can become an organization-wide liability when agents operate across multiple systems and no responsible team has been designated to handle incidents. He said the governance architecture must be built before anything goes wrong, not after. He said accountability in AI governance is distributed across leadership rather than concentrated in a single function.

The same IBV study found that 63 percent of surveyed organizations reported CEO involvement in ensuring effective AI governance, while approximately one in three had a CEO directly accountable for it. An IBV study cited by Doromal found that only 9 percent of surveyed global executives fully understood their dependencies across AI vendors, models and infrastructure. Organizations reported an average of six AI-related disruptions over the preceding two years, with vendor services identified as the leading cause. The study also found that 81 percent of executives expected a major AI vendor outage to significantly disrupt operations, while 71 percent said switching their primary AI vendor or model would be difficult. Doromal cited IBM watsonx Orchestrate as an open, hybrid enterprise agent management platform designed to manage agents regardless of where they were developed or which technology they use.

IBM Sovereign Core is intended for organizations seeking greater operational control through a customer-operated control plane built on open standards. Doromal said poor data management is the single most commonly cited barrier to effective AI governance, and that every AI model and agent sits downstream from the data it uses. He recommended testing governance processes through one high-impact use case before extending them across the organization. He said governance should be embedded in the workflow, not the calendar, adding that policy update cycles should be measured in days rather than quarters. The IBM IBV 2026 CEO Study found that 80 percent of Philippine CEOs surveyed said they were comfortable making major strategic decisions using AI-generated insights.

However, only 63 percent of Philippine executives surveyed said they had a clear vision of how AI would deliver a competitive advantage for their organizations. The study also found that 73 percent admitted the risk of falling behind was driving them to invest in technologies before fully understanding the value those technologies would bring. Doromal said the gap between investment and preparation makes governance a business concern, not merely a technical or regulatory requirement. He advised local organizations to work with technology partners that support skills transfer and strengthen internal capabilities, rather than leaving businesses dependent on external providers. He said governance maturity is not built in a single initiative, but is forged in the daily decisions that mitigate risks and accelerate value.

Organised by Eco-Business in partnership with the United Nations Development Programme, the inaugural Unlocking AI for Sustainability forum convened over 100 senior delegates to explore how AI can support sustainable development while managing its risks. AI technologies could add up to US$15 trillion to global GDP by 2030 by optimising trade, power grids and operational efficiency, including an estimated US$1 trillion for Asean economies, if properly deployed and governed, said UNDP. Edward Vrkić, Resident Representative for UNDP Malaysia, Singapore and Brunei Darussalam, said AI governance needs to account for stakeholders who lack the economic clout or infrastructure to manage and respond to the technology's risks. He said there is disparity between countries, but as concerningly, within countries, and that these are not just geographic but also demographic. He said this demands more inclusive design that ensures no one is left behind, highlighting how women are twice as exposed to job losses brought on by AI automation.

Jessica Cheam, Founder and CEO of Eco-Business, said Asean has a rare chance to rewrite the rules of its digital economy by putting people at the centre. She said the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement, signed on 14 November and the first region-wide pact of its kind, is a step in the right direction by setting common rules for digital trade while helping the region's digital economy to grow to US$2 trillion by 2030. She said AI, digital rules and energy security are now on the same regional agenda, and that with Singapore taking over as Asean chair, this gives a real opportunity and a real responsibility to turn diverse AI provisions into practice across all 11 member states. Benoît Sauveroche, First Counsellor for Digital Transformation, Research and Innovation at the European Union Delegation to Singapore, said AI partnerships should look beyond investing in technological systems alone and into people and institutional and regional capacity as well. He said the most valuable innovation is innovation that people can trust, and that AI must be anchored in trusted infrastructure, sound governance, quality data, strong skills and a clear commitment to fundamental rights.

Sauveroche said the European AI Office, responsible for developing and enforcing AI guardrails, is developing the AI for Public Good initiative to leverage AI models. Leaders warned that the data centres and computing infrastructure needed to power AI place mounting pressure on electricity grids, land and water systems. Without deliberate policy choices, investment and capacity-building, AI could deepen existing technological and digital divides across and within countries. Vrkić also emphasised AI-driven gains in areas such as town planning, urban management and delivering greater efficiencies in basic services when well governed. The forum convened key decision makers to deliberate issues ranging from technological deployment, infrastructure investment, governance, energy and climate strategies.

stories.Headline: SpaceX subsidiary Cursor considers phasing out Chinese AI models to reduce geopolitical risk
stories.Summary:
Cursor, an artificial intelligence coding platform owned by SpaceX, is considering the removal of Chinese developed models from its systems. This decision follows a months long investigation conducted by the House Select Committee on China and the House Committee on Homeland Security. The company had previously built its Composer 2 model using Kimi K2.5 from the Chinese laboratory Moonshot AI. SpaceX completed its acquisition of Cursor in August after first announcing a formal agreement to buy the firm in June.

The transition would involve phasing out open weight models from the People's Republic of China to reduce geopolitical risk. This shift occurs after SpaceX acquired Cursor at an implied equity value of 60 billion dollars. The House report suggests that American firms adopted these models because of their low cost, customization options, and near frontier performance. Lawmakers are now recommending a national American open weight initiative to provide competitive alternatives for the market.

The House committees stated that Beijing intends to use these technological gains to create long term global dependence. They also suggested expanding an October order that banned DeepSeek from federal civilian agency systems to include all Chinese models in federal contracts. While Cursor, SpaceX, and DoorDash did not respond to requests for comment, Airbnb declined to speak on the matter. The report emphasizes that the United States currently lacks an open weight alternative that meets market demands for price and performance.

The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security announced an interim final rule on Monday to stop Chinese companies from accessing AI chips remotely. Washington is specifically concerned about the use of overseas data centers and the process of distillation to train new models. These measures aim to protect the American tech stack as the battle for AI supremacy between the two nations intensifies in 2026. The government continues to monitor how Chinese models are integrated into the infrastructure of private American companies.
