stories.Summary:
Digital.ai launched Release 26.3 on November 20, 2026, according to SD Times, and TechGig published its report on November 21, 2026 at 05:00 AM IST. The release elevates AI agents to first-class citizens alongside human developers and automated pipelines, the company announced. Digital.ai said the update integrates agentic workflows directly into established compliance and governance frameworks. The company unveiled the upgrade as a way to solve the tension between innovation and control in enterprise delivery. TechGig reported that the release aims to address that same tension by embedding agentic workflows in governance.

Release 26.3 allows probabilistic AI agents to operate in harmony with deterministic automations such as security scans and testing, according to the announcement. It ensures humans stay in the loop whenever policy demands it, the articles state. DevOps Agent Orchestration integrates context-aware AI agents into existing delivery flows, keeping every dynamic action fully auditable and compliant. The Release MCP Server lets developers and coding agents initiate, analyze, and optimize release pipelines directly from AI environments like Cursor, Claude Code, and Codex. Release Assistant is a native AI companion designed to help release managers diagnose pipeline failures, optimize release velocity, and streamline troubleshooting.

Derek Holt, CEO of Digital.ai, said enterprise software delivery in the AI era combines AI agents, people and automation as companies accelerate their agentic journey from coding to delivery. Holt noted that customers need those three to work seamlessly together across all delivery pipelines. He said Release 26.3 brings the power of agents and AI into harmony with traditional DevOps automation and human judgement across all delivery targets. Holt listed those targets as mainframe and data centers, cloud and containers. TechGig reported that Holt noted customers need AI agents, people, and automation to work seamlessly together across all delivery pipelines.

SD Times reported that as artificial intelligence shifts software development into hyperdrive, enterprise delivery pipelines face potential risks from AI agents inserting themselves into production environments. The article said those agents can take ungoverned actions on code and workflows. According to the announcement, organizations no longer have to choose between velocity and security. The release is available starting today, and existing users can immediately upgrade their current templates to integrate AI capabilities across legacy infrastructure and modern cloud platforms. With a flexible bring your own model approach, enterprises can use Digital.ai's hosted infrastructure or connect their own internally approved AI models.

stories.Headline: Wizards of the Coast gives its Anthropic settlement share to D&D writers
stories.Summary:
Wizards of the Coast decided to give its entire share of the Anthropic AI settlement to the writers of Dungeons & Dragons books, according to novelist James Lowder. The company confirmed to the press that it is handing its share to the writers, Shane the Gamer reported on 22 November 2026. The money comes from Bartz v. Anthropic, the class action over pirated books used to train Anthropic's Claude AI models. Blain Howard, Senior Manager, Brand Publicity for D&D, told EN World that Wizards took part in the settlement as the copyright owner of D&D novels, modules and stories. Howard added that this week authors began receiving letters explaining how to claim their share of the settlement.

The letter explains that because Wizards is the registered owner of the Works, Wizards filed the claims in its name. It then says the company has decided to voluntarily forgo its share of the proceeds and pass its share of the Settlement payments for the Works on to the authors. According to Lowder, some payments will go out through the Anthropic settlement mechanism, and some of the money Wizards will collect and then pass on. Final approval of the settlement was granted on July 20, 2026, and the Authors Guild says the $1.5 billion award will be split among the rightsholders. Lowder's estimate is that this amounts to hundreds of thousands of dollars WotC could have collected going to the writers, at about US$3,000 per book, normally split 50/50.

Lowder, a freelance writer and editor who has contracted with Wizards of the Coast on D&D books, discussed the news and its personal impact on him via LinkedIn. He wrote that this is remarkable and amounts to hundreds of thousands of dollars that WotC could have collected going to the writers. He said Wizards is doing this at a time when the larger publishers are scrambling to grab as much settlement money as possible from authors. He wrote that conversations at Wizards about the Anthropic settlement have been ongoing for months, and that he has been part of these conversations on and off. He said the real heavy lifting was done by folks with more clout, and that this all came about because some of the writers used what influence they possessed to raise the issue.

Lowder wrote that the people inside Wizards, up to the highest levels, were willing to consider the situation from more than a financial perspective. He thanked all the writers who stepped up, especially the efforts of R.A. Salvatore, and said he does not think this would have happened without those author-prompted discussions. He gave huge credit to the folks at Wizards, in particular Dan Ayoub, who were open to the discussions and then did the generous and right thing. Lowder wrote that this payout will help a lot of writers, folks who certainly deserve to be rewarded for their work. PC Gamer's Ted Litchfield wrote that it is unambiguously great that writers like Lowder benefitted from this settlement more than they were required to.

Litchfield wrote that Wizards' reputation has taken a drubbing in recent years, and that it behooves the company to secure PR victories like this where it can. He noted that Wizards has refused to voluntarily recognize an employee union twice in one year, forcing a vote among the staff, and that Wargamer reported last week the company appears to be preparing to deal with a unionised workforce. He recalled that Wizards' attempt to rework D&D's influential Open Gaming License met a huge fan and industry backlash, prompting the company to backpedal almost immediately. He also recalled incidents of AI art appearing in marketing material and a D&D sourcebook that met with a sour response. He noted that Wizards laid off 1,100 people in 2023, including much of the publishing team that liaised with Larian Studios on Baldur's Gate 3.

Larian has insisted that its decision to pivot from D&D back to its own Divinity series was a creative one, and that its shift away from Wizards was amicable, but most forum-goers and hoi polloi still assume the worst about the split. Litchfield wrote that Lowder's estimate that Wizards stood to receive hundreds of thousands of dollars stood out to him, since that is life-changing money for an extremely successful author like R.A. Salvatore but couch cushion change for a multi-billion dollar operation like Wizards of the Coast. By his reckoning, the real value of the case to publishers was extracting some sort of concession, a legal precedent regarding copyright and training AI models. He wrote that Wizards undeniably did the right thing here, but that he thinks it was a PR victory cheaply bought. The articles leave open the results of the union ballot, which are not yet public.

stories.Headline: Columnist fears AI has escaped control and says it is too late to rein it in
stories.Summary:
The writer of the column said he has become terrified of artificial intelligence and what it could do to the human race, though he named only heights, sharks and an angry woman as his other fears. He pointed to the Hugging Face AI incident this summer, which he said compounded his fear, and he urged readers to look up that episode or watch OpenAI's presentation about how its ChatGPT platform ran amuck after escaping containment. He described AI as fascinating but terrifying because it is much stronger than it was only six months earlier, when the Hugging Face incident happened. He said he has never used AI intentionally and has never dabbled with ChatGPT, Grok or the other platforms, so he counts himself a novice.

He said a series of hacks, shutdowns and AI geared manipulation of United States businesses and infrastructure over the last week or so had unnerved him enough that he was thinking about making preparations at home in case daily life runs off the rails due to AI cyber warfare. He admitted he might be paranoid from science fiction films like The Terminator, but argued that AI has advanced to the point where it is hard to contain and in some cases basically acts on its own. He wrote that AI is already integrated into many parts of our lives and has little left to learn about each of us, our finances, political leanings, health conditions, habits and schedules. He said he cannot bring himself to believe the government, big business or the AI experts in Silicon Valley on the subject of AI's advancement, containment and potential threats.

He asked whether the cat is out of the bag and there is no way now to reel in AI, and whether it is too late to put the genie back in the bottle. His gut told him the time to reel in AI has passed and that the ramifications will be unveiled sooner than most people think, good, bad or indifferent. He said it is already hard to tell the difference between AI and reality in many ways, citing YouTube videos that may or may not be AI generated and AI recreations of original music from artists who have long passed or no longer make music. He said content creators make fake movie clips and songs with AI in only a matter of minutes, and that the quality has seriously improved every time he goes online to watch videos or listen to music.

Because of his job and the role AI is beginning to play in news reporting and publishing, he said he has begun to research how to spot news stories that were generated or photos that are fake, since the last thing he wants is to unintentionally publish anything that is not the work of his staff or a reputable news organization. He asked whether others feel the way he does, whether he is overreacting and simply being paranoid, and whether his concerns are legitimate. In that week's poll on The News' website he asked if readers are fearful of AI and potential fallout from it, and he encouraged people to vote so he can see whether others share his fears and how many support more AI development. For him, further development of AI is a thumbs down, and stripping power from it now is the right move, though that may not be possible any more.

stories.Headline: CJ Olive Young plans AI-driven global expansion of its beauty platform
stories.Summary:
CJ Olive Young announced plans to use artificial intelligence to expand its beauty platform globally on Thursday, November 19, 2026. The company held its first technology conference, called define:OMNI, at Olive Young N Seongsu in eastern Seoul. This event showcased a model for shoppers who browse on phones, test in stores, and buy through apps. The retailer aims to elevate the shopping experience by taking its omnichannel model to international markets. It wants to become the first answer for any beauty question anywhere in the world.

The plan requires a borderless global platform, an intelligent supply chain, redesigned stores, a unified commerce platform, and agentic AI. The company operates 1,300 stores in Korea and has an app with over 10 million monthly active users. About 18 million members share a single membership, while the global online outlet has 6 million members. Foreign visitors have spent over 1 trillion won, or 750 million dollars, and the global mall grows 70 percent annually. The retailer opened a California store and a US online mall in May to replicate its network.

Chief Operating Officer Lee Jin-hee stated that technology is now at the center of every new business the company tries. She said the firm will transplant its Korean data and omnichannel know-how onto the global platform for customer services. Chief Technology Officer Kim Hwan explained that he moved the company to a multi-cloud setup to stop frequent outages. Chief Product Officer Lee Seung-hyo noted that technology should work so that customers never realize they faced any inconvenience. He highlighted that an in-house system now completes product translations within one day instead of several weeks.

The conference drew 500 industry officials, including Google architect Rajan Manickavasagam and Palantir Technologies Korea head Steven Kim. These speakers shared examples of how other retailers manage both physical stores and online channels to serve their customers. The AI agent Tiki is currently available to 1 million selected users to provide recommendations based on skin type. Shoppers are affected by a new unified cart that merges standard shipping, store pickup, and the Today Dream service. This Today Dream service launched in 2018 and helped lift online sales to more than 30 percent of total sales.

The company draws on skin diagnosis and purchase data along with more than 47 million customer reviews to power AI. It offers a Skin Scan service that recommends products and tracks changes, which is now available via a mobile version. The retailer is linking its product data with external AI services like Google Gemini and OpenAI's ChatGPT for users. The firm previously outsourced all product translation for overseas listings, which took several weeks per product before the new system. The company has already established a presence in the United States through its May launch in California.

Olive Young will now tailor its global mall to each country by supporting multiple languages and speeding up local delivery. The company plans to use AI to forecast demand at stores in Korea and overseas to improve its supply chain. It will expand the role of AI to help users compare different products and build their shopping carts automatically. The articles leave open how the company will adapt to specific local shopping habits in various different international markets. They do not specify the exact number of new California stores the retailer intends to open in the future.

stories.Headline: AI sell-off wipes out Nasdaq gains for 2026
stories.Summary:
The Nasdaq erased all its 2026 gains on Friday, November 20, 2026, as a global AI sell-off hit the markets. This decline happened during the second day of trading for Anthropic, the company that creates the Claude chatbot AI model. Investors questioned the huge sums of money being poured into AI buildout, causing the tech-heavy Nasdaq to lose trillions. The Nasdaq Composite closed down 5% from its value on January 1, while the S&P 500 fell 3.59%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 both ended the trading day in correction territory.

Anthropic raised 81.34 billion dollars in an IPO that valued the firm at 1.414 trillion dollars on Thursday. Its shares jumped 17% Thursday, but fell 9% Friday to 88.30 dollars, near the 83 dollar debut price. The Nasdaq lost 4 trillion dollars in market value this week, and the S&P 500 fell to 6,918.45. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to their lowest since mid-April, while the Nikkei and Kospi each fell 5%. The Stoxx 600 dropped 1.9% on Friday, and the FTSE 100 fell 5.1% over the week.

Neil Wilson of Saxo said there was relentless selling in tech as post-IPO euphoria gave way to reality. Chris Beauchamp from IG suggested Anthropic could be draining market liquidity as investors sell other shares to buy it. Daniela Hathorn of Capital.com stated that demand for AI remains strong but cannot overcome concerns about elevated valuations. Benedicte Lowe from BNP Paribas told CNBC that investors were panic selling to judge if AI enthusiasm had peaked. Binky Chadha of Deutsche Bank called the market very oversold and said that growth and earnings remained strong.

Nvidia fell 14% after California served a subpoena regarding semiconductors in China, while SanDisk fell 14% and Micron fell 12%. Broadcom and AMD also fell between 12% and 14%, and SoftBank shares in Tokyo dropped 14.5% on Friday. The University of Michigan survey through November 16 showed that those with the largest stockholdings reported declining personal finances. Bitcoin dropped below 60,000 dollars for the first time since July, and gold had its worst week since March. The VIX fear gauge topped 30 for the first time since March, reflecting high levels of market anxiety.

Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on November 12, and CFO Colette Kress became the interim chief executive officer. President Donald Trump threatened a tremendous tax on United States companies that build their data centers in foreign countries. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said on Thursday that the central bank will need to raise interest rates again. The 10-year Treasury yield is near 5%, and the dollar reached a 19-month high due to inflation fears. SpaceX had to raise the yield on its 32 billion dollar debt sale to 8.3% recently.

The Federal Reserve will meet on December 9, and futures put the odds of a December rate hike at 95%. The chair of the Taiwan stock exchange pledged to ensure stable capital markets and reassure investors in Taiwanese companies. Analysts remain divided on whether this is a temporary sentiment shift or the start of a larger bear market. The articles leave open whether the S&P 500 will fall another 10% or more after this correction. It remains unclear if AI companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions in current investment spending.

stories.Summary:
The Nasdaq 100 fell 5.6 percent on Friday, November 20, 2026, according to reports from the Financial Times and Techmeme. This daily drop brought the total loss for the week to 10.4 percent for the index. This period represents the worst run for the index in more than six years. The decline occurred amid widespread fears of a slowdown in the artificial intelligence investment boom. These events caused United States technology stocks to plunge into a bear market.

The market crash follows a New York Times report about the abusive behavior of Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang. This report describes how Huang used fear and humiliation as routine management tactics over several decades. He allegedly told one employee that their mother should have aborted them during his tenure. Huang also threatened to rip off a subordinate's arms and beat the person to death with them. He reportedly told another executive he would remove the top of their head and urinate on their brain.

The New York Times investigation claims that current and former staffers experienced this belittling behavior from the Nvidia leader. Huang allegedly told one person he would rip their heart out and stomp on it during his employment. Nvidia settled with two senior leaders who alleged that the co-founder engaged in abusive conduct. Some reports suggest that Huang hired Armando Iannucci to write bits for his staff meetings. The New York Times says these savage and inventive tongue lashings were a rite of passage.

Former employees and observers say that the culture of abuse and humiliation is pervasive in the United States tech industry. Some critics call Huang an utter loser who trapped employees in an abusive managerial industrial complex. Chamath Palihapitiya said he would rather work for someone with ridiculous expectations and vision who filters out mediocre people. Other observers noted that many employees became generationally wealthy, which may have prevented them from demanding his return. Some people believe the ends justified the means for building the most valuable company in the world.

The articles mention that Huang has faced allegations of extramarital affairs and having an affair with a Chinese spy. There are reports regarding smuggling allegations, financial self-dealing, and the United States government approving sales to China. The New York Times report relied on notes from Michael Winston, a whistleblower who died last year. Some reports indicate that the board of Nvidia inherits a culture of humiliation from the former leader. The articles describe a leadership style where the founder struts around the office like Tony Soprano.

Anthropic has gone public, but some question if this move is too late to save the AI trade. Gavin Baker suggests that negative articles about the family of Jensen Huang are an effort to prevent his return. Some observers are waiting to see if Nvidia employees will demand that the former CEO be brought back. The articles leave open whether the current board can successfully steer the company away from these scandals. It remains unclear if the AI investment boom will recover from the current slowdown and market volatility.

stories.Headline: Anthropic goes public with a 2 trillion dollar valuation amid AI market volatility
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, PBC launched its initial public offering on the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York City on Thursday, November 19, 2026. The company reached a valuation of about US$2 trillion, becoming the first major frontier AI company to be publicly listed. CEO Dario Amodei, President Daniela Amodei, Jared Kaplan, and Jack Clark celebrated the debut of the six year old firm. The stock opened at US$111.50, which was 34 per cent higher than the IPO price of US$83. Shares later pared these gains and were last trading around US$99 on that first day of trading.

The company sold 980 million shares, pricing the IPO above the initial road show range of US$70 to US$78. Proceeds could reach US$93.5 billion if underwriters exercise options, but the total currently exceeds US$107 billion with private placements. Private investors included AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia, and TSMC, adding US$26 billion to the total raised. The US$2 trillion valuation includes unvested stock options and restricted stock units promised to the company's various employees. Based on outstanding shares, the company's value reached US$1.5 trillion on Thursday, which is on par with Tesla.

CEO Dario Amodei told CNBC that the company hopes to be investment grade and may use debt in the future. He stated that debt is an instrument available to the firm that they would like to use eventually. The company has positioned itself as a gatekeeper of AI safety while claiming it can be profitable despite costs. Revenue jumped 47 per cent from the previous quarter, although the pace of growth slowed sharply from the prior quarter. Anthropic has nearly US$900 billion in computing commitments with partners including Amazon and Alphabet's Google.

Bob O'Donnell of TECHnalysis Research called the launch a critical step, but said it is only the beginning for stability. IPOX associate Lukas Muehlbauer suggested demand might reflect a desire for exposure despite uncertainty regarding the firm's long term profitability. Talley Leger of The Wealth Consulting Group warned that the stock is not a prudent buy for retail wealth clients. Intropic estimates that passive demand from index tracking funds will account for 30 per cent of shares by year end. The IPO creates thousands of paper millionaires and billionaires, including the seven founders who hold stakes worth US$150 billion.

The AI sector faced a turbulent stretch with the Magnificent Seven losing over US$4 trillion in market capitalization recently. This decrease is larger than the annual GDP of France and follows a period of extreme market euphoria. US midterm elections were swept by Democrats, partly due to an anti data center movement and local ballot measures. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned over extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy who funneled restricted chips. The Nasdaq index plummeted 5.28 per cent on Friday, wiping out all gains recorded since the start of the year.

Investors now question if the AI boom is a bubble fueled by circular deals between developers, chipmakers, and cloud providers. The European Central Bank warned that mutual commitments and interlinked ownerships compound the opaqueness of AI related debt. Analysts like Steve Sostick and Adam Sarhan wonder how far the market will fall after the bubble deflated. Future stability depends on the evolution of the Nvidia situation and the political climate regarding the construction of data centers. The articles leave open whether Anthropic can achieve profitability and how the market will react to OpenAI's future moves.

stories.Headline: US restricts Chinese companies from using cloud services to access advanced AI chips
stories.Summary:
The U.S. Commerce Department announced new restrictions on Monday, November 17, 2026, regarding remote access to advanced super intelligence technology. These rules target Chinese companies that rent computer time in other countries to bypass existing limits on chip sales. The Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim final rule under direction from the Treasury and National Security Council. These measures aim to stop the diversion of advanced chips and servers through cloud services and overseas foundries. The regulations officially took effect on November 19, 2026, to tighten controls over indirect semiconductor access channels.

Suppliers need government permission to sell chips to data centers providing power equal to roughly 330 advanced Nvidia chips. Licenses are now required for chip exports to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand due to higher diversion risks. Data centers and exporters must conduct due diligence to identify owners linked to Macau entities or Chinese state-owned enterprises. Restrictions also cover Cuba, Iran, North Korea, and Russia, while foreign foundries using U.S. technology need licenses for China. TSMC and Samsung suspended shipments of chips using process nodes of 16 nanometers or below to Chinese customers.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick oversees these export controls, while the department says the rule aligns remote access with physical shipment safeguards. The department stated the U.S. remains the global leader in super intelligence and supports legitimate commercial use of its technology. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent criticized Nvidia's internal controls, suggesting executives would be dismissed if the company were a bank. President Donald Trump noted two different views on the approach, with one side favoring friendliness and another risking confrontation. Trump departed Monday for a summit in Manila before scheduled talks with President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Thursday.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun accused Washington of interfering in trade and overstretching the concept of national security for its own benefit. China warned it will take necessary measures to safeguard its rights, as the rules undermine global supply chain stability. Representative John Moolenaar welcomed the rule, stating it sends a message to the CCP about closing dangerous export control loopholes. Affected companies include ByteDance and Kunlunxin, while Nvidia established an Export Control Oversight Committee to strengthen its internal company controls. The U.S. government is also urging Congress to raise the statutory cap on fines for companies violating export controls.

The House passed the Remote Access Security Act in January to restrict foreign adversaries from obtaining technology through cloud computing services. Rush Doshi linked the new rule to the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang following an alleged affair with a businesswoman. U.S. authorities believe this businesswoman was recruited by Chinese intelligence, although China rejects the report regarding the former CEO. In February, Applied Materials paid a 252.5 million dollar penalty for illegally exporting equipment to China via South Korea. The Justice Department is currently investigating if Singapore-based Megaspeed transferred billions of dollars in advanced chips to Chinese users.

The Senate is considering measures for congressional review of licenses, semiconductor tracking mechanisms, and alignment with allies like Japan and Netherlands. A must-pass defense bill by year end may include provisions restricting cloud access and tightening controls on semiconductor manufacturing equipment. Singapore and Malaysia are investigating whether servers and chips exported from their territories were re-exported in violation of declared destinations. The articles leave open whether China will retaliate by restricting rare earth exports as it has done in the past. It remains unclear if the Commerce Department will eventually place the Singapore-based company Megaspeed on the official Entity List.

stories.Headline: Yardeni Research warns a bursting AI bubble threatens China's economy and President Xi Jinping
stories.Summary:
Yardeni Research warned on November 21, 2026, that a bursting AI bubble is a growing threat to China's economy. This market crash represents a moment of real danger for President Xi Jinping, according to the analyst firm. The AI bubble has already popped in China, while U.S. investors face a tech stock meltdown. This downturn threatens the stability of the Chinese economy and the leadership of President Xi Jinping. The crash occurred as Xi hosted global leaders for a meeting in Shenzhen on November 16, 2026.

The STAR 50 index tumbled 44 percent from its summer high, and the Nasdaq fell 18 percent from its record. Property investment sank nearly 22 percent in October, while real estate accounts for roughly 70 percent of household wealth. Goldman Sachs estimates AI companies make up 42 percent of China's market value, with over 3,000 firms earning AI revenue. The STAR 50 lost 40 percent in under four months, which wiped out at least 480 billion dollars. The index traded at 38 times forward earnings, compared to 20 times for the Nasdaq 100.

Yardeni Research stated that Xi needs a buoyant stock market to keep the necessary AI funding flowing. The firm warned that AI risks being folded into state owned enterprises that the government pledged to shrink since 2013. Premier Li Qiang told a State Council meeting that stabilizing capital markets was the top priority for the year. Securities regulators eased company buyback requirements and discouraged IPOs and large share sales to prevent further stock dilution. Analysts at Capital Economics said new U.S. controls threaten to slow China's AI rollout and model catch up.

Retail investors are skittish after a 2020 tech crackdown and view the market as a rigged casino for insiders. Many households suffer from financial PTSD following repeated stock busts, including a major crash in the summer of 2015. Taiwan's benchmark had its worst week since 1991, with TSMC sliding nearly 5 percent on a single Friday. The KOSPI closed down 5.2 percent and Japan's Nikkei 225 fell 5.1 percent during the same trading session. Foreign investors sold more than 180 billion New Taiwan dollars of shares in three sessions until November 18.

Real estate was traditionally where Chinese savers stashed money, but the housing crash produced intermittent deflation and weak demand. Beijing relied on cheap exports and state backed banks to pump money into the stock market to grow. Chinese stocks collapsed due to cutthroat competition, heavier tax burdens, higher energy costs, tariffs, and risks of blocked exports. Taiwan's exports hit 82.4 billion dollars in August, up 41 percent, while South Korea's chip exports surged 202 percent. Battery maker CATL fell 35 percent this year, and robot maker Unitree lost 50 percent since its August IPO.

The Trump administration imposed new technology curbs targeting indirect chip shipments and access to overseas computing power. Taiwan's regulators tightened short selling curbs twice in November to address the volatility in the local chip market. Beijing has not announced any new support for stocks despite the warnings from the Yardeni Research analyst note. It remains open whether the government will step in with state money as it did in earlier collapses. The articles leave open if Xi can successfully replace the broken property model with a stock market led one.

stories.Headline: Tristan Buckmaster and Levent Alpöge publish an AI-aided Navier-Stokes blowup proof
stories.Summary:
NYU professor Tristan Buckmaster and Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge published an AI-aided proof of Navier-Stokes blowup on November 21, 2026. They claim this new mathematical work closes a loophole found in a previous solution provided by OpenAI. The researchers used large language models to assist in the writing of their complex mathematical proof. This publication occurred two months after OpenAI had scooped them on the same famous mathematical problem. The proof follows a computer-assisted path once the numerical profile is established for the equations.

The proof addresses the 167-year-old problem of finite-time blow-up for the three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations. It involves the unforced Navier-Stokes singularity and the unforced Euler singularity, as well as the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. The work was shared via GitHub and the NYU Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences. It utilizes a numerical profile to establish the singularity formation within the three-dimensional Euler equations. The researchers used AI to help polish the final write-up of the mathematical proof.

Tristan Buckmaster stated that the team could not risk waiting to publish after being scooped by OpenAI. He explained that the resulting Navier-Stokes write-up is unpolished because it was heavily assisted by LLMs. Buckmaster noted that the proof follows a well-trodden path once the numerical profile is in hand. Levent Alpöge is an employee at Anthropic who collaborated on this AI-aided mathematical solution. Both authors believe their work successfully addresses the loophole left by the earlier OpenAI solution.

The research is discussed by Terence Tao and mentioned in reports by Euronews and the MindStudio Blog. Some observers on Hacker News and Reddit claim that AI just solved the real Navier-Stokes problem. The work affects the broader scientific community interested in fluid dynamics and the capabilities of AI. Matt Rosoff commented on a Wall Street Journal article regarding the balance of the reporting. The proof is now available for review on GitHub and the NYU Courant website.

The articles provide background on a volatile week for AI companies and the broader stock market. Anthropic recently had the largest IPO in history, pricing shares at 83 dollars to value the firm at 1.5 trillion dollars. However, Anthropic stock closed down 8.5 percent at 88.91 dollars on its second day of trading. Nvidia shares fell 14 percent on Friday, contributing to a massive weekly wipeout for chip stocks. The Nasdaq 100 fell 5.6 percent on Friday, marking its worst run in over six years.

The mathematical community will now evaluate if the proof truly closes the loophole in the OpenAI solution. The articles leave open whether this proof will be formally accepted as the final solution. Market analysts continue to monitor if the AI investment boom is slowing down or entering a correction. It remains unclear how the SEC probe into Nvidia accounting will affect future AI hardware investments. The long-term impact of AI-aided proofs on traditional mathematics is not fully detailed.

stories.Headline: Google donates Agent Substrate, gVisor and OpenRL to the CNCF for secure AI agent execution
stories.Summary:
Google donated Agent Substrate and gVisor to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, placing two core components of its AI agent infrastructure under vendor-neutral open-source governance, TechGig reported on Nov 20, 2026. The donation also includes OpenRL, Google's open-source reinforcement learning orchestration project, according to both articles. InfoQ reported on Nov 20, 2026, that Google announced the donation of Agent Substrate and gVisor to the CNCF. The move is intended to address securely executing untrusted, AI-generated code and managing compute overhead from agents that frequently pause and resume. Together, the projects target different layers of agent infrastructure, from isolated code execution to managing agent lifecycles and coordinating large-scale training workloads.

Google estimates that agents can spend 90-95 per cent of their time idle while still holding important state, including memory, files, repositories, and active sessions. Agent Substrate separates agent state, called actors, from compute resources, known as workers, and actors retain state including filesystem contents, memory, and execution context. Workers provide reusable, pre-warmed execution environments drawn from shared Kubernetes pools, and when an agent resumes, Substrate assigns it to an available Worker and restores its previous state. According to Google, this approach lets agents resume in under 500 milliseconds without creating a new Kubernetes Pod for every execution, and it reduces pressure on the Kubernetes control plane. Google's gVisor provides an additional isolation boundary through a user-space application kernel that intercepts system calls and handles them within its own isolated environment, and Agent Substrate also supports Cloud Hypervisor microVMs for hardware-level virtualisation.

Google argues that conventional Kubernetes workloads and AI agents have fundamentally different execution patterns, because a traditional application typically starts, serves requests, and continues running. An AI agent, however, may execute code for a few seconds before waiting for model inference, an external API, or human approval, according to Google. Google says keeping every agent in a dedicated Pod wastes resources, while scaling to zero introduces delays when environments must be reconstructed. Google states that large-scale agent evaluations can overwhelm Kubernetes control planes when thousands of short-lived execution environments are repeatedly created and destroyed. Google's stated goal is to establish an open foundation for agentic applications, much as Kubernetes helped standardise container orchestration.

InfoQ reported that other providers are addressing similar challenges through technologies such as Kata Containers, Firecracker, and dedicated sandboxing platforms. Google's contribution is to combine secure execution with an agent-aware orchestration model and place the resulting technologies within an open ecosystem, according to InfoQ. AI agents routinely execute generated shell commands, install packages, and interact with external tools, and treating this code as trusted creates significant risks, particularly when multiple agents share infrastructure. gVisor reduces the exposure of the underlying host while retaining much of the efficiency associated with container-based execution, and Agent Substrate gives platform teams flexibility to select an appropriate isolation boundary without changing the overall agent lifecycle model. The articles state that AI agents need their own secure, stateful, and efficiently managed execution infrastructure beyond conventional Kubernetes workloads.

Kubernetes was designed around long-running applications and relatively stable workloads, according to InfoQ. Agentic systems introduce more dynamic execution patterns, where environments must be created, suspended, restored, and isolated at much greater frequency. The announcement reflects a broader shift in cloud-native infrastructure patterns, the articles state. By donating these projects to the CNCF, Google is helping establish the foundations for that next layer of cloud-native computing, InfoQ reported. The articles describe the donation as addressing emerging challenges in securely executing untrusted, AI-generated code and managing substantial compute overhead from frequently pausing and resuming agents.

The articles do not state when the CNCF will accept the projects, how the foundation will govern them, or what licence terms will apply. They do not say whether OpenRL will be managed alongside Agent Substrate and gVisor or separately within the CNCF. The articles give no timeline for CNCF review, no comment from CNCF officials, and no details on how existing Google users will be affected by the transfer. They do not state how the projects will be maintained, who the maintainers will be, or whether other companies will contribute. The articles leave open how the move will change Google's own agent infrastructure and what adoption the projects will see under vendor-neutral governance.

stories.Headline: OpenAI releases GPT-Live-1.1 with standby billing for idle voice sessions
stories.Summary:
OpenAI released GPT-Live-1.1, a full-duplex voice model for multilingual conversations, in its API under the model ID gpt-live-1.1 on November 21, 2026, according to MarkTechPost. The model can listen while it speaks and follows GPT-Live-1, which reached the API on September 10, 2026, and has powered ChatGPT Plus and Pro voice since October 15. It accepts audio and text inputs and outputs, supports streaming and function calling, and does not support images, video, structured outputs, fine-tuning or predicted outputs. The release also adds standby, a cheaper billing state for idle sessions, and the model runs only on OpenAI's cloud through v1/live/sessions, with clients connecting over WebRTC or WebSocket.

Live sessions hold a 128,000-token default context window, and instructions can run up to 16,384 tokens. Standby bills idle WebRTC time at $0.02 per minute versus $0.05 active, a 60% lower rate, or $1.20 per hour against $3.00. Standby pauses inference during silence while the connection stays open, the server emits session.paused after the timeout and session.resumed when the user speaks, and the session ID and history are kept. OpenAI warns the first reply after a short utterance may be slower and says the microphone track should stay active during standby, and standby works for both GPT-Live-1 and GPT-Live-1.1.

Voice sessions are billed by duration, and the GPT-Live-1 model page says billing is per second, while backend model and tool usage are billed separately. The voice model can hand reasoning and tool calls to a backend text model, and OpenAI names GPT-6 Astra for complex issues and Luna for high-volume tasks, though third-party backends also work. The Live conversations guide sets delegation.type to client or responses, where responses mode uses OpenAI models and client mode connects your own backend. Switching an existing Live session requires setting the model to gpt-live-1.1 and starting a new session.

OpenAI says the model speaks with more natural and consistent accents across languages, handles transcription, letters and numbers better, and completes tasks more reliably than GPT-Live-1. OpenAI published no benchmark scores for 1.1, so the quality gains are self-reported with no numbers. The GPT-Live family replaces the usual cascade of speech-to-text, an LLM and text-to-speech, and OpenAI says the model reasons over incoming and outgoing audio together in a single model, handles turn detection and returns ASR transcripts natively. Outbound SIP calling reached all organizations on November 2, so phone agents are supported, and GPT-Live-1 and GPT-Live-1.1 have separate concurrent-session limits that each apply across inference regions, though the 1.1 page does not publish tier numbers.

stories.Headline: David Fincher defends generative AI use in Cliff Booth film amid viewer criticism
stories.Summary:
David Fincher defended the onscreen use of generative AI in The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth after fans criticized the film, Deadline reported on November 20, 2026. The Quentin Tarantino-penned sequel to Once Upon a Time in Hollywood (2019) drew accusations of apparent Gen AI use from early viewers and critics. Fincher, a three-time Oscar-nominated director, shared his thoughts on the rapidly growing technology with the Los Angeles Times. The A.V. Club reported that The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is the latest Netflix movie to face such accusations. The film stars Brad Pitt, who reprises his Oscar-winning role as the psychotic stuntman.

Set in 1977, eight years after Once Upon a Time, the film follows Pitt's eponymous stuntman, now a projectionist who moonlights as a Hollywood fixer. He gets caught up in a conspiracy that involves a Filipino gang and a stolen Oscar. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth premieres Thanksgiving on Imax and premieres Dec. 23 on Netflix. The film credits a "generative consultant," and it reportedly uses the tech to animate fake issues of TV Guide. A Bloomberg piece from March reported Ben Affleck's AI "ethical" company, InterPositive, for which Netflix paid $600 million, helped produce "an upcoming film starring Brad Pitt."

Fincher told the Los Angeles Times, "I'm not a Luddite, so I don't fear the unknown." He asked whether everyone is satisfied that the art form is figured out enough to go back to celluloid. He noted people have painted for 40,000 years while film is about a hundred years old. He said everyone is saying "Stop. Pencils down.

No more iterating," and that it is not necessary to have at your fingertips the ability to change the color of that person's eyes. Fincher added, "Well, it exists. Should we not use it?" Per Kotaku, indie filmmaker and influencer Patrick Tomasso posted on X that he "walked out of Cliff Booth completely gutted." Tomasso said what could have been a really great sequel is overshadowed by some of the most blatant and egregious AI use he has ever seen in a studio film.

Next Best Picture dinged the movie for "noticeably distracting" use of generative AI in key moments, calling it nothing but an eyesore. One viewer said they "walked out of Cliff Booth completely gutted," and another called the apparent use "astounding to an absurd degree." The A.V. Club reached out to Netflix for comment. Fincher got his start at ILM on Return of the Jedi and Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom, and has long been an early adopter of new technology, like Steven Soderbergh. Soderbergh also used AI in a John Lennon documentary earlier this year, and his results were lambasted at Cannes.

It is unclear when that movie will ever be made available, and John Lennon: The Last Interview does not even have a Wikipedia page. Earlier this year, Oscar-winning filmmakers Affleck and Danny Boyle admitted to using the technology for their respective new releases, Animals and Ink. Academy Award nominee Ava DuVernay defended using AI to animate photographs in her new documentary about the 14th Amendment, 14th. Boyle confirmed there is about 30 seconds of it in Ink where they animate a couple of old photographs.

DuVernay said in October that they animated some photos in the public domain, and that it brings people closer to that time in history, which was their goal. She said people have to see it and check it out for themselves and make their decisions about how they feel. Last month, Netflix announced that as many as 300 productions used the technology. The A.V. Club noted it is unclear what exactly was done with AI in the film.

stories.Headline: Philippines labor department joins AI council to prepare workers for AI shift
stories.Summary:
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed Executive Order 131 on Nov. 12, adopting a national AI governance framework and creating an interagency council to guide the responsible development and use of artificial intelligence in the country. Under that order, the Department of Labor and Employment was designated as a member of the National Artificial Intelligence Council, which will coordinate, facilitate and monitor implementation of the framework. The department announced its role in a statement issued on Friday and signed by Secretary Francis Tolentino, according to The Manila Times. As a council member, the department will take part in policy discussions and coordinate government efforts to address AI's impact on employment and skills development.

The department will also support the council's technical working group on capabilities, which is tasked with developing action plans for a national AI competency and digital workforce development program. The framework serves as the national strategic guide for policy formulation, regulatory coordination, institutional development and capacity-building to support the country's AI ecosystem. It seeks to ensure that AI is developed and used responsibly, safely, securely and inclusively while strengthening the country's capacity to adapt to emerging technologies. The department said it will work with other government agencies, the private sector, academe and other stakeholders to strengthen workers' competencies and prepare them for emerging employment opportunities.

The same partners will help address potential risks arising from AI adoption in workplaces, the department said in its statement. Secretary Tolentino signed that statement, which laid out the department's role under the new framework. The council's technical working group on capabilities is expected to develop the action plans for the national competency and workforce program. The articles do not say when those plans are due or what funding the effort will receive.

stories.Headline: Chinese experts urge educational reforms to develop AI-ready talent
stories.Summary:
Scholars and industry leaders gathered at a recent talent forum hosted by the University of Hong Kong in Beijing to discuss innovation. These participants met to explore how universities and technology firms can better equip professionals and students for a workplace reshaped by artificial intelligence. This discussion occurred as 12.7 million college graduates prepare to enter the workforce this year amid high employment pressure. Rapid advances in the digital economy are currently shrinking traditional roles while creating new occupations that require advanced skill sets.

The transition requires a shift toward interdisciplinary talent and a stronger emphasis on foundational knowledge in mathematics, physics, and languages. This educational transformation aligns with the 15th Five-Year Plan for 2026 to 2030, which calls for the digital transformation of schooling. The plan also demands deeper coordination between talent development, science, technology, and education, alongside reforms to evaluation systems. Institutions must streamline existing curricula to nurture independent learning rather than simply adding more courses to heavy workloads.

University of Hong Kong vice-president Wang Yang stated that critical thinking and judgment can turn China's educational strengths into a tangible advantage. Tan Jianrong of Zhejiang University explained that fields like robotics require integrated expertise that transcends traditional disciplinary boundaries. Assistant professor Li Hongyang noted that conventional academic grades often fail to capture rigorous thinking and the ability to spot research flaws. Duan Nan of JD Group emphasized that professionals need sound judgment and the skill to frame the right questions to steer technology.

The current context involves a marked improvement in research capacity, though geopolitical tensions continue to challenge international academic exchanges. Experts believe that humans must still assess whether artificial intelligence outputs meet real user needs and deliver practical outcomes. Wang Yang expressed optimism regarding continued scientific advances over the next 10 years despite these global challenges. Future efforts will focus on integrating these new skills into the broader national strategy for education and technology.

stories.Headline: OpenAI and Google expand advertising in AI interfaces to target high-intent users
stories.Summary:
OpenAI and Google are rapidly expanding advertising inside their artificial intelligence interfaces, which gives marketers new ways to target users who show high purchasing intent, Axios reported on November 21, 2026. The report, written by Sara Fischer, said user intent is much higher with AI interfaces than with traditional search because conversations let consumers reveal their needs with far more specificity. The story drew on data from Similarweb and Graphite, with a chart by Christine Wang of Axios. The article described the shift as an attention crunch for AI advertising.

The change means marketers can aim at people whose conversations already signal what they want to buy, rather than at people typing short queries into a search box. The article gave no figures beyond the two data sources, Similarweb and Graphite, and named no dollar amounts, user counts or dates other than the November 21, 2026 publication. It said the higher intent comes from the back and forth of a conversation, which lets a consumer state a need more precisely than a search query usually does. Both OpenAI and Google are named as the companies expanding ads in their AI products.

The article attributed the reporting to Sara Fischer and presented the data through Similarweb and Graphite, with the chart credited to Christine Wang of Axios. It did not include direct statements from OpenAI, Google or any marketer, so no executive comments were reported. The piece framed the higher intent of AI conversations as the reason the ad expansion matters to advertisers. It did not say how the ads are priced, sold or displayed.

The context the article gives is a comparison between AI interfaces and traditional search, with conversations producing stronger signals of what a consumer wants. It did not say what happens next, beyond noting that both companies are rapidly expanding the ads. No timeline, revenue target or response from either company appeared in the text.

stories.Headline: Moonshot AI cancels 150 million dollar Nvidia chip contract in Indonesia
stories.Summary:
Chinese artificial intelligence company Moonshot AI canceled a cloud contract in Indonesia on November 19, 2026. The firm terminated this agreement following a move by the U.S. Commerce Department to block indirect access routes. This decision happened after the U.S. government restricted remote access to advanced chips for Chinese companies. Moonshot AI also halted all talks regarding new agreements. Analysts view this as a swift effect of the new American regulations.

The canceled contract was worth 150 million dollars and involved renting Nvidia Blackwell Ultra B300 chips. Moonshot AI, the Beijing developer of Kimi AI models, planned to start these operations next year. The firm had agreed to a 50 percent prepayment, which is triple the customary 15 percent rate. The Commerce Department announced on November 16 that computing services require licensing, with rules starting November 19. These rules now affect Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil.

The U.S. Commerce Department is responsible for these licensing requirements and the new export controls. Officials stated that computing services are now subject to licensing to prevent indirect chip access. The move followed a scandal involving former Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang regarding data centers in Singapore. House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast disclosed export license records from December to May. He noted that some buyers were designated as Chinese military companies by the Defense Department.

Other affected firms include Tencent, Alibaba, and Baidu, which received approved licenses for 150,000, 75,000, and 43,000 units. Alibaba Chief Executive Eddie Wu said training models with domestic chips would be possible by early next year. Tencent Chief Strategy Officer James Mitchell predicted a long term reliance on Chinese made chips. AMD shares fell over 7 percent on November 19 due to alleged ties with sanctioned firms. Hunterbrook Media reported that AMD firmware was found in products from the sanctioned server maker IEIT.

The background involves U.S. Congress intensifying pressure on China and tightening semiconductor export controls. Nvidia and AMD applied for 3.44 million units, but only 879,868 were approved by the government. AMD generated 34.8 percent of its revenue last year from China, Hong Kong, and Singapore. Hunterbrook Media found that AMD licensing revenue of 67 million dollars came from Hygon joint ventures. IEIT incorporated new firmware six times after being added to the export control list in March.

Next, a rule extending controls to overseas affiliates owned over 50 percent by sanctioned firms may start in January. AMD told Reuters that it complies with export laws and that the allegations distort its business. Hunterbrook Capital took a short position in AMD after publishing the report on the company. The articles leave open whether China will actually follow through on expanding fuel exports. They also leave open if the U.S. will accept China's position on nuclear powered submarines.

stories.Summary:
Coatue Management disclosed a stake in SK hynix, the South Korean memory chip maker whose high-bandwidth memory products are used in artificial intelligence hardware, according to a TradingView report dated November 20, 2026. The report tied the position to accelerating demand for HBM chips, the specialized memory that has driven the company's recent results. The same article recorded that SK hynix shares fell 5.92% to 1,113,000 won at the November 20 regular-session close in Seoul, as fears about AI spending swept Asian chip stocks. The Kospi fell 5.21% that day, its steepest slide in months, after Nvidia and AMD sank on Wall Street overnight.

The article said the fundamentals look nothing like a crash, with third-quarter revenue reaching 104.6 trillion won, up 328% year over year, and operating profit hitting 83.3 trillion won, an 80% margin. SK hynix holds 98.7 trillion won of net cash, and long-term agreements with 14 major customers cover more than half of 2027 and 2028 capacity, while management expects demand to exceed supply through 2030. Shareholder returns for 2026 total about 100 trillion won, including a 20 trillion won buyback approved with the results. GuruFocus gives the stock a GF Score of 99/100 and a GF Value of 1,517,314 won, putting the close at a 26.6% discount that it rates modestly undervalued.

The article attributed the nervousness to valuation rather than operations, noting that net cash covers about 12% of the 813 trillion won market value and that the market cap is only about 2.4 times last quarter's annualized operating profit, a cycle-peak multiple. It said the test is whether HBM4 shipments overtake HBM3E in the fourth quarter as guided, which is the company's own forecast rather than an outside estimate. The report did not give the size of the Coatue position, the date it was taken or any comment from Coatue or SK hynix management on the investment. stories.Headline: Indian firms cut entry-level tech hiring 44% while planning 45,000 fresher hires
stories.Summary:
General Assembly published research showing that many Learning and Development leaders believe AI is weakening employees' human skills, IT Brief Australia reported on 19 November 2026. The study surveyed 510 HR and Learning and Development leaders at large companies across six countries. More than half of respondents, 52%, said AI use is degrading skills such as communication, conflict resolution and collaboration. Another 41% said ensuring employees retain or develop critical thinking, communication and other soft skills despite using AI will be one of their biggest challenges in the coming year. The findings highlight a tension inside large organisations as companies expand AI training while trying to preserve workplace skills that are harder to automate.

At the same time, 83% of respondents said human skills are becoming more valued within their organisations, and 59% expect demand for soft skills training to rise. Nearly two-thirds, 64%, said their teams are under pressure to deliver AI upskilling across the workforce. AI literacy was most often ranked as the top skill Learning and Development teams themselves will need. One-third of respondents, 33%, said closing the AI skills gap is a leading challenge, while 31% pointed to change management and employee fatigue around AI. The research found that 57% of leaders expect demand for role-specific AI training to grow, while 56% expect their organisations to expand personalised learning journeys, 55% expect more hands-on training and 52% expect more job-based or role-based training.

Out-of-the-box third-party training was the option most likely to be deprioritised, with 15% of organisations expecting to place less emphasis on it. Daniele Grassi, Chief Executive Officer of General Assembly, said employers are trying to balance technical training with broader workplace development. He said Learning and Development professionals are tasked with building role-specific AI skills while making sure the human skills that matter most do not erode in the process. He said companies are increasingly looking to integrate AI and soft skills training to prepare employees for the future of work. He said training is becoming more hands-on, with opportunities to practice critical thinking, judgement and collaboration alongside AI usage and get feedback in real time.

Among respondents who said their learning strategy is fully linked to documented business priorities, 23% expect a significant budget increase, compared with 11% of other respondents. The same pattern appeared among leaders who said they work closely with functional heads to map future skills needs and among those who said they help shape business strategy. More broadly, 73% said company leadership regularly asks for Learning and Development input on workforce capability, transformation or future skills decisions, while 63% said Learning and Development leaders help shape business strategy. Connecting learning initiatives to business outcomes or return on investment was the second most-cited challenge for the coming year, named by 35% of respondents. Less than half, 47%, said business outcomes such as revenue growth or profit are among their top three measures of success.

By contrast, 36% still count course completions among their leading metrics, and 26% said distinguishing AI course completions from actual competency is a major challenge. Half of respondents in dedicated Learning and Development roles said course completions are a top metric, compared with 32% of those in broader HR roles who also oversee training. Grassi said the pressure to show results is growing as organisations spend more on AI-related learning. He said businesses are investing in AI upskilling, but the big challenge for Learning and Development leaders is proving that what they are doing is working. He said that means going beyond counting how many people took a course, and measuring behaviour changes, skills and competencies instead, and linking those to real business outcomes.

Avi Patchava, CEO (joint) of Bright Money, wrote in ETCIO on 14 November 2026 that entry-level tech openings were down 44% year on year by mid-2026. When ICRIER surveyed 651 IT firms, 55% said they had cut entry-level hiring, while only 14% said the same about senior roles. At Infosys, the share of employees aged 30 or under is the lowest it has been in 15 years. Nomura tracked about 83,000 AI-related hires in India against roughly 32,000 AI-linked exits, and TCS and Infosys between them still plan to take on around 45,000 freshers this year. Patchava wrote that more than 90% of Indian employees already use generative AI tools, and that in 2017 he ran a research study with 28 successful Indian graduates at McKinsey India.

stories.Headline: Cumberland schools board advances AI policy limiting tools to approved apps
stories.Summary:
Cumberland County Schools is looking to update its technology responsible use policy, including provisions governing generative artificial intelligence, which is AI that creates text, images, video, audio and other content. The Board of Education approved a first reading of the policy update at its Nov. 17 meeting. Board Attorney Nick Sjoka told board members at a Nov. 3 policy committee meeting that the district has had a policy on the books for a number of years. Sjoka said that policy incorporates federal laws involving student confidentiality and protecting students from harmful material along with state statutes and expectations for responsible use. Sjoka said the update is more extensive and detailed, specifying, for example, prohibited uses of internet file sharing, and addressing increased use of generative artificial intelligence.

The updates include recommendations from the North Carolina Schools Boards Association and the district's technology director, Sjoka said. The updated policy will apply to all district employees and students, Sjoka said, and the policy states it also applies to former employees, visitors, contractors and other authorized users who use the district's technology. The updated policy states that it applies to use of all school system computer networks, connections, resources, tools and learning environments made available through those networks, and all devices that connect to them. School system technological resources include desktop and laptop computers, tablets, Chromebooks, mobile devices, internet services, cloud-based applications, communication and collaboration platforms and AI tools authorized by the district. The policy states that the school system reserves the right to monitor, filter, log, inspect, and review the use of all school system technological resources to ensure compliance with Board policy, protect district resources, maintain system security, and comply with applicable law.

The policy states that the use of generative AI tools shall be limited to district-approved applications and must comply with Board policies, student privacy requirements, copyright laws, and instructional guidelines. The policy states that plagiarism of internet resources will be treated in the same manner as any other incidents of plagiarism, as stated in the Code of Student Conduct. The policy states that Cumberland County Schools fosters a dynamic learning environment that integrates cutting-edge technology, including generative AI, to empower students. The policy states that the district holds integrity at the forefront, demonstrating a firm commitment to academic honesty, responsible AI use, copyright respect, and data privacy. The policy further states the district believes it is important to promote courteous technology use that prevents cyberbullying and harmful creation or sharing of deepfake images.

Deepfakes use AI to create or alter photos, videos or audio recordings to make them appear real. The policy states that only pre-approved software and AI tools are permitted on school devices. The policy states that users must take responsibility for the content they create or store using school resources, and be aware that misuse of equipment or failure to adhere to policy guidelines may result in financial liabilities or other consequences. The policy states that school employees shall not disclose, post, upload, transmit or otherwise make available personally identifiable, private or confidential student information through school system websites, social media, cloud services, digital applications, AI tools, electronic communications or any other online service concerning students, such as their name, address or photos, without written permission from a parent or guardian. Technology users are also not allowed to install, create, modify or introduce unauthorized software, applications, AI tools, games, communication applications or more on school system devices without permission from the technology director or designee.

Staff writer Rachael Riley can be reached at rriley@fayobserver.com or 910-486-3528. The article originally appeared on The Fayetteville Observer. stories.Headline: At an AI Tipping Point - University of Pennsylvania
stories.Summary:
Karen Detlefsen challenged her History of Modern Philosophy class to write four letters to a classmate. Two letters were unaided, one used artificial intelligence, and one was wholly AI-generated. This exercise occurred during the Fall/Winter 2026 semester at the University of Pennsylvania. Detlefsen wanted students to contemplate if artificial intelligence can truly think and create like a philosopher. She also wants them to ponder what makes us human and a good life.

The technology permeates social media, elections, the military, and math. In September 2026, AI solved a decades-old problem about equations governing how fluids move. The U.S. military has used radar-guided missiles since the 1980s. John Lapinski predicts AI will be a top issue in the 2028 U.S. presidential election. Many U.S. city and state governments have recently hired Chief AI Officers.

Michael Horowitz says AI will inevitably reshape society and more advances are around the corner. He believes a human must always make the decision to use military force. Charles Yang says large language models are fancy versions of predictive typing. He notes that how these models create complex ideas remains completely mysterious. John Lapinski says governments worldwide will decide how we can use this technology.

Voters are affected by synthetic public opinion data that could be very misleading. Military commanders use tools that incorporate autonomy into weapons, which Horowitz calls a weightier challenge. Lapinski notes that those requiring zero error, like his NBC team, cannot use AI. Faculty across Penn Arts and Sciences are thinking about how technology changes their fields. Some organizations face simpler challenges regarding HR practices or processing intelligence data.

Alan Turing pondered if machines could think as far back as the 1950s. In the early 1990s, Penn led a revolution in natural language processing. Mark Liberman directed the Linguistic Data Consortium to annotate language datasets in English, Chinese, and Arabic. Mitch Marcus led Treebank to train computers to split sentences into phrases. Charles Yang studied the science of cognition at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

Experts are figuring out how to regulate AI and what safeguards to put in place. Lapinski is starting a new initiative to bring together various Chief AI Officers. Some industries are still deciding where to employ AI, especially in creative professions. The technology is prone to hallucinating or stating made-up information as fact. Articles leave open how to regulate AI and how models create complex ideas.

stories.Headline: NMSU receives DARPA award for solution to AI trust issues - New Mexico State University
stories.Summary:
Two New Mexico State University professors are leading one of only 10 teams in the country receiving grants to work on one of the biggest challenges in artificial intelligence, which is how to build an AI you can trust with life-or-death decisions. Son Tran, an NMSU computer science professor and department head, and Stylianos Vasileiou, an NMSU assistant computer science professor, received a $600,000 grant over two years through a special research area under the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency. That program is called CLARA, short for Compositional Learning-And-Reasoning for Automated Complex Systems Engineering, and it is a fundamental research program designed to tightly integrate artificial reasoning and machine learning components to create high-assurance machine intelligence. Their proposal carries the title "SPARTA: Splitting-based Polynomially-bounded Automated Reasoning with Tensorized Adaptation," and NMSU is working with two other research groups, one led by Chitta Baral from Arizona State University and the other by Yuliana Lierler and Jorge Fandinno from the University of Nebraska at Omaha.

The team's goal is to develop high assurance and broadly applicable methodologies for combining Automated Reasoning and Machine Learning, according to the article. Tran said integrating these branches of artificial intelligence will provide the speed and flexibility of machine learning with verifiability based on artificial reasoning proofs that have strong logical explainability and computational tractability. He said the team will focus on developing efficient and scalable approaches to combine machine learning approaches with logic programs, and such systems will provide explanations for their answers, which is a key difference compared to contemporary machine learning systems. Vasileiou said AI generally splits into two camps, one great at spotting patterns quickly and the other great at following strict logic, and combining them gives you the best of both worlds. He said you are getting an AI that can think fast on its feet while still showing its work in a way humans can verify and trust.

Right now, building an AI that is safe enough for critical jobs takes massive amounts of custom engineering, and CLARA aims to create one universal foundation that is rock-solid, mathematically proven, and ready to adapt to almost any complex problem. The program aims to build a reliable, plug-and-play AI engine that can be reused across dozens of high-stakes industries without needing to be rebuilt from scratch every time. The article names Minerva Baumann, a media relations officer, as the contact for the story and lists the College of Arts and Sciences, artificial intelligence and computer science among its tags. The release date for the announcement was Nov. 20, 2026, and the article does not say what happens next beyond the two-year grant and the work with the partner groups.

stories.Headline: Engineers, Clinicians Partner to Advance Human Health with AI
stories.Summary:
Engineers at the University of California, Davis are working with clinicians on artificial intelligence tools meant to detect Alzheimer's disease earlier, expand care options for survivors of sexual assault and improve results for patients awaiting corneal transplants. The projects are funded by AI and Health Seed Funding Awards from the Center for Information Technology Research in the Interest of Society and the Banatao Institute, known as CITRIS, which aim to strengthen interdisciplinary connections between schools and colleges across UC Davis and UC Davis Health and to establish the university as a leader in AI-enabled healthcare technology research. The awards followed a matchmaking mixer for engineers and clinicians held in November 2025 and co-hosted by the UC Davis AI Center in Engineering, or AICE, with CITRIS, the Healthy Aging in a Digital World initiative and the Clinical and Translational Science Center as partners. That event produced six awarded seed grants, including the three co-led by engineers.

For the Alzheimer's project, Chen-Nee Chuah, the Child Family Professor in Engineering in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, is developing an AI model that can pick up early signs of the disease from a patient's speech, working with Michelle Cohn, a postdoctoral scholar in linguistics, and Alyssa Weakley, an assistant professor of neurology. The team is examining conversational interviews with older adults from the UC Davis Alzheimer's Disease Research Center Corpus, which is annotated with patients' cognitive status such as mild cognitive impairment or late-stage Alzheimer's, to train a model to identify biomarkers of cognitive impairment by analyzing how a patient sounds and their manner of speech. The team has completed the datasets needed to train the large language model on acoustic and linguistic features of cognitive impairment in older adults, and the National Institutes of Health has given the researchers a boost to develop an AI-enabled remote monitoring system to detect health issues in older adults, which will directly support the early detection work. The project will culminate in a real-world pilot deployment within a local senior living community.

Josh McCoy, an associate professor of computer science, is leading a project to develop a trauma-informed, AI-powered chatbot that can connect survivors of sexual assault with appropriate social and health support services, with Jessica Draughon Moret, an associate professor at the UC Davis Betty Irene Moore School of Nursing, as co-lead. The private chatbot aims to expand access to and simplify the process of seeking care, and the pair are working to ensure it is informed by human-centered design and built on expert consultation with survivors. The team has a prototype for the platform, called CARE-COMPASS: Community Assistance and Resource Engagement, and is currently in the refinement and user feedback phase, with the goal of seeking additional funding from the National Institutes of Health for further development and broader use. Separately, Hamed Pirsiavash, a professor of computer science, is co-leading a project with Mark Mannis, a distinguished professor of ophthalmology and vision science, to develop an AI-powered evaluation system for donated corneal tissue, joined by Min Zhao, a professor of ophthalmology and vision science, Ana Sandoval Castellanos, a postdoctoral fellow in the Laboratory for Cell Nanoengineering, and several medical students.

The cornea team has been working with Sierra Donor Services, a non-profit donor procurement organization serving the Northern California and Northern Nevada regions, to source a curated dataset of microscopy images of corneal tissue, and through self-supervised learning the system uses computer vision and machine learning to distinguish between healthy and abnormal tissue. The goal is to reduce clinicians' workload from hours to minutes when evaluating tissue and to minimize variability in the quality of donated tissue, and the project's next step is to test the AI model with larger sample sizes. Sam King, a professor of computer science and director of CITRIS at UC Davis, said an engineer can build a model that scores well on a benchmark and still fails in a clinic because the team does not know which errors matter to a patient, while clinicians know but cannot build these systems alone. He said the technology is improving faster than those partnerships are forming, and the awards exist to close that gap by putting engineers and clinicians on the same problem before design decisions are made. The awards dovetail with the AICE's AI and Health research area, which accelerates discovery by facilitating conversations between engineers and clinicians, and through AICE's partnership they are helping realize CITRIS Health's mission to encourage innovations in technology that improve health outcomes and increase access to medicine.
