stories.Headline: Elementl Power and Google use Gemini AI to speed nuclear project delivery
stories.Summary:
Elementl Power and Google said on Tuesday that they have agreed to work together to use Google Cloud's artificial intelligence technology to help bring nuclear projects onto the grid sooner, according to a press release from the Washington, D.C. headquartered project development company. The collaboration will build on Elementl Power's project delivery tool, which is named Elementl Lattice, and the company's AI system is based on Google's Gemini. Elementl Power said the system will continue to leverage Google Cloud's technological expertise to create a standardized and scalable project approach for nuclear development. The companies are additionally working together to create a single, controlled record of a nuclear plant's design, licensing requirements and approved changes, according to the release. Elementl Power said this effort will directly assist with creating shorter timelines and more regulatory certainty for future projects, which the company framed as the purpose of the arrangement.

The collaboration deepens the partnership between Google and Elementl Power after the companies signed a strategic agreement last year. In May 2025, the two companies agreed to develop three advanced reactors, with each project being at least 600 megawatts. The Tuesday announcement did not give a value for the new agreement, a schedule for the work, or a date for when any reactor project might reach the grid. The articles do not name the executives who signed the agreement or give direct statements from either company beyond the release language paraphrased above. Elementl Power is described as a nuclear power project development company headquartered in Washington, D.C., and Google's role is through its cloud computing unit and its Gemini AI system.

The release casts the AI work as a way to standardize how projects are delivered and to keep design, licensing and change records in one controlled place. No independent party is named as overseeing or reviewing the collaboration. The context given is the earlier May 2025 agreement between the two companies to develop three advanced reactors of at least 600 megawatts each, which the new collaboration builds on. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the work described in the release, and they give no timeline for the AI tools or for the reactor projects themselves. More to follow.

stories.Headline: AI industry workers in Westminster propose a national regulator and stronger whistleblower protections
stories.Summary:
A coalition of organizations representing artificial intelligence industry workers gathered in Westminster on November 20, 2026, to advocate for regulation and labor rights. This group, which included whistleblowers, civil society organizations, and unions, held a conference titled AI: Worker Voice as Critical Internal Condition. The event aimed to establish a network that empowers workers to act as a force for regulating the sector. Participants sought to create formal channels so that those who build and are ruled by AI can influence its deployment.

The coalition proposed strengthening whistleblower protections in Britain and establishing a national AI regulator, which the country currently lacks. They called for a negotiated slowdown of development between private companies to ensure the frontier is governed by workers and government. John Chadfield of the Communication Workers Union suggested that contracts for data workers, content moderators, and defense staff include statutory ethics clauses. These clauses would grant employees the legal right to negotiate over matters concerning public safety.

John Chadfield based his suggestions on discussions with workers at Google DeepMind to encourage these contractual changes. Adam Cantwell-Corn from the TUC tech project stated that his organization is leading the movement to define what workers want from AI. He noted that this includes collective bargaining in the workplace and shaping the economy through industrial strategy. Alex Sobel, the Labour and Co-operative MP for Leeds Central and Headingley, argued that Britain should model global behavior by moving first on regulation.

The conference was hosted by the Center for Labor and a Just Economy at Harvard and the Institute for Ethics in AI at Oxford. Alex Sobel compared the need for immediate AI legislation to the passing of the Climate Change Act in 2008. He suggested that the global reach and universities of a middle-ranking power like the UK make it well-positioned to lead. The group believes that workers within AI firms should decide how the technology is designed and when it is released.

Articles.Title: AI industry workers gather to fight for their rights and regulation

stories.Headline: India's chief justice says clear AI rules beat a ban for legal education
stories.Summary:
The Chief Justice of India, Justice Surya Kant, said on Saturday, November 21, 2026, that setting clear rules to regulate the use of AI tools would be a better option than a total ban for legal students and the legal profession. He made the statement while delivering the inaugural address at the first annual international conference on legal education, which was convened by the Commonwealth Legal Education Association in Hyderabad. The Chief Justice observed that generative artificial intelligence had unsettled the assumption that an answer sheet reflects the knowledge of a student. He also said that assessment methods should be improved so that written works are supported by oral explanations, and that a law school must ultimately be able to certify with confidence what the students it had produced had learnt.

On legal education in the country, the Chief Justice noted that practical training can strengthen doctrinal teaching only if it is genuine, and that a student learns the strength of law in a supervised moot trial better than in an examination. He said Indian regulations already require clinical courses and a legal aid clinic in every law school, and that such clinical teaching requires trained supervisors, meaningful assessment and clear ethical safeguards. Justice P.S. Narasimha of the Supreme Court said students develop their legal reasoning through repeated drafting of petitions, analysing facts and finding legal solutions on their own. He warned that students who depend on AI tools for legal solutions without undergoing this rigorous training in drafting and legal reasoning might lose the capacity to analyse and fail to distinguish between right and wrong.

Attorney General R. Venkataramani said legal education must respond to the challenges brought about by globalisation, technology and artificial intelligence, and that law schools should evolve into centres of research and innovation while AI tools are used to assist them. He said AI should not be the master but an assistant. P. Sam Koshy, the Acting Chief Justice of the Telangana High Court, said it was high time everyone examined whether the next generation of legal professionals was being prepared merely to understand the law as it existed or was being equipped to shape the laws the future demands. He said the present legal professional cannot be confined to the legal framework of one jurisdiction, and that while learning a domestic law governing a dispute, one should also be aware of its international dimensions. He added that the future of the Commonwealth's legal tradition will not be secured by merely preserving its past, but by its capacity to learn, adapt and evolve without losing its foundational principles.

Articles.Title: AI regulation rather than ban is better option: CJI

stories.Headline: Pat Gelsinger says AI needs a 10,000-fold efficiency gain beyond incremental chip upgrades
stories.Summary:
Former Intel chief executive Pat Gelsinger used a fireside chat called “Reality Check: Beyond Chips” at the COSM Technology Summit 2026 in Scottsdale, Arizona, to argue that small generational chip upgrades cannot meet the demands of artificial intelligence, which he said needs a 10,000-fold gain in computing efficiency. He appeared alongside technology theorist George Gilder and Heritage Foundation director Bret Swanson. After the event he wrote on X that Moore’s Law should be woken up rather than declared dead. He said the revival depends on fundamental breakthroughs across five engineering fronts.

Gelsinger said the needed advances span light, power, cooling, composition and packaging, and that turning one gigawatt of electricity into ten gigawatts of AI token output requires far more than shrinking transistors. He pointed to U.S. energy capacity growing only in the low single digits over the past decade, gas turbine supply backlogs of eight years and nuclear projects that take a decade to build. He cited NVIDIA’s Kyber racks built on the Blackwell NVL72 architecture, which push power needs to 600kW, enough to supply 500 homes, and a Harvard study finding U.S. data centers consume as much electricity as Chile. He also noted that major AI foundation models now ship roughly every four weeks.

Since joining the venture firm Playground Global as a general partner in March 2025, Gelsinger has backed startups aimed at these hardware bottlenecks, including the government-supported lithography venture xLight, which seeks to move past ASML’s 13.5nm extreme ultraviolet wavelength barrier, and the nuclear capacity firm Alva Energy. His roadmap also points to optical interconnects and silicon photonics to carry data with light instead of copper. He said that after more than 40 years in semiconductors he believes the greatest innovations are still ahead. On an earlier occasion he called HBM a hideous memory while conceding it is the best technology the industry has now, and he proposed Z2RAM as an alternative with potentially better density, performance and power draw.

stories.Headline: Standard Bank Group automates generative AI risk checks in its own AWS account
stories.Summary:
Standard Bank Group, working with AWS Professional Services, deployed an automated assessment that scores each generative AI use case against international AI standards and its own policies, as described in an AWS blog post dated November 20, 2026. The post is co-written by Tala Qraitem from AWS and Jörg Fischer from Standard Bank Group. The assessment produces reports and a dashboard showing what is already in place, what is working well, and what still needs mitigation. The bank already had a model risk practice covering explainability and fairness, and a change risk process that assesses each new use case by its level of risk before it goes live. Generative AI increases complexity because models and tooling change every three to six months, yet each use case must still meet the same high security and compliance bar.

The assessment runs entirely in Standard Bank Group's own AWS account, with documents, code, and test results kept in an Amazon Simple Storage Service bucket there. The AWS Well-Architected Tool handles intake, AWS Step Functions orchestrates the pipeline, and a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock evaluates the evidence using a technique called LLM-as-a-judge. The custom lens in the Well-Architected Tool holds about 40 questions, each covering a risk event such as incomplete technical documentation or insufficient human oversight, and Standard Bank Group customized the lens with judge questions built from its own standards, bringing the total to more than 300. A pre-assessment agent running on AWS Fargate scans the use case's code repository and documentation, maps relevant files to each question, and pre-populates the lens with answers and links to the evidence. The pipeline calls the application through its AWS Lambda function or API, adds a built-in set of jailbreak attempts and off-topic questions, sends the same prompt several times in original and reworded forms, and uses an embedding model on Amazon Bedrock to check that answers stay consistent in meaning.

Jörg Fischer, Group Chief Information and AI Officer at Standard Bank Group, said the assessment demonstrates how the bank is working with AWS to embed intelligent, automated risk management into its AI journey, allowing it to accelerate meaningful business value while maintaining the trust and controls that banking demands. He said the bank believes responsible AI is not about slowing innovation down but enabling it to build and scale with confidence. Review and approval stay with the risk committee, which now bases each decision on consistent evidence collected the same way across use cases. Sri Elaprolu, Director of Frontier AI Science & Engineering at AWS, said most organizations treat policy as something you read, while Standard Bank Group treats it as something you run. He said that when every rule becomes a check that runs against the live system, a policy update stops being a memo and becomes a test, which fundamentally changes how fast a bank can scale AI responsibly.

Each risk receives a likelihood score, the share of required evidence the model couldn't find, and a fixed severity level that the bank's risk team can adjust, together producing a rating from Very low to Critical. Each missing piece of evidence maps to a specific mitigation and to the clause of the standard or policy it came from, so a risk officer can trace any findings back to their source when explaining decisions to a regulator. The checks cover eight AWS responsible AI dimensions: veracity and robustness, privacy and security, transparency, fairness, safety, controllability, governance, and explainability. Every AI model interaction is protected by Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, and each evaluation runs multiple times to measure how consistent the answers are, with inconsistent findings flagged in the review interface. The pipeline delivers results as an executive presentation, a mitigation checklist, a detailed technical report, and an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard that tracks scores across use cases over time.

The assessment fits into three stages of the use case lifecycle: during a proof of concept it is optional, at the build stage it becomes mandatory, and the approval gate draws on its results as formal evidence. Today the assessment runs in Standard Bank Group's production environment, evaluating use cases before they go live, and after live workloads are connected it will rerun on a schedule or whenever code or configuration changes. The bank's teams already trigger assessments on their own through a central system where use cases flow from intake to evaluation in a single workflow. The assessment produces evidence against controls but does not certify compliance with any regulation, and Standard Bank Group remains responsible for its own regulatory determinations. Model availability varies by AWS Region, so the post advises checking the supported models by Region before deploying.

At Standard Bank Group, the assessment reduced a traditionally manual two-week review to a comprehensive risk report generated in approximately two hours, demonstrated across six assessments. It also delivered a 14% improvement in use-case risk scores after remediation, which the post says strengthens responsible AI governance and reduces compliance bottlenecks. The post states that Amazon Bedrock doesn't share the bank's prompts or model outputs with model providers and doesn't use them to train models, and that the bank controls access to the model through AWS Identity and Access Management. Because Amazon Bedrock offers many foundation models through one API, the team can move to a newer judge model by changing a configuration setting instead of rebuilding the pipeline. The assessment uses the judge model as-is with no fine-tuning or customization, and a question factory generates extra judge questions from internal documents so that a policy change becomes a test change.

Articles.Title: How Standard Bank Group automates AI risk assessment for generative AI

stories.Headline: Senator Mark R. Warner leads a bipartisan bill requiring AI-using companies to disclose governance and financing risks
stories.Summary:
A bipartisan group of senators plans to introduce a sweeping securities disclosure bill. This legislation targets companies that use artificial intelligence or are involved in the AI industry. The announcement regarding this new bill was made on November 21, 2026. It aims to increase transparency regarding AI operations and transactions. The group also wants to know if board committees provide AI oversight.

The AUDIT AI Act is led by Senator Mark R. Warner of Virginia. Senators John Kennedy, Angela Alsobrooks, and Mike Rounds are co-sponsors of the proposed legislation. Section 3 requires the SEC to issue rules within 180 days of enactment. Covered issuers are companies required to file annual reports under Exchange Act Section 13 or 15(d). These companies must disclose AI governance policies and board expertise or explain their absence.

Senator Mark R. Warner stated that AI has enormous potential to transform the economy. He noted that trillions of dollars pouring into the technology come with real financial risks. Warner believes investors and policymakers deserve to know where that money is going. He also wants clarity on how deals are financed and what risks are involved. These statements were provided in a press release from the senator.

The bill affects non-financial covered issuers, excluding banking, insurance, lending, investment management, and securities trading. It targets round-trip financing arrangements between AI chip providers and other hardware or software components. Some AI industry observers have described these specific financing arrangements as a concern. The bill protects private fund investor identities unless they are defined as covered entities. Covered entities include joint ventures, special purpose vehicles, or variable interest entities.

Some group members previously served on a small team under then-Majority Leader Chuck Schumer. That team was tasked with creating a legislative framework for AI several congresses ago. Prior legislation proposing similar board expertise disclosures for cybersecurity never advanced beyond the introductory stage. The SEC previously rejected cybersecurity expertise rules, noting that broad business knowledge is often sufficient. The Commission stated that cybersecurity processes are largely administered at the management level.

The SEC must amend Form 10-K within 180 days to include standardized AI risk sections. This section will cover foundation model dependence, compute provider concentration, and training cost volatility. The SEC must also study AI research and development reporting and publish results after one year. A report on automated investment strategies and market efficiency is due within 120 days. The articles leave open whether the bill will pass or how the SEC will implement flexibility.

stories.Headline: Julie Menin leads New York City Council plan to vote on AI bills in January 2027
stories.Summary:
The New York City Council plans to begin 2027 by voting on a set of artificial intelligence bills, according to two people with knowledge of the timing who were granted anonymity to discuss private deliberations. The legislation is being led by Council Speaker Julie Menin, a Manhattan lawmaker who has become a foil to Mayor Zohran Mamdani on several issues, including AI regulation. The package would place the city at the forefront of efforts to rein in frontier AI technology, amid growing concern about its existential threats to society. The measures are meant as a counterpoint to federal inaction on AI, which the article describes as amounting to a regulatory vacuum. The vote is expected in January, though a spokesperson for Menin said the bills are still undergoing review and that no exact date has been set for a vote.

The article gives no other numbers, dates or names beyond the January timing, the 2027 start, Menin, Mamdani and the two anonymous people. It does not specify how many bills are in the package or what any of them would require. The article also does not say what penalties or obligations the legislation would create. Menin is the lawmaker responsible for shepherding the legislation, and her spokesperson said the bills remain under review while confirming that a vote date has not been fixed.

The article does not include further comment from Menin, Mamdani or other council members on the substance of the bills. It also does not say whether the mayor supports or opposes the package. The two people who confirmed the January timing spoke on condition of anonymity because the deliberations were private. The context given is federal inaction on AI, which the article says has left a regulatory vacuum that the city measures are intended to counter.

The article does not say what happens after a January vote, such as whether the mayor would sign the bills or whether further steps are required. It also does not describe any federal proposals that the city effort is responding to. No other details on the next steps are provided. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Yuehua Li and Pengfei Li review explainable AI methods for hepatocellular carcinoma research
stories.Summary:
A comprehensive narrative review by Yuehua Li and Pengfei Li was published in the Journal of the Egyptian National Cancer Institute on explainable artificial intelligence in hepatocellular carcinoma research. The review synthesizes recent methodological advances and clinical translation challenges in applying explainable artificial intelligence to hepatocellular carcinoma research. Hepatocellular carcinoma is a malignancy with significant global incidence, mortality, substantial inter-tumor and intra-tumor heterogeneity at molecular, pathological, and imaging levels, and poor clinical prognosis. Deep learning and machine learning models have shown considerable diagnostic and prognostic accuracy across oncology workflows. Their clinical deployment has been constrained by an opaque black-box architecture where decision-making logic remains concealed.

The authors examine how explainable artificial intelligence methods turn opaque predictions into interpretable findings across four clinical domains: imaging diagnosis, multi-omics biomarker discovery, treatment response prediction, and postoperative prognostic evaluation. The review systematically outlines technical bottlenecks that prevent post-hoc explanations from functioning as direct, actionable clinical interventions. In imaging diagnosis, explainable frameworks visualize model focus and align automated classifications with established clinical frameworks such as the Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System. Techniques like Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping and SHapley Additive exPlanations decode internal feature activations into standardized clinical indicators, including non-rim arterial phase hyperenhancement. Post-hoc attribution methods accurately highlighted the tumor margin and peritumoral boundary zones as decisive features for predicting microvascular invasion, aligning artificial intelligence outputs with histopathological realities.

Multi-task learning frameworks have linked routine macroscopic magnetic resonance imaging performances with underlying tumor grading. Specialized ultrasound and magnetic resonance sequence evaluations confirmed the adaptability of explainable systems across diverse imaging acquisitions. In whole-slide image analysis, explainable architectures apply attention-based visualizations and activation maps to render histological evaluations of nuclear atypia, tissue architectural distortion, and stromal alterations transparent. Explainable systems have successfully decoded the biological foundations of specific magnetic resonance imaging phenotypes by linking macroscale imaging features to underlying cellular microenvironments. This integration marks an evolution toward multi-scale explainability that unifies radiological, histopathological, and spatial molecular data layers into an auditable diagnostic continuum.

Explainable artificial intelligence functions as a high-dimensional mining engine and hypothesis generator across multi-omics data layers, including genomics, single-cell transcriptomics, metabolomics, pathomics, radiomics, and routine clinical records. Methodological frameworks using tree-based feature attribution, automated machine learning, and multi-model feature selection have established reproducible pipelines to pinpoint robust candidate biomarkers while reducing false discoveries. Intrinsically interpretable deep learning structures and pathway-directed post-hoc models have mapped prediction weights directly to known biological cascades, including the cyclic GMP-AMP synthase and stimulator of interferon genes signaling pathway. Interpretable deep learning models processing hematoxylin and eosin slides have identified aggressive macrotrabecular structural patterns to predict microvascular invasion. Multimodal architectures such as token-guided fusion mechanisms and dual-branch exploratory networks simultaneously evaluate whole-slide morphological features, quantitative tumor-stroma ratios, and bulk gene expression profiles.

In transarterial chemoembolization, attribution modeling with SHapley Additive exPlanations has unraveled drivers of variable patient responses. Studies analyzing pre-treatment contrast-enhanced computed tomography parameters and dynamic trajectory tracking of albumin-bilirubin scores have identified distinct responder subtypes and revealed that splenic and renal imaging characteristics significantly inform outcome estimates by reflecting systemic inflammatory states. For systemic therapies encompassing targeted agents and immune checkpoint inhibitors, explainable models have linked baseline radiographic features and cellular pathomic signatures, such as tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte density, to therapeutic responsiveness and specific molecular pathways. Multimodal nomograms and random survival forest models incorporate computed tomography and magnetic resonance radiomics to quantify the biological invasiveness of tumors, reliably forecasting postoperative recurrence in hepatitis B-related malignancies and large hepatocellular carcinomas. Explainable models tailored to specific sub-populations have provided personalized outcome forecasts for alpha-fetoprotein-negative patients, individuals with concurrent diabetes mellitus, and patients at elevated risk for spontaneous tumor rupture or post-hepatectomy liver failure.

The review highlights three fundamental methodological bottlenecks inherent to the prevailing post-hoc explanation paradigm. Post-hoc methods remain fundamentally correlational rather than causal, highlighting statistical dependencies within historical datasets without confirming whether highlighted features represent genuine biological drivers or incidental epiphenomena. A persistent semantic gap separates low-level, pixel-oriented saliency heatmaps from the high-level semantic reasoning utilized by clinicians, leaving models vulnerable to shortcut learning where predictions rely on artifacts rather than disease mechanisms. Current predictive architectures operate as static snapshots trained on historical cohorts, rendering them incapable of self-updating alongside evolving clinical guidelines or actively comparing alternative therapeutic outcomes. The authors delineate a paradigm shift centered on causal inference, concept-driven interpretability, and dynamic collaborative systems.

Methodologies such as double machine learning and causal forests provide mathematical rigor to control for high-dimensional confounding, enabling the estimation of true treatment effects and identifying heterogeneous patient cohorts that derive differential survival benefits from specific interventions. Concept Bottleneck Models offer an architectural solution to bridge the semantic divide by forcing intermediate network layers to predict human-interpretable clinical concepts, such as arterial phase washout or histological nuclear atypia, prior to generating final classifications. Mechanistic interpretability techniques utilizing sparse autoencoders show promising capability in disentangling the complex, polysemantic latent representations of large-scale pathology foundation models into individual, monosemantic biological concepts. The review concludes by emphasizing that the ultimate maturation of explainable artificial intelligence depends on transitioning from passive, retrospective explanatory tools into active, interactive clinical decision partners. stories.Headline: Principals lobby Congress for school funding increases and AI limits
stories.Summary:
Three hundred school leaders and students from across the nation fanned out across Capitol Hill on Nov. 17, 2025, as part of a two-day National Advocacy Summit organized by the National Principals Association. They met with their state representatives and senators to ask for more funding to support public education. The summit took place in Washington, D.C., and the principals met with their state representatives on Capitol Hill. On their agenda were requests to raise federal funding to expand student mental health services, curb school choice programs, and put guardrails on how schools use artificial intelligence. After a long day of lobbying, most principals said they felt hopeful, a decided vibe shift from when they last appealed to Congress in March 2025.

Principals asked their representatives for an increase in Title I funding to $19 billion from $18.4 billion to help high-poverty school districts meet students' needs. They sought an increase in Title II funding to $2.4 billion from $2.14 billion and Title IV-A funding to bolster teacher and principal pipelines and support and expand access to quality mental health care for educators and students. The Federal Scholarship Tax Credit program will go into effect on Jan. 1, 2027, and individuals can claim a federal income tax credit up to $1,700 for qualified cash contributions to certain scholarship-granting organizations. Scholarships can be used for students' approved expenses such as tutoring at a public school or tuition at a private school. Governors of 31 states have opted into the program, fifteen states and the District of Columbia are still undecided, and four have said they will not participate.

Erin Sieh, the principal of Freeman Elementary School in Adams, Neb., said the March 2025 layoff announcement came out hours before they were going to go to the Hill and it felt like their bubble had been burst. Sieh said it felt very defeating and like education wasn't valued, with a lot of uncertainty that was very frightening. Mike Rubin, who leads Uxbridge High School in Uxbridge, Mass., said there's a palpably positive feeling around the willingness to support education and to hear their messages more than the last two or three times they've been here. Rubin said he feels like there's an alignment with what are students' needs and actual next steps to support these needs. Lucas Pugh, the principal of Connolly Middle School in Tempe, Ariz., said the current funding levels are insufficient to retain high-quality educators, provide wraparound student services, and meet testing and graduation requirements.

Jeff Linden, the principal of the approximately 1,000-student Hastings High School in Nebraska, said schools are doing everything they can to work with what they have and find the resources to get creative, but at the same time we need help. At Hastings High School, 54% of students belong to low-income households and 30% require special accommodations in school. Jay Dostal, the principal of Westside High School in Omaha, Neb., said his family is in generational debt trying to teach the youth of tomorrow and asked how we incentivize the youth to continue teaching. Anna Thoma, the assistant principal of Millard High School in Millard, Neb., told an aide to Republican Sen. Pete Rickett that the funding is finite and school vouchers dilute the funding for public schools. Greg Johnson, the longtime principal of West Liberty-Salem High School, an hour outside Columbus, said even policymakers who supported private school choice were open to his view that these programs pull money away from public school students.

Over the past two years, the Trump administration has gutted the Education Department and frozen several federal grants that help schools cover food and medical costs for students. There were cuts to teacher and principal training programs as well, though some grant funding has been restored. The Trump administration has argued that in shutting down the Education Department, they are returning power to the states and to parents by giving them the right to choose the type of education they want for their children. The principals' top fear, of reduced Title 1 and other federal funding, has somewhat dissipated since Congress voted to maintain the existing levels of funding for public education for fiscal year 2026. A group of Republican senators has also proposed a spending package that again preserves virtually all current federal education funding for fiscal year 2027.

Other principals credited the shift in mood to the Democratic takeover of both houses of Congress after the midterm elections and the rise of the so-called blue wave. Rubin and Wiltshire, from Massachusetts, told an aide in Democratic Sen. Ed Markey's office that multiple students from their schools had been hospitalized for mental health conditions. An aide for Markey said their office had written to Google about its decision to bundle AI features with the search function, a move that several prominent school districts have pushed back against. Democratic Rep. Jim McGovern indicated to the Massachusetts contingent that he intends to push to regulate AI sooner than Congress had acted on curbing social media exposure for students. Virginia's newly elected governor Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, reversed her Republican predecessor's decision and pulled out of the program this week.

stories.Headline: Federal contractors face False Claims Act liability for overstated AI capabilities, BCLP partners say
stories.Summary:
Federal contractors that exaggerate or misrepresent artificial intelligence capabilities in bids and billing for government work could face liability under the False Claims Act, according to a Bloomberg Law analysis published on November 20, 2026 by Emmet P. Ong and Susan Carney Lynch, both partners at BCLP. The authors point to regulators who have already pursued misleading claims about AI, including the Securities and Exchange Commission, which has acted against companies for misrepresenting their AI use, and the Federal Trade Commission, which has challenged deceptive claims about AI-enabled products. They describe examples such as a defense contractor claiming its drones can autonomously identify and track targets despite testing that showed undisclosed human intervention, or a medical-device manufacturer overstating diagnostic capabilities to win placement on government supply schedules. The risks also extend to contracts for AI development, where a contractor might falsely report completed model training or successful testing to obtain milestone payments, or bill for AI-enabled analysis never performed.

The analysis says not every promotional claim supports liability, since vague descriptions such as AI-powered differ from specific representations about autonomous operation, detection accuracy or deployed safeguards. It cites the Department of Justice's Civil Cyber-Fraud Initiative as a precedent, noting a university-affiliated defense research contractor that settled allegations last year that a cybersecurity assessment score submitted under defense contracts was based on a fictitious or virtual environment rather than an actual covered system, and a medical-services contractor that settled allegations in 2022, including failing to disclose that patient records were not consistently stored in the secure electronic medical-record system for which it billed the government. Applying established False Claims Act theories would raise questions about materiality, scienter and damages, complicated by the technology's evolving capabilities, and the authors note that under United States ex rel. Escobar v.

Universal Health Services a contractual or regulatory violation does not automatically establish liability because a misrepresentation must have a natural tendency to influence, or be capable of influencing, the government's payment decision. They also cite United States ex rel. Schutte v. SuperValu Inc. for the point that a defendant's subjective beliefs matter, so an objectively reasonable interpretation does not necessarily protect a contractor whose internal communications show it understood its AI representations were false.

On damages, the authors cite United States v. Science Applications International Corp., where the court applied a benefit-of-the-bargain measure to account for the value of services received, and they say evidence that the government would have withheld payment does not itself establish damages. They recommend that federal contractors incorporate reviews of material AI representations into existing contracting and compliance controls, and they set out four practical steps: substantiate claims before making them by comparing proposals, demonstrations and billing submissions with documented testing and actual capabilities; ensure testing supports representations by documenting testing conditions, limitations and results; preserve records connecting commitments to performance, including milestone reports, acceptance tests, deployment records and internal assessments; and reassess representations during performance, since model updates, disabled controls or changes in human oversight may make later claims or certifications inaccurate even if earlier statements were sound. The authors conclude that DOJ may not need a dedicated AI-washing initiative to pursue misrepresentations about AI capabilities, and that as AI becomes embedded in federal procurement and healthcare, contractors should expect greater scrutiny of the gap between promised capabilities and actual performance.

stories.Headline: Incoming Democratic Congress plans stricter AI oversight and safety regulations
stories.Summary:
The artificial intelligence industry is preparing for more aggressive oversight as a Democratic-controlled Congress takes power on November 20, 2026. These incoming lawmakers intend to use their control over congressional committees to investigate tech companies and demand that executives testify in hearings. The new majority plans to introduce various bills that establish safety guidelines for capable models, protect the labor force, and address child safety. These legislative efforts require federal safety requirements for advanced developers and the mandatory reporting of safety breaches. Some proposed rules would force companies to maintain the ability to shut down AI systems if they spiral out of human control.

This shift follows two years of minimal regulation under a Republican-led Congress and President Donald Trump, who believes the industry can self-police. Trump has prioritized winning the AI race against China and has favored voluntary commitments over federal restrictions. Representative Don Beyer of Virginia stated that the government cannot wait for a major catastrophe before implementing meaningful safeguards. Representative Nathaniel Moran of Texas argued that the United States does not have to choose between innovation and safety. Senators Maria Cantwell of Washington and Mike Rounds of South Dakota recently urged National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton to take immediate action against cyberattacks.

They claimed that current defenses are not keeping pace with the ability of AI to exploit software weaknesses. The push for regulation comes as voters express negative attitudes regarding how data centers impact electricity prices and jobs. Recent tech outages at Apple, JPMorgan Chase, and Microsoft have further highlighted the vulnerabilities of interconnected digital infrastructure. While these outages were not linked to cyberattacks, they have spurred calls for a more proactive federal role in protecting financial institutions. Lawmakers are now forming bipartisan caucuses to create legislation that balances industry growth with necessary risk mitigation.

Articles.Title: AI industry braces for tougher oversight under incoming Democratic Congress - WBFF

stories.Headline: Senate passes bill to speed permits for energy projects and data centers
stories.Summary:
The Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, S.5653, on Nov. 19, 2026, by a 62-33 vote, with 14 Democrats and one Democratic-caucusing independent joining most Republicans. Thirty Democrats and one Democratic-caucusing independent voted against the bill. The bill's sponsors are Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Republican Sens. Mike Lee of Utah and Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance vouched for the legislation in a Nov. 20 news conference. The bill must win approval in the House to advance, and the House could amend it, which would require the Senate to approve the new text.

The bill would limit the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the National Historic Preservation Act and the Endangered Species Act. The Natural Resources Defense Council's analysis concluded that under the bill a court "can never invalidate a permit" based on a violation of the National Environmental Policy Act or the National Historic Preservation Act. The bill would cut the time to build a major new transmission line from 10-plus years to five or six. About 2,000 gigawatts of proposed generation and storage are waiting to connect to the grid, and 85 percent of that capacity is solar, wind, or storage. The bill requires data centers to pay for their impact on electricity supply rather than shifting those costs to ratepayers.

Juniper Katz, a University of Massachusetts-Amherst assistant professor of public policy, said there are priorities both sides want and the bill "is not perfect." Geoffrey Henderson, a University of Michigan assistant professor of environmental policy and planning, said it is reasonable to be concerned that development of each kind of project Ruffalo mentioned could be facilitated by the bill. Henderson also said the bill's impacts are highly uncertain, depending on political, market, geopolitical and legal outcomes. The NRDC analysis said that if the Trump administration issued a blanket grant of all permits for oil and gas infrastructure without any environmental review, the bill provides no clear mechanism for a future administration to revoke those permits. Ruffalo's representative did not respond to an inquiry for the article.

Mark Ruffalo said in a Nov. 18 video viewed 22 million times that the bill would fast-track AI data centers, pipelines, mines, power plants and ICE camps while sacrificing clean water, tribal rights, public lands and endangered species. Groups supporting the bill include the Solar Energy Industries Association, the AFL-CIO, the American Petroleum Institute and the Edison Electric Institute. Groups opposing it include the Sierra Club, the Natural Resources Defense Council, the Climate Justice Alliance, a range of tribal organizations, the NAACP and the American Civil Liberties Union. Opponents say their concerns about ICE facilities stem from the use of the National Environmental Policy Act to oppose ICE facilities in court in Maryland, Arizona and Florida. Ezra Klein, a New York Times columnist considered left of center, said he was "unnerved" by conflicting interpretations of certain provisions but still supported the bill.

The bill grew out of concerns from both fossil fuel backers and renewable energy supporters that opponents could stymie projects for years in the courts. Supporters said growing energy demand and rising electricity prices meant a failure to build new infrastructure would consign the United States to a spiral of insufficient energy supplies and higher costs. Critics say the bill effectively guts tools to prevent local governments, citizens, Native American tribes and other local interests from blocking harms caused by such projects. Critics also say the Trump administration, which refuses to acknowledge the possibility of emissions-driven climate change, could wield the law to advance fossil fuel projects over renewable energy infrastructure. The NRDC analysis devotes almost 1,000 words to describing what it considers the bill's positive features, including improving electric capacity by increasing how much power existing transmission lines can carry and enabling construction of new lines.

The bill's fate in the House is uncertain, and the potential for updated language and the difficulty of predicting how courts would interpret its provisions make it difficult to know whether Ruffalo's scenario will come to pass. The bill could also boost non-energy projects that have faced long-running challenges in the courts, including rail and transit, affordable housing and broadband access, Klein wrote. The bill does not directly address ICE detention facilities. The articles leave open whether the House will amend the bill and whether the Senate would then approve new text.

stories.Headline: SpaceX plans to lease 47.3 billion dollars in chips for orbital data centers and AI satellites
stories.Summary:
Space Exploration Technologies, known as SPCX, plans to lease 47.3 billion dollars in chips over approximately five years. This agreement requires payments to continue even if the equipment fails, including a 25.2 billion dollar tranche with an 8.259 percent annual yield. The company also acquired Cursor in August through an all-stock deal valued at about 60 billion dollars. Additionally, SPCX raised 85.7 billion dollars during its June IPO after underwriters utilized their overallotment option.

The company will utilize Nvidia Vera CPUs and the Vera Rubin system for its orbital data centers and the first-generation Starmind AI satellite. Anthropic is expected to pay billions of dollars every month to SpaceX for AI computing capacity. Regarding the IPO, banks earned roughly 500 million dollars in fees, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley each receiving 20.5 percent. The company's prospectus outlines goals for making humanity multi-planetary, creating artificial general intelligence, and building solar-powered data centers in space.

CEO Elon Musk expressed optimism regarding the Terafab chip project and the expansion of data centers. He mentioned that SpaceX and Tesla are increasingly aligned and might be better together, although he announced no deal. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei praised the services provided by SpaceX but noted that the future infrastructure mix for Anthropic remains uncertain. Meanwhile, Anysphere, the parent company of Cursor, informed Congress that it may phase out Chinese AI models due to geopolitical risks.

Space Exploration Technologies advanced its rocket recovery and reuse capabilities over the most recent weekend. The company continues to integrate advanced hardware to support its ambitious goals for space-based computing. Future developments depend on the successful deployment of the Starmind AI satellite and the orbital data center network. These initiatives aim to expand the reach of artificial intelligence beyond the limits of Earth.

stories.Headline: Microsoft and JPMorgan Chase outages and a US flight grounding stem from technical upgrades, not attacks
stories.Summary:
A series of technical failures disrupted American infrastructure and global services starting on Friday, November 14, 2026. Federal aviation authorities ordered a nationwide grounding of planes, while a Microsoft outage affected millions of users worldwide. These events were followed by a widespread outage at United Airlines on Monday afternoon and significant transaction slowdowns at several top United States banks. Other strange occurrences on Friday included a tanker hitting a cruise ship in New Orleans, drones over a British air base, and a bomb discovery in Illinois.

The aviation crisis required a ground stop lasting more than four hours because a technology upgrade overloaded antiquated air traffic control equipment. Microsoft reported that its own service disruption resulted from a network capacity upgrade that surfaced after a recent network change. Financial instability began when a technical issue at JPMorgan Chase created ripple effects across the broader banking system. United Airlines stated that its Monday technical problems specifically impacted departing flights rather than aircraft already in the air.

Bryan Bedford of the Federal Aviation Administration and representatives from Microsoft both stated that no malicious activity caused these failures. A spokesperson for Chase confirmed that their banking issues were not the result of a cyberattack and that they were working to restore services. While some citizens expressed fear that these events signaled a coordinated attack on the economy, officials maintained that the causes were prosaic. The Federal Aviation Administration indicated that airline schedules should have returned to normal by late Sunday.

stories.Headline: ICC re-elects Jay Shah as Silicon Valley Unicorns use AI to make mid-match cricket decisions
stories.Summary:
The article, a Guardian opinion column by Barney Ronay published on 20 November 2026, concerns Jay Shah, who was re-elected unopposed this week as president of the International Cricket Council. The article also concerns the San Francisco Unicorns, a Major League Cricket team that uses artificial intelligence in making mid-match decisions on the field. Ronay first heard about this in an interview with Ravichandran Ashwin in the Cricketer Magazine. The article also discusses Jensen Huang, president of Nvidia, and proposals to regulate new global T20 leagues.

The proposals to regulate more aggressively the rush of new global T20 leagues were postponed to the next ICC conference. The Unicorns are the brainchild of Anand Rajaraman and Venky Harinarayan, Silicon Valley types whose stated aim is treating a cricket team like a startup. Their key tool is called Cric Lens, which provides real-time stats, pitch data and player information plus the predictive power of every T20 game ever played. The process is described as Human-in-the-Loop Execution. The Unicorns' roster includes celebrity endorsements such as Pat Cummins.

Shah was re-elected unopposed at a meeting in Bali, where the article says he wore his usual glazed facial expression. The article says Shah is the son of Indian prime minister Narendra Modi's oldest political ally. Rajaraman and Harinarayan are Stanford graduates of the mid-90s turned Bay-Area digital rainmaker types, like Huang. One of the founders says the ideas are at the level of human civilisation and cannot be kept contained, and that it is cricket for now but why not the NFL, football or soccer. The article says Huang has spent years perfecting a machine that can make every other person's job vanish.

Finn Allen, a New Zealand batsman for the Unicorns, spoke enthusiastically about the effect of the tool in the season just past. Allen said it is not all AI or no AI but the perfect amount of contribution, after an eight-wicket win against Washington Freedom. The article says the Unicorns' backstory reads like a pitch for an app, with endless giddy chat about scaling up the product. The article says AI is already present in elite football scouting systems, and that Formula One is already a machine-led activity now embracing robo-integration. The article says there is a theory big tech companies have begun to buy into sport, citing Bezos at Liverpool, as a hedge against AI.

The article says the latest suggestion being punted about is that Huang is irreplaceable as president of Nvidia. The article says the ICC conference was widely seen as disappointingly inconclusive. The article says captaincy is a skill and sport is a live test of human capacity, and that using a machine to make captaincy decisions should obviously be regulated, understood, debated and capped at source. The article says the Unicorns may be the tiniest twinkle in the sporting sky right now but carry a potentially significant contagion. The article says AI would undoubtedly be better at managing Manchester United than the lost souls currently passing through those gates.

The article says the 20th century gave visions of a flowering of culture and the death of human drudgery. The article says the current version is one in which four people become incredibly wealthy while the rest live in an asbestos box, face clamped into a smartphone. The article says the Luddites actually had some pretty good points about the industrial loom. The article says sport, the human spectacle, is seen as safe from new technology, like buying gold when currencies go haywire. The article says so much of football is essentially guesswork, sniff-test and hunch-based, all of the stuff artificial intelligence exists to replace.

The article asks whether we will ever have the will and the collective backbone to resist and regulate this stuff and police its limits. The article ends by urging readers to resist the machines and release Finn Allen from the Phantom Zone. The article says the proposals on T20 leagues will go to the next disappointingly inconclusive ICC conference. The article does not say when that conference will be held. The article gives no response from Shah, the ICC, the Unicorns or Huang to its claims.

stories.Headline: Researchers propose AI-assisted roadmap to overcome SuperDEM-CFD bottlenecks in gas-solid reactor simulation
stories.Summary:
Researchers published a peer-reviewed review in ENGINEERING Chemical Engineering on November 21, 2026, examining the state of SuperDEM-CFD technology for simulating gas-solid reactors, according to a report by Blake Davidson on Scienmag. The work focuses on systems where gas-solid multiphase flows govern operations, including fluidized bed reactors, packed bed catalytic units, and facilities conducting thermochemical conversion of biomass and plastics. Because most actual particles feature non-spherical geometries rather than ideal spheres, capturing their complex multi-scale behavior remains fundamentally challenging for engineers seeking process intensification and reliable scale-up. The discrete element method coupled with computational fluid dynamics, commonly designated as DEM-CFD, serves as an established technique for resolving particle-level collisions, hydrodynamics, heat transfer, and mass exchange, but extending it to non-spherical particles through the superquadric equation, an approach known as SuperDEM, introduces severe mathematical and computational complications.

The review identified four critical bottlenecks restricting industrial deployment of SuperDEM-CFD technology, the first being anisotropic contact hydrodynamics and persistent numerical singularities that arise at sharp particle edges. The remaining three obstacles encompass incomplete frameworks for modeling heat transfer, immature reaction models tailored to non-spherical surfaces, and exceptionally heavy computational expenses when simulating systems containing massive particle counts. To overcome contact mechanics failures, the researchers proposed adopting a reduced-space Newton iteration method designed to circumvent numerical singularities at sharp edges, and for thermal modeling they recommend developing generalized shape-factor Nusselt correlations. Modeling chemical transformations in irregularly shaped particles also requires specialized formulations, so the authors put forward a shrinking core reaction model adapted directly to superquadric coordinates to accurately capture progressing reaction fronts.

To tackle the prohibitive computational burden of simulating large-scale particulate systems, the roadmap outlines a strategy combining coarse-grained particle models with graphics processing unit acceleration to drastically expand accessible system sizes. The roadmap emphasizes the transformative role of artificial intelligence, noting that deep learning algorithms can construct universal drag and heat transfer correlations by training on detailed direct numerical simulation datasets. Furthermore, AI techniques can generate interpretable chemical reaction kinetics while accelerating stiff numerical solvers to significantly reduce computational overhead during intensive calculations, and machine learning workflows can assist engineers in analyzing numerical convergence and optimizing mathematical stability when formulating new computational solvers. Together, these mathematical formulations and computational strategies provide a clear development roadmap for next-generation SuperDEM-CFD modeling platforms.

By resolving longstanding physical and numerical bottlenecks, the researchers aim to advance predictive reactor design and establish real-time digital twins for industrial gas-solid reactors, supporting more sustainable and efficient chemical processing systems. The review states that modern chemical engineering faces significant hurdles in scaling up reactors and supporting carbon neutrality, particularly in systems where gas-solid multiphase flows govern operations. The articles give no further details on the authors, their institutions, or a publication date beyond the November 21, 2026 report, and they do not say what happens next beyond the stated aims of the roadmap.

stories.Headline: Rep. Vince Fong introduces bipartisan bill to place private AI experts inside CISA
stories.Summary:
Representative Vince Fong introduced a bipartisan bill on November 20, 2026, to strengthen cybersecurity in the United States. This legislative action follows several widespread technical outages that have recently impacted various systems across the entire country. These outages included a nationwide plane ground stop and issues affecting the National Security Agency and multiple banks. Other entities impacted by these technical failures included Apple, United Airlines, and the Outlook service provided by Microsoft. The bill aims to bolster national defenses against a surge of cyberattacks that are related to artificial intelligence.

The Bridging Resources for Innovative Defense and Government Expertise in Artificial Intelligence Act is the formal name of the bill. It would authorize the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, known as CISA, to collaborate with private sector AI professionals. The legislation calls for a pilot project that would allow about 100 private sector workers to serve within CISA. If approved, the bill would also require a semi-annual report regarding the status and potential improvements of the program. These measures are designed to help the government better defend critical infrastructure from sophisticated and frequent AI-related attacks.

Representative Vince Fong, a Republican representing Bakersfield, stated that communities and critical industries are struggling to keep up with AI attacks. He noted that cyberattacks in the Central Valley have increasingly targeted water systems, hospitals, and schools to steal sensitive data. Fong argued that bringing in emerging technology specialists ensures that national experts have the tools needed to modernize systems. He believes these specialists will help address vulnerabilities and protect the essential services that Americans rely on every day. Fong emphasized that these real threats are not waiting for the government to catch up to the technology.

Representative Josh Gottheimer, a Democrat from New Jersey, co-authored the bill and stated that adversaries use AI to attack networks. He claimed that the agency on the front lines of defense does not have enough capacity to keep pace. Gottheimer described the act as a common sense fix to bring in the best tech minds to hunt intruders. He believes these experts can patch vulnerabilities and stress-test AI tools before they are exploited by any hostile actors. He stated that protecting national security, water systems, and families should not be treated as a partisan political issue.

The articles provide background on the necessity of the bill by citing recent technical failures across various American sectors. These failures include the aforementioned ground stop for planes and the outages at the National Security Agency and several banks. The legislation is a response to the increasing frequency and sophistication of cyberattacks targeting critical infrastructure and sensitive data. Specifically, the text highlights how schools and hospitals in the Central Valley have become targets for these digital attacks. This context establishes the perceived urgency for the government to integrate private sector expertise into its cybersecurity framework.

The next step for the legislation is to seek approval to authorize the pilot project for the private sector workers. The bill would then establish the requirement for semi-annual reports to monitor the progress and effectiveness of the program. The articles do not state if the bill has been scheduled for a vote or a formal debate. They leave open whether other members of Congress support the measure beyond the two named authors of the bill. It remains unclear how the 100 private sector workers will be selected or compensated for their service.

stories.Headline: Law Society issues practice note tying solicitors' AI use to existing duties and insurance checks
stories.Summary:
The Law Society published a new practice note on 21 October 2026 that brings together existing professional obligations and practical guidance on using AI in legal practice. It follows the SRA's strongly worded warning notice in August, which Hogan Lovells Cadwalader examined at the time. The note distinguishes AI used in the "practice of law", such as legal research, drafting and analysis, from AI used in the "business of law", such as billing and marketing. It states that there is no AI-specific regulator for the legal sector, so solicitors' use of AI sits within existing professional, data protection and cybersecurity frameworks, including the SRA Standards and Regulations. The note also addresses insurance, highlighting the potential implications of firms' use of AI for both professional indemnity and cyber insurance.

The note says the SRA has not certified AI products and that responsibility for work produced using AI remains with the solicitor and cannot be transferred to the technology provider. It states that AI cannot reliably verify its own output, so lawyers should check AI-generated material against authoritative sources rather than asking the same, or another, AI system to confirm it. It cites Ayinde v London Borough of Haringey and Al-Haroun v Qatar National Bank [2025] EWHC 1383 (Admin), in which the High Court addressed the use of false authorities and emphasised lawyers' responsibility for material put before the court. It cites SRA v Kumar, in which a Registered Foreign Lawyer was removed from the Register of Foreign Lawyers after repeatedly relying on false or unsupported AI-generated authorities, including following an express warning. It cites R v FGD [2026] EWCA Crim 918, in which the Court of Appeal warned that using AI to prepare a witness for cross-examination may amount to coaching and, in an extreme case, create sufficient unfairness for the court to consider excluding evidence.

The note states that although there is currently no general obligation to disclose the use of AI, transparency may be appropriate where AI has been used materially in preparing documents. It states that a witness statement must remain the witness's own evidence and accurately reflect their recollection. It cites the Civil Justice Council's final recommendations on AI use in court documents, published on 29 October 2026, which propose that factual witnesses should declare that AI has not generated or influenced the substantive content of their statements, with a different disclosure requirement for expert evidence. It cites R (Munir) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2026] UKUT 81 (IAC), in which the tribunal highlighted the potential confidentiality and privilege consequences of uploading client material to a publicly available AI tool. It states that using an "enterprise" or specialist "legal AI" product does not remove these risks, and that information described as anonymised will only fall outside data protection law where individuals are genuinely no longer identifiable.

The note states that AI may create new categories of potentially relevant material, including prompts, draft outputs and audit logs, whose treatment under existing privilege principles remains largely untested. It states that a business user may ask AI for legal advice and create unprivileged material, even if it is later sent to the legal team. It states that professional competence increasingly includes understanding the systems lawyers use and their limitations, and that one particular concern is automation bias, where users place undue confidence in an output simply because it has been produced by technology. It states that professional liability could eventually arise from failing to use AI where a reasonably competent lawyer would have done so, and that there is currently no positive professional duty to use AI, but the applicable standard of care may evolve as increasingly reliable tools become embedded in legal practice.

It states that the risks become more significant with AI agents and agentic AI, which can take actions and carry out multi-step processes across systems with reduced human intervention. The note states that firms should limit systems' permissions to what is genuinely necessary and build in appropriate human review and approval points as autonomy increases. It states that firms need effective AI governance even if they have not formally adopted AI, because staff may independently use publicly available tools, creating the risk of "shadow AI". It states that appropriate controls may include an AI-use policy, approved-tools list, restrictions on the information that may be entered into AI systems, staff training and clear processes for escalating errors or data breaches.

It states that clients should receive appropriate information about how AI may be used on their matters, which firms can address upfront through engagement letters or terms of business. It states that where work is billed by time, firms should not charge for the hours the task would have taken without AI, and that any separate AI or technology charge should be transparent, agreed appropriately and should not duplicate other fees. The note states that AI risks extend beyond hallucination and confidentiality, and include bias and discrimination, cybersecurity, operational resilience and concentration risk arising from dependence on particular technology providers. On professional indemnity insurance, it recommends that firms consider whether their use of AI changes their professional indemnity risk profile or falls outside the considerations upon which their insurance was arranged.

It recommends that firms check whether their existing professional indemnity policy, proposal form or renewal documentation asks about matters such as the use of AI, automation and legal technology. It recommends that firms consider their disclosure obligations including in respect of risks that the firm ought to be aware of, in addition to those which the firm is aware of. It recommends that firms maintain clear supervisory documentation and evidence of risk management, as insurers may be interested in the firm's AI governance processes and may ask about the extent of human oversight of AI-assisted work. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Hybrid Artificial Intelligence Framework Calibrates Urban Traffic Fundamental Diagrams in Jordan
stories.Summary:
Transportation engineers developed and tested a hybrid calibration framework combining video trajectory analytics, mobile smartphone telemetry, and machine learning optimization to measure how vehicles move along congested urban roadways. Researcher Laith D. Alomari conducted the study, published in the Journal of King Saud University ,  Engineering Sciences, evaluating macroscopic traffic fundamental diagrams across thirty heterogeneous road segments in Irbid, Jordan. The experimental campaign gathered empirical field observations across thirty distinct locations throughout Irbid, including major arterials, intersection approaches, roundabouts, and mid-block road segments. Each site was monitored for thirty to sixty minutes during multiple weekdays, covering both peak and off-peak travel periods. In total, the field deployments produced approximately 3,000 validated observation points.

The investigation treated each monitored road segment and intersection approach as an independent link-level traffic system rather than merging all data points into a single city-wide diagram. Data collection relied on thirty high-definition video cameras recording at 1080p resolution and thirty frames per second, processed using YOLOv8 with Deep SORT. The team also gathered mobile sensor telemetry from volunteer drivers operating approximately twenty participating vehicles, logging GPS coordinates and accelerometer signals at 1 Hz. The validated microscopic trajectory records were aggregated into macroscopic traffic variables using fifteen-second observation intervals. Speed curves declined sharply once traffic density reached approximately 35 to 40 vehicles per kilometer, while flow-density plots peaked within a critical density boundary of 30 to 35 vehicles per kilometer.

The researchers implemented a sequential, artificial intelligence-assisted optimization routine pairing a Genetic Algorithm with Bayesian Optimization to refine model parameters while maintaining physical interpretability. The Genetic Algorithm conducted a global parameter search, capping free-flow speed between 40 and 120 kilometers per hour and jam density between 80 and 250 vehicles per kilometer. Bayesian Optimization then applied a Gaussian process surrogate model with exploration-exploitation acquisition functions to locate optimal basins of convergence with high numerical stability. The two-stage routine yielded parameter variance of less than 8 percent across test iterations and showed smooth convergence within fifteen to twenty-five generations. The authors emphasized that reported numerical parameters characterize link-level performance across specific road sections and roundabouts rather than serving as network-wide macroscopic fundamental diagrams or universal engineering standards.

Baseline formulations yielded free-flow speeds generally estimated between 62 and 68 kilometers per hour and jam densities clustering around 130 to 160 vehicles per kilometer. At Site S02, the baseline Underwood model achieved a coefficient of determination of 0.93 and a root mean square error of 4.9 kilometers per hour, outperforming the linear and logarithmic alternatives. The refinement process reduced root mean square errors by approximately 15 to 25 percent across the evaluated sites compared with standard baseline regression, while lifting the coefficient of determination for the Underwood formulation up to 0.96. A Support Vector Regression model with a radial basis function kernel, evaluated on a 70 percent training, 15 percent validation, and 15 percent testing split, achieved a coefficient of determination of 0.97 and a root mean square error of 3.9 kilometers per hour. The authors noted its functional black-box nature, which prevents direct physical interpretation of structural roadway indicators such as roadway carrying capacity or spatial vehicle packing thresholds.

Classical analytical expressions, originally introduced decades ago under assumptions of uniform vehicular streams and strict lane compliance, often diverge from empirical observations in rapidly growing developing cities. In these environments, mixed fleets, weak lane discipline, and volatile flow transitions complicate standard theoretical assumptions, creating an operational need for low-cost, localized calibration methods. The investigators initially fitted four canonical analytical formulations using standard nonlinear least-squares regression: the linear model proposed by Greenshields, Greenberg’s logarithmic formulation, Underwood’s exponential decay structure, and the multi-regime exponential-polynomial model introduced by Drake and colleagues. The vehicular mix mirrored standard developing urban streams, comprising passenger automobiles, minibuses, motorcycles, and light commercial vehicles. Data collection relied on a dual-modality sensing strategy designed to bypass expensive fixed roadway detectors such as inductive loops or radar systems.

The framework integrated the calibrated models into a physics-guided hybrid architecture, with the evolutionary-optimized analytical equations defining the base physical trajectory and the Support Vector Regression component acting as an adaptive residual corrector predicting localized deviations. When aggregated across all field study locations using observation-weighted metrics, the resulting empirical dataset yielded an average free-flow speed of approximately 65 kilometers per hour, a critical density of approximately 32 vehicles per kilometer, and a jam density of approximately 145 vehicles per kilometer. The field empirical trials were confined to thirty locations within a single city, excluding broader environmental variables such as inclement weather, variable geometric grades, and dynamic traffic signal splits. Because traffic density was derived through flow and speed calculations, comparative evaluations measured relative mathematical fit rather than causal transport mechanisms. The research team identified the low-cost sensing workflow and hybrid algorithmic framework as scalable and transferable tools for developing metropolitan regions, while cautioning that direct operational deployments require localized parameter recalibration.

Articles.Title: Hybrid Artificial Intelligence Framework Calibrates Urban Traffic Fundamental Diagrams in Jordan

stories.Headline: Researchers find phone accelerometer models detect quakes best at higher sampling rates and tight false alarm budgets
stories.Summary:
Researchers published a comparative evaluation showing that deep learning models running directly on smartphones can detect earthquake signals from built-in accelerometers, but how well they perform depends heavily on sensor sampling rates and the allowed number of false alarms. The team tested five neural network architectures to tackle long-standing problems in crowd-sourced earthquake early warning, including severe data imbalance, limited computing power on phones, and the difficulty of modeling signals over time. Crowd-sourced warning systems use accelerometers inside everyday smartphones to widen seismic monitoring across earthquake-prone regions, yet deployment has been held back by the huge imbalance between constant human vibration and rare earthquakes. To benchmark the architectures rigorously, the investigators built a unified dataset of 35.4 million two-second windows drawn from roughly 186,000 recordings, covering broadband seismometer traces, shake-table smartphone experiments and human-activity data in a 60-gigabyte archive.

The team handled training difficulties with a stratified majority-class under-sampling approach based on a sampling index, which kept the original 60-gigabyte archive while balancing the test-set positive-to-negative ratio from 79.74 to 1 down to 1 to 1. The same method cut the number of training windows per epoch by a factor of 8.6, making training more practical. Model comparisons showed contrasting strengths: an attention-augmented network combining convolutional layers, bidirectional recurrent units and Bahdanau attention reached an area under the curve of 0.9617 with the smallest generalization gap, an absolute difference of 0.004. A dilated temporal convolutional network reached a higher overall area under the curve of 0.9688, but because broadband seismometers made up 99.99 percent of positive test windows, the researchers stratified validation by sensor provenance.

Discrimination stayed robust at 0.944 to 0.962 when seismic and non-seismic classes shared the same instrument type, but accuracy dropped to between 0.86 and 0.92 for earthquakes recorded on 50-hertz smartphones. Performance fell to chance levels on devices sampling at 25 hertz, where the crucial 0.5 to 20 hertz seismic band is only partly observable. On the deployment side, 8-bit quantized models occupied between 44 and 138 kilobytes, while built-in operator variants on Android devices needed 239 to 486 kilobytes and ran inferences in 3.2 to 6.4 milliseconds per window. Under a budget allowing 100 false alarms per device-day, the Bahdanau attention architecture detected 76 percent of seismometer-recorded events and 61 percent of smartphone-recorded events, while the dilated temporal convolutional network detected 53 percent and 33 percent respectively.

The evaluation was carried out by Şara, Almaqtari, Eken, Koç, Arslan, Kahveci and Atay, and their paper, Real-time seismic detection with edge-AI: a balanced comparison, appears in Cluster Computing, volume 30, issue 1, Article 47, with DOI 10.1007/s10586-026-06833-z. The findings show that the ranking of models by unconstrained receiver operating metrics can reverse once realistic false alarm budgets are applied, which matters for anyone choosing an architecture for a phone-based warning system. The results also indicate that sensor bandwidth sets a hard limit, since phones sampling at 25 hertz cannot reliably capture the seismic frequencies the models depend on. The articles do not say what deployment or follow-up work comes next.
