stories.Headline: AI coding tools reduce engineer satisfaction and change valued skills
stories.Summary:
Software engineers say artificial intelligence coding tools are reducing the satisfaction they get from solving difficult problems, and the shift is changing which technical skills are valued while raising concerns about how junior developers are trained. Gemma Rodgers, a UK-based software developer, told CNBC that reaching a working solution feels less rewarding when AI produces it quickly, and she worried that engineers could lose essential technical abilities if they lean too heavily on automated answers. A 2026 Stack Overflow survey found that 83 per cent of software developer respondents use at least one AI tool. Rodgers, who began studying computer science in 2002, said the joy of spending weeks fixing a hard bug has been somewhat removed by AI, and she described the satisfaction from AI-generated solutions as a breadcrumb of joy rather than a full meal of joy.

The growing use of AI is also changing what companies expect from developers, who are now more often required to review AI-produced code for usefulness rather than write every line themselves. James Broadhead, Chief Technology Officer at Taktile, told CNBC that developers who once took three weeks to build a prototype can now generate ten in an afternoon, and he said the challenge lies in identifying which versions are effective. He added that engineers are no longer reading all the AI-generated code, which can complicate understanding how a project is organised. Joshua Whle, Chief Executive Officer of Mindstone, believes the trend is creating a widening gap between employees who can use AI effectively and those who cannot, and he suggested AI could foster what he called 100X engineers compared with the earlier idea of 10X engineers. Whle acknowledged that developers who enjoy traditional coding might find the change difficult, because skills they honed for years are no longer necessarily the most valued.

The shift also poses concerns for people entering the software industry, since junior engineers typically learn by writing basic code, debugging and solving problems, and AI could automate those tasks and cost them crucial chances to develop practical skills. Chris Sees, Chief Executive Officer of Hoxton Mix and a software engineer with more than 20 years of experience, said routine tasks are vital for young developers' learning. He advised companies to integrate AI into training rather than let it become a shortcut, and he described AI as a junior engineer that requires human supervision. Rodgers, while not against AI, prefers using it for repetitive tasks and keeping challenging problems for herself, because she believes struggle is essential for job satisfaction.

stories.Headline: Developer builds a Redis cache before a RAG system to cut AI token costs
stories.Summary:
During the World Cup this year, the author built Rune Score, a sports analytics chatbot that looks simple from the outside. Under the hood it is a distributed system handling the freshness of sports data, user rephrasing, extraction failures, LLM call costs, streaming, memory, fallbacks and security. The author's first move was not a vector database but a Redis cache built around a simple labeling rule. Identical requests get an identical key, something like the football matchup Argentina vs. Spain. The savings were immediate, as the author documented in a LinkedIn article on Rune Score.

Redis is defined as an open-source, in-memory data structure store used as a database, cache, message broker and streaming engine. RAG, short for retrieval-augmented generation, is defined by AWS as a technique used to augment a large language model with external data, such as a company's internal documents. Without the cache, a fresh extraction followed by an analysis can consume up to 23,000 input tokens: scraped content, context, history. With a cache that hits the same key, that number drops to about 5,000 tokens, a 4.5-fold reduction in the single most expensive part of the pipeline. In the Rune Score experiment, a RAG hit brings a request down from 20,000 to 8,000 tokens, a 60% reduction.

The author says it is usually smarter to start simple, because a basic cache is cheap and fast and teaches you what people actually want. The author says a simple cache has one weakness: it only recognizes a question if it is asked the exact same way. The author says a smarter memory system costs a little more to run and can feel slightly slower, but that trade is worth it. The author says the best refactor is not the one that is theoretically right but the one that lets you roll back in seconds if the real metrics do not hold up. The author says to build the cheap, fast cache first, let it teach you what your users actually ask for, and only then invest in a full retrieval system.

According to Google Cloud's documentation, the closer objects are in the embedding space, the more semantically similar they are, and greater distances indicate greater semantic dissimilarity. TechTarget defines garbage in, garbage out, or GIGO, as the idea that in any system, the quality of output is determined by the quality of the input. Redis's own engineering blog says the consistent takeaway across these studies is that combining retrievers tends to surface more relevant results in the top positions than either method on its own. People might write "FC Barcelona vs Real Madrid" or "Barça ,  Madrid," and a strict cache treats each variant as a completely different request.

If 10 people ask your product the same question within a reasonable time window, rerunning the full, expensive pipeline 10 times is money burned for no reason. The author says AI cost usually comes from what you repeat unnecessarily. The author says the biggest quality bottleneck in a RAG system usually is not the retrieval technology itself but what feeds it. The author says every time he cut corners on how much content got extracted from a source, the resulting analysis got visibly worse downstream.

The author says trusting a single relevance score is fragile, and combining exact keyword matches, meaning-based search and how recent the information is, then merging those into one ranking, beats relying on any single signal alone. Redis is precise and cheap but rigid, while RAG is more flexible and durable but costs more to run. The author says Redis and RAG are not competing choices but sequential ones. The author says RAG buys tolerance for how people actually phrase things, memory that outlives a cache's expiration window and an architecture that is reusable well beyond the one product you built it for.

The author says the gap between the 80% reduction from an exact Redis hit and the 60% reduction from a RAG hit is not a strike against RAG. The author says what he learned building Rune Score applies to almost any AI product that has to stay fast, cheap and accurate at the same time. The article gives no further plans or next steps. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Software factory creator builds Squid to automate coding while humans steer planning and final review
stories.Summary:
A software factory is a system that automates software creation by turning raw inputs such as bug reports and feature ideas into shipped software, according to an O'Reilly Media article reported by TechGig on November 21, 2026. The author of that article built a software factory named Squid to manage small and medium projects with reduced human oversight. The approach focuses on combining good software principles with coding agents rather than on constantly changing labels like prompt engineering or context engineering. The article says the concept is gaining traction for automating development and aims to generate clean, maintainable code with minimal human intervention. The factory runs through eight stages grouped into three categories, which are what to build, actual building and checking, and self-improving.

The first category covers triage, brainstorming and planning, the second covers implementation, review, CI and release, and the third covers monitoring and incident response, which feeds production signals back in as new tasks. A context layer supplies user analytics, competitor analysis, research and documentation to guide agent decisions across the stages, and the article says this layer is often implemented as an LLM Wiki. Humans stay indispensable during brainstorming and planning, where taste and high-leverage decisions are made, while agents handle implementing, testing and initial review, and humans return for the final pull request review and merge. Zach Lloyd, the CEO of Warp, is quoted as saying that software engineering will become factory engineering. The article says effective planning with powerful models like Fable lets cheaper models such as Opus or Sonnet execute tasks efficiently, while a weak plan can lead to more retries, more tokens and higher overall costs.

The author advises against overbuilding factories and stresses the need for granular control and human intervention points so workflows can be debugged or redirected. The article presents the shift as a move toward actionable outcomes over evolving engineering labels. The article does not say what happens next beyond describing the structure and roles, and it gives no timeline for adoption. It frames the software factory as a way to redefine roles in the Software Development Life Cycle, with humans steering the early and final decisions and agents doing the intermediate work. The author's guidance is to keep human checkpoints in place rather than removing oversight entirely.

stories.Headline: Yunhong Han and co-authors present ReactNexus, a generative framework that maps reaction networks from reactants alone
stories.Summary:
A paper posted to arXiv on 21 November 2026 by Yunhong Han and 18 other authors describes ReactNexus, a generative framework that produces transition-state candidates directly from reactant graphs without requiring products to be specified in advance. The framework then predicts the chemical species those candidates connect and refines the resulting pathways using a reactive machine-learned potential to guide exploration of the reaction network. Its models were trained on a quantum-chemical database of 130 million structures drawn from 1.1 million reaction records, covering 11 elements and multiple charge and spin states. The authors say the work shows how generative models can extend mechanistic analysis to increasingly complex reaction mixtures.

On held-out reactions, 93.6% of the generated candidates refined to valid transition states at the density functional theory level, and 83.3% connected the supplied reactants to distinct products. Across decomposition, complex rearrangements and organocatalysis, ReactNexus showed how competing mechanisms shape product formation and uncovered pathways that previous studies had missed. In a multisite nucleophilic aromatic substitution, it identified diarylation products that explained LC-MS signals which had initially gone unassigned, with the structural assignments supported by NMR after isolation. ReactNexus also predicted an additional product family that was not detected under the initial conditions, and later experiments at higher temperature provided LC-MS evidence supporting its formation.

The authors frame the work as a response to a specific difficulty, noting that automated saddle-point searches can explore from reactants alone but their computational cost rises sharply as competing pathways accumulate across successive steps. They also observe that machine-learning approaches to transition state generation typically require predefined products, even though identifying those products is a central goal of exploration. ReactNexus is presented as a way around both constraints, generating candidates from reactants and then refining the pathways with the reactive potential. The abstract highlights the potential of generative models to extend mechanistic analysis to increasingly complex reaction mixtures.

The paper is titled Generative discovery of chemical reaction networks, and its author list runs from Yunhong Han and Gaopeng Ren through Chenru Duan and Qiyuan Zhao. The work was posted on arXiv along with a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source, and the posting carries the standard arXivLabs notice describing that framework for collaborators who develop and share features on the site. That notice states that individuals and organizations working with arXivLabs have accepted values of openness, community, excellence and user data privacy, and that arXiv works only with partners who adhere to them. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the higher-temperature experiments already reported.

stories.Headline: Researchers develop compact visual latents to improve remote sensing for large language models
stories.Summary:
Meng Tang, Siyuan Du, Yuxin Liu, Shuaishuai Cao, Di Wang, and Haonan Guo published a research paper on November 21, 2026, regarding ultra-high-resolution remote sensing. The researchers developed a method to compress detailed image crops into short sequences of continuous visual latents to help multimodal large language models. This approach addresses the problem where global overviews hide small objects and detailed crops use too much computational context. By encoding high-resolution crops into latent memory tokens, the team sought to determine if these compact forms could retain fine-grained evidence.

The system utilizes a 64-token memory that achieves a compression rate between 7.6 and 9.9 times compared to retained crop tokens. When tested across two generations of Qwen-VL on the LRS-GRO dataset, this method improved accuracy by 2.5 to 4.8 percentage points over using only downsampled global images. The researchers also observed consistent behavior on the XLRS-Bench to validate the predictive utility of the latent memory. Substituting memory from different images or regions reduced accuracy by 5.8 to 7.4 percentage points, which was worse than removing the memory entirely.

The authors explained that these results prove predictions depend directly on the encoded regional evidence stored within the compact visual latents. They noted that restoring the original source crop within the same model reduced the accuracy loss caused by zeroing or removing the memory. This evidence suggests that the availability of specific local data is the primary factor governing how these latents contribute to model performance. The findings establish that compact visual latents can successfully retain useful local evidence for complex remote sensing tasks.

Articles.Title: Out of Sight, Into Memory: Compact Visual Latents Retain Local Evidence in Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing

stories.headline_source: Out of Sight, Into Memory: Compact Visual Latents Retain Local Evidence in Ultra-High-Resolution Remote Sensing

stories.Headline: Researchers recover pruned MoE experts without training through gated reuse
stories.Summary:
Linliang Chen, Yan Zhong, Wang Kang, Sai Li, Ji Wu and Ji Liu posted a paper to arXiv on 21 November 2026 describing a method for recovering the work of pruned experts in Mixture-of-Experts large language models. Mixture-of-Experts models activate only a few experts per token while generally keeping all experts in GPU memory for high efficiency, and expert pruning reduces that memory footprint but discards the contribution of the pruned experts. The authors report that the functionalities of pruned experts can be efficiently reconstructed from the activated remaining experts. They propose GEAR, which stands for Gated Expert Activation Reuse and reuses the scaled outputs of reliable activated experts without any training or additional expert computation. They also propose GEAR$^2$, which adds an ultra-lightweight residual to further recover what reuse cannot express.

The work was tested on five Mixture-of-Experts large language models ranging from 16B to 106B parameters, with 25% and 50% of experts pruned. GEAR improves over its training-free counterparts in nearly every setting, by up to 4 percentage points in terms of accuracy. GEAR$^2$ outperforms baseline approaches by up to 2.75 percentage points in every setting across nine zero-shot benchmarks. The authors report larger advantages, up to 2.72 percentage points higher, under more aggressive pruning of up to 50%. The paper contrasts its approach with existing remedies that rely on static substitutes, merge experts at the cost of altering their functions, or require costly recovery training.

The paper lists Linliang Chen, Yan Zhong, Wang Kang, Sai Li, Ji Wu and Ji Liu as its authors, and the abstract presents the findings and the two proposed methods in the authors' own account. The authors state that GEAR reuses the scaled outputs of reliable activated experts without any training or additional expert computation, and that GEAR$^2$ adds an ultra-lightweight residual for what reuse cannot express. They describe the reconstruction of pruned experts' functionalities from the activated remaining experts as a finding of the paper. The abstract frames the motivation around the GPU memory footprint that expert pruning reduces and the discarded contribution of pruned experts that existing remedies handle in other ways.

The articles provide no information on what happens next, such as release of code, further testing or publication beyond the arXiv posting. The abstract reports results on nine zero-shot benchmarks and on models from 16B to 106B parameters, with pruning at 25% and 50%. The arXiv listing notes that a PDF, experimental HTML and TeX source are available for the paper. It also describes arXivLabs as a framework allowing collaborators to develop and share features directly on the arXiv website, and states that arXiv is committed to openness, community, user data privacy and partnership with organizations that adhere to those values.

Articles.Title: GEAR$^2$: Pruned Experts Live On through Gated Reuse of Activated Experts and a Missing-Mass Residual

stories.Headline: International Court of Justice rules Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
stories.Summary:
The International Court of Justice ruled on Thursday, Nov. 19, that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, the first time the UN's highest court has held a state responsible for the crime. Delivering the judgment in The Gambia v. Myanmar in The Hague, ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said Myanmar had also failed to prevent and punish genocide. Judges voted 9-6 that the military's 2017 crackdown in northern Rakhine state was carried out with intent to destroy the mainly Muslim minority, and the court estimated about 10,000 Rohingya were killed. The judgment is final, binding on the parties and cannot be appealed.

The court found that Myanmar's security forces and other state organs committed acts prohibited by Article II of the 1948 Genocide Convention, including killing members of the group, causing serious bodily or mental harm and imposing measures intended to prevent births. It found that nearly 400 villages, about 40% of those in three northern Rakhine townships, were partly or totally destroyed, and that some 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh. Myanmar must pass legislation giving full effect to the convention, investigate and where warranted prosecute and punish suspects, and provide guarantees of non-repetition. It must also allow the safe, voluntary return of displaced Rohingya, reunite families and compensate them, with the amount set in a later phase and a report to the court due within two years.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called the judgment a powerful recognition of the Rohingya victims of genocide. The Gambia, which brought the case in 2019 with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, called it a historic day for international justice and urged Myanmar to comply fully and without delay. Myanmar's opposition National Unity Government said it respects the court's authority, while the military-backed government had not responded when NPR published. Ed Miliband said the United Kingdom had ordered the expulsion of Myanmar's defence attache, summoned its charge d'affaires and called for an urgent UN Security Council session, with further measures to follow. Antonia Mulvey of Legal Action Worldwide said all countries should review trade ties with the junta, including arms and jet fuel supplies, and that the ruling will bear on other cases such as South Africa's case against Israel.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave owes $47 billion as analysts question whether its AI-cloud financing can withstand pressure
stories.Summary:
The Guardian published an examination on November 21, 2026, regarding the financing of AI-cloud provider CoreWeave. This report reveals that the company currently owes a total of 47 billion dollars. More than 10 billion dollars of these obligations are due in 2027. Analysts are now scrutinizing whether the company's funding can withstand financial pressure. The company uses Nvidia chips and customer contracts to back its borrowing.

Nearly 25 billion dollars in borrowing is backed by GPUs and customer contracts. Nvidia owns about 11 percent of CoreWeave and will buy 6.3 billion dollars of capacity. CoreWeave uses a six-year depreciation schedule for its chips in its financial planning. The company reported 1.7 gigawatts of active capacity and 132.5 billion dollars in commitments. Third-quarter results showed a 709 million dollar net loss and 846 million dollar interest.

CoreWeave says its funding strategy is lowering the average cost of its borrowing. A spokesperson stated that customers sign multiyear commitments for older GPUs at high prices. CEO Michael Intrator said the company would not use unsecured debt at current yields. The company points to strong contracted demand as support for its growth. They claim older equipment is already winning business beyond its depreciable life.

Jordan Chaflin of CreditSights says used GPUs still have buyers because AI capacity is scarce. He noted that this capital-intensive model is not unique to the company. Brian Hopkins of Forrester says prepayments supplied roughly two-thirds of the generated cash. TechCrunch reported third-quarter revenue of 3.66 billion dollars, which is up 168 percent. These figures affect lenders who favor predictable payments over shorter, higher-priced deals.

CoreWeave rents computing power by buying Nvidia chips and installing them in data centers. The company has shifted toward customer prepayments, contract-backed loans, and shorter customer deals. This model funds expansion but leaves the company exposed to chip-value declines. Revenue growth has been strong, but it has not eliminated the overall financial strain. Prepayments bring money in early but leave the company with work to perform.

Interest keeps accruing when permitting disputes or local restrictions delay data center construction. Revenue from that capacity only starts once the facility is finally delivered. Some market watchers warn that chips could depreciate faster than the company assumes. The durability of protection from long-term customer contracts remains a contested point. It is unclear if customers will remain able to pay their commitments.

stories.Headline: Federal court orders plaintiff to produce expert AI prompts in Shell environmental case
stories.Summary:
A federal court yesterday ordered a plaintiff to produce the AI prompts its expert used to analyze documents in a pending environmental case, holding that the prompts are part of the expert’s methodology and fully discoverable under Rule 26. The order came in Conservation Law Foundation v. Shell Oil Co., an environmental enforcement action pending in Connecticut, Civil No. 3:21-cv-00933 (VDO) (D. Conn.). The ruling is among the first to directly address whether expert AI prompts are discoverable, and it adds an important new piece to an emerging framework that courts have been constructing to address the use of AI in litigation. In preparing her expert report, CLF’s expert Dr. Naomi Oreskes used AI tools to review Shell’s document production and identify a subset of documents for closer analysis.

When Shell and its co-defendants sought discovery of the prompts Dr. Oreskes used in that process, CLF resisted on three grounds, and Magistrate Judge Thomas Farrish rejected all three. The court held that the process by which Dr. Oreskes used AI to narrow defendants’ document production into a workable subset was part of her methodology and therefore discoverable under Rule 26(b). CLF argued that a Rule 29 discovery agreement between the parties protected the prompts from disclosure, and the agreement excluded discovery of “expert notes, drafts, or communications needed by, and made during, the report drafting process.” The court declined to read the agreement that broadly, holding that before a court will deny otherwise-relevant discovery based on a Rule 29 agreement, that agreement “must be quite clear.” CLF also argued it had nothing additional to produce because Dr. Oreskes had not used “prompts,” only “search terms,” which CLF said had already been produced.

The court noted that a party’s good-faith representation that no additional responsive materials exist ordinarily resolves the matter, but that principle gives way when the requesting party has an evidence-backed reason to doubt the representation. The court found that an earlier declaration by Dr. Oreskes’ research assistant had specifically referenced “prompt[s],” giving defendants an evidence-backed reason to doubt CLF’s representation that no additional responsive materials existed. The order in Conservation Law Foundation v. Shell Oil Co. is available on PACER at ECF No. 970, D. Conn., May 18, 2026. The article was published by Arnold & Porter, a firm with over 1,000 lawyers across 16 offices worldwide, and authored by Melissa Weberman and Michel Marchand.

The article states that courts have now addressed attorney-crafted prompts, likely protected as opinion work product, and prompts generated without counsel’s involvement, where protection depends in part on whether the platform maintains confidentiality of user inputs. The article states that courts have also addressed expert prompts as part of disclosed methodology, today’s case, and the use of AI tools on discovery materials generally, where courts are requiring closed AI tools through protective orders. The article states that the thread running through all of these decisions is that protection turns less on the technology and more on who created the prompts, for what purpose, and under what terms of service. The article states that if you are retaining an expert who will use AI, you should treat the prompts as part of the expert’s methodology from the beginning, preserve them, understand how they are used, and assume they may need to be disclosed. The article states that prompts that reflect a disciplined analytical approach may strengthen the credibility of the expert’s work, while poorly defined prompts may invite challenges to the methodology itself.

The article states that parties should address AI use explicitly in engagement letters, discovery protocols, and Rule 29 agreements, and that the parties here had an agreement that covered some of this ground, but its silence on AI tools specifically was enough to defeat CLF’s position. The article states that if you are opposing an AI-assisted expert, the prompts are a legitimate discovery target, and they can reveal the assumptions underlying the analysis, the parameters the expert set for document selection, and any disconnect between what the AI was instructed to do and what the expert ultimately claims the documents show. The article states that the ruling is the latest in a line of decisions addressing AI prompts in litigation. The article states that an agreement that does not expressly address AI prompts and outputs may not protect them from discovery.

The article states that the content is intended to provide a general guide to the subject matter and that specialist advice should be sought about specific circumstances. The article lists related articles, including one titled Protecting AI Work Product Without Blocking Expert Discovery, published by Duane Morris LLP. The article lists a related article titled California’s New AI Law: Implications For Lawyers And EDiscovery Teams, which states that California’s Senate Bill 574 introduces statutory duties for attorneys using generative AI, including mandatory citation verification and court disclosure requirements starting January 1, 2027. The article states that it addresses the full framework in a companion post.

The article states that the ruling has practical implications for both sides of an expert dispute. The article states that the order is available on PACER at ECF No. 970, D. Conn., May 18, 2026. The article states that the case is an environmental enforcement action pending in Connecticut. The article states that the ruling is among the first to directly address whether expert AI prompts are discoverable.

Articles.Title: Court Rules Expert’s AI Prompts Are Fair Game Under Rule 26 - Legal 500

stories.Headline: Pennsylvania governor Josh Shapiro signs AI ad disclosure law taking effect in December
stories.Summary:
Governor Josh Shapiro signed Pennsylvania's Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act, known as SB 806, into law in late October 2026. The law takes effect December 21, 2026. Under it, an advertiser may not run an ad that uses synthetic content in a way that creates a false consumer perception about the nature, origin, or authenticity of what is being sold, unless the ad carries a clear disclosure. Synthetic content covers any image, video, audio, or text that AI has significantly modified or generated.

The disclosure must say that the ad contains content modified or generated using artificial intelligence, though the law does not require any particular wording. It must be easy to notice and understand given its size, contrast, duration, and volume, it must appear in the consumer's language, and it must show the first time the content appears and in the same medium. Where technically feasible, it must be permanent or very hard to remove. The law exempts content that is evidently fictional, parody, satire, commentary, criticism, and text-only content. The Attorney General or a district attorney may seek an injunction or sue, and courts may award damages, fines of up to $3,000, and attorney fees and costs, but there is no private right of action.

The law applies to advertisers who create and disseminate an ad or cause it to be created and disseminated, and earlier drafts limiting it to knowing, reckless, or willful conduct were removed. Because it covers all advertising shown in Pennsylvania, it reaches commercials made in other states or countries as well. Commentators have noted that terms such as "significantly modified" are subjective, and the broad exemptions for parody and commentary may leave advertisers room to maneuver. Unlike California and New York laws aimed at synthetic performers, this law appears to focus more on consumer protection.

Companies will need to decide when a disclosure is needed. A strict reading suggests none is required unless AI use creates a false consumer perception, but regulators have not yet said how they will enforce that standard. Some companies may therefore adopt a conservative approach and disclose more broadly. Observers expect that Pennsylvania's law is part of a wider trend of states regulating AI in advertising.

stories.Headline: Delaware court sanctions lawyer over hallucinated citations but exonerates firm with AI guidelines
stories.Summary:
On November 13, 2026, the Delaware Court of Chancery issued an order sanctioning a lawyer who signed a brief with hallucinated citations, according to an Above the Law article by Stephen Embry. The lawyer submitted fabricated quotations and mischaracterized legal authorities in a brief, and after the other side outed him he owned up to it, sort of. He filed a corrected brief that removed quotation marks from the original hallucinated citations but retained the inaccurate legal propositions. The lawyer blamed a paralegal and then tried to blame the other side for failing to meet and confer before alerting the court. The court sanctioned the lawyer under Delaware's version of Rule 11 but exonerated his law firm because it had proper AI use guidelines in place.

Delaware's Rule 11 provides that absent exceptional circumstances a law firm must be held jointly responsible for a violation committed by its partner, associate, or employee. The court also cited the Delaware Lawyers' Rules of Professional Conduct, which require law firm leadership to make reasonable efforts to ensure compliance with ethical rules. It referenced ABA Formal Opinion 512, which calls on firms to establish clear policies on permissible AI use. The firm barred the use of unapproved GenAI tools in March 2023, formed a working group to evaluate GenAI tools and study ethical guidance in 2024, and adopted a comprehensive GenAI policy in July 2025. That policy required an experienced lawyer to review GenAI output for accuracy and completeness.

The court found the exceptional circumstances that relieved the firm of joint responsibility, determining that the firm had undertaken substantial institutional efforts to prevent the very problem at issue. The court said the firm warned of GenAI risks, established clear verification policies, and trained its personnel through a substantial, multi-layered approach. The court said the firm acted reasonably to prevent GenAI misuse and should not be sanctioned for an individual lawyer bypassing those controls. The court said there is nothing to negotiate or compromise when an attorney submits false citations to a tribunal. The judge made sure the lawyer paid the monetary sanctions out of his own pocket.

The firm developed an internal training program addressing hallucinations and the recommendations of Opinion 512, and it addressed professional obligations concerning competence, confidentiality, meritorious claims, candor, and supervision. Delaware's Commission on Continuing Legal Education accredited the program for an hour of enhanced ethics credit. Embry wrote that AI use guidelines must be a three-legged stool, with a thorough policy, training and education, and guidelines that stay evergreen. Embry wrote that lawyers are naturally skeptical and independent and most believe they are special snowflakes. Embry recalled being told to use the firm's VPN at all times when working remote, but it was slow and clunky and a pain in the ass.

Embry wrote that if the firm's approved GenAI tools are slow and clunky, lawyers will jump to tools that aren't. Embry wrote that guidelines created in 2023, for example, would be unlikely to address the use of AI agents, which is getting more and more common today. Embry wrote that firms need someone, or perhaps several someones, to keep up with AI developments, risks, and the evolving law. Embry wrote that someone must spend nonbillable time monitoring those developments and ensuring the guidelines are frequently revised. Embry wrote that the firm must have a mechanism to approve revisions that doesn't take six months and involve never-ending partner meetings.

Embry wrote that judges are growing increasingly impatient with hallucinations in court filings. Embry wrote that hallucinations could lead to embarrassment, potential malpractice claims, or at the very least, unhappy clients. Embry wrote that law firms absolutely must have AI use guidelines and must train partners, associates, paralegals, legal professionals, and everyone else in the firm about them and why they're necessary. Embry wrote that firms absolutely must keep those guidelines up to date and must have a mechanism for promptly approving needed revisions. Embry wrote that this is simply a cost of doing business in these days and times, so roll up your sleeves and get to work.

stories.Headline: India's chief justice warns law schools that AI detection software cannot prove student cheating
stories.Summary:
At the CLEA international conference on legal education in Hyderabad on Saturday, Chief Justice of India Surya Kant cautioned law schools against treating AI-detection software as proof of misconduct. He delivered the inaugural address at the first Annual International Conference on Legal Education organised by the Commonwealth Legal Education Association at Novotel, Hyderabad. The conference theme is "Globalising Legal Education: Reimagining Law Schools, Legal Learning and the Future of the Legal Profession for a Commonwealth in Transition". The address responded in turn to the five questions set by CLEA for the conference's sessions. Those questions covered technology and academic integrity, citation, clinical learning, research in the age of artificial intelligence, and legal aid clinics.

The CJI said software claiming to detect machine-written essays is "far from reliable" and cannot by itself justify a finding of academic misconduct. He referred to a 2023 study finding that seven widely used detectors, though almost flawless with essays written by schoolchildren in the United States, wrongly flagged more than three in every five essays by non-native speakers of English as machine-generated. The speech text identifies the study as "GPT Detectors Are Biased Against Non-Native English Writers" by Weixin Liang, Mert Yuksekgonul and others, published in Patterns by Cell Press in 2023, which tested seven detectors on 91 TOEFL essays and 88 essays by students in the United States. He cited the Supreme Court of Singapore, which permits Court users to employ such tools but holds them fully responsible for everything they file. The speech text refers in a footnote to that Court's Registrar's Circular No. 1 of 2024, the Guide on the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools by Court Users.

He said an honest student could be branded a cheat on the strength of a number that no one can explain, and that no student should be held guilty of misconduct on the word of a machine alone. He rejected an outright prohibition, saying a ban would be neither practicable nor wise and would only drive this use out of sight, where it can be neither guided nor examined. He said the safeguard lies in clarity offered before an assessment begins rather than after it ends, with students knowing which uses are permitted, which must be disclosed, and which would amount to handing over the very thinking the assessment is meant to test. He suggested assessment evolve so that written work is supported by an oral explanation, a defence of the authorities relied upon, or an exercise in spotting the errors in a machine-generated answer.

He said a law school must be able to certify, with confidence, what its graduates themselves know and can do. On citation, he acknowledged the Supreme Court of India was "not entirely blameless" on inconsistent practice, observing that even Kesavananda Bharati is cited in some judgments in the SCC format and in others in the AIR format. He said he would favour beginning with a common core rather than replacing every existing guide with a single compulsory code, and that where a Court has assigned a neutral citation, as the Supreme Court has done since 2023, that citation should serve as its principal identifier. He said a shared minimum format giving the year, the Court, the decision number and the paragraph would allow any judgment to be traced and verified across borders.

He said such a framework should not depend on expensive commercial databases and must make room for translated judgments and for customary sources that rarely find their way into law reports. He said that to teach students to cite accurately, and to verify what they cite, is itself to teach them to practise law responsibly. On clinical legal education, he used the rule against leading questions to illustrate the gap between knowing a rule and using it, saying a student truly learns what the law is for when drawing out a frightened witness without putting words into his mouth. He noted that Indian regulations already require clinical courses and a legal aid clinic in every law school, and asked whether practical learning should remain confined to a separate corner of the curriculum or should also shape the teaching of core subjects such as Evidence, Criminal Procedure, Family Law and Constitutional Law.

He gave the examples of a Contract Law student drafting and negotiating a simple agreement, a Constitutional Law student tracing a denied entitlement to its remedy, and a Family Law student taking part in a mediation exercise. He said such reform must be introduced with care, since clinical teaching demands trained supervisors, meaningful assessment and clear ethical safeguards, and clients must never bear the cost of inadequate supervision. He proposed a common core for citation built on neutral citations and suggested that a minimum period of legal aid work be made compulsory for every student to graduate. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Congress pushes for tighter export controls after Commerce Department approves 879,000 AI chips for China
stories.Summary:
The Commerce Department approved the sale of over 879,000 advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, as revealed by Representative Brian Mast. This disclosure occurred during hearings this week, sparking an urgent push from members of Congress to tighten export controls. The revelation comes while the semiconductor industry is already reeling from a scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang. Lawmakers are now demanding a complete overhaul of the regime that governs how America exports its strategic technology. These approved shipments include advanced processors from multiple chipmakers, specifically including products from both Nvidia and AMD.

The proposed legislation would create a presumption of denial for AI chip exports to China and require annual audits of licenses. It would also impose criminal penalties on executives who knowingly facilitate the diversion of these chips to military end users. This bill represents the most aggressive export control proposal since the original restrictions were first imposed in 2022. The new rules would require chipmakers to prove sales will not enhance Chinese surveillance or military capabilities in the United States. These changes target advanced AI accelerators, such as the AMD MI300 series and the Nvidia H200 chips.

Representative Brian Mast, who chairs a key subcommittee overseeing technology exports, is leading the bipartisan effort to pass this legislation. He stated that the volume of approved chips far exceeds what most lawmakers believed was flowing to China under current restrictions. Meanwhile, Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress announced that the company would halt all H200 chip sales to China entirely. This voluntary halt by Nvidia occurred despite the fact that the White House had previously approved such sales. The Commerce Department has not commented on the specific figure of 879,000 chips approved for export.

National security hawks in Congress are alarmed that these chips were shipped while the Jensen Huang scandal unfolded behind closed doors. They are concerned that Beijing can deploy this compute capability for military-grade computer vision systems and large language models. AMD CEO Lisa Su now faces pressure to voluntarily restrict sales beyond what current regulations require to appease Washington. Investors are also affected, as Nvidia stock has fluctuated wildly while its China business became a significant political liability. The broader semiconductor industry is watching nervously as these political fights overshadow recent better-than-expected quarterly earnings reports.

The background of this crisis involves a disconnect between the national security apparatus and the trade bureaucracy of the United States. Intelligence agencies had raised red flags about previous shipments, yet the Commerce Department continued clearing massive export licenses. The Jensen Huang scandal forced the founder to depart and reshaped the leadership of Nvidia during this turbulent period. This situation transformed a technical discussion about compute thresholds into a political fight about funding a strategic global competitor. Chip giants had previously ignored calls for AI safety pauses to meet the insatiable demand for advanced hardware.

Legislation is expected to move quickly through committee, as Senate co-sponsors have already lined up to support the new bill. The industry must now decide whether to accept these stricter restrictions or fight back against the proposed Congressional mandates. It remains open whether other chipmakers will follow Nvidia's lead in voluntarily halting sales to avoid further political blowback. The global AI hardware market will be reshaped by whether the government shifts the burden of proof onto the companies. Future outcomes depend on how fast Congress can pass these laws to slam the door on Chinese exports.

stories.Headline: Virginia Beach school leaders weigh AI guardrails as survey shows 60% of high schoolers use AI to explain concepts
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is already a common part of the high school experience in Virginia Beach, and school leaders are now weighing how to make sure students use the technology responsibly while still gaining its educational benefits, according to WTKR. A survey by Virginia Beach City Public Schools found that 60% of high school students surveyed said they have used AI to explain difficult concepts, while 46% said they have used it to study for quizzes or tests. The same survey found that 36% of the students said they have used AI to check homework answers, and the district reported that 91% of high school students surveyed know their school's rules for using AI on assignments. The discussion came before the School Board as the technology becomes another tool available to students, and the district's current rules say open generative AI is not allowed for elementary or middle school students.

Under those current rules, high school students can use approved tools, including Gemini, with teacher guidance and district safeguards in place. School Board member Melinda Rogers said the conversation also needs to include the ethical boundaries surrounding AI use, noting that the technology is used a lot to deceive people in society and that an ethical standard should reflect that just because you can does not mean you should. School Board member Kimberly Melnyk asked district officials for data on the percentage of students who refuse to use AI, and a district official responded that no current data was available. That means the district has information about how surveyed students say they are using AI but does not currently have data showing how many students are choosing not to use the technology.

Kathleen Brown, of District 10, said there has been some conversation about generative AI, which she described as entering a prompt and getting a generated feedback loop, and she said families in the community are very concerned about that. The discussion reflects a broader challenge for Virginia Beach schools, which is determining how AI can help students learn while establishing clear expectations for when and how the technology should be used. The district survey and the board's questions show that leaders are still gathering information about student use, including the group of students who decline the technology. The articles do not say what specific guardrails, if any, the board will adopt or when any further action is expected.

stories.Headline: John and Nisha Whitehead argue humans, not machines, pose the real danger
stories.Summary:
A cascade of technological failures struck in late 2026, beginning with a massive Microsoft outage that disrupted Outlook and other online services around the globe. A nationwide ground stop then brought air travel across America to a standstill, disrupting thousands of flights and leaving travelers stranded. Major banks experienced problems with their online systems, and United Airlines grounded departing flights after yet another computer failure. Reports followed that the highly classified network the National Security Agency uses for internal communications had gone down, and Apple joined the growing list of technology giants with widespread disruptions. Users reported problems accessing iCloud, the App Store, Apple Music and other services, and millions of Americans were reminded how dependent their daily lives have become on technologies they neither understand nor control.

Speculation pointed at artificial intelligence, especially after the nationwide airline shutdown, because the Trump administration had only recently expanded the FAA's new SMART artificial-intelligence system to air traffic control centers across the country. The administration has aggressively promoted AI, or SI for Super Intelligence as Trump insists it be called, as the answer to everything from government inefficiency to national security, while pushing to reduce regulatory barriers and expand automated systems. Yet the Trump administration insists AI had nothing to do with the airline shutdown, and federal officials blamed a malfunction involving aging air traffic control infrastructure, with problems arising as equipment was being replaced and communications systems updated. The FBI issued a report about autonomous AI hacking tools such as Artex AI being used to launch cyberattacks across the U.S. and globally and breach networks in under three hours. The articles ask who is responsible when technological systems fail, who is accountable when officials and executives embrace new technologies without safeguards, infrastructure and human oversight, and what happens when people can no longer distinguish a machine's failure from the failure of the human beings entrusted with its operation.

John and Nisha Whitehead wrote the article, published by The Rutherford Institute on November 18, 2026, and they argue we have been asking the wrong question about artificial intelligence. They say the real danger may not be machines becoming smarter than human beings but the human hunger for power and our willingness to surrender control to those who wield it. They cite Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey, in which the computer HAL 9000 turns against the astronauts who entrusted their lives to its control, and Pixar's WALL-E, in which humanity has abandoned an uninhabitable Earth for a massive spaceship where machines anticipate nearly every need. In WALL-E people no longer walk, no longer work, barely notice the world around them, and are entertained, fed, transported and distracted by systems that make virtually every decision for them. The Whiteheads say the machines never needed to wage war against humanity because human beings surrendered their independence willingly, trading responsibility for convenience and freedom for comfort, and even the ship's captain must struggle to reclaim his authority from an automated system programmed to maintain the status quo.

The Whiteheads say we have confused technological progress with human progress, and that none of our achievements has necessarily made us wiser, more compassionate, more ethical or more capable of restraint. They note that in August 1945 the United States dropped atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, killing tens of thousands of people immediately and many more in the aftermath, and that the bombs did not decide to destroy those cities but human beings did. They say the same computers that revolutionized medicine, science, education and communication have helped give rise to a surveillance state capable of monitoring and tracking entire populations, and that the internet, once hailed as an instrument of free expression and democratized knowledge, has also become a tool for collecting personal information, manipulating behavior and monitoring dissent. According to the FBI, hackers have used ARTEX, originally developed to help cybersecurity professionals identify weaknesses in computer networks, to automate cyberattacks against financial institutions, government agencies and private companies, with some attacks progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in less than three hours. Google's Threat Intelligence Group warns that malicious actors are increasingly deploying autonomous AI systems capable of identifying vulnerabilities and carrying out attacks at machine speed with dramatically reduced human intervention.

The Whiteheads say artificial intelligence has not eliminated human greed, arrogance or the lust for power but has given those impulses greater reach, greater speed and greater power. They warn that government agencies increasingly defer to computers as intermediaries between the government and the populace, and that computers can be wrong, algorithms can be biased, databases can contain errors, and automated systems can perpetuate and magnify the mistakes, prejudices and political agendas of those who build and operate them. They say the ability to do something has never been the same as the right to do it, and that the government does not acquire a constitutional exemption merely because its abuses are carried out by a computer rather than a human being. Fifty years ago, they write, the Senate's Church Committee exposed extensive abuses by America's intelligence agencies, including surveillance operations directed against citizens exercising their constitutional rights. The first article's text ends mid-sentence at that point, with the word "warn," and the second article's text also ends mid-sentence, at "those who."

The articles leave open who or what actually caused the airline shutdown, since the administration blamed aging infrastructure while speculation pointed at AI. They leave open the outcome of the FBI's report on Artex AI and the response to Google's warning about autonomous AI attacks. They leave open what the Church Committee's history means for the present, because the first article's text stops at "The warn" and the second stops at "those who." They leave open what, if anything, should be done about the responsibility and accountability questions the authors raise. They leave open how the cascade of failures, from Microsoft and the banks to United Airlines, the NSA network and Apple, will be resolved.

stories.Headline: Goa cabinet approves AI policy 2026 and five flagship schemes with 10 crore rupees
stories.Summary:
The Goa Cabinet approved the Goa AI Policy 2026 and five flagship schemes on November 20, 2026, in Porvorim, India. These initiatives were proposed by the Department of Information Technology, Electronics and Communications to strengthen the state's artificial intelligence ecosystem. The policy seeks to promote the development, adoption, and responsible use of AI across the state of Goa. It provides a framework for building an ecosystem through innovation, skill development, entrepreneurship, and stronger technological infrastructure. The cabinet sanctioned 10 crore rupees for the implementation of these schemes during the 2026-27 financial year.

The policy allocates 60 percent of the budget to AI skilling, 20 percent to startup promotion, and 20 percent to infrastructure. The AI Ready Goa Scheme includes AI labs in 50 government schools, training for 500 teachers, and a 100-expert coach network. The Konkani AI and Research Excellence Scheme will develop a Konkani LLM and translation infrastructure via BHASHINI using consent-based corpus. The Udyam AI Scheme aims to support 200 MSMEs annually through diagnostic support, DPDP readiness checks, and outcome-linked deployment assistance. The Goa AI Infrastructure and Compute Access Scheme provides 100 GPUs or equivalent hours through CDAC, AIRAWAT, and IndiaAI Compute Capacity.

Chief Minister Dr. Pramod Sawant stated that AI skilling will cover all levels, integrating school and college students into the technology roadmap. He emphasized that training is not just for those in polytechnics and ITIs but for students from school to graduation. Minister Rohan A. Khaunte said the policy advances the Goa AI Mission 2027 and equips innovators across every taluka. Khaunte noted that the government is actively executing real schemes on the ground rather than just drafting a policy document. He highlighted a total allocation of 250 crore rupees under the Innovation Fund for these technological advancements.

The policy affects students, teachers, local MSMEs, young innovators, and government officials through workshops, bootcamps, and certification courses. It targets research-led enterprises and technology firms through incubation, prototyping support, hackathons, and government challenge statements. The Udyam AI framework provides MSMEs with advisory support, access to compute tools, and structured handholding for AI adoption. Sectoral Centres of Excellence and the Goa AI Lab will serve as flagship hubs for co-working and prototyping. The government will reserve 10 percent of the compute capacity for priority and sensitive public-sector use cases.

The policy was formulated by the Department of Information Technology, Electronics and Communications to drive AI adoption across various sectors. It envisions coordinated efforts between government departments, educational institutions, industry, startups, and research institutions to create tailored solutions. The background objectives include promoting entrepreneurship and ensuring the responsible use of AI with safeguards for privacy and transparency. The state aims to position itself as a testbed for AI innovation and a leader in regional language computing. This framework focuses on building an AI-ready workforce and promoting ethical AI practices across the entire state.

The government now aims to produce 50,000 graduates by 2030 to realize the vision of the Goa AI Mission 2027. For the next quarter, 10 crore rupees are allocated, with 60 percent for skilling and the rest for infrastructure. The state will continue partnerships with empanelled cloud providers and approved data-centre partners to maintain the required compute access. The articles do not state the specific timeline for the completion of the 50 government school AI labs. They also leave open the specific details regarding the selection process for the 100-expert AI Coach Network.

stories.Headline: Marc Miller and Evan Solomon name members of Canada's AI and culture advisory council
stories.Summary:
On November 19, 2026, the Honourable Marc Miller, Minister of Canadian Identity and Culture and Minister responsible for Official Languages, and the Honourable Evan Solomon, Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation and Minister responsible for the Federal Economic Development Agency for Southern Ontario, announced the members of the new Advisory Council on Artificial Intelligence and Culture. The announcement was made in Gatineau, Quebec, according to a press release dated November 19, 2026. The ministers also convened the council for its inaugural meeting. The council follows Canada's first-ever National Summit on Artificial Intelligence and Culture, which was held in Banff, Alberta last March. The members were selected based on their expertise and experience.

The council includes twelve members: Samuel Bischoff of the Directors Guild of Canada, Jeremy de Beer of the University of Ottawa, Jonathan Dewar of the First Nations Information Governance Centre, Stéphanie Hénault of the Association nationale des éditeurs de livres, Yves Jacquier of Ubisoft La Forge, Samantha Kaine of the Independent Media Producers Association of Creative Talent (IMPACT), Pascale Landry of Compétence Culture, Margaret McGuffin of Music Publishers Canada, Brenda O'Farrell of the Consortium of Official Language Minority Community Media / Quebec Community Newspapers Association, Sean Power of Musical AI, Amor Provins of the Alberta Machine Intelligence Institute, and Afsoon Soudi of the Creative AI Hub at Toronto Metropolitan University. Its membership will rotate over time to ensure a broad range of expertise informs its work as new questions and emerging issues arise. The council will provide ongoing advice and insight to guide implementation of Canada's National AI Strategy, with a focus on the unique challenges facing the sector and the opportunities for adoption and innovation that responsible AI development can create for Canada's creative industries. The National Summit on Artificial Intelligence and Culture was held in Banff, Alberta, from March 15 to 17, 2026, presented in partnership with the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity.

Miller said that at the Banff Summit the government heard clearly that building trust in AI will require the cultural sector to play a role in shaping how these technologies are developed and used. He said the council is being established to ensure that AI reflects the values, priorities and realities of Canada's cultural sector. Solomon said the future of Canadian culture cannot be shaped by technology alone and has to reflect the voices and value of the people who create it. He said the council brings creators, researchers and technology leaders together to help seize new opportunities, protect the value of human creativity and build a stronger cultural economy. Solomon said the goal is clear: AI that earns trust, expands opportunity and strengthens Canada's culture and identity.

The council includes technology experts, researchers, industry and labour leaders, cultural practitioners and civil society stakeholders. The summit convened leaders from the cultural, government, technology, academic and civil society sectors to shape a shared vision for the future of culture in the age of artificial intelligence. The release states that AI is changing how Canadians create and experience culture. It states that Canadian creators, cultural organizations and creative businesses must have a voice in ensuring it strengthens our cultural sector, protects Canadian creativity and diversity of expressions, and delivers shared prosperity. The council will help the government and the cultural sector navigate the rapid changes driven by AI.

Canada's National Artificial Intelligence Strategy: AI for All sets out six pillars to build a strong, trusted AI ecosystem that creates opportunity and strengthens Canada's sovereignty in AI. The strategy brings together actions to support AI adoption and skills, build infrastructure and advance the safe and responsible development of AI. It includes a $50-million investment in a new Creative Technology Program. The summit was presented in partnership with the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity. The release was sourced from Canadian Heritage.

The council will provide ongoing advice and insight to guide implementation of Canada's National AI Strategy. Its membership will rotate over time as new questions and emerging issues arise. The articles do not state when the council will next meet or what its advice will cover beyond the National AI Strategy. The articles do not name the council's chair or give its size beyond the twelve members listed. The articles do not say how often the membership will rotate.

stories.Headline: Anthropic completes largest IPO in history with 1.5 trillion dollar valuation
stories.Summary:
Anthropic completed the biggest initial public offering in history on November 19, 2026. The San Francisco company became the first major artificial intelligence lab to list publicly. This record breaking debut occurred despite recent jitters among some investors regarding the AI sector. The company raised a total of US$81 billion through the offering of its shares. This event marks a superlative debut for the maker of the Claude AI system.

The company offered 980 million shares at a price of US$83 each before trading began. Shares opened at US$111.50 and closed at US$97.17, creating a first day value of US$1.75 trillion. At noon Eastern time, the valuation spiked to US$2.01 trillion, which is 1am Singapore time on November 20. This exceeds the US$75 billion raised by SpaceX in June and US$26.5 billion by SK Hynix in July. Saudi Aramco previously raised US$25.6 billion in 2019, while SpaceX ended its first day at US$2.1 trillion.

CEO Amodei is the person responsible for taking the safety approach of the company public. He decided to proceed with the listing despite growing unease among the public about technology risks. The company leadership pushed forward even with fears that artificial intelligence might be running amok. They aimed to establish the lab as a publicly traded entity during the current AI boom. This move allows the company to join a small group of tech giants with 13 digit wealth.

Investors expressed worry about market volatility and the possibility of a wider artificial intelligence bubble. The general public remains uneasy about the overall risks associated with this powerful new technology. Eleven companies in the S&P 500 have reached the trillion dollar club, including Apple, Microsoft, and Nvidia. Apple leads this group at US$5.1 trillion, followed by Microsoft at US$3.8 trillion and Nvidia at US$3.6 trillion. SpaceX and Anthropic have also joined this club, although they are not yet in the S&P 500.

Apple was the first corporation to pass the trillion dollar threshold back in the year 2018. A trillion US dollar bills laid end to end would stretch 156 million kilometres, surpassing the distance to the sun. One trillion is a thousand times greater than one billion and a million times more than one million. The US Census Bureau states there are more than 8.2 billion people currently living on Earth. Dividing one trillion dollars among everyone would give each person almost US$122.

The market cap of SpaceX has fallen to closer to US$1.95 trillion since its own record debut. Anthropic finished its first day of trading over 17 percent higher than its initial public offering price. The company now stands as the second business to debut with a value over one trillion dollars. Future performance on the public market remains uncertain as the company navigates these high valuations. The articles leave open how the company will fare as investors monitor the stability of the AI boom.

stories.Headline: California Attorney General subpoenas Nvidia over potential chip leaks and CEO misconduct
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as the top executive of Nvidia last week after admitting to a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy. The sixty three year old co-founded the Santa Clara company in 1993 but stepped down following the revelation of his affair. He also allegedly had a second affair with the vice president of healthcare and a third with another subordinate employee. California Attorney General Rob Bonta served the multitrillion dollar company with an investigative subpoena on Thursday, November 19, 2026. This legal action seeks to determine if the company misled the public and investors regarding the handling of this scandal.

The subpoena asks if confidential information or advanced artificial intelligence chips were sent to China, which would violate national security interests. Bonta is evaluating if Nvidia violated California law, similar to a lawsuit his office filed against OpenAI over misleading claims. The board appointed Colette Kress, the chief financial officer and executive vice president since 2013, to serve as interim CEO. On Tuesday, the company reported third quarter revenue of 115.8 billion dollars, which is an increase of 103 percent. Nvidia also stopped reporting its Singapore revenue separately just as scrutiny of the Singaporean company Megaspeed began to arise.

Attorney General Rob Bonta stated that companies cannot mislead their investors and that the conduct of Huang and Nvidia raises red flags. Nvidia launched an internal investigation and claimed there is no reason to believe that national security or company secrets were compromised. Chairman Harvey C. Jones said the board unanimously accepted the resignation and acted in the best interest of all stakeholders. Jensen Huang posted on X that he made serious mistakes in his personal life and did not meet expected standards. He stated he would be honored to return as CEO to help the company navigate complex geopolitical and market dynamics.

Over 180,000 people signed a petition for the return of Huang, an effort supported by Elon Musk and other tech executives. President Donald Trump believes the former CEO had no idea he was targeted by a spy, though the FBI is investigating. House Democrats are investigating if Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick improperly influenced the chip business because his family has holdings in Nvidia. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent criticized the Commerce Department for failing to blacklist Megaspeed over possible violations of export rules. The shake up has rattled markets and raised questions about whether the U.S. Commerce Department was complicit or incompetent.

The Commerce Department is conducting a years long investigation into Megaspeed for allegedly skirting export rules governing the powerful AI chips. This investigation included an interview with Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed chief executive and the woman with whom Jensen Huang had an affair. U.S. intelligence officials suspect Alice Huang may be a Chinese spy, and she left her role at Megaspeed in 2025. Megaspeed is conducting its own internal investigation into the matter while the Justice Department pursues criminal conduct. The Commerce Department claims a strong track record of bringing semiconductor smugglers to justice through its own excellent work.

The board confirmed on Tuesday that Jensen Huang would not be reinstated as CEO despite calls from President Trump and his allies. Democrats in Congress will gain greater investigative and subpoena powers in January after winning control of both chambers in midterm elections. The California Department of Justice has not released further information regarding the current status of its investigation into the company. It remains open whether the Commerce Department's failure to blacklist Megaspeed was a result of incompetence or intentional influence. The articles leave unresolved whether any specific confidential data or advanced chips actually reached China through these romantic relationships.

stories.Headline: Harvard researchers estimate US data centers emit as much greenhouse gas as Denmark
stories.Summary:
Harvard University researchers published a study on Monday regarding pollution from the largest data centers in the United States. This research estimated that 403 of the biggest centers produced 28.3 million tons of carbon dioxide. Simultaneously, negotiators at the COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, launched a voluntary clean energy pledge. This initiative encourages companies and countries to power data centers with clean energy and disclose their emissions. The pledge also suggests using artificial intelligence to help solve the difficult problem of global climate change.

The Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge requires cleaner electricity, efficient water systems, and transparent reporting of energy and emissions. It was launched by the International Telecommunication Union and Turkey, with Germany, Brazil, and South Korea signing. Alibaba was the only major technology company identified as a supporter, while Microsoft, Google, Meta, and Amazon did not. Amazon separately plans to reduce its electricity carbon intensity by 65 percent by 2030 against a 2019 baseline. The study analyzed electricity use between May 2024 and April 2025, finding 82 terawatt hours of total consumption.

United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said that future emissions savings cannot excuse the rising pollution happening now. COP31 President Murat Kurum stated that world leaders must openly discuss energy consumption and start setting the terms. ITU Secretary-General Doreen Bogdan-Martin argued that international cooperation is necessary to make artificial intelligence more sustainable and accessible. Harvard professor Francesca Dominici noted that emissions are two to three times higher than what previous studies showed. She added that plans for 2,000 more data centers make the current pollution levels more worrisome for the future.

Former Vice President Al Gore expressed hope that computing power can find novel ways of fighting climate change. Caleb Max of the National Artificial Intelligence Association said that fears about energy and water consumption may be overblown. Conversely, Philip Newell of Climate Action Against Disinformation claimed that companies are selling hope while hiding the harms. Cornell scientist Fengqi You stated that environmental impacts cannot be managed effectively without reliable measurements and open disclosure. The report by Climate Action Against Disinformation found that tech electricity consumption rose 240 percent between 2022 and 2025.

The International Energy Agency estimated that data centers consumed 485 terawatt-hours of electricity worldwide in 2025, up 17 percent. AI-focused facilities saw consumption rise 50 percent, which is substantially faster than the overall global electricity demand. Data centers produced more heat-trapping gas in one year than the entire nation of Denmark did before the boom. The IEA warns that delayed connections and equipment shortages could constrain expansion and affect electricity prices for consumers. Some developers are turning to onsite gas-fired generation when grid connections are delayed, which complicates decarbonization targets.

The IEA projects worldwide data center electricity consumption could reach 950 terawatt-hours by 2030, roughly double the 2025 level. European Commissioner Dan Jørgensen said Europe must replace imported fossil fuels by capturing waste heat and tapping geothermal. BaRupOn is building a Texas campus to generate electricity from recaptured heat and planning a North Dakota center. The IEA estimates that captured waste heat could provide for 10 percent of European homes by the year 2030. The articles leave open whether voluntary commitments can influence an industry that is investing heavily in computing infrastructure.

stories.Headline: Huawei showcases AI scaling capabilities for the financial sector at Singapore FinTech Festival 2026
stories.Summary:
Huawei presented its financial AI scaling capabilities at the Singapore FinTech Festival 2026 on November 20, 2026. The company shared insights regarding accelerating financial AI at scale and advancing agentic finance with industry partners. Jason Cao and Alvin Feng delivered keynotes on the Festival Stage and the Frontier Stage during the event. Huawei showcased various solutions for central banks, securities, insurance, application modernization, and resilient infrastructure for global institutions. These presentations included joint solutions from the RONGHAI Financial Partner Program and achievements from the 4-Win ecosystem collaboration.

The Fintelligent AI Solution requires an open architecture, standardized engineering, and shared assets to ensure security and scalability. This framework uses an open hybrid AI infrastructure and three intelligent factories called the Agent, Token, and Data&Knowledge factories. Huawei is exploring a specific architecture that utilizes two super agents and multiple specialized agents for banking capabilities. The Customer Super Agent and Employee Super Agent handle user intent while specialized agents support risk and wealth management. These systems allow banks to turn expertise in credit judgment, marketing strategies, and compliance rules into reusable AI capabilities.

Jason Cao, the CEO of Huawei Digital Finance, stated that the competitive focus is shifting toward enterprise-grade system capabilities. He explained that an open ecosystem makes AI affordable, while extreme engineering makes the technology effective for business. Cao noted that scaling AI for growth requires hybrid infrastructure combining public cloud options with on-premises deployment for flexibility. He emphasized that financial institutions must own their data, knowledge, and business logic to maintain a differentiated competitive advantage. According to Cao, these core assets must be integrated deeply with business processes to create financial-grade AI capabilities.

Alvin Feng, President of Huawei International Financial BU, discussed owning AI and advancing agentic finance during his keynote speech. He explained that the new framework addresses the critical needs of sustainability, scalability, and security for global financial institutions. Customers and employees are affected as they will increasingly rely on their own AI agents to plan and act. Banks must ensure their services can be understood and invoked by these agents to create Customer-AI-Friendly Finance. This process involves building an AI flywheel that links data, execution, learning, and feedback to improve the user experience.

The articles state that Huawei has served more than 7,100 financial customers over the last 16 years of operation. This client base includes 54 of the world's top 100 banks that have used Huawei's various financial technologies. Jason Cao identified four characteristics of Chinese institutions, including hybrid infrastructure and ongoing application modernization known as Zero Legacy. These institutions use enterprise-grade AI architecture for centralized management and integrate AI into core workflows like mobile banking. Such integration into credit and risk control processes is intended to reshape business processes and enhance overall competitiveness.

Huawei will continue helping banks connect employees and customers while coordinating business tasks through its super agent architecture. The company aims to capture and refine expert intelligence to build self-evolving systems for the global financial sector. The Token Factory will manage the full lifecycle of tokens, while the Data&Knowledge Factory provides high-quality data. The Agent Factory will remain responsible for the development and governance of AI agents within the Fintelligent AI Solution. The articles leave open how specific global banks will implement these factories or the timeline for widespread agentic adoption.
