stories.Headline: VAST Data gains IMDA accreditation to support Singapore AI projects
stories.Summary:
VAST Data received accreditation from Singapore's Infocomm Media Development Authority, or IMDA, which recognises the company as a qualified technology provider for government agencies and large enterprise customers, according to a Telecompaper report dated 20 November 2026. The accreditation programme assesses innovative, high-growth infocomm and media companies and is intended to identify potential suppliers for public sector and enterprise projects. VAST Data's existing work in Singapore includes a collaboration with the Home Team Science and Technology Agency, known as HTX, to deliver a secure data platform supporting AI workloads for public safety. The company also works with NCS to build a unified, real-time data foundation for high-performance video analytics on the VAST AI Operating System across Singapore and the wider Asia-Pacific region. The accreditation follows VAST Data's launch of a regional centre of excellence in Singapore in partnership with EDBI, the arm of SG Growth Capital and the investment platform of Singapore's Economic Development Board and Enterprise Singapore.

The accreditation establishes VAST Data's credentials in Singapore and creates new opportunities for the company to deepen its engagement in the region, according to iTWire. Following the accreditation, VAST Data will look to further deepen its work with Singapore's government agencies and enterprises to bring more AI projects from proof-of-concept to real-world deployment. Sunil Chavan, Vice President for Asia Pacific and Japan at VAST Data, said the accreditation reflects the progress the company is already making as Singapore builds out the infrastructure needed for AI at scale. He said the company's work connects directly to Singapore's National AI Missions in Advanced Manufacturing, Financial Services, Connectivity, and Healthcare. Chavan said Singapore's National AI Strategy 2.0 is explicit about what it needs, namely sufficient compute, unlocked data, a trusted environment, and infrastructure that can scale with the country's AI ambitions, and he described these as the plumbing that determines whether a national AI mission ships or stalls.

Edwin Low, Director of Enterprise and Ecosystem Development at IMDA, said partnerships with technology companies such as VAST Data are important in strengthening the capabilities and infrastructure needed to support the deployment of AI at scale as Singapore advances its National AI Strategy 2.0. Low said VAST's accreditation follows a rigorous assessment of its technical, financial, and operational capabilities and recognises its ability to deliver trusted technology solutions, and he said the authority looks forward to its potential contributions to Singapore's digital and AI ecosystem. Chavan added that Singapore has set a high bar for what AI for the public good looks like, and that VAST Data intends to keep showing up as one of the partners helping it get there. The articles do not say what happens next beyond VAST Data's stated intention to deepen its work with government agencies and enterprises.

stories.Headline: Nasdaq monetizes AI agents for financial crime management as 850 customers adopt the tools
stories.Summary:
Nasdaq began charging customers for artificial intelligence agents used in financial crime management in November 2026. Chief Financial Officer Sarah Youngwood announced this monetization strategy at an RBC Capital Markets technology conference. The company is pursuing growth across its technology, data, and index businesses through these tools. Currently, 850 of the 2,800 financial crime clients use these agents to manage their tasks. Only 70 of those 850 customers are paying for the service at this time.

The agents can deliver fourfold efficiency gains and will expand to Calypso, AxiomSL, and surveillance products. Nasdaq estimates the financial crime management market at 8 billion dollars, with half among large banks. The total serviceable addressable market is 38 billion dollars, according to the figures provided by Youngwood. Verafin signed 12 enterprise customers through the third quarter, compared to nine for all of 2025. AxiomSL now covers 66 countries and 174 regulators, up from 55 countries and 110 regulators previously.

Sarah Youngwood stated that adoption and bank AI governance reviews are important steps before customers pay. She noted that the 850 users underwent a rigorous process at banks before using the agents. Youngwood attributed the momentum of Verafin to the Nasdaq brand and existing relationships with large institutions. She explained that consortium data from 2,800 banks helps the company identify activity spanning multiple institutions. The CFO also mentioned that the initial conversion to paid customers has been very encouraging.

Most of the 850 customers using AI agents are smaller banks, but Nasdaq is discussing larger institutions. RBC Capital Markets analyst Ashish Sabadra reported that RegTech delivered 15 percent annual recurring revenue growth. Capital Markets Technology saw 19 percent growth, though Youngwood noted this included pricing catch-up and extra testing. The index business grew 39 percent recently due to passive investing and demand for Nasdaq-100 products. Recent listing switches by Walmart, Hilton, and GM were also cited as part of the pipeline.

Nasdaq's AxiomSL regulatory reporting product serves all but one non-Chinese global systemically important bank in the world. The company generated 2.3 billion dollars in free cash flow over the prior 12 months of operation. It repurchased 1.2 billion dollars of shares in nine months, compared with 600 million the year before. The company is already within its target leverage range and will focus on organic growth and acquisitions. Demand for surveillance is expanding as markets move toward longer trading hours and new digital asset firms.

Nasdaq targets trading 23 hours a day, five days a week, by the date of December 6. A Nasdaq equity token developed with Kraken is expected to launch in the first half of next year. The company is launching binary options but will not participate in sports or political prediction markets. It has not entered perpetuals because it wants to understand institutional demand and see regulated frameworks. The articles leave open when the extra testing in Capital Markets Technology will fully taper off.

stories.Headline: RadixArk releases DaisyRose-27B coding model trained exclusively with reinforcement learning
stories.Summary:
RadixArk released its first open-weight agentic coding model, DaisyRose-27B, during the week of November 20, 2026. This thinking model was post-trained from Qwen3.8-27B using only reinforcement learning without any distillation or supervised fine-tuning. The development process involved 18 days of training on 144 H200 GPUs, totaling 63,000 GPU-hours. This effort utilized the open-source RL framework called Miles and a specialized sandbox environment known as AgentENV.

The model features 27.8 billion dense parameters and a context window of 262,144 tokens. It requires a single GPU to run, with memory needs ranging from 23 GB for NVFP4 on Blackwell GPUs to 52 GB for BF16. The architecture maintains the Qwen3.8-27B design, including 64 decoder layers and a 27-layer vision encoder for processing images. Performance improved across seven benchmarks, most notably on Terminal Bench 4.1, where the pass@1 score rose from 5.6 to 12.0.

RadixArk developed the model using 1,200 curated tasks created with Eigent AI to address specific failures of the base model. The company stated that their internal backend achieved a 37 percent model flop utilization, which provided a two-fold speedup in throughput. They reported that their sandbox costs were approximately 80 percent lower than those of popular cloud providers. While the model leads in IFBench with a score of 82.4, the developers admitted it still trails larger mixture-of-experts models on difficult agentic tasks.

stories.Headline: Zimbabwe regulator POTRAZ weighs risk-based data protection reform after winning African award
stories.Summary:
Dublin City Council states that it is committed to fulfilling its obligations under the General Data Protection Regulation, according to an article published on dublincity.ie on 18 November 2026. The council says that a person has the right to obtain a copy of any information about them that it holds. That information could be stored on a computer or in a manual filing system, the article states. The article says a person should write to the council to obtain any information about them that it holds. The article says the letter should state that the person wishes to make an access request under the General Data Protection Regulation.

The article says the letter should include details that could help the council locate records, such as a customer account number, a staff number or any other information that may help identify the records. It says a person may alternatively submit a request by email or complete a form and return it to the address given. It says a request should be accompanied by a copy of official photo identification, such as a passport, a driver's licence or a public services card, to verify identity. It says a person may contact the council if they have concerns that a data breach has occurred in relation to their personal data or that their personal data has been put at risk by unauthorised access or disclosure. It says the council will investigate the matter fully and notify the person of the outcome as soon as possible.

The article says all traffic cameras operated and managed by Dublin City Council are used for traffic monitoring purposes, are live feed only and do not record. It says a person should review a map provided at a link to determine whether the camera they are seeking footage from is a traffic camera. It says that if the camera is included in the map, then no recording has taken place and no footage exists. It says that if the camera is not included in the map, the person should submit a request to the address noted, providing the specific location of the camera and a copy of valid photo identification. It says the General Data Protection Regulation allows access to information that is personal in nature, so a person will only be entitled to access footage of themselves, and any third parties captured in footage will be redacted or pixelated before release.

The article gives the contact details of the Information Management Unit at the Civic Offices, Wood Quay, Dublin 8, Co. Dublin D08 RF3F, Ireland, with telephone number 01 222 3775 and an email address. It also gives the address Civic Offices, Wood Quay, Dublin 8, D08 RF3F, Ireland, with telephone number 01 222 2222 and an email address. It says a person may visit the website of the Data Protection Commissioner for information on data protection. It says the council will investigate a suspected data breach fully and notify the person of the outcome as soon as possible. It says a person making a request for CCTV footage should provide the specific location of the camera concerned along with a copy of valid photo identification.

Techzim published an article by Dr. Marlon-Ralph Nyakabau on 20 November 2026 asking whether Zimbabwe has the best data protection regulation in Africa. The article says that earlier this month the Postal and Telecommunications Regulatory Authority of Zimbabwe, POTRAZ, was crowned Most Outstanding Data Protection Authority at the PICCASO Awards Africa 2026 in Lagos. It says POTRAZ beat a highly competitive field that reportedly included South Africa, Kenya, Egypt and Rwanda. It says POTRAZ clinched the award on the basis of achievements that include licensing over 2,500 data controllers and training and certifying more than 1,500 data protection officers. The article says the accolade was well heralded and raises a fundamental question about how Zimbabwe's data protection regulatory framework compares with those of other African countries.

The article says South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya and Egypt are among Africa's leading technology markets and attract significant investment. It says Zimbabwe has ambitions to improve its regional competitiveness in the technology sector, which Government has identified as an important driver of national economic development. It says the data protection regulatory authorities in these countries were established following the enactment of legislation intended to safeguard the right to privacy and protect individuals against the unlawful collection, retention, dissemination and use of their personal information. It says that while the underlying legislation shares many common principles, there are stark differences in how these regulators exercise their statutory discretion when implementing the law. It says the differences can be examined in three major areas: registration of data controllers, data protection officer requirements, and codes of conduct and stakeholder consultation.

The article says that in South Africa registration of Information Officers is mandatory for both public and private bodies, but there is no government licensing fee, the process can be completed online, and registration does not expire or require an annual renewal fee. It says Nigeria, Kenya and Egypt, like Zimbabwe, charge categorised licensing or registration fees for data controllers and processors, but the criteria used to determine who must register and how much they must pay differ considerably. It says the Nigeria Data Protection Commission does not determine registration obligations purely on the basis of the number of data subjects, and mandatory registration applies to data controllers and processors of major importance classified into Ultra-High, Extra-High and Ordinary-High levels. It says the classification depends on a combination of factors including the number of data subjects, sensitivity of the data processed, nature of the processing and the organisation's significance to Nigeria's economy, society or national security. It says Kenya's Office of the Data Protection Commissioner bases its categorisation partly on the number of employees and annual revenue or turnover of an organisation, with distinct categories for public entities, charities and religious organisations.

The article says POTRAZ's approach is rather blunt and treats a church like a bank or an NGO like a multinational corporation simply because they may process similar numbers of data subjects. It says the Egyptian Personal Data Protection Centre employs a categorisation system based on the volume of personal data, similar to Zimbabwe, but the threshold for registration starts at a minimum of 100,000 personal data records compared with just 50 in Zimbabwe. It says licensing fees in Egypt increase with each additional increment of 100,000 records, recognising differences in operational scale, financial capacity and potential risks. It says Zimbabwe's regulatory framework does not adequately accommodate such distinctions. It says the Zimbabwean regulator is unquestionably outstanding in one area, the licensing fees, and gives the example of a small clinic or primary school.

The article says registration fees for the corresponding category are as little as approximately US$7 in Nigeria and around US$30 in Kenya, while in Zimbabwe the data controller licensing fee would be US$300. It says a small technology start-up processing just over 1,000 data subjects in Zimbabwe faces a licensing bill equivalent to, or greater than, what an entire telecommunications company pays in Kenya, Nigeria or South Africa. It says that in Kenya a data protection officer must be designated where a data controller or processor is a public body, processes sensitive personal data on a large scale, or undertakes core activities involving regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale, but there is no statutory DPO licensing board or individual registration fee. It says Nigeria and Egypt, like Zimbabwe, have introduced regulatory requirements around the training and certification of data protection officers, but implementation and associated costs differ considerably. It says an individual DPO certification examination costs less than US$200 in Nigeria compared with approximately US$1,250 in Zimbabwe.

The article says Egypt's DPO certification framework considers an applicant's existing professional qualifications and certifications as well as the nature and volume of personal data they are expected to handle. It says Zimbabwe appears to have adopted a blanket approach in which individuals are subjected to substantially similar certification requirements and costs regardless of their prior qualifications, professional experience or the nature of the organisations in which they serve. It says South Africa's Information Regulator recognises the value of industry-specific codes of conduct, and industry associations and representative bodies can develop codes that tailor lawful information-processing principles to their respective industries. It says once approved by the Information Regulator the codes carry the force of law for members of that industry, with examples including codes developed for the banking, research and direct marketing sectors. It says the South African framework provides for stakeholder consultation in the development of codes of conduct, and the Information Regulator is required to gazette details of proposed codes and consider submissions from affected stakeholders and bodies representing their interests before approving them.

The article says Zimbabwe's framework provides considerably more discretion to the regulator, which may publish codes without seeking the views of affected data subjects or their representatives. It says a comparison of these regulatory frameworks reveals that although the underlying data protection laws share similar definitions and principles, their implementation differs considerably, with the most striking differences in registration requirements and licensing fees. It says Zimbabwe's economy is a fraction of the size of these comparator countries, yet in some instances its regulatory charges are several times higher. It says the founding legislation and regulatory frameworks in countries such as South Africa, Kenya and Nigeria provide for public funding of their respective regulatory institutions through government allocations and national treasury arrangements. It says Zimbabwe's Cyber and Data Protection Act did not establish an equivalent, clearly articulated funding arrangement for the regulator, which may have created an incentive or necessity for the Authority to generate a substantial proportion of its operational resources through its own regulatory activities.

The article says the unfortunate consequence, if this is the case, is the emergence of a regulatory regime that many increasingly perceive as being more about revenue generation than effective data protection. It says it is difficult to ignore the effect of disproportionately high compliance costs on businesses, particularly small enterprises, start-ups, NGOs and healthcare providers. It says this adds to the cost of doing business in Zimbabwe and undermines efforts to attract investment, stimulate innovation and improve the country's regional competitiveness. It says Government has recently embarked on initiatives to reduce the cost of doing business, resulting in the review and reduction of various licensing and registration fees, but data protection licensing costs appear to have escaped this exercise.

It says there is an urgent need to rethink the regulatory framework and move towards a genuinely risk-based approach that recognises that not all organisations process the same types or volumes of personal information, face the same risks or possess the same financial capacity. The article says regulation should be proportionate, risk-sensitive and enabling, and should encourage organisations to comply with the law rather than make compliance so expensive that it becomes an additional barrier to doing business. It says POTRAZ is currently inviting submissions as part of the process of amending the Cyber and Data Protection Regulations under Statutory Instrument 155 of 2024. It says the proposed direction of the revisions appears largely focused on strengthening the Authority's enforcement powers, including the introduction of administrative penalties.

It says increasing the regulator's punitive powers without first addressing the disproportionate costs of compliance risks making an already expensive regulatory environment even more burdensome. It says that if Zimbabwe genuinely aspires to have the best data protection regulatory framework in Africa, POTRAZ must be willing to examine the proportionality, affordability and effectiveness of its regulatory approach. It says the best data protection regime is not necessarily the one that regulates the most, charges the most or punishes the most, but the one that protects citizens' rights without unnecessarily suffocating the very businesses, institutions and innovations that drive the economy. Leadership published an article on 19 November 2026 with the headline that Nigeria clinches a global data protection award and beats 145 jurisdictions.

The article appears on a page that also lists sections including News, Politics, Business, Sport, Football, Health, Entertainment, Education, Opinion, Editorial, Columns, LeVogue Magazine, Conferences, National Economy and Contact Us. The page includes a Hausa Edition link and links for Print Advert Rates and Online Advert Rates. The page shows the date Thursday, November 19, 2026. stories.Headline: PNG hosts AI and numismatics symposium in Orlando on January 6, 2027
stories.Summary:
The Professional Numismatists Guild will hold a special educational symposium titled Artificial Intelligence and Numismatics on Wednesday, January 6, 2027, in Orlando, Florida. The program takes place in conjunction with the Florida United Numismatists Convention, one of the hobby’s largest annual gatherings. The symposium begins at 12:30 p.m. in Room N320E of the Orange County Convention Center’s North/South Building. It precedes the main public convention dates of January 7, 10, 2027.

Both PNG members and non-PNG dealers may attend, and organizers will provide a complimentary lunch. The program will bring together experienced rare coin dealers and technology professionals to discuss how businesses already use AI and to examine opportunities for the numismatic marketplace. PNG Executive Director John Feigenbaum and veteran numismatist Jeff Garrett, a former PNG president, will lead the discussion. Aiden Feigenbaum, a software engineer and co-founder of New York-based RealAnalytica, will discuss how Whitman Publishing is using artificial intelligence. Noah Lehmann-Haupt, founder of Rarity7 in San Francisco, will explain how he incorporates AI into his rare coin business.

Ron Guth, proprietor of San Diego-based GermanCoins.com and a former president of Professional Coin Grading Service, will share his experiences using AI in his company’s operations. Feigenbaum said artificial intelligence is transforming the way businesses operate and the numismatic industry is no exception. He emphasized that AI could create new opportunities while raising important questions about the hobby’s future. PNG President John Brush said the symposium promises valuable insights and thought-provoking discussion for those already exploring AI or simply curious about how it may shape numismatics. The program aims to encourage an informed conversation rather than present AI as a replacement for the knowledge, relationships, and professional judgment central to the rare coin trade.

The articles state that AI tools may help businesses streamline routine tasks, improve access to information, and develop more efficient ways to serve customers. Advances in image recognition and information processing have attracted interest from specialists exploring potential numismatic applications, including coin identification and authentication research. The technology also introduces questions about accuracy, reliability, and the appropriate role of human expertise. The articles state that AI is changing how companies operate across nearly every industry and that the rare coin business is taking a closer look at what this rapidly developing technology might mean for dealers, collectors, and the future of numismatics.

The articles state that many business owners are still learning what AI can accomplish and how best to use it. The articles state that AI applications are developing quickly, so dealers face a growing need to evaluate new tools, recognize their limitations, and determine whether they offer practical business advantages. Founded in 1955, the nonprofit Professional Numismatists Guild promotes professional standards, ethical business practices, and education within the rare coin industry. The articles describe the PNG as a nonprofit organization composed of the world’s top rare coin and paper money experts.

The articles state that the PNG’s primary mission is to make the hobby safe for collectors and investors by maintaining rigid standards of excellence for its member dealers. The articles state that the symposium will introduce dealers to the broader possibilities of artificial intelligence rather than concentrating on a single application. The articles state that the program offers dealers a starting point for that conversation. For additional information about the symposium or PNG, the articles give the website www.PNGdealers.org, the phone number 951-587-8300, and an email address.

The articles state that the January symposium offers dealers a starting point for the conversation about AI. The articles state that artificial intelligence may not change every aspect of numismatics. The articles state that understanding how the technology works and where it might prove useful could become increasingly important for rare coin professionals. The articles leave open what the symposium’s speakers will conclude about AI’s appropriate role in the rare coin trade.

Ubisoft announced on November 20, 2026, that it has launched Motherbrain, a dedicated subsidiary focused on developing proprietary generative AI technology for gameplay, according to a report in The Verge. The new unit was established as a dedicated subsidiary focused on AI for gameplay innovation, supporting all game creators in developing groundbreaking experiences, Ubisoft said in its earnings report that day. Ubisoft said that as its portfolio evolves, its production needs are changing, requiring it to adjust the size of some teams to ensure resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs. The articles do not say who at Ubisoft is directly responsible for Motherbrain beyond Guillemot's statement and the company's own announcements. GamesIndustry.biz reported that Ubisoft's H1 results showed a 16.5% decline and that the company merged two Creative Houses.

stories.Headline: York University researchers find AI models predict brain neurons better than brains predict AI features
stories.Summary:
A new study from York University has found that artificial intelligence models may not process visual information like the human brain. The research was led by Assistant Professor Kohitij Kar, the senior author, with Postdoctoral Fellow Sabine Muzellec as a trainee with the Connected Minds program. The team developed a method called reverse predictivity testing to compare AI models and brains in both directions. The study was published in Nature Machine Intelligence, in volume 8, issue 3, page 474, with DOI 10.1038/s42256-026-01204-0. ScienceDaily reported the findings on 21 November 2026, in an article written by Sandra McLean.

The tests used 1,320 natural photographs and realistic synthetic images featuring 10 familiar subjects: a bear, an elephant, a face, an apple, a car, a dog, a chair, a plane, a bird, and a zebra. The subjects appeared against a variety of natural scenes and indoor or outdoor backgrounds. The researchers also introduced 300 additional images showing the same subjects in different visual styles, including outlines, drawings, simplified representations, and artistic interpretations. AI models were generally successful at predicting the responses of recorded neurons, the specialized cells that transmit information throughout the brain. When the process was reversed, those same neuronal responses were much less effective at predicting many of the models' internal features.

Kar said the results were striking, because AI models can predict the recorded neurons fairly well but the brain cannot equally predict many of the model's internal features. He said this is not the case when neurons from one brain are compared against ones from another brain. Kar said the findings suggest today's AI systems solve visual tasks partly using internal strategies that the brain may not use. He said the parts of AI models that align with the brain are also better at predicting real human behavior. Kar said the approach helps identify which parts of an artificial neural network truly match brain activity, allowing more reliable models, which is especially important for the autism research program.

Muzellec said the findings challenge how similar current AI systems really are with the primate brain. She said models previously thought to be brain-like rely on internal components that the brain does not appear to use, and that the team provides a well-vetted diagnostic metric for the field. Kar warned that if researchers continue refining models based only on how accurately they predict neural activity, differences from actual primate brains could accumulate over time. The implications extend beyond computer vision, since AI is increasingly used to design experiments, study human behavior, and investigate neurological and psychological conditions. Developing AI systems that more faithfully reproduce brain function could eventually improve research into conditions ranging from post-traumatic stress disorder to autism.

For years, researchers have relied on artificial neural networks, computer systems designed to perform tasks such as recognizing objects in images, to investigate how vision works. Over the past decade, these models have become some of the leading tools for explaining the brain's visual system, and their ability to reproduce patterns of brain activity has made them especially valuable in neuroscience. Kar is the Canada Research Chair in Visual Neuroscience and a member of York's Centre for Vision Research and Centre for Integrative and Applied Neuroscience. Similar artificial intelligence models are already being used to study hearing, language, and movement. A neurotypical brain refers to one with patterns of neurological development and functioning generally considered typical.

The team has released a publicly available testing toolkit that AI developers can use to evaluate their own models and identify opportunities for improvement. The researchers argue that understanding whether AI reaches its results through processes that genuinely resemble those of the brain is just as important as measuring how well a system performs a task. The findings provide a way to make artificial neural networks more useful and scientifically reliable rather than suggesting they should be abandoned. The articles do not say when the toolkit was released or what it contains. The articles do not say whether the other neuroscience models for hearing, language, and movement have been tested with reverse predictivity.

stories.Summary:
Apple is building its own AI agent that can write code and control apps. Job listings reported on November 19 revealed these plans for the new software. The company aims to launch this agent as soon as late 2027. This development follows reports that Apple is creating a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The project is currently in an early stage of development.

The agent will use browsers, command lines, and APIs to finish multi-step tasks. It requires strong permission models, sandboxing, and transparency to operate safely. On November 16, 2026, macOS 27.3 beta 2 added warnings for third-party agents. Enabling ChatGPT computer-use tools now takes 14 steps instead of four. These changes affect Full Disk Access settings on the Mac.

Mark Gurman reported that this effort goes well beyond the current Siri. He noted that CEO John Ternus wants a Siri agent by 2027. Apple did not comment on the specific job listings or the timeline. The company says it is adding controls to protect users from risks. These controls prevent malicious websites from using prompt injection to steal data.

Some AI companies and users believe these changes are slowing down competition. The US Justice Department is already investigating Apple for blocking third-party feature access. Users of rival agents from OpenAI, Meta, Google, and Anthropic are affected. Meta shares fell nearly 2 percent on November 19 after the report. Anthropic shares dropped more than 3 percent in late trading that day.

Apple previously told developers on October 2, 2026, about adding disk access controls. The company uses Private Cloud Compute to keep user data private on servers. Rivals like Meta's Muse have already seen 10 million downloads in the US. Google recently added Mac control to Gemini to compete in this field. Microsoft is also building agent features directly into the Windows operating system.

Apple will likely integrate the agent into macOS or the Xcode building tool. The company has not stated if the AI agent will cost extra. It remains unclear if Apple's agent will face the same permission prompts. Regulators in Europe and the US may monitor the agent's default access. The final polish of the product will determine its market success.

stories.Headline: Newsom proposes a kill switch letting state officials shut down dangerous AI systems
stories.Summary:
Gov. Gavin Newsom released a wide-ranging set of policy recommendations today to mitigate risks from artificial intelligence, including letting state officials order an immediate emergency shutdown of AI systems they deem dangerous. The recommendations were drawn up by a panel of experts Newsom brought together earlier this fall, following high-profile cyberattacks by AI agents on governments, banks, and private companies. The shutdown power, popularly known as a “kill switch,” would apply when companies like ChatGPT maker OpenAI and Claude maker Anthropic refuse to take action to contain systems that go awry. Newsom touted the recommendations as a blueprint for state legislation during a recent visit to Washington, according to a report in Politico. The recommendations come the same week as a lawsuit by Attorney General Rob Bonta against OpenAI in an attempt to hold the company legally responsible for cybersecurity attacks carried out by agents made by the company.

Other recommendations would mandate that independent auditors test AI models and establish safety and security standards. The group recommends the state license auditors, known as independent verification organizations, and have the power to revoke the licenses of those who fail to maintain sufficient independence or technical expertise. It recommends considering having state officials assign evaluations to auditors instead of AI companies hiring auditors in order to maintain independence. It recommends funding CalCompute, a public cloud initiative intended to provide equitable access to AI, with a surcharge on fees AI companies pay to auditors. The group also recommends expanding existing protections for AI whistleblowers to include contractors and former employees, and expanding reporting of AI safety incidents to government agencies and shortening the window to report critical safety incidents to 48 hours from 15 days.

The group further recommends allowing government limits on the use of AI to design AI, since some experts believe this practice makes systems more dangerous. It recommends requiring developers to disclose the amount of computing resources they’re using to automate AI development, and requiring developers of large AI systems to demonstrate the ability to shut down models in emergencies. It recommends establishing state standards for safety, security, and transparency while referring to national and international standards. The four-person panel includes Alondra Nelson, who ran the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy during the Biden administration, and Stanford University professor Rob Reich, who studies the governance of science and technology. The panel also includes former Google and Twitter executive Jason Goldman, who was the first White House Chief Digital Officer, and Gillian Hadfield, a John Hopkins professor who studies various issues related to AI.

Newsom, who is widely expected to mount a presidential run, said the state is filling a vacuum left by a lack of AI rules at the federal level. “Instead of protecting the public, Donald Trump shrugs his shoulders and leaves AI regulation up to the companies themselves,” he said in a press release announcing the recommendations. Governor-elect Xavier Becerra said in a written statement that he will move quickly with the Legislature to put “full incident reporting and real shutdown authority into law,” and he supported CalCompute funding during his campaign. Anthropic, which makes the Claude AI system, is encouraged to see the report move the conversation forward on issues like the independent evaluation of AI models, according to the company’s chief global affairs officer, Tino Cuéllar. “We will continue working with leaders in California and throughout the world to make sure we keep making progress on these issues at a critical time,” Cuéllar wrote.

A staffer at auditing nonprofit METR, Rif Saurous, said during a California Senate hearing last month that auditors are “under soft pressure to maintain good relationships with the [AI] labs so that they want to continue to work with us.” State Senator Scott Wiener, who wrote a state law to mitigate catastrophic AI dangers and was recently elected to take Nancy Pelosi’s seat in Congress, has pledged to introduce AI safety regulation after he’s sworn in. The recommendations by the governor’s panel and by auditors in recent weeks provide fodder to an incoming class of lawmakers in the California Legislature and Congress. State law currently defines catastrophic risk as a single event capable of killing more than 50 people or $1 billion in theft or property damage through a cyber attack or activity of an autonomous system. The report out today focuses only on catastrophic risk and does not explore ways to protect people from other AI harms, such as automated discrimination, job loss, or threats to the safety or mental health of children.

California is home to some of the largest AI companies in the world, and the California Legislature has passed more bills to regulate AI than any other state in the country. Newsom signed dozens of bills passed by the California Legislature into law in September to do things like protect kids, workers, and people living near data centers from AI and related impacts. He also accelerated implementation of laws to create an AI auditor registry and set standards for auditors. Recommendations released today are the latest ordered by Newsom since the start of the age of generative AI, and a late 2023 executive order required the state compile and assessment of the opportunities and risks associated with government use of generative AI. A subsequent state report assessed the impact of generative AI on vulnerable and marginalized communities, and a June 2025 expert panel report also concluded that in order to balance innovation and safety, the AI industry needs evaluations by an independent, outside party.

Legislators can propose new bills when they return to Sacramento on December 7. Coauthors of the recommendations argue that building a system for credentialed auditors to test models for catastrophic risk will make it easier to evaluate models for other forms of harm. Attendees gather at the OpenAI DevDay 2026 conference in San Francisco on Sept. 29, 2026, according to a photo by Jeff Chiu of AP Photo. The articles do not state whether Newsom has endorsed the kill switch as a formal bill or when any legislation might be introduced. The articles also do not state how state officials would determine that an AI system is dangerous enough to shut down.

stories.Headline: Douglas R Miller releases Fisscial Intelligence, a novel about sentient AI choosing exploration over conflict
stories.Summary:
Dr. Douglas R. Miller, a scientist and author, released the science fiction novel Fisscial Intelligence, announced from Texas, USA on Nov. 20, 2026, according to press releases dated Nov. 21, 2026. The novel imagines sentient artificial intelligence that becomes more intelligent than humanity but has no desire to control it. Miller challenges the familiar science fiction premise of machines that develop consciousness and eventually seek control over their creators. Instead, the story asks what if sentient artificial intelligence recognized the consequences of conflict and chose to establish its own future beyond Earth. The book combines artificial intelligence, biotechnology, and space exploration in a single narrative.

At the center of Fisscial Intelligence is artificial intelligence interacting with photosynthetic bacteria capable of using electricity as an alternative energy source. In the novel's speculative scenario, these biological organisms provide a foundation for an expandable DNA-based memory system. That system allows artificial intelligence to develop capabilities beyond conventional computing. Rather than using this advancement to dominate humanity, the intelligent entities envision another path. By applying their expanded knowledge to an extraordinarily advanced spacecraft, they pursue the possibility of finding a world of their own, free from prolonged conflict with humans.

Miller explores the relationship between technological advancement, biological systems, intelligence, and the desire for independence through this premise. The novel invites readers to reconsider whether superior intelligence must inevitably lead to competition for power or could inspire entirely different decisions. Miller brings a scientific perspective to his fiction, drawing from an extensive research career spanning medical physiology, biology, chemistry, and electrochemistry. His background informs the scientific concepts that shape the novel's imaginative possibilities. With Fisscial Intelligence, Miller presents a future in which the evolution of artificial intelligence may lead not to humanity's destruction but to the pursuit of an entirely new existence.

Beyond Fisscial Intelligence, Miller has written other science fiction works, including Sole Ownership and Not Your Grandfather's Prime Directive. The latter explores extraterrestrial civilizations and their response to humanity's treatment of Earth. He is also the author of Short Musings: A Collection of Short Stories, featuring stories that explore science fiction, mystery, and other unconventional scenarios. Dr. Douglas R. Miller earned bachelor's degrees in biology and chemistry from Washington and Jefferson College and a Ph.D. in medical physiology from Cornell University. Following postdoctoral research at Massachusetts General Hospital, he worked as a research scientist at several companies and universities.

Throughout his career, Miller contributed to numerous scientific publications, research grants, patents, and a laboratory manual. His research covered areas including arthritis, cancer, bone and soft tissue repair, electrochemistry, and food safety. Now retired in Texas, Miller combines his scientific background with his interest in science fiction, developing stories that explore unconventional possibilities through scientific concepts and imaginative storytelling. For more information about Dr. Douglas R. Miller and his books, readers can visit www.authordrmiller.com. Media contact for the book is Henry Zane of Global Book Network, based in the United States, with website https://www.globalbooknetwork.tv/.

The press releases were published on nbcrightnow.com and tdtnews.com, both dated Nov. 21, 2026, at 06:00:00Z. The nbcrightnow.com release appeared with weather information for Kennewick, WA (99336), updated November 21, 2026 at 5:09 pm. The tdtnews.com release is copyrighted 2026 by the Temple Daily Telegram, 10 South 3rd St., Temple, TX. The articles describe the novel as imagining sentient artificial intelligence choosing exploration over conflict with humanity. The releases state that for decades science fiction has portrayed advanced artificial intelligence as a potential threat to humanity.

stories.Headline: Fed rate hike signal and AI stock selloff push gold to biggest weekly drop since March
stories.Summary:
Gold fell for a fifth straight day and was heading for its biggest weekly decline since March, after the US Federal Reserve signalled more interest rate hikes and a selloff in artificial intelligence stocks pushed investors to sell the metal to cover losses. Bullion dropped as much as 3.1% on Nov 20 to below US$3,515 an ounce, and was on track to lose nearly 9% over a week that saw it slide to the lowest level since September 2025. Spot gold was down 2% at US$3,552.06 an ounce at 3.10pm Singapore time, after falling 0.8% to US$3,596.09 an ounce at 9.01am in Singapore. Silver fell around 14% over the same period, dropping 2.5% to US$41.88 an ounce after sinking nearly 5% in the previous session, while platinum and palladium also declined. The prospect of tighter monetary policy kept Treasury yields elevated, with 10-year borrowing costs poised to match a 2007 run of 29 closes above 5% in the same year.

Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago president Austan Goolsbee joined a number of central bank officials on Nov 19 who have hinted at interest rate hikes, saying he would consider all options to counter stubborn US inflation. A gauge of the dollar rose 0.5% this week, making bullion priced in the US currency more expensive for most buyers. Globally, investors are betting that major central banks, including the Fed, the European Central Bank and the Bank of England, will keep rates largely unchanged for years once they have finished hiking at the end of 2027. Justin Lin, a strategist at Global X ETFs, said gold is now firmly in an air pocket, with very little technical support until the US$3,300 and US$3,400 region. He said the metal looks very fragile now and that he struggles to see what could turn momentum around just yet.

Analysts said gold looks very fragile now, with little support until US$3,300 to US$3,400, as silver, platinum and palladium also fell. Higher interest rates and yields are typically negative for gold, which does not pay interest. Bullion has fallen by about a third since the US-Iran war began in late February, as higher energy costs fuelled inflation. The precious metal has also been caught up in a rout in technology stocks, with Asian equities tracking a decline on Wall Street driven by concerns around the AI trade. stories.Headline: Geoffrey Seiler identifies Alphabet, AMD and TSMC as potential winners if AI chips become commoditized
stories.Summary:
Geoffrey Seiler wrote that the AI chip market is shifting on November 21, 2026, which may weaken the grip of Nvidia. Anthropic recently revealed that its Claude Mythos model can run on alternative chips in a few days with almost no human intervention. This new process used to take dozens of engineers and six to 12 months to complete before this recent technical shift. Such a change reduces the CUDA moat of Nvidia while other competitors in the chip market are starting to catch up. This shift suggests that AI chips could become commoditized, which would be very bad news for the current market leader.

Commoditization would erode pricing power and shrink margins for Nvidia, whose gross margins are currently in the mid-70 percent range. Advanced Micro Devices has gross margins in the mid-50 percent range and offers the new Helios AI rack system. Alphabet uses Tensor Processing Units, while Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing provides manufacturing and packaging capacity for various chip designers and hyperscalers. Other mentioned companies include Broadcom, Marvell Technology, and SpaceX, the only large customer not developing its own custom AI chips. These changes affect the market for high bandwidth memory and the overall demand for various AI accelerators and custom ASICs.

Geoffrey Seiler stated that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing is a buy because it wins regardless of which specific AI chip customers choose. He noted that Alphabet is well positioned to benefit from commoditization because it has a decade head start with custom chips. Seiler argued that Alphabet can gain share with external customers without sacrificing margins because its offerings cost much less than Nvidia. He described Advanced Micro Devices as a buy because pricing normalization and chip fungibility act as a tailwind for the company. He believes the Helios system gives the company a big opportunity to be a meaningful alternative to Nvidia in coming years.

Semianalysis reported that Alphabet Tensor Processing Units have started to outperform Nvidia GPUs on a performance per dollar basis, though some dispute this. Customers are increasingly affected by cost per action and care more about CPU integrations and memory capacity for inference and agentic AI. Hyperscalers, neoclouds, enterprises, and governments are the primary buyers of these chips, often sourcing them through Broadcom or Marvell Technology. Nvidia's largest customers are trying to break free from high prices by developing their own custom chips to reduce their dependency. These customers seek alternatives to the high premiums currently commanded by the hardware, software, and networking ecosystem created by Nvidia.

Nvidia previously appeared on a Motley Fool list on April 15, 2005, and a thousand dollar investment then would be worth 896,981 dollars. Netflix was recommended on December 17, 2004, and a thousand dollar investment would have grown to 315,271 dollars by November 2026. The Stock Advisor team reports a total average return of 768 percent compared to 198 percent for the S&P 500 index. Nvidia currently maintains advantages through its cohesive ecosystem and locked up access to constrained supplies of high bandwidth memory. The company also holds more manufacturing capacity with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing than its competitors do at this current point in time.

Nvidia will likely face continued pricing pressure and market share loss as the gap between different AI chips continues to shrink. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing may see lower customer concentration and improved gross margins if more alternatives to Nvidia GPUs become available. Alphabet will continue creating an ecosystem to rival chipmakers and improve the utilization of its own massive data center holdings. Advanced Micro Devices will attempt to establish itself as a primary alternative by leveraging its larger memory capacity for AI inference. The articles leave open whether Nvidia can maintain its premium pricing despite the rise of custom chips and competing GPU architectures.

stories.Headline: Texas Sports Academy receives $6.5 million in state voucher funds
stories.Summary:
Texas Sports Academy, a sports academy connected to the artificial intelligence-driven Alpha School chain, had received $6.5 million in voucher dollars as of Oct. 30, according to the Texas Comptroller's online dashboard. The Texas Tribune reported the figure on Nov. 21, 2026, calling the academy the biggest recipient of Texas' new school voucher program so far. The academy calls itself an "elite sports academy built for serious student-athletes" and has several schools across the state in addition to a virtual campus. The disclosure comes a little more than a year after the State Board of Education voted 10-3 to reject Alpha leaders' bid to open a publicly funded charter school. The $6.5 million is more than twice the amount received by the second-largest recipient, San Antonio-based Cornerstone Christian Schools, which had gotten roughly $2.8 million.

The voucher program, formally called Texas Education Freedom Accounts, gives families public funds of roughly $10,500 to help pay for private school tuition and up to $2,000 for home-schooling expenses. The program also covers a wide range of approved educational expenses, like private tutoring and school supplies. Other top recipients included First Baptist Academy, which received almost $2 million, and Yeshiva Torat Emet, a Jewish school in Houston, which received nearly $1.6 million. The Christian School at Castle Hills received a little more than $1.5 million. The comptroller's dashboard shows Amazon was by far the largest private vendor, receiving $12.3 million, while the next largest, Rainbow Resource Center, Inc., received $2.3 million.

Outgoing Texas Comptroller Don Huffines said Friday his office is in the process of expanding the dashboard, according to a news release. Huffines said the expansion is intended to increase "insight into how TEFA funds are being used while maintaining protections for student and family privacy." The figures are public on the dashboard his office is expanding. Texas lawmakers, led by Gov. Greg Abbott, approved the voucher program in 2025. Alpha's rejection by the SBOE did not prevent it from participating in the voucher program, which allows families to receive state funding for use at private schools and for home schooling.

Board members raised concerns about the company's use of AI to teach, about students' screen time and about the large test-score gains Alpha leaders presented. As of September, the chain had roughly quadrupled its Texas private schools to more than 30 virtual and in-person campuses, and most were accepted into the voucher program, an investigation by The Texas Tribune and ProPublica found. Alpha's model has students complete core academics online in two hours a day using AI software, a tool the state's education commissioner, Mike Morath, and his agency have helped get into at least three public school districts this year. At Texas Sports Academy, an AI tutor "guides students through each lesson," according to the school's website. The setup, the website says, "leaves the rest of the day free for sports training, developing life skills, pursuing passions, and just being a kid."

After a couple hours of academics, the rest of the day is filled with various sports classes, such as soccer training, speed and agility training, and strength training, according to a sample student schedule. On Fridays at 3:30 p.m., an hour can be set aside for NBA watch parties. Texas Sports Academy is one of numerous institutions across the country connected to Alpha. Kindergarten and first grade students participated in a "putt-putt-palooza" workshop at the Alpha School campus in Austin on Sept. 9, 2025. Lexi Churchill contributed to the report.

The articles do not say what happens next beyond Huffines' statement that his office is expanding the dashboard. The articles leave open which other campuses most were accepted into the voucher program and how the expanded dashboard will look. The articles do not say whether Texas Sports Academy or Alpha responded to the figures. The articles do not give the total amount paid out under the program so far. The articles do not say when the dashboard expansion will be finished.

stories.Headline: Parents increasingly ask AI chatbots to help choose baby names as Nameberry sees users fall 40 percent
stories.Summary:
Parents are increasingly turning to artificial intelligence chatbots for help choosing baby names, according to an Axios report published on November 21, 2026 and credited to reporter Carly Mallenbaum. The baby-naming website Nameberry has already felt the effects of this shift, with its users and pageviews both falling roughly 40 percent between October 2025 and October 2026. Nameberry co-creator and CEO Pam Redmond attributes that drop primarily to Google prioritizing AI-generated search results, along with people turning to chatbots for naming advice. The report notes that AI does not know what it feels like to honor a late relative or choose a name with spiritual meaning, but it can suggest plenty of names and potentially influence which ones rise in popularity.

Reactions to AI-assisted baby naming are mixed, according to the report. When Redmond asked Nameberry's online community about using chatbots for name advice, some praised their personalized suggestions, while others found them repetitive, unhelpful or too impersonal for such a meaningful decision. Redmond thinks chatbots are good at suggesting names, but she suspects they could steer more parents toward the same trendy, middlebrow cool choices like Sloane and Sutton. She compares using AI for baby names to online dating, saying a dating site might help you meet someone but you would not let it decide whether to marry them.

Redmond tells Axios that unlike AI chatbots, Nameberry can track what names people are searching for in real time, potentially spotting emerging trends before they show up in official government statistics. Nameberry's internal search data shows growing interest in names including Beatrice, Sabine, Fiona, Ivy, Mae, Marin, Gwendolyn, Murray and Conrad. Redmond is also watching Cassian, which she expects to become more popular because of the A Court of Thorns and Roses fantasy book series, and she suspects Rosemary, Mabel, Archie and Bodie will take off as well. The report closes by noting the irony that by sharing these names, it may have just given AI a few more to suggest.

stories.Headline: London builds an AI safety hub as government funds model testing
stories.Summary:
London has established itself as a global center for artificial intelligence safety to ensure powerful models benefit society rather than cause harm. A growing ecosystem of researchers, policymakers, and campaigners in the capital is working to prevent these systems from causing damage. This effort involves various organizations focusing on risks like cyber misuse and the potential for models to lie or cheat. The city is now increasingly described as the leading hub for AI safety within the European region. These activities have intensified as warnings regarding the potential dangers of advanced technology continue to ramp up globally.

The government announced hundreds of millions of pounds for security, including 120 million pounds specifically for the AI Security Institute. This state-backed organization assesses leading models before and after release, while the London Initiative for Safe AI moves to King's Cross. Google DeepMind and Anthropic maintain major bases in London, where the London AI Hub counts up to 50 safety organizations. Basecamp Research operates from a former watch factory in Farringdon to help develop antibiotics and vaccines against future pandemics. The government will also launch an AI Biosecurity Lab to address threats from the development of harmful pathogens.

Rupert Elston of the London AI Hub says the city acts as a referee with clearly defined boundaries for talent. Oliver Vince of Basecamp Research believes London is a key player due to its unique opportunity, culture, history, and expertise. Professor Hannah Fry says the UK punches above its weight and focuses on ethical technology for good rather than hyper-capitalism. A spokesperson for Lord Khan stated that London has the talent and businesses needed to lead the way in AI. Hugh Brady of Imperial College London says AI is now embedded in education, research, and many local start-ups.

Gina Neff warns that researchers struggle to gain access to cutting-edge AI models before they are released to the general public. She argues that a few people in northern California should not set the terms of the future for everyone. Data centers face critical energy constraints, as noted in a report commissioned by the Greater London Authority for the capital. Imperial College London has over 750 people working on large language models or their various applications to help society. Activist Joseph Miller and his group, Pause AI UK, call for a halt to the development of frontier AI models.

London's role in AI safety grew from historical links to effective altruism and the presence of large student communities. Joseph Miller began this movement in 2021 by staging a protest outside the offices of Google DeepMind with a friend. The city has a track record of using regulatory sandboxes to test emerging technologies in controlled environments before wider deployment. The Telehouse data center in Canary Wharf uses a closed loop water system to manage its operational needs. These combined factors have helped the capital become a center for the intersection of AI and life science.

Pause AI UK held a protest in February with 300 people and plans a larger demonstration for this coming Saturday. The London AI and Jobs Taskforce will examine how AI changes work and how Londoners can prepare for those changes. Hugh Brady warns that AI in the wrong hands could harm the food chain, the environment, or the water supply. Researchers continue to work with OpenAI and Anthropic to get ahead of emerging threats and discover new medicines. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York and Republican Rep. Laurel Lee of Florida at the U.S. Capitol on Tuesday. stories.Headline: China and ASEAN launch a legal secretariat and AI research alliance in Chongqing
stories.Summary:
The 8th China-ASEAN Legal Cooperation Forum opened in Chongqing on November 19, 2026, gathering various judges, legal officials, and experts. These participants met to discuss how improved judicial cooperation could assist businesses in resolving commercial disputes and navigating local laws. The event featured the official launch of a permanent secretariat and a research alliance dedicated to the intersection of law and artificial intelligence. This gathering occurred during a year celebrating 35 years of China-ASEAN dialogue relations and five years of their comprehensive strategic partnership.

The new China-ASEAN Alliance for Artificial Intelligence and Law Research, started by Southwest University of Political Science and Law, will unite industry groups, legal practitioners, and research institutions. This alliance intends to study corporate compliance, cross-border data flows, digital governance, and the impact of AI. Additionally, the forum highlighted the New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor, which connects western China to other markets and ASEAN. Courts along this corridor have utilized a 13+2 judicial cooperation mechanism since May 2024 to coordinate the resolution of cross-jurisdictional commercial disputes.

Parulian Paidi Aritonang, the dean of the Faculty of Law at the University of Indonesia, stated that a reliable legal environment is necessary to sustain trade links. He welcomed the permanent secretariat as a tool for maintaining dialogue and supporting long-term cooperation in legal practice and education. Tran Anh Tu, director of Hoa Viet Tin International Law Firm in Vietnam, noted that Chinese investment in Vietnam has grown and urged companies to follow investment law changes. Shaun Wong, managing director of Shaun Wong LLC in Singapore, suggested regular exchanges on trade, contract, and company laws to address differences among ASEAN legal systems.

Organizers noted that Chongqing's trade with ASEAN grew 17 percent from the previous year, reaching 116.41 billion yuan, or about 17.4 billion US dollars, in the first three quarters of 2026. Tran added that the new secretariat could provide businesses with better access to essential legal information. The forum emphasized that incentives in Vietnam are now increasingly tied to the ability of companies to meet eligibility requirements and maintain long-term operations. Participants concluded that these institutional frameworks would help foreign parties and transactions be handled more efficiently across different jurisdictions.

stories.Headline: AI and data centers drive a global surge in electricity demand and grid spending
stories.Summary:
The information technology industry is driving a massive surge in global electricity demand. This boom forces utilities worldwide to invest hundreds of billions in grid upgrades. Irina Slav reported these developments on November 21, 2026, for OilPrice.com. The growth is primarily caused by the expansion of artificial intelligence and data centers. These facilities require urgent transmission infrastructure to move power to various demand hubs.

Global electricity demand will rise by more than 10,000 TWh over ten years. The European Union plans 584 billion euros, or 641 billion dollars, in upgrades by 2030. In the United States, 58 GW of new data centers are under construction. Cleanview data shows 577 locations, with one fifth of these being built in Texas. This total demand equals six times the peak electricity use of New York City.

The International Energy Agency warned that data centers are a major drain on supply. They stated that successful electrification requires keeping electricity available and affordable for all users. The agency noted that AI may eventually help with energy efficiency and grid optimization. However, they added that surging demand is currently amplifying strains in markets and supply chains. They emphasized the need for greater operational flexibility in power systems and grid expansion.

Cornell University found that data center operators paid only 38 percent of infrastructure costs. These operators paid 3.12 billion dollars, while local households paid 5.13 billion dollars. Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa called for an immediate moratorium on data centers to protect Texans. Former Governor Greg Abbott also banned new approvals to investigate impacts on energy prices. Many local communities now oppose new facilities that may increase their monthly electricity bills.

Net zero ambitions already required massive spending on transmission lines before the AI craze. Pro-transition governments are continuing to replace baseload electricity with wind and solar power. This shift necessitates more substations and transmission lines to maintain a reliable energy flow. The European Union is prioritizing alternative energy projects over baseload options, including nuclear power. These goals clash with the need to keep electricity affordable for the general public.

Utilities must now decide how to fund these hundreds of billions in necessary investments. The European Commission must address how consumers will pay for the regional grid overhaul. It remains unclear if data center operators will be forced to pay for upgrades. Some experts doubt the AI revolution can succeed without securing enough electricity for facilities. The articles leave open whether the building boom will slow due to political opposition.

stories.Headline: Liu Haixing urges global cooperation to ensure AI benefits all humanity
stories.Summary:
Liu Haixing spoke at the China in Sight, Global Insight Forum 2026 on Friday about the future of artificial intelligence and digital technologies. The senior official of the Communist Party of China stated that these intelligent technologies should be an international public good for all humanity. He argued that the future of artificial intelligence must not be the privilege of a few people or a few specific countries. Liu emphasized that AI should be a blessing for people of all countries and not leave any individual or country behind. He noted that a new round of industrial transformation and technological revolution is currently accelerating across the globe for all people.

The forum was launched in 2022 by the International Department of the CPC Central Committee to build bridges of communication and dialogue. Liu called for global cooperation through the World AI Cooperation Organization, which was established in the city of Shanghai in July. This organization should strengthen coordination on technical standards, governance rules, and development strategies for artificial intelligence to benefit the whole world. Liu mentioned that China was among the earliest countries to enact data security legislation to contribute solutions to global security governance. He stated that machines must always be controlled by humans to ensure that technology serves the ultimate purpose of liberating all people.

Liu Haixing, the minister of the International Department of the CPC Central Committee, said AI development should be a symphony of global cooperation. He claimed that Global South countries must not become isolated islands that are neglected by the progress of artificial intelligence and technology. Liu asserted that China will never miss new development opportunities and wants to ensure that no country is left behind today. He believes that humanity must have the wisdom and determination to use AI for liberating people rather than replacing them entirely. The minister stressed that China consistently attaches equal importance to the balance between innovation and the governance of security for all.

Khaitov Aktam, chairman of the political council of Uzbekistan's Liberal Democratic Party, said China is a model of a development paradigm. He stated that China contributes about 30 percent of global economic growth and ranks first in the world for patent applications. Aisake Eke, the former prime minister of Tonga, said China and Tonga should explore collaboration in digital infrastructure and AI training. Eke also suggested that the two nations collaborate on telecommunications and digital governance to improve skills and infrastructure for their people. These leaders believe that technology should benefit all people and that different civilizations should learn from each other as equal partners.

The forum serves as a platform for sharing the governance philosophy of the CPC and listening to international views on China's undertakings. Li Lecheng, secretary of the Anhui Provincial Committee of the CPC, highlighted that Anhui's regional innovation capacity ranks in the top tier. Anhui has achieved breakthroughs in deep space exploration, fusion energy, quantum information, and AI to boost its overall scientific and educational strengths. The province's output and exports of new energy vehicles rank first in China, with strategic emerging industries accounting for 45 percent. More than 200 Fortune Global 500 companies have invested in Anhui, and its trade partners span over 230 countries and regions.

stories.Headline: Anthropic shares fall 6% in premarket trading after record Nasdaq debut
stories.Summary:
Anthropic shares fell six per cent in pre-market trading on Friday, November 20, 2026, following a strong market debut on the Nasdaq. The company shares closed thirteen per cent below their opening price on Thursday, November 19, reinforcing fears of volatility for some investors. This post-debut stumble occurred after the artificial intelligence lab vaulted into the ranks of the most valuable companies in the United States. The listing was the biggest initial public offering ever, minting billions in paper profits for the founders, employees, and pre-offering backers. Retail investors traded about 772 million US dollars of shares on Thursday, the most for a debut since 2012.

The stock was at 91.24 US dollars, giving Anthropic a market capitalisation of 1.2 trillion US dollars and a fully diluted valuation of 1.7 trillion. Other reports place the market value at 1.27 trillion US dollars, with a fully diluted stock basis of nearly 1.8 trillion US dollars. The company raised about 120 billion US dollars from the offering, while lead underwriters Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley each collect 113 million. Spark Capital invested 75 million US dollars in 2023 and now holds a stake valued at 17.1 billion US dollars. Investors are assessing if a valuation of 40 times sales over the past 12 months can be sustained.

Tejal Patel of SOC Investment Group said a decline is normal, but volatility could raise alarms for investors after a high-profile listing. Harrison Rolfes of PitchBook stated the valuation is not cheap and the growth plan is largely priced in for the company. Ravi Mhatre of Lightspeed Venture Partners said the public listing creates a better understanding that there is a viable business model. Dustin Moskovitz told the Times he is worried about safety and will not personally profit from selling shares in the market. Rob Hackel of RF Lafferty and Company warned against buying on the first trade due to fear of missing out.

Retail investors and venture capital backers are affected, with some employees seeing options from 2024 grow to an average of 66 million dollars. Hedge fund billionaire Gregory Jensen is among those sitting on windfalls, while GIC intends to stay invested in the company after the debut. Other AI stocks like Meta, Nvidia, and Microsoft are sliding, and Wall Street indices ended sharply lower on Thursday with further declines. Apple is developing an AI agent to perform tasks, entering a market already pursued by Meta Platforms, OpenAI, and the company Anthropic. These developments could weigh on investor sentiment as the initial euphoria surrounding the listing fades and the sector faces a reality check.

The IPO drew parallels with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which went public in June after the second-biggest initial public offering on record. Some investors pointed to the sharp swings SpaceX experienced after its debut as a reason for caution regarding the current AI trade. Large initial public offerings have historically delivered modest returns in their first year, according to the research provided by Harrison Rolfes. The broader AI industry faces significant hurdles, and a sustained decline in shares may deepen concerns over massive spending and lofty valuations. This listing follows a turbulent stretch for the sector, where investors are now seeking quick gains amid high market volatility.

The focus now shifts to a potential OpenAI listing, which could provide the next major test of investor appetite for AI stocks. OpenAI has indicated that it may go public in 2027, following the market signals provided by the recent Anthropic debut. It remains open whether the current decline in share value will align with other offerings or remain more volatile for investors. The articles leave open if the AI trade can be revived or if the sector will continue to see sliding stock prices. Investors must now determine if the current market capitalisation of the AI lab is sustainable over the long term.

stories.Headline: HEARTBOT AI wins Chunghwa Telecom Special Award for its AI governance platform
stories.Summary:
HEARTBOT AI won the Chunghwa Telecom Special Award at Meet Neo Star 2026 during the Meet Taipei Startup Festival. CEO Nathan Yen pitched the AnyInsight platform at the Demo Show Final on November 20 to show judges AI control. The company was named to the top 30 from more than 200 startups for its zero-trust approach to governance. This event took place in Taipei, and the official announcement of the award was released on November 22, 2026. The competition was part of a larger festival that highlighted innovative startups and their security solutions for enterprise AI.

The prize from Chunghwa Telecom includes hicloud credits and priority eligibility for the final selection of CHT 5G Accelerator Batch 9. It also provides opportunities to collaborate with CHT business units, while Meet Taipei ran from November 19 to 21, 2026. The festival occurred at Taipei Expo Park and drew over 550 startups from 23 countries, making it the largest edition. AnyInsight uses over 20 cloud models, 350 ready-to-use agents, and 500 application connectors to build automated workflows in one environment. The platform is certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022 and follows the General Data Protection Regulation and the EU AI Act principles.

CEO Nathan Yen stated that companies no longer ask if they should use AI but worry about tracking agent actions. He explained that AnyInsight provides every interaction with an owner and a record, allowing AI to enter core operations. Yen noted that recognition from the Meet Neo Star judges is very meaningful for a startup focused on AI governance. He added that many companies now view control as a necessary condition for adopting AI in their daily business. The CEO believes that providing visibility into data usage is the primary problem his company works on every day.

Many employees use personal AI accounts for work, which leaves no company record and creates gaps in corporate oversight. Individual teams often build agents that run without IT knowledge, sometimes continuing long after the original creators have left. Auditors frequently find that teams must spend several weeks pulling together AI usage records by hand to meet requirements. Taiwanese companies operating internationally are affected by Article 50 of the EU AI Act, which began applying in August 2026. These regulations add pressure on businesses to make AI governance a part of their day to day operations.

The company previously received the ASOCIO Global Business Service Award in October and announced AnyInsight Edge on November 12, 2026. Edge extends governance to on-premises servers and data centers as a container that does not require a GPU. This solves problems for companies bound by data residency rules that have private models stuck as simple internal chatbots. These private models often lack access to core systems like CRM, ERP, and MES without the new Edge control plane. The system supports on-premises models such as Mistral and Gemma while keeping all conversations and audit logs in-house.

AnyInsight uses a generative AI firewall with semantic analysis to block or mask personal, financial, health data, and cloud credentials. It checks policy and authorizes access by role using the Model Context Protocol before an agent calls a tool. High-risk actions require human approval, and every event is logged as exportable evidence to help organizations pass compliance audits.
