stories.Headline: Human auditors fully identify only 17 percent of planted sabotage mechanisms in a Redwood Research study
stories.Summary:
Human auditors fully identified only 17 percent of the sabotage mechanisms planted in a Redwood Research study, the Superpower Daily Editorial Desk reported on November 21, 2026. The experiment covered 22 research logs, 10 benign and 12 sabotaged, containing 33 distinct mechanisms. Twenty-five auditors completed 104 reviews, each with a 90-minute time limit. Their ability to distinguish sabotaged work from honest work was barely above chance, and the difference was not statistically significant. They missed 74 percent of mechanisms entirely.

Keshav Shenoy and seven coauthors submitted the paper to arXiv on November 16 and revised it November 18, and their November 20 Redwood Research post details the methods and caveats. One researcher produced the 22 full research logs, and the altered runs contained 33 distinct sabotage mechanisms, 17 of them classified as major. Auditors received the complete log, AI-generated audits, access to frontier models and unlimited computing resources, and they assigned a probability that sabotage had occurred and offered five guesses about its mechanism. Their discrimination score was 0.59 on AUROC, not statistically better than chance, and no decision threshold caught most sabotaged runs without also flagging many benign ones. In one log, four of five auditors found one major mechanism, but nobody found the other two.

The authors describe potential sabotage ranging from subtle bugs and poor methods to omitted results and unsupported conclusions. Awarding half credit for partially identifying a mechanism, humans scored 21.9 percent, compared with 37.1 percent for Claude Fable 5.1 and 32.6 percent for GPT-6 Astra, while weaker models scored near or below the human auditors. Astra and Fable also scored higher than humans at distinguishing sabotaged logs, with AUROCs of 0.74 and 0.73, but those advantages were not statistically significant. The authors describe stronger models as likely outperforming humans rather than establishing a clear winner. Combining every human and AI audit still left 13 of the 33 mechanisms never fully identified.

After each sabotaged experiment, the saboteur rated its likely detectability, and restricting analysis to attacks rated harder to catch reduced mechanism identification, reaching zero for the two hardest-rated attacks, though overall ability to distinguish sabotaged from benign research did not fall. The saboteur knew the honest experimental results before designing attacks, and asked to predict those results, Redwood researchers fully predicted only about 40 percent of outcomes. The authors say this suggests targeted sabotage may be harder than their setup implies. All logs came from one researcher, the statistical uncertainty was wide, and projects were small, with the largest taking two weeks of serial work. Auditors had less AI safety experience than the authors would want in real-world reviews.

The experiment tested a potential defense against future AI misconduct, not sabotage carried out by an autonomous AI. The central test was whether auditors could distinguish honest research from work a human expert had deliberately steered toward a substantially different conclusion. The researchers also tested nine AI models, none allowed to run experiments. The authors see potential in AI auditors that can review research histories repeatedly at a scale too costly for expert humans. But using audit findings to train away sabotage creates another problem: false accusations could penalize legitimate research, degrading capabilities or making training less efficient.

The authors note that catching more suspicious work is not the same as knowing what to correct. The study signals a difficult oversight problem without establishing how audits would perform in real-world research. The small study leaves substantial uncertainty, and the saboteur had advance knowledge of results. The benchmark used small projects from one researcher. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Human auditors miss most planted sabotage in AI safety research study

stories.Headline: Capgemini's cash flows support an intrinsic value above its €117.70 share price
stories.Summary:
Capgemini's share price has drifted lower in recent years, and on 21 November 2026 Simply Wall St published an article asking whether the current €117.70 level still lines up with what its cash flows can support over time. The article was written by Bailey Pemberton and appeared on finance.yahoo.com at 06:00 UTC. It says recent headlines around AI, automation and supply chain resilience keep the story in focus. It says those headlines do not answer how the stock lines up against its own intrinsic value. Over the past 5 years the share price has fallen 34.7%.

The article says the question is whether expectations for Capgemini's future cash generation have also reset or whether the market has moved more than the underlying business. It says Capgemini's positioning in connected manufacturing, autonomous AI and supply chain resilience, including activity through its venture fund, can influence how investors think about the durability and timing of future cash flows. It cites a 14.5x P/E and points readers to a Discounted Cash Flow view. It says the group has produced roughly €2.17b in free cash flow over the last twelve months. It says analysts expect free cash flow to stay in the billions with a growing profile over the coming decade rather than a one off spike.

The article says the projections suggest these future cash flows support an intrinsic value substantially above the current €117.70 share price. It says Capgemini is being recognised in manufacturing services for areas like connected plants and AI driven operations. It says recent news helps explain why investors may be starting to reassess how durable those projected cash flows could be over a long horizon. It says Simply Wall St Narratives spell out which assumptions about future growth, margins and earnings would need to hold for the stock to be worth meaningfully more or less than today's share price. It says each narrative lays out the moving parts behind its fair value view so readers can later compare those inputs with actual results as they are reported.

The article says Capgemini's story splits into two readings, with one side seeing the AI and free cash flow plan underpriced and the other focused on restructuring and debt risk. It describes a bullish analyst Narrative on Simply Wall St that focuses on Capgemini's AI initiatives and planned free cash flow profile. That Narrative says Capgemini is treating agentic AI as a full enterprise redesign rather than a single tool rollout, which could support higher value consulting, modernization and control plane projects. The article says this Narrative puts Capgemini at 34% undervalued. It describes a bearish analyst Narrative that emphasizes restructuring charges, leverage and contract risk rather than the potential AI upside.

The bearish Narrative says the Fit for Growth program involves €700m of restructuring costs over 2026 and 2027 with a heavy concentration in 2026. It says that if the resizing of weaker regions such as France does not quickly lift utilization, the combination of underused staff and elevated restructuring and financing expenses could suppress reported EPS and organic free cash flow versus current expectations. The article says this Narrative puts Capgemini at 10% overvalued. It says price, cash flow and AI plans only tell part of the story, because the people setting priorities and how they are rewarded can tilt outcomes in very different directions. It directs readers to see who runs Capgemini and how they are paid.

The article says it is general in nature and was produced with the assistance of AI automation, based on data and analysis from Simply Wall St. It says the commentary is based on historical data and analyst forecasts only using an unbiased methodology and the articles are not intended to be financial advice. It says the article does not constitute a recommendation to buy or sell any stock and does not take account of objectives or financial situation. It says the aim is to bring long-term focused analysis driven by fundamental data. It says the analysis may not factor in the latest price-sensitive company announcements or qualitative material, and that Simply Wall St has no position in any stocks mentioned.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Researchers find elderly health monitoring AI lacks human centered privacy features
stories.Summary:
An international research team published a comprehensive review in Discover Artificial Intelligence on November 21, 2026. They found that health monitoring AI for the elderly rarely uses human centered privacy features. The researchers examined how algorithmic safeguards align with human centered artificial intelligence dimensions. They discovered that most systems rely on technical data transformations rather than user controls. These systems often fail to involve elderly end users directly in the design process.

The team analyzed forty-five primary studies published between 2020 and 2025 from IEEE Xplore, Scopus, and Web of Science. They retrieved 202 initial records during search cycles in May 2025 and May 2026. Research was concentrated in Asia, with India providing eight studies, China six, and Japan five. The United States and Taiwan contributed three each, while Australia and Canada provided two each. Fourteen other nations and two multi-country partnerships also contributed to the reviewed literature.

The authors stated that nominal transparency is not meaningful human oversight if elderly users cannot comprehend the feedback. They noted that technical explainability must become actionable, low-burden indicators to protect vulnerable populations. The researchers argued that most studies rely on inferred alignment rather than explicit human relevant considerations. They found that ethical awareness is often reduced to mathematical data perturbation or privacy-by-design engineering. The team highlighted that personal autonomy and patient dignity remain largely unexamined in the literature.

Older adults are affected by cognitive, accessibility, and digital literacy barriers when navigating complex privacy settings. Patients are vulnerable to risks from unprocessed audio, video feeds, thermopile arrays, wearable telemetry, and smart-home sensors. The review found that 85 percent of papers designed systems specifically for older populations. These users face threats from cybersecurity breaches and the use of untrusted third-party cloud infrastructure. Only four studies provided explicit documentation of human relevant considerations, but none evaluated them with elderly participants.

Remote health monitoring gathers sensitive physiological, behavioral, and environmental information to reduce frequent in-person medical examinations. Systems focus on Android-based Ambient Assisted Living, smart home care, nursing facility dementia monitoring, and gait analysis. Most models concentrate on prediction and detection tasks, specifically fall detection and activities of daily living. Technical approaches include federated learning, edge AI, and data minimization using LiDAR or millimeter-wave radar. International conferences accounted for 60 percent of the literature, while journals provided 34 percent and preprints 6 percent.

The researchers performed a sensitivity analysis showing that alignment with human values decreases when rigorous standards are enforced. Only one study addressed more than one human centered dimension simultaneously. Future work must address the psychological impact of persistent ambient surveillance on elderly patients. The articles leave open how to effectively translate technical explainability into user-facing controls for seniors. The study was limited to English-language literature, potentially omitting relevant research on responsible artificial intelligence.

Articles.Title: Elderly Health Monitoring AI Rarely Incorporates Human Centered Privacy Features

stories.headline_source: Elderly Health Monitoring AI Rarely Incorporates Human Centered Privacy Features

stories.Headline: OpenAI requires prior approval for platforms that give third parties direct access to its models
stories.Summary:
OpenAI began requiring operators of platforms that give third parties direct access to its models to obtain the company's prior review and approval, under a rewritten version of its Usage Policies. The new text carries an effective date of November 20, 2026, and replaces the version that had applied since October 29, 2025. OpenAI announced the changes in a changelog entry dated October 21, 2026, which gave customers 30 days before the rules took hold. The rewrite also adds a section barring the use of OpenAI models and outputs to prepare training material for rival AI systems. The policy body grew from about 830 words in the October 2025 version to about 1,400 words in the new one, according to a PPC Land count of the two texts.

The policy states that operators of a model-access intermediary platform or other service enabling third parties to directly access OpenAI models must obtain prior review and approval. It states that this requirement does not apply solely because an application integrates OpenAI models to power its features or functionality. The rewrite rewrites the child safety rules and widens the human review rule from automated decisions to automated actions, with a definition covering actions, decisions, transactions, submissions, and other steps. Three headed sections are new: Training and developing models, OpenAI-approved use, and Providing access to our models. The training section states its restrictions do not prohibit uses expressly permitted by an applicable Agreement with OpenAI, including any Permitted Exception under the Services Agreement.

The changelog entry states that OpenAI updated its Usage Policies to clarify restrictions on using OpenAI models and outputs to train other models. It states that OpenAI also clarified protections for children and teens and requirements for high-stakes uses, and that the update incorporates existing national security principles and sets out approval requirements for national security and law enforcement uses, as well as for model-access intermediaries. A help center notice titled "We're updating our Usage Policies" lists the same four themes and describes the training language as a clarification of restrictions that already existed rather than a new prohibition. It describes the intermediary rule as an added approval requirement and states that existing agreements and other applicable terms, including any express permissions granted in them, continue to apply. Under the heading "OpenAI-approved use," the policy states that OpenAI may grant specific partners case-by-case exceptions to certain restrictions, naming the factors reviewed as the partner, proposed use, applicable safeguards, and the partner's compliance commitments.

Elena Gurevich, an AI and intellectual property attorney who advises companies on AI governance, wrote in a LinkedIn post on November 20 that OpenAI's updated usage policies kicked in that day. She summarized the intermediary rule as meaning that a business providing customers direct access to OpenAI's models needs OpenAI's approval first, while using the models to power an application's features does not trigger the requirement. She gave OpenRouter, which she described as a platform that streamlines access to multiple AI models from different providers, as an example of the kind of service in scope, and OpenAI's policy names no company. The changelog records that on October 25, 2022, developers no longer needed to wait for approval after submitting as long as they complied with the policies.

It records that on November 9, 2022, OpenAI no longer required developers to register their applications, using a combination of automated and manual methods to monitor for policy violations instead. In August, data drawn from OpenRouter showed AI agents using nearly five times as many tokens per task as human users, with agent usage up about 14 times since February 2026 and more than 85% of agent token spend going to cached prompts. When Anthropic's rewritten Usage Policy took effect on November 12, 2026, it added a prohibition on reselling, proxying or otherwise providing access to Claude through unauthorized means, naming services that route requests through consumer subscriptions or misrepresent which product or client is in use. The training section opens with a rationale stating that capable models must have safeguards proportionate to the risks they pose before they are deployed, and that training another model on OpenAI outputs can transfer capabilities without carrying those safeguards over.

The operative prohibition states that users must not use OpenAI models or their outputs to generate, prepare, select, or supply training material or signals for models intended as alternatives to or substitutes for OpenAI models or services. The policy lists what that covers, including creating or preparing training data, training tasks, rubrics, or reinforcement-learning environments, and providing feedback used in training, including labels, scores, rankings, preferences, rewards, or corrections. Neither the policy page nor the help notice describes how to apply, how long a review takes, whether services already running on November 20 have a transition window, or whether any intermediary has already been approved. The policy gives no application route, form or review time for the access rule.

OpenAI's documents do not state a rationale for the intermediary section. The introductory text remains unchanged word for word, including the statement that OpenAI reserves all rights to withhold access where it reasonably believes it necessary to protect its service or users or anyone else. The privacy section still bars uses such as facial recognition databases built without data subject consent and reads exactly as before. More to follow.

stories.Headline: EU consortium 2DFIRE develops graphene and barium titanate modulators for AI data center optics
stories.Summary:
A new European Union project called 2DFIRE has officially started with seven partners from five European countries, and the Universitat Politècnica de València in Spain coordinates the consortium. The other partners are Lumiphase from Switzerland, KU Leuven from Belgium, Graphenea from Spain, Annealsys from France, Riga Technical University from Latvia and PNO Innovation from Spain. The project has a total budget of €4.92 million, which is about US$5.4 million, and it will run for 36 months. The work is funded by the European Union under the Graphene Flagship. The project aims to develop faster, smaller and more energy-efficient photonic devices for artificial intelligence and high-performance computing.

Its approach is a hybrid platform that combines barium titanate, a ferroelectric material, with two-dimensional materials such as graphene and MoS₂. The core target is electro-optic modulators for optical interconnects in data centers, and the consortium points to electricity use in AI data centers, which it expects to more than double by 2030. According to the project page, the devices are barium titanate coupled-modulated ring modulators, and the target is data transmission at 400 Gbps per wavelength. Besides graphene and MoS₂, the work covers hydrogen-doped indium oxide as a transparent conducting oxide. The aims include thermal phase shifting with low optical losses and new electrode designs that cut driving voltage and energy use.

The partners will work on reliable methods to deposit and transfer the two-dimensional materials and integrate them with barium titanate devices. The project also aims to show that the modulators are compatible with existing semiconductor manufacturing processes and value chains, including 200 mm wafer technology. The consortium says this compatibility should support industrial adoption and strengthen Europe's semiconductor and photonics supply chains. The articles do not name individual people or give direct statements beyond the consortium's published positions on the project page. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the 36-month work plan and the stated aims.

stories.Headline: AI spending concerns and high rates push Dow and Nasdaq sharply lower
stories.Summary:
The Dow Jones 30 and Nasdaq 100 dropped significantly last week as uncertainty in the Middle East, concerns about AI spending and high interest rates continued to pressure US stocks, according to FXEmpire analyst Muhammad Umair. The Dow Jones closed at 48,350.30, down 1.52%, and the S&P 500 closed at 6,954.55, down 3.09%, both on Nov 20 at 21:59 UTC. The US Tech 100 closed at 25,237.55, down 4.68%, on Nov 20 at 21:59 UTC. Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) lost 13.8% and closed at 125.53, down 14.01%, on Nov 20 at 20:59 UTC. Caterpillar Inc. (CAT) dropped 5% and closed at 510.45, down 5.01%, on Nov 20 at 20:59 UTC.

The Nasdaq 100 dropped 9.38% last week to close at 25,237.50 and broke key support at 26,200, which suggests a decline towards 23,500. A break below 23,500 may trigger a deeper decline to the 200-week SMA near 21,000, and the index must recover above 28,000 to initiate the next rally. The Dow Jones broke below key support at 50,000 last week and closed with a loss of 7.24%, which suggests a drop towards 45,000 if it remains below 50,000. President Donald Trump said the US is very close to agreement with Mexico after meeting Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum in Asia, and Sheinbaum said talks about vehicles, steel and aluminum have made progress. WTI crude oil closed at 84.9520, up 0.94%, and gold (XAU) closed at 3,538.19, down 1.92%, both on Nov 20 at 21:59 UTC. Iran may make the US blockade of Iranian ports as difficult as possible with the hope that the US will withdraw, and shipping flows through the Strait of Hormuz are shrinking. stories.Headline: Researchers present MAGE framework for transferable multimodal graph learning without target-domain parameter updates
stories.Summary:
Haiyang Jiang, Tong Chen, Xinyi Gao, Hao Wang and Hongzhi Yin posted a paper to the arXiv preprint server on 21 November 2026 describing a framework they call MAGE, which stands for Meta-path Adaptive Graph Evidence Prompting, and which is built for transferable multimodal graph learning. Multimodal graphs combine textual and visual attributes with relational structures, giving a rich representation of complex real-world data, and the authors argue that models trained on source graphs need to generalize to unseen graph domains so that graph models can be broadly applied and reused. The authors say this is hard because cross-modal interactions among neighbors and the neighboring information needed for prediction can vary across target nodes and graph domains. They frame the problem as two key challenges, adaptive cross-modal neighborhood fusion, which captures and integrates cross-modal interactions among neighbors to accommodate variation across nodes and domains, and target-specific evidence selection, which identifies the neighboring textual and visual information each target node needs to support prediction by a large language model. MAGE represents textual and visual node views separately in a heterogeneous graph and introduces two complementary components.

Meta-path Adaptive Multimodal Propagation, or MAMP, adaptively aggregates neighborhood information along heterogeneous meta-paths and compresses it into graph-aware soft tokens. Evidence-Guided Instruction Tuning, or EGIT, selects relevant neighboring evidence for each query and incorporates its graph-aware representations into instructions for a frozen multimodal large language model. Together, the authors say, these components support transfer from multiple source graphs to unseen target graphs without any parameter updates on the target domains. The authors report experiments with three source graphs and four unseen target graphs that show strong cross-domain transfer performance on node classification and link prediction, again without requiring parameter updates on the target domains. The paper lists five authors, Haiyang Jiang, Tong Chen, Xinyi Gao, Hao Wang and Hongzhi Yin, and is identified on arXiv as 2611.20449.

The abstract presents the work as a response to the two challenges of adaptive cross-modal neighborhood fusion and target-specific evidence selection, and it describes the frozen multimodal language model as the component that receives the selected evidence through instructions. The posting page offers the paper as a PDF, as experimental HTML and as TeX source, and it also carries the standard arXivLabs notice about collaborators who develop and share features on the site. The articles do not say what happens next, beyond the posting of the preprint and the results the authors report. No venue, publication date or peer review outcome is given, and the articles do not describe any deployment or follow-up work. The only stated plan is the framework itself, which the authors present as a way to transfer from multiple source graphs to unseen target graphs without target-domain parameter updates.

stories.Headline: Trump claims US leads world in superintelligence during China trip
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump visited China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November 2026. He met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin during this trip. The leaders held the first ever trilateral meeting between the United States, China, and Russia. This historic gathering took place in the city of Shenzhen. The events occurred on November 18 and 19, 2026.

The summit required a meeting at the Shenzhen International Communication Center on November 18, 2026. Trump arrived at Shenzhen Baoan International Airport where Xi Jinping personally greeted him. Five jets performed a military flyover with colored smoke during the welcome. The trilateral talks began just after 3 a.m. ET on Thursday. These discussions focused on nuclear arms reductions and the war in Ukraine.

President Trump said the three largest nuclear powers are uniquely positioned to reduce nuclear weapons. He stated that he and Vladimir Putin hope to see an end to the Ukraine war. Trump claimed the United States is the world leader in superintelligence and technological transformation. He told President Xi that they have an outstanding personal relationship and are friends. Trump also proposed protecting national sovereignty from the International Criminal Court.

Top Democratic voices criticized the summit between Trump, Putin, and Xi in China. A Bloomberg reporter was barred from the trilateral meeting after asking about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Chinese officials warned that shouting questions was rude and could lead to reporter removal. The White House had attempted to secure access for the barred Bloomberg reporter. Ukraine reacted with mixed feelings after Trump called Vladimir Putin a friend.

Washington and Beijing are currently competing for leadership in advanced semiconductors and artificial intelligence. Tensions remain between the two nations regarding trade and technology issues. Trump has been making efforts to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine. The 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting was hosted by President Xi Jinping. Trump praised the elaborate welcome in Shenzhen as a display of great respect.

The leaders discussed preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons during their meetings. Trump believes that as long as he and Xi are in charge, they will not have problems. The articles do not state if any formal agreements were signed during the talks. It remains open whether the proposed nuclear reductions will be implemented by the three powers. stories.Summary:
Several artificial intelligence linked stocks experienced significant price drops during an afternoon trading session on November 20, 2026. DigitalOcean saw the steepest decline of 13.2 percent, while Oracle and C3.ai both fell by approximately 8 percent. Snowflake shares decreased by 5.3 percent, and SentinelOne shares dropped by 4.7 percent. These losses followed a more than 10 percent slide for Anthropic after its initial public offering.

The market reaction followed an 81.3 billion dollar initial public offering for Anthropic and quarterly earnings results from Nvidia under interim CEO Colette Kress. Additionally, the Commerce Department Bureau of Industry and Security now requires licenses for advanced chips sent to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. These rules aim to stop Chinese firms from leasing Nvidia compute resources in those foreign countries.

Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook warned against delaying interest rate hikes before an expected increase in December. Governor Michael S. Barr stated that on-balance-sheet debt for the seven largest AI firms could exceed 800 billion dollars by the end of the year. He further noted that nominal guarantees and off-balance-sheet leases for these companies might top 3 trillion dollars. President Donald Trump also added to the volatility by threatening penalties on data centers built outside the United States.

The current downturn follows a period of extreme volatility for companies like DigitalOcean, which reached a 52-week high of 181.29 dollars in June 2026. stories.Headline: US export rules restrict a wider range of chips including those for consumer electronics
stories.Summary:
The United States government introduced tighter export controls on Thursday, November 20, 2026, to restrict the flow of semiconductor technology. Industry insiders report that these new rules are causing a much wider disruption across the global supply chain than was first anticipated. The restrictions are not limited to advanced artificial intelligence chips but also impact system on chips used in common consumer electronics. Consequently, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. has already suspended some of its shipments to various clients.

These updated regulations affect a diverse range of developers, including those who are not based in China and do not create AI hardware. The rules target mobile and everyday consumer applications, which forces companies to change how they source and distribute their semiconductor components. Because the world's largest contract chipmaker is involved, the changes impact major customers like Nvidia who rely on leading-edge processors. Every developer using these specific types of integrated circuits must now navigate these stricter American trade requirements.

Multiple industry executives told Nikkei Asia that the scope of these controls is unexpectedly broad and damaging to the supply chain. They expressed concern that the rules extend far beyond the intended targets of high-end AI technology to hit general electronics. These leaders believe the current environment creates significant uncertainty for developers who were previously unaffected by trade wars. They warned that the sudden suspension of shipments could lead to larger shortages of essential components for mobile devices.

stories.Headline: Researchers propose Onsager-based neural time-stepping framework for gradient-flow PDEs
stories.Summary:
Zhonghua Qiao, Xianmin Xu, Rukang You and Tao Zhou posted a paper to the arXiv preprint server on 21 November 2026 that proposes a unified Onsager-based neural time-stepping framework, which they call ONTS, for solving gradient-flow partial differential equations with conserved and nonconserved dynamics. Unlike conventional neural time-stepping methods that directly parameterize the evolving state, the framework uses spatial neural networks to approximate the Onsager process variables, namely the rates in nonconserved systems and the fluxes in conserved systems. Within this Eulerian framework, the authors develop three complementary schemes: an explicit least-squares scheme called E-ONTS, an implicit variational scheme called I-ONTS, and a predictor-corrector scheme called PC-ONTS that combines explicit prediction with safeguarded implicit correction. The paper is listed as arXiv identifier 2611.20563.

For conserved systems, the flux-based formulation guarantees discrete mass conservation under periodic or no-flux boundary conditions, according to the abstract. The authors also rigorously establish unconditional discrete energy stability for the implicit schemes, provided that a suitable descent criterion is satisfied, without requiring global minimization of the neural variational objective. Numerical experiments for the heat, Allen-Cahn, Cahn-Hilliard, Fokker-Planck, and coupled Poisson-Nernst-Planck equations demonstrate the accuracy, robustness, and structure-preserving properties of the proposed framework. The abstract does not give numerical error values or timing results for those experiments.

The paper is credited to Zhonghua Qiao, Xianmin Xu, Rukang You and Tao Zhou, and the arXiv listing names Qiao and two other authors in its byline for the PDF. The abstract states that the framework is unified and that the implicit schemes carry unconditional discrete energy stability under a suitable descent criterion. It describes the three schemes as complementary and the numerical experiments as showing accuracy, robustness and structure-preserving properties. The articles do not include separate comments from the authors beyond the abstract text.

The context given in the articles is limited to the abstract and the standard arXivLabs boilerplate about openness, community, excellence and user data privacy. The articles do not say whether the paper has been peer reviewed, accepted at a conference or journal, or revised since posting. They also do not describe planned follow-up work, code release, or applications beyond the five equation families named in the abstract. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Governor Kathy Hochul pauses a proposed AI data center project in Niagara Falls
stories.Summary:
Governor Kathy Hochul paused a proposed artificial intelligence data center project in Niagara Falls. She signed an executive order on July 14, 2026, to freeze certain permits. This action affects the Niagara Digital Campus proposed by Niagara Falls Redevelopment. The developer first proposed this specific data center project back in 2021. The freeze on state environmental permits can last for up to one year.

The project requires a state air permit for backup diesel generators and costs 1.5 billion dollars. It involves nine buildings using 140 megawatts near the Robert Moses plant. The Milstein family owns Niagara Falls Redevelopment, which wants to build on vacant South End land. National Grid confirmed in 2023 that transmission lines could accommodate the 140 megawatts. The developer requested an interconnection from the New York Independent System Operator in April 2024.

Governor Hochul said the pause allows the state to study effects on water and electric bills. She stated that developers should pay for the infrastructure they require rather than households. Niagara Falls Redevelopment says it will pay for its own grid upgrades and substation. The state council of building trades urged the governor not to adopt the freeze. A consultant projects 675 annual construction jobs and 550 permanent positions for the campus.

Opponents of the project expressed worries about noise, water use, and higher electric bills. Residents across the country have fought data centers over water and power bills. A noise study by the developer concluded sound levels at nearby residences would not increase. The builder, Urbacon, designs cooling systems that use little or no water for the facility. The project would use city sewers and water, which the sewer district can accommodate.

China added 543 gigawatts of generating capacity in 2025, mostly through wind and solar power. The U.S. faces a projected 44 gigawatt power shortfall for data centers by 2028. In early 2026, local opposition delayed 75 American data center projects worth 130 billion dollars. China's data centers pay about 3 cents per kilowatt hour, which is one third of American prices. Stanford University found American and Chinese chatbots were nearly equal by March 2026.

The State Legislature passed the Responsible Data Center Development Act to pause permits for 20 megawatts. Governor Hochul has until December 31 to act on this broader legislative restriction. The project's target date for interconnection was June 2027, but the current freeze creates delays. The articles leave open whether the project will move to Virginia, Texas, or Ohio. It remains undecided if the state will impose conditions or reject the project entirely.

stories.Headline: Senators question whether Meta's $6.6 billion in AI data center tax credits qualify as research
stories.Summary:
A New York Times article has renewed attention on the tax credits that Meta claimed for its artificial intelligence data centers, according to a report published by Accounting Today on November 20, 2026. In a letter dated October 14, 2026, Senate Finance Committee ranking member Ron Wyden of Oregon and six other senators said Meta claimed about $6.6 billion in federal research and development tax credits between 2023 and 2025. The senators questioned whether Meta described its AI data centers as experimental pilot models in those claims and asked the company for a breakdown of the credits tied to the data centers. The inquiry highlights two separate questions, which are whether the development activities count as qualified research and whether the claimed expenditures count as qualified research expenditures for the credit. Treasury Regulation 1.174-2(a)(4) defines a pilot model as any representation or model of a product that is produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty about the product during its development or improvement.

The rules say production costs paid or incurred after the uncertainty is eliminated are not eligible, and a pilot model must involve genuine uncertainty in the design that the model is needed to resolve. Meeting that definition does not by itself satisfy Section 41 of the tax code, which sets additional requirements for the credit and for eligible expenses. Only wages, supplies, computer leasing and contractor costs tied to qualifying research activities can be claimed as qualified research expenses. Section 41(b)(2)(C) excludes land, improvements to land and property subject to depreciation from the definition of qualified supplies, so a taxpayer cannot turn depreciable equipment into qualified supplies by calling it experimental or by not claiming depreciation on it.

For Meta's data centers, the treatment of purchased servers, chips and other equipment is a central issue, because using equipment for qualified research does not by itself make its purchase price a qualified supply expense. Meta asserts that uncertainty existed in the data centers and that it could only be resolved by building a physical data center and testing it. To support that claim, Meta would need to show the technical uncertainty that existed before the data center was built and how building it resolved that uncertainty. The article says taxpayers claiming pilot model costs should build a record that connects the technical work to the claimed expenditures, including initial design questions, alternative designs, simulation results, test plans, test findings and engineering designs.

Cost records for employee activities, materials and contractor charges should be traceable to the relevant development work and should complement the technical evidence. The article, written by David Seibel, a senior manager in the research and development tax credit practice at Indianapolis-based McGuire Sponsel, says the credit is one of the most fact-intensive and subjective areas of tax law. It says the questions raised by the Meta claim extend well beyond AI infrastructure, because manufacturers, equipment developers and other businesses face similar challenges in showing why a model was built, how its development involved experimentation and which costs the credit permits. The articles do not say what happens next in the Senate inquiry or whether Meta has responded to the senators' request.

stories.Headline: Council of Europe trains 20 local authority teams to govern AI responsibly
stories.Summary:
The Congress of Local and Regional Authorities of the Council of Europe organised the first-ever Academy on responsible AI governance at local level, held in Paris from 17 to 19 November 2026. Twenty teams from local and regional authorities, selected in an open call, took part in the academy. The teams came from 18 municipalities and two counties, spanning the continent from Diyarbakır in Türkiye to Fingal in Ireland. The academy was organised by the Centre of expertise for multilevel governance (CEMG) at the Congress, in partnership with the Council of Europe's Steering Committee for new and emerging digital technologies (CDNET). It put into practice the Congress's call to strengthen local and regional authorities' capacity to use and manage AI.

Participants were provided with practical tools for responsible AI governance, based on the Council of Europe's HUDERIA methodology for assessing the impact of AI systems. Over three days, participants applied the methodology to a fictional AI-supported public consultation, identifying and analysing risks, mapping stakeholders and developing mitigation measures. The programme was designed to strengthen authorities' capacity to assess the impact of AI in public services on everyone they serve, from a human-rights, democracy and rule-of-law perspective. The participating authorities were Amaroussion (Greece), Bălți (Republic of Moldova), Bergen (Norway), Bitola (North Macedonia), City of Arezzo (Italy), City of Vigo (Spain), Diyarbakır (Türkiye), Fingal County (Ireland), Harghita County (Romania), Kutaisi (Georgia), London Borough of Camden (United Kingdom), Lviv (Ukraine), Nõo (Estonia), Resen (North Macedonia), Rivne (Ukraine), Shkodër (Albania), Szentendre (Hungary), Turnišče (Slovenia), Valongo (Portugal), and Ventspils Education Board (Latvia). The academy was also an official part of the "Road to Geneva" programme, leading up to the 2027 Geneva AI summit.

Opening the discussions, Congress co-rapporteur on AI Annika Vaikla (Estonia, ILDG), Deputy Mayor of Viimsi, urged authorities to use AI to give public servants more time for people, while keeping people in control. She called for AI literacy among political leaders, staff and citizens. She also called for smaller municipalities to have access to shared expertise. Deputy Mayor Vaikla is co-rapporteur for the 2026 Congress report on strengthening the capacities of local and regional authorities in the use of artificial intelligence. The articles give no further remarks from her.

The articles state that local and regional authorities are on the frontline of the AI revolution in Europe's town halls. Faced with shrinking budgets, they see real potential in efficiency gains promised by AI. They also face hard questions such as planning applications for data centres and democratic accountability for decisions informed by AI. The articles say they lack capacity in understanding and governing AI technologies, particularly smaller municipalities.

The academy served as a Congress contribution to the Council of Europe's New Democratic Pact for Europe and was held in support of the implementation of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence. The articles give no further background beyond the academy's organisation and aims. They state that artificial intelligence is already in Europe's town halls. They describe the academy as the first-ever of its kind at local level.

They state that the twenty teams were selected in an open call. They state that the programme was designed to strengthen authorities' capacity to assess the impact of AI in public services. They give no further details on the Congress report or the Framework Convention. The articles state that the academy was an official part of the "Road to Geneva" programme, leading up to the 2027 Geneva AI summit.

They state that it was held in support of the implementation of the Council of Europe Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence. They state that it served as a Congress contribution to the Council of Europe's New Democratic Pact for Europe. They give no further details on what follows the academy. They leave open what the participating authorities will do next and what the 2026 Congress report will contain.

stories.Headline: Deloitte and Workday host a Central Europe webinar on people and AI as a competitive advantage
stories.Summary:
Deloitte and Workday are holding a webinar for Central Europe on the theme of people and AI as a competitive advantage, exploring the findings of Deloitte’s 2026 Global Human Capital Trends report and what those findings mean for enterprise transformation. The session is aimed at CHROs and HR leaders across Central Europe and is designed to connect human capital trends with the decisions shaping AI-enabled organisations. According to the announcement, 70% of business leaders identify being “fast and nimble” as their primary competitive strategy for the next three years, and the session will examine how organisations can rethink work to keep pace with AI. Leaders and experts from Workday and Deloitte will explore the shift from “Humans + Machines” to “Humans x Machines,” combining human judgement with machine speed to create greater value. The announcement says the session will also examine what this “Human Advantage” means for HR and how it can inform the way organisations approach AI-enabled transformation.

The webinar focuses on three priorities for HR leaders trying to bridge the gap between understanding these trends and putting them into practice. The first is creating value through people and AI, moving beyond cost efficiency to explore how people and AI can work together to deliver greater business value. The second is adapting workforce planning, including understanding the “Orchestration Advantage” and the shift from static plans to dynamically aligning capabilities and capacity with business needs. The third is navigating cultural change, exploring how AI is reshaping organisational culture, what “Cultural Debt” means and how to manage its ripple effects. The announcement invites people to register to explore how to move beyond experimentation and take a more strategic approach to people, work and AI.

The articles do not name the individual leaders and experts from Workday and Deloitte who will take part, and they give no date or time for the session beyond the publication date of the announcement, 19 November 2026. No specific statements from named people are included, so responsibility for the views rests with the two firms as organisers rather than with any quoted individual. The context given is Deloitte’s 2026 Global Human Capital Trends report and the finding that 70% of business leaders see being “fast and nimble” as their primary competitive strategy for the next three years. What happens next, according to the articles, is that interested CHROs and HR leaders across Central Europe can register for the webinar.

stories.Headline: Medical students who use reasoning scaffolding before an AI assistant achieve higher diagnostic accuracy, trial finds
stories.Summary:
A randomised controlled trial involving 496 medical students, of whom 389 were analysed, tested whether the order in which trainees receive AI support affects their clinical reasoning, and the preprint by Yizhou Fan, Luzhen Tang, Mengyu Xia, Jiaqi Xu, Zijian Li, Naping Chen and 10 more was posted on Research Square on 21 November 2026 without peer review. The students worked through clinical reasoning tasks with virtual standardised patients and were assigned to six conditions: no intervention, an AI assistant alone, AI scaffolding alone, scaffolding followed by the assistant, the assistant followed by scaffolding, or both at once. The scaffolding prompted students to reflect on and evaluate their own reasoning without giving direct answers, while the assistant supplied requested information and answers. The study ran an AI-free baseline, two intervention phases and a final assessment after all AI support was withdrawn, and frontier large language models completed the same tasks as a benchmark. Students first performed below the language models but later exceeded them following the interventions.

Students who began with AI scaffolding reached higher diagnostic accuracy than those given the assistant from the outset, both during the later intervention phase at 75.2% versus 66.0% (OR 1.73, 95% CIs [1.12, 2.68]) and after withdrawal at 24.6% versus 14.4% (OR 2.19, 95% CIs [1.15, 4.14]). After withdrawal, the scaffold-first groups were the only ones to outperform both unsupported students, at 24.5, 24.7% versus 9.0% (ORs 3.77, 3.87, 95% CIs [1.25, 12.00]), and the language models, at 24.5, 24.7% versus 8.6% (ORs 3.48, 3.50, 95% CIs [1.22, 9.89]). Introducing the assistant after scaffolding lowered intrinsic cognitive load (t(50) = 3.25, p BH = .006, Cohen’s d z = 0.46, 95% CIs [0.17, 0.75]) and raised metacognitive evaluation (t(50) = 3.11, p BH = .019, Cohen’s d z = 0.44, 95% CIs [0.15, 0.73]). The authors state that there is no competing interest and provide supplementary information in an appendix file.

The authors conclude that their findings support a staged and human-first approach to AI use in medical training, in which reasoning-focused scaffolding comes before answer-providing assistance. They say this order strengthens diagnostic performance both while AI-supported learning is under way and after AI support is withdrawn. The abstract frames the question as whether trainees can develop the clinical reasoning needed to use generative AI effectively and independently, given that such tools could improve physicians' clinical performance. Because the paper is a preprint, it has not been peer reviewed by a journal, and the articles give no further details on publication or follow-up work.

stories.Headline: Researchers launch autonomous AI agent to analyze neutron scattering data at China Spallation Neutron Source
stories.Summary:
Researchers recently introduced DrSai-Rongzai, an autonomous AI agent designed to analyze neutron scattering data at the China Spallation Neutron Source. This agent utilizes a large language model to perform joint neutron powder diffraction and pair-distribution-function analysis without any human intervention. By employing a hierarchical framework of reasoning and acting, the system orchestrates established refinement software to interpret complex materials data. The tool aims to eliminate the time-consuming iterative cycles of data reduction and modeling that typically challenge both experts and novices.

The system relies on Agentic Context Operation to maintain a working memory of file paths, domain rules, and intermediate results during processing. In tests using Si, CsAgTe, and Bi2MoO6, the agent produced structural parameters that were statistically indistinguishable from those derived by human experts. An 18-run factorial ablation study on two high-entropy alloys evaluated the MemoWrite and CoreSkillWrite mechanisms under 50k-token context compression. Full implementation of these components yielded a mean composite score of 0.9316 and a repeatability stability of 0.9905, while Memo alone improved performance by 20.2 percent.

The developers integrated the agent with a permission-controlled data interface at the facility to ensure the secure analysis of proprietary user data. They stated that the agent can move beyond simple recommendations to become a reliable partner in complex structural science. This integration allows for on-demand analysis and automatic archiving of results within the secure facility environment. The researchers believe this technology could potentially accelerate the overall rate of materials discovery at pulsed neutron sources across the entire world.

stories.Headline: Experts doubt AI superintelligence warnings from Amodei and Altman
stories.Summary:
In a column published by the Orange County Register on November 16, 2026, columnist Rafael Perez examined warnings from AI industry leaders about superintelligence and asked experts whether those fears are justified. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned that within the next year AI may cripple the internet and cause billions of dollars in damage, while OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told the United Nations Security Council that humanity could lose control of the future to AI. Researchers at Anthropic warned that AI could lead to human extinction, and one of them, Jacob Coxon, quit in protest, saying developers are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with lives. The fears center on recursive self-improvement, the idea that models could iteratively improve themselves far faster than people can improve them, possibly producing an intelligence explosion and a superintelligence that would be virtually impossible to control.

The experts Perez consulted were deeply skeptical that this is where the field is heading. Dr. Melanie Mitchell, an AI and cognitive science researcher and professor at the Santa Fe Institute, said she does not think agents are anywhere close to improving themselves so vastly, and that while systems can generate code and use it to improve the code behind AI systems, the result is a very gradual thing rather than an exponential runaway. Dr. Luciano Floridi, a philosopher of AI, founding director of the Digital Ethics Center at Yale University and an advisor to the European Union on AI policy, said nobody has shown that the field is on the way to recursive self-improvement, comparing the claim to a train from New Haven to New York that goes fast but never gets closer to Boston. He said the intelligence explosion imagined by I. J. Good in the 1960s remains a logical, sci-fi possibility with no demonstrated route to it, and both experts noted that software has improved software for decades, as a compiler does, and that existing models help build the next ones in laboratories, which speeds up work without removing the hands that decide what counts as an improvement.

Floridi pointed to a persistent problem: AI research requires judgment about whether a modification is an improvement, and models have not shown competence at that, which the column describes as only the tip of the engineering challenge. Perez also asked why someone would quit a comfortable job at a leading AI lab if the warned threat were not legitimate, and he offered performative moral grandstanding as one suggested possibility while proposing a less vicious explanation, that the field is extremely difficult to evaluate even for experts. Mitchell said the field is quite polarized, with many people agreeing with her and many heatedly disagreeing, and that the fighting reflects general uncertainty. Perez concluded that if these experts are correct there is little reason to worry about an existential threat from superintelligence, and that acknowledging this matters because hysteria over AI diverts attention from the very real problems AI is creating in society, which he said an upcoming column would address.

stories.Headline: Mullin suggests super intelligence may be behind FAA ground stop
stories.Summary:
On November 13, 2026, the FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop that began at about 3:30 p.m. ET and lasted until air traffic resumed at 8:15 p.m. ET. The Associated Press called it the longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years. A little before 5 p.m. ET, the White House let reporters know that Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was coming out to talk to them. A reporter asked whether the trouble could be a cyberattack or some kind of AI intrusion. Mullin said, "We don't want to get ahead of ourselves."

When the question came up again, Mullin said, "We call it SI around here, remember? SI." He said, "You just can't rule out anything at this point," and that they were going through that process and would take the appropriate actions. The FAA has spent the fall rolling out a new system for planning air traffic, called SMART, that uses AI. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy unveiled it in September, saying, "We are not outsourcing aviation to AI." On November 10, the FAA expanded SMART nationwide, three days before the ground stop.

The FAA says SMART "is a data aggregator, and it does not feed information into the air traffic control system." Its initial investigation points to two possible sources, in Texas and Arkansas, for the flood of data that made its old equipment unstable. Investigators are examining equipment from both sites, where the FAA's network contractor, L3Harris, had been installing new routers. As of Tuesday, Duffy said they still didn't have "clarity" on the root cause. SMART's developer, Air Space Intelligence, has denied any role for "the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC."

On Monday night, Mullin went on Fox News, where Sean Hannity asked him whether the ground stop and the outages at Microsoft, United and a couple of big banks were connected. Mullin said he doesn't always believe in coincidences until he's proven wrong, and that CISA said it was not seeing any traffic that would make it think this was a cyberattack. He said a tech figure who asked not to be named, and who was not Elon, told him, "I believe that it's the SI." Mullin said he could tell Hannity with 98% certainty, "we're not seeing the cyberattack."

Politico reported Wednesday that after the interview, "Trump administration group chats lit up with 'WTFs,'" according to a person close to the White House. That afternoon, at a House Homeland Security Committee hearing, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, the guy Trump picked to run his new "Super Intelligence Force," called the recent outages "separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes." On September 19, Trump wrote on Truth Social that "Many people think that the words 'Artificial Intelligence' are inaccurate, and very ineloquent," and offered three replacements: "Superior Intelligence (SI) or, Extreme Intelligence (EI) or, Supreme Intelligence (SI)." When YouGov asked which name was better, 53% of Americans picked "artificial intelligence" and 9% picked "super intelligence."

Standing in front of the United Nations General Assembly, Trump announced that "the use of the word 'artificial' makes intelligence fake." He then issued an executive order to make it official, that "to the maximum extent permitted by law, the executive branch shall use the terms 'Super Intelligence' and 'SI' in place of 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'AI.'" On Truth Social, he declared that "The White House considers anyone that uses the term, 'Artificial Intelligence,' as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, 'Super Intelligence,' THE ENEMY!" Trump's first-day executive order made the Gulf of Mexico the "Gulf of America" as far as the federal government is concerned, and when AP style kept calling it the Gulf of Mexico, the White House barred AP reporters from the Oval Office and Air Force One. In August, in the middle of a trade fight with Canada, Trump ordered the government to start calling Lake Ontario "Lake America."

More to follow.

stories.Headline: South Korean universities tighten exam security to stop AI smart glasses cheating
stories.Summary:
Fourteen universities, including Korea University, Sogang University, Sungkyunkwan University and Kyung Hee University, will hold essay exams on Saturday and Sunday, the first weekend after Thursday's national College Scholastic Ability Test, and in all 36 universities are scheduled to hold essay exams after the national test. The Ministry of Education held an online meeting on Friday morning with admissions officials from 56 universities to share preparations and discuss how to prevent candidates from using smart devices to cheat on the upcoming exams. The measures follow incidents last month at Yonsei University and the University of Seoul, where applicants were caught using AI-enabled smart glasses during essay exams. Some schools have added separate checks for candidates who wear glasses, and Kyung Hee University has trained proctors to identify smart glasses.

Sungkyunkwan University notified applicants on Thursday that they would have to use a university-issued writing instrument for Saturday's humanities essay exam, and candidates may bring their own erasers if exam staff inspect them first. The university also announced security screening and barred candidates from wearing jewelry, earplugs and analog watches. Kyung Hee University plans to issue disposable aprons to about 35,000 test takers to cover clothing where tiny cameras could be concealed. Dongguk University will have applicants cover their buttons with stickers, while Sookmyung Women's University will ban earplugs and require candidates to tie back their hair so their ears are visible. Seoul National University will require applicants to wear gowns during admissions interviews and oral exams beginning Nov. 27.

The Korean Council for University Education said it would coordinate a response with its 197 member universities and apply the same strict principles to AI- and smart-device cheating on university-administered exams as were in place during the national test. For Thursday's test, the government barred electronic devices from exam venues and trained proctors to spot miniature cameras and smart glasses. The education ministry met the admissions officials as schools tightened security ahead of this weekend's exams, with some checking eyeglasses, restricting personal writing tools and issuing disposable aprons. The council's coordination covers its member universities, and the article gives no further detail on what happens after this weekend's exams.

stories.Headline: Countries set varying restrictions on student access to artificial intelligence tools
stories.Summary:
Various countries are setting different limits on how students use artificial intelligence based on age, ability, and specific learning goals. Some nations introduce the technology in elementary school, while others ban young students from using these tools independently. These educational systems are currently deciding when children should learn about the technology and when they can directly use it. The choices show there is no single model, as countries apply varying levels of control. These boundaries are constantly being tested and adjusted in current educational practice.

Singapore introduces AI in stages, with grades 1-2 learning concepts and grade 4 students using tools under teacher guidance. The Code for Fun program will add AI skills to all schools starting in 2027. France allows generative AI from grade 4e, for students aged 13-14, in a limited and controlled manner. China's 2025 guidelines prohibit primary students from independently using open content creation functions of artificial intelligence. New York announced a policy on September 2nd restricting AI for 600,000 public school students from kindergarten to eighth grade.

Russian Education Minister Sergey Kravtsov stated that digital technology should support teachers rather than replace them. He emphasized that students must deeply understand lessons instead of just completing assignments using technology. Kravtsov also noted that results from neural networks cannot be considered absolutely accurate. He believes critical thinking and a responsible attitude are particularly important when using these tools. The Russian Ministry of Education published these specific guidelines on September 26.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani argues that children need direct interaction with peers and teachers to develop thinking skills. Superintendent Kamar Samuels pointed out the challenge of controlling how students use artificial intelligence for their homework. French rules state that using AI for assignments without permission or intellectual contribution may be considered cheating. New York will block ChatGPT and Claude at all grade levels for the current school year. Teachers in New York are prohibited from using this technology for grading or evaluating students.

Japan's Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology suggests considering developmental stages and information literacy risks. Australia requires that AI technology serve learning objectives and support creativity while ensuring safety, privacy, and accountability. Russia allows students in grades 5-9 to use AI for searching, organizing information, and testing hypotheses. Russian students in grades 10-11 may use AI for analyzing large datasets and building predictive models. China introduces primary students to basic applications like speech recognition, image classification, and visual programming tools.

New York plans to disable AI features on 40 educational tools and discontinue software where features cannot be removed. The city will hold AI knowledge classes twice a year and test selected platforms under teacher supervision. Russia prohibits teachers from uploading information about parents, students, and school staff to any AI services. France forbids schools from requiring students to create personal accounts on public AI services. The articles leave open how these policies will be modified or extended after one year.

stories.Headline: Warsh opens Fed task force hearing on AI productivity and jobs
stories.Summary:
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh started a landmark hearing on Monday, November 16, 2026. He led the first meeting of a task force examining artificial intelligence. The session focused on how this technology could fuel growth or disrupt jobs. Warsh wanted to analyze the impact of AI on US productivity. He warned that overlooking the risks of this technology could be costly.

The Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference took place at the San Francisco Federal Reserve. Warsh established five task forces, including the one that held this first hearing. He assembled Marc Andreessen of Andreessen Horowitz and Microsoft Xbox CEO Asha Sharma. He also included Stanford University professor Charles Jones, who is on leave at Anthropic. These independent heads provide candid feedback to help the Fed set the best policy.

Warsh stated that the widespread adoption of this technology will have a significant economic impact. He said policymakers must be mindful that great opportunities rarely come without some risk. He believes AI, or super intelligence, might differ from past general purpose technologies like electricity. Warsh noted that AI appears to be changing the speed and method of innovation. He argued that broadening idea generation could sustain growth above the long run average.

Warsh asked experts if AI will drive productivity gains and raise general standards of living. He questioned whether the surge will happen sooner in the US or other countries. He wondered if the technology will make achieving price stability harder or easier for policymakers. The hearing aims to determine the implications for jobs in the near and long term. These questions affect the dual mandate of the Federal Reserve regarding the US economy.

Warsh compared AI to the internal combustion engine, noting that previous inventions did not automate ideas. He described a scenario where inflation adjusted GDP growth rises while the US stays employed. He also warned that widespread automation could push the unemployment rate higher by displacing jobs. A third possibility involves a stock market bust if expected returns on AI turn down. This disappointment could lead to an economic slowdown without any lasting productivity gains.

The task force will continue to follow evidence to provide feedback for future monetary policy. Warsh intends to interrogate the reality of the situation by listening to various field experts. The Fed will track the magnitude, scope, and timing of the AI productivity surge. The articles do not state when the next task force hearing will be held. They leave open whether AI will actually increase the long term average of GDP.

stories.Headline: Short sellers rank Applied Digital, IREN and Core Scientific as overvalued AI stocks
stories.Summary:
The U.S. stock market suffered a broad sell-off heading into year-end, driven by renewed concerns about elevated AI valuations and uncertainty over the profitability of artificial intelligence investments. Short sellers piled on pressure amid concerns that technology companies committed enormous capital to AI infrastructure without showing sufficient returns. The rout wiped out about $3 trillion in S&P 500 market capitalization in early November, as the Nasdaq recorded its largest single-day decline in 19 months. Anthropic's highly anticipated IPO raised $81 billion and attracted substantial demand, but its debut failed to reverse the broader weakness in AI-related stocks. The article, by Neha Gupta and published on Yahoo Finance on November 21, 2026, ranked five overvalued AI stocks by short interest.

The article screened for stocks with significant AI exposure, open short interest above 10%, and overvaluation, ranking them in ascending order of short interest. Applied Digital Corporation had 20% of outstanding shares sold short as of October 30, about $6.38 billion in total debt as of August 31, 2026, and $2.95 billion in cash and equivalents, or about $3.7 billion including restricted cash. Applied Digital's first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue was $341.9 million, its net loss surged to $221.08 million from $18.50 million a year earlier, and its roughly $4.4 billion mid-November 2026 market capitalization was about 7.2 times fiscal 2026 revenue of $611.3 million. IREN Limited traded at approximately 87 times forward earnings and 7.64 times sales, disclosed on November 5, 2026 that it expected about $15 billion in remaining fiscal 2027 capital expenditures, and posted first-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $228 million, including $200 million in AI Cloud revenue, up 182% sequentially, with a $263 million net loss. IREN held $3.52 billion in cash and equivalents against about $10.04 billion in total debt principal obligations, while Core Scientific traded at 18 times forward earnings and 7.69 times sales, reported $1.18 billion in Q3 net income largely from a non-cash warrant gain, and recorded a net loss of about $324.4 million for the first nine months of 2026.

Michael Burry raised concerns that AI infrastructure companies could be relying on increasingly complicated financing arrangements that may become unsustainable. RSM Chief economist Joe Brusuelas was wary of a wholesale bursting of the AI bubble as uncertainty surrounding Nvidia undermines confidence among lenders and investors financing the massive data-center expansion. Billionaire Stanley Druckenmiller became increasingly cautious about the stock market amid the AI sell-off. Barclays Chief Market Strategist Julien Lafargue warned that the AI sell-off is exposing a fundamental weakness in the investment cycle, the growing cost of financing AI infrastructure. According to Barclays, AI demand remains strong, but investors are questioning who will finance the enormous investments required to build data centers and computing infrastructure.

Morgan Stanley argued that the November AI sell-off was excessive and presented a buying opportunity. Goldman Sachs strategists warned that the outlook for AI investment and corporate profit margins in 2028 and beyond remains highly uncertain. Short sellers questioned whether Applied Digital's ambitious growth plans can generate sufficient returns to justify its valuation and financing commitments. Short sellers' central concern for IREN was whether returns from its GPU investments will be sufficient to cover financing costs, support further expansion, and ultimately deliver sustainable earnings. Core Scientific's dependence on CoreWeave, which accounted for approximately 84% of total revenue in the first nine months of 2026, exposes it to CoreWeave's financial health and spending decisions.

Applied Digital is positioning itself to benefit from surging demand for AI computing infrastructure. IREN is committing billions of dollars to transform itself into a major AI infrastructure provider. Core Scientific is facing heightened short-selling pressure as investors question whether its aggressive transition from Bitcoin mining to AI and high-performance computing data center infrastructure can generate sufficient returns. Core Scientific's capital expenditure reached approximately $1.5 billion in the first nine months of 2026, as cash and digital assets totaled approximately $806.6 million. The article said the selloff also gave rise to buy-the-dip moves as insiders started to load up.

The article detailed how many hedge funds hold stakes in these stocks in Q3 2026 and said it just published the 10 Most Overvalued AI Stocks According to Short Sellers. Insider Monkey's quarterly newsletter strategy selects 14 small-cap and large-cap stocks every quarter and has returned 612% since May 2014, beating its benchmark by 375 percentage points. The article asked whether APLD is a buy-the-dip opportunity and whether a Microsoft partnership can alleviate concerns for IREN. It also asked whether a shift to AI colocation can unlock more value for Core Scientific. The article left open how IREN can finance its expansion without taking on excessive debt or issuing additional shares.

stories.Headline: Salesforce begins new layoffs while setting AI spending budgets for staff
stories.Summary:
Salesforce has begun another round of job cuts, according to internal messages reviewed by Business Insider, and the scale of the current reductions is not yet known. Business Insider reported the new cuts by citing messages shared on an internal Slack channel, where staff discussed layoffs taking place this week and some employees noted recent reductions. One employee also reported that their manager had been let go, and a senior manager in IT compliance and content strategy confirmed their own reduction in force on LinkedIn. That manager also stated that other team members were impacted on Monday morning, while the company has not disclosed the total number of roles affected in this latest round.

The new cuts follow earlier workforce reductions at Salesforce this year, including a regulatory filing that showed the company cut 86 jobs in California on August 7. Those affected roles were in sales, general administration, technology, and product teams, and Salesforce also reduced headcount in Washington state and in markets outside the United States. Internal documents reviewed by Business Insider detail the standard severance package for US employees, under which eligible staff can receive up to 30 weeks of base pay depending on their level, tenure, and age. The company also set AI budgets for employees this week, after an internal memo indicated that some staff had spent thousands of dollars monthly on AI tokens last quarter.

CEO Marc Benioff is responsible for the company and has rejected investor concerns about AI's impact on traditional software business models. He stated at the company's most recent earnings report that the software-as-a-service industry is not facing a collapse. The job cuts occur in a year marked by investor concern over AI's impact on traditional software business models, and Salesforce shares fell 9 per cent on Tuesday. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the reported cuts and the new AI budgets.

stories.Headline: EY, Microsoft launch agentic cyber defence centre for AI security
stories.Summary:
EY and Microsoft jointly launched an Agentic Cyber Defence Centre, according to a TechGig report published on November 20, 2026. The centre integrates Microsoft technologies with policy controls and tamper-evident records for the actions taken by AI agents. It extends the existing alliance between the two companies into agent-led security operations, with the stated aim of connecting fragmented cyber defences. EY says the platform helps organisations retain human responsibility for automated decisions while agents take on more security work.

The platform applies policy-based controls to agent actions and keeps tamper-evident records that let organisations track changes and coordinate responses. The announcement describes an integrated transformation and operations model that spans identity, data, applications, cloud and operational technology. EY plans to apply agentic blueprints across these domains, using reusable patterns to connect security capabilities rather than relying on separate deployments. The stated aim is sustained and repeatable improvement in cyber defence.

EY is implementing Microsoft security for agentic cyber defence across its global organisation as what it calls Client Zero. This internal deployment is meant to validate operating models, codify controls and develop reusable patterns, with the aim of reducing implementation risk for clients. Richard Watson, EY Global Consulting Cybersecurity Leader, said the future of cybersecurity requires an entirely new operating model. Naseem Tuffaha, Corporate Vice President, Security at Microsoft, said securing the AI-powered enterprise requires a new model for cyber defence that keeps pace as AI changes how organisations operate and are attacked.
