stories.Headline: CoreWeave and Humatica release a study on scaling proprietary enterprise AI
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave and Humatica released a joint study on November 20, 2026, regarding the scaling of proprietary enterprise artificial intelligence. This research examines how large organisations turn technological ambition into durable competitive value through resilient data architectures and internal governance. The study drew on insights from 252 enterprises across 14 industries and more than 30 interviews with senior executives. The report finds that 66 percent of surveyed organisations operate models or processes that would fail if their systems were switched off. Only 35 percent of enterprises have a formal operating model, while executives cite organisational barriers 2.4 times more than technological limits.

Seventy-three percent move critical workloads to self-controlled infrastructure for proprietary intellectual property, followed by data security at 55 percent and control at 45 percent. Cost and predictability motivate 36 percent of these moves, while 42 percent of production use cases started in business units. Finally, 24 percent of these AI projects were launched independently by employees or small teams. Chen Goldberg, the CoreWeave Executive Vice President of Product and Engineering, stated that businesses are becoming dependent on AI faster than they can run it. She explained that bringing managed PostgreSQL into Kubernetes clusters reduces latency by keeping data calls local and handles replication, patching, and backups.

Goldberg also noted that the connections between compute and data require the same engineering attention as the components themselves. She highlighted that CoreWeave achieved target quality on DeepSeek-V3 2.7 times faster than its GB200 run in MLPerf results. Andy Knobloch, a Partner at Humatica, said that winning leaders are those who decide who owns each AI system and how it improves. He noted that almost half of production AI started in business units without a formal budget or an executive sponsor. The study affects enterprises that rely on AI for core functions but lack the governance to secure and monitor production systems.

These organisations face vulnerability as initial pilots transition into mission-critical applications that require scalable deployment and strict security. The articles state that CoreWeave is the first cloud to publish multi-rack Vera Rubin results in MLPerf and holds Platinum rankings in SemiAnalysis ClusterMAX. CoreWeave also holds first-place inference speed and price-performance rankings from Artificial Analysis for Moonshot AI's Kimi K2.6 and Kimi K2.7 Code. The company partners with CrowdStrike for security, VAST Data for storage, and ClickHouse for real-time analytics. Other partners include Wayve for autonomous driving and PhysicsX for industrial physics AI, while Humatica works with GloCoach for leadership development.

Next, enterprises can use CoreWeave Forge for scalable deployment and the ARIA tool to transform institutional knowledge into proprietary assets. The CoreWeave Zero Trust AI Framework provides security, while Mission Control offers real-time infrastructure visibility across the entire lifecycle. Companies may also use CoreWeave Direct-to-Expert support to pair internal domain knowledge with external engineering expertise. The articles leave open how many more enterprises will establish formal operating models to bridge the gap in organisational readiness.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang's foundation commits $350 million to buy CoreWeave computing time for open science
stories.Summary:
The charitable foundation of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori, committed $350 million to buy computing time from CoreWeave, according to reporting on the foundation's tax disclosures. The arrangement gives universities and nonprofit research institutes access to powerful chips for open science and AI research. For CoreWeave, it brings in business from a foundation whose assets are largely tied to the company that supplies its chips. The commitment supports the Computing Initiative for Open Science.

Nvidia previously disclosed in a proxy filing that $108.3 million had already been donated under the arrangement. Researchers receive the computing time through grants, and Nvidia said it planned to offer certain recipients engineering help at no charge. Nearly 90% of the foundation's $12.7 billion in assets at the end of 2025 was held in Nvidia shares, according to GuruFocus. Nvidia also invested $2 billion in CoreWeave in January through a private placement of approximately 23 million Class A shares. CoreWeave rents access to Nvidia's graphics processing units, the chips that power many of its customers' AI workloads.

The pledge adds a source of demand from outside the commercial AI market, according to the investors takeaway in the report. Its value to CoreWeave's business will depend on when researchers use the computing time and how much revenue the company recognizes from it over time. Timing matters because CoreWeave has to fund servers before customers use them. The larger question for shareholders is whether demand from a broader range of customers can keep pace with the company's spending on infrastructure.

Articles.Title: CoreWeave Finds AI Demand Outside the Commercial Market - TradingView

stories.Headline: Nebius shares drop as investors pull back from AI stocks
stories.Summary:
Nebius Group N.V. shares traded lower during the premarket session on Friday, November 20, 2026, as investors pulled back from artificial intelligence stocks. This decline followed a recent rally sparked by the initial public offering of Anthropic PBC and strong quarterly earnings from NVIDIA Corp. The stock fell nearly 5 percent to approximately 92.19 dollars while S&P 500 futures dropped 0.9 percent. The market shift follows Anthropic pricing its IPO at 83 dollars per share, which exceeded the expected range of 70 to 78 dollars. Investors are now questioning if neocloud providers can secure the capital and capacity needed to sustain their growth. Evercore ISI noted that NVIDIA has provided roughly 32 billion dollars in neocloud financing to support an extraordinarily strong demand environment.

CoreWeave Inc. has discussed revenues of 11 million dollars per megawatt, though long-term and short-term contracts can reach 20 million and 40 million dollars respectively. Amit Daryanani, a senior managing director at Evercore ISI, stated that financing and capacity are greater constraints than customer demand. He explained that the long-term success of the sector depends on how durable the current demand for AI infrastructure proves to be. Daryanani also suggested that tighter GPU restrictions on Chinese companies might increase available capacity within the Western ecosystem. He described this potential shift as a secondary benefit rather than the primary driver for these stocks.

Nebius currently holds a Buy consensus rating from 24 analysts with an average price forecast of 240.64 dollars. Recent target adjustments include Citigroup lowering its target to 215 dollars on November 16, while Baird lowered its target to 200 dollars on November 13. DA Davidson also cut its target to 125 dollars on November 13 while maintaining a Neutral rating. The company continues to face intermediate pressure as its current price remains well below its 20-day and 200-day simple moving averages.

The fund had call options in Nebius, Sandisk, Bloom Energy and the Roundhill Memory ETF as of September 30, and the filing did not say whether those holdings were held or liquidated during the October market sell-off. Several AI-linked stocks subsequently suffered significant drops, with SharonAI down 55% in October, IREN down 41% and Nebius down 35%, and Nebius and CoreWeave also saw selling pressure on Monday as investors decreased exposure to AI infrastructure businesses. The new portfolio disclosure comes after reports that Situational Awareness lost 67% of its portfolio value in July as AI-related assets slumped, and the September holdings show its ongoing bet on data centers, memory chips and computer infrastructure notwithstanding market turmoil.

Investors will be looking at the fund's next quarterly filing to see if it lowered its position during the October sell-off, or stayed with its AI-focused investment strategy. stories.Headline: Together AI launches hosted API for Qwen3 TTS to support live assistants
stories.Summary:
Together AI added hosted Qwen3 TTS on November 20, 2026, to provide a managed API layer for the open weights model. The company launched this service to help builders create live assistants rather than focusing on batch narration alone. This release follows the open sourcing of the Qwen3-TTS weights by the Alibaba team earlier in the year 2026. The service is available through serverless inference and dedicated endpoints for users who need steady isolation. Together AI aims to pitch a full stack of services including agent eval work and a Storage Accelerator.

The Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B model costs 20 dollars per 1 million characters, which is more than Kokoro at 4 dollars. It offers nine preset voices including vivian, serena, ryan, aiden, uncle_fu, dylan, eric, ono_anna, and sohee. These voices support ten languages including zh, en, ja, ko, de, fr, ru, pt, es, and it. Users can provide plain language delivery instructions up to 500 characters in the extra_params.instructions field to control the style. The system supports wav, mp3, raw, and mulaw formats with sample rates of 24000 Hz or 8000 Hz.

Together AI claims that its inference team tuned serving so first audio can start in as little as 97ms. Authors Anthony Ji, Charles Duong, Sebastien Beurnier, Sahil Yadav, and Sonny Khan credited the launch post on the company blog. They stated that the model separates who speaks from how they speak by using fixed voices with flexible instructions. The company suggests that this allows one branded voice to work across different European and Asian locales. Together AI notes that the 97ms figure is a hosted claim on their own specific serving stack.

Hacker News commenters noted that the time to first audio does not cap the total end to end conversational delay. Product owners are affected by the pricing, with a call center prototype of 50 million characters costing 1,000 dollars. Builders comparing open TTS options may look at Nari Labs, Hugging Face speech to speech defaults, or Zyphra's ZONOS3-Mini. Some teams may prefer self-hosting to avoid the per character meter or to keep audio on premises for compliance. Others might choose HeyGen on OpenRouter or DeepL Voice Aure when emotional range and translation are more important.

Alibaba's Qwen team released the weights earlier in 2026, leading to various local CPU stacks and serving optimizations. Nari Labs previously reported sub 50ms p95 time to first audio using one H100 with a custom stack. Together AI now provides a single invoice for speech alongside Llama or DeepSeek calls for teams using their platform. The model is positioned as a mid tier option, being cheaper than Cartesia Sonic 2 at 65 dollars. This managed layer removes the need for users to operate their own GPUs for Qwen's instruction steered presets.

Users must now benchmark the latency in their own regions rather than trusting the single blog number provided by Together. The documentation leaves open whether instructions work identically across every language, though demos show aiden reading English and others. There is currently no support for word level alignment or opus, aac, and flac output formats on this model. Seed reproducibility is listed as best effort only when the input, voice, and seed match. The articles do not state if custom voice cloning will be added to the Qwen3 hosted offering.

stories.Headline: OpenAI strengthens GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol safeguards, cutting reasoning extraction attack success from 54.0% to 0.2%
stories.Summary:
OpenAI published a post on November 20, 2026 titled "Combatting adversarial distillation," describing how it detects and disrupts adversarial distillation and how it strengthened protections for its models' protected reasoning. Adversarial distillation is when an actor uses a frontier model's outputs without authorization to train another model with similar capabilities. OpenAI said it combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers, and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated extraction attempts. OpenAI said it strengthened defenses against protected reasoning extraction in GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. In an internal adaptive evaluation using strong automated red-teaming, the average attack success rate fell from 54.0% against GPT-6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2% against GPT-6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards.

OpenAI said its updated safeguards align more closely with those it uses for biology and cybersecurity. OpenAI said it places particular emphasis on preventing attackers from extracting protected reasoning, the intermediate steps a model generates internally while working toward an answer, known as its chain-of-thought. OpenAI said these traces can contain information the final answer leaves out, making them especially valuable training data for another model. OpenAI described a September disclosure of attacks that moved encrypted reasoning from one conversation into another and asked the model to reveal the reasoning in user-readable form. OpenAI said it strengthened protections across user, workspace, organization, and model-family boundaries, including closing a pathway that could expose another user's encrypted reasoning.

OpenAI said that with GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol it ties a model's protected reasoning to the conversation history that produced it. OpenAI said that as new messages are added, the model can build on its earlier reasoning, and that if an earlier message is rewritten, its API drops the reasoning that followed it. OpenAI said it also prevents older model families with weaker safeguards from reading GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol's protected reasoning. OpenAI said that when its systems detect unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns, which often include coordinated attempts to extract its models' reasoning, it investigates the accounts responsible. OpenAI said that when it identifies violations, it enforces against the network of accounts, consistent with its policies and terms of service.

OpenAI said that through investigations of each campaign it generates insights that allow it to upgrade its defenses to better detect similar activity. OpenAI said it shares indicators of compromise with other model providers so they can investigate related abuse on their own services. OpenAI said its consistent-standards policy establishes shared standards for safeguards and coordinated enforcement across providers offering its models. OpenAI said it works closely with partners where appropriate to uphold these standards and strengthen protections across deployments. OpenAI said sharing relevant findings across industry and government where appropriate can help disrupt campaigns and enable model developers and providers to better identify and defend against attempts to distill frontier models.

OpenAI said distillation is a common machine-learning technique in which one model learns from data produced by another, for example another model's answers, its reasoning, or its judgments about which answers are better and why. OpenAI said that beyond intellectual property concerns, unauthorized distillation poses serious safety risks, because a second model can learn advanced frontier capabilities without inheriting the safeguards that govern how the original model can use them. OpenAI said the concern is especially clear in dual-use domains like cybersecurity and biology, where a model that helps defenders find vulnerabilities in software could also help an attacker exploit them. OpenAI said that in an internal study on how cyber capabilities transfer, it used the content normally visible to users, final responses, reasoning summaries, and tool interactions, as its baseline for distillation. OpenAI said it started each training run from the same pretrained student model and created a supervised fine-tuning dataset consisting primarily of trajectories from Astra-level teacher models working on coding and defensive cybersecurity tasks.

OpenAI said each trajectory includes all of the steps a model takes as it works through a task, including any tool interactions and its final response. OpenAI said it evaluated each student after fine-tuning and again after a lightweight round of reinforcement learning in cybersecurity and coding environments. OpenAI said that after supervised fine-tuning, the student trained on exact reasoning traces generally outperformed the student trained on reasoning summaries. OpenAI said that after reinforcement learning, the exact-trace student still scored higher at the largest inference budget tested on both benchmarks shown, while the summary-trained student scored higher at lower budgets. OpenAI said its cyber distillation results suggest that protecting reasoning traces can limit cyber capability transfer, even when the underlying task is one allowed under its usage policies.

OpenAI said that across many such interactions, exact reasoning traces can teach a student skills that generalize beyond the tasks the teacher originally performed. OpenAI said it will continue studying how much additional capability transfers across different student models and distillation training recipes. OpenAI said it defends against adversarial distillation at two complementary levels of its safeguard stack, with model behavior, classifier checks, and API controls at the request level and patterns in request-level and account-level signals at the campaign level. OpenAI said attacks uncovered in investigations become examples for training and testing its safeguards.

OpenAI said its adversarial training teaches models to recognize reasoning extraction attempts and refuse to disclose protected reasoning, while preserving responses to legitimate requests for explanations and assistance. OpenAI said adversarial training examples come from successful attacks identified through internal automated red-teaming, investigations, and responsible disclosures of potential security weaknesses from outside researchers or industry partners. OpenAI said it uses input classifiers to detect attempts to extract protected reasoning and output classifiers to detect leaks of protected reasoning in assistant messages and tool-call arguments, applying to both streaming and non-streaming responses. OpenAI said tool-call coverage is important because a model can expose protected reasoning in a tool's arguments without including it in its final answer, and output classifiers can block suspected leaks before that content reaches the caller.

OpenAI said that in static evaluations it replays a fixed set of previously successful attacks to see which still expose protected reasoning, and in adaptive evaluations automated AI red-teamers adjust their approach based on how the system responds. OpenAI said black-box testing gives testers the same view an external user would have, while white-box testing gives them additional information about the system to help them develop stronger attacks. OpenAI said that in its adaptive black-box evaluation it tested whether attackers could recover protected reasoning the model had generated while answering an earlier request or the current one. OpenAI said that on GPT-6.2 Astra with its updated safeguards, the average attack success rate was below 1% for each attack type, and both rates were substantially lower than on GPT-6 Astra with its original safeguards.

OpenAI said it is now applying selected safeguard improvements to GPT-6 Astra as well. OpenAI said it has seen multiple unauthorized adversarial distillation campaigns on its platform this year. OpenAI said it shared initial findings from those campaigns. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Snowflake engineer says enterprises should fix data layers rather than prompts to make AI answers trustworthy
stories.Summary:
Arjun Danda Sureshbabu, a Staff Software Engineer at Snowflake, wrote in SD Times on 2026-11-20 that a few months into building an AI assistant for finance teams, someone asked it what bookings looked like for one region last quarter. The assistant answered in a few minutes with a table and a summary explaining how it got there, and the number was inaccurate. His first instinct was to blame the prompt, into which the team had put role instructions, worked examples and a long description of the schema. When he analyzed the query, the model had done exactly what was asked, finding a table with an AMOUNT column, a REGION_CD column and a date, and summing it up. The model could not know that the amounts included reversals, that region codes had been remapped after a reorg, and that bookings there means something narrower than every row in that table.

The article says most enterprise data was designed for applications and reports, not for a language model reading it cold, and that a finance table is mostly surrogate keys, status codes, amounts and timestamps. It says what those things mean is written down somewhere else, if at all, in a reporting team's SQL, a spreadsheet of code mappings, or the memory of an analyst who has been around for six years. It says a STATUS column with values 1 through 7 will lead the model to decide for itself what they mean, and it won't ask. It says describing the data in the prompt holds up in a demo with five tables and gets shaky at enterprise scale, because definitions and mappings change every quarter and nobody updates the prompt with each mapping change. It says a rule in the ninth paragraph can stop being honoured after a model upgrade, and you find out when a user does.

The article says the teams that get this right stop trying to explain the business to the model in prose and put that knowledge in the data layer, where developers already have tools to build, review and version it. It says that starts with a semantic layer instead of raw tables: named business entities, ontologies, metric definitions, plain-language descriptions of columns and their allowed values, their synonyms and accurate joins. It says bookings gets defined once, in code, and any change to that definition goes through review like everything else, and the model picks from definitions business teams have agreed on rather than creating on its own. It says access control stays in the database, enforced by the same row- and column-level policies that apply to every other query, so the data the model can reach has already been filtered. It says the third piece is making answers checkable, with verified queries reviewed by the owners of those numbers, and when the model writes something new it shows the query, definitions and filters it used.

The article says a prompt tends to belong to whoever wrote it, often one person tweaking it until the demo works, while definitions, policies and verified queries belong to an engineering team with code review, monitoring and someone on call when an answer goes wrong. It says the developers who do this well understand both the data model and the business it describes, sitting with a finance analyst to find out why a code was remapped two years ago and turning that into a definition the system enforces using patterns such as a verified query repository. It says data engineers and domain experts, who often sit at the edge of AI projects, end up doing some of the most important work. It says a better bar than a good demo is whether known or frequently asked questions return the same report the finance team consistently produces, which a human verifies, and whether each answer can be traced back to its definitions and source data. It says prompts still matter, setting the context surrounding the data and how the model asks a follow-up when it is unsure, but they sit on top of everything else.

The article says the author has seen versions of that failure many times since, and the usual response is to tune the prompt, which he thinks is the wrong place to look. It says you can tell the model not to show compensation data to the wrong person, but that is a request, not a permission check. It says moving to a bigger model does not help much, because it writes a more convincing guess and still has no idea when your fiscal year starts. It says you cannot really test a prompt the way you test code. It says most of this is ordinary engineering, schema design, contracts, authorisation and testing, and the unusual part is the consumer, which won't tell you when it's confused or fails silently.

The article says that when an enterprise AI system gives a confident wrong answer, the prompt is usually the last thing the author would change, and he would look first at what the data tells the model, the context layer and grounding factors, and at what it leaves the model to guess. It says the teams keep test sets of real questions with known answers, which is how they tell whether a change actually made things better or just felt like it did. It says the author designs and runs production AI systems that answer questions over enterprise finance data for finance teams and thousands of employees. It says a good answer in a demo tells you very little. It does not say what the finance teams did after the inaccurate answer, or when any of the changes it describes were made.

Articles.Title: Prompt engineering won’t make enterprise AI trustworthy. Data engineering will. - SD Times

stories.Headline: Lenexa Medical wins three VIC AI Awards including Best in Australia
stories.Summary:
Lenexa Medical, a Victorian health technology startup, won three prizes at the VIC AI Awards 2026 in Melbourne, where it was named Best Use of AI in Healthcare, AI Startup of the Year and Best in Australia, the awards recognising projects across technical and creative artificial intelligence categories with winners drawn from Victoria, elsewhere in Australia and overseas. The company was the biggest winner on the technical side of the program through its LenexaCARE product, and it has also been recognised by TIME Magazine as one of the world's top Health Technology companies. Other technical winners included Rostrum AI, which took the Best Enterprise AI Tool award for RostrumLink with Orato, and SPQR Technologies, which won Best AI for Safety for Aegis Runtime Control: Independent Execution Authority for AI Agents. The creative awards covered art, film, music and advertising made with AI tools, with Annelise (Wink.) Clark winning Best in AI Art for Cul-de-Sac Couture and the Best AI Campaign/Commercial prize going to Chapel Street Precinct Film, created by Toby Goodman and the team at CoastGen.

In the film categories, Glamourexia by John Paul DeFazio won Best in AI Short Films, while Edmond Yang took Best in AI Animation for When You Run From Your Mom, and the Best AI Music / Music Videos award went to Is This Not real? by Jason Joseph Dainter. A special Rising Star award went to Peek-a-Boo! A Bunny's Halloween Night, directed by Guillaume Descamps. Matt Kirby, Director of the VIC AI Awards and VIC AI Boom, said the quality of entries stood out before judging began, noting that submissions came from local Victorian individuals and companies alongside international ones and that startups without a profile yet sometimes blew the judges away.

He also pointed to the commercial focus of the technical category winners, saying they are all driven by a real-world need and that it is easy to fall in love with the power of AI but there must be a worthwhile outcome for it to stack up commercially. Kirby said two of the winning filmmakers showed how AI-assisted work could still rely on traditional storytelling strengths, saying both know how to tell a story and that AI is supporting their ideas but it is still driven by human emotion and creativity. The winners reflected a mix of Victorian startups, Australian creatives and international entrants, and the awards were intended to recognise achievements in AI innovation, creativity, consumer work and large-scale business applications. For Victoria's startup scene, Lenexa Medical's result is likely to draw the most attention because of the breadth of its wins, taking category honours in healthcare and the startup competition and then securing the overall Best in Australia award, which placed the company at the centre of this year's judging.

Rostrum AI's award underlined the presence of local business software developers in the field, while SPQR Technologies' win highlighted the attention being paid to AI safety tools as the use of autonomous systems expands. The results come as Australian AI activity continues to spread beyond large technology companies to specialist startups, creative studios and individual artists, and the list of winners suggests judges weighed both commercial application and creative execution across a wide range of work. Kirby said the event left him encouraged by what he had seen from participants, saying VIC AI Boom and the VIC AI Awards came along at the right time and that when everyone else is feeling tired at the end of the year he is feeling inspired by what he is seeing. He added that he cannot wait for the next event.

stories.Headline: MIT and Mecalux find 57% of firms expect AI to make over a quarter of warehouse decisions autonomously by 2028
stories.Summary:
A study by the MIT Centre for Transportation & Logistics and Mecalux found that 57% of organisations expect AI to make or execute more than a quarter of warehouse operational decisions autonomously by 2028, based on a survey of nearly 2,000 supply chain and warehousing professionals across 21 countries. The report, published on 20 November 2026, examined generative and agentic AI in warehouse operations and found that 61% of organisations reported using generative AI at large-scale deployment or full integration, compared with 56% for agentic AI. About three in four deployments had been at their current stage for less than a year, yet 87% of generative AI applications and 81% of agentic AI applications showed at least moderate improvement in their target metrics. Only 39% of generative AI use cases and 36% of agentic AI use cases had significant gains that were both quantified and documented, and where respondents could estimate the scale, the typical gain was about 20% on the main target metric.

Companies are giving AI systems authority in selected areas while keeping tighter controls elsewhere, with inventory movements the area where agents were most often allowed to decide without human approval at 51% of agentic AI use cases, followed by data corrections at 42%. Only 22% of these systems were allowed to make customer-facing commitments and 12% were permitted to make financial decisions, and the most common oversight model was human-on-the-loop, in which AI operates within defined limits while employees monitor and can intervene. Organisations with comprehensive, actively enforced AI governance were about twice as likely to report significant, documented improvements, at 51% versus 26% for generative AI and 46% versus 23% for agentic AI, a pattern that held after accounting for deployment status, region, industry and budget, though the study noted association rather than proof of causation. Legacy system integration was the biggest constraint on scaling generative AI for 40% of respondents, while 54% said better integration with warehouse management and ERP systems would have the greatest effect on adoption.

Matthias Winkenbach, Director of the Intelligent Logistics Systems Lab, said the objective was to move beyond general sentiment and provide practical guidance on where these technologies deliver operational value today and where they remain experimental. Javier Carrillo, Chief Executive Officer of Mecalux, said warehouse decision-makers need AI they can measure and that the research gives clients a clear map of where the technology is working and what it takes to prove it. On employment, 56% of organisations said the technology had mainly shifted staff towards higher-value tasks, while 11% reported reduced headcount and 9% reported increased headcount, and 73% said they were upskilling warehouse-floor staff while 61% were creating new technical roles. Ninety per cent anticipated an increase in AI investment over the next two to three years, with 29% expecting that rise to exceed 25%, broadly in line with the previous year's study, and among companies that had fully integrated the technologies, 70% expected agentic AI to make or execute more than a quarter of warehouse operational decisions autonomously by 2028.

Articles.Title: Study finds AI will run more warehouse decisions by 2028 - IT Brief Australia

stories.Headline: IndexBox forecasts growth for thin wafer processing and dicing equipment through 2035
stories.Summary:
IndexBox released a market report on November 21, 2026, regarding thin wafer processing and dicing equipment. This global market is entering a structural growth phase driven by advanced semiconductor packaging demand. The report provides a comprehensive analysis of the industry from 2026 through 2035. It highlights a shift toward thinner wafers and higher die density for heterogeneous integration. This equipment is now a critical enabler for 3D IC stacking and chiplet designs.

The baseline scenario projects a compound annual growth rate of 6.8 percent from 2026 to 2035. The market index is projected to reach 185 by 2035, using 2025 as a base of 100. Advanced packaging represents 35 percent of demand, while power semiconductors account for 25 percent. Memory and logic devices hold 20 percent, and MEMS and sensors represent 12 percent. Wafers for advanced packaging must be thinned to below 50 micrometers.

IndexBox states that the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals and more disciplined procurement behavior. They note that the supply architecture is now more regionally diversified than it was previously. The report claims that the transition to laser and plasma singulation is accelerating to process brittle materials. These technologies are necessary to achieve near-zero kerf loss for silicon carbide and gallium nitride. The analysts suggest that long-term trajectories remain positive despite some cyclical semiconductor spending.

The report identifies Applied Materials, DISCO Corporation, EV Group, SUSS MicroTec, and Tokyo Electron as representative participants. Other key players include Lam Research, ASM International, Plasma-Therm, and Advanced Dicing Technologies. Electric vehicle manufacturers and 5G infrastructure providers are affected by these technological shifts. High-performance computing and mobile applications also drive the need for fan-out wafer-level packaging. These sectors require precise, damage-free singulation that traditional mechanical blade dicing cannot deliver.

The background includes a shift toward wide-bandgap semiconductors like silicon carbide for use in electric vehicles. Eurostat data shows producer unit values for semiconductor manufacture machines were 666,667.00 EUR per piece in 2025. European Union industry output for other special-purpose machinery rose 35.6 percent year-on-year in August 2026. Producer prices for that same machinery category rose 1.5 percent year-on-year in September 2026. Asia-Pacific is the dominant hub for production, while North America and Europe lead system design.

Future growth depends on the ramp-up of AI accelerators and high-bandwidth memory through 2035. The market must overcome high capital costs and qualification cycles that can exceed 18 months. Geopolitical trade tensions and export controls remain potential constraints on equipment sales to certain regions. Technical challenges include managing breakage and thermal issues when processing ultra-thin wafers. The report leaves open how alternative packaging approaches might reduce the need for dicing.

stories.Headline: Bajaj Finserv and Pennant Technologies invest $4 million in Soket AI as it launches EKA-1 model
stories.Summary:
Bajaj Finserv's applied research initiative Finserv Intelligence invested about $2 million in AI research company Soket AI, and its investee firm Pennant Technologies put in a further $2 million in the same round, for a total of $4 million. Soket AI, which is backed by the IndiaAI Mission, also launched EKA-1, a 26-billion-parameter foundation model under Project EKA, its flagship sovereign AI initiative focused on math, code and reasoning. The model is being built to support over 100 languages, including Indian and Global South languages, alongside programming languages. The investment supports Soket AI's work on indigenous AI solutions for applications where data security, reliability and technological sovereignty are critical.

Sanjiv Bajaj, Chairman and Managing Director of Bajaj Finserv, said in a statement that demand is for AI systems that are not only intelligent but also reliable, secure, auditable and able to operate within trusted environments. He said the group is investing in indigenous research that meets these requirements. Rajeev Jain, Vice Chairman and Managing Director of Bajaj Finance, said the next phase of AI will be defined by outcomes delivered at sustainable cost. He said Soket AI's efficient reasoning-led models can make advanced AI economically viable for financial services while allowing the firm to deploy it securely within its own infrastructure, with full control over data. He added that the startup's depth in Indian languages can help the firm serve customers in the language they are comfortable with.

Abhishek Upperwal, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Soket AI, asserted that the backing of Bajaj Finance and Pennant Technologies reinforces the company's belief that India has the talent and capabilities to develop foundational AI technologies at a global scale. Pradeep Verma, Founder and Managing Director of Pennant Technologies, said the firm is building agentic AI into its lending platform so banks can use AI across their operations while retaining control over their data and decisions. He said there is a clear need for locally built large language models that regulated institutions can run on their own infrastructure and govern under their own policies. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the launch and the funding.

stories.Headline: Mid-cap Indian IT firms buy AI skills as acquisitions outpace organic growth
stories.Summary:
During Coforge's Q2 earnings call, an analyst asked Chief Financial Officer Saurabh Goel to explain the gap between consolidated and organic growth. Revenue grew 10.9% sequentially in constant currency, against organic growth of 3.8%, indicating how much acquisitions are supplementing the company's growth. Goel attributed the difference partly to the consolidation of a full quarter of Encora's revenue in Q2, compared to only two months in Q1. Encora, the digital engineering firm Coforge acquired for ₹22,090 crore, contributed ₹1,382, 1,391 crore in revenue. It contributed about ₹940 crore during the two months included in Q1.

Q2 was busy not just for Coforge, but also for Cyient and Mphasis, which acquired data engineering and decision intelligence firms. Meanwhile, Persistent is expected to complete its acquisition of Nagarro in the first quarter of 2027. Coforge said its AI-led engineering, data integration, and cloud businesses contributed 86% of consolidated revenue. Mphasis said AI-led deals accounted for 66% of its ₹4,380 crore in net new total contract value. Zensar reported that AI-influenced deals made up 36% of its order book, while Sonata Software put AI-led order bookings at 25%.

Gartner's Distinguished Vice President Analyst Milind Govekar tells AIM that most mid-tier companies are acquiring to get new skills and new technology. Coforge has already integrated Encora into its business, and the company no longer distinguishes between the two entities. Coforge's consolidated EBIT margin stood at 16%, against 17% for its standalone business. Integration costs reached about ₹160 crore, exceeding the company's guidance of ₹141 crore to ₹150 crore. Cyient acquired AI-native data engineering firm TAO Digital for ₹2,049 crore, and TAO contributed ₹90 crore in its first month.

Excluding the acquisition, organic revenue grew 1.6% sequentially and 0.4% year-on-year in constant currency. CFO Shrinivas Kulkarni said TAO's annual revenue run rate had risen from about $80 million (₹752 crore) at acquisition to nearly $100 million (₹940 crore). He expects it to reach ₹1,034 crore over the next 12 months, while cautioning against extrapolating from one month's revenue. Cyient now plans to take TAO's AI data engineering capabilities to existing customers.

The company's technology order intake rose 39.7% during the quarter. Persistent secured approximately 94.04% of Nagarro's share capital and voting rights, excluding treasury shares and including its existing holding. The deal awaits RBI approval and foreign investment clearances in Austria and Spain. The acquisition would expand Persistent's European presence through Nagarro's delivery centres in Romania, Portugal, Hungary, and Poland.

Persistent's European revenue fell 8.5% year-on-year in Q2 in US dollar terms, which it attributed to two client-specific events. North American revenue grew 22.5%. Persistent booked ₹185 crore in Nagarro-related transaction costs in Q2, including advisory, financing, and legal expenses. Its PAT margin was 7.5% and operating PAT margin 10.6%.

It expects another ₹235, 282 crore in costs over the next two quarters, taking cumulative one-time expenses to approximately ₹420, 467 crore. Mphasis acquired Canadian decision-intelligence firm Theory and Practice Business Intelligence (TAP) in April and expects to complete its acquisition of IT staffing firm Red Oak Tech's customer contracts, worth up to ₹265 crore, in November. CFO Aravind Viswanathan cited TAP-related amortisation as a pressure on margins during the earnings call. More to follow.

stories.Headline: CPA and learning chief Akhila Chandrashekar argues AI literacy should become a core competency for accountants
stories.Summary:
Akhila Chandrashekar, chief learning officer and a qualified CPA, CMA, CIA and CFE, published an opinion article on November 20, 2026, in Accounting Today arguing that AI literacy should become a core competency for certified public accountants. She opened with a hypothetical in which a CPA asks an AI tool to research a complex tax issue and receives a polished report with regulatory citations and a confident recommendation, only for the CPA to discover the regulation does not exist because the AI fabricated it. She wrote that when something goes wrong the client will not sue the AI company but the CPA, because the accountant remains accountable. The article asks whether AI literacy should become a core CPA competency and notes that the profession's exam already acknowledges AI. The article states that the AICPA's 2026 CPA Exam Blueprints explicitly added artificial intelligence to the Auditing and Attestation section, where students are expected to understand confidentiality risks in using AI tools, recognize how AI adoption could affect the risk of material misstatement, and evaluate the accuracy, completeness, authenticity and potential bias of AI-prepared information.

The 2027 CPA Exam Blueprints, effective January 2027, make what the article calls a nuanced but meaningful change, shifting terminology in AUD17 from information prepared using technologies including AI to information generated using those technologies, and AUD18 explicitly identifies AI-generated information among potential sources of audit evidence. The article stresses that the 2027 blueprint did not introduce AI verification for the first time, since those responsibilities were already reflected in 2026, and it does not create a separate AI examination. Chandrashekar describes the change as a step forward but not a leap, and she argues that foundational AI literacy should be assessed across the CPA exam's Core sections, with more advanced competencies addressed through specialization. Chandrashekar illustrates AI literacy by contrasting two accountants using the same tool, one who copies results into a report and sends it to management and another who checks the underlying data, questions unusual assumptions, verifies calculations, investigates inconsistencies and documents the review. She defines AI literacy not as writing clever prompts or knowing which tool is trending but as understanding AI's limitations, detecting fabricated information, protecting confidential data, recognizing bias and knowing when human judgment must override a machine's recommendation.

She gives sample exam scenarios, including an AI-recommended tax deduction supported by three authoritative-looking citations where one is fabricated, one is outdated and one does not apply, and an AI system that finds no significant revenue anomalies in a dataset that excludes the final month of the financial year. She also raises the case of a CPA who passed the exam 15 years ago and may never have studied generative AI, hallucinations or algorithmic bias yet could now be approving AI-assisted tax advice, supervising automated audits or signing off on AI-prepared financial reports, and she asks whether continuing professional education should evolve to teach identifying errors, challenging outputs, protecting client information and remaining accountable. The article credits the AICPA for recognizing AI-related risks in the 2026 blueprints and for making AI-generated evidence more explicit in 2027, and it concludes that there is a burning need for AI literacy to become a core competency for every CPA. Chandrashekar writes that in a profession built on skepticism, evidence and trust, the greatest risk is not what AI does not know but that accountants may not know what AI does not know. The article does not say what action, if any, the AICPA or state boards plan to take on making AI literacy a core competency or on changing continuing professional education requirements.

stories.Headline: Cloud host reports AI API key exposure as PHP fixes critical flaws
stories.Summary:
A cloud hosting platform disclosed in October that an unauthorized third party may have accessed encrypted environment variables and, for some of them, obtained the decrypted contents. The platform said those variables may contain secrets such as API keys or database and registry credentials. It advised customers to immediately roll all environment variables. The platform said the impact may be limited to a subset of users. It said it believes the incident is part of a series of attacks on platform companies aimed at compromising AI inference providers.

The platform said it has since invalidated all of its API tokens. In a preliminary report, it said the attack was attempting to obtain AI provider API keys. It said at most 1.85% of workspaces had some environment variables potentially compromised. It said it is not yet able to share the specific details and scale of the exploits. The same day, the PHP project released fixes for two critical flaws that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution.

Both PHP flaws are rated 9.2 under CVSS v4.0 and affect all PHP installations serving web requests. The PHP project says there are no complete mitigations and updating is the only safe choice. Versions 8.1 and older are past end of life and get no new official release. For 7.4 through 8.1, the project posted only minimal source patches. Steven de la Fe wrote the Accounting Today article published November 20, 2026, at 9:00 a.m.

EST. De la Fe said an API key is a password that software uses, and an agent often uses one to pull a trial balance or read a client file. He said that if a key leaks from a breached host or an unpatched server, whoever holds it can get whatever the agent could get. He said that makes it a Safeguards Rule issue. In July, the IRS Office of Professional Responsibility said firms in the business of completing income tax returns are defined as covered financial institutions under the FTC Safeguards Rule.

IRS Publication 5708 adds that this holds regardless of size and that a written information security plan is required. De la Fe said the rule requires each authorized user to get only the customer information they need, and customer information to be encrypted at rest and in transit. He said the rule also requires multifactor authentication, monitoring and logging of user activity, and contract oversight of service providers with periodic checks. He said firms that do not qualify for the small-institution exception (314.6) must also run continuous monitoring or periodic penetration testing and vulnerability assessments.

He said none of that mentions AI agents, and he would treat an agent's key like an authorized user. He said the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications names excessive functionality, excessive permissions and excessive autonomy as typical root causes when agents overreach. De la Fe cited a January 2025 technical blog in which NIST's AI safety team, now its Center for AI Standards and Innovation, wrote that many AI agents are vulnerable to agent hijacking. He said the finding came from lab tests in simulated environments, not field data.

He said an attacker hides instructions in data the agent reads, which in a firm includes client emails and uploads. He proposed a one-page AI key and patch policy for a partner to sign, with seven of 10 lines tied to the rule or IRS guidance. He said line 7 follows CISA's advice and lines 4 and 5 are his recommendations. More to follow.

stories.Headline: E2E Networks falls for a fourth day as AI financing worries hit Indian tech stocks
stories.Summary:
E2E Networks shares fell to the lower circuit limit for a second straight session on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, extending the stock's slide to four consecutive days since October 15. The shares dropped 5 percent to Rs 627.15 on the NSE, the lowest level permitted for the day. The weakness spread to other AI-related stocks in India as global AI shares came under selling pressure. Moneycontrol reported the story on the same day, with its report published at 12:53 pm.

Among the other Indian names, Black Box shares slipped 1.55 percent to Rs 880.75 on the NSE. Netweb Technologies India declined 0.36 percent to Rs 4,683 per share at around 12.50 pm. A related headline from the site said Netweb and Black Box had fallen by as much as 9 percent during the broader slide. The article itself gave the smaller figures for the two companies at the time of writing.

The selloff was tied to worries about how the rising costs of AI development and infrastructure will be financed around the world. Concerns about the debt burden carried by CoreWeave added to the pressure on global AI stocks. Fears that higher interest rates could curb spending on AI infrastructure also weighed on technology shares, particularly chipmakers and data centre operators. The article did not name any company or official as having announced a specific decision behind the moves, and it attributed the decline to investor sentiment.

The pattern appears to have built up over several sessions rather than a single day, since E2E Networks has now fallen every day since October 15. An earlier Moneycontrol piece from October 13 carried a headline saying that E2E Networks, Hitachi Energy India and other AI-related stocks had fallen by up to 5 percent amid global jitters over AI. The articles did not say what would happen next for these stocks. The reports left open whether the concerns over financing costs and interest rates would ease or continue to weigh on the sector.

stories.Headline: DOE science chief Gil denies Genesis AI takes 10% from Office of Science research
stories.Summary:
On 20 November 2026, DOE Under Secretary for Science Darío Gil rejected a report that the Genesis Mission AI initiative is paid for partly by taking 10% from the Office of Science’s traditional research budgets. He said this in an interview with AIP’s FYI, speaking with science policy reporter Clare Zhang one year after the White House announced the Genesis Mission. The mission is a DOE-led effort to use AI to double scientific productivity within a decade. Zhang asked Gil about a report in Science that DOE funds Genesis in part by taking 10% from the Office of Science’s traditional research budgets. Gil called that “a total, in my view, mischaracterization of how we’re doing this.”

Gil said each program office began with a science question and that no project was funded unless the science criteria were met. He said “This is not about taking money from High Energy Physics and giving it to ASCR (Advanced Scientific Computing Research) to do SI,” using DOE’s shorthand for superintelligence. He said “I don’t accept the formulation of the 10% thing.” Asked whether Genesis grants are a subset of Office of Science research grants rather than separate, he answered “For sure. We’re not moving any money around.” Gil’s letter to the research community, published by DOE on 12 November 2026, and the AIP interview give figures that are DOE’s own and are presented as Gil states them.

Office of Science funding is at an all-time high of $8.4 billion, according to the Gil letter and the AIP interview. The Office of Science national laboratories’ operating budget is a record $9.8 billion, and laboratory personnel number 28,445, both per the Gil letter and the AIP interview. The Genesis first cohort is 297 teams across 369 institutions in all 50 states, and the first call received over 5,000 proposals, both per the Gil letter. There are 33 National Science and Technology Challenges with over 15 federal agencies, per the Gil letter. Gil also said the response to the open call was the largest in DOE’s history.

In a White House announcement of 22 July 2026, Energy Secretary Chris Wright reported 278 projects selected and more than $5 billion in federal commitments from more than 15 agencies, and the 297-team figure in Gil’s November letter is the later count. Asked about the $300 million, Gil said “I think the overall investments that are going to be required will be larger than that.” He added that the dialogue with appropriators is “very positive” and that “they are the ones that have the responsibility to figure out what is the right level of investment.” His stated top priority for year two is for Congress to take ownership of Genesis in a bipartisan way and codify it in legislation. Asked how to distinguish enthusiasm for Genesis from a general wish for reliable federal research funding at a time of widespread uncertainty, Gil said he could speak only to his own area of responsibility and pointed to the budget, laboratory budget and employment figures, which he called all-time highs, saying “I’m not saying it’s all easy and roses” and acknowledging that advances in computing “create a lot of anxiety.”

The Genesis Mission was launched by an executive order signed in November 2025, and CASRAI has covered it since, including an August 2026 report on the first project selections and a Genesis Mission guide explaining eligibility and how funding works. The Office of Science’s Advanced Scientific Computing Research program, which Gil named in his answer, is one of its research programs. In mid-November, DOE’s Lux system at Oak Ridge debuted on the TOP500 list, which Gil cited as an example of the platform effort. The Senate Appropriations Committee released its Energy and Water Development bill and explanatory statement on 12 November 2026, and according to AIP’s report of 13 November, the Senate proposal would raise the Office of Science budget by about 1% to $8.52 billion, including $120 million in previously appropriated funds, while the House bill would set it at $8.525 billion. AIP also reports that the Senate explanatory statement recommends using up to $300 million within the office’s budget for Genesis Mission research.

The next dated milestone is 11 December 2026, when the current continuing resolution expires, according to AIP, and a lapse would begin on 12 December if Congress does not act. Congress has to reconcile the Senate and House Energy and Water bills, including the Genesis language. Gil also said DOE would decide in early January who will pursue the goal of building a fault-tolerant quantum machine by 2028, a competition that is part of the same effort. The articles leave open how a renewal or continuation will be handled in fiscal 2027 and whether a Genesis-scoped call is expected to be the route. They also leave open whether the Senate and House figures and the Genesis language will survive reconciliation.

stories.Headline: KPMG runs an AI-assisted audit alongside a conventional one for a FTSE 250 company
stories.Summary:
KPMG deployed more than 100 AI agents alongside its conventional audit of an unnamed FTSE 250 company, according to the Financial Times. The agents gathered and analysed information, documented their work and produced draft conclusions. They also suggested next steps. The experiment was reported on 19 November 2026 by Claudine Cassar. KPMG ran two audits alongside each other: its conventional audit and an experimental AI-assisted audit called Project Exponential.

An audit partner signed off the experimental work, but KPMG based its statutory audit opinion on the conventional audit. KPMG did not rely on the AI-assisted exercise when issuing its audit report. KPMG built the agents in four months. Two partners and a director worked with senior managers and junior staff to build and run them, although the firm declined to disclose the team's exact size. Humans set the agents' objectives, supplied information about the business and previous audits, reviewed their work and challenged their conclusions.

KPMG's UK head of audit, Cath Burnet, said that in some situations the technology asked better questions than the human team. Burnet described instances in which the agents investigated issues more deeply, saying "the AI was able to go so much deeper". In one area, a person intervened after an agent failed to match regulations to company documents. KPMG's pilot does not establish better audit quality overall. Deeper questioning still needs to produce reliable evidence.

PwC argued in its 5 August submission to the PCAOB that the use of AI by companies and auditors should become the board's foremost priority. PwC sought guidance on automation bias, explainability, traceability and the ability to reconstruct AI-generated work. PwC identified the need to assess the relevance and reliability of audit evidence and to maintain professional scepticism even when an AI output appears plausible. PwC also identified the need to ensure that agentic workflows allow adequate human oversight and intervention.

Wayne Banks has warned about automation deference, the weakening of scepticism when reviewers become accustomed to plausible, professionally presented AI output. KPMG US has redesigned its audit internship training around fraud scenarios, incomplete information and critical thinking. PwC is introducing critical-thinking and judgement certification for more than 85,000 professionals, including simulations that require employees to challenge AI-generated conclusions. In his examination of Arthur Andersen's training model, William Englehaupt argues that firms must reconsider staffing, promotion and incentives alongside formal instruction.

The traditional audit pyramid distributes work across different levels of experience and provides a route through which recruits become managers, directors and partners. That structure also supports the economics of the partnership, with a relatively small group of senior professionals directing and reviewing work carried out by a much larger workforce. If agents reduce production work, firms could operate with smaller teams. If reviewing their conclusions requires a greater proportion of experienced staff, those teams may also become more senior.

The effect on costs and partner leverage would depend on how much production work disappears and how much review remains. The commercial risk is that firms reduce their staffing pipeline before they understand the sustained demand for human expertise. Firms may need fewer people to produce the work, but they will still need people capable of challenging it. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Keysight launches Chiplet 3D Interconnect Designer for multi-die 3D IC routing and simulation
stories.Summary:
Keysight Technologies has introduced a tool called Chiplet 3D Interconnect Designer, which is meant to streamline the design of chiplet and multi-die 3D IC systems, according to an Electronic Design article published on November 20, 2026. The article, written by William G. Wong, says the tool provides pre-layout workflows for defining, routing, and simulating chiplet interconnects. Wong spoke with Hee Soo Lee, the High Speed Digital Segment Lead at Keysight, about the product in a video that accompanies the article. The tool supports interconnect standards such as UCIe and Bunch of Wires, which is also known as BOW.

According to the article, the designer is used to define silicon and organic interposer systems for chiplet interconnects and to simulate and test those designs. Its electromagnetic-based simulation is described as delivering precise electrical analysis of 3D package interconnects as well as printed-circuit-board designs. The tool can also create microbump maps, vias, and bus interconnects for chiplet and multi-die work. In addition, automated autorouting support for via structures is said to reduce manual operations in the design workflow.

Hee Soo Lee, identified as the High Speed Digital Segment Lead, discussed the tool with Wong, and the conversation is available in the video embedded in the article. The article does not include direct remarks from Lee beyond that discussion, and it presents the tool's features as described above. Wong is the author of the piece and serves as Senior Content Director for Electronic Design and Microwaves & RF. The article lists Marie Darty among its contributors.

The article places the tool in the context of chiplet and multi-die 3D IC design, which it says can be streamlined using Keysight's product. It does not state pricing, availability dates, or performance benchmarks for the designer. The piece also does not say what happens next with the tool or how customers can obtain it. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Sachin Sharma publishes a Claude bug-hunting skills bundle with 83 skills on GitHub
stories.Summary:
ElementalSoul, also named Sachin Sharma, published the Claude-BugHunter bundle on GitHub, and the explainx.ai article about it is dated 2026-11-15T06:00:00Z. The bundle is a self-contained Agent Skills set that teaches coding agents bug-hunting methodology rather than generic hacker prompts. It ships 83 skills, 15 slash commands, and 681 disclosed-report patterns mapped into 24 vulnerability classes. The repository gained about 124 GitHub stars in a day and sits near 5,900 stars total. The article says agent-assisted offensive security is now default curiosity for Claude Code users, and unauthorized use carries legal and platform-policy risk.

The bundle includes explicit in-scope and out-of-scope lists, and its in-scope list covers web apps, APIs, OAuth, SSRF, IDOR, external M365, Okta, vCenter and VPN chains, and cloud IAM misconfigs. Its out-of-scope list covers internal AD attacks, C2 frameworks, persistence, AMSI bypass, and iOS, kernel and binary pwn. The plugin install runs /plugin marketplace add elementalsouls/Claude-BugHunter then /plugin install claude-bughunter@elementalsouls, while the copy install uses git clone plus bash scripts/install.sh, with --all for multi-harness. Option A keeps skills namespaced under claude-bughunter: and updates with plugin bumps, and Option B drops files into ~/.claude/skills and enables the hunt engagement scaffolder plus an optional cbh CLI installed with pipx install git+https://github.com/elementalsouls/Claude-BugHunter. Multi-harness support copies the same SKILL.md files into Codex, Hermes and Antigravity paths when --all is passed, and slash commands remain Claude-Code-only by design.

The README's Authorization section states the skills target assets you own or have written permission to test and points to triage-validation questions on program scope and accepted impact. The README links the Cyber Verification Program and documents Opus 5 model fallback to Opus 4.8 on some higher-risk cyber classes. For defensive work on code you own, the README suggests framing tasks as remediation reviews such as checking against OWASP Top 10 rather than disguising live offensive engagements to bypass classifiers. The README recommends CVP when the work is genuinely offensive, and it describes a 7-Question Gate covering scope, impact class, reproducibility and related program-policy checks before submission. The README lists DVWA, OWASP Juice Shop, Hacker101 and testphp.vulnweb.com as environments the bundle was exercised against.

The article says BugHunter is not a replacement for human judgment on novel logic bugs and encodes patterns triagers already paid for on public programs. It says the bundle's enterprise skills such as m365-entra-attack, okta-attack, hunt-sharepoint, vmware-vcenter-attack and enterprise-vpn-attack encode 2024 to 2026 CVE chains and appliance quirks for Cisco, Fortinet, Citrix, Palo Alto, Pulse, SonicWall and F5. It says agent-assisted recon can parallelize identity-fabric mapping of Entra and Okta with SSL VPN fingerprinting in one session, and the offensive-osint and web2-recon skills feed a ranked surface list shown in the README quickstart transcript with api.acme.com and GraphQL introspection flagged first. It says evidence-hygiene nudges researchers away from screenshots that leak session cookies or victim PII, and red-team deliverables use redteam-report-template instead of HackerOne markdown. It says bugcrowd-reporting gives VRT-aware severity language, and the article says researchers should keep program rules in a scope.md, run the 7-Question Gate before filing, and redact PII in screenshots.

The article says the bundle's 58 hunt-* skills carry payloads, bypass tables and chain templates derived from disclosed bounty reports, and bb-methodology and redteam-mindset cover non-linear recon, hunt, validate and report flows. It says skills load by topic rather than by name, so a plain-language engagement description pulls the right hunt-* module. It says the engine/ folder maps target surfaces to skills deterministically, and the 15 slash commands include /hunt, /recon and /report. It says eight skills vend from shuvonsec/claude-bug-bounty under NOTICE file rules, and the generator public-skills-builder scaffolded the per-class hunt-* skills from disclosed patterns. It says Claude-OSINT is a sister project for recon phases with two skills canonically maintained in BugHunter and re-exported, and installers track manifests and skip duplicate copies.

The README roadmap mentions HackerOne MCP integration, per-engagement memory and quarterly refreshes of enterprise VPN CVE matrices, while Burp MCP is wired today. The article says hunt-fintech-graphql already exists, and healthcare and government compliance hunt skills remain open roadmap entries. It says sponsors ApiSmart and ThreatWatch360 appear in the README footer and do not change the MIT license. It says the README credits Trail of Bits and SecSkills as authoring inspirations without vendoring their trees, and the article recommends reviewing AgentBeam alongside skill installs for defensive agent controls. The article says the README positions the bundle for authorized testing only, and it leaves open whether HackerOne API automation will ship inside the agent.

stories.Headline: SoftBank chairman Masayoshi Son drops plan to acquire SK hynix for $1 trillion
stories.Summary:
Masayoshi Son, the chairman of SoftBank Group, recently explored the possibility of acquiring SK hynix to expand his artificial intelligence empire. He approached several major financial institutions in the United States to discuss how he could raise the necessary funds for this massive purchase. The potential deal was estimated to reach a value of $1 trillion, which is approximately 1,400 trillion won. However, the plan appears to have been dropped at an early stage because it was unlikely to be feasible.

The proposed purchase price of $1 trillion was based on a peak market value for SK hynix plus a 40 percent control premium. Currently, the world's second-largest memory chipmaker has a market value of about $577.7 billion, or 777 trillion won. This acquisition would have given SoftBank control over high-bandwidth memory, a critical component for AI accelerators that is currently supplied by SK hynix, Samsung Electronics, and Micron Technology. Such a move would have complemented SoftBank's existing holdings in Arm, SB Energy, Ampere Computing, DigitalBridge, Intel, and OpenAI.

A spokesperson for SoftBank stated that the company reviews many different opportunities but this specific deal is no longer under active consideration. The company did not confirm that Wall Street banks had actually discussed providing the financing for the acquisition. Market observers generally believe that the idea of a trillion-dollar bid was never realistic given the financial requirements. Despite this, industry officials suggest the approach demonstrates that Masayoshi Son intends to control the entire AI value chain.

Son has a long history of using borrowed money and collateral to fund his large-scale investments in technology. He previously used his holdings in Alibaba to help cover the $32 billion cost of purchasing Arm. In 2017, he launched the $100 billion Vision Fund using money from the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. More recently, he pledged shares of Arm as collateral to finance his stake in OpenAI. These actions show a consistent pattern of aggressive financial maneuvering to secure dominant positions in emerging tech sectors.

stories.Headline: SemiAnalysis finds Apple builds M5 Pro, Max and Ultra as three-die chiplets on TSMC hybrid bonding
stories.Summary:
SemiAnalysis published a die-level teardown finding that Apple's M5 Pro, M5 Max and M5 Ultra are the company's first true chiplet design, splitting the system-on-chip across three separately built dies. The teardown, published on 2026-11-20, reports that the dies are joined with TSMC's SoIC-mH hybrid-bonding packaging instead of solder. SemiAnalysis bought the chips, pulled them apart and measured them rather than relying on a vendor briefing. The CPU chiplet measures roughly 168 mm² and carries 18 cores, four large Thunderbolt 5 PHYs and no efficiency cores. The GPU chiplets are a precise 2:1 scaling of one another at about 300 mm² and 157 mm².

Apple taped out three dies, one CPU die and two GPU dies, a small one and a large one, all on TSMC's N3P process. The M5 Pro pairs the 168 mm² CPU chiplet with the small GPU chiplet of about 157 mm², and the M5 Max pairs the CPU chiplet with the large GPU chiplet of about 300 mm². The M5 Ultra uses two CPU chiplets and two large GPU chiplets and was not measured because the lab had no unit. The large GPU die has 40 GPU cores, 48 MB of System Level Cache and a 512-bit memory interface, while the small die has 20 cores, 24 MB of cache and a 256-bit interface. The CPU chiplet holds 18 CPU cores in three clusters, a 16-core Neural Engine of eight dual-cores, four Display Engines, a 4-lane Display PHY and 16 lanes of PCI-Express, most likely Gen 5, in four 2x2 clusters.

SemiAnalysis said the M5 Ultra's UltraFusion link reaches more than 6x the connection density of the M3 Ultra, which implies hybrid bonding and rules out solder. It said the teardown was inferred, not measured, for the Ultra, reconstructed from a second, larger interconnect on the large GPU die plus Apple's own density claim. It said copper-to-copper bonding can be pitched below 10 µm, versus microbumps stuck at 25 µm, and approaches 3 µm in the most advanced processes. It said the result is the highest quality interconnect you can think of, almost like fusing the metal layers, creating one large coherent chip. It said it is not unlikely that Apple worked on the solution directly with TSMC, and closed with the aside, Can't innovate anymore my ass.

SemiAnalysis said the M1, M2 and M3 Ultra simply took two of the largest dies of a generation and fused them in a classic multi-chip-module arrangement. It said the M3 Ultra used InFO-LSI packaging with a local silicon interconnect and solder-based microbumps, and that measurements show a 25 µm bump pitch. It said the SoIC-mH is the same hybrid bonding behind AMD's 3D V-Cache, but deployed side by side rather than stacked, and that the mH stands for molding horizontally. It said placing the chips side by side avoids the heat trapping of a vertical sandwich, citing the A20 Pro's move to WMCM packaging with memory moved beside the chip. It said the twelve new P-cores, internally called M-cores, are split into two mirrored six-core clusters, each with 8 MB of shared cache and a dedicated matrix engine, and that the S-core cluster is slightly asymmetrical with two S-cores above and four below a shared 16 MB cache.

SemiAnalysis said the CPU die, at roughly 168 mm², is actually larger than a base M5, and that the small GPU die is essentially the large one cut in half, which it suggests shortens development time. It said the four Thunderbolt 5 PHYs outclass the M-cores in size and are not far behind an S-core, and flagged how big analogue SerDes are becoming and how much space the command-and-control area is taking up. It said the 16-core Neural Engine has since been doubled on the M6, and that only the M5 Ultra gets twice the AI hardware because it uses two CPU chiplets. It said it speculates the two-cluster split may be for power management, letting an entire cluster shut off when idle. It said hybrid bonding raises bandwidth and cuts the energy cost of moving data, making it a packaging moat as much as a process one, and puts TSMC's advanced packaging roadmap at the center of Apple's silicon story the way N3P once was.

SemiAnalysis said the first physical analysis of the M5 Ultra will either confirm the two-Max construction or complicate it. It said the other thread worth watching is whether side-by-side hybrid bonding spreads to other Apple products, given the company's apparent shift toward heat-conscious packaging across the A20 Pro and M5 lines. It said the signal for investors is that advanced packaging is becoming a competitive battleground in its own right. It said to watch whether AMD, NVIDIA and the hyperscalers' in-house silicon follow Apple into side-by-side hybrid bonding, and whether TSMC's packaging capacity, not its wafer capacity, becomes the binding constraint on the next generation of high-end processors. It said Apple had access to hybrid bonding for some time, as other TSMC customers did, but waited for the side-by-side implementation.
