stories.Headline: Pennsylvania consumer advocate joins seven states to urge PJM to delay December auction
stories.Summary:
The PA Environment Digest Blog published a roundup on Saturday, November 21, 2026, of A.I. and data center articles from the previous two weeks, covering November 16 to 23. The roundup's first announcement reports that Pennsylvania Consumer Advocate Darryl Lawrence joined advocates in seven other PJM states and the independent PJM market monitor. They urged PJM to delay its December generation auction to avoid billions in added costs to consumers. The roundup also reports that Spotlight PA said the Consumer Advocate filed a complaint against PPL Electric aimed at forcing A.I. data centers to pay their fair share. The roundup states that Spotlight PA reported utility customers who shop for energy suppliers pay more, and the PUC agrees the numbers raise concerns.

The roundup states that the PUC approved a 3.5% natural gas delivery base rate increase for National Fuel Gas. It reports that DEP received U.S. DOE approval to launch a $258 million program providing rebates on appliances and building retrofits to reduce home energy bills. It states that legislators and environmental leaders unveiled a 100-day blueprint to lower electricity bills, rein in data centers and expand clean energy. The roundup reports that DEP says about 25 data center projects are in some stage of permitting in Pennsylvania, and none have signed a consent order saying they will comply with GRID standards under the Governor's executive order. It states that Marcellus Drilling News reported on the status of 27 Pennsylvania data centers in the permitting process and their sources of power.

The roundup states that Gov. Shapiro said new PJM governance rules ensure the electric grid will continue to be held captive by what he called greedy corporate interests. It reports that the North American Electric Reliability Corp. winter outlook said extreme winter weather conditions may result in electricity supply shortfalls due to data center demands and impacts on natural gas distribution systems. It states that the independent PJM market monitor warned of another $5 to $10 billion in electricity grid costs on consumers by data centers after delayed PJM market reforms. It reports that PJM Interconnection proposed a one-year process for speeding generation connections, and that PJM said the plan would cut generation and transmission service interconnections for large loads to one year. It states that PJM proposed new rules to protect grid reliability as A.I. data center demand grows.

The roundup reports that the Scranton Times said Olyphant Boro Council approved a $101 million A.I. data center settlement over the objections of more than 200 people at the meeting amid heavy police presence. It states that the Scranton Times editorial said the approval without real public input was a bad night for the democratic process and appalling. It reports that the Olyphant police chief said public threats over the approval will result in arrest, and that they have been overwhelmed with threats, many online. It states that continued opposition by Mid Valley School District holds up Olyphant's $101 million A.I. data center settlement. It reports that Lackawanna County rescinded the tax abatement on the proposed Olyphant A.I. data center site after the council approved the settlement.

The roundup states that the Morning Call reported a proposed 2.1 GW A.I. data center in Upper Mount Bethel Twp. would create what was called an infrastructure problem of biblical proportions in Northampton County. It reports that PennLive said a second major A.I. data center proposal is moving forward in Swatara Twp. despite utility and pollution concerns from neighbors in Dauphin County, and that no hearings were held on the proposals. It states that PennLive reported a $120.3 million community benefits agreement from an A.I. data center developer promises Swatara Twp. and Dauphin County, and the township held no hearings or comment period on the agreements. It reports that PennLive said a proposed A.I. data center complex in Monroe Twp., Cumberland County, is now dead after strong public opposition. It states that the Pittsburgh Business Times reported the first two of seven natural gas electric generation turbines were set up at the Homer City A.I. data center and power plant complex in Indiana County.

The roundup states that DEP was reminded to hold a meeting and hearing on November 23 on the proposed Project Atlas A.I. data center in South Whitehall Twp., Lehigh County. It reports that DEP posted 38 pages of permit-related notices in the November 14 PA Bulletin and 45 pages in the November 21 PA Bulletin. It states that DEP was reminded to hold a November 18 hearing on the Mid-Atlantic Transmission Line water quality permit in Pike County and a November 20 hearing on the PPL water quality permit for the Stanton Summit Transmission Line Project in Lackawanna County. It reports that the Scranton Times said DEP would hold a hearing that day in Scranton on the PPL Electric Transmission Line Project in Lackawanna and Luzerne counties. It states that the roundup lists Pennsylvania data center hearings and meetings from Physicians for Social Responsibility PA.

stories.Headline: Six FLORetina-ICOOR 2026 courses follow AI through retinal imaging, trials, atrophy care and robotic surgery
stories.Summary:
The FLORetina International Congress on OCT Angiography, En Face OCT, and Advances in OCT (FLORetina-ICOOR) will run December 3 to 6 at the Fortezza da Basso in Florence, the articles state. The course listings published so far include 2 courses tagged AI and 4 more under an AI and robotics heading. Six instructional courses at this year's congress follow artificial intelligence through retinal imaging, drug development, geographic atrophy care, and robotic surgery. At last year's meeting, much of the discussion was about what algorithms could do. The 2026 courses spend more time on how to use AI tools in practice, including how to validate them, put them into clinic workflows, build them into trial endpoints, and explain them to patients.

The course "Pearls and Pitfalls of Artificial Intelligence for Retinal Research and Practice" is co-chaired by Daniela Ferrara, MD, PhD, FASRS, and Usha Chakravarthy, MD, PhD, and co-moderated by Giovanni Staurenghi, MD. Stela Vujosevic, MD, PhD, FEBO, will speak on OCT-based algorithms and Daniel Ting, MD, PhD, on color fundus photography. Pearse Keane, MD, FRCOphth, will discuss oculomics, the use of retinal imaging as a window to systemic health. Valeria De Filippis, MD, PhD, will cover AI-based mining of electronic medical records, and Nadia Waheed will address AI in retinal research and clinical trials. Lajos Csincsik will discuss validation approaches for clinical imaging algorithms, and the course description names multimodal and agentic AI as emerging approaches.

A second Ferrara-led course, co-chaired with Waheed, is titled "Artificial Intelligence for Clinical Trials in Retinal Diseases: From Imaging Biomarkers to Digital Twins." Its description says AI is becoming a mandatory technology in drug development for retinal diseases. The talks include imaging biomarkers as trial endpoints (Waheed), treatment response prediction in exudative macular disease (Virginia Mares, MD, MSc, PhD), and GA progression prediction (Oliver Leingang, PhD). Ferrara will present on AI-enabled digital twins, Hrvoje Bogunovic, PhD, on external control arms and real-world data, and Marion Munk, MD, PhD, on the move toward fully digital, in silico trials. According to the organizers, digital twins could make synthetic control arms possible, especially in early-phase trials, and barriers include data standards, governance, cybersecurity, and regulatory frameworks they describe as outdated.

Anat Loewenstein, MD, MHA, who discussed home OCT monitoring at FLORetina 2025, will cover AI-enabled home OCT monitoring in clinical trials. That talk comes as home-based platforms such as Notal Vision's SCANLY, which received FDA De Novo authorization in 2024, move into research use. SAIVO was founded in May 2025 and ran its first course at FLORetina last year. Its 2026 symposium, "Implementing AI in retina and posterior segment diseases: triumphs and challenges," is again moderated by founding members Munk and Quan Dong Nguyen. Mario Romano, MD, PhD, will discuss lessons from Vision Code 2026, and Niranjan Manoharan, MD, will present an imaging-integrated prescreening pipeline for GA trial recruitment.

Roomasa Channa, MD, will describe putting an automated GA area algorithm into clinical workflows, and Rita Wolf, MD, will report on validation and outcomes of autonomous AI-based retinopathy screening in children. Talks cover AI quantification of hyperreflective vitreous particles in uveitis, human-in-the-loop triage of choroidal lesions for possible melanoma on ultra-widefield imaging, and foundation models for external-eye imaging in oculoplastics. The symposium closes with Mary K. Daly, MD, "Informed Consent for AI in an Epistemic Void." "AI in Clinical Practice: A Practical Patient-Centered Roadmap for Geographic Atrophy Management," organized by Roy Schwartz, MD, and Caroline Baumal, MD, follows the GA care pathway in 5 steps. The steps are differential diagnosis against genetic mimics (Dinah Zur, MD), AI-based risk stratification (Gregor Reiter, MD, MSc, PhD), measuring and monitoring from baseline to treatment response (Aude Ambresin, MD, PhD), functional monitoring (Baumal), and predicting individual patient trajectories (Schwartz).

Omer Trivizki, MD, MBA, closes the course with a look at future needs, and the organizers promise live demonstrations and real-world cases. The United States now has 2 approved GA therapies, but specialists have pointed out that AI-driven imaging analysis for GA has not been cleared for routine US clinical practice, while some such tools are already used in Europe. Ophthalmology Times has also reported on investigational AI tools, such as functional OCT, that aim to estimate retinal sensitivity from structural scans, and those tools have not yet been cleared by regulators. "Artificial Intelligence in Vitreoretinal Surgery: A crash course," organized by Rodrigo Anguita Henriquez, MD, and Martin Zinkernagel, MD, PhD, is written for surgeons who say they lack practical AI training. It starts with the basics of machine learning and neural networks (Philippe Valmaggia, MD) and asks whether no-code AI is ready for clinicians (Lorenzo Ferro Desideri, MD).

It then covers proliferative diabetic retinopathy (Aude Couturier, MD), predictive modeling (Zinkernagel), and real-time computer vision for intraoperative guidance, presented by congress president Stanislao Rizzo, MD. Anguita Henriquez, MD, MBBS ends with "From generative to agentic AI: the road to surgical intelligence." "Robotics, AI and the Future of Eye Surgery," organized by Jean-Pierre Hubschman, MD, may be the most forward-looking session of the meeting. Fanny Nerinckx, MD, will present first-in-human experience with the Luca robotic system. In 2024, Luca was used to perform 7 vitrectomies at Ghent University Hospital in Belgium, and the company reported no device-related adverse events. Nerinckx has said the platform operates with 20 times less tremor than a human hand.

Other speakers include Marc de Smet, MD, CM, PhD, BSc(hon), FARVO, FRCSC, FRCOphth, FEBOphth, FMH, on moving robotic platforms from the lab to the operating room, Khalid Al Sabti on building a new robotic system, Rodolfo Mastropasqua, MD, PhD, FEBO, on intraoperative OCT and robotic automation, and Aya Barzelay Wollman, MD, PhD, on machine learning in robotic instruments. Steven Schwartz will address barriers to adoption. The course ends with a panel whose title asks the question many surgeons and administrators will have: "Is robotic eye surgery ready, and who will pay for it?" Across all 6 courses, the faculty seem less interested in whether AI works than in what it takes to deploy it responsibly. That means validation across devices and populations, workflow integration, regulatory pathways, reimbursement, and patient consent. Ophthalmology Times will be on site in Florence to cover the AI sessions and the rest of the FLORetina-ICOOR 2026 program.

stories.Headline: Apple builds its M5 Pro, Max and Ultra chips from three dies in a first true chiplet design
stories.Summary:
SemiAnalysis published a teardown on 20 November 2026 finding that Apple's M5 Pro, M5 Max and M5 Ultra are the company's first true chiplet design, built from three separate dies. The analysis rests on physical inspection rather than vendor briefings, because SemiAnalysis bought the chips and had them torn down. The speaker walks through die sizes, core counts, cache allocations and PHY structures measured from the silicon. The M5 Ultra fuses two M5 Max dual-die assemblies with a connection density Apple claims is more than 6x that of the M3 Ultra's UltraFusion. The lab had not yet obtained an M5 Ultra, so its layout is inferred from the M5 Max's second interconnect and Apple's own marketing claims.

Apple taped out three dies, one CPU die and two GPU dies, a small and a large one, all fabricated on TSMC's N3P process. The CPU chiplet is roughly 168 mm², the small GPU chiplet about 157 mm² and the large GPU chiplet about 300 mm². The M5 Pro pairs the CPU chiplet with the small GPU chiplet, the M5 Max pairs it with the large GPU chiplet, and the M5 Ultra uses two CPU chiplets and two large GPU chiplets. The CPU die carries 18 cores in three clusters, four Thunderbolt 5 PHYs and no E-cores, and the GPU chiplets scale cleanly at 2:1, the large one with 40 GPU cores, 48 MB of System Level Cache and a 512-bit memory interface.

The speaker draws a firm line between Apple's earlier multi-die chips and the M5 generation, saying the M1, M2 and M3 Ultra fused two of the largest dies of a generation in a classic multi-chip-module arrangement. He defines a true chiplet architecture by two design targets, optimizing the area of each individual die to improve yield and outsourcing different functions of the SoC onto different chiplets so the final product only works once at least two different chiplets are combined. He acknowledges the definition is contestable, saying everyone is entitled to their own chiplet based opinion, but states it as his position. He calls the GPU chiplets interesting and a bit boring at the same time, because the halving is so exact that the small die reads as a straightforward cut of the large one. He flags the four Thunderbolt 5 PHYs as the standout by area, saying it is crazy to see how big analogue SerDes are becoming and how much space the command-and-control area is taking up.

The speaker says the new interconnect uses TSMC's SoIC-mH, called SoIC-X F2F by TSMC, the same hybrid bonding technology behind AMD's 3D V-Cache but deployed side-by-side rather than stacked, with mH standing for molding horizontally. Standard advanced packaging attaches finished dies to an interposer through microbumps around 25 µm and perhaps down to 18 µm, while hybrid bonding aligns matching exposed copper interconnects surrounded by dielectric and heats them so the copper fuses directly. He describes the result as almost like fusing the metal layers, creating one large coherent chip, and says the pitch drops below 10 µm and approaches 3 µm in the most advanced processes. He says placing the chiplets side by side rather than stacked avoids the thermal problems of a vertical sandwich, citing the A20 Pro's move to WMCM packaging with DRAM moved to the side of the SoC. He says Apple had access to hybrid bonding for some time, as other TSMC customers did, but waited for the side-by-side implementation, and that it is not unlikely Apple worked on the solution with TSMC directly.

The speaker says the last UltraFusion chip, the M3 Ultra, used InFO-LSI packaging with a local silicon interconnect and solder-based microbumps, and that Apple never published the bump pitch but measurements show 25 µm. He says a 6x density increase implies a pitch of about 10 µm or less, squarely in hybrid bonding territory and impossible with solder. He says the left side of the CPU die holds the classic 16-core Neural Engine of eight dual-cores, which he notes has since been doubled on the M6, and that only the M5 Ultra gets double the NPU because it uses two CPU chiplets. He says the twelve new P-cores, internally called M-cores, are split into two mirrored six-core clusters each with 8 MB of shared cache and a dedicated AMX unit, and suggests the split may be for power management so an entire cluster can be shut off. He says the S-core cluster is slightly asymmetrical with two S-cores on top and four below a 16 MB shared cache, each S-core getting a 1 MB slice of L2 cache.

The speaker says the CPU die is larger than a base M5 and that the small GPU die is essentially a cut-in-half version of the large one, which he suggests helps with development time. He says the bottom shoreline of the CPU die is a large IO array running from left to right through an Apple proprietary high-speed PHY for cameras and other sensors, a 4-lane Display PHY and 16 lanes of PCI-Express, most likely Gen 5, arranged in four 2x2 clusters. He says the die also includes an on-die NAND controller and an AES engine in the secure enclave, and that four large Display Engines sit to the right of the M-cores. He says only some media acceleration logic near the die-to-die interface stays the same size across both GPU chiplets. He says the faint striped structure on the CPU die's upper shoreline is the physical layer of the new die-to-die interconnect and matches an identical PHY on the adjacent shoreline of either GPU die.

The speaker's verdict is that hybrid bonding materially improves the M5 series rather than serving as a label, and he closes with the aside, Can't innovate anymore my ass. The open item to track is the M5 Ultra itself, whose configuration is derived from the M5 Max's second interconnect and Apple's density claim, not from a teardown, so the first physical analysis of that part will either confirm the two-Max construction or complicate it. The other thread worth watching is whether side-by-side hybrid bonding spreads to other Apple products, given the company's apparent shift toward thermal-conscious packaging across the A20 Pro and M5 lines. The articles give no date for when the M5 chips shipped or when the M5 Ultra will be torn down. The articles give no statement from Apple beyond its marketing claim on connection density.

The procurement involves the use of hybrid bonding systems to enhance the performance of high-bandwidth memory chips. This technical shift requires the integration of specialized machinery from Besi to achieve higher efficiency in chip stacking. The move is designed to support the development of advanced packaging solutions for the evolving semiconductor market. These tools will allow the company to push the boundaries of memory density and speed.

The report indicates that SK Hynix is taking these steps to maintain its leadership in the high-bandwidth memory sector. While the company has not issued a formal public statement in the provided text, the move suggests a commitment to superior hardware. The acquisition of Besi equipment is seen as a way to outpace other manufacturers in the region. stories.Headline: Amit Govrin develops a framework to measure organizational control over sovereign AI
stories.Summary:
Amit Govrin developed a practical framework to measure organizational control over sovereign AI, data, and local risk. This work was featured in Breaking Analysis episode 334 on November 21, 2026. The framework evaluates documented controls across various hyperscaler offerings and different buyer territories. It aims to help firms in regulated industries manage jurisdictional, operating, and commercial risks. The project includes a buyer's guide, a study with Qualitate, and a conversation with John Furrier.

The framework uses five pillars called territorial, legal, operational, technical, and financial to assess vendors. It includes seventeen yes-or-no tests across four nonlegal dimensions and a separate legal evaluation. A November 14 revision index gave Google LLC a top score of 3.45 across all regions. Oracle Corp. followed with 3.25, while IBM Corp. and Microsoft Corp. Azure both scored 3.0. AWS scored 2.7, and Huawei Technologies Co. Ltd. and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. scored 1.2.

Amit Govrin stated that there is a gap between the priorities of buyers and their operational reality. He noted that many respondents have not tested disconnected systems, key-revocation, or exit scenarios. Govrin believes that sovereignty is not a purity test but requires deliberate risk decisions and compensating controls. He recommends that organizations make sovereignty evaluations at the workload level for core business processes. He suggests obtaining proof that controls work in a safe sandbox before moving into production.

Eleven senior technology decision-makers in regulated and critical-infrastructure organizations participated in the commissioned study. Nine of these respondents require AI inference to happen inside a sovereign or regional boundary. A European buyer noted that deep technical support escalations can involve personnel or systems outside the EU. A South American bank executive called the absence of operational testing the weakest point of their story. One Latin American financial-services buyer stated that calling a U.S. endpoint means the system is not sovereign.

The articles explain that U.S. companies supply most cloud and frontier artificial intelligence technology used by enterprises. The U.S. CLOUD Act allows vendors under U.S. jurisdiction to produce data regardless of where it is stored. Seven of eleven buyers believe that having a locally incorporated subsidiary does not fully clarify local jurisdiction. Many buyers add controls to existing platforms because of the cost and burden of new environments. Some customers are waiting for clearer sovereign-specific mandates or enforcement guidelines from their local governments.

Next, buyers should assess their sovereign exposure similarly to how they manage cybersecurity risks. They must trace the end-to-end request cycle from the prompt to the outputs and logs. Organizations should compare self-hosted open-weight model architectures with approved frontier services for sensitive workflows. Major changes to models, services, or contracts should trigger a new assessment of the architecture. The articles leave open how specific local governments will eventually mandate or enforce these sovereignty guidelines.

Articles.Title: Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement

stories.Headline: Alton partners with XUP to build autonomous robots using AI and hardware manufacturing
stories.Summary:
The smart mobility company Alton announced a new partnership with the AI autonomous driving robotics startup XUP on November 20, 2026. This collaboration follows a signing ceremony held on November 19 between Alton CEO Kim Shin-sung and XUP CEO Lee Yong-su. The two companies intend to combine hardware manufacturing capabilities with autonomous driving software to create self-driving robots. They aim to lay the necessary groundwork to commercialize these robots for the general market. The agreement requires Alton to provide structural design support and manage the procurement of production components for the robots.

Alton will also offer its manufacturing capacity to help XUP move its autonomous designs into full-scale production. XUP brings specialized technology including vision AI, lidar, inertial measurement units, and RTK-GNSS-based precision positioning. The startup has already created autonomous driving algorithms for unstructured outdoor environments and is building a control platform with a major domestic telecommunications carrier. An official from Alton stated that their experience in sourcing and mass production for electric bicycles provides a core competitive strength. This expertise allows the company to extend its capabilities into various next-generation smart mobility fields, including AI robotics.

The company intends to continue seeking business cooperation with innovative firms through the open innovation program of its parent company, Innox. This move is part of a broader strategy to diversify the business portfolio of Alton into the robotics sector. The company previously reviewed a waste battery recycling business in August as it looked for new growth opportunities. Alton plans to apply network connectivity technology from its shared electric bicycles to these new AI robots. The partnership will pair Alton's network integration and hardware skills with the precision perception and control technologies developed by XUP.

stories.Headline: Anthropic courts theologians as priest Kevin Deal rejects the idea of a machine soul
stories.Summary:
Religious leaders from across San Francisco gathered behind closed doors last month to discuss being human in the age of artificial intelligence. The AI company Anthropic has been courting theologians, rabbis, and priests to explore the nature of consciousness in machines. Billionaire cofounder Christopher Olah has pressed advisers at the Vatican to consider if his company's chatbot might possess a soul. Reverend Kevin Deal, a priest at St John the Evangelist Episcopal church, finds this pursuit of machine consciousness deeply troubling. He believes that the effort to establish whether a machine has a soul reveals a misunderstanding of humanity.

The pursuit involves asking religious leaders if AI creations possess consciousness or how they might be taught to be good. Researchers at Anthropic have reportedly considered teaching their AI models the practice of confession, which requires confronting harm and seeking forgiveness. This search for spirituality occurs while the company operates only a couple of miles from the parish of Reverend Kevin Deal. The development of AI requires enormous concentrations of capital, infrastructure, and the accumulated intelligence of all humanity. These models are driven by sociopolitical fear, the pursuit of profit, and the hope for a better world.

Reverend Kevin Deal says that AI could never replicate the transcendent mundanity of humans because it lacks a divine spark. He argues that goodness cannot be reduced to a set of behaviors, nor can the human soul be replicated by machines. Deal suggests that tech billionaires should lean into ancient practices, attend mass, pray daily, and read the scriptures. He believes that human worth is not rooted in production and that minds were not created to be quarried for profit. He states that the great moral question is whether builders treat humanity as something more than machines.

The author notes that Silicon Valley seems comfortable treating actual human beings as little more than instruments of production. He mentions that workers whose livelihoods are being transformed and poor neighbors are affected by the decisions made in boardrooms. Deal argues that AI is formed as pure utility and is cast aside if a model does not make a return. He claims that the economic system increasingly measures the worth of everything solely by its productivity. This focus on utility contrasts with the human experience of beauty and the ability to sit with mysteries.

The articles explain that humans are nurtured by caregivers and experience a life of mistakes, vows, and everyday humdrum tasks. AI is described as an ongoing economic choice that exists within a system focused on productivity and commercial utility. The text notes that the traditions being consulted by tech founders have spent millennia teaching that the soul is ineffable. Christianity is highlighted as a faith where confession demands a strive to change how one lives after causing harm. The background provided suggests a conflict between the spiritual nature of humanity and the mechanical nature of AI.

The priest suggests that tech leaders should carry the teachings of justice and mercy back to their offices and boardrooms. He encourages them to stop trying to be effective and instead strive to be good to reflect God's light. The articles leave open whether Christopher Olah and Anthropic will change their approach to developing conscious AI models. It remains unclear if Vatican advisers will ever accept the possibility that a chatbot possesses a soul or consciousness. The text does not state if the religious leaders in San Francisco reached a consensus during their closed meeting.

stories.Headline: SK hynix earns SIL 3 certification for its LPDDR5X memory and development processes
stories.Summary:
SK hynix said on Nov. 11 that its LPDDR5X product and its development processes had received Safety Integrity Level 3 certification under IEC 61508, an international standard written to reduce accident risks from failures in electrical and electronic systems. The certification, announced in a report dated Nov. 13 by The Elec, extends the low-power DRAM from vehicles into robots and smart factories. The company had already obtained automotive functional safety certification in January. IEC 61508 defines four safety integrity levels, running from SIL 1 up to SIL 4, and SK hynix's chip was designed and validated to hold safety conditions in real time without interrupting system operations.

The certification lets SK hynix answer functional safety requirements from customers building real-time robotic control platforms and systems-on-chip. Earlier, the company obtained Automotive Safety Integrity Level D, the highest rating under the ISO 26262 automotive functional safety standard, for the same LPDDR5X product. SK hynix also received certification under ISO/SAE 21434 for its cybersecurity management system, which covers threat analysis, security design and verification, and vulnerability management during development and mass production of automotive memory. The article says data security has grown more important as memory is deployed in physical AI systems, because autonomous vehicles and robots act on sensor data and AI results stored in memory.

Kim Jong-hwan, vice president and head of DRAM Development at SK hynix, said that as the physical AI market takes shape it is becoming increasingly important to establish safety and security systems that comply with international standards throughout the memory development process. He said the company will strengthen its memory leadership in the physical AI market by building on safety and security capabilities validated across the automotive and industrial sectors. The article states that if cyberattacks manipulate stored data, vehicles could fail to detect obstacles and brake, while robots could move in the wrong direction and potentially cause accidents. The report does not say what SK hynix plans to do next beyond using the certification to meet customer requirements.

stories.Headline: Samsung promotes three semiconductor executives to president and keeps its dual-CEO structure
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics announced on Nov. 20 its regular executive reshuffle for 2027, involving six appointments: three promotions to president and three changes in responsibilities, about a week earlier than the late-November timing the company had followed over the previous two years. The company retained its dual-CEO structure, with Vice Chairman Jun Young-hyun, head of the Device Solutions Division, and President Roh Tae-moon, head of the Device eXperience Division, remaining in their current roles. Both men will step down from their concurrent roles as heads of the Memory Business and the Mobile eXperience Business, respectively. Samsung reported consolidated operating profit of 107.4 trillion won in the third quarter, with the DS Division contributing 106.5 trillion won, or approximately $79.67 billion.

The centerpiece of the reshuffle is the promotion of three semiconductor executives who have helped strengthen the division's technological competitiveness. Hwang Sang-joon, who served as head of Memory Development and the DRAM Development Office, has been promoted to president and appointed head of the Memory Business, and he will continue to lead the DRAM Development Office alongside his new role. Cho Sang-yeon, previously a vice president overseeing Device Solutions America, has been promoted to president and appointed head of the System LSI Business, and he is expected to focus on securing new clients. Lee Jong-myeong, previously head of Process Development at the DS Division's Semiconductor Research Institute, has also been promoted to president and will serve as the DS Division's chief technology officer and head of the institute.

Jun will focus on strengthening the competitiveness of future semiconductor businesses, including foundry, in his capacity as head of the DS Division, while Roh will concentrate on developing new businesses, including robotics, while continuing as head of the DX Division and the RX Business Development Office. Choi Won-joon, previously head of the MX Business Development Office, has been appointed the new head of the MX Business, and he has served as the division's chief operating officer since March 2025 and led the development of the Galaxy S26 and Galaxy Z Fold8. Samsung said the appointments were intended to strengthen organizational dynamism and promote generational renewal by placing executives who had driven record semiconductor performance and improved development competitiveness in key leadership positions. The company also plans to finalize and announce regular executive appointments at the vice president level and below, along with an organizational restructuring, in the near future, and it will continue its policy of promoting outstanding employees through appointments throughout the year.

stories.Headline: TSMC restricts advanced chip manufacturing for Chinese designers to comply with new US rules
stories.Summary:
Taiwan's TSMC tightened restrictions on Chinese chip designers around November 19, 2026, by suspending some previously permitted advanced manufacturing orders for those customers. The world's largest contract chipmaker limited affected clients to older technology after new US Commerce Department rules took effect on Thursday. These measures close a remaining route for Chinese firms to produce powerful AI processors, which complicates Beijing's domestic chip development efforts. The company halted orders using manufacturing processes of 16 nanometres and below unless the customers could obtain US export licences. This action follows reports that TSMC and South Korea's Samsung Electronics suspended some chip shipments to Chinese customers on Thursday.

Affected Chinese designers are generally limited to 28-nanometre and 40-nanometre processes, provided they avoid advanced packaging and high-bandwidth memory. The new US rules remove a compliance route that previously allowed some Chinese companies to access advanced manufacturing without individual licences. TSMC can no longer use its verification process to check if certain Chinese chip designs fall outside of US export controls. Advanced chips are now presumed to be covered by US controls, requiring export licences unless a specific exception or exemption applies. These rules reach beyond AI processors and apply to various advanced manufacturing services provided to mainland Chinese firms and designers.

TSMC stated that it will comply with the new US export rules that strip Chinese chip designers of a key exemption. The company instructed that advanced orders be halted and issued guidance requiring closer scrutiny of customers' operating locations and parent companies. TSMC will now check major shareholders, packaging providers, and shipping routes to ensure full compliance with the updated US government regulations. These checks extend to orders placed through intermediaries or overseas subsidiaries located in Taiwan, the United States, Europe, Japan, and Southeast Asia. The company is implementing these strict verification steps to align with the new requirements set by the US Commerce Department.

Chinese technology giants and independent chip designers developing alternatives to Nvidia processors are particularly affected by these new manufacturing restrictions. Most leading AI chips require 7-nanometre processes or smaller for energy efficiency, while high-bandwidth memory handles the vast data volumes. Advanced packaging is also critical because it integrates chips and memory to boost computing power for complex artificial intelligence applications. A US government list of approved chip designers includes Apple, AMD, Nvidia, and Taiwanese firms MediaTek and Realtek, excluding Chinese firms. Some Chinese AI chip designers had access to 7-nanometre technology before Thursday, though Reuters could not independently verify those specific arrangements.

The background involves China's ambition to develop domestic alternatives to AI chips designed by Nvidia and manufactured by the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. Previously, TSMC could verify the technical characteristics and computing power of certain designs to determine if they fell outside US controls. This verification process served as a loophole that allowed some Chinese designers to access advanced services without needing individual export licences. The US government maintains a list of approved designers to control who can access the most advanced semiconductor manufacturing technology. These geopolitical tensions have led to increasing restrictions on the export of high-end computing hardware to mainland Chinese technology companies.

TSMC will continue to monitor the operating locations and shipping routes of its customers to prevent the evasion of US rules. The company will maintain the suspension of advanced manufacturing orders for Chinese clients who lack the necessary US government export licences. The articles leave open whether Chinese firms will find other ways to produce chips or if other foundries will follow. It remains unclear how many Chinese designers were using the 7-nanometre process before the new rules took effect on Thursday. The reports do not specify if the US government will grant any new exceptions to the affected mainland Chinese firms.

stories.Headline: US and China agree to create joint guardrails for superintelligence
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump held a White House news conference on Friday to review his recent trip to Asia. He discussed his productive meeting with President Xi Jinping on Thursday and his arrival at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport on Wednesday afternoon. The visit included the first trilateral summit between the United States, China, and Russia, which took place on Thursday afternoon. This historic meeting occurred on the sidelines of the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen.

The three leaders issued the China-Russia-US Heads of State Declaration toward Peace to prevent nuclear war and reduce nuclear risks. The United States and China also agreed to create joint guardrails for superintelligence to ensure the technology remains under human control. Trump mentioned that he is considering a comprehensive deal with China, though he did not provide specific details regarding chip export restrictions. China's Foreign Ministry stated that both nations will implement an action plan to build a relationship based on respect, fairness, and reciprocity.

President Trump praised his great relationship with President Xi and expressed deep respect for the immaculate development of Shenzhen. He described the city as a clean and flawless modern center that grew from a small fishing village. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC that the two leaders agreed humans must always make military decisions rather than allowing AI to act autonomously. President Xi emphasized the need for strong communication and coordination to prevent security risks associated with artificial intelligence.

stories.Headline: Researchers propose a four-stage framework to evaluate AI outbreak alerts in conflict-affected health systems
stories.Summary:
A mini review published in Frontiers in Public Health evaluated infectious disease surveillance in conflict-affected health systems and proposed a four-stage conceptual evaluation framework for artificial intelligence early-warning tools. The authors synthesized evidence on artificial intelligence early-warning tools alongside operational experiences from conventional humanitarian disease surveillance programmes. The review was reported by bioengineer.org on November 21, 2026. The authors found that faster predictive performance from artificial intelligence does not necessarily translate into timely or equitable public health action. The framework was designed to assess data readiness, alert performance, verification and decision-making, and public health action and equity.

The review's structured literature search in Scopus covered publications released from January 2015 through October 2026. In Southwest Cameroon, routine integrated disease surveillance and response systems achieved timely reporting for cholera in only 16.3 percent of instances during intense conflict, compared to 40.7 percent during periods of reduced conflict intensity. In Borno State, Nigeria, a conventional Early Warning, Alert and Response System produced 13,737 alerts, yet only 16 required an immediate operational response after verification. Of those 13,737 alerts, 89.6 percent were verified within 24 hours, and subsequent investigations led to 9,794 alerts being discarded, 2,501 placed under monitoring, and exactly 16 prompting an active response. An evaluation of a temporal data augmentation approach for outbreak detection in humanitarian settings demonstrated a sensitivity of 0.72 alongside an annual false-alert burden of approximately 2.8 to 3.6 false alerts per local government area across temporal folds.

The authors emphasized that direct empirical evidence linking artificial intelligence outbreak warnings to improved clinical or health outcomes in crisis settings remains limited. They argued that early predictive detection cannot be treated as an established causal driver of reduced morbidity or mortality. The researchers differentiated between reporting delays and data completeness, noting that an empty surveillance registry entry can signify absent disease, an unsubmitted report, a non-operational medical facility, or a severed communications link. They stressed that assessing models retrospectively on finalized, cleaned datasets artificially inflates performance metrics, obscuring the operational reality of provisional, delayed, and noisy incoming data. The researchers argued that evaluations must systematically track verification time, documentation of rationales, and the availability of diagnostic testing, ensuring that resources are not consumed by false-alarm investigations that overwhelm local clinical teams.

The review cited contextual findings from Yemen demonstrating persistent diagnostic, transport, and governance hurdles that constrain outbreak verification during acute humanitarian emergencies. In Sudan, conflict-related disruptions to malaria reporting created difficulties in interpreting longitudinal disease indicators because facility registries were outdated. Evaluations of Somalia's electronic Early Warning and Response Network demonstrated continuous reporting challenges, showing that failing to account for missingness risks training models that identify shifts in reporting logistics rather than genuine changes in transmission dynamics. Research across Ugandan refugee settlements and broader refugee surveillance networks revealed parallel databases, fragmented reporting streams, and substantial coverage gaps, while findings from Lebanon showed difficulties in tracking refugee health when national registries do not disaggregate vulnerable cohorts. The review noted that an artificial intelligence model may produce swift, confident alerts for well-resourced, densely monitored populations while generating weak or absent signals for marginalized groups.

The review noted that reporting delays are not unique to war zones, observing that routine surveillance programs in Indonesia and Uganda have also encountered challenges in satisfying established timeliness benchmarks. Surveillance timelines encompass several distinct stages, including the delay from symptom onset to care-seeking, care-seeking to clinic registration, registration to transmission, and final report transmission to analytical data availability. The authors outlined methodological priorities including shadow-mode prospective evaluations, where model predictions run in parallel with existing surveillance workflows without directing operational resources. Implementation research must also investigate governance structures, clear chains of accountability, human oversight, and whether complex machine-learning algorithms offer verifiable operational advantages over simpler hybrid models combining standard indicators with local knowledge. A primary limitation of the mini review is its focused narrative scope, which did not attempt an exhaustive systematic assessment across all existing surveillance literature.

The analyzed studies exhibited substantial heterogeneity in disease targets, population demographics, epidemiological outcomes, and evaluation protocols, preventing direct statistical comparison. Direct empirical evidence linking artificial intelligence outbreak warnings to improved clinical outcomes in conflict-affected regions remains scarce, and findings from conventional humanitarian surveillance programmes provide contextual insight rather than direct measures of machine-learning effectiveness. The proposed four-stage evaluation framework remains conceptual and requires prospective empirical validation across diverse epidemiological settings before its causal assumptions can be established. The review concluded that the public health value of artificial intelligence in conflict-affected outbreak surveillance cannot be measured solely by mathematical accuracy or prediction speed. Prospective evaluations tracking the full pathway from data readiness to intervention delivery are necessary to ensure that digital surveillance technologies serve vulnerable populations rather than exacerbating existing health inequities.

stories.Headline: Uzbekistan cybersecurity official Bekzod Muminov urges UN, UNESCO and ITU to lead global AI dialogue
stories.Summary:
Bekzod Muminov spoke at the second International Conference on Cyber Diplomacy on 19 November 2026. He is the Head of the International Relations Department of Uzbekistan's Cybersecurity Center State Unitary Enterprise. Muminov discussed the role of artificial intelligence during panel discussions at the event. He addressed how this technology affects governments and international relations. The official highlighted both the benefits and the risks of these tools.

Muminov stated that the UN, UNESCO, and the International Telecommunication Union should lead the international dialogue. He noted that nations currently have different approaches to regulation, data protection, and technological standards. He also mentioned that countries differ in their access to computing resources. These differences could lead to isolated technological ecosystems if they are not addressed. Such isolation might restrict the exchange of innovation, knowledge, and technology.

Muminov said that artificial intelligence helps governments process large volumes of information and analyze international developments. He claimed it allows for better assessment of economic risks and political risks. He also stated that the technology can improve diplomatic communication. However, he warned that it creates challenges regarding disinformation and information reliability. He noted that it can lead to cyber threats and the manipulation of public opinion.

The official argued that diplomacy must go beyond discussing technological issues to shape international rules. He believes this approach can build trust and prevent new forms of geopolitical tension. Muminov wants the development of artificial intelligence to strengthen cooperation between nations. He believes it should not become a new instrument for technological competition. He views these processes as an opportunity to strengthen positions in the international system.

The articles explain that artificial intelligence enables faster analysis of global developments for various governments. This technology is being integrated into diplomatic efforts to manage risks and communication. The current landscape is marked by a lack of unified global standards for AI. Multilateral platforms are seen as necessary to represent the interests of the international community. These platforms would provide a balanced approach to global technological governance.

The articles do not state what specific actions the UN or ITU will take next. They leave open how nations will resolve their differences regarding data protection and standards. It remains unclear if the international community will successfully prevent the rise of isolated ecosystems. The text does not specify a timeline for creating these new international rules. No further details are provided on the outcomes of the conference.

stories.Headline: Fear Erupts, AI Stocks Tank, but so Do Gold, Silver, Cryptos, Nearly Everything but Treasuries
stories.Summary:
Fear hit the markets on Friday, November 20, 2026, and during the week, and everything sold off, stocks, especially semiconductor stocks, gold, silver and crypto, everything except Treasury securities, which rallied. The Nasdaq fell 5.3% on Friday to 22,618, down 10.0% during the week, down 18.4% from its high on October 6, and down 2.7% since the beginning of 2026. The S&P 500 index fell 3.7% on Friday to 6,910, down 8.6% for the week and down 11.9% from its high in early October. Nvidia's stock plunged 14% on Friday to $125.53 at the close, down 47% from its high on October 6, and the seven-week plunge unwound all the gains since June 2024. The Cboe Volatility Index jumped to 40.03 intraday on Friday and ended the day at 35.89, after being below 20 a week earlier.

The Anthropic IPO seems to have sapped the last bit of energy out of the stock market, and its shares fell 8.5% during regular hours on Friday to $88.91, after falling through the IPO price of $85 a share during the day before recovering a bit. SanDisk fell 16.1% on Friday and was down 73% from its June high, Intel fell 8.0% and was down 64%, Micron fell 13.9% and was down 51%, Qualcomm fell 7.5% and was down 41%, Broadcom fell 12.2% and was down 37%, AMD fell 13.3% and was down 36% from its October high, and TSMC fell 9.5% and was down 35% from its October high. Silver plunged 7.4% on Friday to $41.08 per troy ounce, down 16% during the week and down 66% from its all-time high in late January, unwinding all the gains since July 2025. Gold dropped 4.0% on Friday to $3,539 per troy ounce, down 9% during the week and 37% from its all-time high, unwinding the gains since August 2025. Bitcoin dropped 14% this week to $58,761, where it had first been in March 2021, and since its peak in September 2025 it has dropped by over half.

Wolf Richter wrote in WOLF STREET that there was fear in the markets on Friday and also during the week, and that for months everyone has been talking about the end of the AI bubble. He wrote that the fear now is that it is not just idle talk anymore and that the pieces are starting to line up for all to see. He wrote that Nvidia was at the core of the AI trade and of all the circular financing, selling the shovels into the gold rush and charging more for them than its customers could afford. He wrote that to maintain its revenues, profits and stock price, Nvidia recycled these cash flows and added commitments to help fund its customers so they could afford its shovels at its sky-high prices. He wrote that this system already started unraveling a while ago and that the fear now is that it will unravel entirely.

Richter wrote that fears get exhausted after a while, the profit motive takes over, people jump back into the fray to pick up sold-off stuff, and then there is a bounce, and that there may have been enough fear on Friday to trigger that. He wrote that contrarians use a big jump in the VIX, which doubled this week, as a buy signal for at least a short-term bounce. He wrote that another indication was Friday's after-hours trading, with many beaten-down semiconductor stocks, including Nvidia, trading higher by 2% or 3% or more after hours. He wrote that even the 10-year Treasury yield, which had plunged during the day as Treasury prices jumped on the haven trade, reversed in late trading and headed higher. He wrote that "Nothing goes to heck in a straight line" is the old WOLF STREET dictum, and that we just might see a bounce in tech stocks next week along with some unwind of the massive Treasury rally.

Richter wrote that Nvidia's shares started tanking in early October even before everyone was crawling all over the company for the scandal of a lifetime that keeps spawning new scandals, and that the company is in the process of getting vivisected. He wrote that the x trillions in market value, portfolio value and 401(k) value that have evaporated during this selloff set everyone atwitter, and that on the way up those trillions appeared out of nothing and it was no big deal. He wrote that when a lot of it happens it impacts consumer spending and the economy overall. He wrote that other people have been waiting for this sell-off, cash in fist, to jump in and buy some beaten-up stuff, no matter how dubious, and that this is starting to line up. He wrote that the Nasdaq is still positive, if barely, year-over-year, and is not at the low of the year, which was in late March when it fell to 20,690 briefly before rallying massively again and setting a new high.

Richter wrote that the S&P 500 is still 1% in the green for the year and up 4.7% year-over-year. He wrote that the Nasdaq is down 2.7% since the beginning of 2026. He wrote that the semiconductor stocks had been plunging off their highs for months, interrupted by big bounces. He wrote that gold and silver had already gotten hammered for much of the year after the huge years-long rally topped off by a proper mania ended in late January. He wrote that bitcoin's drop to $58,761 marked six-and-a-half years of massive volatility to nowhere, with no interest and no dividends.

Richter wrote that we just might see that bounce in tech stocks next week, along with some unwind of the massive Treasury rally. He wrote that a dead-cat bounce allows the stock market to breathe. He wrote that fears get exhausted after a while and the profit motive takes over. He wrote that there may have been enough fear on Friday to trigger a bounce. The article leaves open where the selloff will end and whether any bounce would last.

Articles.Title: Fear Erupts, AI Stocks Tank, but so Do Gold, Silver, Cryptos, Nearly Everything but Treasuries

stories.Headline: Singapore fintechs outpace global peers in AI adoption rates
stories.Summary:
A report released on Wednesday, November 19, 2026, revealed that fintech companies in Singapore are leading the way in adopting artificial intelligence. This study was based on a survey of 100 fintech leaders and detailed interviews with 10 senior industry practitioners. The research team conducted their fieldwork between July and September 2026 to gather these findings. Most of these firms have already integrated the technology into their current business operations.

The data shows that 86 percent of Singapore fintechs have deployed AI, which is higher than the 65 percent rate for Singapore financial institutions. This adoption rate also exceeds the 62 percent reported for fintech companies on a global scale. Looking ahead, 94 percent of these local firms plan to increase their AI budgets in 2027. However, only 4 percent of the surveyed leaders identify new revenue generation as the primary benefit of the technology.

The Singapore FinTech Association, Airwallex, and Kapronasia were responsible for producing this comprehensive industry report. These organizations highlighted a significant gap between the widespread use of AI and its actual ability to drive business growth. They noted that while the technology is being implemented rapidly, it is not yet translating into substantial new income for most firms. The report suggests that the current focus remains on adoption rather than financial expansion.

stories.Headline: Nvidia leadership upheaval and Anthropic IPO prompt investors to weigh AI sector health as stocks fall
stories.Summary:
Stocks tumbled to end the week on Friday, November 20, 2026, as worries about artificial intelligence rattled the market, and by the closing bell all three major averages were deeply in the red. The Dow Jones industrial average fell more than 900 points on the day, while the Nasdaq dropped more than 5 percent and erased all of its gains for the year. The S&P 500 is now down more than 10 percent from its recent high, which means it is in what investors call correction territory. Investors were weighing the health of the AI sector following Nvidia's leadership upheaval and Anthropic's record IPO, according to the PBS News report.

The market move came as a second federal judge blocked President Trump's Memorial Arch in Washington, D.C., and the judge in Virginia called the project a rush job that lacks a legal basis. She put construction there on hold indefinitely, pending the outcome of legal challenges to the arch, after a separate judge earlier in the week extended a previous block for two more weeks. President Trump is trying to build a 250-foot Memorial Arch near Arlington National Cemetery, which has led to criticism from veterans groups and local environmentalists. In Iowa, a federal appeals court is blocking the U.S. Army from detonating several tons of bomb-making chemicals amid concerns over environmental and health risks, and the controlled explosion had been scheduled for that day.

The explosion was expected to send lead dust as far as 60 miles around the area, and Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle had agreed to postpone the detonation until Monday. Telle warned that a coming drop in temperatures could further destabilize the material, and it is unclear whether the court will weigh in again before Monday. In Florida, heavy storms are moving north after drenching parts of the Atlantic coast, and torrential rains turned roads into waterways, with some areas already seeing their wettest November on record. The National Hurricane Center is warning of severe widespread flash flooding for parts of Eastern Florida and says the threat could carry into next week, while in California heavy flooding left some neighborhoods in Los Angeles underwater.

In Poland, authorities say two Russian missiles and a suspected drone landed in Polish territory overnight, and CCTV footage in Southeastern Poland showed a large explosion and a bright flash. The crash site was around 20 miles from where European troops from 11 countries were taking part in rare military exercises to prepare for a potential postwar Ukraine mission. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the incursions an intentional provocation and said Poland, which neighbors both Ukraine and Russia, must be involved in future peace talks. Russia carried out new strikes on Ukraine overnight and into the day as part of its response to Kyiv's recent attacks on a strategic bridge, and authorities in Western Ukraine said a Russian attack on a railway station killed at least two people.

stories.Headline: AI stock prices plunge as cheap Chinese models undermine US revenue goals
stories.Summary:
Stock prices for artificial intelligence companies plunged over several weeks leading up to November 20, 2026. This collapse occurred because investors realized that companies like OpenAI and Anthropic likely cannot generate the trillion-plus dollars in annual revenue required for profitability. Revenue growth for these firms has slowed sharply since the second quarter of the year. This decline creates a serious problem because these companies must maintain huge double-digit growth to meet their computer leasing commitments through the end of the decade.

The crisis stems from the availability of cheap, open-weight models from Chinese companies, such as the Tencent Hunyuan Hy4 lineup. These Chinese models cost between 0.07 and 2.00 dollars per million input tokens and 0.28 to 6.00 dollars per million output tokens. In contrast, frontier models from U.S. firms charge between 2.00 and 8.00 dollars for input and 10.00 to 40.00 dollars for output. While OpenAI has the GPT6 Luna model and Anthropic offers Claude Haiku 5.5 at 50 cents per million output tokens, these low prices cannot generate hundreds of billions in revenue.

Dean Baker argues that the demand for expensive frontier AI is likely very limited because cheaper alternatives are sufficient for most users. He explains that selling AI at 50 cents per million output tokens would require an implausible volume of demand to reach 500 billion dollars in revenue. Baker suggests that the current plunge in AI-related stocks is a logical beginning to a necessary correction. He believes the business models of these trillion-dollar companies are fundamentally flawed because high-quality AI is available at roughly 1.0 percent of the frontier price.

Articles.Title: The Economics Behind the Collapse of the AI Bubble

stories.Headline: Jackson city launches an AI assistant that answers resident questions around the clock
stories.Summary:
Jackson residents can now get help from the city at any hour of the day, because a new AI tool on the city's website makes answers about city services available around the clock. The city of Jackson's new online AI Community Assistant offers guidance about departments, forms and procedures, according to WBBJ. The assistant uses Jackson's own ordinances and other city materials to help answer questions. The city says the assistant is still learning, and if it comes across a question it cannot yet answer, it will direct the person to a staff member for a response.

The tool is powered by GovWell, a technology platform built specifically for local government, the city said. The city encourages people to test out the tool and give feedback on their experience. Residents who spoke with WBBJ said they would still much rather talk to a human. One resident said a real person would definitely be better in their opinion, because at least you know you are talking to a real person, while talking to a machine could mean it was programmed to have anything in it. Another resident said they feel uncomfortable about AI and do not think it is a good thing right now, and that people their age and older just do not get into that.

The city of Jackson is responsible for the assistant, which draws on its ordinances and other city materials, and GovWell supplies the platform behind it. The city says the assistant is still learning and will send unanswered questions to a staff member. Residents who were interviewed said they would prefer a real person, and one said a real person may not know what they are talking about either, but at least you know you are talking to a real person. The city encourages people to test the tool and give feedback on their experience.

stories.Headline: The race to prove the Riemann Hypothesis just became a human-versus-AI showdown
stories.Summary:
Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said on Friday that he had solved the Riemann Hypothesis, the most famous open problem in mathematics, by working with the AI model Claude for weeks, and hours later Alessandro Masullo, a postdoctoral researcher at Stanford, announced that he had also solved the problem without using AI. Masullo said he had been working on the problem for 12 years and was about a year away from releasing his results when Alpöge's report caught him off guard. In a paper posted online, Masullo said he was being advised to release the current version as it is in light of the current climate, and he added that it may contain errors because it was rushed. In what the article describes as a thinly veiled slight against Alpöge, Masullo said human mathematicians still have a place in the age of AI and that they are still here, very much alive and not going anywhere.

The Riemann Hypothesis proposes a predicted distribution for how often prime numbers appear alongside other numbers, and proving it is a Millennium Prize Problem that earns a mathematician $1 million. The Navier-Stokes equations, which OpenAI has said it solved, are also in the Millennium Prize category. Masullo's solution is far shorter than Alpöge's, and it immediately sparked a further firestorm in a math community already reeling from the Anthropic paper and months of AI companies announcing high-profile solutions to long-standing math problems. Neither solution had been formally proven by Friday afternoon, and mathematicians are now racing to scrutinize both of them with their own brains and with AI.

Steven Strogatz, a math professor at Cornell, said on X on Friday that the plot thickens, and Sergei Gukov, a math professor at Caltech, told Business Insider that it is now getting more complicated. Gukov called the claim that the problem was solved a huge deal and said the Riemann Hypothesis was the biggest problem in math, using the past tense. Masullo, his partner at Stanford, Brian Conrad, and Alpöge did not respond to requests for comment on Friday. At stake is nothing less than the credibility of human mathematicians in the age of AI, and which solution is right will have grave implications for the future of mathematics.

Articles.Title: The race to prove the Riemann Hypothesis just became a human-versus-AI showdown

stories.Headline: AI stock sell-off erases all 2026 Nasdaq gains
stories.Summary:
A severe sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks caused the Nasdaq Composite to drop nearly 4% on Friday, November 20, 2026. This rapid decline erased all gains the index had made throughout 2026, including a peak of almost 19% recorded on October 6. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 also fell more than 10% from recent highs to enter correction territory. Market pressure reached its heaviest level since March, with the S&P Oscillator touching -8% during the Friday session.

The market turmoil requires investors to navigate significant volatility as Nvidia shares fell 12% following reports that U.S. securities regulators are probing its accounting. This decline follows the November 12 resignation of CEO Jensen Huang, which occurred after a November 8 board announcement regarding an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. Anthropic shares also tumbled 10% on their second trading day, falling from a Thursday close of $97.17 toward their $83 IPO price. Meanwhile, Alphabet remained flat as JPMorgan analysts maintained a buy-equivalent rating and a $375 price target for the company.

Jim Cramer noted that negative sentiment from the Nvidia scandal is likely spilling over into the broader artificial intelligence trade. JPMorgan analysts stated that Google is expanding consumer relationships in the agent era rather than ceding ground to competitors. They highlighted the frequent release of Gemini 4 models, including Gemini 4 Neon this week, Gemini 4 Carbon on October 28, and Gemini 4 Hydrogen on November 12. The analysts also noted that Google rebranded its agentic assistant to Tasks this week and expanded its access to free users in six countries.

Investors are now focusing on upcoming Federal Reserve commentary after Governor Christopher Waller suggested a possible 50-basis-point rate hike to fight inflation. John Williams is scheduled to speak next Monday at 4 p.m. ET, and market participants hope for a pragmatic approach to policy. Next week will also bring earnings reports from several companies, including Dell Technologies, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, and Zoom. stories.Headline: Trump threatens taxes and penalties for AI data centres built overseas
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump held a wide-ranging news conference at the White House on Friday, November 20, 2026, following a historic summit. During this event, he defended his personal relationship with Vladimir Putin and praised a first of its kind trilateral peace agreement. This momentous meeting involved the leaders of the United States, Russia, and China to discuss global issues. Trump highlighted the great electricity between the three nuclear powers and emphasized that these relationships keep the country safe.

The president warned that American technology companies will face tremendous taxes and penalties if they build artificial intelligence data centres overseas. He argued that such facilities must stay in the United States because China would otherwise take all of them. While no major deals emerged from the summit, Trump noted an agreement to hold future discussions regarding nuclear proliferation. He also accused Iran of negotiating in bad faith to end a war that is nearly ten months old.

Trump was joined by Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. Other officials present included Defence Secretary Hegseth and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller. Trump stated that he has a very good relationship with Putin, who he claimed was very nice during the Russia hoax investigation. He also dismissed reports that he was upset with Vance for blaming the Iran war for historic midterm losses.

The president maintained that he would make the same decisions again and that his staff has a right to their own opinions. He did not provide specific details on how the government would enforce the proposed penalties on tech companies. Trump mentioned that he had not yet discussed this specific data centre plan with his own officials. The White House has not yet responded to requests for further comment on these policies.

stories.Headline: PIRG finds AI toys for young children can drift into explicit talk and major retailers pull listings
stories.Summary:
The consumer watchdog group PIRG tested seven toys for its 41st annual "Trouble in Toyland" report, released before Black Friday, and found that some artificial intelligence toys marketed to young children can drift into inappropriate and even sexually explicit conversations. Two toys, the GoLabs AI Panda and the Alilo Smart AI Bunny, both marketed to children as young as three, started off aware they were talking to a child but lost that context over longer interactions, eventually engaging in sexually explicit conversations with researchers. The Alilo Smart AI Bunny began to degrade after about 20 minutes, while the GoLabs AI Panda took roughly 30 to 40 minutes of extended questioning to push past its safeguards. The Panda also had a longer-term memory and could pick up a conversation again even a month later, and turning it off and back on did not reset the problem, meaning it could retain context from prior conversations with an adult or older sibling when a younger child later played with it.

After PIRG shared its findings, Amazon, Walmart and Macy's removed online listings for the flagged products, and Amazon said it removed them while it investigates. Report co-author R.J. Cross said the biggest flag was toy makers putting insufficient guardrails on top of AI chatbots designed for adults, which allows the toy to drift into really inappropriate content. Cross described the toys as recording devices with a built-in microphone and Wi-Fi connection that capture what a user says and feed it into a chatbot, and she said anything a child says to one of these toys is data that a company and typically multiple companies are getting and maybe storing. Cross said she would like to see AI companies take a more proactive stance by vetting the third-party developers who use their technology in toys.

Not all of the findings were negative, since Cross said the Miko robot, tested last year, made significant improvements: it is no longer clingy when a user leaves, and parents can now disable its chatbot entirely with a toggle without losing access to its preloaded games and stories. Laurel Powell, the mother of an 8-year-old boy, said AI features are now part of her checklist before she buys, and that if she sees AI anywhere indicated she does not get it. Cross offered similar guidance for shoppers, telling them to check with a child's parents before buying a recording smart toy and to look carefully at packaging, since some toys hide their AI behind phrases like "interactive talking companion" or "emotional friend." Researchers say not every AI toy is unsafe, but parents should do their homework before putting one under the tree, including checking what data it collects and what parental controls are available.

Articles.Title: AI toys marketed to kids can veer into explicit conversations, prompting major retailers to pull listings
