stories.Headline: French health data chief says hospitals worldwide cannot measure whether medical AI improves patient outcomes
stories.Summary:
Emmanuel Bacry, Scientific Director of France’s Health Data Hub, said at the Bengaluru Tech Summit on November 20, 2026, that hospitals worldwide are ill-equipped to assess whether artificial intelligence systems deployed in their facilities actually improve patient outcomes. He estimated that there are perhaps only six or seven hospitals in the whole world today that are able to evaluate medical devices deployed in their systems. Hospitals struggle to access and integrate patient information to track outcomes after discharge, including recovery rates and mortality, which makes it difficult to establish the real impact of AI-based medical technologies. He said hospitals do not know how to compute the return on investment of such technologies, and asked what would happen if they adopted AI.

Mr. Bacry cited an alert system based on rules-based AI, or an expert system, designed to warn intensive care unit staff about severe kidney failure. Despite functioning effectively, the system was associated with a doubling of deaths in two of the six US hospitals where it was deployed in 2022, and he did not identify the study. While researchers had offered hypotheses, the precise cause remained unknown, and he suggested that the absence of a tested response protocol among hospital personnel could have contributed. He said replacing a human alert with a device alert changes the whole thing, and stressed integrating AI into clinical workflows rather than treating it as a standalone technology. He also cautioned against judging diagnostic AI tools solely by laboratory accuracy, saying a system with 95% accuracy against a doctor’s 90% might not perform better in clinical settings, and that once deployed in real life those scores can be forgotten.

He flagged that AI systems can identify patterns even their developers cannot explain, citing research in which one model predicted ethnicity from chest X-rays with approximately 85% accuracy and another inferred sex from eye images with 95% accuracy. Such hidden correlations could influence medical decisions without clinicians understanding the basis, potentially introducing unintended bias into diagnosis and treatment. In a separate interaction with The Hindu, he warned that healthcare AI development is heavily skewed towards Western populations, estimating that nearly 70% of global healthcare AI training data came from male, white and Western populations. He said the field is developing an Occidental AI and even narrow types of Occidental AI, and advocated smaller, locally tailored models trained on representative population data, arguing that deploying large general-purpose models without adaptation could have disastrous consequences, particularly in developing countries. Mr. Bacry heads the Health Data Hub, established under French law in 2019 to facilitate secondary use of health data for research, and is also a research director at France’s National Centre for Scientific Research at Université Paris Dauphine, PSL.

stories.Headline: Air India and Air India Express extend Jeddah flight suspension to November 24
stories.Summary:
Air India and Air India Express announced on Friday, November 20, 2026, that they were extending the suspension of flights connecting Jeddah until November 24, citing the prevailing security situation in Saudi Arabia. The two airlines had already suspended services to and from the Saudi Arabian cities of Riyadh and Dammam until November 30. Earlier, the services to Jeddah had been suspended only until November 21. The announcement was made in a post on X by Air India. The extension means that Air India and Air India Express flights to and from Jeddah will now remain suspended until November 24, 2026, while operations to and from Riyadh and Dammam will continue to stay suspended until November 30, 2026.

Passengers holding confirmed bookings for travel to or from Jeddah up to November 24, made on or before November 20, may avail a complimentary rescheduling subject to availability or opt for a full refund upon cancellation. The same provision applies to guests with confirmed bookings for travel to or from Riyadh and Dammam up to November 30, made on or before November 10. Air India is responsible for the announcement, which it issued in a post on X explaining that the region's prevailing situation had led to the extended suspension. The airline said passengers with confirmed Jeddah bookings up to November 24, made on or before November 20, could take a complimentary rescheduling subject to availability or a full refund upon cancellation.

It added that the same provision covers guests holding confirmed bookings for travel to or from Riyadh and Dammam up to November 30, made on or before November 10. The suspensions come as various Saudi Arabian cities and infrastructure have come under attack from Houthis in recent months. Other Indian carriers have also acted, with IndiGo extending the cancellation of flights connecting Saudi Arabian cities until November 30 on November 18. Akasa Air has cancelled its flights to and from Riyadh and Jeddah until November 30.

stories.Headline: Researchers find data infrastructure gaps limit AI use in ESG financial intelligence
stories.Summary:
Researchers Miehleketo Mathebula, Abiodun Modupe, Vukosi Marivate, and Elda Du Toit conducted a systematic literature review. They published their investigation in the journal Discover Artificial Intelligence by November 21, 2026. The study assessed how artificial intelligence is applied across environmental, social, and governance financial intelligence. They examined 70 peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2017 and 2025. The authors wanted to find the cause of operational limitations in sustainable finance analytics.

The review requires moving past proprietary data dependencies and incompatible metadata schemas. It identifies gaps in unstandardised disclosure environments across the Global Reporting Initiative and Sustainability Accounting Standards Board. The Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures also creates inconsistent reporting structures. Researchers used IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, and MDPI databases starting January 7, 2026. They analyzed 1,623 candidate records before narrowing the final corpus to 70 articles.

The authors stated that computational model architectures have significantly outpaced the required data infrastructures. They argued that principal constraints arise from institutional disparities rather than algorithmic complexity. The researchers urged the community to stop treating commercial ESG ratings as objective ground-truth labels. They also said that post-hoc explainability cannot compensate for unverified data provenance. They claimed technological interventions cannot fix absent semantic crosswalks.

The study affects the research community and those using high-stakes financial environments. It notes that African institutions contributed only eight studies compared to larger volumes from Asia, Europe, and North America. South Africa produced 11 documents but showed very low global integration. The review found that most tasks were executed in isolation on curated benchmark corpora. These tasks rarely demonstrated integration with live compliance verification or supervisory auditing pipelines.

The background shows a shift from traditional machine learning to generative language modeling. Traditional machine learning appeared 40 times, while deep learning appeared 36 times. Natural language processing had 26 implementations, and general large language models had 15. The review used a six-criterion appraisal framework to score studies up to ten points. This process involved two independent reviewers who achieved a Cohen’s kappa coefficient of 0.82.

Next, the authors propose a conceptual architecture for preprocessing, semantic standardisation, and governance oversight. They illustrated this using a South African report prepared under the King IV governance code. The articles leave this architecture as an unvalidated design blueprint rather than a deployed solution. Future progress requires concerted global investments in open-access benchmark datasets. The researchers leave the actual deployment of these software solutions open.

Articles.Title: Data Infrastructure Gaps Limit Artificial Intelligence in ESG Financial Intelligence Review

stories.headline_source: Data Infrastructure Gaps Limit Artificial Intelligence in ESG Financial Intelligence Review

stories.Headline: Scaler cofounder Anshuman Singh launches Arcfront to sell expert decision data for AI training
stories.Summary:
Scaler cofounder Anshuman Singh has unveiled Arcfront, an AI research and training data venture he is building with Naman Bhalla, Scaler’s former head of AI products and an ex-Google software engineer, according to Inc42. In a post on X, Singh said Arcfront also has what he described as deep support from Scaler cofounder Abhimanyu Saxena. Singh claimed that four of the five frontier AI labs became Arcfront’s customers within less than a year of operations, though he did not identify the labs. Singh’s LinkedIn profile lists November 2025 as the end of his tenure at Scaler and the start of his work on Arcfront, and Bhalla’s profile indicates he began working on the venture around the same time.

Arcfront operates under Evaratus Inc., according to its website’s legal disclosures, and company recruitment material identifies Evaratus as formerly Scaler AI Labs, Scaler’s frontier AI research and engineering division. Scaler’s privacy policy also lists Scaler AI Labs Inc. among its group companies, but the public disclosures reviewed do not establish Evaratus’ current shareholding or whether the business has been separated from the Scaler group. Inc42 has reached out to Arcfront’s founders for clarity on its ownership structure and relationship with Scaler, and the story will be updated based on their response. It also remains unclear whether Singh retains any operational responsibilities at Scaler or how the transition relates to Scaler AI Labs’ subsequent identity as Evaratus.

Arcfront is commercialising records of expert decision-making to help AI developers train and test models on professional tasks that require judgement beyond producing correct answers. Singh argued that models capable of solving difficult coding and mathematical problems can still struggle when placed in professional roles such as finance management. Arcfront aims to address this by working with organisations to reconstruct how experts reach decisions, including the options they reject, the revisions they make and the eventual outcomes, an approach the startup calls Decision Arc Data. It converts these records into training data, reinforcement learning environments and evaluations for frontier AI labs, covering software engineering, site reliability engineering, cybersecurity and collaborative workplace tasks, and it also builds sector-specific evaluations using workflows from healthcare, life sciences, legal services and finance to identify where models fail.

Separately, angel investor and former Google, Facebook and DoorDash executive Gokul Rajaram identified Arcfront as the company behind his earlier claim about a startup reaching a $1 Bn annualised revenue run rate faster than any other company. In the earlier post, Rajaram said the unnamed company had no revenue in November 2025 and generated $80 Mn in September 2026, putting it on course to reach a $1 Bn annualised run rate within 11 months of starting operations. Arcfront joins a growing group of startups building training datasets, testing tools and simulated work environments for AI developers, a field in which Deccan AI raised $25 Mn in March to expand its post-training data offerings, research and enterprise infrastructure. A related opportunity is emerging in physical AI, where startups including Human Archive are building data pipelines using footage of workers performing physical tasks, and Humyn Labs raised $47 Mn this week, comprising $26 Mn in equity and $21 Mn in venture debt, to expand its data collection and robot deployment operations.

stories.Headline: Japan insurers report a surge in cyberinsurance claims as AI-driven attacks grow
stories.Summary:
Japan’s biggest property insurers are reporting a sharp jump in cyberinsurance claims as artificial intelligence-driven attacks grow more sophisticated and hacking incidents surge nationwide. Tokio Marine Holdings received three times as many cyberinsurance claim notifications in October as usual, according to the company. Sompo Holdings said claims in October were running at 2½ times higher than the average over the one-year period ending Sept 30, 2026. Both insurers disclosed the figures at earnings briefings on Nov 19. Attackers are using increasingly sophisticated methods as AI advances, and unauthorised access has led to a string of personal data leaks in Japan.

The increase in claims raises the risk of costly payouts even as rising numbers of incidents fuel demand for protection. Payouts on cyberpolicies could rise, but the surge has yet to translate into a significant earnings hit. Yoshinari Endo, a managing executive officer at Tokio Marine, said his company expects some impact on full-year results, though it is managing the profit risk and expects losses to stay within the assumptions of its initial annual plan. Junsuke Koike, an executive vice-president at Sompo, said inquiries about raising coverage amounts or adding coverage items had tripled from normal levels.

Japan’s experience mirrors a broader rise in cyberclaims globally, with US insurers reporting more than 56,000 cyberclaims in 2025, up 20% from a year earlier. Cyberpolicies typically cover damages owed for data breaches, recovery costs and profits lost from disruptions, making insurance a growing part of corporate risk management. Cyberinsurance penetration in Japan remains low for smaller companies, as a 2025 survey by the General Insurance Association of Japan found that only 8.8% of small- and medium-sized business owners said they had cyberinsurance as a defence against attacks. Yasuko Fukuda, a senior executive officer at MS&AD Insurance Group Holdings, said at an earnings briefing on Nov 19 that there is significant room for the market to expand.

The insurers are trying to limit losses by helping customers prevent attacks, and starting in December, Sompo will offer a new service with Trend Micro and others that monitors for vulnerabilities on the internet. Insurers are being selective about underwriting, and Tokio Marine may cap payouts or tighten coverage terms depending on a customer’s risk profile, Endo said. The company expects its cyberinsurance business to remain profitable in the fiscal year through March 2027. Standard total payout limits in Japan and overseas run from about 100 million yen, or S$812,000, to several hundred million yen per contract.

stories.Headline: Higher-income parents more often encourage kids to use AI for schoolwork, RAND finds
stories.Summary:
A report from the research group RAND, published in Education Week on November 20, 2026, found a connection between how much money parents make and how often their kids use AI for schoolwork. The report was written by Arianna Prothero. RAND surveyed nationally representative groups of parents and teens in the winter and spring of 2025 and the spring of 2026. The more parents earn, the more likely they are to use AI themselves and encourage their kids to use it to complete schoolwork. Parental encouragement is positively correlated with teens’ AI use.

There was a 15-percentage-point gap in AI use among high- and low-income parents in February 2025, with the former using AI more. That gap grew to 21 percentage points in May 2026, even as AI use increased among all income groups. About two-thirds of parents who made $150,000 a year or more said in the most recent survey they had encouraged their kids to use AI for schoolwork compared with just under half of parents making less than $50,000. Nearly 1 in 5 parents in that highest-income category (17%) encourage their kids to use AI whenever possible within school rules. Four in 10 teens reported in May 2025 that they used AI to complete schoolwork, rising to nearly 5 in 10 a year later.

Heather Schwartz, the vice president and director of education, employment, and infrastructure for RAND, said the report shows parents are encouraging their children to use AI for school in greater numbers than might have been realized. She said parents therefore need messages about when AI can be helpful and when AI is harmful. Schwartz said many students are unfamiliar with their schools’ AI policies, if they even exist. She said schools should have coherent AI policies and communicate them to parents, and need buildingwide rules rather than depend on teachers to craft their own in individual classrooms. Schwartz said the all-essential ingredient is how higher-income teens are using AI, and that if teens are using AI to do the work for them, this could harm highest-income teens’ performance.

Among parents who don’t think that AI harms their kids’ critical thinking, most encouraged AI use, but even among parents who believe that AI use undermines critical thinking, more than half (53%) still encouraged their kids to use it. In a subset of survey data that matched parents with their own children, which was not a nationally representative sample, teens whose parents reported frequent AI use were more likely to use the technology themselves to help with homework than their peers whose parents didn’t use AI (63% vs. 40%). Teens from high-income families were more likely than their peers to use AI for schoolwork: 57% of teens in the highest-income families (those making more than $150,000 a year) reported using AI to do their homework in 2026 compared with 43% of teens from the lowest-income families (those making less than $50,000 a year). AI use among those wealthiest teens grew by 17 percentage points from May 2025 to May 2026. Teachers accounted for the loudest voices discouraging AI use, with 57% of teens saying teachers discouraged them from using the technology.

Among parents who nudge their kids to use AI for schoolwork, most say they counsel them to use restraint, such as using AI as a brainstorming partner rather than allowing it to do all their thinking for them. Teens are getting mixed messages on AI use from the people in their lives, whether parents, other family members, friends, teachers, or other school staff. If parents, friends, and teachers discouraged teens from using AI, they were much less likely to do so, but if at least one group was pushing for AI use, teens were significantly more likely to use it for homework. Schwartz said that if teens are using AI to supplement their thinking, such as asking a tool for feedback after writing the first draft of an essay themselves, that’s a more enriching way to use the technology that could boost learning. Schwartz said that in the real world, she thinks kids are using AI as a shortcut and, in general, they’re getting AI to do the work for them.

Whether this gap in AI use will harm or hurt wealthier students is to be seen, Schwartz said. Schwartz said schools need to give parents clear talking points about either recommended or mandated do’s and don’ts on their children’s AI use for school. The report states that families play a crucial role in teaching students healthy AI habits that won’t undermine their learning. The articles do not say what specific policies schools have adopted in response to the findings. The articles do not say whether further RAND surveys are planned.

stories.Headline: Clark Hill lawyers present a webinar on three emerging legal threats in healthcare AI
stories.Summary:
Clark Hill, a law firm, announced a webinar titled Healthcare AI in 2027: Three Emerging Legal Threats You Haven't Been Warned About, scheduled for December 16, 2026, from 10:00 to 11:00 AM Pacific Time and running through the corresponding hours in Mountain, Central and Eastern time. The session will be presented by Paul F. Schmeltzer and John F. Howard, according to the firm's announcement dated November 20, 2026. The webinar is aimed at the growing integration of artificial intelligence into healthcare operations and clinical decision-making, which the firm says is producing a new generation of legal, cybersecurity and patient safety risks. The firm states that the discussion will go beyond traditional AI governance and HIPAA compliance to examine three cutting-edge threats.

The first threat covered is autonomous AI agents that make or influence clinical decisions with limited human oversight. The second is AI-targeted cyberattacks, including prompt injection and data poisoning, which can manipulate AI systems, compromise clinical workflows and potentially put patients at risk. The third is AI-driven operational failures that can lead to patient misidentification, inaccurate medical records, or automated decisions that are difficult to reconstruct or explain. The presenters will examine the evolving legal and regulatory implications of these threats, including cybersecurity obligations, medical malpractice exposure and vendor liability.

The firm also plans to address the importance of continuous monitoring, meaningful human oversight and safeguards meant to prevent the uncritical acceptance of AI-generated decisions. Clark Hill lists the webinar under its healthcare industry group and its cybersecurity, privacy and technology litigation and data privacy, protection and cybersecurity practice areas. The announcement does not name any clients, patients or specific AI products affected by the threats described. It also does not state whether the webinar carries continuing legal education credit or what the registration fee is.

The page offers a registration link for the event but gives no further details on the agenda beyond the three threats and the legal topics listed. No enforcement actions, lawsuits or regulatory deadlines are mentioned in connection with the webinar. The announcement appears alongside other Clark Hill legal updates, including one on expanded Medicare revocation powers and one on a federal court ruling vacating a Department of Homeland Security rule. Nothing in the announcement indicates what, if anything, will follow the December 16 session.

stories.Headline: Trump orders federal agencies to replace artificial intelligence with super intelligence
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump ordered federal agencies to replace the term artificial intelligence with super intelligence on September 29. He signed an executive order for this change because he believes the word artificial makes the technology sound fake. On October 4, the president established a super intelligence force to coordinate government efforts and maintain American global leadership. This new body reports directly to the president and his chief of staff to streamline federal actions. The task force has 120 days to submit a report regarding the risks and opportunities of this technology.

The force is led by Jay Clayton, who serves as the director of national intelligence and was previously the chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission. Other members include Federal Trade Commission chair Andrew Ferguson, Pentagon technology chief Emil Michael, and federal workforce leader Scott Kupor. This initiative follows a morally binding accord signed by firms such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and Nvidia for internal evaluations and audits. Private investment in the United States reached 285.9 billion dollars in 2025, which is roughly 23 times the 12.4 billion dollars spent by China. Major American tech companies are expected to spend more than 650 billion dollars on capital investments this year.

Jay Clayton stated that the risk of the United States not being first in this race is high. However, Democratic senator Mark Warner criticized the move as merely renaming the technology while telling private companies to regulate themselves. Critics argue that the White House has not disclosed a budget or clarified if the force has regulatory powers. They also note that the performance gap between the best American and Chinese models narrowed to 2.7 percentage points by 2026. The lack of an enforcement mechanism for the voluntary industry accord suggests that the government may have limited leverage.

The effectiveness of this strategy depends on whether the body secures a budget and gains authority over infrastructure and hiring. Recent midterm elections shifted control of Congress toward the Democrats, which could change future funding and oversight. Because the president revoked Joe Biden's previous executive order on his first day in office, these new actions could also be undone. There is a tension between the goals of winning a global race and protecting the public from potential harms. The leadership comes from defense and intelligence sectors rather than from experts focused specifically on safety.

stories.Headline: Flagship Pioneering invests £100 million to build AI-driven biotech companies in the UK
stories.Summary:
Flagship Pioneering said on Monday that it is opening its first lab for creating companies outside the United States, putting £100 million, or about $131.94 million, behind a new UK-based effort to fund and build AI-driven biotech companies. The move is a first for a firm that has created more than 130 companies, including Moderna, and that had operated only from the United States for more than 25 years. The announcement came after three years of groundwork in Britain, during which the company opened a London office in 2023 near the Francis Crick Institute in King's Cross. Its local team has since built partnerships with academia, government and regulatory groups.

The Flagship Origination lab will be anchored at the firm's London office, and the company hopes its £100 million will attract £500 million or more from partners. Flagship expects to recruit about 50 scientist-entrepreneurs and operators in Britain initially, and it said it will not buy into existing companies. Instead it plans to cast a wide net for partnerships with universities, corporations and funders. AI will run through every stage of the lab's work, from invention to clinical trials, according to the firm.

Noubar Afeyan, founder and CEO of the venture firm and chairman of Moderna, told Reuters that the company concluded this might well be the right next step in its evolution. He said the country's main draw is the National Health Service and the patient data it has gathered, which lets researchers begin with real-world evidence to find disease targets before developing drugs. He cautioned that the use of AI in the field is still early, saying he thinks AI's most fundamental contribution in the first instance will be to shed light on what is happening mechanistically in diseases. Flagship companies are already testing that approach, including drug developer Generate Biomedicines, which completed an early-stage trial of an AI-designed drug for asthma in Manchester.

stories.Headline: LG Group keeps affiliate chiefs and promotes robotics and AI executives in its 2026 reshuffle
stories.Summary:
LG Group began its executive reshuffle on Thursday, November 19, 2026, keeping its key affiliate chief executives in place while promoting executives who specialize in robotics and artificial intelligence. LG Electronics promoted 44 executives, including Baek Seung-tae and Lee Sang-woo to president, along with three executive vice presidents and 10 senior vice presidents, up from 33 promotions last year. Across the whole group, 132 executives were promoted, including 89 newly appointed executives, and the changes take effect on January 1. LG said it chose research and development specialists for 30 percent of its new vice president appointments to strengthen its leadership in future technologies.

Baek Seung-tae, who joined LG Electronics in 1990 and previously headed its Living Solution and Kitchen Solution businesses, was recognized for driving growth in the Home Appliance Solution division despite tariff pressures and rising raw material costs. Since taking charge of that division last year, he has worked to commercialize robotic actuators as part of preparations for future growth. Lee Sang-woo, management strategy head at LG Corp., will move to LG Electronics to lead its Media Entertainment Solution division and display business, after earlier roles in TV business planning, strategy and operations. Robotics executives stood out among those promoted to senior vice president, including Robotics Business Head Song Si-yong, Data Factory Division Leader Park Kie-bum and Robotics Lab Chief Research Engineer Lee Jae-wook.

LG Uplus promoted Enterprise AI Business Group Head Ahn Hyurng-gyoon and Network Infrastructure Group Head Noh Seong-joo to senior vice president in the fields of AI data centers and network automation. LG Innotek promoted Cho Ji-tae, head of its Package Solution Business, to executive vice president as part of efforts to strengthen its semiconductor substrate business. Seven of the 89 newly appointed executives across the group were women. The group said it particularly emphasized executives capable of driving progress in key AI sectors, including physical AI and AI infrastructure.

stories.Headline: Education experts urge Seoul universities to invest in AI detection for high-stakes exams
stories.Summary:
Global higher education experts urged Seoul universities to embrace artificial intelligence and rethink student assessments during a November 2026 summit. These experts called for stronger detection technology for high-stakes exams like the College Scholastic Ability Test to stop AI-assisted cheating. Kuancheng Huang, a professor from Taiwan, visited Korea University to attend the Times Higher Education Innovation and Impact Summit. He told The Korea Times that authorities must invest in technology to prevent cheating because such measures are very important. This push for better security follows growing fears about the misuse of smart glasses and other wearable devices in Korea.

Authorities will deploy at least one trained supervisor at each of 1,300 test sites to identify prohibited AI glasses. Prime Minister Han Seongsook's office is considering shutting down public Wi-Fi and requiring students to hand over their smart devices. More than 500,000 students took the College Scholastic Ability Test on Thursday, November 20, 2026, amid these heightened security concerns. National Tsing Hua University president John Kao requires students and faculty to disclose AI use, similar to citing academic research sources. These changes target high-stakes exams, university admissions, campus tests, and professional licensing tests where traditional testing methods are hard to replace.

Kuancheng Huang stated that technology to counter sophisticated cheating devices is available, but the challenge is the spending level. He suggested that universities shift their focus from final answers to the reasoning and problem-solving processes of the students. John Kao argued that restricting emerging technologies would not stop cheating because those who cheat always find new tools. He emphasized the need to promote academic ethics rather than simply taking away the tools that students use to cheat. Dawn Freshwater urged universities to teach students to think independently and produce original work supported by AI, not driven by it.

Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin rejected calls from lawmakers to postpone the national exam, stating a delay would cause larger disruptions. Han Won-seok, a tax accountant test taker, admitted using a concealed camera and generative AI to receive answers on smartphones. Han scored 397.5 out of 400 on a multiple-choice test in April and 663 out of 800 in July. Other affected students include those caught using AI-powered smart glasses on an English standardized test in June and university essays. These incidents have spooked the nation and left authorities scrambling to prevent fraud before the all-important college entrance exams.

The College Scholastic Ability Test is a high-stakes annual event in a country known for its intense academic competition. Prospects for marriage, social standing, and jobs often depend on which university a person attends in the South Korean system. To ensure an ideal environment, the country delays the workday and stock market trading to ease traffic for test-takers. Police officers use motorcycles to escort late students, and the military sometimes suspends training near the various testing sites. Flights are even paused during the English listening section to prevent noise from disrupting the students during the exam.

Police are currently investigating Han Won-seok, who stated in a YouTube video that he would cooperate with the legal process. Universities must now decide how to integrate AI as an inevitable part of education while ensuring students develop ethical judgment. Experts believe traditional assessments are becoming less effective at measuring actual abilities as AI tools grow more sophisticated over time. The articles leave open whether the government will officially implement the proposed Wi-Fi shutdowns and device collections at sites. It remains unclear how much authorities are actually willing to spend on the detection technology recommended by Kuancheng Huang.

stories.Headline: South Korea invests $1 trillion to become a top three global AI power by 2030
stories.Summary:
South Korea is pursuing an ambitious strategy to become a global hub for artificial intelligence research and education. The government aims to establish the nation as one of the top three AI powers in the world, trailing only the United States and China. This initiative involves attracting international scholars and students to nurture the engineers and scientists necessary to lead the AI revolution. Recent data shows a surge in interest, with 33,349 applications for 2,067 spots at four government-run science universities for the 2027 class.

The strategy requires integrating AI with robotics to develop physical AI that can sense and act in the real world. To achieve this, the government has designated the integration of AI and robotics as one of three mega projects. These projects, which also include AI data centers and semiconductors, will receive at least $1 trillion in public and private investment. The ultimate goal is for South Korea to become the world's leading physical-AI power by 2030. This transition leverages the country's current status as the world leader in industrial-robot density, with 1,220 robots per 10,000 workers.

Lee Kun-woo, the president of the Daegu Gyeongbuk Institute of Science and Technology, believes the country can successfully attract global talent. He noted that many foreigners have high hopes for the future of AI in Korea and aspire to conduct research there. To support this, universities are creating contract departments where companies like Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix fund tuition in exchange for job commitments. Lee highlighted that the AI College at his institution will connect students with local companies through joint research programs in mobility and robotics.

The push for AI dominance comes as Korea already produces the third-largest number of new AI models according to the Stanford AI Index 2026. The country is also capitalizing on research funding cuts in the United States under the Trump administration to draw more international scholars. While Korean universities currently lag behind leading American institutions, they are transforming into international technology hubs to close the gap. Future efforts will focus on combining AI with autonomous manufacturing, smart cities, and biomedical technology to maintain a competitive edge.

stories.Headline: DARPA awards New Mexico State University $600,000 to develop verified AI reasoning architectures
stories.Summary:
The Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency awarded a research grant to New Mexico State University on November 20, 2026. This funding supports the development of verified neuro-symbolic artificial intelligence architectures for safety-critical defense engineering. The agency provided 600,000 dollars for this specific research effort over a two-year period. Computer scientists at the university will pair machine learning pattern recognition with formal logical proofs. This work falls under the Compositional Learning-And-Reasoning for Automated Complex Systems Engineering program.

The project, called Project SPARTA, involves New Mexico State University, Arizona State University, and the University of Nebraska at Omaha. Professor Son Tran and Assistant Professor Stylianos Vasileiou lead the effort at New Mexico State University. Professor Chitta Baral directs the Arizona State University group, while Professors Yuliana Lierler and Jorge Fandinno lead the Nebraska team. The program requires native algorithmic compositionality instead of using post-hoc validation filters on large models. It utilizes splitting-based logic programming, polynomially-bounded automated reasoning, and tensorized adaptation interfaces.

Principal investigator Son Tran stated that integrating these AI branches provides machine learning speed with verifiability. He noted that reasoning proofs offer strong logical explainability and computational tractability for practical engineering. Tran emphasized that computational tractability is the make-or-break criterion for real-time deployment in industrial systems. The goal is to replace unverified statistical guesses with rigorous logical guarantees. This approach ensures that mathematical proofs execute within deterministic processing budgets.

Superpower Daily reported that this initiative represents fundamental basic science rather than a commercial product. The outlet noted the challenge of scaling formal verification across complex systems beyond laboratory benchmarks. Defense contractors building unmanned aerial systems or radar signal processors are affected by these outputs. These contractors could eventually integrate reusable verification libraries into safety-critical firmware. University research offices must also manage subawards and export controls like ITAR and EAR.

Deep neural networks rely on correlation rather than deduction, which creates vulnerabilities in safety-critical domains. Failures can occur in flight control software, aerospace trajectory synthesis, autonomous naval navigation, and power grid automation. DARPA's Defense Sciences Office identified the current serial configuration of AI safety as fundamentally brittle. The CLARA program was solicited as a Disruption Opportunity to fast-track high-risk basic research. McAllister and Quinn noted that these opportunities challenge prevailing commercial assumptions.

During the first twelve months, teams will establish theoretical formalisms and engineer prototype mapping modules. The second year involves integrating algorithms into a unified open-source toolchain for rigorous benchmarking. Researchers will measure verification runtime, proof validity, and model generalization using DARPA-supplied engineering challenges. The articles leave open whether formal verification can remain scalable across arbitrary complex systems. They do not state if the project will meet all its technical milestones.

stories.Headline: Education minister Choi Kyo-jin admits he cannot detect AI cheating as 550,000 students sit a chaotic exam
stories.Summary:
The 2027 College Scholastic Ability Test took place on a Thursday at 1,312 testing centers across South Korea. About 550,000 students sat for the exam amid a major controversy regarding cheating using artificial intelligence. The government failed to prepare for these risks, which left many innocent students bearing the consequences. This event was described as a textbook case of government failure and administrative incompetence. It was the most confused and anxious exam since the test was introduced over thirty years ago.

The process required students to cover buttons with stickers and place their bags in hallways to prevent cheating. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook reportedly spearheaded these specific anti-cheating measures to address the fears surrounding AI technology. During the exam day, emergency disaster alerts sounded three times, which likely unsettled many of the applicants. The ministry of education introduced outdated and hastily devised countermeasures that only served to deepen the general confusion. These disruptions occurred while students were attempting to complete their crucial college entrance examinations across the entire nation.

Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin bears particular responsibility for the lack of preparation and poor crisis management during the test. Choi is a former middle school Korean-language teacher and a regional leader of the Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union. He also served as a three-term superintendent of education in South Chungcheong before taking his current ministerial role. When asked by the National Assembly's Education Committee if he could detect AI cheating, he said he likely could not. He attributed this inability to his age, a comment that subsequently provoked significant public outrage across the country.

The tech industry expressed doubts about whether the government can actually catch those who used AI to cheat. Parents opened up about their frustrations regarding the potential for AI cheating during the high stakes testing day. Many believe that the entire examination administration system has now been exposed to international ridicule due to these failures. The government is facing calls to answer for the inadequate preparation and the chaotic nature of the exam. Students who spent years preparing for the test deserved a fair and orderly environment instead of government negligence.

The Anti-Corruption and Civil Rights Commission had already received 44 petitions calling for measures against AI-assisted cheating via its portal. AI cheating had previously surfaced in a national examination in May and during a university essay exam last month. These repeated warnings were unheeded by officials, raising questions about their understanding of rapidly advancing technology and its risks. The government failed to respond effectively to these early signals before the 2027 College Scholastic Ability Test began. Systematic planning and coordination among agencies were missing, leading to the crisis seen during the recent examination.

Authorities must now work with telecommunications companies and investigators to determine if AI-assisted cheating actually occurred during the test. They should also examine how extensively AI was used for cheating in previous exams since generative AI became available. The government must identify which officials are responsible for the failures in oversight and emergency communication during the day. A fundamental overhaul of the administration system is required to restore public confidence in the national testing process. The articles leave open whether Minister Choi Kyo-jin will resign or if other officials will face accountability.

stories.Headline: South Korea inspects buttons and bags to stop AI cheating in 550,000-person exam as 98 violate device rules
stories.Summary:
Authorities conducted a strict anti-cheating crackdown during the College Scholastic Ability Test on November 19, 2026. About 550,000 test-takers sat for the high-stakes exam under these tight measures. Officials focused on preventing AI-assisted cheating through extraordinary lengths. They inspected clothing buttons for miniature cameras and issued emergency alerts. The government will also probe suspected cheating from last year's exam.

The Ministry of Education reported 98 examinees violated smart device restrictions at 1,312 test centers nationwide. Three emergency alerts identified 49 people, while 44 others were caught using Wi-Fi signal detection. Five students tried to photograph papers or use phones in restrooms. In Yongin, Gyeonggi, a 20-year-old had a miniature camera and earphones. Other devices found included smart glasses in Cheonan and a phone in a shoe insole in Seocho District.

The Ministry of Education stated they are looking into reports of arguments between proctors and examinees. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook reportedly spearheaded the idea to cover buttons with stickers and move bags. She ordered that last year's exam papers be kept in storage until further instructions are issued. The government is pursuing legislation to extend cheating bans from one year to 10 years. These officials aimed to stop the use of concealed devices during the test.

Some students, including 18-year-old Yang, said inspection methods varied and some proctors were more lenient. Examinee Bang and another student named Lee reported different frequencies of glasses checks at one school. One online post claimed proctors skipped identity checks to focus on clothing buttons. Student Kim Han-bi expressed worry that smart glasses could lead to unfair perfect scores. A parent surnamed Kwon ensured their son wore a buttonless sweatshirt to avoid suspicion.

Last year, 30.1 percent of 279 cheating violations involved electronic devices like smartphones. This year, 54,338 registered examinees were absent, which is a 9.97 percent absentee rate. This figure is an increase of 3,042 people from the previous year's 9.4 percent rate. Some people speculate that the stricter supervision contributed to this increase in absences. The government is now extending its scrutiny to previous exams to ensure integrity.

The final tally of violations is scheduled for release on Friday. Seoul National University and Kyung Hee University will require disposable gowns for upcoming admissions tests. These measures aim to prevent the use of miniature cameras during essays and interviews. The government will continue investigating suspected cheating and imposing penalties after the exam. The articles leave open whether the new legislation for longer bans will pass.

stories.Headline: Olive Young develops an AI-powered omnichannel platform for shopping, logistics and supply chains
stories.Summary:
CJ Olive Young said in Seoul on Thursday that it will develop its online platform into an omnichannel service connecting online and offline shopping for consumers in Korea and overseas. Chief Operating Officer Lee Jin-hee said the company aims to build an AI-powered platform spanning inventory, store layouts, delivery logistics and supply chains. The company was established in 1999 and now serves 18 million members, Lee said. Olive Young operates 1,300 stores, and Chief Technology Officer Kim Hwan said accurately sharing each store's stock status with customers is difficult.

The company introduced a shopping cart service a month ago that combines same-day delivery, regular delivery and store pickup. Olive Young has more than 47 million customer records covering skin conditions, analyzed solutions and product reviews, which it plans to use to support consultations through agentic AI. Lee said foreign visitors have contributed 1 trillion won to sales this year and account for 6 million memberships at Olive Young's online global mall. She said those foreign visitors drive 70 percent of the company's annual growth, and Olive Young's California stores use the same technologies as its Korean stores.

Lee said the company is now leading a global commerce trend that integrates online and offline channels into a single marketplace. She said everything from checking stocks to in-store product arrangement, delivery logistics and supply chains will work on a singular platform. Kim said the company at first saw its online infrastructure tumble frequently because of errors, and that implementing cloud technology brought failures as well as chances to improve. Lee said Olive Young aims to move beyond keyword searches and scrolling through lists of results, and that its online traffic and offline stores together offer a next-generation K-beauty media platform.

stories.Headline: South Korea covers buttons and checks glasses to stop AI cheating on the CSAT
stories.Summary:
Proctors began checking test-takers’ IDs and collecting their phones at 8:10 a.m. on Nov. 19, the day of the College Scholastic Ability Test, which had 551,864 applicants this year. Test-takers wearing clothes with buttons were handed small stickers and told to put one over each button under new nationwide measures against AI devices that could be used to cheat on the exam. In one exam room, test-takers who walked in at 7:40 a.m. nervously studied four notices taped side by side on the blackboard.

The notices spelled out the penalties for cheating with smart devices and listed banned and permitted items. Proctors also had to check every test-taker’s eyewear at each period to make sure none were smart glasses. The Ministry of Education said in its Nov. 9 guidance that merely wearing smart glasses during the exam would count as cheating. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook announced last-minute checks, including the button stickers, on Tuesday, Nov. 17, and the government ruled out postponing the CSAT. Tuesday’s measures added checks of buttons, sleeves and collars.

Public Wi-Fi within 100 meters of test sites nationwide was switched off for 24 hours from 6 p.m. on Nov. 18 to curb AI-assisted cheating, though officials said mobile networks could not be blocked. At 8:30 a.m., the government sent a nationwide emergency alert that sets off a 10.5-second alarm on any phone that is switched on, so that any phones test-takers had not handed in would go off. Test-takers’ phone and AI service records will be checked after the exam, and the government plans to bar anyone caught cheating from retaking the CSAT for 10 years, raised drastically from one. During the exam, test-takers may write only with black pencils or the writing tools the ministry provides.

This year’s test-takers are also the last to sit the CSAT under the 2015 revised national curriculum, and from next year elective subjects are dropped and all test-takers will be tested on the same subjects. Police were dispatched to a test site in Yangsan, South Gyeongsang, Thursday morning after a report that someone planned to cheat with AI glasses. The Ulsan Metropolitan Police Agency received the report at around 8:45 a.m., according to the Gyeongnam Provincial Police Agency, passed it to the South Gyeongsang agency two minutes later, and police reached the school at around 8:51 a.m. and informed the proctors. No smart devices or other irregularities had been found so far, and a police official said, “We are checking whether the post is genuine.”

The person who reported it had seen a post in the chat window of a YouTube channel on college admissions consulting that said, in effect, “I will take the exam wearing AI glasses,” and named a specific test site. On Sunday, police opened an investigation after the tax exam’s top scorer turned himself in, confessing he cheated with a hidden miniature camera and generative AI. The Human Resources Development Service of Korea, which runs the test, has said it will file a criminal complaint against the test-taker and revoke the passing result. Suspected cheating with AI-powered smart glasses and miniature cameras has surfaced in a string of recent exams. “My son was very angry about the cheating controversy,” Noh Jeong-dae said, adding that he calmed him down by telling him, “Ignore it and just show what you know,” but still feels upset.

“If the government had postponed the exam by just one week, it could have come up with something more reliable than stickers,” Noh said. “Many students say they feel as if what they built over more than 10 years of hard work has been stolen by cheaters,” a teacher at Seoseok High School in Gwangju said, adding that the school went to great lengths to calm students shaken by the recent controversy. At Namnyeong High School in Jeju City, most test-takers arrived in padded jackets, hoodies or other clothes without buttons, and a teacher there said he told students yesterday to avoid clothes with buttons if they could. “The detailed guidelines changed so suddenly that there could be confusion on site,” Park Su-ji, a third-year homeroom teacher at Chuncheon High School, said, adding that she told her students to get a proctor to check any item before using it. “What I told my students most often was, ‘Hold your nerve,’” Cho Su-yeon, a teacher at Yongin High School, said outside Dongnae High School, a test site in Busan, adding that some students were worried by rumors that the mechanical pencil leads provided at test sites were poor quality.

“I cheer on students outside the test site every year,” Woo Hyeong-geun, a third-year homeroom teacher at Daewon High School in Daegu, said, adding that this year problems like AI cheating meant one change after another right up until the exam. “They are the last generation under the 2015 revised curriculum, and now the AI issue has come up as well,” another teacher in Jeju said, adding that the tax accountant case blew up and that it is actually a good thing it has led to steps against cheating. “I do not know what the world is coming to,” a woman waiting at a bus stop outside Hakseong High School in Ulsan said, adding that she worries about the children who will have to live in a society where trust has broken down. “The government did rush out anticheating measures,” Jung Jae-uk, a parent outside the Cheongseok High School test site in Cheongju, North Chungcheong, said, adding that given how advanced technology has become they do not seem satisfactory and that there should be changes to how the CSAT assesses students or how it is proctored. “Cheating is fraud against everyone who studied hard,” Lee Jeong-in, who came to Cheongseok High School to cheer on a younger sibling, said, adding that once this CSAT is over the government should come up with firmer measures.

“Once this year’s exam is over, it is my child’s turn next year,” said a parent surnamed Son, whose child is a second-year high school student in Jeju, adding that she is worried about AI cheating but that there will always be people like that and it pays to take a wider perspective of life. “My child usually wears glasses, and I worry they might be wrongly suspected or feel intimidated during the checks,” a parent outside Hakseong High School said, adding that stopping cheating is important but so is letting children who prepared diligently take the exam without feeling anxious. In a fourth-floor study room of Myeonggok Library in Changwon, South Gyeongsang, about 20 people were studying for teacher recruitment, civil service and licensing exams, and a library-goer surnamed Lee, preparing for the special education teacher exam for secondary schools, said the alarm did not feel like much of a disturbance. Outside Chuncheon High School in Chuncheon, Gangwon, first- and second-year students from Seongsu High School cheered on test-takers. A mother cheered on her child outside the test site at Myungduk Foreign Language High School in Gangseo District, western Seoul.

Proctors collected banned items and handed out writing tools at Gwangnam High School in Gwangjin District, eastern Seoul, and a proctor checked a test-taker’s glasses for smart glasses at Yeouido Girls’ High School in Yeongdeungpo District, western Seoul. Test-takers got ready for the exam at Yongsan High School in Yongsan District, central Seoul, and a smartphone at Ewha Girls’ High School in Jung District, central Seoul, showed the emergency alert sent nationwide on the morning of Nov. 19. A public Wi-Fi device is installed in front of a CSAT site in Seoul, and a miniature camera was placed next to a button on a sweater in an image released by NEWS1. The library-goer surnamed Lee said, “This problem will surely come up not only in the CSAT but also in the teacher recruitment exam I am preparing for,” adding, “I think I would be really angry if I failed because of people like that,” and that there need to be harsh punishments for AI cheaters and a government way to weed them out. The article was originally written in Korean and translated by a bilingual reporter with the help of generative AI tools, then edited by a native English-speaking editor, with all AI-assisted translations reviewed and refined by the newsroom.

Prime Minister Han Seong-sook was reportedly behind the idea to spearhead anticheating measures for the college admissions test. The CSAT is Korea’s college entrance exam, and the tax accountant exam’s top scorer confessed on Sunday to cheating with a hidden miniature camera and generative AI. The government announced the extra measures only days before the college admissions test was to be held, which induced anxiety in some test-takers and aggravation among parents and teachers. More to follow.

stories.Headline: South Korea targets AI cheating as 550,000 students sit college entrance exam
stories.Summary:
South Korea conducted its toughest crackdown on cheating during the 2027 College Scholastic Ability Test on Thursday, November 19, 2026. Authorities targeted AI assisted cheating as about 550,000 students sat for the nationwide college entrance exam. Proctors caught a 20 year old repeat test taker with a miniature camera and earphones in Yongin, Gyeonggi. Police also found a phone in a shoe insole in Seocho District and other banned items in Jung District. In Yangsan, South Gyeongsang, police responded to a YouTube chat claim about someone wearing AI glasses.

Proctors at 1,312 test sites required students to remove glasses, roll up sleeves, and place stickers over clothing buttons. Public and carrier Wi-Fi within 100 meters of sites was shut off, and 8,400 additional inspectors were dispatched. The government used the emergency alert system at 8:30 a.m., 2:21 p.m., and 2:57 p.m. to find unsubmitted phones. This system uncovered 22 phones across nine cities and provinces, according to the Ministry of Education.

Prime minister Han Seong-sook reportedly spearheaded the ideas for button stickers and placing bags in hallways. The Ministry of Education stated that the emergency alerts helped identify phones that students had not surrendered to proctors. The government vowed to keep pursuing cheating after the exam through tougher penalties and new incentives to report it. President Lee Jae Myung ordered a plan to pay bounties of up to 100 million won for reporting cheating. The ruling party and government are pushing a legal revision to extend the retake ban from one to 10 years.

Officials also asked provincial offices to keep last year's test papers instead of destroying them. Some people claimed online that they did not receive the emergency alerts or that no alarms sounded at all. Critics argued that shutting off Wi-Fi cannot stop smuggled devices from using mobile data to send photos of questions. Parent Jeong Jae-wook in Cheongju, North Chungcheong, said the hastily prepared measures were not enough and assessment methods must change.

Lee Jeong-in believed the government should create more definite measures to protect the efforts of students who studied hard. These concerns highlight doubts about whether current security can stop increasingly sophisticated AI assisted cheating. The crackdown followed AI cheating scandals on other national exams, including a certified tax accountant exam top scorer who used AI. Last year, electronic devices were used in 84 of 279 cheating cases, which is 30.1 percent, according to Ko Min-jung.

These devices included 31 digital watches, 23 e-cigarettes, 16 phones, eight Bluetooth earphones, and six tablet PCs. Lee Jin-woo, who took last year's CSAT and aced the Legal Education Eligibility Test, died by suicide on Thursday. He had faced allegations of using AI to achieve his perfect score on the law school entrance exam. Police will now investigate if the repeat test taker in Yongin photographed questions or communicated with people outside the site.

The government continues to push for the legal revision regarding the ten year ban for those caught cheating. Authorities are still finalizing the bounty system for reporting cheating under the orders of President Lee Jae Myung. It remains unclear if the current security measures can truly prevent the use of advanced generative AI tools. The Education Ministry is still reviewing last year's test papers following the allegations against Lee Jin-woo.

stories.Headline: Rep. Nathaniel Moran co-founds House AI caucus to balance safety and innovation
stories.Summary:
Representative Nathaniel Moran of Texas co-founded a new House AI caucus on November 21, 2026. This legislative group aims to address the rapid growth of artificial intelligence within the United States government. The representative believes that Congress must act quickly to manage the evolving landscape of this technology. He intends to lead efforts that balance safety with the need for technical progress.

The initiative requires the creation of specific safeguards to mitigate the potential risks associated with artificial intelligence. These measures must be carefully designed so they do not stifle innovation or slow down domestic development. Representative Moran argues that overly strict regulations could allow China to gain a significant competitive advantage. He believes the United States must maintain its leadership in the global technology sector.

Representative Moran is responsible for championing this balanced approach to legislative oversight of artificial intelligence. He stated that the government should protect the public without hindering the growth of new tools. The congressman emphasized that the goal is to secure the nation while fostering a pro-innovation environment. He believes that strategic oversight will prevent risks without sacrificing the speed of American discovery.

stories.Headline: LG Electronics promotes 44 executives and forms a CEO-led AI partnership team to speed AI and robotics growth
stories.Summary:
LG Electronics announced on November 19, 2026, that it promoted 44 executives and reshuffled its leadership to improve its competitive edge during the AI era. The company created a new AI partnership team that reports directly to CEO Lyu Jae-cheol to strengthen ties with global tech firms. These changes aim to accelerate growth in future businesses such as robotics, mobility, smart factories, and data center cooling. The organizational restructuring will take effect on December 1, while the executive promotions become official on January 1.

The reshuffle includes promoting Baek Seung-tae, the head of the home appliance business, and Lee Sang-woo, the head of management strategy at LG Corp, to presidents. Lee Sang-woo will now lead the TV and display business, while Baek Seung-tae continues to manage home appliances and robot actuator commercialization. LG Electronics is establishing a new applied business unit under its Eco Solution division to expand its data center cooling operations. Additionally, a new unit under the vehicle division will focus on advanced driver assistance systems and high-performance computing.

Company leadership stated that these moves are intended to speed up decision-making and respond more quickly to changing market conditions. To achieve this, regional heads for Asia, Europe, North America, Latin America, the Middle East, and Africa will now report directly to the CEO. The company is also leveraging a multibillion-dollar deal to supply chillers for data centers with a combined capacity of 5 gigawatts. LG Electronics aims to reach 1 trillion won in annual chiller sales as early as next year.

To support this growth, the company plans to establish a manufacturing subsidiary in Virginia next year to meet rising demand. This strategy builds on the creation of a robotics business center in July that also reports directly to the CEO. The electronics maker continues to streamline its global management structure by reducing layers between regional operations and headquarters. These efforts are part of a broader push to develop robotics and AI infrastructure into primary growth engines.

stories.Headline: Police in Seoul continue investigating alleged AI cheating by perfect LEET scorer Lee Jin-woo after his death
stories.Summary:
Lee Jin-woo was found dead in Seoul on Thursday, November 20, 2026. He was the first person to earn a perfect score on the Legal Education Eligibility Test. Police are investigating allegations that he used artificial intelligence to cheat on several exams. He died before he could perform a planned livestream to dispel these cheating claims. Authorities found the 32 year old man in Gangdong District at around 1:12 p.m.

The IDA admissions research institute planned a verification event at a studio in Gangnam District. This event required metal detectors and ear endoscopy checks to rule out any hidden devices. Lee was to solve the Korean language section of the current College Scholastic Ability Test. He previously entered Korea University in 2024 and Seoul National University dental school in 2026. The 2026 exam was held in November 2025.

Police said they will continue the investigation to establish the substantive truth of the case. They received a criminal complaint from lawyer Park Eun-sun and assigned it to a specific team. This team is the financial crimes investigation team of the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency. Park stated that it is important to uncover the cheating methods and any accomplices. Lawyer Kwak Joon-ho said an investigation can still proceed to establish the facts.

Lawyer Jeong Joon-yeong said meaningful results are difficult without a statement from the involved person. Some test takers say the state is failing to manage exams properly in the AI era. A 22 year old student said national exams have lost their credibility because of cheating. This person mentioned the tax accountant exam cheating case and the LEET case. Others view the failure to appear at the event as a tacit admission.

Lee once placed in the sixth to eighth tiers on the national college entrance exam. He later claimed to have developed his own study method to improve his test scores. He avoided giving clear answers about his LEET answer sheet and suspicious private tutoring in life science. His death follows a wave of AI cheating scandals that prompted tightened security for the CSAT. Prime minister Han Seong-sook reportedly spearheaded these anticheating measures for the college admissions test.

Police plan to determine the exact cause of death through a forensic examination and autopsy. They applied for an order to preserve Lee's answer booklet at Younghoon High School in Gangbuk District. A short note found with the body did not address the cheating allegations. The articles leave open whether any accomplices will be identified without Lee's statement. It remains unclear if the investigation will produce any further meaningful evidence.

stories.Headline: Korea weighs unannounced alerts during exam to catch AI cheaters
stories.Summary:
The government is considering sending unannounced disaster alert messages during this week's annual college entrance exam to catch cheaters using their phones and prevent cheating assisted by artificial intelligence, an interior ministry official said Wednesday. Authorities have been mulling measures to root out cheating during the College Scholastic Ability Test on Thursday following a recent cheating scandal in the certified tax accountant exam using AI. As part of anti-cheating measures unveiled Tuesday, the government said it would send an emergency alert message before the start of the exam to detect any unsubmitted devices. The official said the government is considering sending alerts unannounced in addition to the planned alert scheduled to be sent between 8:25 and 8:30 a.m. President Lee Jae Myung said Tuesday he had instructed authorities to review sending additional alerts, even during testing, to catch cheaters.

The government will send another disaster alert at an unspecified time during this week's annual college entrance exam, the interior ministry said Wednesday. While the first alert will be sent at 8:30 a.m., just before the start of the test, the ministry plans to send another message at an undisclosed time to find any test takers with unsubmitted phones. The ministry said the alerts will ring for 10.5 seconds at full volume, urging the public not to be alarmed. The education ministry notified schools nationwide Wednesday that it will allow test takers to only bring in pencils inside CSAT exam rooms, revising its list of permitted items. Authorities earlier notified test takers that they were allowed to bring black marker pens, correction tape, erasers, pencils and mechanical pencil lead for the exam, and under the revised rules, stationery items except for pencils will be provided at the test sites.

President Lee Jae Myung called on officials Tuesday to thoroughly prepare anti-cheating measures for the nationwide college entrance exam set to take place this week, describing cheating as a grave crime that undermines social trust. Lee made the remarks during an emergency meeting to inspect the country's readiness for the CSAT, also known in Korean as Suneung, scheduled for Thursday, following widespread concerns over cheating using AI. Lee said the Suneung is a symbol of fairness and a ladder of opportunity in our society during a video meeting held from Manila, as he wrapped up his visit to the city for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. Lee added that officials must take strict action against those who engage in misconduct, adhering to a zero-tolerance policy, while asking them to come up with response measures against AI-assisted cheating. In a subsequent social media post, Lee said the government plans to offer a reward of over 100 million won, or US$74,805, per case to those who report instances of cheating involving advanced gadgets, should the case be confirmed.

Anti-cheating measures announced earlier Tuesday include physically checking all glasses worn by test takers, covering buttons on their clothes with stickers and blocking Wi-Fi networks inside and near the test sites. The government also warned that test takers caught cheating will be banned from the CSAT for the next 10 years, while facing criminal punishment. The move appears to reflect concerns of misconduct involving miniature cameras hidden inside personal items brought by test takers. South Korea has recently been rocked by the recent confession of the top scorer on this year's certified tax accountant exam that he had cheated with the help of AI and digital devices.

The incident has deepened worries of such cheating on the upcoming CSAT, widely seen as a major life event in South Korea, where the university one goes to can heavily influence career prospects. The anti-cheating measures were unveiled Tuesday, and the education ministry notified schools nationwide Wednesday of the revised permitted items list. The first alert will be sent at 8:30 a.m. just before the start of the test, while the planned alert was scheduled to be sent between 8:25 and 8:30 a.m.

The interior ministry official said that if the time is known, there would effectively be no point in additional alerts. stories.Headline: Sitespace co-CEO Lee Ju-yeon demonstrates smart glasses at Seoul education office training for CSAT staff
stories.Summary:
Lee Ju-yeon, co-CEO of the nonprofit startup Sitespace, is the woman shown wearing black smart glasses and looking at a test paper in recent articles about exam cheating using artificial intelligence glasses. The photo was taken on the 11th at the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education in Yongsan-gu, Seoul, during a training session for dedicated smart-glasses headquarters staff for the College Scholastic Ability Test. Sitespace had first contacted the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education to propose introducing the functions of smart glasses, which led to the event. At the training, they demonstrated functions such as taking photos with smart glasses, solving test questions, and communicating with a smartphone. Reporters flocked in to film the demonstration, and photos of Lee appeared in multiple outlets after suspicions emerged on the 12th about cheating with smart glasses by the top scorer in the tax accountant exam.

The session taught staff assigned to test sites in Seoul about the features of smart glasses and how to identify them. Co-CEO Jeong Jin-seorang said they first went to show the actual glasses to supervisors at the education office, and after they asked that teachers also be allowed to handle them directly, it turned into a training session. The other woman photographed with Lee was a practicum guide hired short-term for the day's training. Sitespace assisted with smart-glasses identification at test sites on the 19th, the day of the CSAT, identifying models by checking photos sent by the education authorities when a device suspected of being smart glasses was found. A smart-glasses identification aid app developed by Sitespace, which detects nearby Bluetooth and Wi-Fi signals and helps determine whether glasses are AI-enabled based on photos taken from multiple angles, was also used by CSAT proctors.

Lee said in a phone call with Kyunghyang Shinmun on the 19th that AI glasses can be used for public-interest purposes as well, but it seemed like public opinion was becoming too negative. She said they told the education office they wished to explain the functions of the glasses free of charge for the public good. Lee said she was there for work, so she wore comfortable clothes with no makeup, and she did not expect reporters to come. She said that because the proctor teachers have portrait rights issues, she told them it would be better to photograph us doing the demonstration instead. Lee said that at first she was flustered, but now she thinks she has come to enjoy it a bit, and that she is glad many people have learned that there are AI-glasses services like ours engaged in public-interest work.

Jeong recalled that she finished a lecture for teachers in the basement auditorium and came upstairs, and Lee was surrounded by cameras firing flashes like a movie scene. They said they had attended without knowing the event would be open to the press. After the articles ran, people with visual impairments and related institutions reportedly inquired about trying out the app. Jeong said they received many identification requests, but most turned out to be ordinary glasses.

According to the Ministry of Education, one case of cheating using smart glasses during the exam was uncovered that day at a CSAT test site in South Chungcheong Province. Sitespace launched after winning the top prize in April at the startup competition of Hongik University, the alma mater of the two co-founders. Jeong said they at first envisioned a docent service in museums based on smart glasses, but after meeting many people with visual impairments, they realized what was truly needed was technology that helps with mobility. Sitespace is developing an app that uses the cameras and speakers of commercially available smart glasses to provide audio guidance about the surrounding environment, recognizing objects in the user's line of sight with the camera and conveying them through sound.

Instead of long sentences, it is designed to deliver only the necessary information quickly and concisely, such as sliding door, automatic door, and half open. They are currently improving functions through pilot use. After CES 2027 in Las Vegas, USA, next January, they plan to officially release the app on the Apple App Store and Google Play Store. Lee said that AI glasses and ultra-miniature cameras are being used in negative ways, but technology continues to advance.

She said they want to let people know that there are organizations that use technology for the public good. The articles do not say what became of the cheating case uncovered in South Chungcheong Province. The articles do not say how the identification requests were resolved beyond most turning out to be ordinary glasses. The articles do not give the outcome of the tax accountant exam cheating suspicions.
