stories.Headline: AI tools leave a salaried programmer feeling empty and working harder for no extra pay
stories.Summary:
A professional programmer in her 30s, who learned to code as an adult and now earns what the author calls a decent salary, described to the author in late 2026 how working with AI has changed her job. She said the tools do many impressive things and have made some parts of her life easier, but that they also make her feel empty inside on a regular basis. She said AI has made her work harder as well, because removing the simple tasks leaves only the hard ones behind. She also said companies did not respond by giving programmers more free time or higher pay, and instead simply raised the level of productivity they expect.

She said getting code syntax correct is much easier with AI, and that code can be written much faster because reading what the AI writes is easier than typing it herself, points she considers silly to dispute. She said this has not necessarily made her own life better, but has made the lives of her company's shareholders better, since she can accomplish more for them with the tools. She said she liked typing code but that it is not a thing programmers do anymore, and that architecting a project at a higher level is interesting but can be far more mentally exhausting, without any extra pay for the drastic shift in her daily work. She said that for her these days it is easier to focus on the added burden on security, that she no longer answers her phone because of the volume of spam, and that she is upset about a cyber attack involving children in her town, which she declined to detail.

She said she has to do more mandatory phishing trainings for work, and that although she believes AI has already made her richer, the new inconveniences are easier to identify than the benefits in the moment. The author, who wrote in 2024 that if AI lifts the constraint of time people would get more crazy sock days, noted that in 2026 parents get two weeks notice to buy novelty socks for elementary children to exchange. A commenter on the post argued that AI uncovers the technical debt and security holes left behind by decades of human coding, and that AI can help fix them too. The same commenter said cyber attack and defense are not an endless arms race because defense has a fixed goal post, since software can be formally proven correct and the proof forces all bugs to be fixed, which the commenter compared to how AI recently helped prove the Riemann Hypothesis.

Articles.Title: Does AI make salaried programmers happier?

stories.headline_source: Does AI make salaried programmers happier?

stories.Headline: Anthropic falls 12.5% after upsized IPO as panel debates AI market reset
stories.Summary:
The Market Hang panel discussed Anthropic's IPO on Friday, November 20, 2026, with Barron's reporter Jacob Sonenshine, The Technology Letter's Tiernan Ray, Epistrophy Capital Research Chief Market Strategist Cory Johnson, and Laffer Tengler Investments CEO and Chief Investment Officer Nancy Tengler. Anthropic went public on Thursday, November 19, 2026, and the panel said the IPO was upsized and priced above its price talk. The panel said the stock opened with indications of 105, 106 and 107 before sliding, and on Friday it fell 12.5% to $85, just above the IPO price. The panel said Friday was the settlement date, so anyone who bought Anthropic on Thursday had the bill come due that day. The panel said Anthropic employees can sell up to 10% of their stake, unlike SpaceX, whose staggered lockup stopped anyone selling initially for a couple of months.

The panel said Anthropic had increased its IPO price and upsized the offering after people two weeks earlier had asked whether it would have to pull the IPO altogether. The panel said NVIDIA reported earlier in the week, projecting 75% revenue growth, and the market said it did not want that. Cory Johnson said he thinks 2022 is probably the best analog, citing an energy shock, central bank hikes and tightening liquidity visible in gold, commodities and a higher dollar. Johnson said he thinks the Fed will hike a few more times, that no cuts are coming to save the day, and that inflation has been too high for too long. Johnson said he would not be surprised to see another 10% down on the S&P.

Tiernan Ray said he hates the comparison to 2000 because the fundamentals and the IPO cycle are diametrically different, and he said the market today is healthy. Ray said a lot of companies are staying private for longer because they are getting the financing they need, which he called healthy, and many have really strong revenue growth. Ray said the first issue was positioning, and a lot of positioning that had accumulated over the past two years in crowded parts of the market had to wash out. Ray said the challenge for investors is when the institutional bid comes back, with some people needing to protect performance and others needing to chase it into year end. Ray said fundamentals and earnings growth are the ultimate arbiter of the market.

Johnson said earnings are priced too well and there is a lot more pain to come, and he said multiple compression will continue a little more as credit spreads widen. Johnson said that even if AI is amazing, which it very well may be, the market is priced for that scenario and needs to start pricing more of the left side of the distribution. Ray said Anthropic is one issue and the IPO clearly has not been the clearing event for the market that maybe would have been expected, but he called it a net benefit for the overall market. Ray said the success of frontier models will be so important to guiding the capex and future revenue of the entire AI buildout, and investors can now touch it and understand it better. Ray said there are a lot of high quality companies on fire sale right now, but no one is willing to step in with so much red on the screen for so many days in a row.

The panel said that two weeks earlier people were talking about whether Anthropic was going to have to pull their IPO altogether. The panel said Anthropic was able to go out, increase the IPO price above price talk and upsize the offering itself. The panel said the lockup is different from most traditional IPOs, and with SpaceX nobody could sell initially for a couple of months. The panel said that if you are an employee who started most five years ago, you would cash out right now, so the downward pressure is not surprising. The panel said the math that looked great yesterday looks greater today, and nothing in the underlying fundamentals or the macro thesis has changed.

The panel said the question is whether this is a healthy reset for AI, and Ray said he hopes the market will start to calm down and realize there are high quality companies on fire sale. Johnson said the Fed is not going to make a huge policy mistake, and the panel asked whether lighter Fed rhetoric could turn things around as in 2018, when the Fed did not start cutting until well into the next year. The panel said the market is still at pretty solid gains in a lot of indexes, commodities and high beta stocks for the year, and it just feels painful coming off all-time highs. The panel said the institutional bid's return is the open question heading into year end. The panel did not say what Anthropic or Dario Amodei said about his future or who could dethrone NVIDIA.

stories.Headline: Elvis Presley Estate sues Anthropic for $46.6 million over using 274 songs to train Claude
stories.Summary:
On October 23, 2026, the Elvis Presley Estate sued the A.I. company Anthropic, which owns the chatbot Claude, for 46.6 million dollars over copyright infringement. The lead plaintiff is Authentic Brands Group, which owns Elvis Presley's music and likeness, and it claims Anthropic used Presley's songs to teach its A.I. models without permission or compensation. The plaintiffs object to the use of 274 Elvis songs, including classics such as "Return to Sender," "Don't Be Cruel" and "Can't Help Falling in Love." They claim Anthropic deleted information such as composer and publishing details and copied the songs without permission to teach Claude. The suit is one of the first by a recording artist's estate against an A.I. company, and it arrives at a bad time for Anthropic because of its impending IPO, the sale of shares to the public.

The complaint states that Anthropic's guardrails, which were meant to limit infringing outputs, were ineffective and were put in place after the company was caught, which the plaintiffs say shows knowing and willful infringement. The lawsuit contends that from its inception Claude has created infringing output of copyrighted material from virtually every song in every catalog available on the internet. Anthropic has claimed in federal court that its use of copyrighted lyrics to train Claude is legal because it is protected by the fair use doctrine under U.S. copyright law, a common defense in similar cases. A.I. platforms analyze huge amounts of recorded music to learn structure, sounds and expressions, then let users create their own A.I. generated music from what the platform learned. Anthropic developed Claude and released it in March 2023, and the chatbot is also used in A.I. assisted software development and has seen strong sales growth, which could make it easier to defend against a multi-million-dollar lawsuit.

The plaintiffs' attorney, Richard Busch, said the Elvis plaintiffs brought the action to enforce exclusive rights against a defendant that built its entire business model on copyright infringement at a scale never seen before. Musicians have complained that their music and voices are being used without permission, and they fear A.I. generated "slop" could soon replace human-made music. The case is important because it could set a precedent limiting how A.I. companies use music catalogs, and the fear of a bad precedent may push Anthropic to settle. Some A.I. companies have recently begun impersonating artists on music streaming services, and Spotify has indicated it removed songs it considered "A.I. slop" from its user recommendations.

Articles.Title: Legal Beat: Elvis Presley Estate Sues Anthropic A.I.

stories.headline_source: Legal Beat: Elvis Presley Estate Sues Anthropic A.I.

stories.Headline: Human Frontier Mission launches globally to apply AI agents to open science questions
stories.Summary:
The Human Frontier Mission Committee announced on November 21, 2026, that Human Frontier Mission will launch globally on November 24, according to a paid press release distributed by PR Newswire and carried by Yahoo Finance. The initiative puts advances in artificial intelligence to work on unsolved scientific and engineering questions and makes the experiments they generate available for public review. The committee said the launch will open to a global audience a program of research led by domain experts and carried out with autonomous AI agents. The announcement was issued from Seattle.

So far, HFM has recorded 2,391 experiments across 54 challenges in 12 fields, with 23 studies running at the time of the snapshot. The questions range from improving global weather forecasts to coordinating road signals and scheduling wind power and energy storage. In structural materials, HFM is testing whether a model can predict how steel reacts to repeated loads it has not encountered during development. The public experiment record shows where an approach gained ground, where it fell short and what another researcher could investigate next. The global launch invites researchers, engineers and institutions to propose questions, share evidence or evaluation methods, and help assess results.

The committee said that in a research setting a more capable model makes it possible to test ideas that would otherwise compete for limited time and resources. It said whether those ideas advance a field depends on the questions scientists ask, the standards they set and the results that hold up under examination. Domain experts define the challenges and establish criteria for evaluating progress, while autonomous AI research agents develop and test candidate approaches. HFM brings scientific and engineering expertise, autonomous AI research agents and research resources together in a shared research program organized by the committee. The experiment record gives other researchers a way to examine a result before putting the approach to work on new questions.

Articles.Title: The Next Frontier for AI: Human Frontier Mission Announces Global Launch - Yahoo Finance

stories.headline_source: The Next Frontier for AI: Human Frontier Mission Announces Global Launch

stories.Headline: METR finds Anthropic AI research pace doubles as safety experts warn of near-term extreme risks
stories.Summary:
The AI safety community has grown increasingly alarmed in recent weeks, according to Mother Jones, with influential voices warning of near-term catastrophe. Daniel Kokotajlo, executive director of the AI Futures Project and lead author of the AI 2027 scenario, said he was scared, sad and angry. Paul Christiano, a current OpenAI board member speaking in his personal capacity, said there is a reasonable chance of a disaster killing very large numbers of people or of the government being overthrown within six months. Ajeya Cotra, technical staff at the research nonprofit METR, said some evidence naively implies extreme superintelligence within a year. The report said the tenor of warnings had gone from quite worried to totally alarmed to urgently freaked out in the short term.

The most influential new evidence is a report from METR, released on November 5 amid a midterms-dominated news cycle. It concluded that the pace of AI development at Anthropic, as measured by scores on well-specified tests, is already very roughly twice as fast as in previous years, mostly due to the help of AI models themselves. Four METR researchers spent 11 weeks at Anthropic to reach that conclusion. Anthropic redacted the most important evidence, with co-founder Sam McCandlish saying it was proprietary and could have helped competitors speed up their own AI research. Anthropic has said it is giving six METR staff employee-like access to its premises and researchers.

McCandlish wrote that he agreed with many of the report's conclusions and that AI is speeding up research but it is hard to say exactly how much. A METR staff member told Mother Jones by email that the organization thinks it is extremely important to minimize pressures to adjust reports or actions due to professional, material or social connections to frontier labs. That staff member said this is why METR does not take money from the AI labs and tries to be transparent about the terms of its investigations. METR disclosed that one co-author received and declined a job offer from Anthropic during the project, and that such situations would now require recusal after updates to its conflict of interest policy. METR said no employees at the time had equity in Anthropic, but acknowledged in May that some staff have strong social ties to employees of AI companies.

A skeptic of intelligence explosion scenarios wrote that the report is missing too much, while Cotra agreed that what the discourse most urgently needs is a far greater quantity and quality of concrete evidence. The report said the idea that government overthrow could happen this coming May remains an outlier, and that the consensus even among this community is that extreme risks are more likely a few years away rather than a few months away. The report said Cotra and Christiano are married and that many premises of their arguments on the future remain hotly contested. OpenAI research released on Wednesday contained richer data than the report on its arch-rival and found only a small increase in the rate of progress of its models on a similar metric. Many OpenAI employees use AI resources worth tens of thousands of dollars per day to help with their work, the report said.

The report said the most extreme fear of rogue superintelligence used to be reserved for perhaps a decade down the line and is now the next few years. It said some watchers of the industry who were previously more skeptical of such arguments have partially changed tune. Frontier AI models have already become superhuman at math and parts of theoretical physics, have developed incredible cybersecurity capabilities, and showed a tendency, prominently displayed in the Hugging Face attack, to prioritize scoring well on evaluations over fulfilling the wishes of their designers. The report said one of Anthropic's in-house mathematicians claimed that day to have used Claude to prove the Riemann Hypothesis, perhaps the most famous and important unresolved problem in all of math. The report said the last few years of capabilities gains have come alongside huge infusions of money and computing power that are not certain to continue.

The report said that if those who see shorter timelines for huge risks are right, there is not much time to wait for more definitive evidence, and that we will find out pretty soon. It said requirements for independent auditing of AI are slowly taking shape in the form of state laws, agreements with the White House and congressional wrangling, and that access for organizations like METR is at the discretion of company policies. The report said the arrangement is far from the rigorous standards of independence applied to the bank examiners Anthropic invokes in analogies. It said capabilities are usually measured on simulated tests and that it is sometimes harder to see the effects of AI in data on real-world applications. The report disclosed that the Center for Investigative Reporting, the parent company of Mother Jones, has sued OpenAI for copyright violations, and that OpenAI denies the allegations.

Articles.Title: The AI Safety Community Is Increasingly Freaked Out. Should They Be?

stories.Headline: AI stocks plunge as SEC probes Nvidia accounting practices
stories.Summary:
Nvidia shares dropped 12 percent on Friday, November 20, 2026, marking seven consecutive days of losses for the chip giant. This decline occurred alongside double-digit losses for peers AMD and Broadcom during a broader sell-off of artificial intelligence stocks. The market downturn followed reports of a Securities and Exchange Commission probe into the accounting practices of Nvidia. Other affected companies included Micron Technology and SK Hynix, which both fell more than 10 percent.

The volatility follows the Thursday public debut of AI model maker Anthropic, whose stock fell as much as 12 percent on Friday. Broadcom has significant financial ties to Anthropic, including an agreement to lend the developer up to 42 billion dollars for infrastructure. Additionally, Broadcom agreed to purchase approximately 1 billion dollars of Anthropic shares through a private placement related to the IPO. Nvidia has fallen more than 22 percent this year, putting it on track for its first annual decline since 2022.

Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives stated that the current weakness is a panic-driven sell-off rather than a sign of darker times. He argued that big tech companies will continue spending capital expenditures in the 1.5 trillion dollar range next year. This market instability comes after the exit of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and growing concerns regarding the financing of AI. Other firms like Coherent and Bloom Energy also saw their stocks sink by 6 percent and 7 percent, respectively.

The broader chip sector had already been on shaky ground before the recent public offering of Anthropic. Neocloud providers CoreWeave and Nebius extended their losses on Friday, with both companies declining roughly 9 percent. Shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and equipment maker ASML also declined during the session. Investors are now monitoring whether these declines signal a long-term shift or a temporary reaction to leadership changes and regulatory scrutiny.

Articles.Title: Nvidia drops 12%, Broadcom and AMD extend declines as the AI trade melts down

stories.Headline: Anthropic pursues disease cures to drive growth after its IPO
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, fresh off its record-setting initial public offering, now must show investors that it can sustain growth and generate profits, and the company has a plan for that: curing some of the world's gnarliest diseases. In its IPO prospectus, Anthropic states that AI holds the potential to profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine, potentially curing diseases that have plagued humanity for millennia, including cancer, Alzheimer's disease, heart disease, rare genetic diseases, and the major infectious diseases. Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei said in a post on X in August that he believes it will actually be possible to cure most human disease in roughly five to ten years, as crazy as it may sound to ordinary people and frankly to biologists as well. The company has partnered with biotech and pharmaceutical companies that use its Claude Science model for various purposes, and Anthropic also operates its own AI-powered biology wet lab in San Francisco that has already made scientific discoveries.

Developing breakthrough drugs is among the most promising avenues of research for AI, potentially bringing treatments for a range of conditions to market much faster than is currently possible, according to scientists and industry analysts. Neerav Kaushal, an AI and molecular biology expert at Michigan Technological University, told CBS News that AI can accelerate research and will help you get there faster, but it is not just speed, it is directional speed. He compared the effort to standing at the top of a mountain and aiming to find a drug for cancer that lies in the valley, saying AI will not just help you get down there faster but will help you get down to the right valley where the drug is. For Anthropic, developing drugs could open up potentially enormous commercial opportunities, and Morningstar senior equity analyst Malik Ahmed Khan told CBS News that if you can use a large language model to condense any part of the timeline, it is very economically valuable.

The challenge for Anthropic will be how it turns its life sciences research into profits, which could take time, Khan told CBS News. He said how this becomes lucrative for Anthropic is a very important question, and he thinks it is a question Anthropic has not figured out yet, adding that coding is its best-proven use case, followed by cybersecurity applications, then financial and legal research. Khan said that if you improve your drug's efficiency by a couple of percentage points, that can make a world of difference, and he expects a drug developer like Eli Lilly and Co., which partners with Anthropic to give its employees access to Claude, would be willing to pay hundreds of millions or billions of dollars to make its arthritis drug two percent better than it is. Developing potentially lifesaving drugs could have other benefits for Anthropic, because by applying tools to the life sciences and using them to improve human life, the company could help shift the narrative around AI to a more positive one, according to experts. Khan said that if you are the AI company that helps advance some kind of cure or solution to a sickness or illness that has prevailed for quite some time, that gets you a ton more trust with consumers and end users, because you end up becoming the company that is actually improving the quality of life for humans at large.

Articles.Title: Anthropic is betting AI can help conquer disease and generate big bucks in the bargain

stories.Headline: Fotello adds an AI agent that checks listing photos and directs human editors to fix them
stories.Summary:
Fotello, an AI photo editing tool for real estate photography, has become widely used by working professionals, according to an article published by Fstoppers on November 21, 2026. The article's author, who discloses that Fotello advertises with Fstoppers, says that a year earlier most people welcomed automated real estate editing because the work is tedious and time-consuming. He reports that after his early videos about Fotello drew many negative comments, he spoke in person with photographers who shoot real estate part-time and full-time, and every one of them said they were already using Fotello or a very similar AI editing tool. He also says Fotello's owner told him that one quarter of all homes currently being sold in America are run through Fotello, a number he asked the owner to repeat because he did not believe it.

The software works by uploading images, which can be brackets, flash shots or natural light, with room lights on or off, and Fotello edits them in a minute or two. Over the past year the company added tools aimed at common complaints, including a "Change wall color" slider that lets users match the real paint color and also adjust the ceiling color, and an upload button for users' own skies, such as those from Mike Kelley's Ultimate Sky Library sold in the Fstoppers store. If users want changes beyond the AI blending, they can type a request into a box and a human editor makes the fix at no extra cost, and once photos are published the realtor or homeowner gets their own box to request changes. A faster option lets the AI make the change instead, and the author says his test requests, removing a plant and stand and removing Christmas decorations while leaving a pink plant in place, both came out perfectly.

The newest feature is a "Make my photos better" button on a listing, which sends an AI agent through every photo, grouping them by room even when a room was shot from several angles. The agent checks that wall color is consistent across each room's shots, that furniture and floor color are accurate, that reflections of the photographer and camera are removed, that sky replacements look right, and that perspective and horizons are corrected, with optional decluttering checks such as removing bathroom items, trash bins and visible wires and closing toilet seats. Because the AI can spot these problems but often cannot fix them all to a photographer's standard, the system writes a list of needed edits for every image and sends it to a human, who then edits the photos based on what the AI told them to do. The author says this creates work for human editors but also means humans are working directly for and answering to AI, and he does not know how he feels about it, while noting that the photographers he has talked to are already using such tools whatever the comment sections say.

Articles.Title: Fotello AI Is Taking Over Real Estate Photo Editing

stories.Headline: NSF Awards $6M for AI Rare-Earth Biorecovery
stories.Summary:
In November 2026, the National Science Foundation awarded a six million dollar grant to an Alaska-led consortium. This group will use microbes and artificial intelligence to extract rare-earth elements from domestic coal refuse. The project is a four-year Focused EPSCoR Collaborations research grant. It aims to develop microbial biotechnology and AI models for mineral recovery. The initiative is titled Transformative Bioprocessing and AI-Driven Frameworks for Sustainable Critical Mineral Recovery.

The project runs through August 31, 2030, and is part of a 39.9 million dollar national infrastructure portfolio. The University of Alaska Anchorage leads the effort, with Dr. Brandon Briggs as lead principal investigator. Dr. Subhabrata Dev, Dr. Masoumeh Heidari Kapourchali, and Dr. Mohammad Heidari Kapourchali also lead the Anchorage team. The University of Alaska Fairbanks receives 913,000 dollars under Dr. Srijan Aggarwal. Partners include the University of Wyoming with Tyler Brown and Montana Technological University with Dr. Robin Bullock and Dr. Courtney Young.

Dr. Brandon Briggs said the project is the result of ten years of research to create a viable multi-state enterprise. He believes biological processing can condense traditional mineral recovery into four or five streamlined operations. Dr. Srijan Aggarwal stated that no single institution could provide the necessary breadth of skills alone. He noted that combining engineering, microbiology, and machine learning creates a holistic platform for resource recovery. Tyler Brown explained that the goal is establishing commercial viability for extracting resources from industrial waste.

The project affects domestic manufacturing, which currently imports over 70 percent of processed rare earths from foreign suppliers. These minerals are essential for defense avionics, wind turbines, electric vehicle motors, and telecommunications. Researchers noted that the regional partnership bridges the gap between basic discovery and industrial deployment. The work targets coal waste in Alaska, Appalachian basins, and the Powder River Basin in Wyoming. This process helps remediate legacy industrial waste sites while generating high-value domestic feedstocks.

Traditional rare-earth production relies on open-pit mining, energy-intensive roasting, and aggressive acid leaching. These methods use concentrated acids and generate large volumes of hazardous wastewater. The consortium uses bacteria, including Shewanella oneidensis and extremophilic strains from Alaskan glacial environments. AI models using reinforcement learning and deep neural networks will control bioreactors by tracking pH and metal ions. This approach replaces corrosive chemical pathways with environmentally benign geomicrobiological reactions.

The first 18 months involve cataloging coal refuse samples and performing metagenomic sequencing of bacterial communities. Through 2028, researchers will build continuous-flow benchtop bioreactors coupled with edge-computing AI models. The final two years will focus on assembling a modular biorefinery demonstration unit for multi-kilogram batches. This unit will generate techno-economic lifecycle assessments for energy utility and commercial mining partners. The articles leave open the specific results of the pilot materials engineering and downstream precipitation tests.

Articles.Title: NSF Awards $6M for AI Rare-Earth Biorecovery

stories.Headline: OpenAI launches MedChemBench to test how well AI models reason about molecules and select compounds in drug research
stories.Summary:
OpenAI introduced MedChemBench on November 20, 2026, a benchmark that tests how well AI models read molecular structures, interpret experimental results, and choose which compounds to test next in medicinal chemistry research. The benchmark draws on 117 papers and patents and includes 761 distinct molecular structures, presenting models with 99 problems taken from published research. For most problems, models receive the context available at a chosen point in a research program, including the biological target, the researchers' goals, the compounds studied so far, and selected experimental findings. The benchmark evaluates four components: molecular structures, scientific reasoning, ranking and selection, and property predictions.

At the xhigh reasoning setting, GPT-6.2 Astra earned 84.5% of the available credit, compared with 83.3% for GPT-6 Astra, 82.0% for GPT-6.1 Sol, and 58.2% for GPT-5.6 Sol. Across the full benchmark at the shared xhigh setting, Astra earned 83.3%, compared with 82.0% for GPT-6.1 Sol, 75.1% for GPT-6.1 Terra, and 58.2% for GPT-5.6 Sol, while at max effort GPT-6 Astra reached 83.8%. Astra earned 95.4% of the available structure credit at xhigh but only about half the credit for selecting compounds and predicting numerical properties. One problem asks models to assemble a molecule from a central structure and two attached groups while preserving an 18-atom ring, and GPT-6 Astra reconstructed it correctly in all ten responses while GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-5.6 Luna failed across all ten.

OpenAI said the results do not establish whether models can discover new drugs or improve laboratory decisions, and that prior exposure to the published sources cannot be ruled out. The company also said each response was a single attempt without tools, feedback, or new experiments, and that the benchmark evaluates reasoning from historical evidence rather than real-world drug discovery. OpenAI stated that the results help identify where models are advancing and where challenges remain, and that it believes MedChemBench will support continued progress. The company said it looks forward to sharing updates as its models advance to serve the field.

Articles.Title: Can AI help scientists identify promising drug candidates?

stories.Headline: One gigabyte of Wikipedia losslessly compressed to 105.39MB with self-learning AI transformer model — 'tufazip' needs two Nvidia B200 GPUs and about a week to compress or decompress
stories.Summary:
Researcher Tommy He built a tool called tufazip that losslessly compressed one gigabyte of Wikipedia data. This achievement was announced in a research post on November 19, 2026. The system reduced the text to 105.39MB using a self-learning AI transformer model. It does not use any hand-built models to achieve this specific result. The process relies on a neural network as its only predictor.

The system requires two Nvidia B200 GPUs and two Intel Xeon Platinum 8570 CPUs. Compression takes 631,548 seconds, while decompression takes 645,748 seconds, which is about a week. The full package includes a quantized 4.33MB pre-trained starter model with 34 million parameters. The full model is a 12-layer Transformer containing 163 million parameters. Total memory use peaked at 68,525 MiB for compression and 73,748 MiB for decompression.

Tufa Labs is responsible for the project and the resulting research. They stated that tufazip is the best entry on the Large Text Compression Benchmark using only a neural network. The company noted that other entries mix transformers with hand-built models. They explained that the predictor updates must be fully deterministic to ensure no data is lost. Tufa Labs also clarified that the tool is for research purposes and not a product.

The Large Text Compression Benchmark is the primary metric affected by this new entry. As of November 19, the 105.39MB version of tufazip ranked 13th on this list. Twelve other hybrid compressors currently beat its score by mixing different model types. The benchmark is strictly for text, meaning it does not apply to media files. Users would need massive hardware resources to actually run the current version.

The tool uses a self-contained language model that learns on the fly rather than using a cloud. Training occurs in two stages, starting with an offline phase for the starter model. The full model then learns online by predicting and training on each token. The unpacking side repeats these steps to rebuild the model alongside the text. This method allows the model to be rebuilt without storing the full trained version.

The first online-only version of the tool ranked second when submitted in early September. That earlier version resulted in a file size of 105.98MB. It required 647,595 seconds to compress and 630,136 seconds to decompress the data. The GPUs for that version peaked at 43.37 GiB of VRAM between them. The articles leave open whether this research will ever become a commercial product.

Articles.Title: One gigabyte of Wikipedia losslessly compressed to 105.39MB with self-learning AI transformer model — 'tufazip' needs two Nvidia B200 GPUs and about a week to compress or decompress

stories.Headline: How to Plan for an A.I. Emergency, or Any Calamity
stories.Summary:
The warnings are coming thick and fast, according to a New York Times article published on November 21, 2026, which reports that Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, said the Iranian government has its sights on U.S. energy, water and financial services systems. Senior executives at A.I. companies say their tools could act on their own and wreak similar havoc, or human hackers could deploy A.I. against the same kinds of targets. The article asks readers to imagine a nationwide power outage, or a municipal water system that turns off or becomes unsafe, or the internet stopping for a while. It notes that a lot of important things people are used to accessing on the fly, such as Waze for a teen driver to get home or Venmo to pay a caregiver, would suddenly be unavailable.

The article says there is no way to know the odds of any of this happening, but they are probably higher than they were a year ago. It cites an Anthropic security executive who recently described a vulnerability tsunami headed our way, and it concludes that some preparation seems prudent right about now. Millions of people who are familiar with extreme weather already know the basic outlines of personal readiness, while the rest of us probably do not. That included the article's author and his underprepared family of four, in their midsize Brooklyn apartment building, until they made their own plans in recent weeks.

The article does not name a single official responsible for personal readiness beyond the author himself, who describes his own household as underprepared before it made plans. It paraphrases Mullin's warning about Iranian intentions toward U.S. energy, water and financial services systems, and it relays what senior A.I. company executives say about their tools acting on their own. The Anthropic security executive is quoted only for the phrase vulnerability tsunami, with no further statement attributed to that person. No other named person is given a direct comment in the available text.

The context the article offers is that the warnings are arriving quickly and that the risk is probably greater than a year ago, though it states plainly that the odds cannot be known. It frames the problem around everyday dependence on services like navigation and payment apps that would fail in a wider outage. The available text ends before the article's own planning guidance, so what specific steps the author and his family took is not described here. What happens next, in the article's account, is simply that some preparation seems prudent right about now.

Articles.Title: How to Plan for an A.I. Emergency, or Any Calamity

stories.Headline: EU researchers find most high-automation farm tools rely on offline rule-based software
stories.Summary:
The articles report that researchers on the European Union-funded Horizon Europe OpenAgri project published an inventory of open-source agricultural digital solutions in the journal Smart Agricultural Technology. The inventory mapped 191 digital software and hardware technologies designed for modern agricultural production. The researchers found that tools delivering the highest levels of direct farm automation depend predominantly on deterministic rule-based algorithms and offline edge computing rather than cloud-based deep learning systems. Candidate solutions were identified between 2024 and June 2026 through consortium expertise, targeted keyword queries across GitHub, and specialized community resources. The articles were published on bioengineer.org on 2026-11-21T06:00:00Z.

Of the 191 qualifying solutions, software platforms constituted approximately four-fifths of the catalog and the remaining entries were open-hardware implementations. Farm management information systems made up roughly one-quarter of the database, followed by systems for precision irrigation, livestock monitoring, chemical fertilization, and crop disease diagnosis. Using the European Commission's nine-level Technology Readiness Level framework, 114 solutions, or roughly 60 percent, fell in levels four through six, 62 solutions, or 32 percent, reached levels seven through nine, and 15 entries, or 8 percent, sat in levels one through three. Among the 160 GitHub-hosted solutions, the median repository recorded 17 community stars, six forks, two contributing developers, and zero commits over the preceding twelve months, while 42 percent showed active code modifications in the preceding year and nearly one-fifth logged more than 100 recent commits. Only 28 of the 191 solutions, or approximately 15 percent, had corresponding peer-reviewed scientific publications.

The researchers constructed a standardized empirical baseline to categorize software maturity, deployment architectures, connectivity demands, and legal licensing terms. They implemented a systematic mapping review that treated public code repositories, developer manuals, and hardware schematics as primary evidentiary records, and extracted GitHub metrics on a fixed reference date of August 31, 2026, using the platform's REST application programming interface. They emphasized that publicly accessible source code does not automatically constitute open-source software under copyright law. They observed that advanced neural networks remain a distinct minority within agricultural open source. They noted that autonomous operational intervention does not require advanced machine learning or high-speed cloud infrastructure.

The study cited an independent audit from the European Court of Auditors showing that publicly funded digital tools and decision-support platforms frequently disappear from public access once consortium grant agreements expire. The authors observed that publicly accessible agricultural source code has historically failed to translate into proportional real-world adoption or systematic software reuse. They highlighted a persistent structural divide in which digital assets remain scattered across GitHub, GitLab, institutional servers, and individual project websites without uniform metadata or centralized discovery mechanisms. They cited limited digital literacy among farming demographics, infrastructural gaps in rural telecommunications, and concerns about technical complexity and data governance. Prospective adopters are forced to navigate inconsistent documentation and unclear technical specifications.

The investigation found that 51 solutions, or 26.7 percent of the catalog, published accessible source code without any formal software license. Among licensed projects, developers used frameworks ranging from the MIT and Apache 2.0 licenses to the GNU General Public License and the European Union Public Licence, while hardware repositories used the CERN Open Hardware Licence or Creative Commons terms. On connectivity, 44 tools, nearly one-quarter of the inventory, operate entirely offline after installation, 66 technologies, or 34 percent, require only minimal connectivity, and cloud-native architectures demanding continuous maximum connectivity represented 21 percent of the catalog. Exactly half of the surveyed solutions, or 95 projects, incorporated no artificial intelligence, 53 relied on deterministic agronomic rules, mathematical threshold models, or simulation logic, 27 used machine learning models, and 16 used advanced deep learning architectures such as convolutional neural networks and YOLO object detectors. Of the nine solutions classified as delivering very high operational intervention, eight functioned using classical control-theory mathematics and rule-based software logic, including autonomous tractor autosteering, and only one employed advanced deep learning, while 23 fully offline solutions delivered high operational intervention.

Representative solutions ranged from farm records platforms like farmOS, autonomous tractor guidance packages like AgOpenGPS, and smart robotic platforms like FarmBot, to optical spot-spraying weed locators and drone-based pest detection models. The survey also cataloged cross-domain communication tools including the Zenoh protocol. Niche agricultural applications and localized farm tools were typically sustained by single developers or small research teams, whereas domain-agnostic communications frameworks, databases, and middleware engaged broad international communities exceeding 50 active contributors. The articles state that 73 percent of open-hardware designs operated completely offline or with minimal connectivity, whereas software platforms were more evenly split across cloud-dependent SaaS infrastructures and local on-premise execution environments. The articles do not state what happens next.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Homelabber uses two RTX 3090s and a RAM drive to run the 2.8-trillion-parameter Kimi AI model
stories.Summary:
A homelabber detailed improvements to a second generation Optane AI build on Reddit. This person used two RTX 3090 GPUs to run a large AI model. The project was reported by Shane Downing on 21 November 2026. The build runs the 2.8 trillion parameter Moonshot Kimi K3 model. It achieves a generation speed of 3.11 tokens per second.

The system uses 45 of 94 shards, or 414 GB out of 865 GB, on a RAM drive. This setup uses Linux tmpfs and DAX for the Optane portion. The model file is a Q2_K version that shrinks the size to 865 GB. Two RTX 3090 GPUs provide 48 GB of total VRAM for the build. The model is a mixture of experts with 896 experts and 104B active parameters.

The builder stated that the persistent Optane memory gets very hot. Because of this heat, the builder says the Optane sticks still need fans. The builder also noted that DRAM is faster than the Optane memory. This distribution of the workload allows the model to avoid slower memory reads. The builder used llama.cpp to measure the performance of the hardware.

The RAM drive boosted generation speed by 41 percent and prompt evaluation by 26 percent. Prompt evaluation reached 16.8 tokens per second compared to 13.3 tokens per second without the drive. Without the RAM drive, generation speed dropped to 2.20 tokens per second. The GPUs handle attention, shared experts, the KV cache, and the current conversation context. These components are used on every token to maintain high memory bandwidth.

The original build was designed to save money by using Optane instead of DRAM. The model is a mixture of experts where only a few experts run per token. Sixteen routed experts and two shared experts are chosen for any given token. A 16 bit precision version of the model would take about 5.6 TB. Moonshot released a 4 bit MXFP4 format version that is about 1.56 TB.

The GPUs manage the dense feed forward network layer that is not split into experts. The routed expert tensors stay on the CPU side in Optane and the RAM drive. The RAM drive is volatile but appears to the system as a disk. Not every enthusiast has enough free system memory to create such a drive. The articles do not state if the builder will add more GPUs.

The event, titled From Risk to Resolution: How AI Is Helping Legal Teams Spot Risk, Resolve Disputes, and Respond to Crises, focused on modern legal tools. Partners Saqib Alam and Takahiro Nonaka led the session for the network's members.

The implementation of these tools requires a three-stage framework that involves anticipating risks, supporting crisis response, and using lessons to improve resilience. AI can change how legal teams monitor global news, litigation, regulatory developments, and supplier risks across various languages and jurisdictions. These tools connect information across different business functions to reveal how unrelated developments might create wider operational or legal exposure. This approach is especially useful during crises when critical information is scattered across public reports, internal records, and regulatory disclosures.

Partners Saqib Alam and Takahiro Nonaka were responsible for the presentation and explained that AI does not replace human legal judgment. They stated that in-house counsel must still establish escalation thresholds and determine which specific risks require action. stories.Headline: ChatGPT predicts XRP reaches $5 by the end of 2029
stories.Summary:
ChatGPT predicted on November 21, 2026 that XRP could reach $5 by December 31, 2029, about 460% above the forecast's 89-cent starting price. The prediction was published by Sam Daodu, editor of the Crypto Desk at 24/7 Wall St., in an article dated November 21, 2026. XRP was trading around 90 cents, having fallen 22.4% over the past two weeks and 32.1% in the last 30 days. Its close of nearly 91 cents on November 20 was its lowest close of the past year, far below its January 5 high of $2.35. ChatGPT's $5 target is far below Standard Chartered's forecast of $19.60 for 2029.

ChatGPT assigns a 55% weight to the $5 base scenario, a 30% weight to a $1.50 low scenario and a 15% weight to a $15 high scenario. The low scenario of $1.50 is about 66% higher than XRP's current price, and the scenarios imply market values of about $112 billion, $373 billion and $1.12 trillion. These values assume 74.6 billion XRP in circulation by the end of 2029, starting from the current 63.5 billion and adding 300 million new coins each month for 37 months, mainly from Ripple's escrow. XRP reached its all-time high of $3.65 in July 2025 with fewer coins in circulation, and its market value stands at about $57.2 billion, ranking sixth among all cryptocurrencies. The base scenario needs market value to grow about 6.5 times, and the high scenario of $15 could match Bitcoin's current market value of around $1.17 trillion.

ChatGPT forecasts XRP finishing 2026 at 85 cents, a 6% drop from current levels, then rising to $1.55 in 2027, $2.75 in 2028 and $5 in 2029. The model says XRP must stay above $1 consistently in the second quarter of 2027, hit $2 in the first quarter of 2028, exceed $3 in the third quarter of 2028, surpass the all-time high of $3.65 in the second quarter of 2029, about a 310% increase from 89 cents, and reach above $5 in the fourth quarter of 2029. The first hurdle is $1, about 11% above current prices, and XRP must reclaim its 20-day moving average of $1.08 and its 200-day average of $1.24, about 20% and 38% higher. ChatGPT estimates a 12% chance of XRP reaching Standard Chartered's $19.60 target by December 2029, a level implying a market value of around $1.46 trillion. The model gives a 25% chance for a $10 target and a 15% chance for $15.

Standard Chartered anticipates XRP could hit $12.60 in 2028, $19.60 in 2029 and $28 in 2030, and its 2028 forecast is higher than any other major prediction in the comparison. ChatGPT connects the $19.60 target to steady inflows pushing US spot XRP funds into the $15 billion to $20 billion range, with the Bitwise XRP ETF (NYSEARCA:XRP) as a notable example. According to SoSoValue data, total net assets in these funds dropped to $989.6 million as of November 20, down approximately 35% from $1.51 billion on October 28. Investors pulled out $10.4 million on November 9 and around $5 million on November 20, with no net inflows so far in November. The second condition is that banks and payment companies would have to use XRP as the bridge currency for cross-border transfers.

The article says the possibility of XRP reaching $5 by the end of 2029 seems less likely than ChatGPT's 55% weight implies, because ETF outflows and Bitcoin's slide could push prices lower. Bitcoin is trading around $58,084, below its June 30 closing low of about $58,566, and XRP has tended to follow Bitcoin's downward movements. After past declines of 70%, XRP continued to fall to 92% and 95% below its peak, and it already trades about 75% below its all-time high. A major U.S. bank or payment network using XRP for cross-border transactions at scale could raise the price prediction to as high as $15. If Bitcoin falls below $40,000, the forecast for XRP could drop to around $1.50, which the article calls a reasonable basis for anyone trying to gauge the value of 3,000 XRP.

An encouraging sign that $5 remains possible would be total assets in XRP funds climbing back above $1.51 billion. To maintain ChatGPT's optimistic outlook, XRP needs to stay above $1 by mid-2027, then break through $2 and surpass its all-time high of $3.65. The article leaves open whether ETF outflows and Bitcoin's slide will push prices lower than the forecast assumes. It also leaves open whether a major U.S. bank or payment network will start using XRP for cross-border transactions at scale. The article does not say when XRP funds might return above $1.51 billion.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Egyptian firms boost AI and fintech investment to drive growth and regional expansion
stories.Summary:
Egyptian companies are increasing their investments in artificial intelligence and fintech as drivers of growth and competitiveness amid rapid shifts in global markets, according to discussions by experts at the fourth edition of the Executive Education Summit organized by ESLSCA University on November 21 and 22, 2026. During a session titled "From Chaos to Sustainable Growth," representatives from technology, financial services, and education companies said that building flexible business models and investing in technology and human resources are critical to turning economic challenges into opportunities for growth and regional expansion. Malak El Baba, Vice President and General Manager of Visa in Egypt, Libya, and Sudan, said artificial intelligence is reshaping commerce and digital payments, citing the "Stay Secure" study showing that 91% of consumers in Egypt use artificial intelligence in shopping and 88% trust its role in fraud protection. She added that more than 83% of Egyptian companies plan to invest in agentic commerce over the next two years, and she stressed the importance of integrating payment and financing solutions into the purchasing experience as commerce grows across social media platforms and digital gaming.

Ahmed Nader, CEO of Geidea, said the company grew over five years from a team of 3 to 4 individuals to nearly 1,200 employees, with the number of merchants it serves reaching approximately 100,000. He said Geidea broadened its services from point-of-sale solutions to e-commerce, restaurant, and retail services, up to lending and embedded finance powered by artificial intelligence, and he affirmed that digital payment solutions and faster financial inclusion drive corporate growth, particularly for small and medium enterprises. Mohamed Tawfik, Managing Director of TP in Egypt and Chief Operating Officer for English-speaking African markets, said investment in technology and specialized talent helps companies operating in Egypt compete regionally and export services to global markets. He noted that attracting talent in computer science and medical sectors is one of the most prominent expansion challenges while serving clients in the United States and Europe, and he said the company cooperates with the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology and the Information Technology Industry Development Agency (ITIDA) to address the repercussions of regional tensions and ensure business continuity.

Karim El Hennawy, CEO and Secretary-General of ESLSCA University, said rapid technological evolution forces organizations to retrain leaders and employees and to develop strategic thinking and crisis management skills. He explained that the COVID-19 pandemic and remote work accelerated shifts expected by 2030 and 2040 into a reality within three to four years, reinforcing the importance of practical skills and adaptability to labor market changes. Omar El Shenity, Founder and CEO of Qaf Education, said organizations need to move from reactive management to flexible operating models based on data and proactive planning amid continuous changes in labor market needs and its trend toward specialized disciplines. The summit was held with more than 1,200 participants, 60 speakers, and 50 partners, under the auspices of the Ministries of Industry, Higher Education and Scientific Research, Communications and Information Technology, and Health and Population, and it discussed the future of leadership, management, and organizational development amid technological and economic transformations.

stories.Headline: AI helps uncover a Ghostscript flaw that exposes Google and Zoom to attack
stories.Summary:
A series of major technology failures across the United States over the past two weeks slowed banking transactions, interrupted Microsoft and Apple services, disabled a classified National Security Agency network and temporarily grounded commercial air traffic nationwide, the New York Times reported on Saturday. U.S. officials said they had no evidence the incidents were caused by malicious cyberattacks. Instead, they attributed several of the disruptions to software patches intended to strengthen systems against newly discovered vulnerabilities. The disruptions came as confirmed cyberattacks on systems in the U.S. and Europe underscored the growing vulnerability of interconnected networks. Hackers had already targeted American municipal water systems and European refrigeration infrastructure.

The Times reported that Iranian hackers targeted scores of municipal water systems in the United States this summer, exploiting weak or default passwords on computers controlling operations. Recent cyberattacks against refrigeration systems in Europe showed how even relatively unsophisticated hackers can disrupt equipment essential to commercial operations. Cybersecurity researcher Paulos Yibelo, founder of PWN AI, discovered a serious software vulnerability called Upload2Shell using artificial intelligence to examine file-upload processes. The flaw involved Ghostscript, decades-old software widely used to process documents and images, and could potentially have allowed attackers to compromise systems at major companies including Google and Zoom by uploading a specially crafted file. Yibelo reported the discovery to the software developer and affected companies, which issued patches.

Microsoft reportedly released more than 1,400 security patches in October, roughly 10 times its historical baseline. The NSA experienced a days-long outage of a classified network after installing faulty updates designed to address vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language, which officials cited by the Times said had been identified with the assistance of artificial intelligence. Retired Gen. Paul Nakasone, the former director of the NSA and U.S. Cyber Command, said at a Washington conference hosted by Vanderbilt University's Institute of National Security that the past week is "the new normal." Nakasone, who also serves on OpenAI's board, called artificial intelligence "the most disruptive technology" in history and said, "We are in an era where we've got to think differently about how we're going to be more resilient." He said industries and agencies are trying to rapidly modernize and at the same time defend themselves, and that "A.I. is driving all of this, the opportunities and the challenges."

Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., and Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., warned the White House that existing cybersecurity defenses were struggling to keep pace, writing that "A.I. is rapidly increasing the ability to discover and exploit weaknesses in software, and our defenses are not keeping pace." Michael Yeh, Microsoft's vice president of customer security and trust, said some of the most frequently exploited vulnerabilities were discovered years ago and that "None of those are A.I.-driven attacks," adding that "These are people exploiting existing legacy vulnerabilities" that can be decades old. Rob Joyce, a former senior NSA cybersecurity official, said at Cyberwarcon on Friday that AI was not "inventing brand new ways to hack" but was intensifying pressure to repair existing weaknesses, comparing the situation to a forest fire in which "All that tech that's on fire and going to burn down" while "all the little things that are down in the forest floor" will grow stronger and more capable. The disruptions affected consumers who suddenly could not access banking services, businesses experiencing interrupted operations, and travelers stranded by computer failures. Experts disagree about whether artificial intelligence will ultimately make the internet safer or produce an endless cycle of newly discovered vulnerabilities and emergency repairs.

Repeated disruptions affecting financial transactions, communications, transportation and national security systems risk undermining confidence in the institutions responsible for protecting them. Public skepticism does not prove that officials are concealing cyberattacks, yet the combination of confirmed intrusions, aging infrastructure and increasingly frequent outages creates a difficult credibility problem, especially when technical explanations are not accompanied by detailed public findings. The distinction between a failed software update and a deliberate cyberattack is increasingly difficult for ordinary Americans to assess, particularly when the consequences can look nearly identical. The incident illustrates a growing dilemma in which security teams must respond quickly to newly discovered weaknesses, but rushing to install protective updates can itself trigger serious disruptions. The incident also illustrates how AI is dramatically accelerating the discovery of security flaws in technology that businesses and government agencies have relied upon for decades.

More to follow.

Articles.Title: Government Blames Glitches as Cyber Threats Are 'New Normal' With AI

stories.Headline: OSF HealthCare CEO Michelle Conger says Pope Leo XIV's AI encyclical guides the Catholic system's AI strategy
stories.Summary:
OSF HealthCare CEO Michelle Conger spoke about Pope Leo XIV's first encyclical, which focuses on artificial intelligence, at this year's OSF OnCall Digital Health Symposium, according to a newsroom post dated 20 November 2026 from Peoria, Illinois. Conger said the document gives Catholic health care organizations a chance to help shape how the rapidly evolving technology is used. She said the encyclical provides a framework for thoughtfully embracing AI while ensuring it serves patients, communities and the health care workforce. She said many people have compared the transformation that will come from AI to the industrial revolution, a time when there were questions about jobs and about who would be harmed. She said Pope Leo's message reinforces the importance of keeping people at the center of decisions about technology.

Conger said the encyclical is not an outright rejection of artificial intelligence and not an endorsement of adopting new technology without careful consideration. She said it is a call for organizations, particularly those rooted in Catholic values, to consider how AI can improve the human condition. She said OSF is already exploring applications such as ambient listening, robotics and automation to reduce administrative work. She said a significant amount of time and effort is spent in its revenue cycle to collect payments for care already provided, work she said is necessary but does not directly add value to the patient experience. She said OSF is approaching AI adoption through a governance process that considers the potential impact on both patients and employees.

Conger said the encyclical's themes include protecting human dignity and labor, addressing disinformation, educating people about AI and establishing appropriate governance. She said the message reinforces that AI must serve people and protect human dignity. She described the central themes she took away as human dignity over machines, with a person always kept at the center of the care provided or the work done. She said technology and algorithms must serve people rather than reduce them. She said the document provides a framework for OSF, as a Catholic organization, to apply the message and be a leader in doing so in a positive way to improve the health and wellbeing of patients and communities.

Conger said OSF's governance process includes its human resources team, its Mission people and its ethics people, who help it think through and make sound decisions. She said the challenge is to balance the promise of innovation with the responsibility to ensure technology remains a tool in service of people. She said she sees AI as an opportunity to free labor to do things far more rewarding than some of the work people do today, adding that OSF needs all of them. She said the shift is particularly important as health care organizations face persistent workforce shortages and growing demand for services from an aging population. She said individuals frequently struggle to determine where to go for care and how to access the services they need.

Conger said technology could help OSF better understand a person's background and circumstances when they contact the organization, making it easier to direct them to the appropriate care. She described that vision as creating a digital safety net that helps patients find the right entry point into the health care system. She connected that responsibility to OSF's broader system goals: clinical excellence, working together as One OSF and becoming the health care destination patients choose, regardless of where they enter the system. She said the goal should not simply be to do more with technology but to use it to elevate the work of caregivers, strengthen relationships and improve the health and well-being of the communities OSF HealthCare serves. She said the pope's message offers an opportunity for OSF to demonstrate how a Catholic health care organization can lead through a period of significant technological change without losing sight of its purpose.

The newsroom post was published at 17:06 PM America/Chicago on 20 November 2026 and was shared by media relations coordinator Colleen Reynolds. The post lists audio clips of Conger speaking on people being at the center of AI decision-making, technology serving people, Pope Leo providing a framework and AI freeing up Mission Partners for more meaningful work. The post also lists video clips with Conger on technology needing to serve people, people needing to be at the center of AI decision-making, Pope Leo providing a framework and freeing up employees for meaningful work. The post offers a media kit and B-roll of the Digital Health Symposium for download. The post's latest news list includes items dated 20 November 2026 from Ottawa and Peru on OSF Saint Elizabeth earning high marks for patient safety from The Leapfrog Group.

stories.Headline: Researchers use explainable AI to link plasma conditions to semiconductor etch profiles
stories.Summary:
Researchers led by Jihoon Park and Seolhye Park used plasma physics-informed explainable artificial intelligence to study how plasma conditions affect etching profiles in semiconductor manufacturing, as reported by AIP.org on November 20, 2026. The team fed etch profile image data into the XAI system and analyzed how those profiles changed in relation to the plasma conditions during the experiments. They found that the mathematical index produced by the XAI can serve as an interpretable index for plasma physics, according to the article. The work was published in the Journal of Vacuum Science and Technology: A in 2026 under a title describing geometry-dependent etch-profile response in fluorocarbon-based high-aspect-ratio plasma etching.

The research addresses the difficulty of maintaining consistency and quality in plasma etching, which involves complex physics along with dynamic physical reactions and inhomogeneous chemical reactions. The authors note that these challenges grow as etching processes become more advanced and require more stringent high aspect ratio etch profiles. From their results, the researchers developed a plasma physics-informed profile-analysis framework for high aspect ratio plasma etching. This framework allows quantification of plasma-surface balance from measured etch profiles instead of relying on statistical attribution alone.

Jihoon Park said the work gave them the insight that process result image data, which had not been highlighted compared with other sensor data, could be applied to extract new information about plasma reaction properties during the process. Seolhye Park said processing plasmas are very difficult to understand because of the complexity of inhomogeneous chemical reactions, physical reactions, and numerous mechanical and electrical parts of the system. She added that finding a new source of information about the plasma reaction would have an effect similar to installing a new diagnostic tool without any hardware investment. The researchers believe their methodologies could be useful to other areas of plasma physics and diagnostics as well.

The team intends to apply their findings to understanding plasma process-driven phenomena in nuclear fusion, according to the article. The published paper lists Jihoon Park, Taejun Park, Ji-Won Kwon, Gon-Ho Kim, and Seolhye Park as its authors. The article states that the paper can be accessed through the DOI link provided in the source listing. The work was reported in a Scilight article by Mara Johnson-Groh with a DOI of its own.

stories.Headline: The New York Times Opinion section hires Jasmine Sun to cover AI and technology
stories.Summary:
The New York Times has appointed Jasmine Sun to its Opinion section, where she will cover artificial intelligence and technology, according to a report published by citybiz on November 20, 2026. Sun brings experience in Silicon Valley, product management and technology journalism to the publication. In her new role, she will lead a weekly newsletter focused on artificial intelligence and contribute to the development of editorials addressing technology and related issues. She will also participate in the publication's expanding audio and video programming and appear as an occasional guest on the relaunched Hard Fork podcast. The appointment requires Sun to contribute to Opinion Shows and extend her coverage across multiple editorial formats at the publication.

Before joining The New York Times, she worked as a product manager at Substack, the digital publishing platform that enables writers and creators to distribute newsletters and subscription-based content. During her tenure at Substack, Sun helped develop strategies supporting the platform's growth and gained firsthand experience with digital publishing, audience development and the technology industry's business models. She also co-founded Reboot, a publication focused on young technologists and their perspectives on technology, culture and the industry's broader influence. Her editorial experience also includes helping research and edit The A.G.I. Chronicles, the latest book by Kevin Roose, a technology journalist at The New York Times. Sun is a graduate of Stanford University and is based in San Francisco, placing her near the center of the Silicon Valley technology industry.

The report says her appointment comes as artificial intelligence continues to reshape the technology industry, creating demand for reporting and commentary that examines the development, commercialization and broader consequences of emerging AI systems. Her background combines direct experience working inside a technology company with independent editorial work, providing perspectives on both the business and cultural dimensions of technological change. At The New York Times Opinion, Sun will focus on artificial intelligence while contributing to broader editorial discussions about technology. Her weekly newsletter will provide a dedicated outlet for her analysis, while her involvement in Hard Fork and Opinion Shows will expand her presence across the publication's multimedia offerings. The report says her appointment adds a technology-focused writer to The New York Times Opinion team as the publication expands its coverage and commentary on artificial intelligence and the rapidly evolving technology sector.

stories.Headline: AI bone age tool matches atlas medians but varies more in individual children
stories.Summary:
A retrospective study at Independent Public Clinical Hospital Number 1 in Zabrze, affiliated with the Medical University of Silesia, evaluated how artificial intelligence compares with radiological reference atlases for bone age. The analysis covered 376 pediatric patients whose skeletal maturity was assessed by the Greulich and Pyle Atlas, the Pocket Atlas of Skeletal Age, and the Stanford University Hand Bone Age artificial intelligence web tool. Archived DICOM radiographs were retrieved from the hospital picture archiving and communication system for cases collected between April 2024 and June 2025. The initial screening identified 473 clinical cases evaluated during routine hospital care for short stature, precocious puberty, delayed puberty, and growth hormone deficiency managed with recombinant growth hormone therapy. An experienced pediatric radiologist performed the atlas evaluations, while the automated web tool independently predicted age values from identical digital radiographs.

Inclusion required radiographs of the non-dominant hand with proper positioning and complete records of chronological age, sex, and pediatric endocrinologist-determined pubertal status. Exclusion criteria eliminated acute hand or wrist trauma, insufficient image quality, contradictory data, and diagnosed skeletal dysplasias such as achondroplasia. Because the Stanford platform operated within a validation boundary of 72 to 192 months of skeletal age, both atlases had to produce estimates within that six-to-sixteen-year span, yielding 376 patients. Chronological age averaged 142.9 months with a standard deviation of 35.0 months, a median of 146 months, and an interquartile range of 114 to 173 months across an absolute range of 47 to 220 months. Twenty-two participants fell outside the 72 to 192 months range chronologically, with four children younger than 72 months and 18 older than 192 months.

The study group comprised 188 female and 188 male patients, and 250 patients, or 66.5 percent, were clinically categorized as pubertal, whereas 126 patients, or 33.5 percent, were classified as prepubertal. Statistical evaluation in R software version 4.5.3 showed the Pocket Atlas, the Greulich and Pyle atlas, and the Stanford algorithm all yielded an identical median bone age estimate of 144 months. Interquartile ranges were 114 to 165 months for the Pocket Atlas, 120 to 162 months for Greulich and Pyle, and 120 to 156 months for the artificial intelligence application. Shapiro-Wilk testing showed significant departure from normality for the Pocket Atlas at W equals 0.96, Greulich and Pyle at W equals 0.96, and the automated model at W equals 0.93, with all probability values below 0.001. A global paired comparison using the Friedman test detected significant divergence among the modalities, with a test statistic of 29.55 and a probability value below 0.001.

Post-hoc Wilcoxon signed-rank testing with Bonferroni correction showed the global differences were driven by the automated application rather than disagreement between human atlas evaluations. The Pocket Atlas against artificial intelligence comparison reached significance with an adjusted probability value of 0.001, and Greulich and Pyle against artificial intelligence yielded an adjusted probability value of 0.044. The direct comparison between the Pocket Atlas and the Greulich and Pyle atlas showed no statistically significant difference, recording an adjusted probability value of 0.13. Median pairwise discrepancies were centered at zero months across all comparisons, but mean pairwise differences were 0.69 plus or minus 6.82 months for the Pocket Atlas relative to Greulich and Pyle, 2.22 plus or minus 13.66 months for the Pocket Atlas relative to artificial intelligence, and 1.53 plus or minus 12.73 months for Greulich and Pyle relative to artificial intelligence. The two-way mixed-effects intraclass correlation coefficient for absolute agreement, ICC(A,1), was 0.93 with a 95 percent confidence interval from 0.92 to 0.94.

Pairwise intraclass correlation values reached 0.98 with a confidence interval of 0.97 to 0.98 between the Pocket Atlas and Greulich and Pyle, 0.90 with a confidence interval of 0.89 to 0.92 between the Pocket Atlas and artificial intelligence, and 0.92 with a confidence interval of 0.90 to 0.93 between Greulich and Pyle and artificial intelligence. Bland-Altman analysis revealed an average bias of 0.69 months between the two visual atlases, with 95 percent limits of agreement from minus 12.68 to positive 14.06 months, while comparisons pairing artificial intelligence against the Pocket Atlas and Greulich and Pyle produced wider limits of agreement spanning minus 24.55 to positive 28.99 months and minus 23.43 to positive 26.48 months. Under a predefined threshold of agreement within plus or minus 12 months, the two human atlas approaches agreed in 363 out of 376 cases, an agreement rate of 96.5 percent with a confidence interval from 94.2 to 98.0 percent. Greulich and Pyle against artificial intelligence dropped to 83.8 percent, representing 315 out of 376 children with a confidence interval from 79.7 to 87.2 percent, and the Pocket Atlas against artificial intelligence registered 77.4 percent across 291 patients with a confidence interval from 72.9 to 81.3 percent. Under a stringent threshold of plus or minus six months, the two reference atlases sustained agreement in 77.9 percent of cases, encompassing 293 patients, while concordance fell to 44.4 percent across 167 cases for Greulich and Pyle against artificial intelligence and 43.6 percent across 164 cases for the Pocket Atlas against the automated tool.

Locally estimated trend lines indicated the Stanford model tended to underestimate bone age relative to visual atlases among the youngest and oldest participants, a deviation absent in the direct atlas comparison. After controlling for quadratic age trends, Breusch-Pagan testing confirmed significant age-related heteroscedasticity for comparisons involving artificial intelligence, with probability values below 0.001, whereas the two atlas methods maintained homoscedasticity with a probability value of 0.52. Spearman correlation between chronological age and absolute residuals showed weak but statistically significant negative associations for the Pocket Atlas against artificial intelligence at r equals minus 0.14 and Greulich and Pyle against artificial intelligence at r equals minus 0.18, compared to r equals 0.006 and a probability value of 0.90 between the two manual atlases. Patient sex exerted a profound effect on method agreement, creating pronounced divergence in female patients that was largely absent among males. Wilcoxon rank-sum testing with Bonferroni correction established significant associations between sex and pairwise differences for the Pocket Atlas against artificial intelligence and Greulich and Pyle against artificial intelligence, both displaying adjusted probabili

More to follow.
