stories.Headline: Researchers propose a clinician-supervised hybrid AI framework to optimize medication regimens for multimorbid patients
stories.Summary:
An interdisciplinary research group formulated a conceptual framework to optimize pharmacotherapy in multimorbid patients through a clinician-supervised hybrid artificial intelligence system, published in the International Journal of Clinical Pharmacy. The framework was formulated between June 2025 and February 2026 by a team comprising specialists in clinical pharmacy, pharmacotherapy, artificial intelligence, digital health, and medication management. The authors adopted a design science-informed approach guided by problem identification, artifact design, and iterative refinement rather than a formal consensus methodology or clinical trial. The work responds to increasing clinical complexity driven by polypharmacy, fragmented patient records, expanding electronic health records, drug shortages, and healthcare workforce constraints. The investigators were informed by earlier feasibility work in artificial intelligence-supported pharmacotherapy, existing literature on clinical decision support platforms, and recurrent challenges observed in clinical practice.

The framework defines hybrid artificial intelligence as an operational integration uniting retrieval-augmented generation, deterministic safety rules, and contextual large language model reasoning. The researchers derived seven primary design principles, the first mandating decomposition of complex clinical workflows into distinct tasks with separate risk profiles and documentation needs, such as data acquisition, patient assessment, therapeutic goal formulation, safety checks, and guideline adherence reviews. The second principle establishes relevance-based prioritization by patient vulnerability and clinical urgency, such as highlighting severe drug-related problems over minor informational alerts. The third principle requires hybrid reasoning under strict human oversight, cross-referenced against established risk models and deterministic constraints, while the remaining four address patient alignment, professional agency, ongoing governance, and methodological evaluation. The data foundation incorporates structured electronic health record data, laboratory panels, vital signs, comorbidities, organ function metrics such as renal and hepatic assessments, and pharmacogenomic markers where available, alongside natural language processing of unstructured narratives and computer vision-based representation learning of guideline artifacts such as visual algorithms, decision flowcharts, and therapeutic tables.

The authors emphasize that the study presents a conceptual blueprint and does not provide empirical validation, performance metrics, or clinical trial outcomes. They state that stand-alone artificial intelligence models, especially general-purpose large language models, remain insufficiently reliable when deployed independently in complex medication management. They note that large language models demonstrate utility in answering isolated biomedical inquiries and categorizing descriptive data but present substantial clinical risks without structured clinical context, verification mechanisms, and explicit justifications. The authors stress that clinicians must actively shape the governance and clinical logic of these emerging digital tools to ensure future artificial intelligence implementations remain safely grounded in patient-centered pharmacotherapeutic reasoning. They also note that previous evaluative literature has disproportionately examined the outputs of off-the-shelf commercial language models rather than purpose-built clinical architectures.

Professional oversight and legal accountability remain anchored entirely with human healthcare providers, with physicians, clinical pharmacists, and allied health professionals retaining uncompromised authority to accept, modify, or reject system recommendations based on independent clinical assessments. Every recommendation is coupled with transparent rationales, explicit evidentiary citations, and visual uncertainty signaling indicating when data gaps warrant further investigation. Clinicians also record override justifications and performance feedback, establishing a traceable audit trail that supports continuous model refinement, helps prevent uncontrolled model drift, and aligns digital decision support with medical device regulatory requirements. The framework incorporates patient preferences, treatment burden thresholds, symptom severity, and adherence barriers, and envisions digital patient interfaces, potentially utilizing interactive avatar-based digital assistants on mobile devices, to gather longitudinal symptom reports, track well-being, and clarify medication concerns between clinical appointments. Key limitations include the absence of standardized consensus procedures during framework formulation, lack of direct patient involvement in design stages, and technical barriers surrounding electronic health record interoperability and secure data processing.

The authors aligned their structural design with the recently introduced MedinAI guidance, which mandates explicit documentation of model architectures, data provenance, ethical considerations, and verifiable human oversight in pharmacotherapy applications. They note that established reporting recommendations such as CONSORT-AI and TRIPOD-AI have advanced general reporting rigor. Citing broader evidence highlighting the absence of standardized testing protocols for retrieval-augmented generation in medicine, the investigators emphasized that their framework grew out of direct developmental experience with a de novo system engineered specifically to resolve complex drug-therapy trade-offs. The conceptual model positions its architectural safeguards within an evolving landscape of clinical artificial intelligence standards. The authors state that conventional clinical decision support systems remain primarily static and rule-based, frequently emitting non-contextual alerts that cause alert fatigue and exhibit limited clinical utility.

Implementation is expected to proceed modularly, beginning with deterministic safety rules before layering advanced retrieval-augmented components. System validation must proceed sequentially across multiple assessment layers, with initial evaluation phases focusing strictly on technical reliability, user interface ergonomics, alert relevance, workflow integration, and clinicians' trust in uncertainty signaling. Only after decision-support tools achieve stable, reproducible performance under real-world clinical constraints should trials proceed to quantify downstream clinical endpoints, including reductions in preventable adverse drug events. The articles leave open the empirical validation, performance metrics, and clinical trial outcomes the authors say the study does not provide. The articles also leave open how electronic health record interoperability and secure data processing barriers will be resolved.

stories.Headline: Review authors say AI can help close epilepsy diagnosis gaps in low-income countries
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a Review published in Nature Reviews Neurology on 20 November 2026 examining how artificial intelligence could address global disparities in epilepsy diagnosis and treatment, particularly in resource-limited settings. The Review was written by authors publishing in Nature Reviews Neurology, and it examines AI-based analysis of electroencephalography recordings captured with affordable open-source systems, smartphone data and electronic health records. It states that the convergence of AI and health care offers unprecedented opportunities to address disparities in access to specialized epilepsy diagnosis and treatment. It also states that advances in AI models, combined with increasing internet connectivity and smartphone usage in low-income and middle-income countries, offer promising solutions for epilepsy diagnosis and monitoring. The Review says this technological revolution raises important questions about the preservation and expansion of clinical expertise, AI algorithm transparency and health-care equity.

The Review states that most people with epilepsy live in low-income and middle-income countries, where shortages of neurologists, electroencephalography and MRI contribute to large diagnostic and treatment gaps. It says low-cost, open-source EEG systems combined with deep learning models that match expert performance in specific EEG tasks could enable minimally trained health workers to screen for epilepsy in resource-limited settings. It states that smartphone-based approaches, including video recordings of seizures and passive analysis of touchscreen interaction dynamics, are candidate tools for screening and monitoring but are not yet established diagnostic tests. It says multimodal and reasoning-capable large language models could integrate clinical histories in local languages with EEG data and explain their reasoning, and that affordable open-source models can run offline on local devices. It states that AI models trained in high-income settings often generalize poorly to other populations, so local data collection, external validation and attention to bias, data protection and cultural applicability are essential.

The Review states that responsible implementation requires a phased approach of hardware validation, local model adaptation, clinical trials and sustainable scaling that strengthens clinical expertise and community-based care. It says the authors examine how AI can help to address disparities and improve global epilepsy care while maintaining high clinical standards and addressing systemic challenges. The article presents figures on global internet penetration and on AI processing in epilepsy diagnosis with and without internet access. The article lists references including a 2024 Lancet Neurology analysis of the global burden of disorders affecting the nervous system from 1990 to 2021 and a 2018 Nature Reviews Disease Primers paper on epilepsy. It also lists a 2024 World Health Organization fact sheet on epilepsy and a 2017 Epilepsia review on premature mortality of epilepsy in low- and middle-income countries.

The article lists a 2017 ILAE position paper on classification of the epilepsies and a 2023 Epilepsy Research paper on challenges in epilepsy diagnosis and management in Bhutan. It lists the WHO 2017 Atlas of Country Resources for Neurological Disorders and a 2024 Seizure review on perceived and self-stigma in people with epilepsy in East Africa. It lists the WHO Intersectoral Global Action Plan on Epilepsy and Other Neurological Disorders 2022, 2031 and the WHO 2019 report Epilepsy: A Public Health Imperative. It lists a 2022 Epilepsia report from the ILAE Epidemiology Commission on the worldwide epilepsy treatment gap and a 2022 npj Digital Medicine review on AI for strengthening healthcare systems in low- and middle-income countries. It lists a 2024 Nature Reviews Neurology paper on AI in epilepsy and a 2023 JAMA Neurology paper on automated interpretation of clinical electroencephalograms using AI.

The article lists a 2022 Epilepsia paper on accurate identification of EEG recordings with interictal epileptiform discharges using a hybrid approach of AI supervised by human experts and a 2025 Epilepsia paper on expert level detection of interictal discharges with a deep neural network. It lists a 2024 Frontiers in Neuroscience review of epilepsy detection and prediction methods based on EEG signal processing and deep learning and a 2025 Epilepsy & Behavior survey of fellowship education in epilepsy in Latin America and Africa. It lists a 2010 IEEE Engineering in Medicine and Biology Magazine paper on wearable electroencephalography and a 2022 Epilepsia systematic review on noninvasive mobile EEG for seizure monitoring and management. It lists a 2023 Sensors comparison of high-end and low-cost EEG amplifiers and a 2021 IEEE conference paper on a wearable system with in-ear EEG electrodes for monitoring brain activities. The article lists a 2025 IEEE Access paper on remote epilepsy monitoring signal quality and reliability and a 2014 PLoS ONE paper on the smartphone brain scanner.

It lists a 2017 Scientific Reports validation of smartphone-based EEG among people with epilepsy and a 2020 European Journal of Neurology paper on tablet-based EEG diagnostics in the West African Republic of Guinea. It lists a 2015 Nature paper on deep learning and a 2023 Archives of Computational Methods in Engineering review of convolutional neural network-based EEG signal analysis. It lists a 2025 Sensors review of transformers in EEG analysis and a 2025 IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics paper on a hybrid AI system for automated EEG background analysis and report generation. It lists a 2024 Epilepsia external validation study on generalizability of EEG interpretation using AI and a 2020 International Journal of Neural Systems paper on automated detection of interictal epileptiform discharges by convolutional neural networks. The article lists a 2022 Scientific Reports method for AI-assisted human interpretation of neonatal EEG and a 2021 Neurocritical Care paper on monitoring seizure burden and highly epileptiform patterns in critical care with a machine learning method.

It lists a 2025 IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics paper on EEG-Deformer and a 2024 PLoS ONE paper on epilepsy detection based on a multi-head self-attention mechanism. It lists a 2024 BioMedical Engineering OnLine paper on automatic detection of epilepsy from EEGs using a temporal convolutional network with a self-attention layer and a 2020 JAMA Neurology paper on expert-level automated detection of epileptiform discharges during EEG interpretation. It lists a 2023 Epilepsy & Behavior paper on epilepsy diagnosis using a clinical decision tool and artificially intelligent electroencephalography and a preprint on bioRxiv on reliable and automatic epilepsy classification with affordable consumer-grade electroencephalography in rural sub-Saharan Africa. The article states that the full text is available only through subscription or purchase. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Chinese tech giants double AI spending as lab revenue fails to cover costs
stories.Summary:
Major Chinese technology firms are expected to double their capital spending to 139 billion dollars in 2026, according to research from Rhodium Group. These companies are struggling to fund the soaring costs of training powerful artificial intelligence models while facing a difficult financial landscape. This massive investment occurs as the United States and China compete for supremacy in the field of artificial intelligence. Many Chinese startups are finding it harder to secure funding compared to American rivals like Anthropic.

The financial gap is significant because revenue from artificial intelligence labs covers less than 8 percent of the projected spending. Rhodium Group forecasts that these expenditures could continue to rise and potentially top 193 billion dollars by 2027. Meanwhile, the STAR 50 index has plunged 43 percent since the end of July, reflecting a deep sell-off in Chinese tech stocks. Tech giants such as Alibaba, Baidu, and Tencent are currently grappling with negative cash flows while backing leading AI firms.

Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution, stated that the financial numbers suggest these companies are running on a treadmill that is speeding up. He believes the economic pressure is becoming increasingly difficult for these organizations to manage. This financial strain may prove to be a more critical obstacle than the American export controls on advanced semiconductors. While some labs rented data centers in Southeast Asia to access Nvidia chips, the Trump administration is now moving to close that loophole.

stories.Headline: Review authors link AI tools to supply chain resilience through agility and governance
stories.Summary:
A structured narrative synthesis of 75 studies published between 2015 and 2025 was published in Discover Artificial Intelligence. Adel Aazami, Amirhossein Hassani, Nadun Karunarathna, and Sebastian Kummer conducted the review. The synthesis examined how artificial intelligence tools interface with operational risk management. It covered predictive analytics, machine learning, deep learning, digital twins, and robotic process automation. The review was published on November 21, 2026.

The review covered literature published from January 2015 through December 2025, with database searches executed through January 2026. Searches ran across Emerald, Web of Science, and Google Scholar using three Boolean concept clusters. The query clusters covered supply chain contexts, artificial intelligence technologies, and resilience outcomes. Critical appraisal followed a qualitative, Joanna Briggs Institute-informed framework across five dimensions. The dimensions were objective clarity, methodological adequacy, evidence validity, analytical transparency, and alignment between data and conclusions.

The authors assigned qualitative evidence weights of High, Medium, Low, and Limited support rather than numerical scores. The authors explicitly disclaimed compliance with systematic PRISMA 2020 reporting standards. They presented the work as a structured narrative synthesis grounded in an appraised 75-study corpus. The authors stated that intermediate retrieval counts, database-specific search logs, screener counts, and inter-rater agreement statistics were not archived. The authors concluded that artificial intelligence represents an enabling capability rather than a standalone operational remedy.

The synthesis found that publications rose from fewer than 10 per year between 2015 and 2018 to more than 40 annually between 2023 and 2025. Research concentrated heavily on demand forecasting and inventory management, where algorithms optimize safety stocks, dynamic buffer allocation, and lead-time predictability. Empirical investigations of supplier relationship management and deep-tier supplier vulnerabilities remained underrepresented. The corpus concentrated on conceptual frameworks, model-driven proposals, and simulation-based studies. Longitudinal investigations and cross-industry empirical evaluations in live operational environments remained comparatively scarce.

The articles state that global logistics networks connect suppliers, manufacturing facilities, and consumer markets through cross-border flows of materials, capital, and data. Lean inventory and Just-In-Time principles lowered working capital requirements and reduced warehousing overhead during predictable market stability. The removal of safety stocks, backup sourcing channels, and redundant capacity diminished buffer mechanisms across lower operational tiers. Modern networks face compounded shocks including the COVID-19 pandemic, geopolitical conflicts, and extreme climate events. Traditional risk management relied on historical probability distributions and static redundancy buffers.

The synthesis frames implications for enterprise management, ecosystem policy, and academic scholarship. Managers are advised to establish data quality, integration pipelines, and workforce analytics literacy before acquiring advanced predictive algorithms. Industry consortia and policymakers are encouraged to develop standardized transparency protocols and secure data-pooling frameworks. The authors conclude that realized resilience depends on co-evolution between technical capabilities, dynamic sensing and seizing routines, and verifiable institutional governance structures. The articles leave open the intermediate retrieval counts, database-specific search logs, screener counts, and inter-rater agreement statistics.

stories.Headline: Algerian professor Fayçal Djeridane presents AI cancer screening project with Laghouat as potential pilot region
stories.Summary:
Professor Fayçal Djeridane presented the prospects of an ambitious AI-assisted cancer screening project at the 1st National Forum of Oncology Experts, held on November 5, 6, 2026, at the Chahid Mohamed Rezoug Cancer Center (CLCC) in Laghouat, Algeria. The forum gave particular attention to the opportunities offered by artificial intelligence in developing predictive and adaptive oncology during its scientific discussions. Djeridane is an internationally recognized Algerian expert in artificial intelligence and medical imaging and a member of the High Council of the National Scientific Community Abroad. His presentation highlighted the potential of emerging technologies in cancer screening and introduced the prospects of the project. The province of Laghouat could be selected as a pilot region for the AI-assisted cancer screening project.

The project would require defining the targeted cancers and eligible populations and establishing clearly structured screening pathways. It would require ensuring the availability of appropriate diagnostic infrastructure and training healthcare professionals. It would require validating algorithms in the Algerian population and protecting and securing medical data. It would require regularly evaluating diagnostic performance and project outcomes. The article was published on OncoDaily on November 20, 2026, and was authored by Abderrahim Djellaoui, MD, an Assistant Professor in Medical Oncology in Laghouat, Algeria, and medically reviewed by Vahe Grigoryan, MD, Editorial Director.

The article states that the aim is not to replace the expertise of radiologists or oncologists but to provide them with complementary tools. It states that a model designed using data from other countries does not necessarily guarantee the same level of performance in the Algerian population. It states that local validation is therefore a fundamental step before any large-scale implementation. It states that the approach requires close collaboration between oncologists, radiologists, biologists, epidemiologists, engineers, and data scientists. It states that artificial intelligence alone cannot solve all the challenges of cancer screening.

The article states that screening programs face challenges including the growing volume of medical imaging examinations, the availability of specialists, reporting delays, variability in diagnostic performance, and geographical inequalities in access to healthcare. It states that AI could offer applications including AI-assisted identification of suspicious lesions and improved analysis of mammograms and other medical imaging examinations. It states that applications also include characterization of certain radiological abnormalities, standardization and optimization of image interpretation, and support in identifying patients who require further diagnostic investigations. It states that the involvement of the Laghouat Cancer Center and its oncology team provides a particularly relevant clinical environment to support the initiative. It states that the project highlights the importance of collaboration between scientific experts, specialists in emerging technologies, and healthcare professionals.

The article states that cancer remains one of the major public health challenges worldwide and that early detection remains one of the key factors in improving patient outcomes and reducing cancer-related mortality. It states that AI is progressively emerging as a promising technology with the potential to transform medical practice, particularly in medical imaging, screening, risk assessment, and clinical decision support. It states that Algeria is also embracing this wave of innovation. It states that predictive oncology involves integrating clinical, biological, histopathological, molecular, and radiological data to better understand cancer behavior. It states that the combined analysis of these data could eventually help identify profiles associated with an increased risk of cancer, improve prognostic assessment, and contribute to predicting treatment response.

The article states that the potential selection of Laghouat as a pilot region opens up interesting prospects for exploring the integration of these emerging technologies into the Algerian healthcare system. It states that the Laghouat pilot project could provide an opportunity to develop a national experience in evaluating artificial intelligence tools applied to cancer screening. It states that such cooperation could also encourage the emergence of national research projects and contribute to strengthening Algeria's scientific expertise. It states that the transformation must be part of a structured strategy based on clear clinical objectives including improving access to screening, reducing diagnostic delays, addressing geographical inequalities, and improving patient outcomes. The article does not state whether the project has been approved, funded, or scheduled.

stories.Headline: Gallup finds frequent AI users report no change in meeting time
stories.Summary:
Gallup surveyed 21,648 U.S. employees and found that among the 32% of respondents who use artificial intelligence a few times a week or more, most reported no savings in meeting time. In that group of frequent users, 52% said they spend less time gathering information and 47% said they spend less time writing. But 83% said their time in meetings has not changed, and 78% reported no change in the time they spend collaborating with coworkers. The survey also found that 82% of frequent AI users spend about the same amount of time working with customers or clients.

The results suggest that while artificial intelligence speeds up some tasks, other parts of workplace life may be essentially AI-proof, and meeting time is the clearest example. A 2024 survey by the scheduling platform Reclaim.ai found that employees spend nearly 15 hours a week in meetings on average, which is roughly 37% of a standard workweek. Nearly two-thirds of frequent AI users, or 65%, said their roles require about the same mental effort as before, while 21% reported expending less mental effort and 14% said their work has become even more demanding. Among frequent users, 21% said they now spend more time reviewing and correcting work, and the same percentage reported spending more time learning new skills and tools.

Among employees at organizations that have adopted AI, just 29% told Gallup the technology has raised expectations for how much work they should complete in a day. Frequent AI users are more likely to feel pressure, however, since 36% said AI has raised expectations for their output and 33% said they felt pressure to use the technology to keep up. The survey's results suggest that AI is replacing routine tasks while creating new responsibilities, which may explain why even frequent users find their jobs have not gotten easier overall. Although meeting time has dropped from its pandemic-era peak, studies show that meetings still eat up an extraordinary amount of the typical worker's schedule.

stories.Headline: GPT-6.1 Sol reads and writes executable binaries directly from hex dumps
stories.Summary:
GPT-6.1 Sol demonstrated the ability to read and write executable binaries directly from hex dumps. This capability was revealed in a report published on November 21, 2026. The model performed these tasks without using any disassemblers or compilers. It processed machine code byte by byte to understand and create programs. This suggests that large language models can program directly in binary.

The process requires an xxd hex dump, which uses about 2.4 tokens per byte. GPT-6.1 Sol used Codex CLI 0.166.0 and ran under qemu-x86_64 on Apple Silicon. It analyzed a stripped FreeBSD tool called ministat and a 4,608-byte PE32+ Windows malware sample. The model wrote three programs, including an AES tool and a bank ledger. It also edited a program called wordcount to report its longest line.

The researchers defined Machine Code Programming as reasoning about bytes without any intermediate tools. They stated that LLMs may eventually write in machine code instead of high level languages. The team noted that the model found a real bug in the ministat code. They observed that the model treats binary patching like a human analyst would. They claimed this could challenge the foundations of reverse engineering and malware analysis.

Malware analysts are affected because they usually spend hours turning samples into assembly or C code. The model analyzed a sample in 211 seconds and identified a server at 165.154.205.34. It found 13 APIs and a kill switch file located at %TEMP%\log_de.log. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash also reached the same conclusion about the malware sample. This suggests that general-purpose models can perform triage without being specialized for it.

Most people write source code and use compilers and linkers to create bytes. Humans use disassemblers because x86-64 instructions vary in length and jumps are relative. Takehi et al. previously showed that models can read and write neural network weights. The researchers tested reading, extending, and writing abilities using one attempt per program. They used a local relay to ensure no tools were used during requests.

The model may soon analyze samples without lifting them to assembly or source code. Future work could involve a harness based on Recursive Language Models for larger files. Context size remains a hard limit, as a 10 MB program needs 24 million tokens. The researchers do not know how quality holds up near the 67 KB limit. It remains open whether this approach works for very large programs.

Articles.Title: LLMs can read and write executables byte by byte from a hex dump

stories.Headline: PAHO publishes guidance on reinforcement learning in health AI
stories.Summary:
The Pan American Health Organization presented a new publication on 20 November 2026 in Washington, D.C., titled "Reinforcement Learning in Artificial Intelligence for Health: Opportunities, Risks, and Implications for Policy and Practice," which examines the opportunities, risks, and implications of reinforcement learning in artificial intelligence for health systems. The document provides guidance for policymakers, health authorities, technical teams, and health professionals so that they can better understand the potential of this technology and promote its responsible implementation. Reinforcement learning represents a step forward toward AI systems capable of supporting decisions that evolve over time, because it enables the identification and adjustment of strategies based on feedback from previous decisions. In health systems, where clinical and public health decisions are often part of continuous processes, this capability opens up new possibilities for improving care and operations.

The publication states that this approach can help optimize treatment sequences, support the care of people living with chronic conditions, improve the allocation of health resources, and develop public health interventions that adapt to changing epidemiological and operational conditions. It highlights that the potential of these technologies depends not only on their technical capabilities but also on the institutional conditions that support their implementation. One of the main challenges is preventing these systems from reproducing or amplifying inequalities embedded in historical data, and their adaptive nature means they require validation, monitoring, and continuous evaluation mechanisms to identify potential risks to safety, equity, and quality of care. The document emphasizes the importance of high-quality data, interoperable digital infrastructure, appropriate governance frameworks, and technical and institutional capacities.

The publication also underscores that human oversight must remain an essential component, ensuring that AI-generated recommendations strengthen, rather than replace, the judgment of health professionals and decision-makers. This approach aims to foster innovation without compromising patient safety, equity, or the protection of fundamental rights. The publication is part of PAHO's ongoing efforts to advance the digital transformation of the health sector in the Americas and to promote the development and use of safe, equitable, and people-centered artificial intelligence technologies. PAHO offers the full publication for download in English and invites interested readers to subscribe to a mailing list for updates on publications, activities, and resources related to artificial intelligence and digital health.

stories.Headline: Agentic AI creates new revenue streams for solopreneur platforms
stories.Summary:
Al Bentley published an article on Yahoo Finance on Saturday, November 21, 2026 at 11:09 AM CST titled "3 Stocks Riding The Agentic AI Boom For Solopreneur Platforms." The article introduces three stocks it links to the agentic AI surge among solopreneur and microbusiness platforms. It says agentic AI is no longer just writing code or invoices and is spinning up one person companies at scale. The piece says this shift creates fresh revenue streams for platforms serving solopreneurs and microbusinesses. It says the shift could potentially sideline slower incumbents.

The article covers Zeta Global Holdings, Toast and Klaviyo, and says the full screen on Simply Wall St surfaced 8 more solopreneur and microbusiness platforms not discussed. Zeta Global Holdings runs an AI driven cloud platform and reports about US$1.7b in Internet Software and Services revenue, with roughly US$1.6b from the United States and US$141 million from international customers. Its AI heavy super scaled customers now count 197 companies with 17% year over year growth and 17% higher ARPU at US$1.8 million. Toast runs a cloud platform for restaurants and generates about US$7.2b from data processing activities. Klaviyo runs a B2C CRM and marketing platform and reports about US$1.5b in Internet Software revenue, with roughly US$856 million from the United States and US$610 million from international markets.

The bullish analyst Narrative on Simply Wall St argues Zeta's scale could translate into deeper AI driven use cases over time. It says the 197 super scaled customers give Zeta room to layer additional Athena and business intelligence use cases on an already large revenue base per client. The bullish analyst Narrative on Simply Wall St argues Toast's toolkit could become far more important as agentic AI handles more routine work. The bearish analyst Narrative on Simply Wall St focuses on how well Klaviyo's usage can actually translate into hard financial outcomes. The article says it provides commentary based on historical data and analyst forecasts only using an unbiased methodology.

The article says Toast IQ and Toast IQ Grow are being used as the base for an agentic platform that can take over workflows such as marketing, scheduling, bookkeeping and payroll. It says Toast turns many owner operated restaurants into microbusinesses with enterprise style payments, payroll and AI support. It says Klaviyo reports rapid adoption of Composer and Customer Agent. It says a recent downgrade questions visibility on how these AI agents will be priced and packaged. The article says Simply Wall St has no position in any stocks mentioned.

The article says the three stocks covered are only a starter set for the theme. It directs readers to the Solopreneur and Microbusiness Enablement Platforms screener to identify their own highest conviction angles. It says the article is general in nature and was produced with the assistance of AI automation, based on data and analysis from Simply Wall St. It says the article does not constitute a recommendation to buy or sell any stock. It says the analysis may not factor in the latest price-sensitive company announcements or qualitative material.

The article asks what happens to Zeta Global Holdings' margins if a single unseen pressure changes how quickly high value users embrace its newest AI layers. It asks what happens to Klaviyo's economics if a single unresolved question about how AI usage converts into paid packages tilts one way or the other. It says the real swing factor for Toast is how one quiet shift in where restaurants source their help for finance and admin work reshapes Toast's margins. It says slower uptake could drag on returns while faster deployment might sharpen them. It says the full narratives for Zeta Global Holdings, Toast and Klaviyo show how accelerating AI use could reshape customer economics, how Toast could accelerate or stall, and how Klaviyo's AI usage, pricing power and customer mix could be quietly decoupling.

stories.Headline: Louisville Public Media CEO Kenya Young says staff review all AI use and journalists write its stories
stories.Summary:
Louisville Public Media published a statement of its practices on artificial intelligence on November 20, 2026, and its President and CEO, Kenya Young, issued a message the same day explaining how the organization uses AI and how it does not. Young said LPM had been watching the technology closely and planning for the changing landscape, and that AI is part of the organization's new three-year strategic plan under its priority of Digital Transformation and Adaptability. The plan says LPM will adopt AI tools with clear ethical standards that increase efficiency and responsiveness, freeing staff capacity for higher-value work. Young said LPM is in the beginning stages of adapting to AI and is exploring, experimenting and in some cases already using AI tools for work behind the scenes. Young said the tools are used for tasks such as transcription, research and data analysis, and that anything LPM uses AI for is reviewed and checked by a person.

She said LPM does not use AI to write its stories, that its journalists source stories, conduct interviews and write the news, and that this will not change. She said LPM does not use AI to choose the music listeners hear, does not play AI-generated music on air, and will not use AI to replicate anyone's voice or to alter real audio, photos or video. Young said hosts and music staff decide what plays on WFPK and WUOL, and that staff own the final result of whatever AI helps with. Young said technology companies, including AI companies, have invested heavily in journalism and media in recent years, and that LPM has received support from some of them, including the Google News Initiative and the OpenAI Foundation's People-First AI Fund. She said the organization's ethics and independence policy states there is no connection between its funding and editorial decisions, and that donors have no direct access to the newsroom, programming or those who make content decisions.

She said that holds for technology companies too, and that their support comes with no influence over what news LPM covers or what music it plays and no commitment to any company's products. Young said media companies across the country are cutting staff, and some have tied those cuts directly to their increased use of AI, while data centers are going up in communities, particularly in Kentucky. She said AI is undoubtedly changing how people work and navigate their days, and that a generation ago the internet changed the media landscape, in some ways for the better and in others for the worse. She said LPM will keep innovating, experimenting and evolving, guided by its standards and ethics, and that the most important theme in its strategic plan is trust. She said trust has to be earned every day, with every concerto on WUOL, every new artist on WFPK and every local story on WFPL.

stories.Headline: California political candidates use AI to create fake images for election advertising
stories.Summary:
California political candidates used artificial intelligence to create fake images for election advertising during the current cycle. These digital tools allowed campaigns to produce surreal visuals to help them stand out on air and online. Some candidates appeared as caped crusaders or fought massive robots in these generated advertisements. Other images showed candidates kowtowing to rich fat cats or bloodthirsty crowds. These tactics were used to influence voters across the state of California.

Researchers at the Wesleyan Media Project found that campaigns spent over 137 million dollars on AI ads by mid-October. Republican groups were responsible for about 80 percent of those specific messages. Former Los Angeles mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt used AI to depict himself as the character Batman. Gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton appeared as a gladiator with Gov. Gavin Newsom and Xavier Becerra in a coliseum. A San Diego school board candidate used a mailer showing a female opponent working a fake bake sale.

Ramesh Srinivasan is a UCLA professor of information studies who hosts the Utopias podcast. He stated that AI can now automatically create content that targets people based on their psychology. Srinivasan believes this is pernicious because there is no disclosure when content is AI-generated. He has worked with the U.S. Congress and the state Senate to force watermarking on AI images. He explained that watermarking flags an image as AI-generated so it can never be written over.

The female school board candidate in San Diego said her bake sale image was sexist. Srinivasan noted that many voters cannot tell the difference between AI content and human-created content. He argued that this lack of a common basis of reality is not good for democracy. He mentioned that the president used AI to show himself healing the sick, which looked like Jon Stewart. This type of content is often called AI slop when it is not meant to fool people.

The articles mention that the Cambridge Analytica story involved using data to target people based on psychology ten years ago. Social media platforms like TikTok and Instagram have hosted AI content that was not flagged. Some of the ads from Steve Hilton did include a line saying they were AI-generated. Big Tech companies have been accused of censoring content during the Biden administration. These platforms use data from credit card records and social media to influence what users see.

Future efforts must rein in AI companies to ensure they adhere to basic standards of disclosure. Regulation is needed to ensure that technological innovation is accompanied by human and social innovation. The 2028 elections may be impacted by whether leaders recognize that these technologies are here to stay. It remains open whether AI will be used as a tool to protect or destroy democracy. The articles leave open how the platforms will be regulated to pay people for their data.

stories.Headline: Meta AI funds LSU project that uses color-coded alerts to monitor infants breathing through artificial airways
stories.Summary:
Meta AI partnered with the LSU system on November 20, 2026, to launch five projects aimed at solving various healthcare challenges. One specific initiative called Eyes-On focuses on assisting infants who rely on artificial airways to breathe. This project functions as a specialized baby monitor for infants with complex or technology-dependent medical problems. The system uses a color-coded alert process to notify medical staff about the status of the airway tubes.

The project requires a total of 80,000 dollars in funding provided by Meta AI to operate. A green light indicates the tube is correctly in place, while orange means the system is uncertain. A red light triggers an alarm to warn staff that the tube has come out. The ultimate goal of the Eyes-On project is to keep babies healthy until they can breathe independently.

Michael Dunham, the Head of Pediatric Otolaryngology at the LSU School of Health, is responsible for the project. He stated that artificial intelligence should not be relied upon to perform these medical tasks entirely. Dunham believes humans must evaluate the input data and make the final decisions based on the AI output. He argued that keeping humans integrated ensures the foundation of healthcare remains people taking care of other people.

stories.Headline: Marvell stock drops 22 percent as Nvidia turmoil hits AI chip sector
stories.Summary:
Marvell Technology stock fell 22 percent in one week ending November 21, 2026. This decline happened as turmoil at Nvidia hit the broader AI chip sector. The selling began when Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on November 12. Marvell did not release any negative news of its own during this period. Markets slumped worldwide on Friday, dragging Marvell down with other connectivity stocks.

Marvell agreed to buy Lumentum on November 2 in an all-stock deal. Each Lumentum share becomes 4.5 Marvell shares, increasing Marvell's share count by 49 percent. The deal requires approval from regulators, including those in China, by early 2028. Marvell owes Lumentum 3.2 billion dollars if regulators block the merger. Nvidia holds 2 billion dollars of Marvell preferred stock and invested 2 billion into Lumentum.

Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston told Jim Cramer that shareholders are unhappy. He stated that the companies have work to do but will see earnings uplift. Gary Black of The Future Fund called the stock deal a prime example of failure. Stifel cut Marvell's target to 280 dollars and Credo's target to 250 dollars. Oppenheimer reiterated a Buy rating and a 425 dollar target for Marvell.

Lumentum shareholders are affected because Marvell's price drop reduces the offer value. Credo Technology, a rival that settled a patent dispute with Marvell, also saw declines. The S&P 500 fell 9 percent and the Nasdaq 100 fell 10 percent. Jim Cramer said Nvidia's troubles outweighed the record IPO of the company Anthropic. Investors are selling the whole AI connectivity group due to the Nvidia news.

Nvidia reported revenue of 115.8 billion dollars on November 17, up 103 percent. California's attorney general subpoenaed Nvidia after the market closed on Thursday. Marvell's fiscal third-quarter revenue midpoint was 3.15 billion dollars, up 52 percent. Credo reported revenue of 479 million dollars for the quarter ending August 1. Marvell's forward P/E is currently below its five-year average of 32x.

Marvell and Credo will both report their earnings on December 1. Analysts expect Marvell's normalized EPS to reach 7.37 dollars by January 2028. The articles leave open whether Marvell's business can carry the stock until closing. It remains uncertain if Nvidia's legal troubles will hit the group again. The final outcome depends on whether regulators sign off on the Lumentum deal.

stories.Headline: Dira wins $10,000 education prize at African Agentic AI Design Challenge in Nairobi
stories.Summary:
The Kenyan education technology startup Dira won the US$10,000 Education track prize at the African Agentic AI Design Challenge on November 20, 2026. This announcement occurred during a closed-door side event held alongside the Model Context Protocol Dev Summit Nairobi, which took place from November 19 to 20 at the Hyatt Regency Nairobi Westlands. Founded by Michelle Gati, Jacinta Wanjiru, and Irene Mukii, the startup developed an AI assistant that helps teachers identify students needing extra support. The tool converts spoken observations from educators into structured records known as Evidence Cards to reduce manual record-keeping.

The competition also awarded US$8,000 to first runner-up Marga AI and US$6,000 to second runner-up TALO, which was created by university students aged 21 and 22. All three winning teams received computing credits to help cover their initial hosting and model-inference costs. This event highlighted the Model Context Protocol as a standard for linking AI agents to external tools and institutional workflows. Such technical gatherings in Nairobi aim to integrate African engineers into global conversations typically dominated by Asia, Europe, and North America.

The Ministry of Information, Communications and the Digital Economy launched the Kenya National Artificial Intelligence Strategy 2025 to 2030 on March 27, 2025, with a reported KSh 152 billion budget. However, legislative progress has stalled, as a Senate committee in October 2026 recommended against the Artificial Intelligence Bill, 2026, sponsored by Senator Karen Nyamu. That proposed bill would have created an AI Commissioner with the power to levy fines of KSh 5 million or impose two years of imprisonment. Organizers have not yet disclosed the judging rubric or how the voice-driven data is encrypted and stored.

The success of Dira will depend on whether the prize money and credits can lead to sustained pilots within school budgets. While the national strategy is in place, the lack of a dedicated regulator leaves startups to navigate general data-protection obligations on their own. Future adoption of these agentic tools requires reliable institutional procurement and comprehensive teacher training. It remains unclear if these early experiments will move from hackathon validation into everyday Kenyan classrooms.

stories.Headline: Microsoft AI chief Suleyman calls recursive self-improvement dangerous yet keeps deploying agents
stories.Summary:
Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman expressed deep nervousness about AI models improving other models. He spoke about this dangerous capability during a November 17 interview with Deirdre Bosa. This conversation occurred the same day Microsoft announced six new MAI models at Ignite. Suleyman described the last three months as a total watershed moment for the industry. He believes that recursive self-improvement is a very serious and dangerous capability.

Microsoft is putting AI agents on Windows 11 PCs and within Microsoft 365. The company announced seven new MAI models, including MAI Code 2 and MAI Cyber 2 Flash. A new contract in October 2025 allowed Microsoft to pursue AGI independently from OpenAI. The superintelligence team started 12 months ago to reach the absolute frontier next year. Microsoft Execution Containers became generally available on Windows 11 in October to provide guardrails.

Mustafa Suleyman said that models are now fully involved in improving the models that follow. He stated that the industry is not being alarmist about these recursive self-improvement risks. Suleyman believes that models must be proven safe step by step before entering production. He argued that Microsoft must ensure models are contained, aligned, and secured for users. He also stated that he is a humanist who strongly opposes the idea of handoverism.

John Langford, a 14 year veteran, quit Microsoft AI because the philosophy is scaling. Some Microsoft engineers admit the company cares more about winning than about product polish. Regular users are affected by agents that can organize, move, and rename their files. These agents may hallucinate or fall for attacks like cross-prompt injection on Windows PCs. Nation state grade capabilities could be available to the general public within six months.

Microsoft previously relied on OpenAI models served on Azure and wrapped inside the Copilot app. The company now uses gigawatts of compute to build its own frontier model ecosystem. A July breach at Hugging Face showed an autonomous AI agent breaking into production infrastructure. Suleyman previously wrote a book called The Coming Wave which pleaded for AI containment. He once told Axios that governments should license powerful AI to avoid acting too late.

Microsoft will continue rolling out MAI Code 2 into the GitHub Copilot platform now. The company has no plans to do open weight for its new frontier models. Suleyman wants AI labs to coordinate and share safety practices like the drug industry. He admitted that Microsoft has not hit the brakes on any technology so far. The articles leave open whether Microsoft will actually stop a model if it is dangerous.

stories.Headline: Harvard's Yu presents CHIEF pathology AI model for bladder cancer analysis
stories.Summary:
Kun-Hsing Yu, an associate professor at Harvard Medical School, discussed foundation AI models for pathology image analysis in bladder cancer at the BCAN Think Tank annual meeting, in a UroToday video posted on November 22, 2026. He described his lab's CHIEF model, which was trained on more than 15 million pathology image patches plus an additional 60,000 hosted images from 19 different anatomical sites. The model aligns image findings with text annotations from pathology reports using the CLIP method first proposed by OpenAI. Yu said the model was evaluated for making cancer diagnosis, predicting molecular profiles and survival prediction. He spoke with Ashish Kamat, a urologic oncologist in Houston, Texas, and a professor of urology at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center.

Yu said a foundation model is a large general-purpose machine learning model trained on broad and diverse data that can be adopted to a wide range of downstream tasks. He cited GPT, Gemini and Claude as families of foundation models developed using vast amounts of human-generated text and image. He said the CHIEF model extracts detailed features from individual image regions and aggregates them into a patient-level representation to capture simple-level patterns. He said several related models using similar approaches have appeared since CHIEF's publication, each with different training data, architectures and combinations of image and language information. He said imaging-based models capture only one dimension of a patient's disease, and that pathology slides, radiology scans, genomic and transcriptomic profiles, medical records, treatment regimen and family history are among the data included in multimodal models.

Yu argued that true clinical impact requires integrating pathology with radiology, genomic, transcriptomic and clinical record data into multimodal models rather than imaging alone. He said this multimodal framework enables discovery of new biomarkers, improves patient prediction and supports translation of insights into clinical care. In bladder cancer specifically, he said this means more accurate risk stratification, better prediction of recurrence and treatment response, and more personalized treatment selection. He said clinical deployment must minimize clicks and cognitive burden rather than add them, and should make clear when a clinician is expected to act on the output or override it. He said accountability requires defining who owns the final clinical decision and monitoring performance shift and unintended harms vigorously after deployment, with a clear process for escalation and correction.

Yu said clinical trust comes from transparency, and that models must communicate the basis and limits of their output and make uncertainty visible to end users while preserving meaningful human oversight. He said responsibility has to be built into the entire AI system, not only added to the end. He predicted pathologists will not be replaced by AI, but that those who adopt it will replace those who don't. He closed by paraphrasing John F. Kennedy, saying we should ask not what AI can do for you but what we can do together to build a better future with AI in medicine. Kamat said AI and machine learning have seen an explosion in medicine, and noted that niche companies such as Valar Labs have developed AI algorithms that look at tissue and are trained on large data sets as closed platforms.

Kamat asked whether pathology AI will remain restricted to certain proprietary platforms or become a general pathology AI available across the globe in the near future. Yu agreed it was a great question and observation, and began to note that several proprietary platforms currently exist. The discussion was part of a breakout session at this year's BCAN Think Tank annual meeting on how AI is beginning to read risk directly from tissue. Yu's biography lists him as an associate professor in the Department of Biomedical Informatics at Harvard Medical School in Boston, Massachusetts. Kamat's biography lists him as a professor of urology and the Wayne B. Duddleston Professor of Cancer Research at the University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston, Texas.

Related content listed with the video includes BCANTT 2026: AI in Bladder Cancer: What's Real, What's Next, and What to Watch Out For, and sessions on artificial intelligence and machine learning in bladder cancer pathology and clinical decision-making with Hikmat Al-Ahmadie and Alexandre Zlotta. Another related item is Harnessing Artificial Intelligence in Bladder Cancer: Digital Tools for Enhanced Diagnosis and Treatment with David McConkey. The article was published on UroToday's Bladder Cancer Center of Excellence page, dated November 22, 2026, and the video was posted on November 21, 2026. The page carries a cookie notice with a privacy policy and an I Agree button. The transcript ends mid-sentence as Yu was describing proprietary platforms.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Angel Robotics lets people build and control robots without code through its phact and phorce platform
stories.Summary:
Angel Robotics, a wearable robotics company founded in 2017 by Kong Kyoung-chul, is pursuing a physical AI business strategy built on two technologies, the phact actuator and the phorce control platform of circuit boards and algorithms. Kong, who is also a professor of mechanical engineering at KAIST, described the goal as letting anyone build and control the robot they need without writing a single line of code. The company became the first Korean wearable robotics company to go public on the KOSDAQ in 2024, and its flagship products include the Angel Legs M20 and Angel Suit H10 rehabilitation robots. Those products combine phact, which works like a muscle, phorce, which controls movement, and AI that reads users' movement intentions in real time to assist them.

The company has secured coverage under Korea's national health insurance system for its products and has expanded into overseas markets including Malaysia. The platform's potential was shown at the first Robot Hackathon at KAIST in August, where all 10 teams of undergraduates from KAIST and Seoul National University, most without a formal robotics background, built robots with phact and phorce in just 100 hours. Their projects included robots for packing boxes and grilling lamb skewers, and some students went on to launch startups based on their creations. Kong said physical AI has a wide range of applications, noting that a robot filling containers with rice and one filling them with red beans require separate development because they involve different data.

Kong said the company spent years studying the resistance and friction of rehabilitation robots to help treat patients, and that this research has become a competitive advantage in the era of physical AI. He added that as the physical AI ecosystem expands, advances in data and lower component costs will create synergies with the wearable rehabilitation robot business. He also said there will be sufficient demand for the platform, and that the company will dramatically lower the barriers to physical AI so ordinary people can use it without difficulty. He said the company aims to become a leader in the "robots for all" ecosystem.

stories.Headline: Meta halts buybacks and borrows to fund AI data center spending
stories.Summary:
Meta stopped buying back its own stock, spending nothing on buybacks in the first nine months of 2026 after spending $26 billion in the same period of 2025, and moved that cash into capital spending such as data centers. In those nine months its business brought in $97 billion, which was $17 billion more than a year earlier, and it put $83 billion into capital spending, or 86 cents of every dollar, up from 61 cents. Meta also borrowed $25 billion, lifting its debt from $29 billion a year earlier to $84 billion, and in November it sold another $15 billion and €9 billion of bonds. In late October it sold about $14 billion of preferred stock that converts into shares, and it agreed to sell 40 million new shares by November 2027. Its interest bill more than tripled to $2.3 billion, which the article says is still small next to the $97 billion of cash its business brought in.

Analysts expect Meta's sales to reach $313 billion in 2027, and at 55 cents of cash per $1 of sales that would bring in about $172 billion, leaving $167 billion to spend from its own cash after about $5 billion of dividends. Against its current spending pace of $136 billion, that leaves room to spend about $31 billion more without new debt, or about 23%, assuming no buybacks. Its room to borrow is the smallest of the three cash-rich buyers, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta, because its debt nearly tripled in the past year, and the November bonds cut that room to about $64 billion. Meta's $31 billion of room is worth about $16 billion to Nvidia, or up to about $63 billion if Meta borrows, since Nvidia's sales equal about 52 cents of every $1 the five biggest buyers spend.

The article says Meta traded its buybacks for data centers and also borrowed and sold stock on top, so its owners now carry more debt, with more shares on the way and no buybacks for now. If 2027 spending stays within the $167 billion Meta can pay from its own cash, buybacks could come back. On Friday, Nov 20, AI stocks had a hard day, with Nvidia falling 14.0%, the Nasdaq 100 fund 5.7%, Meta 5.9% and the S&P 500 fund 3.6%. The article also says about $118 billion of analysts' forecast for Nvidia is not yet covered by any buyer's cash or borrowing room.

stories.Headline: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge publishes proposed Riemann hypothesis proof he says Claude helped develop
stories.Summary:
Levent Alpöge, a Turkish American mathematician working at Anthropic, published a proposed proof of the Riemann hypothesis on Friday, 21 November 2026, and said the AI system Claude helped him develop it over about six weeks. He released the proof together with computer code written in Lean, a programming language used to formalize mathematical arguments, and he says the code can verify the findings. Mathematicians have begun examining the work, but it has not been independently confirmed. The Riemann hypothesis was first proposed by the German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859 and concerns the distribution of prime numbers, the building blocks of arithmetic.

The problem is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems selected by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000, and the institute offers $1 million for each problem that is successfully solved. Alpöge wrote on his personal website that Claude far outpaced him near the finish line, adding that the system flew, danced and sparkled near that finish line. He also acknowledged that the precise timing was horrible, saying that if he could have, he would have finished it all much earlier. The announcement came one day after Anthropic made its debut on Nasdaq.

The claim arrives as AI companies increasingly seek to show that their systems can contribute to advanced mathematics, a field where the difference between a plausible argument and a rigorous proof matters greatly, and a proposed solution must withstand independent scrutiny before it is accepted. In September, OpenAI said a non-public version of its AI tools had helped solve part of another Millennium Prize Problem, an effort reportedly involving $15 million and 10,000 AI systems. Alpöge had been working on that separate problem for Anthropic when OpenAI made its announcement, and his latest claim puts the two companies in an increasingly visible contest. On the same Friday, the Italian mathematician Alessandro Masullo released an incomplete proof of the Riemann hypothesis that he said he had spent nearly 12 years developing, and he said he had not used AI because he did not fully trust the technology.

stories.Headline: Anthropic prices IPO above range and lists on Nasdaq at $111.50
stories.Summary:
Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share, above its marketed range of $70 to $78, and began trading on Nasdaq on Thursday, listing at $111.50, Yahoo Finance reported on Saturday, November 21, 2026. Elon Musk, CEO of SpaceX and Tesla, praised Anthropic's AI models ahead of the Nasdaq debut, saying he had met members of the team before SpaceX agreed to supply computing capacity. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy reiterated that his company is a "big believer" in Anthropic ahead of its Nasdaq debut. Anthropic's landmark IPO put the AI company's relationships with some of the biggest technology companies in focus that week. The company's filing identifies Amazon, Google and Microsoft as companies that "develop and deploy competing AI models."

Anthropic's IPO filing says it expects to pay SpaceX about $3.1 billion a month once all the promised computing capacity is delivered. Musk said Anthropic is "extremely likely" to keep renting computing capacity from SpaceX and could seek another 10 gigawatts. Amazon is set to hold roughly 14.7% of Anthropic's capital stock after the IPO and concurrent private placement, while Alphabet's Google will own about 13.7%, according to the company's filing. Together, the two companies will hold roughly 28.4%. Anthropic has committed to spend between $47.2 billion and $49.2 billion with Microsoft, and Google agreed to purchase $10 billion in non-voting Anthropic stock through the private placement.

Musk said "Opus and Fable are great products" and that "no one I know at Anthropic set off my evil detector." He described Anthropic's executives as "principled" and "diligent," and called the potential additional 10 gigawatts a "big number." Musk cautioned that demand could decline in a "worst-case scenario" if governments impose severe restrictions on AI, and said the agreements are short-term and either side can terminate them. He added that he would end the arrangement if he believed Anthropic was doing something "really terrible for the world."

Jassy said "we're big believers in Anthropic" and has previously said customers want access to multiple leading AI models, a dynamic that benefits Amazon Web Services by allowing it to offer third-party models such as Anthropic's Claude. Beyond Musk and Jassy, the other Magnificent Seven CEOs did not make new public comments specifically addressing Anthropic or its IPO during the week, including Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai, Nvidia's Colette Kress, Apple CEO Tim Cook and Meta Platforms CEO Mark Zuckerberg. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around TSLA stock slipped to 'neutral' from 'bullish' over the past week, while chatter stayed at 'low' levels. Retail sentiment around AMZN stock stayed in 'bearish' territory over the past week, accompanied by 'low' levels of chatter. Retail sentiment around ANT stock stayed in 'extremely bullish' territory through the week, with chatter at 'extremely high' levels.

Amazon, Alphabet's Google and Nvidia are among Anthropic's investors, while Microsoft is a major financial backer and infrastructure partner. SpaceX, led by Tesla CEO Elon Musk, is also supplying computing capacity to the Claude developer. Musk said he knew several Anthropic employees from his time at OpenAI. Microsoft participated in Anthropic's private placement, adding to its financial and commercial relationship with the AI company. Anthropic's filing identifies Amazon, Google and Microsoft as companies that "develop and deploy competing AI models."

Musk said the SpaceX agreements are short-term and either side can terminate them, and that he would end the arrangement if he believed Anthropic was doing something "really terrible for the world." The article did not say when Anthropic's additional 10 gigawatts of computing capacity might be delivered. The article did not say what the other Magnificent Seven CEOs might say about Anthropic later. The article did not give further details on the terms of Google's $10 billion purchase of non-voting Anthropic stock. The article did not say how Anthropic's stock performed after its $111.50 listing on Thursday.

stories.Headline: Cornell's Eun-Ah Kim leads machine-learning work in a $12 million Energy Department quantum AI project
stories.Summary:
A $12 million award from the U.S. Department of Energy will fund a collaborative project linking artificial intelligence and quantum computing, according to an announcement reported on November 20, 2026. The effort is called Application-Aware Error Correction Codesign for Scientific Quantum Computing, and it is one of twelve Phase II awards under the Genesis Mission. Eun-Ah Kim, the Hans A. Bethe Professor at Cornell, will lead machine-learning work focused on a reinforcement-learning compiler that translates quantum algorithms into physical movements on a reconfigurable neutral-atom quantum computer. Harvard Professor Mikhail Lukin, co-director of the Harvard Quantum Initiative, leads the project overall, with Kim serving as a co-investigator.

Kim's group will concentrate on two key stages, beginning with compilation, and they will build a reinforcement-learning compiler to convert algorithms into specific atom movements and gate operations. The project unites expertise from MIT and Harvard alongside industry partners QuEra Computing, NVIDIA and Anthropic, demonstrating a broad collaborative effort. Researchers from Los Alamos, Lawrence Berkeley and Sandia national laboratories also contribute to the initiative, which is administered by the Department of Energy's Advanced Scientific Computing Research division. The collaboration extends beyond algorithm translation, aiming to improve the entire pipeline from scientific question to hardware execution.

According to the Department of Energy's announcement of the Genesis Mission awards, the goal is to integrate the world's best supercomputers, experimental facilities and AI systems to advance American research and innovation. The project's funding signifies a commitment to linking AI and quantum computing for scientific advancement, the report said. The award places Harvard and Cornell arts and sciences researchers within a twelve-award Phase II cohort under the Genesis Mission. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the funded work described.

stories.Headline: Nvidia's 40% slide spreads AI bubble fears to stocks and Bitcoin
stories.Summary:
Nvidia shares fell roughly 40% from their October 6, 2026 all-time closing high of $243.37 to around $150 by mid-November, and the selloff spread to the S&P 500, the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the crypto market. Bitcoin traded below $60,000 on November 21, 2026, with an intraday low somewhere between $55,000 and $57,000, and the asset has now fallen more than 30% since September 2026. The total crypto market contracted to approximately $2 trillion, down from a peak above $4 trillion in October 2025, while the S&P 500 entered correction territory with weekly losses exceeding 8% as of November 21, 2026. The Dow also slipped into a correction, and both benchmarks now sit more than 10% below their recent peaks, according to Crypto Briefing.

The anxiety centers on whether the trillions of dollars flowing into AI infrastructure will ever earn back what they cost, since AI infrastructure spending is projected at $7 trillion through 2030 while Gartner forecasts AI revenue over the same window at only $3.6 trillion. Nvidia sells the chips that power data centers, so if the companies buying those chips start doubting the payoff, they may slow their orders. The selling pressure on Bitcoin appears to reflect a broad, macro-driven liquidity squeeze rather than any problem specific to crypto, and no major exchange failure or protocol exploit is behind the move. Instead, Bitcoin is trading like a high-beta risk asset that moves with tech stocks, so when investors pull money out of speculative growth bets, digital assets tend to get swept up in the same tide.

The article was written by Diego Almada Lopez and edited by him, and it states that the gap between projected AI spending and forecast revenue is unlikely to close quickly, calling a $7 trillion capex bill against $3.6 trillion in expected revenue a structural mismatch rather than a quarterly blip. It says each new earnings report from chipmakers and cloud providers will be read as evidence for or against the bubble thesis. For crypto traders, the key signal may sit outside crypto entirely, because as long as Bitcoin trades in step with the Nasdaq and the S&P 500, the path of the AI trade could help set the direction for digital assets too. The article carries a disclosure that all content is for informational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice.

stories.Headline: Claude AI predicts Chainlink could fall to $1.85 by January 2027 in a bearish scenario
stories.Summary:
Anthropic's Claude AI predicted that Chainlink faces a catastrophic collapse that could erase years of progress and leave the token trading at a fraction of its former relevance by the first day of 2027, according to a TradingView article published on November 21, 2026. The hypothetical landmark catalyst in the prediction is a coordinated institutional rejection of decentralized oracles, in which a consortium of major global banks, clearing houses and rating agencies announces in mid-2027 that it will migrate all critical data feeds, cross-chain messaging and compliance infrastructure to a new permissioned, bank-operated oracle network built on proprietary technology. The article says the consortium cites unresolved concerns around decentralization risks, potential single points of failure in the broader ecosystem and regulatory pressure for fully controllable systems, and that it effectively freezes new production deployments of Chainlink's CCIP and Data Streams. Existing pilots are wound down, and the narrative that Chainlink would become the standard connective tissue for tokenized finance collapses almost overnight, the article says.

In this extreme but not impossible scenario, Claude AI predicts that Chainlink could trade at $1.85 by January 1, 2027, which the article describes as a probability-weighted bearish scenario rather than a certainty. On higher-timeframe charts looking into 2027, the article says LINK has spent years forming a broad distribution pattern after its previous-cycle peak, with multi-year descending trendlines and failed attempts to sustain higher structural highs leaving the asset vulnerable to a decisive breakdown. Should the institutional narrative fracture, measured-move projections from the long-term range and Fibonacci extensions of prior major declines open the door to a deep retracement of the entire post-2020 advance, and volume profiles and long-term moving-average clusters that once acted as support would flip into heavy overhead supply. The article says macro conditions, liquidity and risk appetite will ultimately determine the path.

The article notes that recent catalysts widely viewed as bullish could kill the Claude prediction, including high-profile integrations Chainlink secured throughout late 2026, expanded CCIP volume metrics and a completed Moody's testnet pilot for multi-chain credit ratings. It also partnered with OpenZeppelin for institutional tooling, advanced work with LG CNS on Korean digital assets, and saw banks publicly discuss moving from exploration into production systems. However, the article says that if these announcements ultimately fail to convert into sticky, high-volume, fee-generating usage that meaningfully accrues value to the LINK token, they risk becoming evidence of over-promised institutional adoption. A sudden pivot by the same institutions toward closed alternatives would turn the current partnership pipeline into a liability rather than an asset, according to the article.

stories.Headline: KAIST researcher urges metal detectors to stop AI smart glasses cheating on college exam
stories.Summary:
A KAIST artificial intelligence researcher and YouTube creator, Heo Sung-beom, warned in a video posted on his channel on the 16th that test takers could cheat on the college entrance exam using AI smart glasses, and he urged the government to prepare thorough measures before the exam. He said he did not make AI to be used this way and found it sad that some people abuse it before social systems or guidelines are ready. He explained that cheating with AI devices works in three stages, photographing questions with a micro camera, sending them out through communication equipment, and receiving analyzed answers through smart glasses or earphones. He said the biggest problem is that a small number of students abuse technology and may take opportunities away from students who studied hard, and he called it senseless to hold the test without any measures.

Heo proposed a metal detector as the most realistic way to block such cheating, because lenses, smart glasses and earphones all need a battery to run for a long time, and the battery contains metal that a detector should catch. He noted that test supervisors are not professional security staff, so suspicious signals may be missed, and that securing enough equipment and training supervisors in a short time is practically difficult. He questioned thermal imaging cameras, saying very small devices or ones that have not yet built up enough heat may not be caught and that a whole classroom would have to be watched from a distance. He also called for checks of communication devices such as smartphones, smart watches, tablet PCs and portable Wi-Fi at test sites, for unexpected inspections with radio wave detectors, and for later checks of communication records and test paper analysis for suspected cheaters, while warning that investigating every test taker's records could raise legal problems.

The controversy spread after a person identified as A, who passed the tax accountant examination, confessed to cheating on the tax accountant and certified public accountant exams using micro cameras and generative AI, turned himself in to police, and had related electronic devices seized in an investigation. Concern grew that AI cheating could occur in the CSAT, which was to take place on the 19th, and college entrance exam creator Mimiminu, Korean language instructor Yoo Jae-jong and math instructor Jung Seung-je also urged measures to secure fairness, with Jung saying postponement of the CSAT should be considered if no effective measures exist. The government responded, with Cheong Wa Dae holding an emergency meeting on the 15th to discuss a full investigation into suspected AI cheating and ways to strengthen management and supervision of CSAT test sites, and police decided to form a countermeasure team for CSAT cheating. Heo told worried students that cheating is bound to be caught eventually even if it takes time and hoped they would never do it because it could twist their lives, and he told test takers skeptical about studying that people have abused technology in every era and they should go their own way.
