stories.Headline: Pasadena councilmember Justin Jones renews call for local AI policy and cybersecurity review
stories.Summary:
Pasadena City Councilmember Justin Jones renewed his call for the city to develop a local artificial intelligence policy and to review its cybersecurity protections, telling Pasadena Now on Thursday that residents should be able to find out how the city uses AI and provide input. His renewed push followed a week of communication outages at email systems, the Federal Aviation Authority, banks and intelligence agencies, and a Microsoft outage that left the city and other organizations unable to send or receive email. No cyberattack has been reported so far, though several legislators have expressed doubts about that claim, and the City Council discussed the need for talks on local technology on Tuesday. Jones first called for a local AI policy at a City Council meeting last month, and Councilmember Steve Madison has expressed support for the policy. Jones said he wants the city to review its cybersecurity protections and its plans for keeping services running through a major technology failure, noting that the city depends on computer systems for emergency communications, public safety, water, electricity, traffic signals and finances.

He said the council needs to understand the city's vulnerabilities and the cost to fix them, and that he will bring the matter to the Municipal Services Committee, which he chairs and which oversees public works, transportation and Pasadena Water and Power. Rick Cole, who also sits on the committee, echoed the call, saying technology is reshaping every aspect of life including the public sector and that Pasadena can lead, follow or get crushed. No date has been announced for a Municipal Services Committee discussion on cybersecurity. The article cites recent attacks on local organizations, including a June 2026 ShinyHunters extortion campaign against Pasadena-based Inter-Con Security that exposed employee and contact records, and a broader cyberattack one month earlier that disrupted access to the Canvas education platform for Pasadena City College and Pasadena Unified School District. In June 2024, a ransomware attack forced network shutdowns across all 36 Los Angeles County Superior Court locations, including the Pasadena Courthouse, and after a 2024 ransomware attack in Columbus, Ohio, its City Council approved $23 million in July 2025 for a new security network.

Jones said a discussion could review which services are most important to protect, whether backups are adequate and how long recovery from a longer outage would take, and that upgrades and a new network could cost millions if the city were hit. Councilmembers are also concerned about data retention, and on Tuesday the city voted to end its contract with Flock Cameras, whose license plate readers store data on an Amazon server out of local control. Councilmember Tyron Hampton called for keeping information obtained by technology in Pasadena, recommending servers owned and operated by city employees, and noted that 300 other agencies and every sworn Pasadena police officer could access the information. Councilmember Jason Lyon called the discussion on mass surveillance and data retention one of the most important of our time, and the Council unanimously agreed that the limited public safety benefits of the technology do not outweigh the privacy risks.

stories.Headline: Apple settles Siri lawsuit for $250 million as claimants seek at least $61 per iPhone
stories.Summary:
In May, Apple agreed to pay $250 million to settle a U.S. class action lawsuit over Siri AI's delayed launch, MacRumors reported on Saturday, November 21, 2026. The report said one month remained to submit a claim through the settlement website. In a court document earlier that week, lawyers said claimants will likely receive at least $61 per eligible iPhone, based on early participation data so far. The article was published at 9:08 am PST and written by Joe Rossignol. The lawsuit alleged false advertising after Apple delayed the personalized version of Siri in March 2025.

Apple will pay a minimum of $25 per eligible iPhone to eligible customers, who can submit a claim via the settlement website until December 21 of this year. The exact payment may be higher or lower than $25 depending on the total number of valid claims submitted and other factors, with the maximum amount set at $95. To be eligible, a person must reside in the U.S. and have purchased one of the listed iPhone models in the U.S. for purposes other than resale between June 10, 2024 and March 29, 2025. Eligible customers should have already been notified by email, which contains a claim ID and a PIN code, though the settlement website also offers an option to submit a claim without this information. The claims form asks for personal information and the eligible iPhone's serial number, and if the serial number is unavailable, it asks for the Apple Account email address and the eligible iPhone's phone number.

Apple denies all of the allegations made in the lawsuit and agreed to the settlement to avoid the costs and risks of a trial. In a statement, Apple touted a range of other Apple Intelligence features it had already released. Nevertheless, Apple agreed to settle the lawsuit "to stay focused" on "delivering the most innovative products and services to our users." The lawyers representing the class members expect payouts of at least $61 per eligible iPhone, unless there is a significant uptick in claims submitted. According to the terms of the settlement, each person who files an eligible claim will receive a per-device payment of $25, but this amount could increase up to $95 if the total number of claims submitted is lower than anticipated.

On November 16, the lawyers representing the class members estimated that claimants will receive at least $61 per eligible iPhone. A final approval hearing is scheduled for February 24, 2027, so payments to customers are not expected to begin until some point next year. The settlement website answers some common questions about opting out of the settlement and other important topics, and the article advised reading it carefully. The article said Apple finally announced Siri AI at WWDC 2026 in June, and Siri AI is available on iPhone 15 Pro models and newer running iOS 27, which was released in September. Siri AI is still considered a beta feature even though iOS 27 is no longer in beta.

In June 2024, Apple previewed new Siri capabilities powered by Apple Intelligence, including understanding of a user's personal context, on-screen awareness, and deeper per-app controls. For example, Apple showed an iPhone user asking Siri about their mother's flight and lunch reservation plans based on info from the Mail and Messages apps. Apple advertised those Siri features in product presentations, on its website, in a TV commercial starring actor Bella Ramsey, and elsewhere. In March 2025, Apple delayed the launch of the personalized version of Siri, leading to the company being hit with a class action lawsuit alleging false advertising. The article noted that in May, Apple agreed to pay $250 million to settle the lawsuit.

The claims deadline is December 21, and the final approval hearing is scheduled for February 24, 2027. Payments to customers are not expected to begin until some point next year. The article said the exact payment may be higher or lower than $25 depending on the total number of valid claims submitted and other factors, with the maximum amount set at $95. The lawyers said claimants will likely receive at least $61 per eligible iPhone, based on early participation data so far, unless there is a significant uptick in claims submitted. The article left open the final number of valid claims and the exact payment amount.

stories.Headline: Berkshire holds 30.2 percent of its 367 billion dollar portfolio in Apple and Alphabet AI stocks
stories.Summary:
Adam Spatacco wrote an article on November 17, 2026, regarding the investment holdings of Berkshire Hathaway. He analyzed how the company manages its large portfolio under the leadership of CEO Greg Abel. The report focuses on the firm's significant exposure to the artificial intelligence sector through specific stocks. It examines the current distribution of assets within a total portfolio valued at 367 billion dollars. The author evaluates which technology investments align best with the long term philosophy of Warren Buffett.

The portfolio holds 30.2 percent of its value in Apple and Alphabet, which are both artificial intelligence stocks. Apple represents 21.9 percent of the holdings, consisting of 228 million shares worth about 80.5 billion dollars. Alphabet makes up 8.3 percent of the portfolio, with a stake worth roughly 30.4 billion dollars. Berkshire bought 17.8 million Alphabet shares in the third quarter of 2025 and increased this to 106 million. A 10 billion dollar investment was made through a private placement in June to fund AI infrastructure.

Warren Buffett personally initiated the investment in Alphabet, while Greg Abel has overseen the expansion of that specific position. Spatacco stated that Apple is the more defensive long term investment because of its sticky ecosystem and brand. He noted that Apple does not need to dominate infrastructure spending to benefit from the adoption of AI technology. Alphabet provides direct exposure to AI through Gemini models, cloud infrastructure, and the development of custom semiconductor hardware. However, the author warned that Alphabet's aggressive capital expenditures introduce uncertainty regarding the company's future financial returns.

Large language models like ChatGPT present challenges to the business model of Alphabet by competing with Google Search services. Investors prioritizing business durability over speculative upside may find Apple more aligned with the preference for established, enduring franchises. Other market participants are watching Nvidia, where founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following a probe into alleged spying. Interim CEO Colette Kress will lead the fiscal 2027 third quarter earnings report after the market closes November 17. This report could affect AI power stocks like Constellation Energy, Bloom Energy, and the pipeline network Energy Transfer.

Berkshire first started building its position in Apple a decade ago, and it became the portfolio's largest holding. By mid 2023, Apple accounted for more than 50 percent of holdings, but Berkshire trimmed this stake in 2024. The company continued reducing its exposure throughout 2025, though it did not sell any Apple shares in early 2026. Nvidia reported second quarter revenue of 96.2 billion dollars, with its data center segment bringing in 89 billion dollars. Constellation Energy has power agreements with Amazon for 690 megawatts and with Alphabet for about 890 megawatts.

Nvidia has projected third quarter revenue of 108 billion dollars, which would be an 89 percent gain over last year. Investors will wait to see if demand for the next generation Vera Rubin platform is progressing as expected. The outlook for the fourth quarter will determine if AI infrastructure demand is accelerating or beginning to moderate. The articles leave open whether Alphabet can maintain its search dominance against new AI competitors and large language models. It remains unclear if Nvidia's leadership crisis will impact the broader spending trends of its global AI customers.

stories.Headline: Major tech firms use existing ecosystems to compete in AI office software as models become commoditized
stories.Summary:
Major Chinese companies recently adjusted their organizational structures for AI office business to concentrate resources and use existing advantages in channels and ecosystems. ByteDance integrated Doubao, Feishu, and Volcano Engine in July, while Liang Rubo explained this arrangement at the September Feishu Conference. Tencent incorporated QClaw into WorkBuddy, and Alibaba merged three products into Tongyi Office under the DingTalk team. Baidu integrated internal products into Baidu Dazi, and Kingsoft Office shifted its main focus toward AI.

Tencent WorkBuddy connects to Hunyuan, DeepSeek, Zhipu GLM, Kimi, and MiniMax, while Doubao Work accesses Kimi, GLM, DeepSeek, and two Doubao models. Tongyi Office launched ten models in mid-November, including self-developed Tongyi, DeepSeek, Kimi, and MiniMax, after briefly accessing external models in August. Microsoft Copilot adopts both OpenAI and Claude models, and packages AI functions into the E7 plan for 99 dollars per user monthly. Alibaba popularized the data mid-platform concept around 2015, but the company began weakening this specific approach around 2020.

Large enterprises claim that holding massive data provides a competitive advantage, but the author says getting departments to coordinate interests is difficult. These companies also argue that connecting systems to core processes creates customer reliance, though this can make product modification very slow. The author notes that the labor cost saved in some RPA projects is not even enough to maintain the software. Satya Nadella integrated OpenAI capabilities into the Office suite rather than making AI an independent product.

Users of WorkBuddy are partly driven by point subsidies and free traffic from WeChat, though this may not translate into long-term usage. Tencent relies on WeChat and WeCom traffic, while Alibaba uses DingTalk enterprise customers and Kingsoft uses government and enterprise channels. Baidu utilizes its search, cloud disk, and intelligent cloud systems, while Microsoft relies on the customer base from Windows and Office. These companies use traditional software industry tactics, making their AI office products increasingly similar to one another.

The articles state that many people initially thought new AI products would replace industry leaders and allow small companies to rise. However, big companies with existing customer relationships and complete product systems still occupy a favorable position because models are now accessible to all. The author explains that sorting messy data into usable information requires long-term accumulation that cannot be solved by simply switching models. This suggests that AI is currently being used by old companies to complete upgrades to their original systems.

The winner among these five major companies remains unknown because it is too early to tell who will prevail in this competition. The articles leave open whether a balance can be struck between product stability and the flexibility needed for models that update every half year. It remains unclear if a new player, developing outside the attention of leading enterprises, will emerge to re-divide the market. The realization process of technological change is described as more tortuous than initially expected.

stories.Headline: Anthropic ports AI models to AMD chips in days without engineers
stories.Summary:
Anthropic disclosed that its Claude Mythos model can move part of its AI workloads onto non-Nvidia chips in just a few days with basically no human intervention, a job that used to take six to 12 months and dozens of engineers. The disclosures came as Anthropic prepares for its IPO, and the headline capability is software that rewrites and tunes AI models to run on different hardware largely on its own. The specific benchmark is AMD's MI355X GPUs, which Claude Mythos can port an AI model to in approximately three days compared to the old norm of 6-12 months. Nvidia's dominance has never rested on silicon alone, because its CUDA software ecosystem is the real lock-in that developers built their tools around.

Anthropic's deal for AMD's Instinct GPUs is projected to reach multi-gigawatt scale, with the first phase set for the first half of 2027. AMD reportedly offers a per-gigawatt system cost that is roughly half that of some Nvidia platforms, and Nvidia's share of contracted future AI compute capacity for frontier labs has declined to around 39% from previous highs of 80% or more. Alphabet stands to benefit because its tensor processing units, or TPUs, are custom chips built for AI workloads that gain when customers can move models onto them without a costly rewrite. TSMC may be the quietest beneficiary, since it manufactures chips for Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom and collects revenue no matter which designer wins the procurement fight.

For Nvidia, the risk is less about losing sales tomorrow and more about losing pricing power over time, with the 39% capacity share figure the number to watch. For AMD, the opportunity is direct, because its biggest obstacle was software friction rather than chip performance, and the Anthropic deal becomes a proof of concept other buyers can point to. The articles note risks to the commoditization story, since Anthropic's results cover part of its workloads rather than all of them, and porting a model is different from running it at peak efficiency across every task. Nvidia also still holds a large installed base and deep relationships with nearly every major AI buyer, while overall demand for AI chips continues to look strong as companies spread purchases across vendors.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Stand for Children releases guidelines for school districts to govern student devices and educational technology
stories.Summary:
A national nonprofit organization called Stand for Children released a new research-backed framework on November 20, 2026. This document, titled Instructional Technology and School-Issued Devices: District Policy Guidelines, helps school districts manage the risks of student devices. The guidelines provide a way for school systems to regulate educational technology without using sweeping bans. These standards were developed with input from national experts to curb digital risks on school hardware.

They aim to preserve essential tools that support academic development and early literacy for students. The framework requires school districts to anchor their technology policies in student safety, data privacy, and student outcomes. Administrators must evaluate if individual tools meet a defined instructional need and protect the privacy of students. The guidelines call for minimizing or eliminating non-instructional screen time based on American Academy of Pediatrics research.

Districts are encouraged to establish a strict review cycle to prune unused or ineffective software platforms. Consolidating approved applications helps K-12 IT teams shrink their cybersecurity attack surface by reducing third-party vendors. The nonprofit organization is responsible for these guidelines and suggests that structured governance addresses direct operational challenges. They argue that unrestricted software access increases data exposure risks and creates significant compliance problems for districts.

The organization warns that blanket bans may push students and staff toward unvetted applications and unmonitored personal devices. Reducing passive digital exposure on district-managed devices limits classroom distractions and narrows windows for cyberbullying. This approach allows schools to balance educational access with the need for student safety. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Ipswich Middle School enforces a new policy banning AI deepfakes and digital impersonation to protect student dignity
stories.Summary:
The School Committee unanimously approved a new handbook resolution on Thursday night for Ipswich Middle School. This policy prohibits the use of synthetic media and generative artificial intelligence to violate the identity or dignity of others. The new rules take effect immediately following a similar resolution passed for the high school last June. This action follows several AI related issues the school has already encountered recently.

The policy forbids cyberbullying and bullying that uses technology to create deepfakes, including audio recordings, videos, or images. Prohibited actions include AI voice cloning, face swapping, and the digital manipulation of a person's likeness for defamatory or mocking purposes. Students may not engage in digital impersonation or the unauthorized use of a person's image and name. These rules apply online, off campus, and during school sponsored activities or on school grounds.

Assistant Principal Sean Fitzgerald stated that the school must investigate and mitigate issues that impact a student's life at school. He explained that the specific AI policy was necessary because the district has already seen related problems. He emphasized that the administration has a duty to ensure all students feel safe when coming to school. Other issues from the past year were handled under the existing anti bullying policy.

Students who violate these rules may face expulsion, suspension, or the loss of school issued technology. The school also reserves the right to report the creation of harmful synthetic media to the Ipswich Police Department. This policy aims to prevent the distribution of content that falsely represents staff members or students. The administration will monitor both on campus and off campus behavior to maintain student safety.

stories.Headline: ICO seeks evidence on agentic AI to shape its statutory code of practice
stories.Summary:
The Information Commissioner's Office published a call for evidence on agentic AI on 8 October 2026, seeking feedback from organisations before 20 November. The call sets out the ICO's challenges and expectations across six themes: data security, transparency, accountability, automated decision-making, fairness and purpose limitation, and lawfulness of processing. The ICO also published a report on 8 October 2026 titled Building trust and transparency into generative AI development: our work to create regulatory certainty. That report followed a supervision programme set up in 2025 under the ICO's AI and Biometrics Strategy, which originally targeted 11 priority foundation model developers. The ICO held its annual Data Protection Practitioners' Conference online on 13 October 2026, with an afternoon programme of twelve practical seminars.

The call for evidence will feed into the ICO's statutory code of practice on AI and automated decision-making, which is set to become a key pillar of UK AI regulation in the absence of standalone UK AI legislation. The ICO's report sets out next steps including developing that statutory code, releasing guidance on emerging technologies such as agentic AI, continued scrutiny of foundation model developers, and engagement with government on special category data use. The report states that broad interests such as training models are unlikely to be a valid and specific interest for processing. It states that effective mechanisms for exercising rights are likely to require a combination of dataset and model-focused measures and output-focused safeguards across the AI development lifecycle. It also states that reliance on Article 11 of the UK GDPR should not be applied broadly.

DRCF Chief Executive Kate Jones said in a keynote speech on 23 September 2026 that one agentic example, an AI agent booking a consumer's holiday, engaged the remits of all four DRCF members. She said technology converges whereas regulation historically specialised, and that AI does not arrive in neat regulatory boxes. She said AI autonomy does not remove organisational responsibility and urged organisations to end internal silos just as regulators have done via the DRCF. The ICO notes that agentic systems can involve multiple organisations, models, agents and tools that may change with the workflow, making it hard to identify who determines the purposes and means of processing. The ICO states that organisations must assess whether Articles 22A to 22D of the UK GDPR apply across the complete workflow, not to agents or decision points in isolation.

The DRCF brings together the ICO, the CMA, Ofcom and the FCA. The ICO's report provides examples of how foundation model developers have implemented data protection improvements, including completing computability assessments, publishing sources used in training, including details about safeguards in legitimate interests assessments, and adopting de-duplication, filtering, testing across different languages and classifiers and hash matching to reduce risks with special category data. The ICO's conference sessions covered the DUAA complaints requirement, AI and automated decision-making, international transfers using Article 49 derogations, and cyber resilience. The ICO recently decided to join the National Cyber Resilience Centre Group's National Ambassador programme. On data subject access requests, the ICO said the use of AI to create DSARs does not change if and how organisations comply with and fulfil them, and that organisations should consider the intention of the request and ask for clarification if needed.

The ICO's report follows a supervision programme set up in 2025 under the ICO's AI and Biometrics Strategy, which selected 11 priority foundation model developers by reference to compliance risk, UK market share and reliance on higher-risk training datasets. The report addresses transparency, lawful basis, data subject rights, whether AI models contain personal data, and special category data. On whether AI models contain personal data, the ICO states that the extent to which a model memorises training data requires a case by case assessment considering factors such as the size of the model and training dataset and the amount of duplication in training data. The ICO considers that the manifestly made public and scientific research processing conditions are potentially applicable to special category data processed for foundation model training. The ICO's conference included a session on the new obligation for controllers to handle data protection complaints under the DUAA.

The ICO's call for evidence closed on 20 November and will feed into the statutory code of practice on AI and automated decision-making. The ICO's report sets out continued scrutiny of foundation model developers through ongoing engagement and continued reliance on legitimate interests. The ICO states that organisations piloting or deploying AI agents should review the report alongside the call for evidence. The articles state that comparable guidance is lacking at EU level, with no European Data Protection Board opinion or guidance, leaving developers and deployers to rely on piecemeal guidance from individual regulators such as the Spanish data protection authority's guide on agentic AI. The articles state that organisations cannot wait for complete regulatory clarity, and that AI developers and deployers are making compliance decisions now.

stories.Headline: Meta pauses business terms on web crawling after publisher backlash
stories.Summary:
Meta has paused proposed business terms that alarmed publishing groups over the possible crawling of websites tied to business accounts, the company said, after Nieman Lab reported on the backlash to the language. The company said it is now collecting feedback from stakeholders and intends to discuss revised terms with publishers and regulators in early 2027 before putting anything into effect. It said the pause followed concerns raised about its web crawlers and noted that it honors the industry-standard robots.txt protocol, which lets sites signal their crawling preferences. The retreat comes as the traffic and advertising economics that have long sustained the media business come under strain from AI-powered search and chatbots, which can answer questions directly instead of sending readers to publishers' pages.

Google said its News AI pilot now covers more than 400 publishers worldwide, including Axios, CNN and the Financial Times, with the company paying participating outlets to license material for specific Google News features such as article overviews and personalized audio briefings. Google is separately testing a broader model that compensates publishers according to how much their content contributes to AI-generated answers across Gemini, AI Overviews and AI Mode. Anthropic signed a licensing agreement with the Associated Press covering real-time election information inside Claude, its first publisher licensing deal. In court documents made public in unsealed filings, OpenAI's head of ChatGPT, Nick Turley, acknowledged that AI products were largely substitutive of publishers' work and represented an existential threat to their businesses, and the same filings showed that OpenAI president Greg Brockman replied with a short approving remark when an employee described a workaround for the New York Times paywall.

Publishers have watched referral traffic from search and social platforms become less dependable, and generative tools threaten to compress it further by summarizing reporting without a click, which has pushed trade groups and individual outlets to press for licensing fees, crawl controls and clearer rules on attribution. For the AI companies, licensing deals give them defensible access to fresh, authoritative material and reduce legal exposure as copyright litigation advances, but each concession raises the cost of training and serving models, and a contribution-based payment model as Google is testing could prove harder to administer at scale than flat licensing fees. The Meta episode shows how quickly proposed terms can become a public fight, and pausing the language buys the company time, but the 2027 timeline means publishers will spend another year without clarity on how their sites may be accessed. Apple, for its part, is hiring to build an agentic AI assistant capable of browsing sites autonomously, moving across apps, generating and debugging code and connecting to outside services, a reminder that the demand for machine-readable content is only going to grow.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns from Nvidia and dissolves the company's AI vertical stack
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia during the week ending November 20, 2026. This leadership change occurred as the Nasdaq fell about 4 percent from Friday through Thursday. Host Steve Eisman reported that the resignation dissolved a virtual holding company structure. He claims this event fractured the single AI trade into separate investments. The resignation coincided with a large Democratic sweep of both houses in the midterms.

The circular financing involved Nvidia providing loans or equity to several AI companies. OpenAI received 30 billion dollars, while Anthropic and SpaceX each received 20 billion dollars. CoreWeave received 2.5 billion dollars, and Nebius received 2 billion dollars. These companies then used the funds to buy Nvidia chips. This structure affected 65 percent of the S&P 500 including utilities and banks.

Steve Eisman is a longtime investor and the host of the Weekly Wrap. He said the Jensen unwind is just starting and will get very ugly. Eisman argued that Nvidia should have withheld guidance to avoid a stock collapse. He stated that stock picking and valuation have returned because AI is no longer one trade. He believes the reported quarter is irrelevant to the forward picture.

The tech world wants Huang back, but Treasury Secretary Bessent has appointed himself watchdog. Banks, private equity, and shareholders are now affected as they evaluate their balance sheets. Investors in the S&P 500 are impacted because info tech is about 40 percent. Tech-adjacent names like Google and Amazon bring that total to roughly 50 percent. Other affected entities include industrial suppliers like Eaton and power providers like GE Vernova.

Nvidia reported revenue of 116 billion dollars, which was an increase of 103 percent. Earnings per share were 2.68 dollars, representing a 111 percent increase year over year. Management guided next quarter revenue to 130 billion dollars, excluding compute revenue from China. The company previously operated as a virtual vertical holding company rather than a chip vendor. This system allowed Nvidia to fund the very customers who bought its products.

The market must now determine how much revenue depended on circular financing and guarantees. It remains unclear if China exclusions cover direct sales or illegal shipments via Asian intermediaries. Eisman suggests that 20 percent of revenue from dicey Asian entities could go to zero. Future growth depends on whether the midterms produce an AI moratorium or construction slowdown. The articles leave open exactly how much Nvidia revenue will fall before it grows.

stories.Headline: Paul Schrader uses AI to write scripts and create synthetic actors for his films
stories.Summary:
Paul Schrader is using artificial intelligence to write scripts and create synthetic actors for his films. The eighty year old director began these experiments over a year ago. He is embracing this technology as he enters the final act of his career. Schrader believes the takeover of cinema by AI is inevitable. He describes the process as opening the cage of a monster.

He is collaborating with Fable, a San Francisco studio, for a horror thriller called The Doors of Perception. This film features AI generated hallucinations of an ayahuasca ceremony in the Peruvian jungle. He is using AI characters for Three Guns at Dawn after Black actors declined roles in September. He is also considering an AI western titled Nine Men from Now. These tools allow him to avoid expensive stars and major studios.

Schrader says he does not see a place for humans in the larger scheme of things. He believes that any story where man defeats AI is just a bogus story. He claims that AI actors are always available, free, and on time. He says the film world is driven by money and unions cannot stop AI. He believes the industry is hearing the last cries of a dying species.

Steven Spielberg and Christopher Nolan express deep scepticism about the use of AI in cinema. The performers union Sag Aftra requires producers to show that AI performers bring significant additional value. The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences banned AI actors and screenplays from winning Oscars this year. These guilds and organizations are trying to fend off copyright infringement and existential threats. Many Hollywood professionals strongly oppose using this technology to create scripts or actors.

Schrader wrote Taxi Driver, Raging Bull, and American Gigolo and collaborated with Martin Scorsese and Robert De Niro. He once lived as a drifter in seedy Los Angeles, which influenced his character Travis Bickle. In March, his wife of forty three years, actor Mary Beth Hurt, passed away. He later took ayahuasca eight times during a two week retreat in Costa Rica. He was disappointed that he did not experience any visual hallucinations during that trip.

Schrader will now test if audiences feel let down by films made with artificial intelligence. He previously felt spooked when AI wrote a script in his own concise tone. He wondered if the technology was his tool or if he was its tool. The articles do not say if his new AI films will be released. It remains open whether the industry can successfully block the use of synthetic actors.

stories.Headline: A CIO says organizational culture and clear responsibilities, not AI tools, determine enterprise efficiency
stories.Summary:
A CIO friend of a company in Lao Yang's group posted on November 20, 2026, that organizational efficiency cannot be improved by tools alone, and that an agile organization can be efficient even via emails. The same passage said that those who pass the buck all day cannot make good use of the best software in the world even if it is given to them free. Lao Yang wrote the article in Xiangjiang Digital Review, published with authorization from 36Kr, and 36Kr said the views are the author's own. Lao Yang recalled that a CIO friend from a manufacturing group was called out by the general manager that day about arguing over cross-departmental account reconciliation in WeChat groups for three days after adopting AI and buying collaboration software. The CIO replied that the problem was not the system but that no one was responsible for the result of the account reconciliation in the first place.

Lao Yang said the ceiling of organizational efficiency usually lies not in tools but in culture, consensus and collaboration mechanisms, and that technology is advancing while collaboration mechanisms stay stagnant. He said top leaders understand digital transformation as deploying systems, purchasing SaaS and installing models, while efficient organizations have transparent information, decentralized decision-making and clear responsibilities. He said that with these three points even primitive emails, asynchronous, traceable and group-sent for synchronization, achieve high efficiency because everyone knows who to turn to, what to respond and when. He said that with fragmented information and ambiguous rights and responsibilities, AI only makes wrong decisions faster and makes buck-passing reasons more technical. He described an enterprise that deployed an intelligent report system where, when data was wrong, everyone blamed the underlying calibers not being aligned and no one took responsibility.

Lao Yang said the tool did not improve efficiency but gave buck-passing a set of professional terms, and he thought of the word entropy. He said to judge an organization's entropy by one small thing: for a cross-departmental demand from initiation to closed loop, how many groups are created, how many hands it passes through and who makes the final decision. He said the more steps and the more chaotic the groups, the higher the entropy, and that in high-entropy organizations AI is not an antidote but an amplifier. He said enterprises must sort out information flow, rights and responsibilities before talking about tools, and that buck-passing reflects a lack of trust and result-oriented contractual spirit. He said AI and digital tools are levers that amplify executive power in healthy organizations and destructive power in organizations used to shirking responsibilities.

Lao Yang said AI's prediction reports become evidence for departments to attack each other and automated processes become an excuse, with people saying the system judged it automatically. He said the primary premise of AI implementation is a matter-oriented rather than person-oriented data culture, and without the courage and consensus to tell the truth with data, advanced AI tools can only write weekly reports or become an excuse. He said tools are neutral and what the organization turns them into depends on the organization itself. He said email suits teams with high self-discipline and high consensus, while many enterprises stuck in the agricultural era deploy interstellar battleship level collaboration software and AI middle platforms, so employees create small WeChat groups to complain and fill in data no one reads. He said AI implementation failures are often caused not by inaccurate algorithms but by collaboration maturity that cannot support tool complexity, which is production relations failing to adapt to advanced productivity.

Lao Yang said AI implementation should advance in small steps and reject the Great Leap Forward, starting with a small scenario with clear pain points and clear responsibility boundaries, such as financial invoice recognition or automatic classification of customer service work orders. He said light tools should come first and a heavy middle platform at the start is useless except for showing off. He said employees pass the buck mostly because of ambiguous areas in the process, and AI intervention only solidifies these holes with code, deeper and harder to find, while managers use diligence in AI technology to replace laziness in management. He gave the example of an approval process with unclear rights and responsibilities where, after AI intelligent approval, people argue about why AI judged this way and who set the rules, so the buck-passing shifts from people to algorithms and the algorithm takes the blame. He said AI is the accelerator of processes, not the repairman, and business process reengineering must come first, cutting off points that cause artificial buck-passing and clarifying responsibility boundaries with systems and SOPs before AI enters.

Lao Yang said the first step of process reengineering is often to write who on earth is responsible for the result into the system, and execution is the key. He said efficient organizations using emails have every sentence correspond to clear action items and responsible persons, a kind of mental digitalization with a common logic. He said the goal of AI is not to teach employees to operate software but to train the organization's best practices and consensus into the default workflow of AI, and without consensus on what a good solution is, AI solutions are picked on and rejected by departments based on their own interests. He said the highest state is system as code, consensus as algorithm, with 80% of efforts to unify business logic, precipitate knowledge assets and clarify evaluation criteria and 20% for purchasing computing power and training models, solidifying review standards into a reusable knowledge base and review checklist. He said not to let the IT department take the blame for poor organizational efficiency, and suggested that before any major AI or digital project, a team be asked whether it could push the matter forward with only emails and Excel without internet and software, solving people's problems first and then letting AI amplify efficiency.

stories.Headline: Republican groups account for about 80% of $137 million in AI-generated political ads
stories.Summary:
Campaigns across the country spent more than $137 million on AI-generated political ads by mid-October of this election year, according to researchers at the Wesleyan Media Project, and Republican groups accounted for about 80% of those messages. Californians saw candidates battle massive robots, appear as caped crusaders and kowtow to bloodthirsty crowds and rich fat cats, all through fake images generated with artificial intelligence to help campaigns stand out online and on air. Many of the spots leaned on humor and exaggeration, such as former Los Angeles mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt depicting himself as Batman and failed gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton appearing as a gladiator in a crowded coliseum that included rival Xavier Becerra and Gov. Gavin Newsom. Other ads were not exaggerations and seemed more realistic, such as a mailer circulating in a San Diego suburb that showed a male school board candidate behind a desk and his female opponent working a fake bake sale, an image she called sexist.

Ramesh Srinivasan, a UCLA professor of information studies who hosts the Utopias podcast, said the president has put out plenty of AI-generated content and that so-called AI slop is almost everywhere. He said the deeper issue is less the slop itself than the way AI is being used to promote and create what could almost be called propaganda-type targeting. He said the Cambridge Analytica story a decade ago involved a third party advising many right-wing and other candidates, using people's data to create content that targeted them based on predictions of their psychology. He said AI systems can now create content in real time that targets a person based on their psychology without the multi-step process of buying data, gathering it and building content from it.

Srinivasan said that if someone can gather and access a range of data about a voter, including credit card records and not just what the person posts on Instagram, that data can influence what the person sees and does not see, which already happens on social media. He said AI can in this case create content that directly targets a person based on data about them, which he called very pernicious because people have no disclosure around when something is or is not AI-generated. He said he has been working with people in the U.S. Congress and in the state Senate to try to at a minimum force third parties to watermark anything created by AI. He described watermarking as something put on an image that can never be written over and that would say the image is AI generated.

stories.Headline: Meta's social media ad business generates cash that cushions its AI spending
stories.Summary:
Anthropic began trading on November 19, 2026, closing its first day at $97.17, which was 17 percent above its initial public offering price of $83. This market entry prompted analysts to compare the new company to Meta Platforms, as both entities hold a market capitalization of approximately 1.5 trillion dollars. While both firms are heavily invested in artificial intelligence, Meta possesses a massive social media advertising business that provides a financial safety net. This existing revenue stream allows Meta to remain stable even if the broader artificial intelligence investment trend fails.

The company reported that its advertising revenue grew by 26 percent in the third quarter, significantly outpacing the 12 percent growth seen at Pinterest. Meta expects fourth quarter revenue to reach between 73 billion and 76 billion dollars, representing a growth rate of 22 to 27 percent. However, capital expenditures of 34.9 billion dollars exceeded the operating cash flow of 32.8 billion dollars during the third quarter. Management has provided a guidance for 2026 capital expenditures ranging from 135 billion to 145 billion dollars. As of September 30, the company held 454.5 billion dollars in commitments that cannot be canceled.

Dan Niles, the founder of Niles Investment Management, stated that Meta has a social media business that generates a ton of cash. He argued that this diversification gives Meta a distinct advantage over Anthropic, which lacks a secondary revenue source. Mike Santoli of CNBC also noted the similar market valuations of the two companies during a November 18 broadcast. Meta management believes that upgrades to ad ranking models are driving better conversions and justifying the heavy spending on compute. These leaders suggest that the current investments in artificial intelligence are already providing tangible benefits to the advertising engine.

The current financial situation creates risks for suppliers like Arista Networks, which saw third quarter revenue jump 58.5 percent to 3.66 billion dollars. Because Microsoft and Meta accounted for 42 percent of Arista's 2025 revenue, any reduction in Meta's spending would hit the supplier first. Investors are currently paying about 19 times forward earnings for Meta, which is below its five year average of 21 times. The market will look for more clarity during the fourth quarter earnings call in late January. Analysts expect total capital expenditures for 2027 to be roughly 210 billion dollars.

stories.Headline: Federal Circuit ruling shows AI patent applicants how concrete claim language shapes eligibility, Phelan says
stories.Summary:
The Federal Circuit recently decided Ceiva Opco, LLC v. Amazon.com, Inc., a patent case about digital picture frames that the court used to show how concrete claim language can change the outcome of a patent-eligibility analysis. The court reversed an ineligibility ruling for one digital picture frame claim while it affirmed that same ruling for representative claims of three related patents. The claim that survived specified the interactions among a physically separable user interface, a server, and a digital frame, and the court found that this combination addressed technological limitations of earlier devices. By contrast, the related claims broadly described desired functions without sufficiently specifying how those results were actually achieved.

Although Ceiva did not involve artificial intelligence, the decision offers a practical lesson for AI patent applicants, according to Marshall, Gerstein & Borun LLP partner Ryan Phelan, who analyzed the ruling in a contribution to IPO Daily News. Phelan wrote that applicants should identify the technical improvement, connect it to shortcomings in existing technology, and claim the features and relationships that produce that improvement. He made the point that concrete claim language can make a meaningful difference in the patent-eligibility analysis. Phelan is a regular contributor to the newsletter's AI Insights column, where he analyzes court decisions, regulatory developments, and other issues affecting patents and emerging technologies, and he also authors the firm's PatentNext blog on artificial intelligence and other next-generation technologies.

The article was published by Legal 500 on 20 November 2026 and carries the headline about the claim-drafting lesson for AI patents. It presents the Ceiva decision as an illustration for applicants rather than as a change in the law, and it does not say what happens next in the case or whether any further review is expected. The piece states that its content is intended as a general guide to the subject matter and that specialist advice should be sought about specific circumstances. Members can read Phelan's latest AI Insights article on the IPO website, according to the article.

stories.Headline: Peter Gabriel endorses AI and predicts humans will become cyborgs
stories.Summary:
Peter Gabriel has said he is in favour of artificial intelligence and believes people will eventually become cyborgs, according to an interview reported by Guitar Player on 21 November 2026. The musician gave his view that humans and technology will merge over time, and he framed the coming change as something to accept rather than resist. The article reports his position as a clear yes to AI, with his remark that we will become cyborgs summing up his outlook. No further details of the interview, such as where or with whom it took place, are given in the article.

The piece does not set out any specific plans, releases or projects tied to his comments, and it gives no dates, figures or names beyond Gabriel himself and the publication. What it records is his stated attitude toward AI rather than any announced use of the technology in his own work. The article presents the remark as his prediction about society generally, not as a description of tools he is currently employing. It offers no timeline for when he expects people to become cyborgs.

Gabriel is the person responsible for the view described, and the article attributes the cyborg remark directly to him. It does not include a longer quotation or any explanation from him of what becoming cyborgs would involve. No other musicians, companies or experts are quoted in the article, and no response from anyone else is reported. The piece does not say whether his comment came in the context of his own music or of the wider debate about AI in the arts.

The article gives no background on previous statements Gabriel has made about technology, and it does not say what prompted this one. It also does not indicate what happens next, whether he plans to work with AI tools or speak further on the subject. Beyond his remark and the publication date, the piece carries little additional detail. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Teachers at WHS debate how to regulate student AI use as departments split on its value
stories.Summary:
For the past four years, educators have scrambled to change curriculums around the emergence of AI in a way that reduces the ability to potentially cheat with AI tools. As the use of AI in schools becomes more prominent and commonly used, debates surrounding the topic have increased. Reports analyzing various advantages and harms to AI in school prompt further conversations on what the role of AI should look like. In a survey by Pew Research Center about 32% of K-12 educators say there is an equal mix of benefit and harm using AI tools in an education background. At WHS, departments share different needs for AI, and in certain subjects teachers argue AI creates a lack of critical thinking, especially in an academic setting.

History Department Head David Schmirer said AI is literally taking away your power to be able to think for yourself. Schmirer said the ability to make critical decisions and choices as you get older is going to become a lot more difficult. Math teacher Emily Grant said AI can be useful in math when students use it to understand how to do problems and not to just get the answers. Grant said if students put in a problem and ask for AI to make a similar problem and show the steps, that can be a really helpful way to learn the material. English Department Head Peter Galalis doesn’t believe there will ever be a use for AI in English classes.

Galalis said writing is a human practice, and it always is going to be. Galalis also points out that writing at a professional level means there are certain legal barriers to producing something written by AI, because AI isn’t protected under copyright. Galalis said it’s going to continue to be really important that human writers produce and own their own words, because what you produce with a chatbot is not the same as something that you’ve written. Galalis argues that the physical act of writing something human can’t be replaced by generative AI. Galalis said writing is something we don’t do just to produce more words for other people to read, and if you outsource that to a chatbot, you rob yourself of those opportunities.

Math Department Head Kanchan Kant believes policies should adapt to focus on teaching what will be helpful for students seeking a math degree in the world of AI. Since AI will have an impact on careers in math, Kant believes a specific part of math jobs will no longer be focused on writing proofs, but instead critiquing what already exists. Kant said if critiquing AI’s work is a part of what our students will end up doing, we should be preparing them for that. Schmirer said AI’s capability and availability has increased so rapidly that it’s really difficult for any teacher at the school to keep up with it. In the history department, Schmirer comments that teachers are allowed to choose their own pathway regarding AI usage.

While some teachers attempt to sway students away from AI by giving students zeroes on assignments completed with AI, Schmirer’s method is to inform students on just how harmful AI can be and encourage them to use their own thinking. Schmirer said ultimately all we can do is appeal to students to make good choices, just like we do in other areas of life. The in-class essay, rather than a take home essay, is becoming increasingly popular as a way to remove AI from the equation. Some teachers assign print-out readings rather than the typical online readings that teachers worry will be copy and pasted into an AI tool. Research shows that reading off a paper, annotating, and taking notes by hand is more helpful in successfully absorbing information than reading a screen.

One anonymous student was given a zero on a homework assignment after it was flagged by an AI detector, and later met with their teacher over the issue to defend their academic integrity, where the student was able to receive full credit. The anonymous student said they were very confused and thinking maybe there was a glitch or something like that. The anonymous student said it should be a bit more holistic with teachers meeting with students before assigning a grade for AI use. Up until last year, take-home essays were common, if not expected, in WHS humanities classes. Junior Archie Baker said they started here in 2024, so in freshman year and sophomore year it was almost entirely take-home essays, which they appreciate a lot more.

English teacher Phillip George said in his first year teaching here in 2023, he thinks he had something like 16 instances of catching students cheating using online resources, and that shocked him. George said that forced him after that first year to start revising his approach. George used the analogy of marathon runners and sprinters, and said now he’s making them sprint, and they are sprinting for at least an hour. George said the in-class essay is great for authentically assessing student thought and writing, but it is very narrow in scope. George said it eliminates the opportunity for revision, improvement, and the drafting process, which is usually so essential to writing, and it limits the kind of time under tension that students experience.

Junior Archie Baker said during an in-class essay they feel much more rushed, and they can’t refine their thoughts, so they just write it and then that’s it. Baker said they’re trying to develop ideas but can’t get as in-depth or as nuanced as they’d like to. George said what is lost is a sense of intellectual endurance, and the reward for the virtue of prolonged thought and hard work. Schmirer said he’d rather get less than good work from a student that’s their own work and that they put time and effort into than something that is just simply not their own at that point. Schmirer describes it as a fluid situation where teachers react in the interest of educating students and preparing them for their futures as new advancements in AI continue to present themselves.

stories.Headline: Fireworks AI discloses customer data exposures that raise questions about Shopify's use of its AI services
stories.Summary:
Fireworks AI disclosed customer data exposures that have prompted questions about how third party systems handle sensitive information, and Shopify uses Fireworks AI services that are now under scrutiny after recent security incidents at the provider. The disclosure was reported by Simply Wall St in an article published on Yahoo Finance on Saturday, November 21, 2026. The article was written by Al Bentley and appeared at 10:08 AM CST. Shopify trades on NasdaqGS under the ticker SHOP. The article asks whether Shopify faces new risks from its AI partner's security issues.

Investors are assessing whether Fireworks AI tools are embedded in parts of Shopify's infrastructure that touch merchant or shopper data. Shopify runs a global commerce platform that powers online and offline stores for merchants of many sizes. The article says Shopify's reliance on external intelligence tools like Fireworks AI directly intersects with how retailers manage and protect shopper interactions across those channels. The Fireworks AI issue feeds directly into Shopify's AI driven commerce catalyst in the Narrative. The article says questions over a vendor's controls can make the cost and efficiency gains from cheaper, open weight models look more complicated, even if Shopify's own systems have not been compromised.

The article says the practical thing to watch is Shopify's future disclosures and earnings call commentary around security reviews, vendor changes or extra compliance spending tied to external AI platforms. It says any explicit update on how third party AI is segmented from merchant and shopper data will show how management is balancing AI expansion with operational and regulatory risk. It adds that one off costs to tighten those connections will also show that balance. The article states that investors are not only judging how well Shopify uses third party AI tools to support merchant workflows. It states that investors are also judging how carefully those tools are integrated so that data use, privacy and security do not undermine the broader push into AI assisted selling and operations.

The article says the Fireworks AI security issues only tell part of Shopify's story, so it helps to weigh them against the broader picture. It says its analysis turns up 3 other big wins for Shopify as well. It directs readers looking beyond the headline toward other ways to play the same theme to 53 AI infrastructure stocks. It advises readers to add Shopify to their Watchlist and get alerts as these catalysts play out.

The article says it is general in nature and was produced with the assistance of AI automation, based on data and analysis from Simply Wall St. It says the commentary is based on historical data and analyst forecasts only using an unbiased methodology and the articles are not intended to be financial advice. It says the article does not constitute a recommendation to buy or sell any stock and does not take account of readers' objectives or financial situation. It says Simply Wall St aims to bring long-term focused analysis driven by fundamental data and that its analysis may not factor in the latest price-sensitive company announcements or qualitative material. It says Simply Wall St has no position in any stocks mentioned and that companies discussed in the article include SHOP.

The article leaves open whether Shopify's own systems have been affected, saying only that they have not been compromised. It leaves open what security reviews, vendor changes or extra compliance spending, if any, Shopify will disclose. It leaves open how third party AI is segmented from merchant and shopper data. It leaves open what one off costs, if any, Shopify would incur to tighten those connections. It leaves open what Shopify's future earnings call commentary will say about external AI platforms.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia head amid infidelity and chip export restriction allegations
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as the head of Nvidia after thirty three years of leadership. He admitted to infidelity with a woman running an Asian chip supply company called Megaspeed. This personal relationship coincided with accusations that Huang bypassed American export restrictions on advanced computing chips. The controversy gained credibility after a major newspaper reported the details of the situation. These events occurred around November 2026 while Nvidia employed nearly 50,000 people worldwide.

The situation involved Megaspeed purchasing at least 4.8 billion dollars of Nvidia hardware. Trump approved further chip sales to China for a reported 25 percent payment to the government. Nvidia contributed 25 million dollars to a ballroom project benefiting the president and his contractors. Trump held a personal Nvidia investment valued between 13 million and 62 million dollars. Howard Lutnick led the Commerce Department, which had the authority to blacklist the company Megaspeed.

Howard Lutnick boasted that he promised Huang easy access to the president of the United States. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed Lutnick for delaying the restrictions on chip sales to China. Donald Trump stated that the country is stronger and that America plays games with China. Huang argued that selling chips to everyone, including China, would strengthen American technological leadership. Trump expressed support for Huang returning, suggesting that the executive had learned a big lesson.

Elon Musk and 180,000 other technology executives, workers, and shareholders signed a petition for Huang's reinstatement. Former NATO ambassador Ivo Daalder said blaming Lutnick spares the president and the silent principals. Many employees in Santa Clara, California, became millionaires through generous stock awards and compensation. Many other workers face displacement and uncertainty as the AI revolution concentrates wealth among infrastructure owners. The existing leadership at Nvidia remains uncertain about whether they should reinstate the former chief executive.

Nvidia began as a gaming chipmaker and reached a market capitalisation approaching 4.8 trillion dollars. Fiscal 2026 revenue reportedly reached 216 billion dollars before the resignation of the founder. Huang arrived from Taiwan at age nine and studied at Oregon State and Stanford universities. The company launched a 500 billion dollar financing platform for AI start ups and cloud providers. US intelligence agencies suspected Megaspeed was connected to the intelligence apparatus of the Beijing government.

Democrats may start congressional investigations after the new Congress takes office on January 3. A probe into illegal sales reportedly stalled after Jeff Kessler allegedly tipped off the company. The articles leave open whether Nvidia will actually reinstate Jensen Huang as its leader. It remains unclear if the AI boom is a speculative bubble that might eventually falter. The text does not say if the Justice Department will resume the stalled illegal sales case.

stories.Headline: Apple develops autonomous AI agents to perform tasks across apps independently
stories.Summary:
Apple is developing its own autonomous AI Agent to perform tasks across apps and plan workflows independently. The company is the last tech giant to enter this market during the first year of AI Agents. Two job postings related to these agents appeared on the official Apple website in mid-November. Apple wants Siri to evolve from giving verbal commands to taking actual actions on its own. This move follows a trend started by generative AI access for ordinary users in 2023.

The system requires a senior engineering manager to develop assistants with proactive service capabilities that operate computers like humans. It must browse the web, run commands, write code, and coordinate multiple specialized sub-agents to execute multi-step tasks. A senior applied AI engineer must establish personal intelligent evaluation benchmarks and use feedback mechanisms to optimize performance. Candidates are required to use Claude Code and Codex in their daily work. macOS 27.3 Beta 2 adjusts authorization for device control and full disk access permissions.

Bloomberg reports that Apple is developing this autonomous AI Agent to enable independent planning of workflows. Apple's job postings describe a vision where AI can select the appropriate tool for each step of a task. The company emphasizes the need for privacy, security, sandbox isolation, and permission management in these roles. Apple aims for the agent to find ways to complete tasks on its own and become more reliable. The company wants to prevent agents from accessing user data and devices at will.

Meta, OpenAI, Anthropic, Tencent, and ByteDance are already pushing AI Agents into real work and life scenarios. Meta's Muse has over 10 million setup users in the US and Canada, with 25 percent using it daily. OpenAI launched Dots in September, which connects to over 4,000 apps and works continuously in the background. Anthropic offers Claude Code and Claude Duet, with the latter currently open for research preview. These competitors have already accumulated millions of users and started generating actual revenue.

Apple relies on a huge ecosystem consisting of the iPhone, Mac, and the App Store. The company is now preparing for the deep involvement of AI within its operating system. Recent updates allow users to authorize specific apps and folders and provide status prompts during AI control. This follows the success of Meta's Muse, which handles travel planning, restaurant reservations, and document sorting. Other agents like Dots and Claude Duet now have their own working environments and external service connections.

Apple considered launching these related products as early as the end of 2027. Development of the autonomous AI Agent is still in the early stage. The company must solve the balance between agent capability and data security together. The articles do not state the exact date the product will be available to the public. It remains open how third-party Agents will be affected by the new macOS permission rules.

stories.Headline: Metal artist Christina Thompson creates The Touch sculpture with AI to explore human and machine connection
stories.Summary:
Christina Thompson, a metal artist and welder of vacuum furnace equipment during the day, created a sculpture called “The Touch” that reflects the rapid development of artificial intelligence and the many possibilities, concerns, and unanswered questions people have about what is going on. She said she wanted to take that conversation and represent it in a physical sculpture, according to an article published by The Fabricator on November 21, 2026. Thompson first picked up a welding torch about 13 years ago when some welders in the fab shop of the Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory, where she worked as an emergency services officer, encouraged her to give it a try. She was hooked from that moment, purchased a small welding machine shortly afterwards, began making metal flowers, and eventually decided to pursue a welding career by taking formal classes and earning her certifications.

For “The Touch,” Thompson wanted the creative process to reflect her motivation as well, so she wanted to collaborate with AI, which meant striking up conversations with ChatGPT. She decided to use Michelangelo’s “The Creation of Adam,” where God and Adam reach out to almost touch fingers, as an inspiration, with the difference being that man is the creator in this scenario. Thompson said she laid a lot of metal while TIG welding the human and robotic hands and then removed a good bit by grinding the pieces into the shapes she wanted, noting that with TIG welding she really can control what she is doing and is basically sculpting with a pencil. Because the sculpture is called “The Touch,” she thought it should be an artistic piece that encouraged the viewer to reach out and touch it, which is where her husband, Darren Thompson, helped by developing an electric base that houses a speaker and wiring.

When viewers push an illuminated button at the base of the sculpture, they hear a three-minute narration about the sculpture, voiced by Christina, which says that the viewer becomes part of the work and completes the circuit between human intention and machine response. The narration says that without touch there is silence and with touch there is creation, and that the piece is not just a sculpture but a question, a warning, and a celebration. Thompson has spent the last year working on “The Touch,” and even with that work and some of her other works displayed at an art gallery, she said she is in no hurry to jump into another large sculpture. She is spending her time working on smaller pieces, like ocean scenes and palm trees, according to the article.

stories.Headline: Former DeepSeek core member Tony Zhang founds Simplex AI to develop personal computer agents
stories.Summary:
Tony Zhang announced the open source of his personal agent product Linger on November 19. He is a former Project Lead of DeepSeek-VL and a core member of that lab. Zhang founded Simplex AI to develop this new AI technology for personal computers. He started his entrepreneurial journey in 2025 after leaving DeepSeek in March 2024. This move marks the first public case of a DeepSeek core author starting a company.

Linger runs on personal computers to operate software, process emails, and enable multiple AI assistants. It uses PolyStrata, a local inference project created by an 18-year-old developer named VecSzn. Simplex AI, also known as Hangzhou Topology Lingxi Technology Co., Ltd., was established February 24, 2025. The company has registered capital of 1 million yuan and secured 6 million US dollars. GL Ventures led this seed round of financing announced in January 2026.

Zhang Bo said he learned the importance of focusing on one thing from DeepSeek's founder. He told his research team to pursue quality over the number of papers they publish. Zhang hopes to bring AI back to personal computers to change the current data center model. He noted that users currently pay per Token for usage of most large AI models. He wants users to have an AI assistant that keeps working without cloud reliance.

Users on the X platform asked if the product could connect to mobile phones. Some users reported encountering model download problems during the installation of the new software. Linger affects ordinary computer users by reducing the cost of running large AI models. The product allows users to avoid paying Token fees to cloud model service providers. However, users must still bear their own costs for electricity and necessary computer hardware.

Zhang earned a bachelor's degree from Zhejiang University in 2013 and a doctorate in 2019. He worked at Microsoft Research Asia on projects like VQ-Diffusion and Rodin before joining DeepSeek. At DeepSeek, he helped develop the first-generation large language model and the DeepSeek-VL project. He later became a PhD supervisor at the State Key Lab of CAD&CG at Zhejiang University. DeepSeek's core team is stable, with only 6.4 percent of paper contributors having departed.

Simplex AI plans to support mobile phone functions within one month of the Linger release. The team is working to fix a reproduced bug regarding the model download process. Simplex AI also plans to launch a hosted version, though the price is not announced. The articles leave open whether ordinary users can actually use the technology in practice. It remains to be seen if third party developers will verify the enterprise test data.

stories.Headline: Anthropic executive Aiden Blake helps drive record $81 billion stock market launch
stories.Summary:
Aiden Blake, a Letterkenny man who serves as Anthropic's Head of Startup Sales for Europe, the Middle East and Africa, was a key part of the AI company's successful stock market launch, according to Donegal Daily. The company's arrival on the stock market set records, raising $81 billion and landing its stock price at $97 a share by closing on opening day. By closing on Friday the price had dipped to $85, but staff at Anthropic's Irish offices are still set for a notable financial windfall. Blake, a former long-time Google executive, has been working with the AI startup since November of 2025.

As one of the company's most senior employees in its Dublin office, Blake is likely to be one of its biggest beneficiaries from the stock market floatation. The company offered €8.4 million in share-based remuneration to its employees in 2025, though its public filings included no specifics relating to a guaranteed sale price in the event of a public offering. Blake is married to Ballybofey native Rachel Heeney, who is herself a long-time Google employee. His father is Laurence Blake, a prominent businessman from Letterkenny, while his mum Denise Blake is a well-known poet and writer.

The article names no one as responsible for the floatation beyond the company itself, and it carries no direct comment from Blake or from Anthropic on the listing or on his likely gain. The only figures it gives are the $81 billion raised, the $97 opening-day closing price, the $85 Friday close and the €8.4 million in share-based remuneration offered to employees in 2025. It states that Blake will benefit massively from the successful IPO launch and that Irish office staff are still set for a windfall despite the dip.
