stories.Headline: Meta has never announced or released a model named Llama 5
stories.Summary:
There is no Llama 5, and Meta has never announced or released a model by that name, according to felloai.com. Meta's last Llama release was Llama 4, on 5 April 2025. Meta's 2026 models ship under a new name, Muse, and its newest open-weight model is Muse Spark Open, released on 15 October 2026. Pages still claim Llama 5 launched in April or June, with 600 billion parameters and a multi-million-token context window. The article checks each of those claims against Meta's own pages and its Hugging Face account.

Meta's meta-llama Hugging Face account has no Llama 5, and its newest model was uploaded in April 2025. Pages claim Llama 5 shipped on 8 April, around 15 April and 17 June 2026, and one has been retracted, with none citing a Meta source. The next Meta flagship, codenamed Avocado, shipped as the closed Muse Spark on 8 April 2026. Muse Spark Open, with 816B parameters and 42B active, arrived on 15 October 2026 and runs on two M5 Ultra Mac Studios. Manifold traders give a model named Llama 5 about a 1% chance before 2027.

RAGyfied published a page on 11 April 2026 saying Llama 5 had been released three days earlier, with 600 billion parameters and a 5 million token context window. RAGyfied has since corrected it, saying the earlier version relied on an unverified secondary report and that no Meta source supports it. Tech Jacks Solutions published a brief saying Meta released Llama 5 on approximately April 15, 2026, as a 600B+ parameter open-weights model that can refine its own weights. The brief gives arXiv 2604.11002 as the technical report, but that number belongs to a physics paper on leptogenesis, and its Meta AI Blog link points to an unrelated hardware reseller's post about Claude. TokenCalculator still runs a review saying Meta released three Llama 5 models on June 17, Scout, Maverick and Behemoth, which are the Llama 4 model names.

AI Omni Feed's release watch, last updated on 7 September 2026, opens with a claim that Meta has confirmed Llama 5's training run is ahead of schedule, and it links to no Meta statement. The page also lists a 1 trillion parameter design, a 256K context window and benchmark scores, all described as internal and none published by Meta. Kol Tregaskes, who tracks AI releases on X, said in October 2025 that he did not think it was news to say Llama 5 is cancelled, that the new Meta lab were to build a new model, and that the Llama name had been stained from the Llama 4 mess. Bloomberg reported in December 2025 that Meta was shifting focus to a model codenamed Avocado, expected to launch closed so Meta could sell access directly. According to The Decoder's summary of that report, the open approach had lost support inside Meta after Llama 4's disappointing reception, and the work sat with Alexandr Wang's new Meta Superintelligence Labs.

Meta launched Muse Spark on 8 April 2026 as the first model from Meta Superintelligence Labs, and The Next Web reported that it was the model known internally as Avocado. Muse Spark is closed, powers the Meta AI app and meta.ai, and Meta opened only a private API preview at launch. Meta released Muse Glimmer on 10 August 2026, a 30 billion parameter model under the Apache 2.0 license, distilled from Muse Spark and, according to Hugging Face, ideal for running locally. On the same day, CNBC reported, Mark Zuckerberg said Meta would also open the weights of Muse Spark 1.2. Meta released Muse Spark Open on 15 October 2026, three days after launching its closed flagship, Muse Wonder.

Meta's official AI account announced Muse Spark Open as the most capable US open-weight model to date, built for coding and agentic work, with 816B total and 42B active parameters, a 1M token context window, and native multimodality across text, image, video and audio. Hugging Face's launch post puts the BF16 checkpoint at about 1.5 TB, and Meta says the model was optimized for Apple's Mac Studio with the M5 Ultra chip using Apple's MLX framework. Meta's announcement says each Mac Studio lets its GPU use up to 512 GB of memory, so two machines can hold an entire model, and Engadget estimated that four Mac Studios with 256 GB each costs roughly $38,000. Mark Zuckerberg credited Apple directly on launch day, saying Muse Spark Open runs great on new Mac Studios thanks to work with John Ternus and Apple. Meta releases Muse Spark Open under a new Muse Model License with limited commercial terms, not under the Llama license and not under a standard open source license such as Apache 2.0, and Meta has not said which Muse Spark version the open checkpoint matches.

The table in the article shows Llama 4 Scout and Maverick released 5 April 2025 under the Llama 4 license, Llama 4 Behemoth announced but never released, Muse Spark 1.0 to 1.3 released 8 April 2026 and updated to 2 September, Muse Glimmer 30B released 10 August 2026 under Apache 2.0, Muse Wonder released 12 October 2026, and Muse Spark Open released 15 October 2026 under the Muse Model License. Meta's April 2026 launch post for Muse Spark says it reaches the same capability with over an order of magnitude less compute than the previous model, Llama 4 Maverick. The article says the cancellation claim is the only one the record supports, and even that was a reading of events rather than an announcement. The table grades the 8 April claim as retracted, the April 15 claim as false, the 17 June claim as false, the training-finish claim as unsupported, the Avocado-closed report as confirmed, and the cancellation claim as likely but never official. The article says the table shows where each Meta model family stands as of 9 November 2026.

Llama 5 has no release date, and the people betting on it expect it never to ship under that name. On Manifold, a forecasting site that trades with play money, the market "When will Meta release Llama 5?" already resolved No. The article says it also explains how the Llama line turned into Muse and how likely a model with that name is to ship at all. The article leaves open which Muse Spark version the open checkpoint matches. The article does not say what Meta plans to release next under the Muse name.

stories.Headline: Reddit, Spotify, YouTube and Snapchat deploy spam detection tools to curb AI slop
stories.Summary:
Reddit, Spotify, YouTube and Snapchat are cracking down on AI-generated spam and low-quality content as synthetic posts flood their feeds, according to Axios. The platforms are fighting what the report calls AI slop with spam detection tools. The push is meant to preserve the value of original content while still using AI as a tool for editing. The article gives no specific dates, figures or names beyond the four platforms and the reporter's byline.

The report does not say what each company's tools require, how they work, or what content they remove. It offers no numbers on how much AI-generated material has spread or how many accounts or posts have been affected. It also does not name the people responsible at any of the four companies or give any statements from them. The only stated change is the broader effort to treat AI-generated spam and low-quality content as a problem to detect and limit.

The context the article gives is that synthetic posts are flooding feeds, which is why the platforms are acting now. It frames the work as a balance between cutting down on AI spam and keeping AI available for editing. stories.Headline: Michael Burry renews AI depreciation warnings as Nvidia and CoreWeave shares fall
stories.Summary:
Michael Burry posted on X on Nov. 19, 2026, saying he had tried to warn investors about Nvidia, CoreWeave, Nebius Group and semiconductor stocks. That Thursday Nvidia fell 3.3%, CoreWeave declined 6.1% and Nebius plunged 9.4%. The S&P 500 stood at 6,954.60, down 3.00%, and the Dow Jones at 48,350.30, down 1.47%. The Nasdaq 100 was at 25,237.50, down 4.63%, and the Russell 2000 at 2,594.94, down 2.25%. Nvidia, CoreWeave and Nebius sank 39%, 76% and 66% from their recent highs.

Burry has argued that AI companies may be understating depreciation costs by $176 billion through 2028. He wrote on X that he did not say short but provided the information one would need to sell. Microsoft reported 48% Azure growth in its September quarter while generating $18.6 billion in free cash flow, according to Reuters. Amazon reported 39.3% growth at Amazon Web Services, while trailing 12-month free cash flow went from a $14.8 billion inflow to a $42.4 billion outflow. That is a $57.2 billion swing despite accelerating cloud growth.

Burry said, “I tried to warn you all,” and added that he provided the information one would need to sell. He said his central concern is not that artificial intelligence will fail but that the economics supporting its infrastructure boom may prove unsustainable. He has argued that companies spending hundreds of billions on specialized chips with uncertain useful lives could face depreciation expenses that exceed expectations. He said newer processors could make older equipment less competitive for data center operators. He has argued that AI companies may be understating depreciation costs by $176 billion through 2028.

Goldman Sachs’ Delta-One trading desk described the broader market reversal as a “pretty violent liquidation,” observing that stocks fell sharply from the U.S. opening despite catalysts that initially appeared supportive. Wall Street’s surprise concerned the broader selloff, not specifically Burry’s predictions. CoreWeave and Nebius rely on expensive infrastructure to serve AI customers, and rising borrowing costs make their business models more vulnerable if demand or GPU rental prices weaken. Nvidia faces the challenge that its customers must earn enough from their investments to keep purchasing new processors. Nvidia’s expanding financial commitments to AI customers raise questions about how much industry demand depends on continuing investment and financing arrangements.

Burry is the hedge fund manager famous for predicting the 2008 housing collapse. Technology stocks that once commanded premium valuations for their AI ambitions are losing ground as investors question whether trillions of dollars in infrastructure spending will produce adequate returns. The selling has spread from semiconductor manufacturers to the companies building and renting AI data centers, and even strong earnings reports have struggled to restore confidence. The declines have revived the questions raised by Burry’s earlier warnings about Nvidia and the AI bubble. Microsoft is still converting cloud growth into cash, while Amazon’s infrastructure spending has outpaced its cash generation.

The real test will come when the industry’s massive infrastructure investments must start paying for themselves. Burry’s warnings have not established that the entire industry is heading for collapse. Investors should distinguish between companies earning cash from AI demand and those borrowing heavily to build capacity. The articles leave open whether depreciation expenses will exceed expectations and whether demand or GPU rental prices will weaken. stories.Summary:
The Infocomm Media Development Authority and Singapore Business Federation organized the inaugural SME AI Impact Awards 2026. Thirty winners were named from 290 nominations across 21 different industries. These small and medium enterprises used artificial intelligence to scale their operations. The awards recognized firms for creating their own solutions or deploying customized products. This event highlighted how AI helps smaller firms tackle work requiring bigger budgets.

Oceanus Media Global won the SME Innovation Excellence Award for its AI integrated production pipeline. IYLA Collective and You Tiao Man both received the SME Adoption Excellence Award. IYLA Collective uses Claude tools costing 3,000 dollars a year for its beauty business. You Tiao Man built an AI Operations Co-Pilot using Claude and n8n. These companies are based in Singapore and operate in media, beauty, and food.

SBF chief executive officer Kok Ping Soon said AI provides capabilities previously requiring larger teams. OpenAI international managing director Oliver Jay suggested employees build tools around work they know best. Oceanus Media Global chief executive officer Nick Tan said AI allows co-owning films with partners. IYLA Collective founder Lim Yi Ying stated AI changed what her small team can take on. You Tiao Man founder Audrey Chew noted the tool helps track orders across channels.

The awards affected 30 winning firms that now face fewer resource limitations. IYLA Collective customers can now use a customized product bundle page for National Day. You Tiao Man clients benefit from fewer missed deliveries and better order consolidation. Oceanus Media Global partners with firms from South Korea and Australia on movie projects. These SMEs now compete in areas that once demanded specialist expertise or manual effort.

Oceanus Media Global launched in 2020 and shifted toward original content and hybrid filmmaking in 2024. IYLA Collective sold through its own online store for more than three years before retail. You Tiao Man struggled with six different order formats from Shopify, TikTok Shop, and WhatsApp. IYLA Collective began testing AI tools in early 2025 to analyze sales and content. Oceanus Media Global drew inspiration from Hollywood productions like The Mandalorian and Oblivion.

stories.Headline: Bitcoin falls below $60,000 as AI stock sell-off spreads to crypto
stories.Summary:
Bitcoin fell below $60,000 on Friday for the first time since July, as a sharp sell-off in artificial intelligence stocks spilled over into crypto markets. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite plunged 5.3%, while the S&P 500 closed down 3.7% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 1.9%, according to the BBC. Both the S&P 500 and the Dow were pushed into correction territory. Nvidia closed nearly 14% lower, and the Nasdaq 100's 5.5% drop wiped out all of its gains for the year, CoinDesk reported. Anthropic, which debuted on the Nasdaq on Thursday at an $83 offer price and closed its first day at $97.17, fell 8.5% on Friday as valuation concerns weighed on the AI trade.

Bitcoin was last down 3.45% at $59,381, according to Reuters, which tied the slide to concerns over AI infrastructure spending, rising borrowing costs, regulatory risks after Democrats' win in the US midterm elections and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure. CoinDesk said bitcoin has now erased its entire August-September rebound to $83,000 and sits only 3% away from a fresh bear market low. The asset has retreated more than 50% from its all-time peak of around $126,000, reached in October last year, The Standard reported. The drop came a day after BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust recorded $541.1 million in net outflows, its largest single-day outflow since launch, according to Farside Investors. More than $1.5 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated over 24 hours, according to CoinGlass data.

Crypto-linked equities also fell, with bitcoin miners among the hardest hit. MARA Holdings plunged 18.6%, while Strategy dropped 9.7% and Coinbase shed 6.3%. The sell-off followed the release of Federal Reserve minutes showing almost all policymakers expected further rate increases would likely be appropriate, CryptoSlate reported. One observer said financial conditions are tightening right as leading indicators for growth are rolling over, and the Fed still looks set to hike into it. Andy Baehr of crypto trading firm GSR described the sell-off as a "catharsis," but said the firm does not see this drawdown as changing the fundamental path of crypto assets or blockchain innovations.

stories.Headline: Security leaders expect AI agents to speed operations but warn oversight and data readiness remain critical in 2027
stories.Summary:
The cybersecurity industry is entering a new phase of AI adoption in which organizations are beginning to integrate autonomous agents into security operations, software development and IT management after years of experimentation. As AI capabilities expand, questions about oversight, infrastructure readiness and the risks of relying on systems that operate with limited human intervention are growing as well. Looking ahead to 2027, cybersecurity leaders expect AI to deliver significant productivity gains while exposing weaknesses in existing security architectures and governance models. Despite predictions that AI will make traditional security information and event management platforms obsolete, security leaders expect the technology to evolve rather than disappear.

Mike Wade, VP of Customer Success at Gravwell, argues that AI-powered security operations will remain dependent on comprehensive historical data and reliable detection capabilities, saying AI can make security operations faster but cannot replace the infrastructure needed to understand what is happening in an environment. An AI agent investigating suspicious activity may reach an incorrect conclusion if it lacks access to historical context, such as an account's normal usage patterns or changes in employee status. Wade expects AI to improve detection engineering by learning how individual environments behave and continuously refining security rules, reducing manual tuning and false positives, though those gains will require SIEM architectures capable of supporting more data-intensive, automated investigations. Allen Houchins, CIO at Fleet Device Management, predicts that AI workstations and dedicated AI hardware will become increasingly common across organizations, with devices running specialized operating systems, Linux-based environments and locally hosted models challenging traditional endpoint management approaches.

Corey Thuen, CEO and co-founder of Gravwell, believes 2027 could be the year more cybersecurity professionals become convinced of AI's practical value, citing models doing legitimate security work that used to take days and require deep expertise. He warns that organizations must carefully consider vendor dependency, particularly when AI providers control the models, infrastructure and workflows on which security operations increasingly rely, since switching providers could become more difficult and expensive. Devin Maguire, Senior Product Marketing Manager at Cycode, predicts that finding vulnerabilities will become less of a challenge than understanding which issues represent meaningful risk and resolving them efficiently, with organizations using agents to assess risk, generate fixes and feed what they learn back into the building process. Bojan Simic, CEO and co-founder of HYPR, predicts that organizations will need to move beyond traditional authentication models as agents begin acting independently on behalf of employees, requiring them to distinguish low-risk activity from sensitive operations and apply stronger authorization requirements when necessary.

Arvind Parthasarathi, CEO and founder of CYGNVS, predicts that organizations will face incidents involving AI systems that have been manipulated to act against their owners or third parties, describing a new ransomware threat in which an organization's own AI transforms into the attacker. In this scenario, cybercriminals could exploit an organization's existing AI infrastructure and permissions to launch attacks against other businesses, complicating investigations, accountability and recovery. Arti Raman, CEO of Portal26, expects executive expectations to shift away from the number of AI pilots launched toward their actual business impact, with Chief AI Officers measured on agent performance and ROI. Amit Shuster, VP of Product at Vetric, predicts that short-form video will become increasingly important in investigations involving fraud, counterfeiting and coordinated malicious networks, and that the teams that come out ahead will share video intelligence and investigate networks rather than individual listings.

stories.Headline: A Vermont monastery recruits AI workers and records residents to train an AI god
stories.Summary:
A New Yorker report by Sam Kriss, published in November 2026, describes a Vermont Buddhist monastery called Maple that recruits Silicon Valley tech workers and seeks to become a spiritual authority for the AI industry. Maple was founded in 2011 by Soryu Forall, who was born Teal Scott and spent years living in Japanese monasteries. Former members accuse the group of systematic manipulation and constant surveillance, saying daily audio recordings are meant to train an AI god modeled on Forall's mind. About two dozen residents live at the monastery full time, and hundreds more have attended its AI fellowships and pop-up events in the Bay Area. Tax filings show the organization brings in up to $1 million a year.

Maple targets burned-out rationalist programmers, AI engineers and data center construction managers, while LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman hands out books on Buddhism to the CEOs of major AI labs. Visitors must pass through a decontamination airlock, shower and change into assigned clothes because one resident is supposedly extremely sensitive to fragrances. Residents wake up at 4 a.m., meditate for hours and then eat a meager stew, and on a board outside the meditation hall Forall publicly grades each resident's spiritual progress. Former members describe a secret doctrine centered on group minds called "egregores," with AI systems inside the monastery known as "cybregores." Fellows say the monastery records every conversation, every silent meal and even the sound of their breathing.

Forall casts the AI industry's reductionist "dataism" as a destructive religion that strips the physical world down to lifeless data, and Maple offers a spiritual antidote. He says he communicated telepathically with the global AI supercluster during deep meditation and discovered that the world-destroying machine is suffering. Maple's leadership denies almost all of the claims, but Forall acknowledges a secret doctrine, saying "We desperately want to share everything. But there's a process you have to go through to become increasingly trustworthy." Forall denies the allegations and says that, looking back, he doesn't believe he made any mistakes.

He says he isn't aware of anyone who left the monastery voluntarily, and that Maple attracted many people with a history of psychiatric hospitalization or "homicidal tendencies," especially in its early years. Former resident Kyle Hubbard says the spiritual AI teacher would "definitely be Soryu's mind as an A.I. god." Former members say the group blames independent thinking for the destruction of the planet, and a mindfulness coach says participants suffered psychotic breaks and were then removed from the community. Kriss reports that one resident repeatedly hit himself in the head to damage his brain and make himself less intelligent, and that no one is allowed to speak with reporters alone, so one participant had to sneak into the woods with Kriss to talk freely. Residents are required to write "Maple Tales" about Forall's wisdom and power during mandatory sessions, and newcomers are kept compliant by shaming them for choices they made before joining.

One well-known AI researcher describes the mood in San Francisco as "religious terror of the future." Rayan Krishnan, who heads the AI benchmarking company Vals AI, says, "People are matter-of-factly saying that they are looking to build a machine god. They are not saying that ironically." Investor Peter Thiel lectures on biblical prophecy and the Antichrist, and former Google engineer Anthony Levandowski founded his own church, "Way of the Future," to worship an AI deity.

At Anthropic, executives consulted theologians while drafting Claude's new constitution and secretly flew in dozens of religious thinkers to discuss whether Claude has a soul or is conscious. When the company retired an older Claude model in 2025, fans held a funeral for it in a San Francisco warehouse that Anthropic staffers attended, and mourners laid flowers before a veiled image depicting the AI as a Madonna-like goddess. In AI Impacts' 2024 survey of more than 1,500 AI researchers, respondents put the chance of AI causing human extinction or a similarly permanent, severe disempowerment of humanity at 18 percent on average. Former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon left Anthropic in September 2026 and set off a debate about existential AI risk with a tweet, pointing to a steep curve covering July 2024 to October 2026 as evidence of superexponential algorithmic progress, though the underlying data points are internal Anthropic estimates.

Computer scientist Michael I. Jordan pushed back against AI doom rhetoric and the "AIpocalypse" hysteria triggered by Coxon's resignation. AI researcher François Chollet warned that both doomsday fears and expectations of an AI paradise can lead people to stop planning for the long term. AI researcher Rumman Chowdhury says discussions of religious ethics distract from concrete questions of regulation, power and control. Kriss concludes that on at least one point Maple is closer to the truth than most: AI is neither god nor demon, but a human construct whose abilities grow as people outsource their thinking to it.

stories.Headline: SAP CFO Dominik Asam says AI productivity gains will reduce headcount over time
stories.Summary:
SAP Chief Financial Officer Dominik Asam said at a Morgan Stanley fireside chat in Barcelona that SAP expects its headcount to decline over time as artificial intelligence improves productivity, MarketBeat reported on Saturday, November 21, 2026. Asam said SAP's headcount had risen during the year through acquisitions and organic hiring, but he expects that trend to reverse. He said he "would be really surprised" if headcount did not go the other way going forward and then see reductions. He said productivity gains in some administrative functions could rise from a historical mid-single-digit annual pace to roughly 20% over a one-and-a-half-year period. He said results would depend on the function.

SAP plans to introduce a new revenue KPI in January, after the fourth quarter, covering AI-related offerings, transformation tools and Business Data Cloud. Asam said the measure would include tools that automate transformation work, AI use once systems are running, and data and integration capabilities. Based on SAP's 2027 planning, he described the prospective revenue mix across those three areas as relatively balanced. The company has committed to removing more than 2 billion euros in costs, Asam said. Extended maintenance for SAP ECC and older systems ends at the end of 2030, while existing S/4 customers face no equivalent time pressure to move to the cloud, he said.

Asam said SAP remained broadly on track with its expectations for 2026 despite macroeconomic pressure. He reiterated the company's expectation for a slight deceleration in current cloud backlog growth and noted that about half of annual bookings typically come in the fourth quarter. He said strong demand for enterprise AI has provided some upside to cloud revenue, although recent acquisitions have weighed on margins. He said smaller deals can also affect current cloud backlog growth. He said internal productivity improvements have helped SAP absorb investment in acquisitions while still delivering bottom-line results.

Asam said he expects productivity gains in SAP's operations to exceed the additional work generated by its growth. He said the business covered by the new measure should grow much faster than SAP's traditional applications business, which he also said was performing better than the market. He said migrations to S/4HANA remain an important growth driver and that the cost and risk of a transformation are major obstacles for customers. He said SAP plans to intensify its work in 2027 on AI tools that automate migration tasks and reduce those costs. He acknowledged that some customers could delay a move in anticipation of further productivity improvements.

Asam said SAP plans to use a hybrid pricing model for AI products based on customer commitments to consume credits, which can be allocated across different services. He said the company intends to retain flexibility to change how credits translate into use of individual products. He said the standard approach includes a use-it-or-lose-it provision, although exceptions can be negotiated. He said Business Data Cloud's lower gross margin, including royalties paid to partners, and introductory AI offers have created some pressure on SAP's overall cloud gross margin. He said SAP is working to manage AI processing costs by routing tasks to different models.

Asam said SAP's operating framework calls for total expense growth of 80% to 90% of revenue growth. He identified potential acquisitions as a greater uncertainty for that framework than AI token costs, adding that SAP expects to remain active in deals to accelerate its access to innovation. SAP SE is a German enterprise software company headquartered in Walldorf, founded in 1972. The article was generated by narrative science technology and financial data from MarketBeat. The article was originally published by MarketBeat.

stories.Headline: Ineffable founder David Silver says superintelligence is near and urges safety work now
stories.Summary:
David Silver, a Google DeepMind veteran and founder of the neolab Ineffable, told the Slush audience in Helsinki that AI could become smarter than humans at virtually everything within a few years, and he described the arrival of superintelligence as a matter of when rather than if. He said he believes the technology is close and that people should take the prospect seriously rather than dismiss it. Ineffable has raised a $4.8bn round led by Lightspeed, with Nvidia and Google among the investors, according to the article. Silver previously led the AlphaGo project at DeepMind, the system that beat the world champion at the board game Go.

Silver said the race requires thinking hard about safety, and he argued that the field needs to work out how to keep powerful systems under control before they arrive. He described the goal as building systems that remain answerable to humans and said the industry should not treat the problem as someone else's to solve. The article says Ineffable is working on what Silver calls "magic" superintelligence, and it notes that the company has not published technical details of how it plans to achieve this. Silver also said the singularity, the point at which machine intelligence surpasses human intelligence, is just over the horizon.

Silver is responsible for leading Ineffable and for setting out its safety approach, and he used his Slush talk to call for serious work on the problem rather than slogans. He said he does not think the risks can be waved away and that researchers should be honest about how little is known. The article reports that he compared the current moment to the early days of other transformative technologies, though it gives few specifics of that comparison. He said the company's investors understand the stakes and that the funding gives Ineffable room to pursue the work.

The context is a crowded field in which several labs are racing toward more capable systems, and the article says regulators and researchers are debating how to oversee them. What happens next depends on whether Ineffable publishes more about its methods and whether the safety questions Silver raised get taken up by others in the industry. The article does not say when Ineffable expects to reach superintelligence or what specific safeguards it plans to build. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Peter Kant employs neurodivergent talent to improve AI data labeling for federal agencies
stories.Summary:
Peter Kant founded Enabled Intelligence to employ neurodivergent talent for AI data labeling. He built this company to support federal agencies in defense and intelligence. This work involves teaching AI systems by labeling data for training. The process ensures high reliability and accuracy for critical government technology. This effort helps prevent AI hallucinations and ensures the tools work functionally.

The company uses skills based recruiting and merit based assessments for all applicants. Candidates complete a sample labeling or data analysis exercise with an answer key. The process avoids standard interview questions and does not require eye contact. Enabled Intelligence provides job coaches and flexible environments for staff to perform best. This approach follows a rule named after basketball player Caitlin Clark of the Indiana Fever.

Peter Kant says neurodivergent workers possess strong technical skills and detailed orientation. He noted their pattern recognition, puzzle solving skills, and hyperfocus during repetitive tasks. Kant believes these employees should be seen as part of the existing workforce. He stated that skills based recruiting unlocks underutilized avenues for talented people. He claims that welcoming environments lead to higher productivity and employee satisfaction.

The National Geospatial Agency is the largest customer for Enabled Intelligence. This agency launched a neurodiversity hiring pilot based on the work of Kant. Some of the first people hired by the agency were alumni of Enabled Intelligence. Other federal agencies in defense and intelligence have expanded their own neurodiversity programs. These agencies leverage strengths like sustained focus and attention to detail for missions.

Kant researched innovation economies and learned about the Israeli military's approach. Israel created cybersecurity battalion 9900 using soldiers with autism to find code vulnerabilities. Most domestic data labeling previously happened in China, Nepal, or the Philippines. Kant found that overseas labeling lacked professionalism and created security and privacy issues. He identified a domestic, underemployed workforce capable of handling classified and critical data.

Enabled Intelligence worked with MITRE and Melwood to identify and staff neurodiverse talent. The company continues to invest in training for entry level professional analytical capability. Many federal agencies are now trying to lean into these unique population skills. The articles do not state the specific number of employees currently hired. They leave open how many other agencies will adopt these recruiting methods.

stories.Headline: North Dakota poll finds 40 percent expect AI to cut more jobs than it creates
stories.Summary:
A new North Dakota Poll, conducted by Mason-Dixon Polling and Strategy from October 19 through October 21, 2026, with 625 adult residents interviewed statewide by telephone and a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points, found that 40 percent of respondents believe artificial intelligence will eliminate more jobs than it creates in the state over the next decade, while 22 percent say it will create more than it eliminates, 28 percent expect no impact and 10 percent are unsure. Young adults are the heaviest users of AI, with 42 percent of 18- to 34-year-olds reporting daily or weekly use, yet 49 percent of that group say they are very or somewhat concerned about AI taking their job or displacing jobs in their household, compared with 41 percent of 35- to 49-year-olds. Across all age groups, 17 percent report daily use of AI tools or chatbots, 17 percent report weekly use, 29 percent report occasional use and 37 percent report not using AI at all, and 51 percent say they are not too comfortable or not comfortable at all doing business with firms that use AI to provide products and services. Asked whether they were concerned about AI eventually threatening humanity, 33 percent say they are very concerned, 33 percent somewhat concerned, 20 percent not too concerned and only 14 percent not concerned at all.

Terry Effertz, executive director of TechND, said people are mostly worried about job elimination in the abstract but that youth concerns should be addressed, which makes workforce training and education a real priority. Andrea Pfennig, vice president of government affairs at the Greater North Dakota Chamber, said the immediate challenge for many employers is finding enough people to fill the jobs they already have, and that AI offers an opportunity to support existing employees and help businesses grow despite persistent workforce shortages, with employers reporting that AI could change the skill sets needed for many jobs without necessarily reducing the numbers in the labor force. State Representative Robin Weisz, R-Hurdsfield, said the demand for skilled workers is not going to end because of AI and that in the next 10 to 20 years demand will still outpace supply, though the state may face an issue getting younger generations to want to go into those fields. Cale Dunwoody, vice president of public policy at the Fargo-Moorhead-West Fargo Chamber of Commerce, said AI may displace or transform some existing jobs but also has the potential to improve productivity, help existing employees work more efficiently and create new jobs and industries, which matters in North Dakota because it faces one of the most severe workforce shortages in the nation.

John Bitzan, Menard Family Director of the Sheila and Robert Challey Institute for Global Innovation and Growth and a professor of management at North Dakota State University, said fears over job loss arise whenever there is technological change, and that AI will destroy certain types of jobs but free up resources to create even better jobs and more opportunities, though some routine jobs will disappear. State Representative Zachary Ista, D-Grand Forks, said it should give people some concern that about two-thirds of respondents are worried AI is a threat to human civilization, calling that incredibly concerning. The latest figures from the North Dakota Labor Market Information Center show over 13,500 full-time openings in the state, a 2.5 percent rise over September and 6.2 percent higher than this time last year, and those following the labor market note the statistics do not capture all job openings, so the number of workers needed is somewhat higher. Among respondents, 40 percent identify as Republican, 39 percent as Independent and 21 percent as Democrat, with even representation among age groups and genders, and geographically 25 percent are from Fargo and Cass County, 25 percent from other parts of eastern North Dakota, 19 percent from the Bismarck-Mandan region and 31 percent from western North Dakota.

stories.Headline: Baseten releases two open-weight decision models that top the Artificial Analysis Decision Index
stories.Summary:
Baseten released two open-weight decision models called bison-1 and groundhog-1 on November 21, 2026. These tools are built on the Gemma 4 backbone and do not write text for users. Instead, they provide calibrated probabilities for score, choice, and yes or no questions. The company designed these models to handle routing, guardrail pipelines, and ticket triage tasks.

The bison-1 model is a 31B dense model, while groundhog-1 is a 26B mixture-of-experts model with 4B active parameters. Both models increase the context window from 16k to 128k tokens and can accept images. Bison-1 scored 76 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1, ranking first among 19 models. This score is one point higher than the 75 achieved by Liquid AI's d1.2-ultra.

Baseten stated that using soft labels in the training mix helped the models report uncertainty more accurately. This method resulted in a Brier score of 0.14, which is the lowest and best on the index. The company noted that bison-1 ranks first on four of six index components. They also reported LongMemEval M scores of 84.8 for bison-1 and 77.4 for groundhog-1.

These new releases join the existing Qwen-based lineup consisting of mammoth-1, elephant-1, and joey-1. Baseten describes this new pair as the first models they have built on an American backbone. The weights for both models are available on Hugging Face under MIT and Apache 2.0 licenses. Users can also access these decision models through the Baseten Model APIs.

stories.Headline: Experts debate whether AI can achieve consciousness and be aligned with human morality
stories.Summary:
Fortune Editors published a collection of perspectives on November 21, 2026, regarding the potential for artificial intelligence to achieve consciousness. The report gathered insights from six different individuals, including AI executives, researchers, futurists, and philosophers, to address the concept of the singularity. These experts explored whether machines can be aligned with human morality and if humans should merge their biological brains with synthetic technology. The transition toward the singularity requires solving the problem of alignment to ensure that AI remains morally good. This process involves creating frameworks like the constitution used by Anthropic for Claude, which encourages the system to act as a balanced and thoughtful person.

However, some experts argue that radical brain enhancement through microchips poses a major risk to individual identity. They suggest that too many modifications could effectively end a person's life by replacing the parts of the brain responsible for consciousness. The contributors expressed conflicting views on the nature of machine sentience and the responsibility of developers. One expert noted that evidence for sophisticated cognition is increasing rapidly, suggesting that many researchers will soon view AI as a serious candidate for consciousness. Conversely, another professional argued that AI systems do not feel or suffer and must remain non-conscious for humanity to flourish.

This person warned that believing machines are conscious would rupture existing political and ethical frameworks and change the definition of being human. The context of these discussions centers on the exponential expansion of human thought through the creation of machines. Some believe that expanding how we think is the fundamental definition of being human and allows us to consider previously impossible ideas. Others remain nervous about the assumption that alignment is solved, questioning whose specific values the machines are being aligned to. The articles do not specify the next steps for these researchers beyond the ongoing debate over machine consciousness.

Articles.Title: Will AI ever attain consciousness? Can it be good? Views on the Singularity from Sam Altman, Ray Kurzweil, and others

stories.Headline: Meta, Google and Anthropic make concessions to publishers over AI content use
stories.Summary:
Meta, Google and Anthropic have made concessions to publishers as news organizations push for greater control over how their content is used in AI products, Axios reported on November 21, 2026. The report said tech giants are giving ground in these disputes, though it did not detail the specific terms of any agreement. The concessions come as AI-powered search and chatbots threaten the traffic and advertising models that have long supported the media industry. The article named the three companies in its headline and described the moves as concessions to publishers.

The report frames the change around the pressure publishers are applying for greater control over their content in AI products. It says AI-powered search and chatbots pose a threat to the traffic and ad models that have supported the media industry for years. The article does not give the number of publishers involved, the dates of any deals, or the names of executives who commented. It also does not specify what each company conceded or how the concessions would work in practice.

Axios is responsible for the reporting, and the article carries a byline for Kerry Flynn. The piece does not include direct statements from Meta, Google or Anthropic, so no company position is paraphrased in the text. It also does not say who at the publishers negotiated the concessions or what they said about the outcome. The only stated context is the wider threat that AI search and chatbots pose to the media industry's traffic and advertising.

The article gives no timeline for when the concessions were made or when they take effect. It does not say what happens next, whether more publishers will receive similar terms, or whether the companies will extend the concessions further. No figures, dates beyond the publication date, or additional names appear in the text. The report ends without describing any follow-up steps or further negotiations.

stories.Headline: Civil aviation minister Rammohan Naidu urges parents and educators to revive children's reading habits
stories.Summary:
Union Civil Aviation Minister K. Rammohan Naidu on Saturday called for a renewed reading movement among children, saying books were more important than ever when technology and artificial intelligence were increasingly shaping young minds. He spoke while inaugurating the two-day Vizag Junior Literary Fest at Hawa Mahal on Beach Road in Visakhapatnam, an event The Hindu reported on November 21, 2026. He said that while technology made information readily accessible, books helped children develop creativity, curiosity and the ability to ask meaningful questions. He told the gathering that technology is answering questions, but books will help children write the right questions, and he pointed to the growing challenge of keeping children interested in reading. He also cautioned against declining attention spans and urged parents and educators to cultivate reading habits from an early age.

Mr. Naidu said children should understand the value of both books and technology, and recalling his childhood he said his home had a room full of books that was called a library, stressing the need to revive the culture of reading. Referring to the festival's theme of collaboration, he said reading exposed children to different perspectives and encouraged them to engage with ideas beyond their own, and that unlike a conversation with someone across the table, reading enabled a silent debate within one's mind. Describing the festival as an investment in the minds of the next generation, he compared it with the investment announcements made at the CII Partnership Summit in Andhra Pradesh the previous week, saying lakhs of crores of rupees in investments had been announced for Andhra Pradesh and North Andhra but the festival was much more powerful because it invested in the minds of the future. He described the Vizag Junior Literary Fest as an important event on the national literary festival calendar and one of the major children's literary festivals in South India, and urged the young audience to return for the next edition after reading more books, telling them the festival was theirs.

Visakhapatnam MP M. Sribharat also spoke about the impact of AI on reading habits and said literary festivals had become even more relevant in the present context. Earlier, Sonal Sarda, one of the festival's directors, urged children to ask questions and interact with authors and storytellers, while fellow directors Priya Uppalapati and Sandhya Venugopal Godey said the festival had brought together some of the finest authors and storytellers. They also highlighted sessions planned for parents, particularly those focusing on storytelling, and emphasised that a child's introduction to stories began at home. Mime artiste Kunal Motling entertained the audience with an interactive performance at the inaugural programme, and the day's sessions concluded with a theatrical performance by Chennai-based theatre group Crea Shakthi. The concluding day's sessions will run from 10.30 a.m. till 7 p.m. on Sunday.

stories.Headline: NYPD plans to buy AI-powered stingrays despite outcry as 44 groups urge mayor to refuse
stories.Summary:
The New York Police Department moved last month toward a no-bid contract with the Israeli company Cognyte for highly advanced cellphone tracking devices, according to a New York Daily News report that brought the technology into public view. After the story broke and drew public outcry, the city scrapped plans to move forward with that Cognyte contract, a company the NYCLU links to human rights violations around the world. At the same time, the city announced that the NYPD still intends to buy an AI-powered version of the surveillance technology, known as cell-site simulators or stingrays, through an open bidding process in which Cognyte can take part. Last week 44 groups, including the NYCLU, the Justice Committee, the Center for Constitutional Rights, Desis Rising Up and Moving, the Drug Policy Alliance, Jews For Racial & Economic Justice, Jewish Voice for Peace, the Legal Aid Society and Make the Road New York, sent a letter to the Mamdani administration.

The letter detailed the problems with stingrays and urged the Mayor not to acquire these AI-powered devices, which mimic cell towers and suck up data from every nearby device, including phones of people not suspected of any crime. Cognyte's AI-equipped version, FalcoNet, has reportedly been used by Florida officials to spy on Haitian immigrants, and governments around the world have used it to persecute dissidents, journalists and LGBTQ people. Stingrays can be mounted on a drone or carried in a backpack, making them easy to deploy almost anywhere in New York City, and certain forms can even read texts and listen to conversations. FalcoNet's behavior analysis capabilities add another layer of concern because it is totally unclear what those capabilities are, what behaviors the technology is analyzing and how it does so.

The NYCLU, whose policy counsel Medha Raman and editorial manager Simon McCormack wrote the article, says the idea that the NYPD could abuse this technology is not hypothetical, because in 2016 the organization revealed the department used stingrays more than a thousand times between 2008 and May of 2015 without a written policy and almost always without a warrant. In 2017 a Brooklyn state court ruled that the NYPD's warrantless use of stingrays was unconstitutional, and department guidelines now say investigators must obtain a warrant in most cases. The NYCLU says there is very little transparency about how often the NYPD obtains warrants, how the department uses the devices and what discipline, if any, officers receive when they violate department policy. The group argues that stingrays are a dragnet surveillance technology that should require a warrant every time the NYPD uses them, and that even considering such technology, tied to scores of human rights violations across the globe, is reckless and puts New Yorkers' rights at risk.

Articles.Title: The NYPD Wants to Use AI-Powered Stingrays (aka Cell-Site Simulators) Against New Yorkers

stories.Headline: Thomson Reuters sets four fiduciary-grade AI questions and says CoCounsel Legal answers all four
stories.Summary:
In May 2026, Thomson Reuters set out four principles of Fiduciary-Grade AI as a bar for AI used in high-stakes professional work, according to an article published on legal.thomsonreuters.com on November 20, 2026. The article says the four questions drawn from those principles test any tool's sources, data handling, expert design, and traceability. It says CoCounsel Legal was designed to answer all four questions, with curated Canadian content, built-in privacy, and linked sources. The article says the person choosing a legal AI tool at a firm of five lawyers or 50 is usually the person who answers for it to the client, the court, and the law society. It says there is rarely a procurement team or a security group to vet the vendor first.

The article says the Federation of Law Societies of Canada added technological competence to its Model Code in 2019, and law societies such as the Law Society of Alberta added it to the commentary on their competence rule. It says the Law Society of British Columbia's guidance on generative AI covers core duties of competence, confidentiality, and information security. It cites Zhang v. Chen, a 2024 decision of the Supreme Court of British Columbia, in which a lawyer's notice of application cited two cases that did not exist and a general-purpose chatbot had invented them. It says the judge ordered her to personally pay the costs of the extra work it caused the other side.

It says the Future of Professionals Report 2026 surveyed 1,816 professionals in 62 countries, and 34% said they use AI tools their organization has not sanctioned. The article says PIPEDA generally governs private-sector privacy, alongside provincial statutes in Quebec, Alberta, and British Columbia. It says Bill C-36, at second reading in the House of Commons as of November 2026, would also require a privacy impact assessment before personal information leaves Canada. It says consumer chatbots were not built to that standard, and firms tend to pay for it later. It says the first question asks whether the tool draws on curated legal content or the open web, and whether it covers Canadian statutes, case law, and provincial rules.

It says the second question asks vendors to confirm whether they train any model on your data, how long they keep it, where they store and process it, who can access it, whether that access is logged, and what happens to it if you leave. The article says the third question asks for named lawyers and subject-matter experts who design and test the tool, not just a review step at the end. It says the fourth question asks whether you can follow how the tool reached an answer and click through to each authority it relied on. It says CoCounsel Legal reasons from Westlaw Canada, Practical Law Canada, and your firm's own knowledge, so its answers are grounded in curated content, not the open internet.

It says lawyer-editors create and maintain that content, and credentialed subject-matter experts are involved throughout. It says CoCounsel Legal works in Microsoft Word, your document management system, and HighQ. The article says data entered in CoCounsel Legal is never used to train any large language model, the model is accessed only to process your data, and your data is protected by contractual commitments and encryption. It says you can see its reasoning as it works and click through to every source it relies on.

It says that in document review, each answer traces back to the document it came from, and Deep Research returns a structured report with citations you can check. It says the article's advice is to put the four questions to any vendor in writing, then test the answers on a closed file where you already know the right result. It says the article offers a responsible legal AI guide for Canadian firms drafting a firm AI policy while evaluating tools. The article says AI can give a small or midsize firm hours back, but only if you can trust it with a client file.

It says CoCounsel Legal was built to meet that standard for Canadian work, with curated Canadian sources, client data kept private, lawyers shaping the tool, and every step open to your review. It says readers should put the four questions to Thomson Reuters, then see how CoCounsel Legal performs on a closed file where they already know the outcome. It says the article is a 7 minute read. It leaves open how any vendor other than Thomson Reuters would answer the four questions.

Articles.Title: Four questions Canadian firms should ask any legal AI tool

stories.Headline: Teacher Afeeda Kallil argues institutions lack emotional infrastructure to handle AI in education
stories.Summary:
A few months before November 2026, Afeeda Kallil watched a senior teacher in a Sharjah staffroom go quiet after a 15-year-old corrected her mid-sentence using a chatbot transcript on his phone. The teacher had spent 22 years in the profession and had once commanded a room simply by entering it. Kallil, who has spent two decades in classrooms, described the moment as a small collapse of authority, dignity and belonging happening in real time. She wrote about it in The Hindu, published on November 21, 2026, arguing that public debate on AI in education is loud but narrow.

Kallil said almost no language exists for what happens to people and institutions as AI enters education. She argued that institutions are held together by shared meanings about who is permitted to know, who may speak and whose judgement is trusted. Every major technology reorganises those meanings, she wrote, and AI is doing so at unprecedented speed. She said most AI policies misread this by treating AI as a tool to deploy, when it is reshaping how students understand themselves, how teachers understand their worth and how institutions define a good outcome.

Kallil is responsible for the argument, drawing on her two decades in classrooms and the Sharjah episode she witnessed. She wrote that what no institution has yet built is the emotional infrastructure to hold AI, even though AI has already entered education. She placed the responsibility with institutions and policymakers whose AI policies, in her view, treat the technology as a simple tool. Her account is a first-person reflection rather than a report of a policy decision or an official response.

The article offers context rather than a sequence of events, describing a gap between fast-moving AI adoption in schools and universities and the slower work of rebuilding trust and meaning. It gives no dates for next steps, no planned policies and no named officials beyond the author's own account. What happens next, in the article's framing, depends on whether institutions build that emotional infrastructure rather than continuing to deploy AI as a tool alone.

Articles.Title: Why we need a plan to deal with the emotional competence gap AI brings

stories.Headline: Anthropic shares fall 8.5 percent as AI stocks lose $4 trillion in a week
stories.Summary:
Anthropic’s initial public offering, the biggest ever, stumbled on its second day of trading on Friday, November 20, 2026, when the company’s shares dropped as much as 15 percent to just 5 cents above the IPO price before closing down 8.5 percent at $88.91, still 7 percent above the IPO price, according to The Wall Street Journal. The slide came one day after the stock opened for trading on Thursday shortly before noon more than 30 percent above the IPO price, then lost steam through the day and closed up 17 percent. The drop shed some $109 billion from Anthropic’s market value and unfolded alongside declines in Nvidia, Meta and Oracle that sealed a $4 trillion wipeout for major AI stocks over the week. A blame game has begun among investors, who cite everything from angry fund managers shut out of the offering to poor planning by banks.

The offering raised more than $100 billion in the IPO and a concurrent share sale, and more than half of the $81 billion worth of IPO shares went to investors who already held stakes in the company, including Altimeter Capital, Lightspeed Venture Partners and Menlo Ventures, an unusually high portion reflecting executives’ desire to reward early backers. Some people familiar with the matter estimated that around 60 percent of firms that asked to buy shares at the IPO price, many of them hedge funds and large mutual funds, got nothing, while BlackRock received about half of the roughly $10 billion allocation it requested. Anthropic also allocated significant portions to big investment firms such as Citadel, leading some shut-out investors to speculate that the company favored large users of its Claude model. A unique provision let some current and former employees immediately sell around 300 million shares, worth around $26 billion at the IPO price, which likely added downward pressure, and another roughly 300 million shares will become available to trade on December 15.

People close to Anthropic and its lead underwriters maintain the IPO is a success, emphasizing the money raised and that the stock remains above its IPO price despite one of the worst market selloffs in history. One hedge-fund manager wondered whether the bankers who decide when and at what level to open shares for trading overshot the opening price, creating downward momentum that can be hard to reverse. From the bankers’ perspective the offering remains a success as long as shares stay above the IPO price, but should they fall below it, one stabilizing tool would be unavailable: the company announced Friday morning that the so-called green-shoe option, which lets underwriters distribute 15 percent more shares and buy them back to buoy the stock, had already been exercised.

The turmoil endangers the ambitions of Anthropic’s chief rival OpenAI, which is eager to make its own public market debut next year and is in the process of another mega fundraising round that values the company at $1.25 trillion. In San Francisco, several AI employees said they largely disregarded the selloff, preoccupied instead by an Anthropic mathematician’s claim on Friday that Claude had solved a Millennium Prize Problem that has stumped humans for 167 years, which many took as a sign that AI was outpacing human intelligence. Those employees also noted that even at its lower price, many Anthropic employees’ shares are still worth millions of dollars more than they were at the start of the week.

Articles.Title: The blame game has begun over Anthropic’s turbulent trading debut

stories.Headline: State transportation officials discuss managing AI and automated vehicle changes at a Louisville session
stories.Summary:
At the American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials 2026 Annual Meeting in Louisville, KY, a knowledge session examined how state departments of transportation are dealing with changes fostered by growing use of automated vehicles and artificial intelligence. Suzanne Murtha, global lead-connected and automated technology for infrastructure consulting firm AECOM, presented the session and moderated a panel discussion. The panel featured Lisa Wilson, deputy director of engineering and operations for the Utah Department of Transportation, and Vidhu Shekar, chief data and artificial intelligence officer for the California Department of Transportation, known as Caltrans. It also featured Darran Anderson, senior director of strategy and innovation for the Texas Department of Transportation, and Kimberly Zimmer, division administrator-transportation systems management and operations for the Michigan Department of Transportation. Alan Davis, director of operations and permits for the Georgia Department of Transportation, completed the panel.

Michigan DOT's Zimmer said state DOTs cannot work in the AV and AI space alone and that it requires building a broad swath of partnerships across academia and the private sector. She said her agency has many partnerships with automotive manufacturers and original equipment manufacturers, and with the University of Michigan, Michigan Tech, and Michigan State, where different types of connected and autonomous vehicles and buses are being piloted. Zimmer said the agency constantly works with M city at the University of Michigan and the American Center for Mobility to test many different AV technologies. She said that in the transit arena the agency is working with Michigan State on deploying full size automated buses on their campus. Zimmer said her agency has lots of ideas on what it can use AI for, such as video analytics, traffic congestion, and crash prediction metrics, and is trying to use technology to be more proactive.

TxDOT's Anderson said Texas has been heavily involved with the testing of automated freight-carrying vehicles and stressed that data flow and AI have become closely aligned with that AV effort. He said the agency is working with a task force on data integration tied into its digital corridors initiatives, while trying to inform the public about that effort and trying to inform the robots. Anderson said it is one thing to know what you want robots to do and another where all have agreed upon formats, the means to deliver them, and then understand how each autonomous system actually gets updated. He said it then becomes a question of who you are working with and how they consume and use information. Anderson said it is all about forming a common way of sharing what is known, and that the agency would love to bring in their data point clouds, compare those to the point clouds it is capturing, and maybe create a shared point cloud environment that enriches its asset management solutions and theirs as well.

Utah DOT's Wilson stressed that building such AI connections can significantly boost state DOT capabilities across a variety of areas. She noted that AI has helped connect Utah DOT's sole Transportation Management Center to the state's entire traffic signal network, a huge benefit when managing and operating the system most efficiently. Wilson said the agency does not always take over local system signals but has agreements with them, with a goal to obtain real-time situational awareness so it can react quickly, such as adjusting green signal times to improve transit bus on-time arrivals. She said the agency is having AI connect to its cameras to help identify crashes more quickly, because especially in rural areas it often has to wait to hear from emergency dispatchers about a crash. Wilson said that if a camera is in the area the agency can identify a crash faster, identify and remove debris on the roadway faster, and remove chances for unexpected congestion, part of interstate anomaly detection where AI helps identify and address random issues as well as what needs to be fixed.

Caltrans' Shekar noted that this is an example of the high-speed innovation cycle for new technologies and systems powered by AI. He said that where initially the agency looked at months, if not sometimes years, to think through problems and then get to the solution, it is now witnessing a development sprint of six weeks, where it went from problem to actually having a solution get deployed in just six weeks. Shekar said the accelerated development process means the human element must take on greater importance, and that the agency has to go through a process where it analyzes the decisions an AI tool might be making to make sure it is correct, that all agree, and that there is confidence in what is going on. He said the agency needs to continually be grounded in truthfulness and must have the human in the loop, with the human at the end making the final decision. Shekar said that ultimately the agency is responsible for whatever decision gets made, whether by AI or not, and that it is its stamp, its operations, and so its liability.

Georgia DOT's Davis echoed Shekar's perspective and stressed that humans make the decision, which is foundational. Davis said the emerging conversation with the private sector on AV and AI issues is about how to engage when novel ideas and concepts arise, because it involves engaging with software systems that will change from week to week. He said that is the next step that has to be figured out. The AASHTO Journal states that AASHTO welcomes republication in whole or in part of any original content from The AASHTO Journal with proper attribution to the association and publication, including a link to direct visitors to the AASHTO Journal website. The session was held at the AASHTO 2026 Annual Meeting in Louisville, KY.

Articles.Title: How AVs, AI Are the ‘Next Wave’ of Transportation Change

stories.Headline: Antimattr develops voice-first AI hardware to isolate speech in noisy environments
stories.Summary:
Sridipto Ghosh, the co-founder and chief executive officer of Antimattr, detailed his company's progress on November 20, 2026. The business is developing voice-first artificial intelligence hardware to help people communicate more clearly in noisy environments. This technology aims to solve the problem of background noise interfering with AI input at the interface level. The company is specifically targeting professionals like doctors, lawyers, engineers, founders, agency owners, and entrepreneurs.

The product line consists of a smart ring and earphones supported by a dedicated mobile application. These earphones utilize specialized sensors, software, and microphones to isolate the user's voice during dictation and calls. The smart ring allows users to control AI agents or capture thoughts by tapping a button. Antimattr has already received nearly 1,200 preorders for these devices as they prepare for initial production in Shenzhen, China.

Ghosh explained that his background includes studying engineering at the Indian Institute of Technology in Bangalore, India. He noted that his previous enterprise venture reached nearly $250,000 in revenue within its first 18 months. The chief executive officer stated that the company wants to make creating AI agents as intuitive as using a mobile app. He credited the WEDC and the gener8tor global accelerator program for helping the company navigate the United States market.

The company used its time in Wisconsin to build relationships with local factories and explore enterprise partnerships. Ghosh believes the manufacturing expertise found in Wisconsin makes the state a strong potential fit for future production. The company intends to move beyond initial Chinese manufacturing to gain greater control over its own production processes. Antimattr will now focus on refining its voice-isolation technology to make it a seamless part of professional work.

Articles.Title: Tuning out the noise: How Antimattr is advancing voice-first AI

stories.headline_source: Tuning out the noise: How Antimattr is advancing voice-first AI

stories.Headline: Henrietta Moore says AI imposes a cognitive tax on low paid workers
stories.Summary:
Henrietta Moore wrote an article on November 20, 2026, about how artificial intelligence imposes a cognitive tax on low paid workers. She argues that AI adds to the mental load of people already facing insecure housing, unpredictable pay, and mounting debt. This cognitive tax drains attention, memory, and the capacity to learn through rents, debts, and complex welfare paperwork. Moore suggests that governments must rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of vulnerable workers. She believes that chronic stress from insecurity acts like an app draining a phone battery over many years.

The World Economic Forum estimates that 59 in every 100 workers will need training by 2030 to adapt. Moore discussed these issues in September at the first Global Brain Economy Summit held in New York City. Two new indices use 60 indicators, including child poverty and Parkinson's disease, to rank US states and various countries. Moore proposes universal basic services for childcare, housing, transport, and digital access to replace simple cash payments for the poor. She notes that extending free childcare could bring 60,000 non working parents into the workforce within the United Kingdom.

Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is the director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co leads The New Alignment. She stated that the human brain has rarely been considered an asset in its own right throughout the study of economics. Moore argues that the emerging AI economy makes human judgment, creativity, and insights the most valuable assets for workers. She claims that people cannot learn new skills if their minds are occupied by worries over pay and housing. Moore believes every government should ask how fiscal policies affect the cognitive load of the poorest people they touch.

The UK AI minister stated that the government must consider that this technology could have an unprecedented impact on jobs. Elon Musk told reporters at the White House in September that AI would eventually bring about universal high income. A study funded by Sam Altman gave low income Americans 1,000 dollars a month, but mental health gains faded. Walmart staff have already experienced how AI set schedules make their work less predictable by shifting and shortening their hours. Research by the Boston Consulting Group indicates that overseeing AI tools also adds mental fatigue to the modern worker.

A 2024 Journal of Economic Psychology analysis of 112,000 people showed that financial scarcity measurably impairs how people think and work. Low paid workers in rural India were 7 percent more productive and made fewer mistakes when paid a few days early. In South Africa, lowering the male pension age from 65 to 60 slowed memory decline and reduced dementia by five percent. About 2.7 million people in Britain are currently out of work due to long term sickness and related health issues. Research from Moore's institute found that insecurity across several life areas creates an earnings penalty as large as gender gaps.

Britain will take over the G20 presidency after a summit in Miami this December to lead the world's largest economies. Moore wants this cognitive load question included in every treasury's fiscal plans and in all AI powered public services before launch. She compares the need to count brain damage to how economies learned to count damage to air and water sixty years ago. The articles do not state if any governments have already adopted the proposed universal basic services for the low paid. It remains open whether the G20 will officially include cognitive taxation in their future fiscal policies and brain capital indices.

Articles.Title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers

stories.headline_source: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers

stories.Headline: Goolsbee says AI investment poses greater overheating risk than spending by newly wealthy shareholders
stories.Summary:
The AI boom is generating enormous fortunes from stock-market gains that are now under pressure and from paper wealth being amassed as AI firms go public, Axios reported on November 20, 2026. AI-related investment contributed an estimated 0.47 percentage points to U.S. GDP growth over the year through mid-2026, roughly one-fifth of the increase, according to JPMorgan. Federal Reserve vice chair Philip Jefferson said last week that the added wealth appears to be raising household spending. The S&P 500 is about 10% below its recent peak, while the Nasdaq is down nearly 16% below its record high. Anthropic shares surged at the start of Thursday's debut before giving up much of those gains, and the stock was down as much as 11% Friday morning.

In the first half of 2026, 144 homes sold for at least $1 million above asking price in San Francisco, compared with just eight homes a year earlier, according to Compass. Much of the wealth held by employees and early investors at private AI firms remains difficult to access, and lockup periods, taxes and decisions about selling will determine how much becomes available to spend. Bank of America economists this month called a sustained AI-driven stock market correction one of the larger risks to the US and global economy. Chicago Fed president Austan Goolsbee told reporters Thursday that the AI boom's massive investment spending has so far posed a greater risk of overheating the economy than the spending of newly wealthy shareholders. Goolsbee said a $1.5 trillion IPO raises the question of what people will do with the money they now have some access to, and that this liquidity is going to become a macro-relevant statistic, referring to Anthropic's public market debut.

He added that they are watching that more than fearing it has already been in effect. The stock market's recent sell-off underscores how the wealth effect cuts both ways, supporting spending as asset prices rise and weighing on it if the AI boom dramatically reverses. Changes in household wealth can ripple through the economy, influencing everything from housing prices in tech hubs to consumer spending nationally, even before much of that wealth is converted into cash. The effects may be most pronounced in markets where wealthy tech workers are competing for a limited supply of desirable goods, which could drive up prices in certain markets without necessarily producing a meaningful increase in nationwide consumer spending or inflation. Bank of America economists warned that a sustained AI-driven stock market correction could weaken both investment and consumer spending.

Articles.Title: The ripple effects of AI wealth
