stories.Headline: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he and Claude prove the Riemann hypothesis in Lean code
stories.Summary:
Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at the AI company Anthropic, claimed on Friday, 20 November 2026, to have discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis working with Anthropic's Claude AI. He published a statement on his website saying he believed he had, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. The Riemann hypothesis was first put forward in 1859 by the German mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It proposes an origin for the prime numbers, namely that they follow a certain pattern. The question is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems, which will award a $1 million prize for an accepted solution.

Alpöge has not published a human-readable version of the proof, saying it would be obviously inappropriate to attempt to post some massive unreadable travesty of slop. He says an unpublished version ran to more than 250,000 pages. Instead he released a version written in Lean, a computer code mathematicians use to mechanically verify proofs as a series of logical steps in a process called formalisation. The process is so thorough that if a theorem comes through intact, meaning the code compiles, it is considered proved correct beyond all reasonable doubt. Alpöge says the proof confirms the generalised Riemann hypothesis, which widens out the concept to different properties of prime numbers.

Alpöge wrote that it is natural to feel that this is an end, in his case a loss of a principal guiding light. He wrote that what he saw during the course of progress so amazed him that he believed it is one dawn across science of something far greater. He wrote that the precise timing is horrible and that if he could have, he would have finished this all much earlier. He says he spoke to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and determined that there was a constraint to respect before the announcement could be made. Anthropic listed on the stock market on 19 November, and Alpöge appears to suggest that he waited to announce the proof until after.

Kevin Buzzard at Imperial College London said let's see if it compiles first, and that it might be a while before we find the relevant experts able to tell us the thrust of the argument. Buzzard said it probably will be true because Alpöge will have a huge amount of egg on his face if the Lean code doesn't compile or is deficient in some way. James McKee at Royal Holloway University of London said there are numerous results conditional on the generalised Riemann hypothesis, and now those are theorems. McKee said most mathematicians believed, or the more cautious ones merely suspected, that GRH was true, so its proof will not be unsettling. McKee said what is both unsettling and tremendously exciting is the rapid progress in recent months towards automated proofs of significant mathematical results, and that it is both a wonderful time and a terrible time to be a research mathematician.

Hector Pasten, a mathematician at the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile, said that if the proof is correct and understood, this completes a dictionary between different branches of math where the connections were only partial, something like a Rosetta Stone. Carlo Pagano, a professor at Concordia University and a visiting researcher at Google DeepMind, said that if true, even from a first high level scan of the summary of the proposed argument, it is very plausible to him that the new ideas in the proof will open up brand new avenues of thinking in number theory. Andrew Sutherland, an MIT mathematician, told Scientific American today after he had independently compiled Alpöge's result in Lean that this is indeed an historic moment and that the world has changed. Sutherland said he knows there will be a wide range of reactions in the community, but to him this is a human triumph and a day for celebration. Sutherland said there is much work to be done to understand the mathematical details of the proof, that he can't wait to dig into them, and that perhaps the single most important step in the proof was building a machine that can think.

In August, Anthropic announced previous work on the Riemann hypothesis, but that stopped short of a full proof. The first chink in the problem's armor appeared in October, when one of the proofs in OpenAI's massive dump of math results made significant progress on making sense of the primes. In July, Alpöge announced that the Jacobian conjecture, which academics have spent decades trying to prove was true, is actually false, giving a tiny, 216-character counterexample as proof. He and Tristan Buckmaster at New York University also announced that they had cracked three significant problems considered stepping stones to the Navier-Stokes problem, hours before OpenAI controversially revealed a full solution. Scientific American reported that Buckmaster implied in September that OpenAI had stolen his and Alpöge's work.

The process isn't without vulnerabilities, and the code and mathematics will need to be thoroughly checked by humans. Issues can arise in Lean, but it shouldn't take long for experts to verify whether the hypothesis is properly coded, and if the proof is correct. Scientific American called the story breaking news and said it will be updated. The Riemann result, if correct, doesn't have any immediate real-world applications, and it won't upend global banking or make the internet run faster. Sutherland once told Scientific American that an AI that can prove the Riemann hypothesis is not one he'd want to meet, and that if that happens, mathematicians having jobs will be the least of our problems.

stories.Headline: TeraWulf begins erecting structural steel at its 480 MW Kentucky AI campus for Anthropic
stories.Summary:
TeraWulf has moved from foundational work to vertical construction at its Justified Data Campus in Hawesville, Kentucky, where the company announced on LinkedIn that the first structural steel is going up at the Hancock County site, according to US Data Center Projects. The 480 MW facility is being purpose-built for the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, and the majority of structural steel for the first building, known as CB-1, has already been delivered and staged, with substantial deliveries also completed for CB-2. TeraWulf described the development as an important transition as it advances large-scale infrastructure built specifically for its customer Anthropic. Engineering, procurement and construction work at the site is being handled by Fluor Corporation, a partnership that has grown beyond the two companies' earlier collaborations. The Justified Data Campus occupies a 790-acre site in Hancock County that was previously used for aluminum processing, and Century Aluminum operated at the location from 1969 until 2022, when TeraWulf acquired the property with plans to convert the long-standing industrial site into digital infrastructure.

The project was announced in February, and the first facility at the campus is due to come online in 2027. Anthropic will lease capacity at the site, with Google acting as a backstop for the arrangement, and the campus is designed to support large-scale AI and high-performance computing workloads. At 480 MW of capacity, the Hawesville campus represents one of TeraWulf's largest commitments to date. Leo Kaid, president of Fluor's advanced technologies and life sciences business line, said earlier this month that Fluor is proud to expand its partnership with TeraWulf and support the delivery of infrastructure needed to meet rapidly growing demand for artificial intelligence and high-performance computing. He added that the company's integrated engineering, procurement and construction capabilities, combined with its data center expertise and skilled workforce, position it to deliver the project with a strong focus on safety, quality and schedule certainty.

The Hawesville development is one of several projects in TeraWulf's expanding portfolio, and the company currently operates a campus outside Buffalo, New York, located at a former coal power plant where it initially mined cryptocurrency at the 180-acre site before beginning to pivot the campus toward AI and HPC uses. Core42 and Fluidstack are live customers at the New York location, and in addition to its operating site and the Hawesville campus, TeraWulf is developing sites in Maryland and Kentucky and is planning a second development in Lansing, New York. The move away from cryptocurrency mining toward AI and HPC infrastructure reflects a broader strategic direction for the company. With the majority of structural steel for CB-1 staged and substantial deliveries for CB-2 complete, the project is positioned for continued above-ground construction activity in the coming months, and the first facility is expected to come online in 2027.

stories.Headline: ABC Corporation uses OpenAI's dots to manage a vinyl greenhouse in a two week trial
stories.Summary:
ABC Corporation, a company based in Nagoya's Nakamura ward, said its research and development division ran an experiment from November 1 to November 15, 2026, in which OpenAI's general-purpose AI agent "dots" served as the core system for managing a vinyl greenhouse used in protected cultivation. The company reported that the trial achieved stable management of the greenhouse. The work drew on procedures the company had built up while operating its own systems. The experiment covered sensing conditions inside the house, managing water, ventilation, liquid fertilizer and nutrient solution, and adjusting lighting according to the crop's growth stage.

The trial addressed six management items, namely temperature and humidity control, water management, rolling up the greenhouse vinyl for ventilation, continuous environmental monitoring, light source management that adjusts the timing and duration of illumination to match growth stages, and liquid fertilizer and nutrient solution management. In the experiment, an IoT box gathering several sensors inside the house was made available to dots, and cameras installed in the greenhouse acted as the agent's eyes. dots grasped conditions from the camera images as well as the sensor readings and made the judgments needed for facility management. The company confirmed that this setup could carry out its existing management procedures. Previously the company had implemented in-house the software framework, or harness, that combined the functions needed for daily management.

The company said that when AI is used in agriculture, one approach is to develop custom programs for each facility and use case, but it sees a problem in that priority tends to go to implementing the functions needed on site, leaving security questions, such as what information to give the AI and which equipment operations to entrust to it, pushed back. For this project it therefore concentrated the core of facility management in dots. When expanding to other greenhouses, it aims to set common rules for the information the AI handles and the scope of operations it performs, so that measures do not vary from facility to facility and a certain security level is secured. It also aims to turn the management methods cultivated in its own house into a form that can be applied to other vinyl greenhouses, and it will study management mechanisms usable according to each facility's equipment and operations.

ABC Corporation is located at 12-8 Tsubakicho, Nakamura ward, Nagoya, in Aichi prefecture, and its representative is Kina Oda. The company was founded in February 2021, has capital of 15 million yen, is unlisted, and lists information and communication as its industry. The experiment ran for about two weeks in early November 2026. The company said it will use the knowledge gained from the experiment to research management systems that can be adapted to the equipment and operation of individual facilities.

stories.Headline: Study Pocket launches AI simultaneous interpretation for schools in April 2027
stories.Summary:
Study Pocket Co., Ltd., a Tokyo-based company led by CEO Ryo Yamaji and CAIO Hiroyuki Tsuruta, announced on November 20, 2026 that it will officially offer its school-oriented web service "Study Pocket AI Simultaneous Interpretation" from April 2027, a tool that interprets conversations between teachers and children and students who need Japanese language instruction as well as parents with foreign roots. The service was first announced in May 2026 as "Study Pocket AI Interpreter" and was provided free of charge during the current fiscal year to teacher accounts of "Study Pocket for TEACHER," after which trial use continued at schools and municipalities that made inquiries. With the official launch the name changes to "Study Pocket AI Simultaneous Interpretation," and the pricing and timing that were undecided at the time of the announcement have now been set. The service runs in the browser of GIGA school devices without any dedicated equipment, and it supports bidirectional interpretation that displays the teacher's Japanese in the other person's language and the child's or parent's words in Japanese on the screen in real time.

The pricing is 50,000 yen per school per year, excluding tax, which covers all faculty and staff and up to five children needing Japanese instruction, with an additional 10,000 yen per year excluding tax for each person from the sixth child, and contracts are made per school and per fiscal year from April to the following March, with quotations and invoices available. The service supports 60 languages including Japanese, with Portuguese, Chinese, Filipino, English, Spanish, Vietnamese and Korean placed under frequently used languages, and it offers a face-to-face mode, full-screen display, adjustable text size, color coding by speaker, conversation records that can be reviewed later, AI summaries after a conversation and export in TXT or CSV formats. Speech recognition and interpretation use the Japan region of the voice AI Soniox, with audio sent directly from the device browser to Soniox, and schools decide the scope of use, as administrators assign children one by one from a roster. According to a May 2026 Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology survey, 84,759 children in public schools needed Japanese language instruction as of May 1, 2025, up 15,636, or 22.6 percent, from the previous survey, of whom 73,313 held foreign nationality and 11,446 held Japanese nationality, and 12,668 public schools, or 39.4 percent of all public schools, had at least one such child, while about 8,300 schools, roughly two thirds, had only one to four.

The company says it developed the service because such children are enrolled in small numbers across many schools and the languages used differ from school to school, making it difficult to station interpreters or native-language supporters at every school, so teachers often combine gestures and translation tools in class and meetings. A teacher at a public junior high school in the Chugoku and Shikoku area who used it during a three-way meeting with a parent from Vietnam said the parent tearfully told the teacher in her native language that she was truly grateful, and the teacher felt that feelings had gotten through beyond the language barrier. The company plans to hold a demonstration at its "StudyPocket Product Day 2026" online event on December 1, 2026 from 15:00 to 16:30, free with advance registration, showing the actual screen and plans for provision in fiscal 2027. Free trial use under this year's demonstration ends at the end of February 2027, and official provision begins in April 2027, with trial and demo requests handled individually.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave funds global datacenter expansion with massive debt backed by Nvidia chips
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave is expanding its global network of datacentres by taking on massive amounts of debt. Former crypto miners now run the company to sell raw compute power for artificial intelligence. The company currently operates a network of 52 datacentres located from Texas to Scotland. This expansion is happening during a period of high risk for the AI bubble. CoreWeave is now seen as a poster child for this increasingly risky business model.

The company owes 47 billion dollars, with 10 billion dollars due in 2026. It bled 709 million dollars last quarter while earning 3.6 billion dollars in total revenues. CoreWeave uses GPU-backed debt, borrowing nearly 25 billion dollars against Nvidia chips and customer contracts. It also issued unsecured senior notes and listed 18 different varieties of debt in an SEC filing. The company expects interest payments to exceed 1 billion dollars in the next quarter.

Jordan Chaflin of CreditSights said the infrastructure buildout is painful from a free cashflow perspective. He noted that this capital-intensive model is common for neoclouds and hyperscalers building for a theoretical economy. A CoreWeave spokesperson stated that customers are signing multiyear commitments for GPUs beyond their depreciable lives. The spokesperson added that the company is using a diverse funding strategy to lower debt costs. They claimed this strategy eliminates reliance on renewals to repay the debt in most cases.

Creditors previously estimated the risk of default at over 60 percent over the next five years. Short-sellers worry that the value of the chips will plummet faster than the six-year timeline suggested. The news website the Verge called the company an Eldritch horror with no obvious path to profitability. Major AI companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are affected because they rent this computational power. These frontier AI companies avoid the cost of building their own massive datacentres.

Nvidia owns about 11 percent of CoreWeave and provided finance for it to buy chips. Nvidia also agreed to a 6.3 billion dollar deal to buy compute that CoreWeave cannot sell. The chip maker further invested in clients like OpenAI and Anthropic to support the ecosystem. This circular arrangement allows Nvidia to improve its balance sheet while others provide the models. CoreWeave acts as the middle layer that takes on the financial risk for both parties.

The removal of Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang creates uncertainty for the scaffolding of the AI economy. Huang admitted to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy before he left the company. Analysts are now watching to see if the current demand for secondhand chips remains tight. It remains unclear how senior note holders would be repaid if the company goes belly-up. The long-term future of CoreWeave and the stability of the AI bubble remain unknown.

stories.Headline: MFour adds Google AI Mode to its consumer conversation feed and collects 2.8 million new AI conversations every 30 days
stories.Summary:
MFour Data Research, Inc., a provider of the largest mobile-app consumer panel in the U.S., announced on November 20, 2026, that it has added Google AI Mode to its AI conversation data feed. The Irvine, California, company said the addition means it now collects 2.8 million new consumer AI conversations every 30 days. Google AI Mode joins ChatGPT and Google Gemini in the feed, which MFour describes as the only platform connecting surveys and behaviors for full journey intelligence from prompt to purchase. The announcement builds on MFour's November 3 announcement that it had added Google Gemini, which expanded its collection from 2.35 million to 2.8 million new AI conversations every 30 days.

The addition gives clients greater scale and a broader view of how consumers use AI to research products and make decisions, according to the release. Google AI Mode lets consumers research products, compare brands and refine their choices through conversations within Google Search, and MFour connects those exchanges to the same consumers' subsequent behaviors. Brands and agencies can ask DANI, MFour's autonomous AI research analyst, to analyze AI conversations alongside connected behavioral and survey data and produce boardroom-ready reports. The AI conversation feed is also available for direct licensing, and MFour says the signals reveal what consumers are considering, what they do next and why.

Chris St. Hilaire, CEO of MFour Data Research, said a company cannot claim to understand its consumer if it is blind to the conversations shaping their decisions. He said customers are asking AI what to buy and which brands to trust, and that MFour connects those conversations to what they actually do next. He said this gives insights teams the power to walk into the boardroom with answers the business can act on, including what consumers want, what is winning their consideration and where to go next. MFour connects conversation data to the same consumer's demographics, web browsing, app usage, GPS-verified store visits, purchases and survey responses through a single identity.

MFour, founded in 2011, says its 14M+ consumer panel generates nine deterministic data streams all connected to a single identity, and that DANI provides analysis across 4 billion monthly buyer signals. The data comes from MFour's first-party panel, whose members opt in and are compensated for sharing their behavioral data and participating in surveys. The company says it is trusted by Samsung, Google, Amazon Ads, Microsoft, Hulu, Keurig Dr Pepper, Papa Johns and hundreds of other global brands. The release offers one free LLM insights report through MFour's website by providing DANI simple guidance on the insights being sought.

stories.Headline: Walmart launches a $120 Sam's Club Plus and Walmart+ bundle as Sparky lifts basket sizes 40 percent
stories.Summary:
Walmart launched a combined membership for Sam's Club Plus and Walmart+ on October 20, 2026, to attract busy households. Chief executive John Furner announced the bundle as a way to create the most essential membership in the United States. The company is also utilizing Sparky, an AI shopping assistant that debuted in June 2025, to increase customer spending. This digital tool operates in French, Spanish, and English across Canada, Mexico, and the United States.

The new bundle costs $120 per year, which is a significant reduction from the $400 cost for separate memberships. Existing Walmart+ members who pay $90 can upgrade to this plan, while Sam's Club Plus members are able to link their accounts. The strategy has already brought in a couple of million new customers for Sam's Club. Third quarter results ended October 31, 2026, showing revenue of $188.8 billion and adjusted earnings per share of $0.65.

John Furner stated that the company is focusing on services rather than just price to drive growth. He explained that Sparky helps families save time by providing recipes and one click ordering for ingredients. Furner noted that the consumer remains resilient and consistent, particularly among higher income households over the last few years. He also mentioned that the company can now reach 96 percent of the U.S. population with three hour delivery.

The company reported that U.S. usage of Sparky rose 129 percent year over year, with users filling baskets 40 percent larger. Walmart raised its full year adjusted earnings per share guidance to between $2.84 and $2.89. However, Sam's Club operating income fell 15.8 percent because part of the membership fees are now allocated to Walmart U.S. The upcoming holiday quarter will test if these memberships and AI tools successfully increase shopper loyalty.

stories.Headline: Ondas, Palantir and Regna AI convene defense leaders to speed AI into the field
stories.Summary:
Ondas Inc., Palantir Technologies Inc. and Regna AI co-hosted the Ondas Defense Technology Summit, a small, invitation-only executive session, on November 18 in Las Vegas. Ondas shared highlights from the summit in a press release dated November 20, 2026, issued from West Palm Beach, Florida and Miami, Florida. Executives and leaders from Ondas, Palantir, Regna AI and Aston Martin Performance Technologies attended, along with other defense technology and AI innovators and industry experts. The day opened with remarks from Ryan Hartman, President and Chief Executive Officer of Ondas Sentinel and Interim Chief Executive Officer of Regna AI. Palantir followed with a demonstration and presentation on sovereign AI for mission-critical operations.

The summit is one of the first activations of Ondas' Global Partner relationship with Aston Martin Aramco Formula One Team, announced as the "Speed to Decision" partnership. The partnership is a multi-year global partnership in the autonomous systems sector that extends through 2029. The Las Vegas Grand Prix will showcase Ondas through brand visibility, engineering collaboration and stakeholder engagement. Four panels covered autonomy in the air and at sea and where unmanned systems go next, investing in defense tech, how industry and the Department of Defense partner to deliver, and defense tech capital markets and mergers and acquisitions. Bob Bell, Business Development Consultant at Aston Martin Performance Technologies, led the session on Manufacturing and Supply Chains for Defense.

Eric Brock, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Ondas Inc., said defense technology is attracting growing demand and investment, and capital is following companies that can pair AI and autonomy with the ability to manufacture at scale. Brock said convening leaders from technology, defense and capital markets with Palantir and Regna AI reflects how Ondas is positioning itself at the center of that shift, turning innovation into fielded capability and creating long-term value for stockholders. Elias Davis, Office of the CEO at Palantir Technologies, said the companies are helping defense partners deploy sovereign AI on their own terms, with control over their data and operations. Davis said co-hosting the summit with Ondas and Regna AI reflects a deep and expanding partnership. Ryan Hartman said bringing the leaders into one room let them focus on how AI is changing the mission and what it will take to get capability into the field sooner.

Hartman said that across the demo and the panels the message was consistent: AI and autonomy only matter if operators can trust them, control them and rely on them. Hartman said that is where industry and government have to keep working side by side. The day closed with Q&A and closing remarks from Hartman. The focused, executive-level format allowed for candid conversations about AI across defense missions, including sovereign AI. The summit reflects Ondas' strategy of bringing together the software, autonomous platforms and production capability that modern warfare requires.

Ondas Inc. (NASDAQ:ONDS) describes itself as a leading provider of advanced autonomous systems and next-generation defense and security technologies. Ondas develops and deploys integrated unmanned and autonomous platforms across air, ground and stratospheric environments, including autonomous drone systems, counter-UAS technologies, robotic ground systems, advanced unmanned aircraft and propulsion solutions, demining and engineering systems, and integrated sensing and communications technologies. Ondas' solutions are deployed globally by government, defense and commercial customers to protect infrastructure, borders, transportation networks, personnel and strategic assets. Regna AI says it is building the sovereign AI layer for defense, putting mission intelligence under the customer's command through specialized AI models that governments and defense organizations can own, control and deploy wherever the mission demands. Formula One is one of the most technology-driven sports in the world, and the engineering, data and rapid manufacturing developed for the track are increasingly being applied in other industries.

stories.Headline: Cipher Digital ranks sixth among most overvalued AI stocks as short interest hits 18 percent
stories.Summary:
Cipher Digital Inc., which trades on Nasdaq under the ticker CIFR, ranked sixth on a list of the ten most overvalued AI stocks according to short sellers, published by Insider Monkey and reported by Yahoo Finance on November 21, 2026. The company's shares had lost more than half of their market value during 2026, as investors grew wary of its aggressive AI data center expansion, its financing needs and its valuation. Short interest in the stock had risen to 18 percent, reflecting bets that the company may struggle to deliver the earnings and cash flow needed to justify its premium valuation. The article frames the central issue as Cipher's ability to complete its transition from Bitcoin mining to AI and high-performance computing infrastructure and to generate sustainable cash flow from that business.

The company's net debt stood at approximately $3.08 billion as of September, a significant burden for a business still scaling its HPC operations, and the article notes concerns that debt-servicing costs and future financing needs will weigh on shareholder returns. Cipher recognized its first HPC lease revenue of $5.85 million in the third quarter of 2026, after rent commenced at its Black Pearl facility, which the article says shows the transition remains relatively early. The company has secured long-term agreements carrying $9.1 billion in contracted revenue, which the article cautions should not be confused with immediate cash flow or guaranteed profits. The stock trades at approximately 18.24 times sales, a valuation the article says leaves little room for execution setbacks, and the company could also come under pressure if data center construction takes longer than expected.

The article places Cipher within a broad market sell-off driven by renewed concerns about elevated AI valuations and uncertainty over whether the huge capital committed to AI infrastructure will generate sufficient returns. It reports that the rout wiped out about $3 trillion in S&P 500 market capitalization in early November, as the Nasdaq recorded its largest single-day decline in 19 months. Michael Burry raised concerns that AI infrastructure companies could be relying on increasingly complicated financing arrangements that may become unsustainable, while RSM chief economist Joe Brusuelas was wary of a wholesale bursting of the AI bubble as uncertainty surrounding Nvidia undermined confidence among lenders and investors. Barclays chief market strategist Julien Lafargue warned that the sell-off was exposing the growing cost of financing AI infrastructure, and Goldman Sachs strategists warned that the outlook for AI investment and corporate profit margins in 2028 and beyond remains highly uncertain. Anthropic's IPO raised $81 billion but failed to reverse the broader weakness in AI-related stocks, while Morgan Stanley argued the November sell-off was excessive and presented a buying opportunity.

stories.Headline: Baltimore Sun replaces dismissed cartoonist with AI images on opinion pages
stories.Summary:
The Baltimore Sun began publishing AI-generated illustrations on its opinion pages after dismissing its longtime cartoonist, Kevin “KAL” Kallaugher, a two-time Pulitzer Prize finalist, and the paper initially ran syndicated cartoons before introducing the generated images. In one example, the image’s own caption disclosed that it had been made using AI tools by the newspaper’s editorial staff, which made the production method clear but did little to settle the dispute over whether the work belonged in a space traditionally associated with an individual artist’s judgement and craft. Kallaugher told Baltimore Fishbowl that the repeated appearance of generated images made the practice seem like an ongoing editorial policy rather than an isolated experiment, and he described it as a case of AI taking people’s jobs while distinguishing between using technology to gather visual references and asking an image generator to produce the finished work.

The Association of American Editorial Cartoonists condemned the Sun’s decision in an open letter, arguing that replacing a human cartoonist with generated imagery diminishes the work of artists and weakens journalism, and the organisation invoked the paper’s history of publishing Kallaugher, whom it described as an internationally acclaimed cartoonist, while urging editors to reject AI for cartoons and other creative content. FAIR’s account describes the Sun’s images as relying on generic figures and explanatory text rather than visual wit or concise satire, so the dispute is not simply about whether an image has been labelled as AI-generated but also about whether automated illustrations can offer the interpretation and originality expected of editorial cartooning. Questions of attribution have become sharper as image generators have produced cartoons carrying signatures associated with real New Yorker contributors, and Nieman Journalism Lab reported on examples bearing artists’ names, including work that the cartoonists said they had neither made nor endorsed, while cautioning that imitation of an artist’s style does not by itself establish copyright infringement.

A report by Cartooning for Peace recommends stronger ways to identify and trace cartoons, greater transparency about the material used to train image generators, and an explicit opt-in approach to including copyrighted work in training databases, and it also calls for mechanisms to address economic or moral harm caused by unauthorised use. FAIR’s account cites AI-written or AI-assisted material across opinion writing and news production, including the Financial Times’ apology after an undisclosed AI process was used to condense a column, and Columbia Journalism Review has separately documented newsroom cuts at McClatchy and journalists’ concerns about the company’s use of automation. The review reported that more than 90 unionised media workers across 17 publications were laid off in September 2026, while noting that a direct link between those cuts and AI plans had not been established, and journalists told the review that AI was being used for some repackaging and content-production tasks amid uncertainty about future policy and the effect of staff losses on coverage.

The immediate controversy is about editorial cartoons, but the underlying question is wider, namely whether publishers will treat AI as a disclosed tool that supports journalism or as a substitute for the people whose judgement, experience and creativity give it value. The professional and policy responses call for transparency and protection for artists, and the challenge for news organisations is to show readers where automation is used without obscuring who is responsible for the work.

stories.Headline: Thinking Machines Lab releases Inkling 2 Mini open-weight model for smaller hardware
stories.Summary:
Thinking Machines Lab released the Inkling 2 Mini on November 21, 2026, as an open-weight looped transformer. This model features 26.4 billion total parameters and utilizes a sparse Mixture-of-Experts architecture. It is designed to process both text and images while returning only text responses. The system reuses its middle layers three times per token to maintain efficiency.

The model requires a 32GB Mac with Apple silicon, one NVIDIA DGX Spark, or GPUs with at least 32GB of VRAM. It keeps the checkpoint near 20GB, allowing it to run on smaller hardware for agentic coding and document work. The architecture includes 24 layers grouped into four blocks, where the two middle blocks share weights. It supports a context window of up to 1 million tokens and is available under the Apache 2.0 license.

Thinking Machines stated that looping the middle layers provided a compute-equivalent gain between 1.51x and 1.91x. They reported that the model is strongest in agentic coding, scoring 79.2 percent on SWE-bench Verified. However, the developers admitted the model has weaker knowledge recall and struggles with multi-turn instruction following. They noted that the model tied with Qwen3.8-27B on the Artificial Analysis Index with a score of 20.1.

This release follows the Inkling 2 Small, which is a 594 billion parameter model launched on November 5. The Mini version is now available on Hugging Face, with fine-tuning and hosted inference provided through Tinker. It also offers GGUF builds via llama.cpp and Unsloth for developers. The company claims the model achieves higher intelligence per watt than competing models from Google and Alibaba.

stories.Headline: Taiwan regulators limit short selling to stabilize chip-heavy markets
stories.Summary:
Taiwanese financial regulators took drastic emergency steps on Saturday, November 21, 2026, to stabilize their chip-heavy markets. These actions followed an intense sell-off in artificial intelligence and technology stocks that rattled global investors. The main trading index in Taiwan, which relies heavily on semiconductor stocks, dropped 17.5 percent over five trading days. This local crash occurred as the Dow and S&P 500 entered correction territory by falling 10 percent.

The Financial Supervisory Commission of Taiwan announced that it would limit short selling starting on Monday. These new rules include a complete ban on short selling any stock below its closing price. However, the regulators stated that securities firms and futures companies may still borrow for hedging purposes. This intervention aims to stop the significant fluctuations currently impacting the Taiwan stock market. Such restrictions may force investors to sell long positions to raise necessary cash.

The Financial Supervisory Commission said these measures were a direct response to recent market volatility. Investor Michael Burry noted on X that he had previously warned about neoclouds and chip makers. He specifically mentioned companies like Nvidia, Coreweave, and Nebius while providing information for those who wanted to sell. Burry did not explicitly tell people to short the market, but he highlighted the risks. Some market professionals now believe the artificial intelligence trade has reached a turning point.

This situation mirrors a 2008 event when the United States Securities and Exchange Commission banned short selling for financial stocks. Former SEC Chairman Christopher Cox stated at that time that such measures should not be necessary in well-functioning markets. The American intervention during the housing market collapse largely failed to stop the decline of those stocks. Current headwinds are now reshaping the outlook for the global technology sector. Investors remain cautious as the AI bubble potentially deflates across multiple international exchanges.

stories.Headline: Writer disables all Galaxy AI features for a week and misses only two
stories.Summary:
Shimul Sood, a writer for MakeUseOf, published an article on November 21, 2026, describing a week-long experiment in which she turned off every Galaxy AI feature on her Samsung phone running One UI 9. She undertook the test after hearing chatter that Samsung might someday put some Galaxy AI features behind a paywall, although Samsung has not officially confirmed anything of that kind. She said she had been using a Samsung phone for months and could not immediately say which AI features she would be willing to pay for. Rather than guessing which features she could live without, she disabled all of them and went about her usual routine for an entire week. By the end, she found she wanted to turn only two features back on, and she said neither had anything to do with One UI 9 itself.

The two features she missed were Circle to Search, which she noted is technically a Google feature also available on Samsung phones rather than something Samsung built for Galaxy AI, and Object Eraser, an existing Galaxy AI tool in Samsung's Gallery app. She said Circle to Search proved useful on Pinterest, where she looks for home decor and interior design inspiration, because images often carry no product link and the feature let her circle a lamp or coffee table and find the item or similar alternatives. She said several of her furniture purchases began with a random picture she found on Pinterest, and that going back to manual searching felt unnecessarily tedious. Object Eraser, she wrote, let her remove unwanted elements from photos in the Gallery app instead of discarding a picture or using a third-party editing app, and while results were not always perfect with complicated backgrounds, it handled her usual fixes convincingly.

Sood stressed that the experiment was not a criticism of One UI 9 or of how Samsung has implemented AI across its smartphones, but rather a reflection of how she personally uses her phone. She wrote that she enjoys trying new AI features when they arrive, but very few become part of her routine, and she would rather have a handful of well-thought-out features than a whole suite of tools she tries once and forgets. She also said that what she missed during the week was not necessarily the AI itself but the convenience she had grown accustomed to. Once the week ended, she was in no rush to turn everything back on, and her device felt just as capable without most of its AI features.

She concluded that if Samsung ever decides to charge for Galaxy AI, she at least knows where she stands, and that it would take a lot more than a growing list of AI features to convince her to open her wallet. The article does not say that Samsung has announced any pricing, timeline or other change to Galaxy AI, and it gives no further details on what happens next beyond her own intention to keep most features off.

stories.Headline: GlobalWafers ramps new 12 inch fabs in Texas, Italy and Japan as retail investors watch
stories.Summary:
Retail investors began watching GlobalWafers after panic selling hit Nvidia and other AI leaders on November 21, 2026. This market shift followed the exit of Jensen Huang, which turned previous excitement into doubt for many investors. The company provides silicon wafers to chip manufacturers and offers upstream exposure to data center and AI demand. GlobalWafers operates across the Americas, Europe, Northeast Asia, and other Asian regions to serve its global customers. It currently holds a market capitalization of NT$233.2 billion according to the provided financial data.

The company generates NT$58.4 billion from its Semiconductor Business Group and NT$0.2 billion from its Renewable Energy operations. It is currently moving its global capacity buildout from construction into qualification and ramp at new 12 inch fabs. These new facilities are located in Texas, Italy, and Japan to expand the company's overall production capabilities. Phase 1 tool installation is nearly complete in Texas, while the Italy line has achieved automotive grade certification. The facility in Utsunomiya, Japan, has already turned profitable and is currently operating with high utilization.

Analysts from Simply Wall St are responsible for the narrative regarding the company's global expansion and earnings potential. They stated that the company is transitioning its capacity buildout into the qualification and ramp phase for new fabs. These analysts link the company's cost base and earnings potential to its strategic expansion in three different countries. They believe the current progress in Texas, Italy, and Japan supports the company's growth in the semiconductor market. The report suggests that these developments are core threads linking the company's global capacity and future success.

The report notes that retail investors are watching the stock as a potential opportunity after recent market pullbacks. These investors are affected by the broader volatility in AI chip stocks following the leadership change at Nvidia. The analysis suggests that solid businesses can move from being crowded to ignored when market expectations reset. Some investors may see the current weakness as a signal of mispricing rather than permanent damage to the business. The text indicates that these investors are seeking established leaders in the AI and semiconductor sectors.

GlobalWafers is described as a large and profitable wafer producer tied into broader semiconductor spending and AI demand. The company's business model relies on supplying the essential silicon wafers needed by chip manufacturers worldwide. It has diversified its sales across multiple continents to mitigate risks and capture various regional market opportunities. The company's current financial standing includes significant revenue from its primary semiconductor business group. This background positions the firm as a key upstream player in the global AI hardware supply chain.

The company will continue the ramp of its new 12 inch fabs in Texas, Italy, and Japan. Future success depends on how quickly these new lines fill and the pricing the company can achieve. The articles leave open whether unseen pressures will change the speed of utilization for these new facilities. It remains unclear how the wafer mix and subsidies will reshape the company's long term financial story. Investors must wait to see if the current ramp speed leads to lasting profitability and margin growth.

stories.Headline: Benton Harbor approves City Detect AI system to scan for code violations
stories.Summary:
Benton Harbor City Commissioners approved a contract at their regular meeting this past week that will allow the city to use a more automated method of detecting code violations citywide, according to News/Talk/Sports 94.9 WSJM. The service, called City Detect, is offered to municipalities and uses vehicle-mounted cameras and artificial intelligence to spot things like building violations and illegal dumping. The department of public safety says the camera would be mounted on a city code compliance truck to conduct inspections. Commissioners amended the resolution approving the contract by adding a requirement that the Public Safety Committee receive regular reports on the program's results, and it was then approved five to three with Mayor Marcus Muhammad not present.

The contract will cost $55,000 per year and will be paid with Community Development Block Grant funds, and commissioners will be asked to renew it yearly. Public Safety told commissioners that City Detect conducted a demonstration for the inspection department, scanning 896 parcels in just a half hour and identifying issues like tall grass, sidewalk problems, boarded up windows, and trash. City Manager Alex Little said the city is not in a position to hire enough people to handle all these inspections, but technology like City Detect can help. Commissioner Sharon Henderson said the city's inspection department will only use City Detect as a first step when issuing potential citations, and that staff get a photograph and review the information rather than writing a ticket immediately.

Commissioner Juanita Henry took issue with the program, saying residents should not be burdened with surprise tickets and little human oversight, and she said she knows AI can do a lot of things but does not think this will work out well for residents because there is no human in it. Henderson said inspectors are still looking at what has been sent to them to make sure, and are not just giving people a ticket based on the system. Henry also said it is all about policy. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the yearly renewal request and the regular reports to the Public Safety Committee.

stories.Headline: Apple adds non-AI features to iOS 27 including better AutoMix and Find My redesign
stories.Summary:
Apple released iOS 27 in September 2026, and while the new Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features drew most of the attention, the update also brought a long list of non-AI changes that 9to5Mac editor Chance Miller highlighted in a piece published on November 21, 2026. In the Music app, Apple updated AutoMix with new transitions that Miller described as noticeably better and more immersive than the version that launched in iOS 26. The Photos app now offers full-resolution sharing in iCloud Shared Albums, and it also lets users save a specific video frame as a photo without taking a manual screenshot. The Clock app gained an independent alarm volume option found in Settings under Sounds & Haptics, so alarms and timers no longer have to match the ringtone volume.

The Home Screen adds an all-new extra-large widget size, including full-screen widgets for apps like Music, Photos, Weather and Calendar, and users can now swipe away the Now Playing widget from the Lock Screen. On the Lock Screen, the clock can be moved to the top widget row so it no longer covers the wallpaper. The Apple Pay checkout flow was significantly overhauled to make switching between payment cards easier, and landscape support arrived in more apps, including Music, Reminders and Weather. The Find My app has a new design with more flexible sharing options that show more specific location information without tapping on a specific person, and a built-in paste shortcut now appears above the keyboard in the next text field after something is copied. CarPlay also gained an audio scrubber for skipping to different parts of a song or podcast on the car's display.

Miller, the editor-in-chief of 9to5Mac who also hosts the site's Daily and Happy Hour podcasts, wrote that he had come to really enjoy these features and called the landscape support great as someone who keeps his iPhone docked at his desk all day. He said he was a big fan of the initial AutoMix in iOS 26 and finds the new transitions better, and he singled out the Find My redesign for showing more specific location information without extra taps. He closed by asking readers to share their own favorite non-AI features in the comments. The article does not say what happens next beyond that invitation.

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike discusses acquiring Zscaler to expand AI-powered cybersecurity defenses
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. is in talks to acquire Zscaler Inc. according to a Bloomberg report on Friday, November 21, 2026. This potential combination would be one of the largest deals in the cybersecurity industry. The two companies are discussing a deal that could come together soon. This move follows a wave of multibillion-dollar takeovers in the security market. These companies are racing to expand defenses against sophisticated attacks powered by artificial intelligence.

The deal involves Austin, Texas-based CrowdStrike and Santa Clara, California-based Zscaler in the 244 billion dollar security market. Zscaler had a market value of 32 billion dollars at the end of regular trading Friday. CrowdStrike has a market capitalization of around 235 billion dollars. Zscaler reached record revenue of 3.35 billion dollars in fiscal 2026 but has not turned an annual profit since 2018. Zscaler serves 11,000 customers in over 185 countries, including more than half of the Fortune 500.

People familiar with the matter said deliberations are ongoing and a transaction is not certain. These sources asked not to be identified because the information is confidential. Representatives for CrowdStrike and Zscaler did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The report caused Zscaler shares to rise about 16 percent after the close of trading. The deal would allow CrowdStrike to monitor threats across more parts of a company's technology infrastructure.

Cloudflare co-founder Matthew Prince said in June that AI agent traffic surpassed human internet traffic for the first time. Businesses are grappling with risks from AI-enabled attacks, benefiting providers like Palo Alto Networks Inc. and Cloudflare Inc. Zscaler's cloud-based products replace traditional VPNs from companies like Citrix and Ivanti Inc. that suspected Chinese hackers have targeted. The "SaaSpocalypse" fear suggests AI tools could allow competitors to recreate software services more cheaply. This threatens the business models of established providers.

CrowdStrike's Falcon product had a botched software update in 2024 that triggered a global IT meltdown. Alphabet Inc. bought Wiz for 32 billion dollars last year, and ServiceNow Inc. bought Armis for 7.75 billion dollars in December. Palo Alto Networks took over CyberArk for 25 billion dollars in February and bought Applied Compute for 4.5 billion dollars this month. Recent US outages affected Microsoft Corp., JPMorgan Chase & Co., United Airlines, and the National Security Agency. Gartner Inc. projects global information security spending will grow nearly 12 percent this year.

The companies will determine if these ongoing deliberations result in a final transaction. A combination would give CrowdStrike a broader role in defending corporate networks and applications. The deal would accelerate a shift toward fewer companies protecting more of the world's computers. The articles do not state when a final decision will be reached. stories.Headline: Luca Guadagnino says Altman has guns as Artificial opens Christmas Day
stories.Summary:
Neon is releasing Luca Guadagnino's film Artificial, about OpenAI co-founders Sam Altman, Ilya Sutskever and Elon Musk, on Christmas Day, 2026. The film premiered at the New York Film Festival and the BFI London Film Fest before its theatrical release. Deadline published its Crew Call podcast interview with Guadagnino on November 21, 2026. The film stars Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman, Monica Barbaro as Mira Murati and Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever. Artificial currently holds a 95% fresh rating on Rotten Tomatoes.

The film opens limited on Christmas Day, a date Deadline calls perfect for a sophisticated adult skewing awards contender. Amazon MGM Studios originally backed the movie but exited out of fear of OpenAI, because Amazon has a $50 billion investment in the Altman non-profit. CAA screened the project for Neon, which Guadagnino says was first and front and center in its passion to take over. The Simon Rich script was shot outside Altman's house in San Francisco. Dario Amodei's Anthropic went public earlier this week creating a $1.18 trillion company, with shares falling from a $111 day-of-market price to $88.91 EOD Friday.

Altman told the Vanity Fair podcast he "did not" coerce Amazon to drop Artificial, adding "I don't know anyone else who did" and "I didn't speak to Jeff Bezos." Altman said he felt like he was in a weird glitch or a simulation when he saw Garfield dressed exactly like him with the same backpack, and emphasized that Garfield "did walk like me." Altman said of the trailer, "I don't think they're going for accuracy," and called the bunker loaded with guns "an example of an inaccuracy," saying "There's no bunker with firearms on the wall." Altman admitted "I have a survivalist mindset" but said "I don't have a setup that is depicted in that trailer." Guadagnino told Deadline, "I have validated the validating information that has been vetted: He does have guns."

Guadagnino said "We were very careful that everything that was in the movie had to be approved legally," and that "the truth in this case is more extraordinary than any fiction." On Amazon exiting, Guadagnino said "I was cool because I like disruptions, very much," and called the decision to let the movie find another home "truly honorable." Guadagnino said of speculation that no studio wanted the movie, "I like to think that there was the need (by the media) to fill blank pages with nothing." On AI as a doomsday threat, Guadagnino told Deadline, "I don't have trust and I don't have faith in humans." Guadagnino's suspicions stem from growing up during the Cold War, and he remembers "very well in 1985 when Chernobyl happened."

Deadline contrasts Artificial with Sony's recent theatrical release The Social Reckoning, which it says arguably didn't resonate with the current tech era. Deadline notes the film arrives as people fear the technology will end us, whether in regards to existence or financial livelihoods. Deadline says there has been zero ill will from Altman or OpenAI about the film, unlike the Facebook camp when The Social Network was released in 2010. Deadline cites concerns about AI including a Chatbot being at the center of 16-year old Adam Raine's suicide, and AI trespassing and impostering another company's security space. The Crew Call episode also covers why Andrew Garfield was right to play Altman and Altman's sincerity about creating guardrails for the technology.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: Economists warn of an AI bubble after Anthropic IPO triggers market volatility
stories.Summary:
The company Anthropic finalized a blockbuster initial public offering on Wednesday, November 19, 2026, which rapidly pushed its valuation to 1.5 trillion dollars. This unprecedented growth has caused economists to worry that the artificial intelligence sector is currently a massive bubble. Investors are increasingly concerned that the trillions of dollars spent on this technology will not provide a return in the near future. These fears were heightened when the Nasdaq fell by 3.7 percent after Anthropic stock tumbled by 12 percent.

This volatile environment requires investors to prepare for a potential economic downturn or a dramatic market retrenchment. Google recently saw its market capitalization drop by half a trillion dollars in one day because AI search features hindered traditional advertising revenue. Some estimates suggest that companies are spending as much as 800 billion dollars every year on AI infrastructure. Meanwhile, SpaceX rebranded as an AI company and predicted annual revenues of 1 trillion dollars by 2030, with future sales potentially reaching 26.5 trillion dollars.

Gary Gensler, an MIT economist and former head of the US Securities and Exchange Commission, stated that the industry is already a bubble. He warned that history shows new technologies eventually plateau after significant investment, suggesting that people should prepare for stormy weather. David B. Yoffie, a professor at Harvard Business School, noted that no company in history has grown so large so quickly. He added that the expectations for continued rapid growth will likely be off the charts.

The market is struggling because corporate customers are rattled by the exorbitant costs of using frontier coding tools. One company reportedly spent 500 million dollars on Claude tokens in a single month, leading many businesses to adopt cheaper Chinese models. This shift toward hybrid spending occurs as AI errors continue to erase productivity gains in the workplace. Experts remain uncertain whether the eventual correction will be a soft recession or a more dramatic collapse.

stories.Headline: One engineer runs an AI podcast network producing over 300 sports shows daily for about 5 cents
stories.Summary:
Beatline Sports, an AI-generated podcast network, launched in August and began flooding the market with daily episodes covering dozens of professional and college teams, but the shows drew little attention until their heavy use of keywords gave them traction on Apple and Spotify's search functions in November 2026, according to a Boston.com column by Chad Finn. The podcasts are hosted by AI voices trained on basic facts about a given team, and the network's graphics look suspiciously like those of the Locked On Podcast Network. A New York-based engineer named Ibnul Jaif Farabi claimed on X.com that Beatline Sports is his creation, writing that one person is producing more than 300 sports podcasts daily using custom models and agents running on CPU only. Finn listened to part of a Friday Patriots episode hosted by voices called Monica and Frank, and he wrote that the product is so lousy that even intentional promotion would not help it.

The network's output requires no human hosts, as the episodes are described as an AI reading of a script of keywords about a real team rather than an actual conversation. Farabi wrote that the whole operation costs him about 5 cents daily, a figure Finn responded to by suggesting Farabi is getting robbed. Finn noted that on a phony Jets podcast, edge rusher Will McDonald IV was referred to as Will McDonald Four, and he said he hoped for something similarly unintentionally funny on the Patriots episode but found no such luck. In the snippet Finn quoted, Monica said the offense was completely suffocated against Detroit and asked whether the team is competitive or just surviving on momentum and hope, while Frank said he felt cautious after a 35-10 loss to the Lions and that without Drake Maye at full health the ceiling is lower than most people will want to admit.

Farabi is the person responsible for the network, and in his X.com post he told doubters to question their profession and said the choice is to compete or perish. Finn wrote that the podcasts entirely miss why people enjoy podcasts in the first place, which he described as hearing a conversation with knowledgeable and often humorous people listeners enjoy spending time with. He added that Monica and Frank will never make listeners wish they were part of the conversation because it is not a conversation at all. Finn wrote that he worries about what happens when AI-generated content starts to look decent and people can no longer tell what is authentic, though he said these Beatline pods are fortunately not that.

In separate media news, a Deadline report cited in the column said ESPN and ESPN2 dropped from 61 million pay-TV subscribers in 2025 to 54 million this year, down from a peak of more than 100 million fifteen years ago. Finn attributed the decline mostly to pay-TV subscriber losses across the board rather than to programming decisions. He also answered a reader question about Boston sports radio shows discussing the Celtics, ranking WEEI's Jones and Keefe and The Sports Hub's Zolak and Bertrand as the top two midday shows and Felger and Mazz at the bottom.

stories.Headline: Nvidia researchers argue huge context windows are often overkill and costly
stories.Summary:
Nvidia researchers have argued that the enormous context windows now common in large language models are often a dead end, because processing entire novels at once is frequently overkill and expensive for the tasks involved. In many of their tests, periodic summaries combined with targeted lookups performed about as well as holding everything in view at once. A model's context window is its working memory, covering everything it holds in view when generating a reply, and that window has grown rapidly over the past few years. GPT-4 launched in March 2023 with 8,192 tokens, while GPT 5.6 Sol today handles around one million tokens, about 120 times as much and enough for Tolstoy's "War and Peace." The research argues that the cost of very large context windows is not always justified by the results, since cheaper approaches such as periodic summaries and targeted lookups worked about as well in many tests.

The comparison the article gives is between GPT-4's 8,192 tokens at launch in March 2023 and GPT 5.6 Sol's roughly one million tokens today, a difference of about 120 times. That larger window is enough to hold Tolstoy's "War and Peace" in view at once, which the researchers say is often overkill. The article does not say what the researchers propose beyond periodic summaries and targeted lookups. The Nvidia research team is responsible for the argument, and the article reports their view that huge context windows are often overkill and expensive rather than describing a product or a policy change. The article does not name individual researchers or give direct statements from them beyond the team's position.

It also does not say when the research was published or where, beyond the date of the article itself, 2026-11-21. No company has announced a change in response, according to the article. The context for the argument is the rapid growth of context windows across the industry, from GPT-4's 8,192 tokens in March 2023 to GPT 5.6 Sol's around one million tokens today. The article does not say what happens next, whether Nvidia will change its own models, or how other companies responded to the research. It also does not say whether the tests covered specific tasks or models beyond what is described.

stories.Headline: UNESCO and the EU launch training for 18,000 Nigerian teachers in digital pedagogy and AI
stories.Summary:
UNESCO and the European Union, working with the Government of Katsina State, launched a training program for 18,000 teachers on November 10, 2026. This initiative focuses on digital pedagogy and the responsible use of artificial intelligence to improve teaching and learning across Nigeria. The national flag-off ceremony took place in Katsina State and included various education stakeholders and traditional leaders. Training activities began on November 10 and will continue through the end of November 2026.

The program requires teachers in Adamawa, Bayelsa, Enugu, Katsina, Oyo, and Plateau states to develop practical digital competencies. It utilizes 13 training modules that were developed after an assessment of more than 10,000 teachers. These modules teach educators how to use technology for lesson preparation, the creation of learning materials, and student assessment. This effort is part of the second phase of the Education and Youth Empowerment Initiative in Nigeria, which is funded by the European Union.

UNESCO Representative Dr. Isaías Barreto da Rosa stated that technology should support teachers and learners without replacing human relationships. Governor Malam Dikko Umaru Radda, represented by Commissioner Yusuf Sulaiman Jibia, noted that these digital tools improve instructional delivery and learner engagement. Ambassador Gautier Mignot of the European Union reaffirmed a commitment to helping Nigeria prepare its education sector for the digital age. These leaders emphasized that professional judgment and empathy remain essential to the learning process.

The initiative adopts an inclusive and ethical approach to ensure that digital transformation does not increase existing inequalities. By strengthening teacher resilience and capacity, the program aims to improve the overall quality of education in Nigeria. Participating teachers are encouraged to apply their new knowledge directly within their classrooms to boost productivity. Stakeholders are now urged to maintain consistent monitoring and evaluation of the program to ensure its long-term success.

stories.Headline: Physician-author argues AI should assist transplant teams rather than decide organ allocation
stories.Summary:
The CBS legal drama Cupertino, in its sixth episode titled "Harper," turned its lens to artificial intelligence and life-or-death medical allocation. In the episode, Harper Gervin, 27, the roommate of Price, Siffre & Associates manager Christy Palladino, lost her long-awaited liver transplant to Albert Ensler, a wealthy venture capitalist, just before surgery. With the organ viable for four hours and Michael Price, Olivia Siffre, and Judge Hornstein stranded in U.S. 101 traffic, they litigated by video. Assuming AI bias disadvantaged Harper, the attorneys learned that the allocation algorithm selected her, but a hospital physician-executive overrode it after Ensler's foundation offered a cancer-research donation. Christy exposed the quid pro quo, restored Harper's claim, and revealed that human corruption poses a greater danger than AI bias.

The article's author, Arthur Lazarus, a physician-author, noted that the television producers decided not to credit his novel Transplant, which examined the nefarious side of transplant allocation. He wrote that in real-world transplant settings, AI has shown more promise than harm as a decision-support tool, though many proposed applications still require prospective clinical validation. Transplant waitlists have long relied on mathematical formulas, such as the Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score, adopted for U.S. liver allocation in 2002, to estimate medical urgency and prioritize candidates. MELD is a statistical risk score, not an autonomous AI, and its current adult version, MELD 3.0, was implemented in 2023 to address disadvantages faced by women. The U.S. transplant system is transitioning toward continuous distribution models that replace rigid allocation categories with weighted point systems, and lung allocation adopted this framework in 2023.

Lazarus wrote that continuous distribution is a policy framework, not inherently an AI system, and that national allocation policies also consider factors such as blood type compatibility and distance from the donor hospital. He stated that modern machine-learning models can analyze vast amounts of complex clinical data to uncover patterns that traditional equations or human committees might miss. Researchers are also developing deep-learning tools to help organ procurement organizations identify hard-to-place organs, such as kidneys, early, so they can be considered for accelerated placement, an approach that could speed placement and reduce organ discard rates. An experimental multi-agent AI system, where separate large language model agents simulate the perspectives of a transplant surgeon, hepatologist, cardiologist, and social worker, achieved approximately 92 percent accuracy in predicting one-year post-transplant survival and 98 percent in identifying contraindications in a retrospective proof-of-concept study. The study combined real transplant-recipient data with artificially assigned contraindications and did not demonstrate safe or equitable performance within a functioning transplant selection committee.

Lazarus wrote that handing the final ranking of transplant candidates to a fully autonomous AI without human oversight remains unrealistic because of ethical, social, and regulatory barriers. He stated that algorithms do not always align with human moral values when making complex ethical trade-offs, and a study examining how large language models weigh competing kidney transplant candidates found that AI systems often prioritized variables differently than human research participants, whose medical training was unspecified. Models sometimes fixated on a single factor, such as drinking habits, and rarely expressed indecision, even when given that option, and these hypothetical comparisons reveal differences in value judgments but do not establish that AI performed worse than physicians making real transplant decisions. He wrote that machine-learning models are trained on past medical records, and historical transplant data reflects longstanding racial, socioeconomic, and geographic disparities in who is referred and approved for organs, so an unmonitored algorithm risks automating and entrenching systemic inequities. This challenge is compounded by the "black box" nature of complex neural networks, which often cannot provide transparent, easily understandable explanations for why one patient was ranked above another.

Lazarus wrote that organ allocation depends heavily on public trust, and patients, families, and clinicians require clear accountability for life-altering decisions. He stated that the urgency of end-stage organ disease and the scarcity of donated organs pose practical and ethical challenges to conducting traditional randomized clinical trials of allocation tools, and these challenges do not eliminate the need for rigorous prospective evaluation, including carefully designed trials where feasible. He wrote that the more defensible near-term approach to AI in transplant medicine is neither purely human decision-making nor complete algorithmic control, but rather a collaborative "human-in-the-loop" model. He stated that AI should serve as a clinical assistant rather than an independent arbiter, with transparent oversight of both its recommendations and human overrides. In practice, he wrote, this could mean integrating validated algorithms to flag high-risk candidates who might otherwise be overlooked by conventional metrics, estimate likely outcomes for specific donor-recipient combinations, and streamline administrative bottlenecks before an organ loses viability.

Lazarus wrote that by pairing the data-processing speed and consistency of machine learning with the ethical judgment, contextual awareness, and accountability of multidisciplinary transplant teams operating under national allocation policies, health care systems can aim to make organ allocation fairer and more efficient while keeping ultimate responsibility for human life firmly in human hands. He has published more than 500 articles and essays across scientific journals, professional publications, and online platforms. He is the author of numerous books on narrative medicine, AI in medicine, and career development. The article appeared on KevinMD on November 21, 2026, and asked readers whether an allocation algorithm would make them trust the transplant list more, or less. The article did not report any real transplant allocation decision, policy change, or official response.

stories.Headline: Goldman Sachs admits the 'AI unwind' has spiraled into something more dangerous — and it's watching for 3 signs of bottom
stories.Summary:
Goldman Sachs reported that an AI unwind became a broader growth downgrade during the week of November 20, 2026. The S&P 500 closed Friday in a correction, falling 3.59 percent to 6,918.45 for its seventh straight loss. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.28 percent and is now down more than 2 percent for the year. This losing streak for the S&P 500 is the longest since February 2020. Goldman Sachs strategists are now watching for three specific signs to identify a market bottom.

Recovery requires confidence in AI earnings, a dovish Fed signal, or a big drop in investor positioning. The Nasdaq is 12 percent below its October 6 record, and Goldman's AI stock basket fell 32 percent since then. The Fed meets December 9, with economists expecting hikes in December and March to reach 4.25 to 4.5 percent. Anthropic raised 93.5 billion dollars in its IPO, passing the 85.7 billion dollar SpaceX record. Nvidia lost 2.7 trillion dollars in market value since October 6 and fell 14 percent on Friday.

Goldman Sachs strategists wrote that the sell-off expanded from an AI unwind to a broader growth downgrade this week. They stated that the AI outlook for 2028 and beyond is highly uncertain for the global market. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said on Thursday that the Fed must raise rates because inflation is too high. Morgan Stanley closed its support position for Anthropic shares, which closed Friday at 88.91 dollars. Goldman noted that hedge fund net leverage is at its lowest level since April 2025.

Arun Sundaram of CFRA Research called the current market situation a meltdown, while David Kelly of JPMorgan called it non-fatal. Investor Dan Niles told CNBC that a price war between Anthropic and OpenAI is hurting both of those companies. Robert Pavlik of Dakota Wealth said investors are skeptical of the market rather than the company Anthropic itself. Chipmakers Nvidia, Broadcom, Micron, and AMD fell between 12 and 14 percent as the AI ecosystem split. US Bank Asset Management said Anthropic's valuation assumes years of rapid growth.

The SEC is probing the accounting practices of Nvidia, where Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on November 12, 2026. CFO Colette Kress is now the interim CEO of Nvidia after its worst day in almost two years. Combined sequential revenue growth for Anthropic and OpenAI fell from 75 percent in the second quarter to 48 percent. Combined losses for those two companies rose from 7.9 billion dollars to about 8.4 billion dollars. The VIX closed at 35.89, which is its highest level in 19 months.

Capital Economics expects further declines, while Goldman's November 20 note gives a range from 5,800 to 8,100 for the S&P 500. The index averaged a 4 percent return over three months after 22 corrections since 1980, rising in 17 cases. E*Trade research notes that five of 14 times since 1983, a 10 percent drop below a record became bear markets. The articles leave open whether Friday's market data supplied the signs Goldman was looking for to call a bottom. It remains uncertain if investors will regain confidence in AI earnings to trigger a recovery.

stories.Headline: Roblox chief creator officer Vlad Loktev says AI is here to stay as 80% of top Roblox games use AI tools
stories.Summary:
A massive experiment in machine-assisted creation is unfolding on Roblox, the online videogame hub, at a time when a reflexive backlash against AI-generated writing, music and advertising is sweeping through the creative world. On Roblox, machine-assisted creation appears to be winning, and the players do not seem to mind, according to an Axios report published on November 21, 2026. The contrast offers a glimpse into the future of entertainment, because audiences still demand human authenticity in traditional art while video game players have shown a pragmatic willingness to accept AI as long as the result is fun. Roblox is becoming a real-time laboratory for the AI era, and a staggering 80% of its top 100 games in October were built with AI tools.

Although some of its 138 million daily users fear the proliferation of homogenized game clones, the ease of building new worlds and games with friends is showing millions a new dimension in the AI creation wars. A 2025 NYU study found that fully AI-created ads achieved up to 19% higher click-through rates than human-created ads, but a simple disclosure of AI's involvement caused clicks to plummet 31.5%. More than 500,000 users have already tried Build, Roblox's natural-language creation environment released in a limited number of markets, and they published over 70,000 games in the process. Since the second quarter, time spent using AI tools has tripled among its top creators, and in September a game created almost entirely with AI broke into the platform's top 10 by concurrent players.

Vlad Loktev, Roblox's chief creator officer, tells Axios that the technology is here to stay and is evolving incredibly quickly, and he predicts that in the future everyone will be a builder. He says the platform's success with AI stems from fundamentally lowering the barrier to creation, and he expects multiple millions of people who could not make games before to suddenly be able to make them. He waves off the idea that AI games are inherently low-effort, noting that he is personally over a thousand prompts deep into building his own game and is also building games with his children. He says it still requires a lot of effort on the creator's side to design something that is actually fun, because models cannot tell you what fun is.

The broader gaming world is currently enjoying Grand Theft Auto VI, a title some players view as the last great, entirely human-made blockbuster, but on Roblox a major transition is already underway. The Axios reporter describes watching the dynamic with his own sons, who are AI power users yet distrustful about AI creation, and says building games on Roblox has helped sell them on the future of AI. His younger son, Clark, 16, is building a game he hopes to launch in the coming months, while Soren, 18, mostly wants to make games he can play with his friends. Soren, who has played Roblox since he was 7, says the problem now is that a lot of games are going by monetization trends and the same type of game becomes popular over and over again.

Articles.Title: "In the future, everyone's a builder." The massive AI experiment playing out in video games
