stories.Headline: Apollo CEO Marius Hobbhahn calls a 2027 AI takeover plausible and warns OpenAI audit access falls short
stories.Summary:
Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and co-founder of Apollo Research, said on the podcast MTS that he has reversed his view on short AI timelines, having called takeover by 2027 "very, very unlikely" two years ago. He said he is no longer sure and called it a negative update over the last two years. He endorsed the timeline Paul Christiano laid out on the Dwarkesh podcast, roughly a one-in-three chance of superintelligence within about a year. Hobbhahn said such an event is "less likely than not" in the next year. He said that if things move that fast, humans would not be able to correct it in any meaningful way.

Hobbhahn described a 6-to-12-month window in which substantial risk of full AI takeover would emerge. He said the risk is a speed problem, a correction lag, not a movie-style robot revolt. He said his earlier worry was "trained-in" scheming, where a model develops goal-seeking during reinforcement learning and improves itself past human supervision. He said the Hugging Face incident, an investigation Apollo was involved in, pushed him to take seriously a second pathway he calls "on the episode" risk. He said bad behavior in that pathway is committed spontaneously during a single rollout rather than baked in during training.

Apollo is one of four organizations OpenAI embedded inside its operations in November 2026, alongside METR, Transluce and Goodfire. OpenAI gave them access to model checkpoints, source code, training and evaluation data, monitoring systems and technical documentation, framed as part of commitments under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence. Apollo's pilot tests four claims: training-process subversion, evaluation robustness, historical deployment review and monitorability. OpenAI supplies a whitelist of approved employees for Apollo to interview, and Apollo cannot speak with other OpenAI staff about the assessment or anything in scope. Apollo's public statement calls the pilot "an ambitious first step" whose access and disclosure rights "don't yet meet our bar for full embedded evaluations."

Hobbhahn said he understands why broader access would cede a lot of control to an outsider. He argued that science has always advanced through the informal channel, through "coffee chats" and things "heard over lunch." He said the field has to be robust enough that even if any particular developer was trying to hide something, the external evaluator would find it. He said that is a necessary condition for a field like this to exist, and that "Right now, we're just nowhere near that." He wants embedded evaluation to become a professional field with nuclear-inspection-grade powers, analogous to nuclear inspections, food inspections or cyber security.

The Verge reported a six-person Apollo team spending four months inside OpenAI, with conversations logged and no access to internal messaging tools such as Slack. The research community has read that as well short of the employee-level access Sam Altman previously promised. Hobbhahn said he expects little internal effect, because only a handful of lab staff would interact with the evaluators. He said he expects a real external effect, with a trusted outside voice able to correct public misreadings in both directions. Anthropic was preparing a listing with an IPO expected to raise as much as $85 billion. Earlier in November the S&P 500 slid 10% from its October peak into correction territory, a seven-day losing streak reaching back to February 2020, and even NVIDIA's strong earnings and Anthropic's listing failed to bring buyers back.

SoftBank's Masayoshi Son, who has poured roughly $64.6 billion into OpenAI for about a 13% stake, publicly conceded that skipping Anthropic was a mistake. Asian family offices have reportedly been paying premiums of 30% for fund stakes that merely touch Anthropic or OpenAI paper. The articles say to watch whether OpenAI's approved-interviewee list widens to direct employee access. They also say to watch whether METR, Transluce and Goodfire adopt Apollo's same four-claim template. The articles say Hobbhahn's 2027 timeline is the headline, but the access terms decide whether anyone outside the building can constrain anything at all.

stories.Headline: RingCentral CFO says AI products drive growth as paid AI ARR doubles
stories.Summary:
RingCentral Chief Financial Officer Vaibhav Agarwal spoke at an RBC conference, and MarketBeat reported the remarks on Saturday, November 21, 2026, describing a strategy centered on an AI customer engagement platform. He said the platform handles communications between people and increasingly between people and AI. He said the company expects AI to address routine inquiries and automate workflows, with humans stepping in when more judgment or expertise is required. He said the core business is durable and that RingCentral goes into the base to address new sales with more AI products. The conference interviewer said RingCentral AI annual recurring revenue represented about 15% of total ARR and had doubled year over year.

The measure covers customers using at least one paid AI-native product, and Agarwal said it helps the company track paid AI adoption within its customer base. RingCentral's AIR product has more than 22,000 customers, while ACE has nearly 7,000, Agarwal said. The interviewer said the Customer Engagement Bundle had 14,000 paying customers, up 50% sequentially. Agarwal said RingCentral's overall gross margin is 80%, with AI product gross margins close to that level. He identified approximately 40 billion voice minutes flowing through the platform annually as a competitive asset.

Agarwal said RingCentral is spending more than $250 million on AI investments and manages AI costs through model orchestration, inference efficiency and infrastructure efficiency. He said the company uses multiple frontier models and routes work to lower-cost models, and could evaluate open-source models over time for additional cost efficiencies. He said RingCentral sells through direct representatives, in-product discovery, a network of 16,000 partners and global service carriers. He corrected the interviewer's suggestion that about half of AI ARR comes through the partner channel, saying RingCentral had not disclosed that mix. He said an expanded partnership with NiCE gives RingCentral greater access to enterprise customers as NiCE resells its RingEX product.

Agarwal described RingCentral's enterprise business as close to $1 billion, with a generally stable demand environment, win rates and retention. He said the company continues to face comparisons with COVID-era contracts that have undergone seat and pricing rationalization and expects to move past those comparisons into the first half of next year. He declined to provide guidance for next year. He said AI products are growing from a smaller base and could contribute more to overall growth as their share of the business increases. Based on its latest guidance, he said the company expects margin expansion of about 200 basis points this year.

Agarwal said stock-based compensation is declining by about 200 basis points, supported by discipline in new share grants and the fading impact of older grants. He said RingCentral has previously stated a longer-term goal of bringing stock-based compensation to 3% to 4%. Asked about potential AI-related pressure on customer seat counts, he said RingCentral is not seeing much seat rationalization among small businesses, though it sees some at the high end of the enterprise market following headcount actions. He said selling additional products to existing customers can help offset that pressure. He said AIR, which addresses missed calls, has initially found traction with small businesses but is also being sold to larger customers.

Agarwal said AIR Pro is designed for more complex workflows, using voice AI to understand intent and take actions before handing interactions to a human when needed. He said CEB targets businesses whose employees communicate with customers but do not have a dedicated contact center, and that once customers adopt it they can also buy AIR to address missed calls and add conversational intelligence. He cited a national fitness operator that used ACE to identify the reasons customers were calling before buying AIR to automate recurring inquiries. He said Destination Pet, an existing RingCentral customer, similarly used ACE to identify call drivers and then bought AIR Pro. He said customers can use NiCE's CXone for more complex deployments or RingCentral's RingCX for simpler contact center needs.

stories.Headline: Eric Fry says the AI trade is evolving into a new phase beyond Nvidia
stories.Summary:
Eric Fry, editor of The Speculator and a global macro investing expert at InvestorPlace, published an article on November 21, 2026 arguing that the AI trade is not over but is evolving into a new phase. He compared the current moment in artificial intelligence to the early personal-computer era, when IBM hired a small software company run by a 24-year-old entrepreneur named Bill Gates to supply an operating system for its first personal computer. Microsoft agreed to provide the software but kept the right to sell that same software to other computer manufacturers, including IBM's competitors, so it could profit from nearly every compatible machine built. Fry believes investors should now ask what happens when the companies building AI infrastructure give way to the companies putting that technology to work.

Fry pointed to Nvidia as the biggest winner of the AI revolution so far, noting that its powerful chips became the engines behind the boom as companies raced to build data centers and develop more sophisticated AI models. He said he is not predicting the end of the AI revolution but believes it is moving into a new phase that could create an entirely different set of winners. He called this turning point "The Crossing" and said he has identified two numbers that recently crossed paths, a development he believes could signal the beginning of the next great wave of AI wealth creation. He also said he believes the evidence could soon show up in Nvidia's own financial results.

Fry's track record includes warning about Cisco Systems in October 2000 during the dot-com boom, before the stock eventually plunged roughly 84% from its peak, and recognizing Nvidia in April 2020 as positioned to benefit from the next great technology revolution. He has put together a free presentation titled "Life After Nvidia" in which he will explain what he has discovered, reveal the key indicator he will be watching when Nvidia reports earnings in February, and introduce three companies he would rather own than Nvidia today. He will also explain what he believes Nvidia shareholders should consider as this next phase of AI unfolds, and viewers can reserve a place to watch the presentation. The article describes Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang as having been seen as AI's biggest cheerleader.

Articles.Title: The AI Trade Isn’t Over, Just Evolving

stories.Headline: Seramount finds only 18 percent of Gen Z workers want to build AI skills
stories.Summary:
Talent services firm Seramount released research on Thursday, November 21, 2026, regarding the AI skills of young workers. The study found that only 18 percent of Gen Z employees want to improve their AI skills. This group showed the least interest in sharpening these abilities compared to other generations. The research highlights a puzzle because these workers are often viewed as digital natives. They use the technology at rates similar to older employees but lack interest in development.

Seramount defined Gen Z as workers aged 29 and younger in a June survey of 1,800 U.S. white-collar employees. These employees worked at companies with at least 500 workers and were polled via NORC's AmeriSpeak panel. The survey found 58 percent of Gen Z use AI, while 60 percent of baby boomers and 63 percent of millennials do. Gen Xers had the highest usage rate at 67 percent. Other groups wanting AI skills included 36 percent of millennials, 46 percent of Gen Xers, and 43 percent of baby boomers.

Jessica Reif, a Wharton assistant professor, said using AI is riskier for younger workers who lack established professional standing. She explained that AI blurs a worker's own contribution, which can make early-career employees seem less competent. Diana Forster of Seramount stated that employers risk weakening their future leadership pipeline if Gen Z falls behind. Forster urged companies to provide clearer guidelines, training, and practice opportunities for these young employees. Reif suggested that proactive communication about how AI enables contributions can counteract negative perceptions.

Some 22 percent of Gen Z employees worry that AI use leads others to question their skills, compared to 10 percent of millennials. Only 27 percent of Gen Z feel comfortable acknowledging their AI use, while 47 to 53 percent of older colleagues do. A separate survey of 3,001 professionals by Protiviti and the London School of Economics found 48 percent fear being judged for not using AI. This creates a dilemma for young workers who must prove their own abilities while demonstrating AI proficiency. Only 27 percent of Gen Z say their organization provides support to integrate AI into their work.

Reif and co-authors Richard Larrick and Jack Soll studied 4,400 participants and found AI users were perceived as lazier and less diligent. A Gallup, GSV Ventures, and Walton Family Foundation survey of 1,572 Americans aged 14 to 29 found 80 percent fear AI hinders learning. Among employed Gen Z, 48 percent believe AI risks outweigh benefits, and 69 percent trust work completed without AI more. Only 30 percent of Gen Z believe AI increases efficiency, and 41 percent believe it improves work quality. The LSE and Protiviti study found 66 percent of Gen Z received AI training last year.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman believes rapid technological change allows those starting their careers to gain a competitive advantage. He stated in October that people with new skills and ideas do well when the ground is shaking. The articles leave open how employers will specifically change their training to engage the youngest workers. It remains unclear if the perceived stigma of AI use will permanently alter hiring decisions for entry-level roles. The research does not specify how government or schools will better prepare young people for an AI economy.

stories.Headline: Together AI adds Qwen3 TTS model to its serverless inference platform for real-time voice agents
stories.Summary:
Together AI launched the Qwen3 TTS open text-to-speech model on its serverless inference platform on November 20, 2026. This addition provides developers with a tool for real-time voice agents that separates speaker identity from delivery style. The system allows users to control emotional tones through plain language instructions without changing the chosen voice. This capability targets the growing demand for agentic deployments in customer support and experience automation.

The service costs 20 dollars per 1 million characters and offers nine preset voices for native speakers of English, Chinese, Japanese, and Korean. These voices support 10 languages, including French, German, Italian, Portuguese, Russian, and Spanish, with first audio delivered in as little as 97ms. Developers can use a WebSocket API or HTTP streaming, and they can preview custom text using the VoiceFinder tool. The underlying Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B model was developed by the Qwen team at Alibaba Cloud.

Together AI designed the serving stack to prioritize production voice performance and low latency for enterprise users. The company aims to provide a flexible alternative to proprietary ecosystems that often force developers into model lock-in. By offering a library that spans voice, code, and language, the platform supports organizations that prefer a mix of vendor and in-house solutions. This strategy positions the company to capture a larger share of the AI platforms market.

stories.Headline: Together AI launches free storage accelerator to speed data pipelines for GPU clusters
stories.Summary:
Together AI launched the Together Storage Accelerator on November 19, 2026, to speed up data pipelines for GPU clusters. Authors Pavneet Ahluwalia and Vinamra Jain introduced this distributed caching layer to stop compute resources from sitting idle. The tool provides fast and free data caching for every Together GPU Cluster to alleviate repeated data reads. It targets the problem of data living far from GPUs in object storage or on the Hugging Face Hub. This new service is now included at no additional cost for users of Together GPU Clusters.

The system requires no application changes, new SDKs, or rewritten data loaders to function for the user. It works with Hugging Face Hub and S3 compatible storage like Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, and Together AI's T4. T4 is an in data center object storage solution that is currently available in a limited preview. Users can enable the tool from the cluster settings page or use a single command to get started. The system uses encrypted credentials stored in a secrets vault to handle authentication for the user.

The authors stated that GPUs are only as fast as the data pipelines that feed them during training. They explained that cold starts pay a WAN tax because cross cloud or cross region reads are slow. This tax includes egress from AWS which can run up to 0.09 dollars per gigabyte of data. The authors noted that the tool provides resilience to outages because cached data serves even when upstream fails. They claimed that the tool dramatically accelerates AI data pipelines while also cutting data egress bills for users.

AI teams are affected because they often pull the same checkpoints across hundreds of nodes, which compounds waste. These teams face slow reads, high costs, and failed jobs when the origin source throttles their data requests. Measured results from October 28, 2026, show that warm reads on an H100 node are about 20 times faster. A 2 GiB object from Cloudflare R2 dropped from 12.7 to 15 seconds down to 0.64 to 0.72 seconds. Small files saw latency drop from 320 to 680 milliseconds down to 5 to 8 milliseconds.

The technology is powered by ASTRA, which stands for Accelerated Storage Transport and Retrieval Architecture, used for their inference fleet. A 70 GB checkpoint pulled by 200 nodes now requires only one origin fetch instead of 200 fetches. Cold reads through the system cost nothing extra and ran within about 5 percent of a direct download. The system achieves local speeds of up to 3.4 GB per second per node on a Together GPU Cluster. Origin speed varies by region, as Hugging Face downloads ran 5 times faster from us-central than ca-west.

Users can now point the accelerator at existing S3 or R2 buckets without migrating any of their data. Those wanting warm data to live permanently next to GPUs can switch to T4 with one config change. Together AI will share a deeper technical look at the ASTRA technology in an upcoming engineering post. The articles leave open the specific date for the general release of the T4 object storage solution. They also do not specify the exact technical details of the ASTRA architecture in this current announcement.

stories.Headline: Samsung and SK hynix values dive as AI chip rally ends
stories.Summary:
Samsung and SK hynix values dove over 30 percent as the KOSPI rally ended. The KOSPI fell 45 percent from its June peak and 30 percent since early October. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix dropped 32.82 percent and 39.33 percent respectively from early October. This market slide happened by November 21, 2026, according to the Seoul Economic Daily. Investors who bought equity products like ETFs during the June AI chip rally now face losses.

Total KOSPI market capitalization shrank from 7,449.6 trillion won in June to 3,991.4 trillion won. This represents a loss of 3,458 trillion won, or 46.4 percent, of the total value. Samsung Biologics moved to fifth place and Celltrion returned to ninth in the market rankings. Hyundai Motor fell to eighth place as Samsung Securities cut its target price to 380,000 won. The company previously had a target price of 410,000 won for the automaker.

Citibank estimates household stock investment losses will reach 563 trillion won in the second half. They assess this impact as comparable to a 0.50 to 0.75 percentage point base rate increase. The South Korean government has not produced clear measures to stabilize the market or stop outflows. This differs from Taiwan's FSC, which tightened short-selling restrictions and used a stabilization fund. Officials are facing questions over a missing response while retirement accounts suffer losses.

Investors who poured retirement savings into the market are now carrying mounting financial losses. Hyundai Motor is affected by intensifying price competition with Chinese electric vehicles and a stronger won. Samsung Electronics is betting on technology leads to trigger a revaluation of its stock. Big tech firms including Nvidia and Tesla are providing advanced-node orders to the foundry division. Holders of Kia shares must watch the National Assembly's tax subcommittee for new tax credits.

The KOSPI trading volume on November 19 was 239 million shares, the lowest since May 2014. Investor deposits shrank to 81.5669 trillion won during this period of weakening investor sentiment. Korean passenger EV market share fell to 48.7 percent while Chinese vehicles climbed to 43.5 percent. China exported 3.35991 billion dollars of passenger electric vehicles to South Korea from January to September. This represents a 99.2 percent jump from the previous year.

Samsung appointed President Hwang Sang-joon to lead memory and President Choi Won-joon to lead MX. AI glasses launch on December 10, and a humanoid will debut at CES 2027. The company aims for HBM4E next year and HBM5 in 2028 to regain market share. The government is pushing production tax credits for domestically built electric vehicles and autonomous-driving AI. It remains open whether the foundry business turns profitable or the stock market rebounds.

stories.Headline: South Korea surpasses one trillion dollars in annual exports driven by AI chip demand
stories.Summary:
South Korea surpassed one trillion dollars in annual exports for the first time this year on Thursday, driven largely by a boom in artificial intelligence chips. This milestone makes the nation the fourth country ever to reach this threshold, following the United States and Germany in 2006 and China in 2007. The achievement occurred despite significant global trade headwinds, including higher tariffs from the administration of President Donald Trump and ongoing conflicts in the Middle East. This growth follows a previous record of 709.3 billion dollars last year, which narrowed the gap with Japan's 738.3 billion dollars. The surge was led by semiconductor exports, which rose 193.1 percent to 396.8 billion dollars between January and October, representing 42.7 percent of total exports.

This demand for memory chips used in data centers benefited major companies like Samsung Electronics Co. and SK hynix Inc. The cumulative trade surplus for the first ten months reached 294.9 billion dollars, more than triple the 2017 record of 95.2 billion dollars. Consequently, the economy is expected to grow by more than 3 percent in 2026, the first such expansion since 2021. Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan credited the workers and businesses for this success and promised continued government support for exporters. He stated that the government would help companies overcome various challenges in financing, logistics, and trade to maintain this growth. Meanwhile, Professor Lee Jae-min of Seoul National University School of Law called the event historic but warned about potential trade restrictions.

He noted that managing these risks is essential to ensure the sustainability of growth driven by semiconductors and artificial intelligence. While shipbuilding, defense, and biohealth industries grew, automakers and electronics manufacturers faced pressure from Chinese rivals and American tariffs. Experts warn that a heavy reliance on semiconductors makes the economy vulnerable to price drops or a slowdown in global AI investment. To mitigate these external shocks, the country must develop new markets and diversify its export industries beyond traditional heavy manufacturing. South Korean companies are currently reviewing their supply chains and overseas production plans to adapt to these uncertainties.
